stem: Fertilisers, hard water and photographic chemicals contain a range of ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of each compound: (i) ammonium phosphate (ii) calcium hydrogencarbonate (iii) iron(II) hydroxide (iv) sodium thiosulfate.
parts.answer: (i) (NH₄)₃PO₄ (ii) Ca(HCO₃)₂ (iii) Fe(OH)₂ (iv) Na₂S₂O₃
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the formula, including charge, of: (i) the nitrite ion (ii) the manganate(VII) ion.
parts.answer: (i) NO₂⁻ (ii) MnO₄⁻
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A and B react in solution. Initial rates were measured at constant temperature.
Expt 1: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, rate = 1.8 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to A and with respect to B. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: First order in A; second order in B
parts.working: B1 expts 1→2: [A] doubles, rate doubles → first order in A; B1 expts 1→3: [B] ×3, rate ×9 → second order in B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, k, including its units.
parts.answer: rate = k[A][B]²; k = 0.20 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 rate equation; M1 k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10²) = 0.20; A1 units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.040 mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Propanone reacts with iodine in acid solution:
CH₃COCH₃ + I₂ → CH₃COCH₂I + HI
The rate equation is rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺]. With [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂] = 0.0020 mol dm⁻³, the initial rate is 3.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the rate equation tells you about the role of iodine in the rate-determining step.
parts.answer: Iodine is not involved in the rate-determining step (it reacts in a later, fast step).
parts.working: B1 zero order → I₂ not in / after the RDS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant and give its units.
parts.answer: k = 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.60 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂] is doubled.
parts.answer: 2.55 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the rate of this reaction could be followed.
parts.answer: Use a colorimeter to measure the decrease in the brown/yellow iodine colour over time.
parts.working: B1 colorimetry (or titrating quenched samples with thiosulfate).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the units of the rate constant for a reaction that is (i) zero order overall (ii) first order overall (iii) second order overall.
parts.answer: (i) mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (ii) s⁻¹ (iii) dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of a graph of concentration of reactant against time for a reaction that is zero order with respect to that reactant.
parts.answer: A straight line with negative gradient (constant rate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of a graph of initial rate against concentration of a reactant for a reaction that is second order with respect to it.
parts.answer: A curve upwards through the origin (rate ∝ [X]², a parabola).

stem:
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with oxygen: 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g). The rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[O₂].
Expt 1: [NO] = 0.020, [O₂] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, rate = 6.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [NO] = 0.010, [O₂] = 0.040 mol dm⁻³, rate = X
Expt 3: [NO] = Y, [O₂] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.054 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, with units, using experiment 1.
parts.answer: k = 1500 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the missing value X (rate in experiment 2).
parts.answer: X = 0.0060 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the missing value Y ([NO] in experiment 3).
parts.answer: Y = 0.060 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rate equation suggests the reaction might occur in a single step, and why this is unlikely in practice.
parts.answer: Rate eq matches the stoichiometry 2NO + O₂ (a termolecular collision); a three-particle collision with correct orientation and energy is very improbable.
parts.working: B1 orders match equation coefficients; B1 simultaneous collision of three particles very unlikely.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student investigates the reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂ using an iodine clock. Each mixture contains 10.0 cm³ of K₂S₂O₈(aq), 5.0 cm³ of Na₂S₂O₃(aq), 1 cm³ of starch, a volume V of KI(aq) and enough water to make the total volume 26.0 cm³. The time t for the blue-black colour to appear is recorded.
V / cm³: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
t / s: 22.0, 27.5, 36.7, 55.0, 110.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the total volume of each mixture is kept the same.
parts.answer: So that the volume of KI solution is proportional to [I⁻] in the mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1000/t for each experiment, giving values to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B2 all five correct (B1 for three or four).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1/t can be used as a measure of the initial rate.
parts.answer: Each run stops when the same fixed amount of iodine has been formed (just enough to use up all the thiosulfate), so rate ∝ amount/t ∝ 1/t.
parts.working: B1 same (fixed) amount of I₂ formed/reacted before the blue-black colour appears in every run.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your values to deduce the order of reaction with respect to iodide ions. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: First order
parts.working: M1 1/t is directly proportional to volume of KI (e.g. halving volume halves 1/t; graph straight line through origin); A1 first order.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State two variables, other than total volume, that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature; concentration/volume of peroxodisulfate (and of thiosulfate and starch).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the reaction X + 2Y → Z, the rate equation is rate = k[X][Y]².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to X, with respect to Y, and overall.
parts.answer: X: 1; Y: 2; overall 3
parts.working: B1 X and Y; B1 overall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the factor by which the rate changes when the concentrations of both X and Y are doubled.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the factor by which the rate changes if [X] is tripled and [Y] is halved.
parts.answer: 0.75 (rate falls to three-quarters)

author: HomiLabs

stem: The decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide, 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), is first order with a constant half-life of 24 minutes at a certain temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original N₂O₅ remaining after 96 minutes.
parts.working: B1 96/24 = 4 half-lives; (½)⁴.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, in min⁻¹, using k = 0.693/t½.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the half-life would change if the initial concentration of N₂O₅ were doubled. Explain.
parts.answer: No change – the half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of the starting concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of a catalyst. The concentration of H₂O₂ is measured over time.
t / s: 0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 600
[H₂O₂] / mol dm⁻³: 0.800, 0.566, 0.400, 0.283, 0.200, 0.100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to show that the reaction is first order with respect to H₂O₂.
parts.answer: Successive half-lives are constant: 0.800→0.400 in 200 s, 0.400→0.200 in 200 s, 0.200→0.100 in 200 s.
parts.working: M1 two or more half-lives found from data; A1 they are equal (200 s), so first order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, using k = 0.693/t½, and give its units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction.
parts.answer: 2.77 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (accept 2.78 × 10⁻³)

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by water in a first-order reaction: rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl], with k = 4.62 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the half-life of the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the concentration of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane to fall to 12.5 % of its initial value.
parts.working: B1 three half-lives.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of water does not appear in the rate equation, even though water is a reactant.
parts.answer: Water is the solvent and in large excess, so its concentration is effectively constant; and/or it is not involved in the slow step (SN1 – RDS is ionisation of the C–Cl bond).
parts.working: B1 water in large excess/constant; B1 RDS involves only the halogenoalkane.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ammonia decomposes on the surface of a hot tungsten wire: 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g).
t / s: 0, 100, 200, 300, 400
[NH₃] / 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³: 2.00, 1.60, 1.20, 0.80, 0.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to ammonia. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Zero order
parts.working: M1 concentration falls by the same amount (0.40 × 10⁻³) in each 100 s – constant rate/straight line; A1 zero order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant and give its units.
parts.answer: 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: M1 0.40 × 10⁻³ ÷ 100; A1 value with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for the first half-life and the time for the next half-life (from 1.00 × 10⁻³ to 0.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³).
parts.answer: 250 s and 125 s

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the rate does not depend on the concentration of ammonia in this experiment.
parts.answer: The tungsten surface is fully covered with adsorbed ammonia (all active sites occupied), so extra NH₃ cannot react faster.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A medicine is removed from the body by a first-order process with a half-life of 6.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the drug remaining in the body 24 hours after a 400 mg dose.
parts.answer: 25 mg
parts.working: M1 24/6.0 = 4 half-lives; A1 400 × (½)⁴ = 25 mg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the first-order rate constant, in h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 0.116 h⁻¹ (accept 0.115 h⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The drug is effective only while at least 60 mg remains. A doctor says a second dose is needed after 12 hours. Use a calculation to show whether this advice is sensible.
parts.answer: Sensible: after 12 h (2 half-lives) 100 mg remains, still above 60 mg; after 18 h only 50 mg would remain (< 60 mg), so the level falls below 60 mg between 12 h and 18 h (at about 16.4 h) and a second dose at 12 h keeps the drug effective.
parts.working: M1 amounts at 12 h (100 mg) and 18 h (50 mg); A1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis.
parts.answer: Homogeneous: catalyst in the same phase as the reactants; heterogeneous: catalyst in a different phase.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of the following as homogeneous or heterogeneous: (i) iron in the Haber process (ii) Fe²⁺ ions in the reaction of S₂O₈²⁻ with I⁻ (iii) platinum/rhodium in a catalytic converter (iv) NO₂ in the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂.
parts.answer: (i) heterogeneous (ii) homogeneous (iii) heterogeneous (iv) homogeneous
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Peroxodisulfate ions oxidise iodide ions: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂. The reaction is catalysed by Fe²⁺(aq).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the uncatalysed reaction between S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻ ions is slow.
parts.answer: Both ions are negatively charged, so they repel each other and collisions with enough energy are rare (high Ea).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write two equations to show how Fe²⁺ ions catalyse the reaction.
parts.answer: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺; 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Fe³⁺ ions can catalyse this reaction equally well.
parts.answer: The two steps occur in reverse order: Fe³⁺ first oxidises I⁻ to make Fe²⁺, which then reduces S₂O₈²⁻ – the catalyst is regenerated either way.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the property of iron that allows it to act as this catalyst.
parts.answer: It has variable oxidation states (+2 and +3).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cars on the roads of Lahore are fitted with catalytic converters containing platinum and rhodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the steps by which the solid catalyst speeds up this reaction.
parts.answer: Reactant molecules adsorb onto active sites on the metal surface; bonds in reactants weaken and molecules are held close together in suitable orientation, so reaction occurs; products desorb, freeing the sites.
parts.working: B1 adsorption; B1 bonds weakened/lower Ea/correct orientation; B1 desorption.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst is spread as a thin coating on a ceramic honeycomb.
parts.answer: Gives a large surface area so more active sites, and uses less expensive metal.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Over industrial cities, sulfur dioxide from burning fuel is oxidised in the air faster when nitrogen dioxide from vehicle engines is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two equations to show how nitrogen dioxide catalyses the oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation numbers of nitrogen in NO₂ and in NO, and of sulfur in SO₂ and in SO₃.
parts.working: B1 N; B1 S.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is described as homogeneous catalysis and how the overall equation shows that NO₂ is a catalyst.
parts.answer: All species are gases (same phase); NO₂ is used in the first step and regenerated in the second, so it does not appear in the overall equation SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃.
parts.working: B1 same phase; B1 regenerated/cancels.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why this reaction contributes to acid rain.
parts.answer: SO₃ reacts with water to form sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction between nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide occurs in two steps:
Step 1 (slow): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO
Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂
parts.working: B1 add steps and cancel NO₃ and one NO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the rate equation. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: rate = k[NO₂]²
parts.working: M1 step 1 is slow/rate-determining; A1 involves two NO₂, CO not in RDS.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the intermediate in this mechanism.
parts.answer: NO₃

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The rate equation is rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr].

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to hydroxide ions and explain what this shows about the mechanism.
parts.answer: Zero order; OH⁻ is not involved in the rate-determining step, which is the slow ionisation of the C–Br bond.
parts.working: B1 zero; B1 explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the two-step mechanism, naming the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1 (slow): (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ (heterolytic fission); Step 2 (fast): (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH. Intermediate: tertiary carbocation.
parts.working: B1 slow step forming carbocation; B1 fast attack by OH⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the effect on the initial rate of doubling [(CH₃)₃CBr] and halving [OH⁻] at the same time.
parts.answer: Rate doubles

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen reacts with iodine monochloride: H₂(g) + 2ICl(g) → I₂(g) + 2HCl(g). The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[H₂][ICl].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a two-step mechanism consistent with the rate equation. Show which step is slow and identify the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1 (slow): H₂ + ICl → HI + HCl; Step 2 (fast): HI + ICl → HCl + I₂. Intermediate HI.
parts.working: B1 slow step contains one H₂ and one ICl; B1 fast step uses second ICl, steps add to overall equation; B1 HI intermediate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate equation cannot be deduced from the overall equation.
parts.answer: Orders come from the rate-determining step, which need not match the stoichiometry; they must be found by experiment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The [H₂] is tripled and [ICl] is reduced to one-third. State the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: No change

author: HomiLabs

stem: A mixture of gases reacts with activation energy Ea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Boltzmann distribution curve for a gas at temperature T₁. Refer to the axes and the start of the curve.
parts.answer: y-axis: number/proportion of molecules; x-axis: energy. Curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak (most probable energy) and falls gradually, never touching the energy axis.
parts.working: B1 axes labelled; B1 starts at origin, single peak, asymptotic to x-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the curve changes at a higher temperature T₂.
parts.answer: Peak moves to higher energy and is lower; curve is broader with more molecules at high energy; area under curve unchanged.
parts.working: B1 peak lower and to the right; B1 same area / more molecules beyond Ea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why the rate of reaction increases with temperature.
parts.answer: A larger proportion of molecules have energy ≥ Ea, so more frequent successful collisions (also slightly more frequent collisions).
parts.working: B1 more molecules with E ≥ Ea; B1 more successful/effective collisions per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The temperature of a sample of gas is increased. Which statement about its Boltzmann distribution is correct?
A The total area under the curve increases.
B The peak becomes higher and moves to lower energy.
C The peak becomes lower and moves to higher energy.
D The activation energy moves to a lower value.
parts.answer: C The peak becomes lower and moves to higher energy.
parts.working: At higher temperature the most probable energy increases and the peak falls; the area (total number of molecules) stays the same, so A is wrong; Ea is unchanged by temperature.

stem:
Marble chips (calcium carbonate, in excess) are added to hydrochloric acid in a conical flask on a balance. The loss in mass, caused by carbon dioxide escaping, is recorded.
t / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240
loss in mass / g: 0.00, 0.44, 0.78, 1.02, 1.18, 1.26, 1.30, 1.32, 1.32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide produced in total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction, in g s⁻¹, over the first 30 s and over the period 60 s to 90 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why the rate decreases during the reaction.
parts.answer: Concentration of acid falls (and chip surface shrinks), so fewer particles per unit volume and fewer collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 concentration decreases; B1 collision frequency falls.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a loose plug of cotton wool is placed in the neck of the flask.
parts.answer: Lets CO₂ escape but stops acid spray being lost (which would add to the mass loss).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to find how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon, collecting the hydrogen in a 100 cm³ gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of HCl; dependent: volume of H₂ (with time); control: mass/length of Mg, volume of acid, temperature.
parts.working: B1 independent; B1 dependent; B1 two control variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 20 s passes through the points (0 s, 12 cm³) and (40 s, 52 cm³). Calculate the rate at 20 s.
parts.answer: 1.0 cm³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in measuring the volume of gas at the start, and an improvement.
parts.answer: Gas lost while inserting the bung after adding Mg; place Mg in a small tube inside the flask and tip it over after sealing (or use a divided flask).
parts.working: B1 error; B1 matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the effect of a catalyst on a reversible reaction is correct?
A It increases the enthalpy change of the forward reaction.
B It lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction only.
C It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally.
D It increases the equilibrium yield of products.
parts.answer: C It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally.
parts.working: A catalyst provides an alternative route with lower Ea for both directions, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged. B is wrong because the reverse Ea is lowered by the same amount.

stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), ΔH = −98 kJ per mol of H₂O₂. The activation energy is 75 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 23 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme catalase (found in potato and liver).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction for the uncatalysed and the catalase-catalysed reactions.
parts.answer: 173 kJ mol⁻¹ and 121 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: Catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea; on the Boltzmann curve the lower Ea lies further to the left; so a greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ Ea and more collisions are successful per unit time.
parts.working: B1 alternative route lower Ea; B1 more molecules have energy ≥ Ea (shaded area larger); B1 more effective collisions per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the catalyst affects the enthalpy change of the reaction.
parts.answer: No effect – ΔH stays −98 kJ mol⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a reaction, k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and k = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 320 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the Arrhenius equation and explain what happens to k as temperature increases.
parts.answer: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); as T increases, −Ea/RT becomes less negative so k increases (exponentially).
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 k increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, calculate the activation energy, in kJ mol⁻¹. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 55.3 kJ mol⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate constant of a reaction was measured at five temperatures.
T / K: 290, 300, 310, 320, 330
k / s⁻¹: 0.00154, 0.00353, 0.00767, 0.0159, 0.0315

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln k and 1/T for the experiments at 290 K and 330 K.
parts.working: B1 each pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A graph of ln k against 1/T is a straight line. Calculate its gradient using your values from (a).
parts.working: M1 Δ(ln k)/Δ(1/T); A1 value (negative).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the gradient to calculate the activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 60.0 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 gradient = −Ea/R; A1 Ea = −gradient × 8.31 ÷ 1000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the graph could be used to find the pre-exponential factor A.
parts.answer: Extrapolate to find the y-intercept, which equals ln A; A = e^(intercept).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a fertiliser factory near Multan, the rates of several gas and solution reactions are controlled carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why increasing the pressure increases the rate of a reaction between two gases.
parts.answer: Same number of molecules in a smaller volume / more molecules per unit volume; so collisions are more frequent (more successful collisions per second).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why powdered zinc reacts faster with dilute sulfuric acid than the same mass of zinc granules.
parts.answer: Powder has a larger surface area exposed to acid; so more frequent collisions between acid particles and zinc atoms.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why increasing concentration does not change the proportion of collisions that are successful.
parts.answer: Concentration does not change the energy of the particles, so the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles but does NOT change the fraction of collisions that have energy greater than the activation energy?
A adding a catalyst
B increasing the temperature
C increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution
D using a reactant with a lower activation energy
parts.answer: C increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution
parts.working: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions, but the energy distribution is unchanged. B raises both the collision frequency and the fraction with E ≥ Ea.

stem: Milk turns sour because of reactions caused by bacterial enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term activation energy.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A rough rule says the rate of a reaction doubles for every 10 °C rise. Calculate the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature of milk rises from 5 °C (in a fridge) to 35 °C (on a hot day).
parts.answer: 8 times
parts.working: B1 three 10 °C rises: 2³ = 8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a small rise in temperature causes a large increase in rate, even though the mean kinetic energy of the particles rises only a little.
parts.answer: The Boltzmann distribution shifts so that the number of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases by a large proportion; only these particles react, so the number of successful collisions per second increases greatly.
parts.working: B1 many more particles with E ≥ Ea; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen and iodine are sealed in a flask at 450 °C: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rates of the forward and backward reactions change from the moment H₂ and I₂ are mixed until equilibrium is reached.
parts.answer: Forward rate is greatest at the start and decreases as [H₂] and [I₂] fall; backward rate starts at zero and increases as [HI] rises; at equilibrium the two rates are equal (and non-zero).
parts.working: B1 forward decreases; B1 backward increases from zero; B1 equal at equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst on (i) the rates of the forward and backward reactions (ii) the position of equilibrium (iii) the time taken to reach equilibrium.
parts.answer: (i) both increase by the same factor (ii) no change (iii) decreases
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. Explain why raising the temperature decreases the equilibrium yield of HI even though both rates increase.
parts.answer: The backward (endothermic) reaction has the larger Ea, so its rate increases by a greater proportion; equilibrium shifts left.
parts.working: B1 endothermic direction favoured/its rate increases more; B1 equilibrium shifts to the left.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which mechanism, SN1 or SN2, is mainly followed in the hydrolysis of (i) 1-bromobutane (ii) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
parts.answer: (i) SN2 (ii) SN1
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react mainly by the SN1 mechanism.
parts.answer: Tertiary carbocation is the most stable because three alkyl groups donate electrons (positive inductive effect) and stabilise the positive charge; the three bulky alkyl groups hinder (steric hindrance) attack by a nucleophile from the side opposite the halogen, so SN2 is difficult.
parts.working: B1 tertiary carbocation stable; B1 alkyl groups electron-donating/inductive effect; B1 steric hindrance prevents SN2 attack.

stem: 1-bromobutane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ions. Describe in words where each curly arrow starts and ends, and describe the transition state.
parts.answer: Arrow from a lone pair on O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br; arrow from the C–Br bond to Br; transition state [HO···C···Br]⁻ with partial bonds and a negative charge, OH and Br on opposite sides of carbon; products butan-1-ol and Br⁻.
parts.working: B1 C–Br dipole (Cδ+, Brδ−); B1 arrow from OH⁻ lone pair to C; B1 arrow from C–Br bond to Br; B1 transition state with partial bonds and overall negative charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the rate equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: rate = k[CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br][OH⁻]

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An isomer of C₄H₉Br reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions. Initial rates at 25 °C:
Expt 1: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.050, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.100, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 3: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.050, [OH⁻] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the orders with respect to C₄H₉Br and to OH⁻, and write the rate equation.
parts.answer: First order in C₄H₉Br, zero order in OH⁻; rate = k[C₄H₉Br]
parts.working: B1 orders from data; B1 rate equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the mechanism and hence the structural formula of this isomer of C₄H₉Br. Explain.
parts.answer: SN1, so the isomer is tertiary: (CH₃)₃CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: M1 rate independent of [OH⁻] → SN1; A1 tertiary isomer (CH₃)₃CBr.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, can undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydroxide ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why 2-bromobutane is chiral.
parts.answer: Carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (H, Br, CH₃, C₂H₅).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane reacts with OH⁻ by the SN2 mechanism. State and explain whether the butan-2-ol formed rotates plane-polarised light.
parts.answer: Yes – OH⁻ attacks from the side opposite Br, so the configuration is inverted and a single enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms, which is optically active.
parts.working: B1 attack opposite to leaving group/inversion; B1 single enantiomer so optically active.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the same reaction occurred by SN1, the product would not rotate plane-polarised light. Explain why.
parts.answer: The carbocation intermediate is planar, so the nucleophile can attack equally from either side; a racemic mixture (50 : 50 enantiomers) forms and the rotations cancel.
parts.working: B1 planar carbocation, attack from both faces; B1 racemic mixture, no net rotation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which halogenoalkane is most likely to undergo hydrolysis by an SN1 mechanism?
A CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl
B CH₃CHClCH₃
C (CH₃)₃CCl
D CH₃Cl
parts.answer: C (CH₃)₃CCl
parts.working: (CH₃)₃CCl is tertiary: it forms the most stable carbocation and is sterically hindered towards SN2. B is secondary and can react by either route, but less readily by SN1.

stem:
Three test-tubes each contain 1 cm³ of ethanol, 1 cm³ of aqueous silver nitrate and three drops of a halogenoalkane, warmed in a water bath at 50 °C: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane.
Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–Cl 340; C–Br 280; C–I 240

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the order in which precipitates appear, fastest first, and state the colour of each precipitate.
parts.answer: 1-iodobutane (yellow AgI) first, then 1-bromobutane (cream AgBr), then 1-chlorobutane (white AgCl) last.
parts.working: B1 order I > Br > Cl; B1 all colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the bond energies to explain the order of reactivity.
parts.answer: C–I is the weakest bond (240 kJ mol⁻¹), so it breaks most easily; C–Cl is the strongest (340 kJ mol⁻¹), so the chloroalkane is hydrolysed most slowly.
parts.working: B1 bond strength decreases C–Cl > C–Br > C–I; B1 weaker bond broken more easily so faster rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student predicts that 1-chlorobutane should react fastest because the C–Cl bond is the most polar. Explain why this prediction is wrong.
parts.answer: Bond strength, not bond polarity, is the dominant factor controlling the rate of hydrolysis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the ethanol.
parts.answer: It is a solvent in which both the halogenoalkane and aqueous silver nitrate dissolve (they mix).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions needed to convert 2-bromopropane into propene.
parts.answer: NaOH (or KOH) dissolved in ethanol; heat (under reflux).
parts.working: B1 ethanolic NaOH/KOH; B1 heat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: CH₃CHBrCH₃ + NaOH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of the hydroxide ion in this reaction.
parts.answer: Base (removes H⁺ from the carbon next to the C–Br carbon).

stem: 2-bromobutane is heated with potassium hydroxide in ethanol. Three different alkenes are formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name all three alkenes formed.
parts.answer: but-1-ene; cis-but-2-ene (Z); trans-but-2-ene (E)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there are two products with the formula CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
parts.answer: Restricted rotation about the C=C bond; and each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis/trans (geometrical) isomers exist.
parts.working: B1 restricted rotation; B1 two different groups on each C of C=C.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product and write an equation when 1-bromopropane is heated with (i) NaOH(aq) (ii) NaOH in ethanol.
parts.answer: (i) propan-1-ol: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + NaBr (ii) propene: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for each product name, 1 mark for each equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the different behaviour of the hydroxide ion in (i) and (ii).
parts.answer: In water OH⁻ acts mainly as a nucleophile, attacking the δ+ carbon (substitution); in ethanol it acts mainly as a base, removing H⁺ (elimination).
parts.working: B1 nucleophile in aqueous; B1 base in ethanolic.

stem: There are four structural isomers with formula C₄H₉Br. Each is heated with ethanolic potassium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the names of the four structural isomers of C₄H₉Br.
parts.answer: 1-bromobutane; 2-bromobutane; 1-bromo-2-methylpropane; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: B2 all four (B1 for three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which isomer(s) give(s) only 2-methylpropene on elimination.
parts.answer: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the isomer whose elimination products include a pair of stereoisomers.
parts.answer: 2-bromobutane
parts.working: B1 gives cis- and trans-but-2-ene.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the isomer that gives only an unbranched alkene with the C=C at the end of the chain.
parts.answer: 1-bromobutane (gives but-1-ene only)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent and conditions convert bromoethane into ethene?
A NaOH(aq), warm
B NaOH in ethanol, heat
C concentrated H₂SO₄, 170 °C
D KCN in ethanol, heat
parts.answer: B NaOH in ethanol, heat
parts.working: Hot ethanolic hydroxide removes HBr (elimination). A gives ethanol (substitution); C is used to dehydrate ethanol, not bromoethane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why chlorobenzene does not undergo nucleophilic substitution with NaOH(aq) under normal laboratory conditions.
parts.answer: A lone pair (p-orbital) on Cl overlaps with the delocalised π-electrons of the ring; so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is stronger/harder to break; the electron-rich ring also repels nucleophiles.
parts.working: B1 p-orbital overlap with π system; B1 stronger C–Cl bond; B1 π electron cloud repels OH⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what is seen when chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane are each warmed with ethanolic silver nitrate.
parts.answer: Chlorobenzene: no precipitate; 1-chlorobutane: white precipitate (slowly).
parts.working: B1 each.

stem: Consider three chlorine compounds: benzoyl chloride (C₆H₅COCl), 1-chlorobutane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl) and chlorobenzene (C₆H₅Cl).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the three compounds in order of ease of hydrolysis, most easily hydrolysed first.
parts.answer: benzoyl chloride > 1-chlorobutane > chlorobenzene

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is observed when each compound is added to water containing AgNO₃(aq) at room temperature.
parts.answer: C₆H₅COCl: immediate white precipitate (and steamy fumes of HCl); 1-chlorobutane: no precipitate at room temperature (slow, faint on warming); C₆H₅Cl: no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 immediate precipitate with acyl chloride; B1 none/very slow for the other two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why benzoyl chloride is hydrolysed most easily.
parts.answer: The carbonyl carbon is attached to both O and Cl, two electronegative atoms, so it is strongly δ+; the planar C=O carbon is easily attacked by water (addition–elimination).
parts.working: B1 two electronegative atoms make C very δ+; B1 attack by water easy (lone pair of H₂O).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine under two different sets of conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the conditions needed to make (i) 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene (and its 2-isomer) (ii) (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, from methylbenzene and chlorine.
parts.answer: (i) AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) catalyst, room temperature, no UV (ii) UV light (or boiling)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mechanism in each case.
parts.answer: (i) electrophilic substitution (ii) free-radical substitution
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the formation of the electrophile in (i).
parts.answer: Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of structural isomers of C₇H₇Cl that contain a benzene ring and name the one with Cl on the side chain.
parts.answer: 4; (chloromethyl)benzene
parts.working: B1 4 (three ring isomers + one side-chain); B1 name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to distinguish (chloromethyl)benzene from 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene. Give the results.
parts.answer: Warm each with NaOH(aq); acidify with dilute HNO₃; add AgNO₃(aq). (Chloromethyl)benzene gives a white precipitate; 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene gives no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 warm NaOH(aq) then HNO₃ then AgNO₃; B1 white ppt with side-chain compound; B1 no ppt with ring-substituted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To neutralise excess OH⁻, which would otherwise form a brown precipitate of silver oxide.

stem: Equal amounts of bromobenzene, 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane are added to separate tubes of warm aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the order in which a cream precipitate appears in the three tubes, fastest first.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, then 1-bromobutane; bromobenzene gives no precipitate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your order for the two halogenoalkanes.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary and reacts by SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation, faster than the primary 1-bromobutane (SN2).
parts.working: B1 tertiary via SN1/carbocation; B1 faster than primary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why bromobenzene gives no precipitate.
parts.answer: The C–Br bond is strengthened by overlap of a Br lone pair with the ring π system, and the π electrons repel the nucleophile, so no Br⁻ is released.
parts.working: B1 stronger C–Br bond (delocalisation); B1 nucleophile repelled.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bromoethane, C₂H₅Br, is a useful starting material in synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions to convert bromoethane into (i) ethanol (ii) propanenitrile (iii) ethylamine.
parts.answer: (i) NaOH(aq), heat under reflux (ii) KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux (iii) excess concentrated NH₃ in ethanol, heat in a sealed tube (under pressure)
parts.working: 1 mark for each reagent and 1 mark for each set of conditions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
1-bromopropane is heated under reflux with KCN in ethanol. What is the organic product?
A propanenitrile
B butanenitrile
C propan-1-ol
D propylamine
parts.answer: B butanenitrile
parts.working: CN⁻ replaces Br, adding one carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂CN is butanenitrile. A forgets that the nitrile carbon is counted in the name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give reagents and conditions for each step of a two-step synthesis of butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane, naming the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → butanenitrile; Step 2: dilute HCl(aq) (or H₂SO₄), heat under reflux → butanoic acid.
parts.working: B1 KCN/ethanol/heat; B1 intermediate butanenitrile; B1 aqueous acid; B1 reflux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this route is useful in synthesis.
parts.answer: It increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of 1-chloropropane with excess ammonia to form propylamine.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Cl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ammonia is used in large excess.
parts.answer: Propylamine has a lone pair and is itself a nucleophile, so it can react with more 1-chloropropane to form secondary and tertiary amines (and quaternary salts); excess NH₃ makes collision of the halogenoalkane with NH₃ more likely.
parts.working: B1 amine product also nucleophile/further substitution; B1 excess NH₃ reduces this.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is carried out in a sealed tube.
parts.answer: Ammonia is volatile; the sealed tube keeps it in (under pressure) when heated.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the secondary amine that could form as a by-product.
parts.answer: (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₂NH

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term nucleophile.
parts.answer: A species that donates a lone pair of electrons (to an electron-deficient carbon) to form a new covalent bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: From the list, identify all the nucleophiles: OH⁻, H⁺, CN⁻, Br₂, NH₃, NO₂⁺, H₂O, AlCl₃
parts.answer: OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O
parts.working: B2 all four and no extras (B1 three correct).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in a halogenoalkane is attacked by nucleophiles.
parts.answer: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar and the carbon is δ+.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, with curly arrows described in words, the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane by water.
parts.answer: Step 1: C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically (arrow from C–Cl bond to Cl) to give (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Cl⁻; Step 2: a lone pair on the O of H₂O attacks the carbocation (arrow from O lone pair to C⁺); Step 3: loss of H⁺ from the –OH₂⁺ group gives (CH₃)₃COH.
parts.working: B1 heterolytic fission arrow; B1 carbocation and Cl⁻; B1 arrow from O lone pair to C⁺; B1 loss of H⁺ to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the rate-determining step.
parts.answer: Step 1 – formation of the carbocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide ions by the SN2 mechanism. Which statement describes the transition state?
A It is a carbocation, CH₃⁺.
B It has a partial C–O bond and a partial C–Br bond and carries a negative charge.
C It contains a full C–O bond and a full C–Br bond.
D It is uncharged, with OH and Br on the same side of the carbon atom.
parts.answer: B It has a partial C–O bond and a partial C–Br bond and carries a negative charge.
parts.working: In SN2, bond-making and bond-breaking happen together: [HO···CH₃···Br]⁻ with OH and Br opposite each other. A describes the SN1 intermediate, not a transition state.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between bromoethane and ammonia to form ethylamine. Describe each curly arrow in words and show the intermediate ion.
parts.answer: Lone pair on N of NH₃ attacks δ+ C of C–Br (arrow N lone pair → C); C–Br bond breaks (arrow C–Br → Br), giving CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ and Br⁻; a second NH₃ uses its lone pair to remove H⁺ from CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ (arrow from N lone pair to H, arrow from N–H bond to N) giving CH₃CH₂NH₂ and NH₄⁺.
parts.working: B1 dipole and attack by N lone pair; B1 C–Br breaks, Br⁻; B1 intermediate CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺; B1 deprotonation by second NH₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mechanism.
parts.answer: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when 1-iodopropane is heated with each reagent: (i) NaOH(aq) (ii) KCN in ethanol (iii) excess NH₃ in ethanol in a sealed tube.
parts.answer: (i) propan-1-ol (ii) butanenitrile (iii) propylamine (propan-1-amine)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the inorganic product in (i).
parts.answer: NaI

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the organic product when 2-bromobutane is warmed with dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A butan-1-ol
B butan-2-ol
C but-2-ene
D butanone
parts.answer: B butan-2-ol
parts.working: OH⁻ replaces Br on the same carbon (C2), giving butan-2-ol. C would need ethanolic NaOH (elimination).

stem: 5.48 g of 1-bromobutane is heated under reflux with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. 2.22 g of pure butan-1-ol is obtained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield of butan-1-ol. [Mr: C₄H₉Br 136.9; C₄H₉OH 74.0]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A different isomer, P, of C₄H₉Br is hydrolysed to an alcohol Q. Q does not change the colour of hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Identify P and Q.
parts.answer: P: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr; Q: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH
parts.working: M1 Q is a tertiary alcohol (not oxidised); A1 both names/structures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change seen if butan-1-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: Orange to green

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give a reagent for converting propan-2-ol into 2-chloropropane, and write the equation.
parts.answer: PCl₅ (or SOCl₂, or PCl₃ with heat, or conc HCl with ZnCl₂): CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + PCl₅ → CH₃CHClCH₃ + POCl₃ + HCl
parts.working: B1 reagent; B1 matching balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions for making bromoethane from (i) ethene (ii) ethane.
parts.answer: (i) HBr(g), room temperature (ii) Br₂, ultraviolet light
parts.working: B1 HBr; B1 Br₂; B1 UV light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why method (ii) is not a good way to make pure bromoethane.
parts.answer: Free-radical substitution gives a mixture of multi-substituted products (e.g. dibromoethanes).

stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is prepared by shaking 7.40 g of 2-methylpropan-2-ol with concentrated hydrochloric acid in a separating funnel at room temperature. The upper organic layer is washed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, then with water, dried with anhydrous sodium sulfate and distilled. 6.94 g of product is collected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of shaking with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and how the pressure in the funnel is controlled.
parts.answer: Removes/neutralises the remaining HCl acid; CO₂ is produced so the tap must be opened regularly (with the funnel inverted) to release pressure.
parts.working: B1 neutralise acid; B1 release CO₂ pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why anhydrous sodium sulfate is added.
parts.answer: It is a drying agent that removes traces of water from the organic layer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield. [Mr: (CH₃)₃COH 74.0; (CH₃)₃CCl 92.5]

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one safety precaution specific to this experiment.
parts.answer: Use concentrated HCl in a fume cupboard / wear gloves (corrosive, gives off HCl fumes); keep the volatile, flammable product away from flames.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name each of the four structural isomers of C₄H₉Cl and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: 1-chlorobutane (primary); 2-chlorobutane (secondary); 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (primary); 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tertiary)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct name with classification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a halogenoalkane is classified as primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: By the number of alkyl groups (carbon atoms) bonded to the carbon atom carrying the halogen: one, two or three.

stem: Water pipes and crates sold in Pakistani markets are often made from poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the repeat unit of poly(propene). Use the form –CH₂–CHX– with X identified.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–
parts.working: B1 continuation bonds shown at both ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula and name of the monomer used to make poly(chloroethene), PVC.
parts.answer: CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene
parts.working: B1 formula; B1 name.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of polymerisation and why no other product forms.
parts.answer: Addition polymerisation; the C=C π bonds open and monomers join with no atoms lost, so the polymer is the only product.
parts.working: B1 addition; B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A polymer has the repeat unit –CH₂–CCl₂–. What is the monomer?
A CH₂=CHCl
B CHCl=CHCl
C CH₂=CCl₂
D CCl₂=CCl₂
parts.answer: C CH₂=CCl₂
parts.working: Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon of the repeat unit, so the monomer is 1,1-dichloroethene. B would give –CHCl–CHCl–.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the monomer and the repeat unit of PTFE, poly(tetrafluoroethene).
parts.answer: Monomer CF₂=CF₂; repeat unit –CF₂–CF₂–
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why PTFE is very unreactive, making it suitable for non-stick cooking pans.
parts.answer: The C–F bonds are very strong (high bond energy) and the polymer is saturated (no C=C), so it resists attack by most chemicals.
parts.working: B1 strong C–F bonds; B1 saturated/non-polar overall, no reactive sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A molecule of poly(ethene) has Mr = 280 000. Calculate the number of monomer units in the molecule. [Mr of C₂H₄ = 28.0]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chain of poly(chloroethene) contains 2000 monomer units. Calculate its Mr. [Mr of C₂H₃Cl = 62.5]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a sample of poly(ethene) is described by an average Mr rather than a single value.
parts.answer: Chains grow and stop at random, so the polymer contains chains of different lengths.

stem: A city council plans to reduce waste from thin plastic shopping bags made of poly(ethene) and from PVC pipes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why poly(alkene)s cause problems in landfill sites.
parts.answer: They are non-biodegradable because they are saturated/non-polar with strong C–C and C–H bonds; microorganisms cannot break them down, so they persist for many years.
parts.working: B1 non-biodegradable; B1 reason (inert, no polar bonds for enzymes to attack).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why burning PVC waste is particularly harmful.
parts.answer: Combustion releases toxic and acidic hydrogen chloride gas (and possibly toxic chlorinated compounds); HCl causes acid rain/respiratory damage.
parts.working: B1 HCl produced; B1 harmful effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of recycling over incineration.
parts.answer: Saves crude oil (raw material) and energy; no toxic gases released.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Part of a polymer chain is shown: –CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–
What is the monomer?
A CH₂=CHCN
B CH₃CH₂CN
C CH₂=C(CN)₂
D CH≡CCN
parts.answer: A CH₂=CHCN
parts.working: The repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(CN)–, from propenenitrile CH₂=CHCN. B has no C=C so cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

stem: A section of a copolymer used for flexible food packaging is: –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two monomers used to make this polymer.
parts.answer: ethene, CH₂=CH₂, and propene, CH₂=CHCH₃
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of polymerisation and give the empirical formula of the polymer if the monomers are present in equal numbers.
parts.answer: Addition; CH₂
parts.working: B1 addition; B1 C₅H₁₀ per pair → CH₂.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw (as a text formula) the repeat unit of the polymer formed from but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
parts.answer: –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of this polymer has an average Mr of 112 000. Calculate the average number of but-2-ene monomer units in each chain. [Mr of C₄H₈ = 56.0]
parts.working: B1 112 000 ÷ 56.0 = 2000 (the repeat unit has the same formula as the monomer, ignoring end groups).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the atom economy of any addition polymerisation and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 100 %; all the atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer – it is the only product.
parts.working: B1 100 %; B1 only one product / no atoms lost.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the polymer from but-2-ene is saturated even though the monomer is unsaturated.
parts.answer: The π bond of each C=C breaks to form new C–C single bonds to neighbouring monomers.

stem: Perspex, a clear plastic used for shop signs, is an addition polymer made from methyl 2-methylpropenoate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the monomer, methyl 2-methylpropenoate.
parts.answer: CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of the polymer.
parts.answer: –CH₂–C(CH₃)(COOCH₃)–

parts.label: c
parts.text: The polymer is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Describe the change to the side groups and name the small molecule released.
parts.answer: The ester side groups are hydrolysed to sodium carboxylate groups (–COO⁻Na⁺); methanol is released. The main carbon chain is not broken.
parts.working: B1 –COOCH₃ → –COO⁻Na⁺; B1 methanol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the polymer backbone survives this treatment while a polyester backbone would not.
parts.answer: The backbone of the addition polymer contains only C–C bonds; in a polyester, ester links are in the main chain and are hydrolysed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A waste incinerator burns PVC pipe offcuts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen chloride, at r.t.p., released when 1.00 kg of PVC is burned completely. Assume each repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl– gives one HCl. [Mr of C₂H₃Cl = 62.5; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³]
parts.answer: 384 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The HCl is removed by passing the gases through powdered calcium carbonate. Write the equation and calculate the mass of calcium carbonate needed. [Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1]
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; 801 g
parts.working: B1 equation; M1 8.00 mol CaCO₃; A1 801 g.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH, can form an addition polymer. Give its repeat unit.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(CH₂OH)–

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the addition polymer from (a) can dissolve in water, whereas poly(propene) cannot.
parts.answer: Each repeat unit has an –OH group that forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; poly(propene) has only non-polar C–H/C–C bonds with instantaneous dipole forces.
parts.working: B1 –OH hydrogen bonds with water; B1 poly(propene) non-polar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether prop-2-en-1-ol alone could form a condensation polymer.
parts.answer: No – it has only one functional group (–OH) able to take part in condensation; a condensation polymer needs two reacting groups per monomer (or two different monomers).
parts.working: B1 only one condensing group; B1 needs two functional groups.

stem: Expanded polystyrene is used to pack electronic goods and to make disposable food boxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the name and structural formula of the monomer of polystyrene.
parts.answer: phenylethene (styrene), C₆H₅CH=CH₂
parts.working: B1 name; B1 formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of polystyrene.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why poly(alkene)s such as polystyrene are chemically unreactive.
parts.answer: They are saturated (contain no C=C in the chain) and have strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of poly(ethene), (C₂H₄)ₙ.
parts.answer: (C₂H₄)ₙ + 3nO₂ → 2nCO₂ + 2nH₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass, in kg, of carbon dioxide produced when 14.0 kg of poly(ethene) burns completely. [Mr: C₂H₄ 28.0; CO₂ 44.0]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why poly(ethene) waste should not be burned in an open fire.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide (and soot).

stem: Nylon-6,6 is used to make fishing nets for boats in Karachi harbour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two monomers used to make nylon-6,6.
parts.answer: hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine (1,6-diaminohexane)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of nylon-6,6.
parts.answer: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–
parts.working: B1 amide link shown; B1 correct numbers of CH₂ groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated and the linkage formed.
parts.answer: water; amide (peptide) linkage –CONH–
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Plastic drinks bottles are made from PET, poly(ethylene terephthalate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the two monomers used to make PET.
parts.answer: HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) and HOCH₂CH₂OH (ethane-1,2-diol)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of PET.
parts.answer: –OC–C₆H₄–COO–CH₂CH₂–O–
parts.working: B1 ester link; B1 rest correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of polymer.
parts.answer: Polyester (condensation polymer)

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the 'nylon rope trick', nylon-6,6 is made at the interface between a solution of hexanedioyl dichloride in an organic solvent and an aqueous solution of hexane-1,6-diamine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the structural formula of hexanedioyl dichloride.
parts.answer: ClCO(CH₂)₄COCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated when hexanedioyl dichloride reacts with hexane-1,6-diamine.
parts.answer: hydrogen chloride (HCl)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two advantages of using the diacyl dichloride rather than hexanedioic acid in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Reaction is fast at room temperature (no heating/catalyst needed); the reaction goes to completion (not an equilibrium).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kevlar is a polyamide used in bulletproof vests and cricket helmets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the monomers used to make Kevlar.
parts.answer: H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂ (benzene-1,4-diamine) and HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) (or the diacyl dichloride)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of Kevlar.
parts.answer: –NH–C₆H₄–NH–CO–C₆H₄–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Kevlar is very strong.
parts.answer: Rigid, flat chains line up parallel; strong hydrogen bonds form between C=O of one chain and N–H of the neighbouring chain.
parts.working: B1 linear rigid chains packed closely; B1 hydrogen bonds between chains (C=O···H–N).

author: HomiLabs

stem: PLA is made from maize or sugar cane and is used for disposable cups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid).
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)COOH

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(lactic acid), PLA.
parts.answer: –O–CH(CH₃)–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how one monomer can form a condensation polymer on its own.
parts.answer: Each molecule has two different functional groups (–OH and –COOH), which react with groups on neighbouring molecules to form ester links.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why PLA is biodegradable.
parts.answer: Its ester links can be hydrolysed (by water/enzymes/microorganisms).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw (as text formulae) the two possible dipeptides formed from one glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) and one alanine (H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH) molecule.
parts.answer: H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH and H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(glycine).
parts.answer: –NH–CH₂–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the linkage formed between amino acids.
parts.answer: peptide (amide) link

author: HomiLabs

stem: A section of a polyester is: –O–CH₂CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–O–CH₂CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the products when the polyester is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH (hexanedioic acid) and HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH (propane-1,3-diol)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the products when the polyester is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: NaOOC(CH₂)₄COONa (sodium hexanedioate) and HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH
parts.working: B1 salt; B1 diol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of reaction in (a) and (b).
parts.answer: Hydrolysis

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the Mr of the repeat unit of nylon-6,6, C₁₂H₂₂N₂O₂, is 226.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A nylon-6,6 chain has an Mr of approximately 33 900. Calculate the number of repeat units in the chain (ignore the end groups).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each repeat unit is formed from one diacid and one diamine molecule. Deduce how many water molecules were eliminated in forming one chain with this number of repeat units. Explain.
parts.working: M1 one H₂O per amide link; A1 300 monomers joined by 299 links.

stem: A section of a polyamide is: –NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–CO–(CH₂)₈–CO–NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–CO–(CH₂)₈–CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two monomers needed to make this polyamide. Give their structural formulae.
parts.answer: H₂N(CH₂)₄NH₂ (butane-1,4-diamine) and HOOC(CH₂)₈COOH (decanedioic acid)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other type of monomer that could replace the dicarboxylic acid.
parts.answer: The diacyl dichloride, ClCO(CH₂)₈COCl

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Addition: monomers contain C=C, no other product, polymer has same empirical formula as monomer; condensation: monomers have two functional groups, a small molecule (e.g. H₂O or HCl) is eliminated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each linkage: –COO– and –CONH–.
parts.answer: –COO– ester (polyester); –CONH– amide (polyamide)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of nylon-6, made from 6-aminohexanoic acid, H₂N(CH₂)₅COOH.
parts.answer: –NH–(CH₂)₅–CO–

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chain of nylon-6, H–[NH(CH₂)₅CO]₅₀₀–OH, has 500 repeat units. Calculate its Mr. [Mr of C₆H₁₁NO = 113.0; H₂O = 18.0]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nylon-6 and nylon-6,6 have very similar properties.
parts.answer: Both have amide links regularly spaced along similar hydrocarbon chains, so similar hydrogen bonding between chains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each monomer or pair of monomers, state whether it forms an addition or a condensation polymer: (i) propenamide, CH₂=CHCONH₂ (ii) hexane-1,6-diol and butanedioic acid (iii) 2-aminopropanoic acid (iv) tetrafluoroethene.
parts.answer: (i) addition (ii) condensation (iii) condensation (iv) addition
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of the polymer formed in (ii).
parts.answer: –O(CH₂)₆O–CO(CH₂)₂CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the complete hydrolysis of one repeat unit of nylon-6,6, –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–, by hot concentrated hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO– + 2H₂O + 2HCl → [H₃N(CH₂)₆NH₃]²⁺ 2Cl⁻ + HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH
parts.working: B1 diacid and diammonium salt products; B1 balanced (2H₂O and 2HCl).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the diamine is obtained as its salt.
parts.answer: The amine groups are basic and are protonated by the excess acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nylon clothing is damaged by spills of acid.
parts.answer: The amide links in the polymer chain are hydrolysed, breaking the chains and weakening the fibres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable while poly(alkene)s are not.
parts.answer: Polyesters/polyamides contain polar ester/amide links that can be hydrolysed (by enzymes/water); poly(alkene)s have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds that are not attacked.
parts.working: B1 ester/amide links hydrolysed; B1 poly(alkene)s non-polar/inert.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a photodegradable polymer and give one structural feature that makes a polymer photodegradable.
parts.answer: One that breaks down when exposed to light (UV); it contains C=O groups that absorb UV and break bonds nearby.
parts.working: B1 meaning; B1 C=O groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nylon-6,6 has a much higher melting point than poly(ethene) of similar chain length.
parts.answer: Nylon chains form hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O of neighbouring chains; poly(ethene) has only weaker instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces, needing less energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonds in nylon; B1 only id–id forces in poly(ethene)/less energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why low-density poly(ethene), with many side branches, is softer than high-density poly(ethene).
parts.answer: Branches stop the chains packing closely, so intermolecular forces are weaker and chains slide past each other more easily.
parts.working: B1 packing; B1 weaker forces.

stem: A large city such as Karachi produces thousands of tonnes of plastic waste every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of incinerating plastic waste.
parts.answer: Advantage: energy released can generate electricity / reduces landfill volume. Disadvantage: releases CO₂ (greenhouse gas) and toxic gases such as HCl from PVC or CO.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why mixed plastic waste is difficult to recycle.
parts.answer: Different polymers have different properties/melting points and must be sorted first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a bag made of a polyester would break down faster in a compost heap than one made of poly(propene).
parts.answer: Ester links are hydrolysed by water/enzymes from microorganisms; poly(propene) has no such polar links.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis of ester; B1 poly(propene) inert.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 12.0 g cup made of poly(lactic acid), PLA, is buried in an industrial compost heap. It loses 25 % of its mass in the first 30 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the cup remaining after 90 days, assuming it continues to lose 25 % of its remaining mass every 30 days. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction by which the PLA cup breaks down and the organic product.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the same cup would break down more slowly in a dry landfill than in moist compost.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis needs water (and microorganisms), which are scarce in a dry landfill.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for each reaction and explain each answer: (i) CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (ii) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (iii) H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) (iv) Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
parts.answer: (i) positive – gas formed from a solid (ii) negative – 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas (iii) positive – liquid → gas, more disorder (iv) negative – free ions in solution form an ordered solid
parts.working: 1 mark each for sign with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the entropy, S, of a system.
parts.answer: A measure of the dispersal of energy / the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy (disorder).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Place H₂O(s) at 0 °C, H₂O(l) at 25 °C and H₂O(g) at 100 °C in order of increasing entropy and explain.
parts.answer: H₂O(s) < H₂O(l) < H₂O(g); particles become more free to move and there are more ways of arranging them and their energy.
parts.working: B1 order; B1 explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K.
parts.answer: Zero

stem: Standard entropies, S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: N₂(g) 191.6; H₂(g) 130.6; NH₃(g) 192.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard entropy change for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
parts.answer: −198.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = 2(192.5) − [191.6 + 3(130.6)]; A1 value with sign and units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the sign of your answer.
parts.answer: Negative: the number of gas molecules decreases (4 → 2), so fewer ways of arranging particles.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Methane (natural gas) from the Sui gas field is burned in home cookers.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: CH₄(g) 186.2; O₂(g) 205.0; CO₂(g) 213.6; H₂O(l) 69.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° for the complete combustion of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
parts.answer: −242.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how ΔS° would differ if the water were formed as steam. Explain.
parts.answer: Less negative (≈ zero): 3 mol gas would give 3 mol gas, and gaseous water has much higher entropy than liquid water.
parts.working: B1 less negative; B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Instant cold packs used by sports teams contain solid ammonium nitrate and a pouch of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water spontaneously although the process is endothermic. Explain this in terms of entropy.
parts.answer: The ordered solid lattice breaks up into freely moving aqueous ions, so ΔS of the system is large and positive; TΔS is greater than ΔH, so ΔG is negative.
parts.working: B1 ΔS positive (ions dispersed); B1 TΔS > ΔH so ΔG < 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of the entropy change of the surroundings for this process and explain.
parts.answer: Negative – energy is absorbed from the surroundings (they cool), reducing their entropy.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Place the following reactions in order of increasing ΔS, without calculation. Explain your order.
W: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g)
X: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
Y: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)
Z: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)
parts.answer: Y < X < Z < W
parts.working: B1 Y lowest/negative – amount of gas decreases (3 mol → 2 mol); B1 X ≈ 0 – 1 mol gas → 1 mol gas; B1 Z forms 1 mol gas from liquids, W forms 2 mol gas from a solid, so W is largest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ΔG = 0 for the vaporisation of a liquid at its boiling point.
parts.answer: At the boiling point liquid and vapour are in equilibrium (neither direction is favoured).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the entropy change of vaporisation of ethanol at its boiling point, 351 K, given ΔH_vap = +38.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: +110 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: For water, ΔH_vap = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K. Calculate ΔS_vap and suggest why it is similar to that of ethanol.
parts.answer: +109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; both involve changing 1 mol of liquid into 1 mol of gas, giving a similar increase in disorder.
parts.working: B1 value; B1 explanation.

stem:
Magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white flame in fireworks.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: Mg(s) 32.7; O₂(g) 205.0; MgO(s) 26.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, unlike standard enthalpies of formation, the standard entropy of an element such as Mg(s) is not zero.
parts.answer: Entropy is an absolute quantity; all substances above 0 K have some disorder (particle motion), so S° > 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° for 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
parts.answer: −216.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and state whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
parts.answer: +130 kJ mol⁻¹; not feasible
parts.working: M1 ΔG = 178 − 298 × 0.161 (ΔS in kJ); A1 value and conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature at which the reaction becomes feasible.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression that links ΔG, ΔH, ΔS and T, and state the condition for a reaction to be feasible.
parts.answer: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; feasible when ΔG is negative (≤ 0).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each combination, state whether the reaction is feasible at all temperatures, at no temperature, only at high temperature or only at low temperature: (i) ΔH −, ΔS + (ii) ΔH +, ΔS − (iii) ΔH −, ΔS − (iv) ΔH +, ΔS +
parts.answer: (i) all temperatures (ii) no temperature (iii) only at low temperature (iv) only at high temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g); ΔH° = −92.0 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = −198.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Ammonia is made at a fertiliser plant in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction at 298 K.
parts.answer: −32.9 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is no longer feasible under standard conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The industrial process runs at about 720 K, where ΔG° is positive. Explain why this temperature is still used.
parts.answer: At 298 K the rate is far too slow; a higher temperature gives an acceptable rate (with an iron catalyst), and high pressure keeps the equilibrium yield economic (conditions are not standard).
parts.working: B1 rate too slow at low T; B1 compromise/high pressure, non-standard conditions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ΔG_f° / kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K: NO₂(g) +51.3; N₂O₄(g) +97.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g).
parts.answer: −4.8 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔG_f° for O₂(g) and explain.
parts.answer: Zero – an element in its standard state is not formed from anything (by definition).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, how the feasibility of this reaction changes as temperature rises.
parts.answer: It becomes less feasible: ΔS is negative (2 mol gas → 1 mol), so −TΔS becomes more positive and ΔG eventually becomes positive.
parts.working: B1 less feasible; B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zinc is extracted by heating zinc oxide with carbon.
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: ZnO(s) −348.3; CO(g) −110.5
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: ZnO(s) 43.6; C(s) 5.7; Zn(s) 41.6; CO(g) 197.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = +237.8 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +190.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature at which carbon can reduce zinc oxide.
parts.working: M1 T = ΔH/ΔS with consistent units; A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
C(diamond) → C(graphite); ΔH° = −1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: C(diamond) 2.4; C(graphite) 5.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° and ΔG° at 298 K for C(diamond) → C(graphite).
parts.answer: ΔS° = +3.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔG° = −2.88 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why diamonds in jewellery do not turn into graphite even though the reaction is feasible.
parts.answer: The activation energy is extremely high (strong covalent bonds must break), so the rate at room temperature is negligible – diamond is kinetically stable.
parts.working: B1 very high Ea; B1 rate negligible/kinetically stable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a reaction, ΔG° = +20.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K and ΔG° = −10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 500 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature, calculate ΔS (in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and ΔH (in kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: ΔS = +150 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔH = +65.0 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at both temperatures; M1 subtracting gives 30.0 = 200ΔS → ΔS = 0.150 kJ K⁻¹; A1 ΔH = 20.0 + 300(0.150) = 65.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which ΔG = 0.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data for thermal decomposition, MCO₃(s) → MO(s) + CO₂(g):
MgCO₃: ΔH° = +117 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = +175 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
BaCO₃: ΔH° = +269 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = +172 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature for the thermal decomposition of each carbonate.
parts.answer: MgCO₃ 669 K; BaCO₃ 1560 K
parts.working: B1 each (T = ΔH/ΔS).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why ΔS° is almost the same for both reactions.
parts.answer: Both form one mole of CO₂ gas from a solid; the gas dominates the entropy change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the cations, why MgCO₃ decomposes at a much lower temperature than BaCO₃.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is smaller than Ba²⁺ (same charge), so has a higher charge density; it polarises/distorts the carbonate ion electron cloud more, weakening the C–O bonds, so less energy is needed to decompose.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ smaller/higher charge density; B1 polarises carbonate anion more; B1 C–O bond weakened, decomposes more easily.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In the Contact process, sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide.
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: SO₂(g) −296.8; SO₃(g) −395.7
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: SO₂(g) 248.1; O₂(g) 205.0; SO₃(g) 256.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = −197.8 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = −187.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 723 K, the temperature of the converter.
parts.answer: −62.0 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is no longer feasible under standard conditions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Daniell cell is made from Zn/Zn²⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺ half-cells. E°cell = +1.10 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), using ΔG° = −nE°cellF. [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: −212 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sign of E°cell tells you whether the reaction is feasible.
parts.answer: Positive E°cell gives negative ΔG°, so the reaction is feasible.

author: HomiLabs
