parts.text: An element in Period 4 forms a 2+ ion with the configuration [Ar] 3d⁸. Identify the element and write the configuration of its atom.
parts.answer: Nickel; [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s²
parts.working: B1 nickel. B1 configuration (4s electrons lost on ion formation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Four elements in Period 4 have atoms with exactly two unpaired electrons in the ground state. Identify all four.
parts.answer: titanium, nickel, germanium, selenium
parts.working: Ti 3d², Ni 3d⁸, Ge 4p², Se 4p⁴. 2 marks all four; 1 mark for three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the electronic configuration of a Ge atom in the form [Ar] ….
parts.answer: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the full electronic configuration of a bromine atom.
parts.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to state, for one bromine atom: (i) the total number of electrons in p orbitals, (ii) the number of electrons in d orbitals, (iii) the total number of orbitals that contain at least one electron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the electronic configurations of a cobalt atom, a Co²⁺ ion and a Co³⁺ ion in the form [Ar] ….
parts.answer: Co [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; Co²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁷; Co³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of unpaired electrons in each of the three species in (a).
parts.answer: Co 3, Co²⁺ 3, Co³⁺ 4
parts.working: 2 marks all three; 1 mark two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the ion of iron that is isoelectronic with Co³⁺.
parts.answer: Fe²⁺
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶.

stem: An ion M³⁺ contains 21 electrons and 28 neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify element M and give the nucleon number of the isotope.
parts.answer: Chromium; nucleon number 52

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the electronic configurations of an M atom and of the M³⁺ ion in the form [Ar] ….
parts.answer: Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cr³⁺: [Ar] 3d³
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the atom does not have the configuration [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
parts.answer: A half-filled 3d sub-shell with one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals (and 4s¹) gives less electron repulsion/is more stable; 3d and 4s are close in energy.
parts.working: M1 3d and 4s close in energy. M1 3d⁵ 4s¹ arrangement minimises repulsion / half-full sub-shell more stable.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the electronic configurations of Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺.
parts.answer: Sc³⁺ [Ar]; Zn²⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A transition element is defined as a d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete d sub-shell. Use your answers to (a) to explain why scandium and zinc are not classed as transition elements.
parts.answer: Sc³⁺ (its only ion) has no d electrons; Zn²⁺ (its only ion) has a full 3d¹⁰ sub-shell; neither has an incomplete d sub-shell.
parts.working: B1 Sc³⁺ empty 3d. B1 Zn²⁺ full 3d.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper forms Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺. Write both configurations and state which ion shows that copper is a transition element.
parts.answer: Cu⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰; Cu²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁹; Cu²⁺ (incomplete 3d)
parts.working: B1 both configurations. B1 Cu²⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the trend in atomic radius down Group 2 from magnesium to barium.
parts.answer: Radius increases; each element has an extra occupied shell, so outer electrons are further from the nucleus (more shielding outweighs extra nuclear charge).
parts.working: B1 increases. B1 extra shell(s) / more shielding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain whether a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, is larger or smaller than a magnesium atom.
parts.answer: Smaller; the ion has lost its outer (3s) shell, and the remaining 10 electrons are attracted by 12 protons.
parts.working: B1 smaller. B1 loses outer shell / greater proton-to-electron ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each pair, state which species is larger: (i) K or K⁺ (ii) F or F⁻ (iii) Na⁺ or Mg²⁺.
parts.answer: (i) K (ii) F⁻ (iii) Na⁺
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a)(iii).
parts.answer: Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ both have 10 electrons in the same shells (isoelectronic), but Mg²⁺ has more protons (12 vs 11), so its electrons are pulled closer.
parts.working: M1 same electronic configuration / isoelectronic. M1 Mg²⁺ greater nuclear charge.

stem: Covalent radii (nm): F 0.071, Cl 0.099, Br 0.114, I 0.133.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the trend in covalent radius from fluorine to iodine.
parts.answer: Increases; more electron shells, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
parts.working: B1 increases. B1 more shells / more shielding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the trend to explain why chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine.
parts.answer: Chlorine atoms are smaller, so an incoming electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded; chlorine attracts/gains electrons more readily.
parts.working: M1 Cl smaller radius / less shielding. M1 so electron gained more easily (stronger attraction).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Atomic radii in Period 2 (nm): Li 0.152, Be 0.112, C 0.077, N 0.075, O 0.073, F 0.071 (boron omitted).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in atomic radius from lithium to fluorine and explain it.
parts.answer: Radius decreases across the period; nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same (second) shell, and shielding stays about the same, so electrons are pulled closer.
parts.working: B1 decreases. M1 increasing nuclear charge / proton number. M1 same shell, similar shielding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict which of these values belongs to boron: 0.064 nm, 0.084 nm or 0.135 nm. Give a reason.
parts.answer: 0.084 nm, because boron lies between beryllium (0.112) and carbon (0.077).
parts.working: B1 0.084 with reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the large increase in radius between Al³⁺ and P³⁻.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (two shells) while P³⁻ has 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (three shells), so its outer electrons are much further from the nucleus.
parts.working: M1 P³⁻ has an extra (third) occupied shell. M1 compare configurations / more shielding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the radius decreases from P³⁻ to Cl⁻.
parts.answer: The three anions are isoelectronic (18 electrons) but nuclear charge rises from 15 to 17, so the electrons are attracted more strongly.
parts.working: M1 same number of electrons / same configuration. M1 more protons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the radius of P³⁻ is than that of Al³⁺. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

stem: Atomic radii (nm): Ti 0.132, V 0.122, Cr 0.117, Mn 0.117, Fe 0.116, Co 0.116, Ni 0.115, Cu 0.117. For comparison: Na 0.186, Cl 0.099.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in atomic radius from titanium to copper and from sodium to chlorine. Give each to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Ti → Cu 11 %; Na → Cl 47 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why atomic radius changes so little across the first row of the transition elements.
parts.answer: Each extra electron enters the inner 3d sub-shell, which shields the outer 4s electrons; the increase in nuclear charge is largely cancelled, so the 4s electrons are at a similar distance.
parts.working: M1 electrons added to inner 3d sub-shell. M1 extra shielding offsets extra nuclear charge.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Radii (nm): Mg atom 0.160, Mg²⁺ 0.072, O atom 0.073, O²⁻ 0.140.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Treating each particle as a sphere, calculate how many times greater the volume of a magnesium atom is than that of a Mg²⁺ ion. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the oxide ion, O²⁻, is larger than the oxygen atom.
parts.answer: O²⁻ has two extra electrons in the same shell but the same nuclear charge (8 protons); increased electron–electron repulsion and lower attraction per electron make the ion expand.
parts.working: M1 more electrons, same number of protons. M1 more repulsion / less pull per electron.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the electronic configurations of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ in the form [Ar] ….
parts.answer: Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶; Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Fe³⁺ (0.065 nm) is smaller than Fe²⁺ (0.078 nm).
parts.answer: Same nuclear charge (26 protons) but Fe³⁺ has one fewer electron, so less repulsion and each electron is pulled more strongly towards the nucleus.
parts.working: M1 same number of protons, fewer electrons. M1 greater attraction per electron / less repulsion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which ion, Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺, has the greater polarising power. Explain.
parts.answer: Fe³⁺; it has a higher charge and a smaller radius, so a higher charge density.
parts.working: B1 Fe³⁺. B1 higher charge and smaller radius → greater charge density.

stem: In an ionic crystal the distance between the centres of neighbouring oppositely charged ions equals the sum of their radii. Measured distances: NaCl 0.283 nm, NaF 0.235 nm, KF 0.271 nm. The radius of Cl⁻ is 0.181 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the NaCl and NaF data to calculate the radius of the F⁻ ion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the KF value to calculate the radius of K⁺ and predict the distance between ion centres in potassium chloride.
parts.answer: K⁺ 0.138 nm; KCl 0.319 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why K⁺ is larger than Na⁺.
parts.answer: K⁺ has an extra occupied shell (configuration of Ar rather than Ne).
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Cl–Cl bond length is 0.198 nm. Explain how this gives the covalent radius of chlorine, 0.099 nm.
parts.answer: The covalent radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms: 0.198 ÷ 2 = 0.099 nm.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The covalent radii of carbon and silicon are 0.077 nm and 0.117 nm. Predict the C–Cl and Si–Cl bond lengths.
parts.answer: C–Cl 0.176 nm; Si–Cl 0.216 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The measured Si–Cl bond length is 0.202 nm. Suggest why it is shorter than predicted, whereas the measured C–Cl bond (0.177 nm) is close to the prediction.
parts.answer: The Si–Cl bond is much more polar (large electronegativity difference), so it has partial ionic character; the extra electrostatic attraction pulls the atoms closer. C–Cl is less polar.
parts.working: M1 Si–Cl more polar / larger electronegativity difference than C–Cl. M1 ionic attraction shortens the bond.

stem: Ionic radii (nm): Na⁺ 0.102, Mg²⁺ 0.072, Al³⁺ 0.053.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge/radius ratio (charge ÷ radius in nm) for Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺. Give each to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why anhydrous aluminium chloride shows considerable covalent character while sodium chloride is ionic.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ has a very high charge density, so it strongly polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the large Cl⁻ ion; electron density is shared between the ions (covalent character). Na⁺ has a low charge density and hardly polarises Cl⁻.
parts.working: M1 Al³⁺ highest charge density / small and highly charged. M1 polarises/distorts Cl⁻ electron cloud. M1 Na⁺ low polarising power so NaCl is ionic.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the maximum number of electrons that the second shell (n = 2) can hold?
A 2
B 6
C 8
D 18
parts.answer: C 8
parts.working: n = 2 has one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals: 4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8. 6 is only the 2p sub-shell; 18 is the third shell.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a ground-state atom of which element is every occupied orbital completely full?
A magnesium
B silicon
C oxygen
D chlorine
parts.answer: A magnesium
parts.working: Mg is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²: every occupied orbital holds two electrons. Si (3p²), O (2p⁴) and Cl (3p⁵) all have at least one half-filled p orbital; chlorine is the trap as it has only one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two similarities and one difference between a 1s orbital and a 2s orbital.
parts.answer: Similarities: both spherical; each holds a maximum of two electrons (with opposite spins). Difference: 2s is larger / further from the nucleus / higher in energy.
parts.working: B1 each point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of orbitals in (i) a 2p sub-shell and (ii) a 3d sub-shell.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List these sub-shells in the order in which they are filled in ground-state atoms: 3d, 2p, 4s, 3s, 4p, 3p.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for one pair out of order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sub-shell that is being filled in an atom of arsenic (proton number 33).
parts.answer: 4p
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the sub-shell that receives the last electron added, in filling order, when building up the ground-state configuration of scandium (proton number 21).
parts.answer: 3d
parts.working: B1 3d: [Ar] 3d¹ 4s² — 4s fills before 3d, so the 21st electron enters 3d.

stem: Zinc is used to galvanise iron roofing sheets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the full electronic configuration of a zinc atom.
parts.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s²
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State (i) the number of sub-shells that are occupied and (ii) the number of orbitals that contain two electrons in a zinc atom.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the arrangement of electrons in the 2s and 2p orbitals of a ground-state carbon atom, including electron spins.
parts.answer: 2s: two electrons paired with opposite spins; 2p: two electrons in separate 2p orbitals with parallel spins; one 2p orbital empty.
parts.working: B1 2s paired. B1 2p electrons unpaired in separate orbitals (same spin).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In methane, carbon forms four equivalent bonds. Describe how one electron is moved to give four unpaired electrons, and state the type of hybrid orbital formed.
parts.answer: One 2s electron is promoted into the empty 2p orbital (2s¹ 2p³), giving four unpaired electrons; these orbitals mix to form four sp³ hybrid orbitals.
parts.working: B1 promotion 2s → 2p. B1 sp³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the bond angle in methane.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of 3d orbitals that contain exactly one electron in each of: Fe³⁺, Cr³⁺, Cu²⁺, Ni²⁺.
parts.answer: Fe³⁺ 5; Cr³⁺ 3; Cu²⁺ 1; Ni²⁺ 2
parts.working: B1 each (3d⁵, 3d³, 3d⁹, 3d⁸).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the rule that explains why the five 3d electrons in Fe³⁺ occupy separate orbitals.
parts.answer: Hund's rule: electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly (with parallel spins) before pairing.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place these sub-shells in order of increasing energy in an isolated potassium atom: 3p, 4s, 3d, 2p, 4p, 3s.
parts.working: 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark for one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your order to explain why the electronic configuration of potassium ends 4s¹ rather than 3d¹.
parts.answer: The 4s sub-shell is lower in energy than 3d in potassium, so the 19th electron enters 4s.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the 4p sub-shell and name the first element in which it is full.
parts.answer: 6; krypton
parts.working: B1 6. B1 krypton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the full electronic configuration of a calcium atom.
parts.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of electrons in (i) s orbitals and (ii) p orbitals in one calcium atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of spherical orbitals that are occupied in a calcium atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two elements in the p-block of Period 4 have atoms with exactly one unpaired electron. Identify them and write their configurations in the form [Ar] ….
parts.answer: Gallium [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹; bromine [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵
parts.working: B1 Ga. B1 Br. B1 both configurations (4p¹ has one unpaired electron; 4p⁵ has two filled 4p orbitals and one half-filled).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of completely filled orbitals in an atom of each element.
parts.answer: Ga 15; Br 17
parts.working: Ga: 1s + 2s + 3 × 2p + 3s + 3 × 3p + 5 × 3d + 4s = 15. Br: 15 + two filled 4p orbitals = 17. B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the three 2p orbitals of an isolated atom are filled singly before any electron pairs up.
parts.answer: The three 2p orbitals have the same energy; placing electrons in separate orbitals keeps them further apart and reduces repulsion (Hund's rule), which is lower in energy than pairing.
parts.working: M1 orbitals equal in energy (degenerate). M1 pairing in the same orbital causes extra repulsion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of unpaired electrons in (i) N³⁻ (ii) O⁻ (iii) a manganese atom.
parts.answer: (i) 0 (ii) 1 (iii) 5
parts.working: (i) 2p⁶. (ii) 2p⁵. (iii) [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s². B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each configuration, state whether it is the ground state or an excited state of a neutral atom, and identify the element: (i) 1s² 2s¹ 2p¹ (ii) [Ar] 3d¹ 4s¹ (iii) [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (iv) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3p¹
parts.answer: (i) excited, beryllium (ii) excited, calcium (iii) ground state, chromium (iv) excited, sodium
parts.working: B1 each (element and state both needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest whether less or more energy is needed to remove the outer electron from the atom in (a)(iv) than from a ground-state sodium atom. Explain.
parts.answer: Less energy; the electron is already in a higher-energy 3p orbital, further from the nucleus/more shielded than 3s.
parts.working: B1 less. B1 3p higher in energy than 3s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When a Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly, what is the mole ratio of nitrogen dioxide to oxygen given off?
A 1 : 1
B 2 : 1
C 4 : 1
D 1 : 4
parts.working: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂, so NO₂ : O₂ = 4 : 1. 1 : 4 reverses the ratio; 2 : 1 comes from forgetting to double the nitrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Strontium carbonate (Mr 147.6) is heated to constant mass. What is the percentage loss in mass?
A 29.8 %
B 44.0 %
C 70.2 %
D 59.6 %
parts.working: SrCO₃ → SrO + CO₂: loss = 44.0 ÷ 147.6 × 100 = 29.8 %. 70.2 % is the percentage of mass remaining; 44.0 % treats Mr as 100 (true only for CaCO₃).

stem: Quicklime is made in a kiln near Chakwal by heating limestone, which is mainly calcium carbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction that takes place in the kiln.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in dm³ at room conditions, released when 250 g of calcium carbonate is decomposed completely. (Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 59.9 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the carbon dioxide released in this process is an environmental concern.
parts.answer: CO₂ is a greenhouse gas / contributes to global warming.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats 0.500 g of an anhydrous Group 2 nitrate, M(NO₃)₂, in a hard-glass tube. The gases pass through aqueous sodium hydroxide, which absorbs all the nitrogen dioxide, and the oxygen is collected in a gas syringe. Volume of oxygen collected at room conditions = 28.4 cm³. Molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the decomposition of M(NO₃)₂.
parts.answer: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of oxygen collected and hence the amount of M(NO₃)₂ heated.
parts.answer: O₂ 1.18 × 10⁻³ mol; M(NO₃)₂ 2.37 × 10⁻³ mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of M(NO₃)₂ and identify M. (Ar: N 14.0, O 16.0)
parts.answer: Mr ≈ 211; Ar of M ≈ 87 → strontium

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the total volume of gas produced could not be measured accurately by collecting the gas mixture over water.
parts.answer: Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in / reacts with water, so it would not be collected and the measured volume would be too low.
parts.working: B1 NO₂ soluble in / reacts with water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 5.00 g mixture of calcium carbonate and calcium nitrate is heated to constant mass. The total loss in mass is 2.60 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for the decomposition of each compound in the mixture.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that heating 1.000 g of CaCO₃ loses 0.440 g, and that heating 1.000 g of Ca(NO₃)₂ loses 0.658 g. (Mr: CaCO₃ 100.1, Ca(NO₃)₂ 164.1, CaO 56.1)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate in the 5.00 g mixture. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trend in the temperature needed to decompose the Group 2 nitrates down the group.
parts.answer: It increases (nitrates become more thermally stable down the group).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend in terms of the cations and the nitrate ion.
parts.answer: Down the group the M²⁺ ion has the same charge but a larger radius, so a lower charge density; it polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the nitrate ion less; the N–O bonds are weakened less, so more heat is needed to break them.
parts.working: M1 cation radius increases / charge density decreases. M1 less polarisation of NO₃⁻ anion. M1 N–O bond weakened less so higher decomposition temperature.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)
stem: Data for MCO₃(s) → MO(s) + CO₂(g): MgCO₃ ΔH = +117 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +175 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; SrCO₃ ΔH = +234 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +171 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; BaCO₃ ΔH = +267 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +172 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG at 1200 K for the decomposition of each carbonate. Give your answers in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: MgCO₃ −93.0; SrCO₃ +28.8; BaCO₃ +60.6 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which carbonates decompose spontaneously at 1200 K, and relate the result to the trend in thermal stability.
parts.answer: Only MgCO₃ (ΔG negative); thermal stability increases down the group, so SrCO₃ and BaCO₃ need higher temperatures.
parts.working: B1 MgCO₃ only. B1 link to increasing stability down the group.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)
stem: At 25 °C, the solubility of barium sulfate is 2.4 × 10⁻³ g dm⁻³ and the solubility of magnesium hydroxide is 9.6 × 10⁻³ g dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the solubility, in mol dm⁻³, of BaSO₄ and of Mg(OH)₂. (Mr: BaSO₄ 233.4; Mg(OH)₂ 58.3)
parts.answer: BaSO₄ 1.03 × 10⁻⁵; Mg(OH)₂ 1.65 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write Ksp expressions for both compounds and calculate each value, with units.
parts.answer: Ksp(BaSO₄) = [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.06 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol² dm⁻⁶; Ksp(Mg(OH)₂) = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² = 1.79 × 10⁻¹¹ mol³ dm⁻⁹
parts.working: B1 each expression. B1 BaSO₄ s² with units. B1 Mg(OH)₂ 4s³ with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the solubilities of the sulfates and of the hydroxides change down Group 2.
parts.answer: Sulfates become less soluble; hydroxides become more soluble.
parts.working: B1 both.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)
stem: Ksp of barium sulfate = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of BaSO₄, in mol dm⁻³, (i) in pure water and (ii) in 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ sodium sulfate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a gravimetric analysis a BaSO₄ precipitate is washed with 100 cm³ of pure water. Calculate the maximum mass of BaSO₄, in g, that could dissolve. (Mr 233.4) Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an excess of barium chloride is added when sulfate ions are precipitated for analysis.
parts.answer: Common ion effect: excess Ba²⁺ lowers the solubility of BaSO₄ (Ksp fixed), so precipitation of sulfate is essentially complete.
parts.working: M1 common ion / excess Ba²⁺. M1 [SO₄²⁻] remaining in solution becomes negligible.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)
stem: Lattice energies (kJ mol⁻¹): MgCO₃ −3122; MgO −3791; BaCO₃ −2614; BaO −3054.

parts.label: a
parts.text: ΔH(decomposition) = −LE(MCO₃) + LE(MO) + X, where X is the same for both carbonates. Show that ΔH(decomposition) of BaCO₃ is 229 kJ mol⁻¹ more endothermic than that of MgCO₃.
parts.working: M1 BaCO₃: 2614 − 3054 = −440 (+X). M1 MgCO₃: 3122 − 3791 = −669 (+X). A1 difference +229; X cancels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ΔS for the decomposition is about the same for both carbonates. Use your answer to (a) to explain why barium carbonate must be heated to a much higher temperature than magnesium carbonate before it decomposes.
parts.answer: Decomposition becomes feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0, i.e. at T ≥ ΔH/ΔS. ΔH for BaCO₃ is 229 kJ mol⁻¹ larger while ΔS is similar, so the minimum temperature for BaCO₃ is much higher.
parts.working: M1 feasible when ΔG ≤ 0 / T = ΔH/ΔS. M1 larger ΔH with similar ΔS → higher temperature for BaCO₃.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Saturated solutions of four Group 2 hydroxides are made at the same temperature. Which solution has the highest pH?
A magnesium hydroxide
B calcium hydroxide
C strontium hydroxide
D barium hydroxide
parts.answer: D barium hydroxide
parts.working: Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2, so saturated Ba(OH)₂ has the highest [OH⁻] and pH. Magnesium hydroxide is the least soluble and gives the lowest pH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Limewater is a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide. Write an equation for the reaction that makes it turn milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through.
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why limewater is always a dilute solution.
parts.answer: Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble in water.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a solution of barium hydroxide could also be used for this test, but magnesium hydroxide could not.
parts.answer: Ba(OH)₂ is more soluble and BaCO₃ is insoluble, so a white precipitate forms; Mg(OH)₂ is too insoluble to give a useful solution.
parts.working: B1 Ba(OH)₂ soluble enough and gives white ppt. B1 Mg(OH)₂ almost insoluble.

stem: A water-treatment laboratory in Peshawar tests river water for sulfate ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how acidified barium chloride solution is used to test for sulfate ions, and give the positive result.
parts.answer: Add dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq); a white precipitate (BaSO₄) shows sulfate.
parts.working: B1 method. B1 white precipitate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an ionic equation, with state symbols, for the positive result.
parts.answer: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solution is acidified first.
parts.answer: To remove carbonate (or sulfite) ions, which would also give a white precipitate with Ba²⁺.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.0100 mol of barium hydroxide is dissolved in water and made up to 500 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution.
parts.answer: 0.0400 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pH of the solution. (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶) Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a solution of magnesium hydroxide of the same concentration cannot be made.
parts.answer: Magnesium hydroxide is much less soluble; it would not dissolve to this concentration.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student filters a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide at 20 °C. 25.0 cm³ portions of the filtrate are titrated with 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Mean titre = 22.00 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of hydroxide ions in the saturated solution.
parts.answer: 0.0440 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of calcium hydroxide in g dm⁻³. (Mr 74.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.63 g dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the solution must be filtered before titration, and one reason why the result might be too high.
parts.answer: To remove undissolved Ca(OH)₂ solid. Result too high: undissolved solid passing through the filter (or left on the pipette/tip) also reacts with the acid, increasing the titre.
parts.working: B1 remove undissolved solid. B1 suspended solid reacting with acid increases the titre.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ barium hydroxide is placed in a beaker with a conductivity probe. 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid is added from a burette and the electrical conductivity is recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction, and explain why the conductivity falls almost to zero at the end-point.
parts.answer: Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O. At the end-point all Ba²⁺ and OH⁻ ions have been removed as insoluble BaSO₄ and water (a weak electrolyte), so very few ions remain.
parts.working: B1 equation. M1 BaSO₄ precipitate removes Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻. M1 OH⁻ and H⁺ form water; few mobile ions left.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of sulfuric acid at the end-point.
parts.answer: 12.5 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe and explain the change in conductivity as more acid is added after the end-point.
parts.answer: Conductivity rises again because excess H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions are now present.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ strontium nitrate is mixed with 30.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Sr²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → SrSO₄(s)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine which reagent is in excess.
parts.answer: Sr²⁺ 0.0100 mol; SO₄²⁻ 0.00750 mol, so strontium nitrate is in excess.
parts.working: M1 both amounts. A1 Sr(NO₃)₂ in excess.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of strontium sulfate formed. (Mr 183.7) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.500 g of a nitrogen fertiliser from a factory near Multan is dissolved in water. Excess acidified barium chloride is added, and the precipitate of barium sulfate is filtered, washed and dried. Mass of BaSO₄ = 0.800 g. Assume all the sulfate comes from ammonium sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of barium sulfate formed. (Mr BaSO₄ 233.4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of ammonium sulfate in the fertiliser. (Mr (NH₄)₂SO₄ 132.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two steps needed to make sure the mass of precipitate is accurate.
parts.answer: Any two: wash the precipitate with distilled water to remove soluble impurities; dry/heat to constant mass; use excess BaCl₂; use fine filter paper / sintered crucible so no solid is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seawater contains 1.29 g of Mg²⁺ ions per dm³. Magnesium is extracted from seawater by first precipitating magnesium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an ionic equation for the precipitation of magnesium hydroxide when calcium hydroxide is added to seawater.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺(aq) + Ca(OH)₂(s) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) (or Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Mg(OH)₂)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the trend in hydroxide solubility, why this reaction works.
parts.answer: Mg(OH)₂ is much less soluble than Ca(OH)₂, so OH⁻ from dissolving Ca(OH)₂ precipitates Mg²⁺ as Mg(OH)₂.
parts.working: M1 Mg(OH)₂ less soluble than Ca(OH)₂. M1 hydroxide solubility increases down the group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of calcium hydroxide, in kg, needed to precipitate all the magnesium from 1.00 m³ of seawater. (Ar Mg 24.3; Mr Ca(OH)₂ 74.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a saturated solution of strontium hydroxide has a higher pH than a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Sr(OH)₂ is more soluble than Ca(OH)₂ (hydroxide solubility increases down the group), so its saturated solution contains more OH⁻ ions.
parts.working: B1 Sr(OH)₂ more soluble. B1 higher [OH⁻].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether strontium sulfate is more or less soluble than calcium sulfate.
parts.answer: Less soluble
parts.working: B1 sulfate solubility decreases down the group.

stem: Solubilities at 25 °C, in mol per 100 g of water: hydroxides — Mg(OH)₂ 2.0 × 10⁻⁵, Ca(OH)₂ 1.5 × 10⁻³, Sr(OH)₂ 3.4 × 10⁻³, Ba(OH)₂ 1.5 × 10⁻²; sulfates — MgSO₄ 1.83 × 10⁻¹, CaSO₄ 4.7 × 10⁻⁴, SrSO₄ 7.1 × 10⁻⁶, BaSO₄ 9.4 × 10⁻⁸.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more soluble barium hydroxide is than magnesium hydroxide, and how many times more soluble magnesium sulfate is than barium sulfate. Give each to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Hydroxides: 750 (7.5 × 10²); sulfates: 1.9 × 10⁶

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to suggest why aqueous sodium hydroxide can be used to distinguish Mg²⁺(aq) from Ba²⁺(aq), while dilute sulfuric acid can be used to distinguish Ba²⁺(aq) from Mg²⁺(aq).
parts.answer: With NaOH, Mg(OH)₂ (very insoluble) precipitates but Ba(OH)₂ does not; with H₂SO₄, BaSO₄ (very insoluble) precipitates but MgSO₄ is soluble.
parts.working: B1 hydroxide argument. B1 sulfate argument.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
0.687 g of barium (Ar 137.3) reacts completely with water. What volume of hydrogen is produced, measured at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)?
A 60.0 cm³
B 120 cm³
C 240 cm³
D 30.0 cm³
parts.answer: B 120 cm³
parts.working: Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂. 0.687 ÷ 137.3 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol Ba gives 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol H₂ = 120 cm³. 240 cm³ assumes 2 mol H₂ per mol Ba (confusing with H₂O).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations when magnesium ribbon burns in air, and write an equation for the reaction with oxygen.
parts.answer: Bright/dazzling white flame (light); white powder/ash forms. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
parts.working: B1 each observation. B1 equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The white powder is shaken with water and universal indicator is added. Suggest the pH and write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: pH about 9–10 (weakly alkaline); MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂
parts.working: B1 pH 8–10. B1 equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of barium with water.
parts.answer: Ba(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ba(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the reaction of barium with water differs from that of calcium with water.
parts.answer: Barium reacts more vigorously/faster; produces gas more rapidly; little or no white precipitate forms (Ba(OH)₂ is more soluble, whereas Ca gives a cloudy suspension).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid differences.

stem: Builders in rural Punjab 'slake' quicklime (calcium oxide) by adding water before making whitewash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with water, and state two observations.
parts.answer: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂; hissing/steam produced; solid crumbles/heats up (exothermic); white powder forms.
parts.working: B1 equation. 1 mark each for two observations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the pH of the solution formed when strontium oxide is added to water, and give a reason.
parts.answer: About pH 13 (strongly alkaline); SrO forms Sr(OH)₂, which is fairly soluble and releases OH⁻ ions.
parts.working: B1 pH 12–14. B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium oxide with hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide needed to react exactly with 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. (Mr MgO 40.3) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of barium oxide with dilute nitric acid and state the type of reaction.
parts.answer: BaO + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + H₂O; neutralisation (acid–base)
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 type.

stem: A student heats magnesium ribbon in a lidded crucible, lifting the lid from time to time. Results: mass of crucible and lid = 22.640 g; mass of crucible, lid and magnesium = 22.880 g; mass of crucible, lid and product after heating to constant mass = 23.032 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts, in mol, of magnesium and of oxygen atoms that combined. (Ar: Mg 24.3, O 16.0)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mg : O ratio to 3 significant figures and deduce the empirical formula.
parts.working: B1 ratio 1.04. B1 MgO.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the experimental ratio is not exactly 1 : 1, and an improvement for one of them.
parts.answer: Some white smoke (MgO) escaped when the lid was lifted; some magnesium reacted with nitrogen to form magnesium nitride; magnesium not fully burned. Improvement: lift the lid only slightly / heat to constant mass / add water and reheat to convert nitride.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons; 1 mark for a matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.150 g of calcium granules is added to excess water in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe. 81.0 cm³ of hydrogen is collected at room conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical volume of hydrogen at room conditions. (Ar Ca 40.1; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 89.8 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the expected volume that was collected. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for the low volume.
parts.answer: Calcium was coated with oxide/hydroxide so less metal reacted; gas escaped before the bung was replaced; some hydrogen dissolved/leaks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a fume cupboard, magnesium ribbon is heated in a boiling tube that also contains mineral wool soaked in water. Steam from the wool passes over the hot magnesium, and the gas leaving the tube is lit at a jet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium with steam and name the white solid formed.
parts.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂; magnesium oxide
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hydrogen is burned at the jet rather than released into the fume cupboard, and why the boiling tube must be made of hard (heat-resistant) glass.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is flammable and can form an explosive mixture with air; burning it as it leaves converts it safely to water. The magnesium is heated strongly, so ordinary glass would soften/crack.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen flammable / explosive mixture avoided. B1 hard glass withstands strong heating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium needed to produce 180 cm³ of hydrogen at room conditions. (Ar Mg 24.3; 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.350 g of a Group 2 metal M reacts completely with water, producing 95.9 cm³ of hydrogen at room conditions (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
parts.answer: Ar = 87.6; strontium

parts.label: b
parts.text: The solution is made up to 250 cm³. Calculate its pH. (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶) Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 1.00 g of a mixture of calcium and magnesium powders is added to excess cold water. Only the calcium reacts significantly, giving 350 cm³ of hydrogen at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium in the mixture. (Ar Ca 40.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the magnesium does not react significantly with the cold water while the calcium does.
parts.answer: Magnesium has higher first and second ionisation energies (outer electrons closer to nucleus, less shielded), so it loses electrons less readily; a layer of insoluble Mg(OH)₂ also slows the reaction.
parts.working: M1 higher ionisation energies for Mg. M1 less readily forms M²⁺ / Mg(OH)₂ insoluble coating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the remaining magnesium could be made to react to produce more hydrogen without using acid.
parts.answer: Heat it in steam.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for (i) strontium with cold water and (ii) magnesium with steam.
parts.answer: (i) Sr + 2H₂O → Sr(OH)₂ + H₂ (ii) Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation numbers of the Group 2 element and of hydrogen before and after reaction (i), and state which species is reduced.
parts.answer: Sr 0 → +2; H +1 → 0; water (hydrogen in water) is reduced
parts.working: B1 oxidation numbers. B1 water reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why magnesium gives an oxide with steam but calcium gives a hydroxide with cold water.
parts.answer: At the high temperature of steam, magnesium hydroxide is not stable and the product is the oxide (Mg(OH)₂ decomposes to MgO); calcium reacts at room temperature where the hydroxide forms.
parts.working: B1 high temperature → oxide.

stem: Barium and calcium metals are stored under oil in a school laboratory because they react with oxygen in air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for the reactions of calcium and of barium with oxygen.
parts.answer: 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO; 2Ba + O₂ → 2BaO
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of the solid oxides and the type of bonding in them.
parts.answer: White; ionic
parts.working: B1 white. B1 ionic.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property increases down Group 2 from magnesium to barium?
A first ionisation energy
B electronegativity
C atomic radius
D charge density of the M²⁺ ion
parts.answer: C atomic radius
parts.working: Each element has an extra shell, so atomic radius increases. Ionisation energy, electronegativity and cation charge density all decrease down the group; charge density is the trap because ionic radius increases.

stem: Ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): strontium 1st 549, 2nd 1064; barium 1st 503, 2nd 965.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy needed to form one mole of gaseous M²⁺ ions from gaseous atoms for strontium and for barium.
parts.answer: Sr 1613 kJ mol⁻¹; Ba 1468 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why barium reacts more vigorously with water than strontium.
parts.answer: Less energy is needed to form Ba²⁺ because its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so barium loses electrons (is oxidised) more readily.
parts.working: M1 lower total IE for Ba. M1 larger atom / more shielding so electrons lost more easily.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict two observations when a small piece of radium is added to water.
parts.answer: Very vigorous reaction / fizzing; metal disappears quickly; solution becomes warm; solution is alkaline.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Ra + 2H₂O → Ra(OH)₂ + H₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why radium is expected to be the most reactive Group 2 metal.
parts.answer: It has the largest atoms, so its outer electrons are furthest from the nucleus and most shielded; it has the lowest ionisation energies.
parts.working: M1 largest radius / most shielding. M1 lowest ionisation energies.

stem: Equal amounts (in mol) of four Group 2 carbonates are heated in turn with the same Bunsen flame, and the gas is bubbled into 5 cm³ of limewater. Time for the limewater to turn milky: MgCO₃ 25 s; CaCO₃ 140 s; SrCO₃ 410 s; BaCO₃ no change after 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to place the carbonates in order of increasing thermal stability.
parts.answer: MgCO₃ < CaCO₃ < SrCO₃ < BaCO₃
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same for a fair comparison.
parts.answer: Any two: amount (moles) of carbonate; volume/concentration of limewater; flame/heat setting and distance; tube size; particle size.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in thermal stability.
parts.answer: Down the group the cation radius increases (same charge), so charge density decreases; the cation polarises the carbonate ion less; C–O bonds are weakened less, so a higher temperature is needed to release CO₂.
parts.working: M1 larger cation, lower charge density. M1 less polarisation/distortion of CO₃²⁻. M1 less weakening of C–O bond.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the difference in the rate of reaction of magnesium and of barium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Barium reacts much faster/more vigorously because it loses its outer electrons more easily (lower ionisation energies).
parts.working: B1 Ba faster. B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid at first, but the reaction soon slows and stops even though both reactants remain. Explain why.
parts.answer: Calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble; it forms an insoluble layer on the metal surface, preventing further contact with the acid.
parts.working: M1 CaSO₄ sparingly soluble. M1 coats the metal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of strontium with hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Sr + 2HCl → SrCl₂ + H₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium with carbon dioxide, and state what is seen.
parts.answer: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C; white solid with black specks (of carbon); magnesium continues to burn brightly.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 observation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of carbon before and after the reaction and identify the reducing agent.
parts.answer: +4 → 0; magnesium
parts.working: B1 oxidation numbers. B1 Mg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a carbon dioxide extinguisher must not be used on a burning magnesium fire in a workshop.
parts.answer: Magnesium continues to react with (is oxidised by) CO₂, so the fire is not put out.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of barium carbonate with hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: BaCO₃ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of CO₂, in cm³ at room conditions, given by 1.97 g of barium carbonate. (Mr BaCO₃ 197.3; 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 240 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Barium carbonate is insoluble in water but is still poisonous if swallowed, whereas barium sulfate is safe for X-ray imaging. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Stomach acid (HCl) reacts with BaCO₃ to give soluble BaCl₂, releasing toxic Ba²⁺ ions; BaSO₄ does not react with acid and stays insoluble.
parts.working: M1 reacts with stomach acid. M1 soluble Ba²⁺ absorbed; BaSO₄ insoluble and unreactive.

stem: Ionic radii (nm): Mg²⁺ 0.072, Ca²⁺ 0.100, Sr²⁺ 0.118, Ba²⁺ 0.135.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate charge ÷ radius (radius in nm) for each ion. Give each to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your values to predict which carbonate releases carbon dioxide at the lowest temperature, and explain.
parts.answer: MgCO₃; Mg²⁺ has the highest charge density so it polarises the carbonate ion most, weakening the C–O bonds.
parts.working: B1 MgCO₃. B1 explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A cement works in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa heats limestone containing 95.0 % calcium carbonate by mass. CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to decompose the calcium carbonate in 1.00 tonne of the limestone. (Mr CaCO₃ 100.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The kiln burns methane (ΔHc = −890 kJ mol⁻¹), and only 60 % of the heat released is used for decomposition. Calculate the mass of methane, in kg, needed. (Mr CH₄ 16.0) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 1.689 × 10⁶ ÷ 0.60 = 2.815 × 10⁶ kJ. M1 ÷ 890 = 3163 mol. A1 × 16.0 = 50.6 kg (accept 50.7 from rounded intermediate values).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why kilns that decompose limestone run at a higher temperature than those decomposing magnesium carbonate.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ is more thermally stable (Ca²⁺ is larger, polarises CO₃²⁻ less), so it needs a higher temperature.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats 2.00 g samples of magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate separately at the same oven temperature for exactly 5 minutes. Mass lost: MgCO₃ 0.80 g; CaCO₃ 0.13 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass loss expected if each sample decomposed completely. (Mr: MgCO₃ 84.3, CaCO₃ 100.1, CO₂ 44.0)
parts.answer: MgCO₃ 1.04 g; CaCO₃ 0.879 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of each carbonate that decomposed in 5 minutes. Give each to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: MgCO₃ 76.6 %; CaCO₃ 14.8 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concludes that MgCO₃ is less thermally stable than CaCO₃. Evaluate this conclusion, giving one weakness of the method.
parts.answer: Supported: a much larger percentage of MgCO₃ decomposed in the same time at the same temperature. Weakness: only one trial each / mass losses (especially 0.13 g) measured to only 2 decimal places / samples may not have reached the same temperature (different particle size or container).
parts.working: B1 conclusion supported by the larger percentage decomposed. B1 one valid weakness (single trial; low precision of mass loss; heating/particle size not controlled).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Radium is the element below barium in Group 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether radium carbonate decomposes at a higher or lower temperature than barium carbonate.
parts.answer: Higher; Ra²⁺ is larger than Ba²⁺, so it has lower charge density and polarises the carbonate ion less.
parts.working: B1 higher. B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether radium sulfate is soluble or insoluble in water and whether radium hydroxide is more or less soluble than barium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Radium sulfate insoluble; radium hydroxide more soluble than barium hydroxide.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of radium nitrate.
parts.answer: 2Ra(NO₃)₂ → 2RaO + 4NO₂ + O₂
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of strontium carbonate with dilute nitric acid, and state what you would see.
parts.answer: SrCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Sr(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂; effervescence/fizzing and the solid dissolves.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 observation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas given off and describe a test for it.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; turns limewater milky.
parts.working: B1 each.

stem: Equal masses (0.120 g) of magnesium and of calcium are each added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid, and the hydrogen is collected in gas syringes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at room conditions, from each metal. (Ar: Mg 24.3, Ca 40.1; 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) Give each to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Mg 119 cm³ (118.5); Ca 71.8 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why calcium gives its hydrogen faster, but magnesium gives the larger final volume.
parts.answer: Rate: calcium has lower ionisation energies (larger atom, more shielding) so it reacts faster. Volume: each mole of metal gives one mole of H₂, and 0.120 g of Mg contains more moles than 0.120 g of Ca because Mg has the smaller Ar.
parts.working: M1 Ca more reactive. M1 reason (IE / radius). M1 more moles of Mg in equal mass.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Power stations remove sulfur dioxide from their waste gases by passing them through a slurry of calcium oxide or calcium carbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of reaction occurring and explain why removing SO₂ from flue gases is important.
parts.answer: Acid–base (neutralisation); SO₂ causes acid rain (damages buildings, lakes, plants).
parts.working: B1 acid–base. B1 acid rain.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O. (Mr: CaSO₄·2H₂O 172.2, H₂O 18.0) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gypsum is used to make plaster for broken-bone casts. State one property of calcium sulfate that makes it suitable.
parts.answer: It is only slightly soluble in water / non-toxic / sets hard.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point (2852 °C).
parts.answer: It has a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attractions between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, needing a lot of energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 giant ionic lattice. B1 strong attractions between oppositely charged ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the melting point of MgO is much higher than that of NaCl (801 °C).
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have double charges and are smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the attraction between ions is stronger.
parts.working: M1 higher charges. M1 smaller ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of MgO that depends on its high melting point.
parts.answer: Lining furnaces/kilns (refractory material).
parts.working: B1

stem: Historic buildings such as the old forts of Lahore were built with lime mortar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lime mortar contains calcium hydroxide. Write an equation for the reaction by which it slowly hardens in air.
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why lime mortar hardens from the outside inwards and why hardening takes many months.
parts.answer: CO₂ comes from the air, so the surface reacts first; CO₂ must diffuse slowly into the mortar, and its concentration in air is low.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ from air reaches surface first. B1 slow diffusion / low CO₂ concentration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for: (i) making quicklime from limestone; (ii) making slaked lime from quicklime; (iii) slaked lime turning back into limestone in air.
parts.answer: (i) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (ii) CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (iii) Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass, in kg, of carbon dioxide released in step (i) for every 1.00 tonne of quicklime made. (Mr: CaO 56.1, CO₂ 44.0) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 784 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of barium chloride-2-water, BaCl₂·2H₂O, needed to make 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution. (Mr 244.3) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one safety precaution needed when handling this solution and explain it.
parts.answer: Wear gloves/avoid ingestion and wash hands, because soluble barium compounds are toxic.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why barium sulfate, which is used in X-ray 'barium meals', is not toxic even though it contains barium.
parts.answer: It is insoluble, so Ba²⁺ ions are not released/absorbed into the body.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hard water from a well in Quetta contains calcium hydrogencarbonate. Write an equation for the formation of 'scale' when it is boiled in a kettle.
parts.answer: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Scale can be removed with vinegar (ethanoic acid). Write an equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why hydrochloric acid would remove scale faster than vinegar at the same concentration.
parts.answer: HCl is a strong acid (fully dissociated) so it has a higher [H⁺] than the weak ethanoic acid (partly dissociated).
parts.working: M1 HCl strong / ethanoic acid weak. M1 higher H⁺ concentration.

stem: Epsom salt, MgSO₄·xH₂O, is used in bath salts. A student heats 2.46 g of the crystals to constant mass. Mass of anhydrous MgSO₄ = 1.20 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts, in mol, of anhydrous MgSO₄ and of water. (Mr: MgSO₄ 120.4, H₂O 18.0)
parts.answer: MgSO₄ 9.97 × 10⁻³ mol; H₂O 0.0700 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the value of x.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student can make sure all the water has been removed.
parts.answer: Heat, cool and weigh repeatedly until the mass is constant.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A textile factory in Faisalabad produces 5000 dm³ of waste water containing 0.0040 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid each day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the neutralisation of sulfuric acid by calcium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + 2H₂O
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass, in kg, of calcium hydroxide needed. (Mr 74.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using calcium hydroxide rather than sodium hydroxide for this purpose.
parts.answer: It is cheaper / less corrosive / only slightly soluble, so excess does not make the water strongly alkaline.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A coal-fired power station in Tharparkar burns 5000 tonnes of lignite each day. The coal contains 1.2 % sulfur by mass. The sulfur dioxide formed is removed with calcium carbonate slurry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur, in tonnes, in the coal burned each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each mole of sulfur is removed by one mole of calcium carbonate. Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate needed, in tonnes. (Ar S 32.1; Mr CaCO₃ 100.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The calcium sulfite is oxidised in air to gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O. Write an equation for this oxidation (with water) and calculate the mass of gypsum formed, in tonnes. (Mr 172.2) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2CaSO₃ + O₂ + 4H₂O → 2CaSO₄·2H₂O; 322 t
parts.working: B1 equation. M1 1.869 × 10⁶ mol gypsum. A1 × 172.2 = 322 t.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one use for the gypsum produced.
parts.answer: Plasterboard / cement manufacture / plaster.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: A magnesium supplement tablet is labelled 'contains 250 mg of magnesium as magnesium oxide'. The tablet is dissolved in 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid (excess). The excess acid needs 14.6 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide for neutralisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of HCl that reacted with the tablet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of MgO with HCl and calculate the mass, in mg, of magnesium in the tablet. (Ar Mg 24.3) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O; 215 mg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnesium content as a percentage of the label value, and suggest why a back titration is used rather than a direct titration of the tablet.
parts.answer: 86.0 %; MgO is insoluble in water / reacts slowly, so it cannot be titrated directly with a sharp end-point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Farmers can treat acidic soil with either slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, or powdered limestone, CaCO₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of each compound needed to neutralise 1.00 mol of H⁺ ions in soil. (Mr: Ca(OH)₂ 74.1, CaCO₃ 100.1)
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ 37.1 g; CaCO₃ 50.1 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more mass of calcium carbonate is needed than calcium hydroxide. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Despite this, many farmers prefer powdered limestone. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Any two: it is cheaper; safer/less caustic to handle; it acts more slowly so soil pH does not rise too high; excess does not make soil strongly alkaline because CaCO₃ is insoluble.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A self-heating can of coffee uses the reaction CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(s), ΔH = −65 kJ mol⁻¹. The 250 g drink (specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) must be warmed by 40 °C, and only 60 % of the heat released reaches the drink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heat energy, in kJ, needed to warm the drink.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of calcium oxide needed. (Mr CaO 56.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one hazard of this design and one reason calcium oxide is suitable.
parts.answer: Hazard: CaO and Ca(OH)₂ are corrosive/alkaline if the can leaks, or overheating. Suitable: cheap, reacts readily and very exothermically with water.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each compound, state one property that makes it suitable for the use given: (i) BaSO₄ — X-ray imaging of the gut; (ii) Mg(OH)₂ — antacid; (iii) CaO — drying ammonia gas; (iv) CaCO₃ — neutralising acidic lakes.
parts.answer: (i) insoluble (non-toxic) and absorbs X-rays; (ii) weak base/slightly soluble so mildly alkaline; (iii) basic, absorbs water and does not react with basic ammonia; (iv) base/reacts with acid, cheap, insoluble so pH doesn't overshoot.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why calcium oxide cannot be used to dry hydrogen chloride gas.
parts.answer: CaO is basic and would react with (neutralise) the acidic HCl.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent gives a positive result with BOTH ethanal and ethanol?
A acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm
B 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine
C Fehling's solution, warm
D sodium metal
parts.answer: A acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm
parts.working: Both a primary alcohol and an aldehyde are oxidised by warm acidified dichromate(VI), which turns from orange to green. 2,4-DNPH and Fehling's react only with ethanal; sodium reacts only with ethanol (O–H group).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound reacts with sodium metal but does NOT react with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A phenol
B ethanol
C ethanoic acid
D ethyl ethanoate
parts.answer: B ethanol
parts.working: Ethanol has an O–H group so it gives hydrogen with sodium, but it is too weak an acid to react with NaOH(aq). Phenol and ethanoic acid react with both. Ethyl ethanoate has no O–H, so it does not react with sodium (it is hydrolysed by NaOH).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test that distinguishes pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Warm with alkaline aqueous iodine: pentan-2-one gives a yellow precipitate (tri-iodomethane); pentan-3-one gives no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 reagent (I₂ + NaOH(aq), warm). B1 both results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which structural feature of pentan-2-one causes the positive result.
parts.answer: It contains a CH₃CO– (methyl ketone) group.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test that distinguishes butanoic acid from its isomer methyl propanoate. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Add aqueous sodium carbonate (or NaHCO₃): butanoic acid gives effervescence (CO₂, turns limewater milky); methyl propanoate gives no effervescence.
parts.working: B1 reagent. B1 both results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps needed to identify the halogen present in an unknown liquid halogenoalkane, X, using aqueous silver nitrate.
parts.answer: Warm X with aqueous sodium hydroxide (hydrolysis releases the halide ion); acidify with dilute nitric acid; add aqueous silver nitrate and observe the precipitate colour.
parts.working: B1 warm with NaOH(aq). B1 add dilute HNO₃. B1 add AgNO₃(aq), note colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To neutralise excess OH⁻ ions, which would otherwise form a brown precipitate of silver oxide.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: X gives a cream precipitate that dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not in dilute ammonia. Identify the halogen and write an ionic equation for the precipitate formation.
parts.answer: Bromine; Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s)
parts.working: B1 bromine. B1 equation.

stem: Three unlabelled bottles contain small samples of phenol, benzoic acid and phenylmethanol (C₆H₅CH₂OH). No other organic solvent is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe tests that would identify each compound. Give the reagent and the observation for each compound in each test.
parts.answer: Aqueous bromine: phenol decolourises it and gives a white precipitate (2,4,6-tribromophenol); the other two show no white precipitate. Aqueous sodium carbonate: benzoic acid effervesces (CO₂); phenol and phenylmethanol do not. Phenylmethanol is the remaining compound; it can be confirmed by warming with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (orange → green).
parts.working: B1 bromine water reagent. B1 phenol result. B1 Na₂CO₃ reagent. B1 benzoic acid result. B1 phenylmethanol identified with a confirming test/result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why phenol does not give effervescence with aqueous sodium carbonate although it reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Phenol is a very weak acid — weaker than carbonic acid — so it cannot release CO₂ from carbonate, but it is acidic enough to be neutralised by the strong base OH⁻.
parts.working: M1 phenol weaker acid than carbonic acid/CO₂. M1 still reacts with strong base.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Four bottles contain butanal, butanone, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, but the labels have fallen off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a sequence of no more than three test-tube tests, each using a different reagent, to identify all four liquids. For each test give the reagent, the conditions and the expected results.
parts.answer: Test 1: 2,4-DNPH — orange precipitate with butanal and butanone; none with the alcohols. Test 2: Tollens' reagent, warm (on the two carbonyls) — silver mirror with butanal only; butanone no change. Test 3: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, warm (on the two alcohols) — butan-2-ol turns orange → green; 2-methylpropan-2-ol stays orange.
parts.working: B1 each reagent with conditions (3). B1 each correct pair of results (3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a single reagent that gives a positive result with both butan-2-ol and butanone but not with the other two liquids, and state the observation.
parts.answer: Alkaline aqueous iodine (warm); pale yellow precipitate of CHI₃.
parts.working: B1 reagent. B1 yellow precipitate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound Y, found in sour milk (dahi), contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of Y. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
parts.answer: CH₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Mr of Y is 90. Deduce its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₃H₆O₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: Y effervesces with aqueous sodium carbonate and gives a yellow precipitate with warm alkaline aqueous iodine. Suggest the structure of Y.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)COOH (2-hydroxypropanoic acid)
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Alcohol A, C₃H₈O, is warmed with an oxidising agent and the product B is distilled off as it forms. B gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify A and B, giving their structural formulae.
parts.answer: A: propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH; B: propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for converting A into B, and explain why the product is distilled off as it forms.
parts.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm, distil immediately; to stop further oxidation of the aldehyde to propanoic acid.
parts.working: B1 reagents/conditions. B1 reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why A cannot be propan-2-ol.
parts.answer: Propan-2-ol (secondary) would be oxidised to propanone, a ketone, which does not give a silver mirror.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the alkene C₄H₈ that reacts with hydrogen bromide to give only one structural product. Give its name and structure.
parts.answer: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃
parts.working: B1 name. B1 structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product and explain why only one structural product forms.
parts.answer: 2-bromobutane; the alkene is symmetrical, so H and Br adding either way round give the same product.
parts.working: B1 name. B1 symmetrical.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether this alkene shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; each carbon of the C=C has two different groups (H and CH₃), and rotation about the C=C is restricted.
parts.working: B1

stem: 0.440 g of a sweet-smelling neutral liquid G, containing C, H and O only, burns completely to give 0.880 g of CO₂ and 0.360 g of H₂O. Its Mr is 88. On hydrolysis it gives ethanoic acid and ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the masses of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in 0.440 g of G. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the empirical and molecular formulae of G.
parts.answer: C₂H₄O; C₄H₈O₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify G and write an equation for its hydrolysis by aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃; CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + CH₃CH₂OH
parts.working: B1 identity. B1 equation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound K has molecular formula C₅H₁₀O. Its mass spectrum has a molecular ion peak at m/z 86 and large peaks at m/z 57 and 29, but no peak at m/z 43. K gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, does not react with Tollens' reagent, and gives no yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use all the evidence to identify K. Explain how each piece of evidence helps.
parts.answer: K is pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃. M⁺ 86 → C₅H₁₀O. 2,4-DNPH positive → carbonyl; no Tollens → ketone, not aldehyde; no iodoform → no CH₃CO– group (rules out pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one); peak at 57 = CH₃CH₂CO⁺, with no peak at 43.
parts.working: B1 structure. B1 carbonyl/ketone evidence. B1 iodoform evidence. B1 fragment 57 = C₂H₅CO⁺.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the fragment responsible for the peak at m/z 29.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂⁺ (C₂H₅⁺)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structure of the product when K is reduced by NaBH₄.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (pentan-3-ol)
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Halogenoalkane L, C₃H₇Br, is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form M. M is heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to form N, which gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify L, M and N and give their structural formulae.
parts.answer: L: 2-bromopropane CH₃CHBrCH₃; M: propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃; N: propanone CH₃COCH₃
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When L is heated with ethanolic sodium hydroxide a gas is formed instead. Name the gas and the type of reaction.
parts.answer: Propene; elimination
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why L cannot be 1-bromopropane.
parts.answer: 1-bromopropane would give propan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, which would be oxidised to an aldehyde/carboxylic acid, not a ketone.
parts.working: B1

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound P, C₄H₇N, is unbranched. On hydrolysis it forms butanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structure and name of P.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CN; butanenitrile
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for (i) the hydrolysis of P to butanoic acid and (ii) the reduction of P to an amine. Give the structure of the amine.

stem: Infrared absorption ranges: O–H (alcohol) 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, broad; O–H (carboxylic acid) 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, very broad; C=O 1670–1740 cm⁻¹; C–O 1040–1300 cm⁻¹. Four spectra show: Spectrum 1 — very broad 2500–3000 and strong 1710; Spectrum 2 — strong 1740 and strong 1240, nothing above 3000; Spectrum 3 — broad 3350 and strong 1050, nothing at 1670–1740; Spectrum 4 — strong 1730 only (no absorption at 3200–3600 or 1040–1300).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Match each spectrum to ethanol, ethanal, ethanoic acid or ethyl ethanoate. Explain your choices.

parts.working: B1

stem: Ibuprofen, a painkiller, has the structure (CH₃)₂CHCH₂–C₆H₄–CH(CH₃)COOH, with the two groups on opposite (1,4) positions of the ring.

parts.text: Compound Q, CH₂=CH–CH(OH)–CH₂–CHO, is tested with 2,4-DNPH, Tollens' reagent, aqueous sodium carbonate and bromine in hexane. State which reagents give a positive result and identify the group responsible each time.

parts.text: 4-aminophenol, H₂N–C₆H₄–OH, is converted into paracetamol by reaction with ethanoyl chloride. Name the two functional groups in 4-aminophenol and the new functional group formed.
parts.answer: Amine (primary aromatic amine); phenol; amide formed
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why, with one mole of ethanoyl chloride, the –NH₂ group reacts rather than the –OH group.
parts.answer: The nitrogen lone pair is a better nucleophile (N less electronegative than O, lone pair more available), so the amine reacts faster.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the formulae of the products when paracetamol, HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃, is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a π bond between two carbon atoms is correct?
A It is formed by end-on overlap of two sp² hybrid orbitals.
B It is formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals, with electron density above and below the bond axis.
C It is stronger than the σ bond between the same two atoms.
D It allows free rotation about the carbon–carbon bond.
parts.answer: B It is formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals, with electron density above and below the bond axis.
parts.working: A π bond forms by sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals; its electron density lies above and below the internuclear axis. A describes a σ bond (end-on overlap). The π bond is weaker than the σ bond (less overlap), and it prevents rotation, so C and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which molecule are ALL the carbon atoms sp² hybridised?
A benzene, C₆H₆
B propene, CH₂=CHCH₃
C cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂
D ethyne, C₂H₂
parts.answer: A benzene, C₆H₆
parts.working: Each carbon in benzene forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) and uses its remaining p orbital in the delocalised π system, so all six are sp². Propene is the main distractor: its CH₃ carbon is sp³. Cyclohexane carbons are all sp³; ethyne carbons are sp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methanal, H₂C=O, is used to make resins for plywood. State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methanal and the approximate H–C–H bond angle.
parts.answer: sp²; about 120°
parts.working: B1 sp²; B1 120° (trigonal planar: three bonding regions, no lone pair on C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the σ bond and the π bond between the carbon atom and the oxygen atom are formed.
parts.answer: σ: end-on (head-on) overlap of an sp² orbital of C with an orbital of O; π: sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbital on C with a p orbital on O.
parts.working: B1 σ bond = end-on/axial overlap of orbitals along the C–O axis; B1 π bond = sideways overlap of p orbitals, electron density above and below the axis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of σ bonds and the number of π bonds in one molecule of methanal.
parts.answer: 3 σ bonds and 1 π bond
parts.working: Two C–H σ + one C=O σ = 3 σ; the second bond of C=O is the π bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂, is used to make synthetic rubber for car tyres. Calculate the number of σ bonds and the number of π bonds in one molecule.
parts.answer: 9 σ bonds; 2 π bonds
parts.working: C–H bonds: 6 (σ). C–C bonds: 3 σ (one in each C=C plus the central C–C). Total σ = 9 (B1). Each C=C has one π: 2 π (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the hybridisation of each carbon atom in buta-1,3-diene.
parts.answer: All four carbon atoms are sp²
parts.working: Each carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond, so sp² (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the approximate H–C–H bond angle at a terminal CH₂ group.
parts.answer: about 120°
parts.working: Three regions of electron density around an sp² carbon: trigonal planar, 120°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Urea, (NH₂)₂CO, is made in Pakistan on a large scale as a nitrogen fertiliser. Its structure has a C=O group with each NH₂ group joined to the carbon atom. Calculate the number of σ bonds and π bonds in one urea molecule.
parts.answer: 7 σ bonds; 1 π bond
parts.working: 4 N–H + 2 C–N + 1 C=O σ = 7 σ (B1); 1 π in C=O (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the hybridisation of the carbon atom and the approximate O=C–N bond angle.
parts.answer: sp²; about 120°
parts.working: B1 sp² (three σ bonds, one π); B1 about 120° (trigonal planar).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon atom and the three atoms bonded to it lie in one plane.
parts.answer: The three sp² hybrid orbitals of carbon lie in one plane at 120° and point towards O and the two N atoms.
parts.working: B1 the three sp² orbitals are coplanar (trigonal planar arrangement); the unhybridised p orbital is perpendicular to this plane and is used in the π bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vinegar contains ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in the CH₃ group and of the carbon atom in the COOH group.
parts.answer: CH₃ carbon: sp³; COOH carbon: sp²
parts.working: B1 sp³ (four σ bonds); B1 sp² (three σ bonds and one π bond).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the approximate H–C–H bond angle in the CH₃ group and the O=C–O bond angle in the COOH group.
parts.answer: about 109.5°; about 120°
parts.working: B1 tetrahedral 109.5°; B1 trigonal planar 120°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of σ bonds and π bonds in one molecule of ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: 7 σ; 1 π
parts.working: 3 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C=O σ, 1 C–O, 1 O–H = 7 σ (B1); 1 π in C=O (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propadiene (allene), H₂C=C=CH₂, has two C=C bonds that share the central carbon atom. State the hybridisation of the central carbon atom and of each end carbon atom.
parts.answer: Central C: sp; each end C: sp²
