parts.working: B1 central C forms two σ bonds and two π bonds: sp (C=C=C linear, 180°). B1 end carbons form three σ bonds and one π: sp².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of σ bonds and π bonds in one molecule of propadiene.
parts.answer: 6 σ; 2 π
parts.working: 4 C–H + 2 C–C σ = 6 σ; one π in each C=C = 2 π.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The central carbon atom uses two p orbitals at 90° to each other to form the two π bonds. Explain why the plane containing one CH₂ group is at 90° to the plane containing the other CH₂ group.
parts.answer: Each π bond needs the end carbon's p orbital to be parallel to one of the central carbon's p orbitals; these two p orbitals are perpendicular, so the two end p orbitals are perpendicular. Each CH₂ plane is perpendicular to its own p orbital, so the two CH₂ planes are at 90°.
parts.working: M1 π overlap requires parallel p orbitals on adjacent carbons; M1 the central carbon's two p orbitals are at right angles, so the two π bonds are in perpendicular planes; A1 each CH₂ group lies in the plane perpendicular to its p orbital, so the two H–C–H planes are twisted 90° to each other (and rotation is prevented by the π bonds).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in a benzene molecule, C₆H₆, in terms of hybridisation, σ bonds and π electrons.
parts.answer: Each C is sp² and forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) in a planar ring at 120°; each C has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring; these six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring to form a delocalised π system containing 6 electrons above and below the plane.
parts.working: B1 sp², three σ bonds per C, planar hexagon 120°; B1 one p orbital (one electron) per C perpendicular to the plane; B1 sideways overlap gives a ring of delocalised π electrons (6) above and below the ring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of σ bonds in one molecule of benzene.
parts.working: 6 C–C σ + 6 C–H σ = 12.

parts.label: c
parts.text: All C–C bonds in benzene are 0.139 nm long. In cyclohexane the C–C bond length is 0.154 nm and in cyclohexene the C=C bond length is 0.134 nm. Explain why the benzene bond length lies between these values.
parts.answer: The π electrons are delocalised evenly over all six C–C bonds, so every bond is identical with a bond order between single and double (about 1.5), giving an intermediate length.
parts.working: M1 delocalisation spreads π electron density equally over all six bonds (no alternating single/double bonds); A1 each bond is stronger/shorter than a single bond but weaker/longer than a double bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the average bond energies (kJ/mol) C–C 347, C=C 612, H–H 436, C–H 413 to calculate the enthalpy change for the hydrogenation of ethene: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃
parts.answer: −125 kJ/mol
parts.working: Bonds broken: C=C 612 + H–H 436 = 1048 (M1). Bonds formed: C–C 347 + 2 C–H 826 = 1173 (M1). ΔH = 1048 − 1173 = −125 kJ/mol (A1). (The four original C–H bonds cancel.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experimental enthalpy change for this reaction is −137 kJ/mol. Suggest why your answer to (a) differs from this value.
parts.answer: Average bond energies are averages taken over many different compounds, so they are not exactly the values for the bonds in ethene, H₂ and ethane.
parts.working: B1 average bond energies are not specific to these molecules (accept: values are means from a range of compounds).

parts.label: c
parts.text: In terms of σ and π bonds, state which bonds are broken and which are formed in this reaction, and use this to explain why the reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: Broken: the π bond of C=C and the σ bond of H–H. Formed: two C–H σ bonds. Two strong σ bonds are formed while only one σ bond and one weaker π bond are broken, so more energy is released than is taken in.
parts.working: B1 broken: one π (C=C) + one σ (H–H); formed: two σ (C–H); B1 π bond weaker than σ (poorer sideways overlap), so energy released by forming two σ bonds exceeds energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule is linear?
A BeCl₂
B H₂O
C SO₂
D OF₂
parts.answer: A BeCl₂
parts.working: Be has two bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the pairs are as far apart as possible at 180°. H₂O and OF₂ have two lone pairs (bent); SO₂ has a lone pair on S (bent, about 120°), so it is the main distractor for students who count only the two double bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of species has the same shape?
A NH₄⁺ and BF₄⁻
B NH₃ and BF₃
C H₂O and CO₂
D PF₅ and SF₆
parts.answer: A NH₄⁺ and BF₄⁻
parts.working: NH₄⁺ and BF₄⁻ each have four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around the central atom: both tetrahedral, 109.5°. NH₃ is pyramidal (one lone pair) but BF₃ is trigonal planar; H₂O is bent but CO₂ linear; PF₅ is trigonal bipyramidal and SF₆ octahedral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon tetrachloride, SiCl₄, is used to make very pure silicon for solar cells. State the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the silicon atom, and give the shape and Cl–Si–Cl bond angle.
parts.answer: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs; tetrahedral; 109.5°
parts.working: B1 4 bp, 0 lp; B1 tetrahedral; B1 109.5°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nitrogen trichloride, NCl₃, has a Cl–N–Cl bond angle of about 107°. Give the shape of NCl₃ and explain why its bond angle is smaller than in SiCl₄.
parts.answer: Pyramidal (trigonal pyramidal). N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair; lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, so the bonding pairs are pushed closer together.
parts.working: B1 pyramidal; M1 3 bp + 1 lp on N (four electron pairs, roughly tetrahedral arrangement); A1 lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, reducing the angle from 109.5° to about 107°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is a fertiliser. Give the shape of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and its H–N–H bond angle.
parts.answer: tetrahedral; 109.5°
parts.working: B1 tetrahedral; B1 109.5° (four bonding pairs, no lone pairs on N).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, the nitrogen atom has three regions of electron density and no lone pair. Give the shape of the nitrate ion and its O–N–O bond angle.
parts.answer: trigonal planar; 120°
parts.working: B1 trigonal planar; B1 120°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the principle used to predict the shapes in (a) and (b).
parts.answer: Electron pairs (regions of electron density) around the central atom repel each other and move as far apart as possible.
parts.working: B1 VSEPR: electron pairs repel and arrange themselves to minimise repulsion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is linear but sulfur dioxide, SO₂, is bent (non-linear). In both molecules the central atom forms a double bond to each oxygen atom. State the number of lone pairs on the central atom in each molecule.
parts.answer: C in CO₂: 0 lone pairs; S in SO₂: 1 lone pair
parts.working: B1 CO₂ none (C uses all 4 outer electrons in bonding); B1 SO₂ one (S has 6 outer electrons, uses 4 in two double bonds).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why SO₂ is bent and suggest its O–S–O bond angle.
parts.answer: S has three regions of electron density (two double bonds and one lone pair) which repel to a trigonal planar arrangement; the lone pair is not part of the shape and repels more strongly, so the molecule is bent with an angle a little below 120° (about 119°).
parts.working: M1 three regions of electron density around S; M1 lone pair repels more than bonding regions; A1 bent, angle just under 120° (accept 115–120°).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which of the two molecules is polar. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: SO₂. Both have polar S=O/C=O bonds, but in linear CO₂ the two dipoles cancel; in bent SO₂ they do not cancel.
parts.working: B1 SO₂ polar; B1 dipoles cancel by symmetry in linear CO₂ but not in bent SO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylamine, CH₃NH₂, is responsible for the smell of stale fish. Give the shape around the carbon atom and around the nitrogen atom, with the approximate H–C–H and H–N–H bond angles.
parts.answer: Around C: tetrahedral, about 109.5°. Around N: pyramidal, about 107°.
parts.working: B1 C tetrahedral; B1 109.5°; B1 N pyramidal (3 bp + 1 lp); B1 about 107°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethanenitrile, CH₃C≡N, is a solvent used in medicine-testing laboratories. State the C–C≡N bond angle and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 180°. The nitrile carbon has two regions of electron density (the C–C single bond and the C≡N triple bond) and no lone pair, so they are as far apart as possible: linear.
parts.working: B1 180°; B1 two regions of electron density (a triple bond counts as one region) with no lone pair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boron trichloride, BCl₃, and phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃, both have three chlorine atoms bonded to the central atom. Give the number of lone pairs on the central atom and the shape of each molecule.
parts.answer: BCl₃: 0 lone pairs, trigonal planar. PCl₃: 1 lone pair, pyramidal.
parts.working: B1 BCl₃ no lone pair (B has 3 outer electrons); B1 trigonal planar; B1 PCl₃ one lone pair (P has 5 outer electrons); B1 pyramidal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both molecules contain polar bonds. Explain why PCl₃ is a polar molecule but BCl₃ is not.
parts.answer: In trigonal planar BCl₃ the three B–Cl dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel; in pyramidal PCl₃ the dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole.
parts.working: M1 symmetrical shape in BCl₃ so dipoles cancel; A1 PCl₃ is not symmetrical (lone pair at the top), so there is a resultant dipole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur trioxide, SO₃, has three S=O double bonds. Sodium sulfite, Na₂SO₃, is used as a food preservative (E221); the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻, has one lone pair on the sulfur atom. Give the shape and the approximate O–S–O bond angle of SO₃ and of SO₃²⁻.
parts.answer: SO₃: trigonal planar, 120°. SO₃²⁻: pyramidal, about 107° (accept 106–109°).
parts.working: B1 SO₃ trigonal planar; B1 120°; B1 SO₃²⁻ pyramidal; B1 about 107°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the shapes are different even though each species has three oxygen atoms around sulfur.
parts.answer: SO₃ has three regions of electron density around S with no lone pair, so they spread to 120° in a plane. SO₃²⁻ has four regions (three bonds plus a lone pair) arranged roughly tetrahedrally; the lone pair repels more strongly, so the three S–O bonds form a pyramid with angle below 109.5°.
parts.working: M1 3 regions vs 4 regions of electron density; A1 the extra lone pair in SO₃²⁻ (from the 2− charge) gives a tetrahedral arrangement and a pyramidal shape.

stem: The O–N–O bond angles in three nitrogen species are: NO₂⁺ 180°; NO₂ (a molecule with one unpaired electron on N) 134°; NO₂⁻ 115°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why NO₂⁺ is linear.
parts.answer: The N atom has two regions of electron density (two N=O bonds) and no lone pairs or unpaired electrons, so the regions are 180° apart.
parts.working: M1 two bonding regions, no non-bonding electrons on N; A1 maximum separation 180°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bond angle in NO₂⁻ is smaller than in NO₂.
parts.answer: NO₂⁻ has a lone pair (two electrons) on N, but NO₂ has only one unpaired electron; a single electron repels the bonding regions less than a lone pair does, so the angle in NO₂ is larger.
parts.working: M1 NO₂ has a single non-bonding electron, NO₂⁻ a full lone pair; A1 the lone pair repels the bonds more strongly, so the angle closes further (115° compared with 134°).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which of the three species are bent (non-linear), and suggest which one could join with another identical particle to form a dimer, giving a reason.
parts.answer: NO₂ and NO₂⁻ are bent. NO₂ forms a dimer (N₂O₄) because it has an unpaired electron, so two NO₂ molecules can pair these electrons to form an N–N bond.
parts.working: B1 NO₂ and NO₂⁻; B1 NO₂ — it is a free radical (unpaired electron), and two unpaired electrons pair up to form a covalent bond.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, is used in cola drinks. The P atom is bonded to one oxygen by a double bond and to three OH groups by single bonds, with no lone pair on P. Give the shape around the phosphorus atom and the approximate O–P–O bond angle.
parts.answer: tetrahedral; about 109.5°
parts.working: B1 four regions of electron density around P (one P=O counts as one region), no lone pair: tetrahedral; B1 about 109.5°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the shape around each oxygen atom of an O–H group and suggest the P–O–H bond angle.
parts.answer: bent (non-linear); about 104.5°
parts.working: B1 O has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs: bent; B1 about 104–105° (lone pairs repel most).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of lone pairs on all the oxygen atoms in one H₃PO₄ molecule.
parts.working: Each of the four oxygen atoms has two lone pairs: 4 × 2 = 8.

parts.label: d
parts.text: In the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻, all four P–O bonds are the same length. Give the shape of PO₄³⁻ and the O–P–O bond angle.
parts.answer: tetrahedral, 109.5°
parts.working: Four regions around P, no lone pair: regular tetrahedron, 109.5°.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pauling electronegativities: Li 1.0, K 0.8, Al 1.6, H 2.2, Cl 3.2, I 2.7, F 4.0.
Which compound has bonding with the greatest ionic character?
A KF
B LiI
C AlCl₃
D HCl
parts.answer: A KF
parts.working: Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference: KF 4.0 − 0.8 = 3.2; LiI 2.7 − 1.0 = 1.7; AlCl₃ 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6; HCl 3.2 − 2.2 = 1.0. LiI is the main distractor because it contains a Group 1 metal, but iodine is much less electronegative than fluorine.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule is non-polar even though it contains polar bonds?
A SiF₄
B CH₂Cl₂
C NH₃
D CHCl₃
parts.answer: A SiF₄
parts.working: SiF₄ is tetrahedral with four identical Si–F bonds, so the bond dipoles cancel. CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ are tetrahedral but have different atoms around C, so the dipoles do not cancel (main distractor); NH₃ is pyramidal and polar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C and is used to line furnaces in steel works. Describe the structure and bonding in solid magnesium oxide.
parts.answer: A giant ionic lattice of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions held by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions.
parts.working: B1 giant (ionic) lattice of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; B1 strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride (801 °C).
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges (and are smaller) compared with Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is much stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.
parts.working: M1 ions have 2+ and 2− charges (vs 1+ and 1−) / smaller ions; A1 stronger attraction, more energy needed to break the lattice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain whether magnesium oxide conducts electricity when solid and when molten.
parts.answer: Solid: no — ions are fixed in the lattice. Molten: yes — ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 solid does not conduct, ions cannot move; B1 molten conducts, mobile ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term electronegativity.
parts.answer: The power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond towards itself.
parts.working: B1 power/ability of an atom to attract the shared (bonding) pair of electrons in a covalent bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the electronegativities Na 0.9, H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, Cl 3.2, F 4.0 to calculate the electronegativity difference in each of NaF, H–Cl and C–H.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to classify each bond as ionic, polar covalent or (almost) non-polar covalent.
parts.answer: NaF ionic; H–Cl polar covalent; C–H almost non-polar covalent
parts.working: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two correct. Large difference → electron transfer (ionic); moderate → polar covalent; very small → almost non-polar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student dissolves sugar (sucrose, a simple molecular compound) in one beaker of water and table salt (sodium chloride) in another. Predict which solution conducts electricity and explain your answer.
parts.answer: The salt solution conducts: it contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are free to move. The sugar solution does not: sucrose dissolves as neutral molecules, so there are no charged particles.
parts.working: B1 salt solution conducts, mobile ions; B1 sugar solution does not, molecules carry no charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sucrose melts at about 186 °C but sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Explain this difference in terms of the forces that must be overcome.
parts.answer: Melting sucrose overcomes only intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds and van der Waals' forces) between molecules, which are weak; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break. Melting sodium chloride needs the strong ionic bonds (electrostatic attractions) throughout the giant lattice to be overcome.
parts.working: M1 sucrose: intermolecular forces between molecules overcome, not covalent bonds; M1 these are relatively weak; A1 NaCl: strong ionic attractions in a giant lattice must be overcome, needing much more energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thin stream of liquid is run from a burette past a charged plastic rod. Predict whether each of water, hexane and trichloromethane (CHCl₃) is deflected. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Water: deflected. Trichloromethane: deflected. Hexane: not deflected. Water and CHCl₃ molecules are polar (permanent dipoles), so they are attracted towards the rod; hexane is non-polar.
parts.working: B1 water and CHCl₃ deflected; B1 hexane not deflected; B1 polar molecules have a permanent dipole that is attracted by the charged rod (the molecules turn so that the oppositely charged end faces the rod).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, contains four polar C–Cl bonds. Predict whether a stream of CCl₄ is deflected and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Not deflected. CCl₄ is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the four bond dipoles cancel and the molecule has no overall dipole.
parts.working: B1 not deflected; B1 symmetrical tetrahedral shape, dipoles cancel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the stream is deflected whether the rod is positively or negatively charged.
parts.answer: Polar molecules rotate so that their oppositely charged end points towards the rod, so they are always attracted.
parts.working: B1 molecules can rotate/align so the end with the opposite partial charge faces the rod.

stem: Melting points of four Period 3 chlorides: NaCl 801 °C; MgCl₂ 714 °C; SiCl₄ −70 °C; PCl₃ −112 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the electronegativity values Na 0.9, Mg 1.3, Si 1.9, P 2.2, Cl 3.2 to calculate the electronegativity difference between the element and chlorine in NaCl, MgCl₂, SiCl₄ and PCl₃.
parts.answer: NaCl 2.3; MgCl₂ 1.9; SiCl₄ 1.3; PCl₃ 1.0
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the type of bonding and structure in each chloride.
parts.answer: NaCl and MgCl₂: ionic, giant ionic lattice. SiCl₄ and PCl₃: covalent, simple molecular.
parts.working: B1 NaCl and MgCl₂ ionic lattice; B1 SiCl₄ and PCl₃ simple covalent molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the large difference in melting point between MgCl₂ and SiCl₄.
parts.answer: Melting MgCl₂ requires overcoming strong electrostatic attraction between ions in a giant lattice; melting SiCl₄ only overcomes weak intermolecular (van der Waals') forces between molecules.
parts.working: M1 MgCl₂: strong ionic bonding throughout lattice; M1 SiCl₄: weak intermolecular forces only, covalent bonds not broken.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sodium chloride dissolves in water. Refer to the interaction between the ions and water molecules.
parts.answer: Water molecules are polar. The δ− oxygen atoms are attracted to Na⁺ ions and the δ+ hydrogen atoms to Cl⁻ ions; these ion–dipole attractions release enough energy to separate the ions from the lattice, and the ions become surrounded (hydrated) by water molecules.
parts.working: B1 water is polar (δ− O, δ+ H); B1 O end attracted to Na⁺, H end to Cl⁻; B1 energy released by these attractions compensates for breaking the lattice; ions become hydrated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sodium chloride does not dissolve in hexane.
parts.answer: Hexane is non-polar, so it cannot form strong attractions with the ions; the energy released would be far too small to overcome the strong ionic lattice.
parts.working: M1 hexane non-polar/only weak van der Waals' attraction with ions; A1 not enough energy to overcome lattice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Iodine dissolves well in hexane but only slightly in water. Explain this.
parts.answer: I₂ and hexane are both non-polar and attract each other by instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces of similar strength to those they replace. In water, I₂ cannot break into the strong hydrogen bonding between water molecules because it cannot form comparable attractions with water.
parts.working: M1 iodine and hexane: similar id–id forces formed and broken; M1 water's hydrogen bonds are stronger than any attraction iodine can form with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature, but silicon dioxide melts at 1710 °C. Describe the structure of each oxide and explain the difference in melting point.
parts.answer: CO₂: simple molecules, O=C=O, with weak intermolecular forces between molecules. SiO₂: giant covalent lattice, each Si bonded to 4 O and each O to 2 Si. Melting SiO₂ requires breaking many strong Si–O covalent bonds; CO₂ only needs weak intermolecular forces to be overcome.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ simple molecular, linear molecules; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent, SiO₄ tetrahedra, Si–O single bonds; M1 SiO₂: many strong covalent bonds broken; A1 CO₂: only weak intermolecular forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why carbon forms double bonds with oxygen in CO₂ but silicon forms four single bonds to oxygen atoms in SiO₂.
parts.answer: Silicon atoms are larger than carbon atoms, so the Si–O distance is longer and the sideways overlap of p orbitals needed for a π bond is poor; Si instead forms more σ bonds to more oxygen atoms. Carbon is small, so its p orbitals overlap well with oxygen's to form π bonds.
parts.working: M1 Si atom larger (outer electrons in n = 3); A1 poor sideways p-orbital overlap, so π bonds are weak/ineffective and single σ bonds to four O atoms are preferred.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Beryllium is a metal, yet beryllium chloride, BeCl₂, melts at only 399 °C, dissolves in some organic solvents and its molten form is a very poor conductor. Electronegativities: Be 1.6, Cl 3.2. Calculate the electronegativity difference and use it, with the data, to suggest the type of bonding in BeCl₂.
parts.answer: 1.6; covalent (polar covalent) bonding
parts.working: B1 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6; B1 moderate difference + low melting point + poor conductivity when molten → mainly covalent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Be²⁺ ion would be very small with a high charge. Explain how this makes the bonding covalent rather than ionic.
parts.answer: Be²⁺ has a very high charge density, so it strongly attracts (distorts/polarises) the electron cloud of a neighbouring Cl⁻ ion, pulling electron density into the region between the nuclei; this electron sharing is covalent bonding.
parts.working: M1 small ion with 2+ charge = high charge density; A1 it pulls the anion's electrons towards itself so that electrons are shared between Be and Cl.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the gas phase BeCl₂ molecules are linear. Give the number of electrons in the outer shell of beryllium in BeCl₂ and state why this molecule can accept electron pairs from other molecules.
parts.answer: 4 electrons; Be has an incomplete outer shell (only two bonding pairs), so it has empty orbitals that can accept lone pairs in dative bonds.
parts.working: B1 4 (two shared pairs); B1 electron deficient — can accept lone pairs (e.g. from Cl atoms of other BeCl₂ units in the solid).

stem:
Data for five solids at room temperature:
P: mp 990 °C; solid does not conduct; molten and aqueous solution conduct; brittle.
Q: mp 80 °C; does not conduct as solid or liquid; soluble in hexane, insoluble in water.
R: mp 1083 °C; conducts as solid and as liquid; malleable; insoluble in water and hexane.
S: mp 3550 °C; does not conduct as solid; insoluble in all solvents; very hard.
T: mp −114 °C (a gas at room temperature); pure liquid T does not conduct; very soluble in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of structure in each of P, Q, R, S and T. Choose from: giant ionic, giant metallic, giant covalent, simple molecular.
parts.answer: P giant ionic; Q simple molecular; R giant metallic; S giant covalent; T simple molecular
parts.working: B1 each. P: conducts only when molten/dissolved → ions mobile only in liquid. Q: low mp, non-conductor → simple molecules. R: conducts as solid and liquid, malleable → metallic. S: very high mp, insoluble, non-conductor → giant covalent. T: low mp, polar solvent soluble, non-conductor → simple molecular (polar).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Substance T dissolves in water to give a solution that conducts electricity. Suggest an explanation that is consistent with T being simple molecular.
parts.answer: T is a covalent molecule that reacts with water to form ions (e.g. like hydrogen chloride ionising to H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻).
parts.working: M1 T reacts with/ionises in water; A1 producing mobile ions — e.g. HCl or SO₂ type molecule.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of attraction is the only force between methane molecules in liquid methane?
A instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
B permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces
C hydrogen bonds
D covalent bonds
parts.answer: A instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
parts.working: CH₄ is non-polar (symmetrical tetrahedron, C–H almost non-polar), so only instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces act between molecules. Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them (main distractor); there is no N–H, O–H or F–H for hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound has the highest boiling point?
A ethanol, C₂H₅OH (Mr 46)
B methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃ (Mr 46)
C propane, C₃H₈ (Mr 44)
D chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl (Mr 64.5)
parts.answer: A ethanol, C₂H₅OH (Mr 46)
parts.working: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds through their O–H groups (bp 78 °C). Chloroethane has a larger Mr and a permanent dipole but no hydrogen bonding (bp 12 °C) — the main distractor. Methoxymethane has no O–H (bp −24 °C); propane has only id–id forces (bp −42 °C).

stem: Boiling points of the noble gases: He −269 °C; Ne −246 °C; Ar −186 °C; Kr −152 °C; Xe −108 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of intermolecular force between noble gas atoms in the liquid state.
parts.answer: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces (London / dispersion forces)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these forces arise.
parts.answer: Electrons move randomly, so at an instant the electron cloud is unevenly distributed, giving a temporary dipole; this induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, and the two dipoles attract.
parts.working: M1 uneven electron distribution at an instant → instantaneous dipole; A1 induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom; attraction between them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in boiling points from helium to xenon.
parts.answer: Boiling point increases down the group because the atoms have more electrons, so larger instantaneous dipoles form and the id–id forces are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the atoms.
parts.working: M1 more electrons down the group; A1 stronger id–id forces, more energy needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Boiling points: methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −0.5 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sold in cylinders in Pakistan is a mixture of propane and butane. Explain why butane has a higher boiling point than propane.
parts.answer: Butane molecules are larger, with more electrons and a larger surface area of contact, so the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them are stronger.
parts.working: M1 more electrons / larger molecule / more contact; A1 stronger id–id forces need more energy to overcome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether pentane (C₅H₁₂) is a gas or a liquid at 25 °C.
parts.answer: Liquid — its boiling point is above 25 °C because the trend continues (pentane boils at about 36 °C).
parts.working: B1 liquid, with reason based on the trend (bp increases by a few tens of °C per CH₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: In very cold weather in the northern areas, an LPG cylinder may still contain liquid that does not turn into gas. Suggest which component remains as a liquid and explain why.
parts.answer: Butane. Its boiling point (−0.5 °C) is above the outside temperature, so it does not vaporise, whereas propane (bp −42 °C) still boils.
parts.working: M1 butane; A1 bp −0.5 °C is above the low temperature, propane's bp is far lower.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each substance, name ALL the types of intermolecular force between its molecules or atoms: (i) argon, Ar  (ii) bromine, Br₂  (iii) hydrogen bromide, HBr  (iv) ethanal, CH₃CHO  (v) methanol, CH₃OH
parts.answer: (i) id–id only; (ii) id–id only; (iii) id–id and permanent dipole–permanent dipole; (iv) id–id and pd–pd; (v) id–id, pd–pd and hydrogen bonding
parts.working: B1 each. Ar and Br₂ non-polar. HBr and CH₃CHO polar (no H on N/O/F, so no hydrogen bonding in ethanal — the H atoms are on carbon). CH₃OH has an O–H group: hydrogen bonds (plus the other forces).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which force is present between the molecules of every substance in (a).
parts.answer: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
parts.working: B1 all molecules and atoms have electrons, so id–id forces are always present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: cis-1,2-dichloroethene boils at about 60 °C but trans-1,2-dichloroethene boils at about 48 °C. Both have Mr 96.9. Explain why only the cis isomer is a polar molecule.
parts.answer: In the cis isomer both C–Cl dipoles point to the same side of the C=C bond, so they do not cancel; in the trans isomer they point in opposite directions and cancel.
parts.working: M1 C–Cl bonds polar; A1 trans: dipoles opposite and cancel; cis: resultant dipole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain the difference in boiling points.
parts.answer: The cis molecules have permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces in addition to id–id forces; the id–id forces are similar for both (same number of electrons), so the cis isomer has stronger intermolecular forces overall and a higher boiling point.
parts.working: M1 cis: extra pd–pd forces; A1 id–id similar (same Mr/electrons), so more energy needed to separate cis molecules.

stem: Boiling points of the Group 14 hydrides: CH₄ −162 °C; SiH₄ −112 °C; GeH₄ −88 °C; SnH₄ −52 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in boiling point from CH₄ to SnH₄.
parts.answer: All are non-polar tetrahedral molecules with only id–id forces; the number of electrons increases down the group, so the id–id forces become stronger.
parts.working: M1 only id–id forces (non-polar molecules); A1 more electrons → stronger forces → higher bp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The boiling points of the Group 16 hydrides are H₂O 100 °C, H₂S −60 °C, H₂Se −41 °C, H₂Te −2 °C. Explain why water does not fit the pattern shown by the Group 14 hydrides.
parts.answer: Water forms hydrogen bonds between molecules because O is very electronegative and small and has lone pairs; hydrogen bonds are much stronger than id–id or pd–pd forces, so water's boiling point is far higher than expected from its small number of electrons. Group 14 hydrides cannot hydrogen bond, so their trend is regular.
parts.working: M1 hydrogen bonding in water; M1 due to highly electronegative O with lone pairs and δ+ H; A1 hydrogen bonds stronger than other intermolecular forces, so much more energy needed. (CH₄ has no lone pair and C is not electronegative enough.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the Group 14 hydrides all have lower boiling points than the Group 16 hydride in the same period (for example SiH₄ −112 °C and H₂S −60 °C).
parts.answer: The Group 16 hydrides are polar (bent shape), so they also have pd–pd forces; the Group 14 hydrides are symmetrical and non-polar.
parts.working: B1 Group 16 hydrides bent and polar → extra pd–pd attraction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of Br₂ and of ICl. (Ar: Br 79.9, I 126.9, Cl 35.5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Iodine monochloride, ICl, boils at 97 °C but bromine boils at 59 °C. Explain why the boiling points are so different even though the Mr values are almost equal.
parts.answer: Both have similar numbers of electrons, so their id–id forces are similar. ICl is polar because Cl is more electronegative than I, so ICl molecules also attract by permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; Br₂ is non-polar. So ICl has stronger intermolecular forces and needs more energy to boil.
parts.working: M1 similar id–id forces (similar number of electrons); M1 ICl polar (electronegativity difference) — pd–pd forces; A1 Br₂ non-polar so weaker overall forces, lower bp.

stem: Four compounds have similar relative molecular masses: pentane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ (Mr 72); butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO (Mr 72); butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (Mr 74); propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH (Mr 74).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place the four compounds in order of increasing boiling point.
parts.answer: pentane < butanal < butan-1-ol < propanoic acid
parts.working: B1 correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the order you have given. Refer to the strongest type of intermolecular force in each compound.
parts.answer: Pentane: id–id forces only. Butanal: polar C=O, so pd–pd forces as well (but no hydrogen bonding, no O–H). Butan-1-ol: hydrogen bonds between O–H groups, much stronger. Propanoic acid: hydrogen bonds from O–H and to the C=O oxygen; molecules form strong hydrogen-bonded pairs (two hydrogen bonds per pair), so the most energy is needed.
parts.working: B1 pentane id–id only (lowest); B1 butanal pd–pd from C=O; B1 butan-1-ol hydrogen bonding; B1 propanoic acid more extensive hydrogen bonding (C=O and O–H, dimers), so highest. Similar Mr means id–id forces are similar for all four.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why comparing these four compounds is a fair test of the effect of the type of intermolecular force.
parts.answer: They have almost the same Mr / number of electrons (72–74), so their id–id forces are similar.
parts.working: B1 similar Mr → similar id–id forces, so differences are due to dipoles/hydrogen bonding.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The enthalpy change of vaporisation of propane is +19.0 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy needed to vaporise 1.00 kg of liquid propane in a gas cylinder. (Mr propane = 44.0) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 432 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: The enthalpy change of vaporisation of butane is +22.4 kJ/mol. Explain why it is larger than the value for propane.
parts.answer: Butane molecules have more electrons/larger surface area, so the id–id forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate one mole of molecules.
parts.working: M1 more electrons/larger contact area; A1 stronger id–id forces to overcome.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When gas is drawn quickly from a cylinder, the outside of the cylinder becomes cold. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: Liquid inside vaporises to replace the gas used; vaporisation is endothermic, so energy is taken from the liquid and the cylinder walls, lowering their temperature.
parts.working: M1 liquid vaporises; A1 endothermic — heat absorbed from the cylinder/surroundings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar, but tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is non-polar. Explain this difference in terms of molecular shape.
parts.answer: Both are tetrahedral. In CCl₄ the four identical C–Cl dipoles cancel by symmetry. In CHCl₃ one Cl is replaced by H, so the dipoles no longer cancel and there is a resultant dipole.
parts.working: M1 both tetrahedral; A1 CCl₄ symmetrical so dipoles cancel, CHCl₃ not symmetrical.

parts.label: b
parts.text: CCl₄ (bp 77 °C) boils at a higher temperature than CHCl₃ (bp 61 °C). Explain why, even though only CHCl₃ has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces.
parts.answer: CCl₄ has more electrons (74 compared with 58) and a larger surface, so its instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces are much stronger. This increase in id–id forces outweighs the pd–pd forces in CHCl₃, so overall the forces between CCl₄ molecules are stronger.
parts.working: M1 CCl₄ has more electrons (calculate: 6 + 4 × 17 = 74 vs 6 + 1 + 3 × 17 = 58); M1 stronger id–id forces; A1 id–id forces are the larger contribution here and outweigh the pd–pd forces of CHCl₃.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what this pair of compounds shows about using 'polar molecules have higher boiling points' as a rule.
parts.answer: The rule only works for molecules with similar numbers of electrons; differences in id–id forces can be larger than the effect of a permanent dipole.
parts.working: B1 must compare molecules with similar Mr/number of electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which description of metallic bonding is correct?
A electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons
B electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions
C shared pairs of electrons between neighbouring metal atoms
D attraction between instantaneous dipoles on neighbouring metal atoms
parts.answer: A electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons
parts.working: Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and the 'sea' of delocalised outer electrons. B describes ionic bonding (the main distractor, as both involve electrostatic attraction); C describes localised covalent bonds; D describes id–id forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why can metals be hammered into thin sheets without breaking?
A Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons continue to hold them together.
B The delocalised electrons can move, so they carry the force through the metal.
C Metal atoms are joined by weak covalent bonds that can re-form easily.
D When layers slide, ions of the same charge come next to each other and repel.
parts.answer: A Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons continue to hold them together.
parts.working: Metallic bonding is non-directional: when a layer of cations slides, the delocalised electrons still attract every ion, so the metal changes shape instead of shattering. B links electron mobility to conduction, not malleability. D describes why ionic solids are brittle (main distractor).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is used for decorative handicrafts and door fittings. Explain why pure copper is malleable.
parts.answer: Copper has layers of identical Cu ions in a regular lattice; the layers can slide over one another while the delocalised electrons keep the bonding intact.
parts.working: M1 regular layers of identical ions; A1 layers slide, metallic bonding not broken (non-directional).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why brass is harder than pure copper.
parts.answer: Zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms, so they disrupt the regular layers; the layers cannot slide over each other as easily.
parts.working: M1 atoms/ions of different size; A1 layers distorted, slip is prevented/more difficult.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium chloride shatters when hit with a hammer.
parts.answer: A blow shifts one layer of ions relative to the next, so ions of the same charge are brought next to each other; they repel and the crystal splits.
parts.working: M1 layers of ions displaced; A1 like charges side by side repel → crystal breaks (brittle).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a block of aluminium bends instead of shattering when hit.
parts.answer: Aluminium ions are surrounded by delocalised electrons; when layers move, the ions remain attracted to the electron sea, so no repulsion develops and the metallic bond is not broken.
parts.working: M1 delocalised electrons surround all ions; A1 bonding is non-directional so layers slide without the structure breaking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each aluminium atom releases three electrons into the 'sea' of delocalised electrons. Calculate the number of delocalised electrons in 1.00 g of aluminium. (Ar Al = 27.0; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 6.69 × 10²² electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the charge on the aluminium ions in the metal lattice.
parts.working: B1 Al³⁺ (three electrons delocalised per atom).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why aluminium conducts electricity in both the solid and the liquid state.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure in both states and carry the charge.
parts.working: B1 mobile delocalised electrons present in solid and liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A copper wire used in a household circuit has a diameter of 2.00 mm and a length of 100 m. Calculate the volume of the wire in cm³ (volume = πr²L) and its mass. (density of copper = 8.96 g/cm³) Give each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: volume 314 cm³; mass 2.81 × 10³ g (2810 g)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume each copper atom contributes one electron to the delocalised electrons. Calculate the number of delocalised electrons in the wire. (Ar Cu = 63.5; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what happens to the delocalised electrons when the wire is connected to a battery.
parts.answer: They drift through the lattice towards the positive terminal, carrying the current.
parts.working: B1 electrons move in one direction (towards positive terminal) — a flow of charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gallium melts at about 30 °C but does not boil until about 2400 °C. Suggest why gallium has a very large liquid range.
parts.answer: On melting only some of the metallic bonding is disrupted so the ions can move past one another, but the ions are still held by the delocalised electrons in the liquid. Boiling requires the atoms to be separated completely, breaking all metallic bonding, which needs much more energy.
parts.working: M1 metallic bonding still present in the liquid (ions and delocalised electrons remain); A1 boiling separates atoms completely — far more energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in liquid gallium that allows it to conduct electricity.
parts.answer: Ga³⁺ ions move randomly close together, surrounded by delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 positive ions close together and mobile; B1 delocalised electrons free to move → conduction.

stem: Standard enthalpy changes of atomisation (kJ/mol): sodium +107; magnesium +147; aluminium +326.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of an element.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions.
parts.working: B1 one mole of gaseous atoms formed; B1 from the element in its standard state, standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend in these values from sodium to aluminium.
parts.answer: From Na to Al the ions have a higher charge (1+, 2+, 3+) and are smaller, and there are more delocalised electrons per atom (1, 2, 3); the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the atoms.
parts.working: M1 increasing ionic charge; M1 more delocalised electrons per atom / smaller ions; A1 stronger metallic bonding, more energy to form gaseous atoms.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Densities: sodium 0.97 g/cm³ (Ar 23.0); aluminium 2.70 g/cm³ (Ar 27.0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of atoms in 1.00 cm³ of each metal, and hence the number of delocalised electrons per cm³ in each (sodium releases 1 electron per atom, aluminium 3). (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) Give each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Na: 2.54 × 10²² atoms and 2.54 × 10²² electrons per cm³. Al: 6.02 × 10²² atoms and 1.81 × 10²³ electrons per cm³.
parts.working: M1 Na: 0.97 ÷ 23.0 = 0.0422 mol; A1 2.54 × 10²² (also electrons); M1 Al: 2.70 ÷ 27.0 = 0.100 mol = 6.02 × 10²² atoms; A1 × 3 = 1.81 × 10²³ electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the density of delocalised electrons is in aluminium than in sodium. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.1 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why aluminium is much harder and has a higher melting point (660 °C) than sodium (98 °C).
parts.answer: Aluminium has many more delocalised electrons per unit volume and higher-charged (3+) ions that are packed more closely, so the electrostatic attraction holding the lattice together is much stronger.
parts.working: M1 higher density of delocalised electrons and 3+ ions; A1 stronger metallic bonding needs more energy to disrupt/deform.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Electrical conductivity at 20 °C: copper 5.96 × 10⁷ S m⁻¹ (density 8.96 g/cm³); aluminium 3.77 × 10⁷ S m⁻¹ (density 2.70 g/cm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the conductivity divided by the density for each metal, and hence how many times better aluminium is than copper per gram. Give your final answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Cu 0.665; Al 1.40 (units 10⁷ S m⁻¹ per g cm⁻³); aluminium is 2.1 times better per unit mass

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why high-voltage overhead power lines use aluminium cables (with a steel core) rather than copper, even though copper is the better conductor per unit volume.
parts.answer: For the same mass, aluminium carries about twice the current, so cables are much lighter for long spans between pylons (and aluminium is cheaper); the steel core provides tensile strength.
parts.working: M1 lighter for same conductance / better conductivity per mass; A1 less load on pylons, longer spans (or lower cost); steel adds strength.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Both metals conduct because of delocalised electrons. Suggest one property of copper, other than conductivity, that makes it preferred for wiring inside homes.
parts.answer: More ductile / easily drawn into thin flexible wires that do not break when bent repeatedly (also resists corrosion at joints).
parts.working: B1 any one valid property: ductile, flexible, does not form an insulating oxide layer at connections.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Melting points of some Period 3 elements: Na 98 °C; Mg 650 °C; Al 660 °C; Si 1410 °C; P (white, P₄) 44 °C; S (S₈) 115 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in melting point from sodium to aluminium.
parts.answer: Metallic bonding in all three; from Na to Al the cations have higher charge, are smaller, and there are more delocalised electrons per atom, so the attraction between cations and electrons increases.
parts.working: M1 metallic bonding; A1 increasing charge/more delocalised electrons → stronger attraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why silicon has the highest melting point in the period.
parts.answer: Silicon has a giant covalent lattice in which each atom is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds; melting requires many of these bonds to break.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent structure; B1 many strong covalent bonds must break.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why phosphorus and sulfur have low melting points, and why sulfur's is higher than phosphorus's.
parts.answer: Both are simple molecular (P₄ and S₈); melting overcomes only weak id–id forces between molecules. S₈ has more electrons than P₄, so stronger id–id forces.
parts.working: M1 simple molecules, weak id–id forces only; A1 S₈ larger molecule, more electrons (128 vs 60) → stronger forces.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium melts at 63 °C but calcium, the next element, melts at 842 °C. Write the electronic configuration of the outer shell for each atom and state the number of electrons each atom contributes to the delocalised electrons.
parts.answer: K: 4s¹, contributes 1. Ca: 4s², contributes 2.
parts.working: B1 configurations; B1 1 and 2 electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the large difference in melting point.
parts.answer: Ca²⁺ ions have twice the charge of K⁺ and are smaller (more protons for the same shells), and there are twice as many delocalised electrons per ion; so the electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalised electrons is much stronger in calcium, and more energy is needed to break down the lattice.
parts.working: M1 Ca²⁺ higher charge; M1 Ca²⁺ smaller ionic radius / more delocalised electrons; A1 stronger metallic bonding → much higher mp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, which metal is the better electrical conductor per atom.
parts.answer: Calcium — it provides two delocalised electrons per atom, compared with one for potassium.
parts.working: B1 calcium, more delocalised electrons per atom (accept a reasoned answer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride, NaCl. Show outer-shell electrons only and give the charge on each ion.
parts.answer: Na⁺: empty outer shell shown (or the full 2,8 shell with no outer electrons) in square brackets with + charge. Cl⁻: eight electrons in the outer shell, seven dots and one cross (the cross is the electron transferred from Na), in square brackets with − charge.
parts.working: B1 sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine; B1 Cl⁻ shown with 8 outer electrons (7 of one symbol, 1 of the other); B1 square brackets and charges 1+ and 1−.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the electronic configurations of the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
parts.answer: Na⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Cl⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for methane, CH₄. Show outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: C at the centre with four shared pairs, one to each H; each pair is one dot (from C) and one cross (from H); C has 8 outer electrons, no lone pairs; each H has 2.
parts.working: B1 four bonding pairs, each one electron from C and one from H; B1 no lone pairs on C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for ammonia, NH₃, and state the numbers of bonding pairs and lone pairs on nitrogen.
parts.answer: N with three shared pairs (one dot from N + one cross from H in each) and one lone pair of two dots from N. 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair.
parts.working: B1 three bonding pairs; B1 one lone pair (both electrons from N); B1 N has 8 outer electrons in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide. Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram of the ions in magnesium oxide, showing outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ in square brackets, with no outer-shell electrons shown (outer shell now the full second shell), charge 2+. O²⁻ in square brackets with 8 outer electrons: 6 dots of oxygen and 2 crosses transferred from Mg, charge 2−.
parts.working: B1 two electrons transferred from Mg to O; B1 O²⁻ shown with 8 outer electrons (6 + 2 distinguished); B1 brackets and charges 2+ and 2−.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons in one Mg²⁺ ion and in one O²⁻ ion.
parts.working: B1 12 − 2 = 10; B1 8 + 2 = 10 (the ions are isoelectronic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen chloride, HCl. Show outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: One shared pair between H and Cl (one dot from H, one cross from Cl); three lone pairs on Cl (all crosses).
parts.working: B1 one bonding pair with one electron from each atom; B1 three lone pairs on Cl.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for water, H₂O. State the numbers of bonding pairs and lone pairs on the oxygen atom.
parts.answer: O shares one pair with each H (one electron from O, one from H); O also has two lone pairs. 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs.
parts.working: B1 two bonding pairs; B1 two lone pairs on O.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the formula of water is H₂O and not HO, using electron pairs.
parts.answer: Oxygen has six outer electrons and needs two more to complete its octet, so it forms two shared pairs, one with each of two H atoms.
parts.working: B1 O needs two electrons → two covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in a molecule of ethene, C₂H₄.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for ethene. Show outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: Two shared pairs (a double bond) between the carbon atoms, each pair made of one electron from each C; each C shares one pair with each of two H atoms; no lone pairs; each C has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 C=C shown as two shared pairs; B1 two C–H shared pairs on each carbon; B1 no lone pairs / octet on each C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of bonding pairs in the molecule and check that it agrees with your answer to (a).
parts.answer: 6 bonding pairs = 12 electrons
parts.working: B1 4 C–H + 2 in C=C = 6 pairs, 6 × 2 = 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium fluoride, CaF₂, occurs as the mineral fluorite. Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why its formula is CaF₂.
parts.answer: A calcium atom loses its two outer electrons; each fluorine atom gains only one electron; so two fluorine atoms are needed for each calcium atom.
parts.working: M1 Ca loses 2 electrons (forms Ca²⁺); A1 each F gains 1 (forms F⁻), so 2 F per Ca.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for calcium fluoride, showing outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: [Ca]²⁺ with no outer electrons shown; two separate [F]⁻ ions, each with 8 outer electrons: 7 of the fluorine's own symbol and 1 of calcium's symbol.
parts.working: B1 Ca²⁺ in brackets, 2+; B1 two F⁻ ions, each 7 + 1 electrons; B1 brackets and 1− charges.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the full electronic configuration of the Ca²⁺ ion.
parts.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for the hydroxide ion, OH⁻. Show outer-shell electrons only.
parts.answer: O and H share one pair (one electron from each); O has three lone pairs; one electron on O is the extra electron that gives the negative charge (shown with a different symbol); square brackets with − charge.
parts.working: B1 one O–H shared pair; B1 three lone pairs on O (8 electrons around O); B1 the additional electron identified, bracket and 1− charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in the hydroxide ion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the hydroxide ion can act as a base (proton acceptor).
parts.answer: The O atom has lone pairs that can form a bond with an H⁺ ion (forming H₂O).
parts.working: B1 lone pair on O donated to H⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂ (H–O–O–H), is used as a mild disinfectant for cuts. Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in one molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for H₂O₂ and state the total numbers of bonding pairs and lone pairs.
parts.answer: One shared pair between the two O atoms (one electron from each); each O shares one pair with an H; each O has two lone pairs. 3 bonding pairs and 4 lone pairs.
parts.working: B1 O–O single shared pair; B1 each O bonded to one H; B1 two lone pairs on each O: 3 bp, 4 lp in total.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Check your answer to (b) against your answer to (a).
parts.answer: (3 + 4) × 2 = 14 electrons
parts.working: B1 7 pairs × 2 = 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N. Show outer-shell electrons only and state the number of lone pairs.
parts.answer: H shares one pair with C; C and N share three pairs (each pair one electron from C and one from N); N has one lone pair. 1 lone pair.
parts.working: B1 one H–C shared pair; B1 three shared pairs between C and N; B1 one lone pair on N, none on C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethyne, H–C≡C–H, has the same total number of outer-shell electrons as hydrogen cyanide. Calculate this number and explain why ethyne has no lone pairs.
parts.answer: 10. In ethyne all five pairs are bonding pairs (two C–H and three C–C); in HCN, N has one more outer electron than C, which with its own electron forms the lone pair.
parts.working: B1 10 (2 × 4 + 2 = 10; 1 + 4 + 5 = 10); B1 all ten electrons are in bonds in ethyne / each C uses all four electrons in bonding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In phosphorus(V) chloride gas, PCl₅, the phosphorus atom forms five single bonds. Calculate the number of electrons in the outer shell of phosphorus in PCl₅.
parts.working: 5 bonding pairs × 2 = 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for PCl₅ and state the total number of outer-shell electrons in the molecule.
parts.answer: P at centre with five shared pairs, each made of one P electron and one Cl electron; no lone pairs on P; each Cl has three lone pairs. Total outer electrons = 5 + 5 × 7 = 40.
parts.working: B1 five P–Cl shared pairs (one electron from each atom); B1 three lone pairs on each Cl, none on P; B1 40.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why phosphorus can have more than eight electrons in its outer shell but nitrogen cannot (NCl₅ does not exist).
parts.answer: Phosphorus is in Period 3 and has available 3d orbitals / its n = 3 shell can hold more than 8 electrons, and the atom is large enough to fit five Cl atoms around it; nitrogen's outer shell (n = 2) holds a maximum of 8 electrons.
parts.working: M1 P has a third shell with d orbitals available (can expand its octet); A1 N's second shell has only s and p orbitals, max 8 electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen monoxide, NO, forms in car engines. Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in an NO molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is impossible for both atoms in NO to have a full octet.
parts.answer: The total number of outer electrons is odd, so the electrons cannot all be paired; at least one atom must have an unpaired electron (and fewer than 8 electrons).
parts.working: M1 odd number of electrons; A1 one electron unpaired, so one atom has 7 outer electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A simple dot-and-cross diagram of NO shows a double bond between N and O. Describe this diagram, giving the lone pairs on each atom and the unpaired electron.
parts.answer: Two shared pairs between N and O; O has two lone pairs (8 electrons); N has one lone pair and one unpaired electron (7 electrons).
parts.working: B1 N=O double bond with two lone pairs on O; B1 N has one lone pair plus a single unpaired electron.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what name is given to a species such as NO, and why it is reactive.
parts.answer: A free radical; the unpaired electron readily pairs up with an electron from another species.
parts.working: B1 free radical, with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in sulfur dioxide, SO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one model, sulfur forms a double bond to each oxygen atom. Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for this model and state how many electrons are in the outer shell of sulfur.
parts.answer: S shares two pairs with each O (two double bonds); S has one lone pair; each O has two lone pairs. Sulfur has 4 × 2 + 2 = 10 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 two S=O double bonds; B1 one lone pair on S and two on each O; B1 10 electrons around S (an expanded octet).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Check that your diagram uses all the electrons from (a), and use it to predict the shape of SO₂.
parts.answer: 4 shared pairs + 5 lone pairs (1 on S, 2 on each O) = 9 pairs = 18 electrons. S has three regions of electron density (two double bonds and a lone pair), so SO₂ is bent (just under 120°).
parts.working: B1 9 pairs × 2 = 18; B1 bent/V-shaped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for boron trifluoride, BF₃, showing outer-shell electrons only. State the number of electrons in the outer shell of boron.
parts.answer: B shares one pair with each of the three F atoms (one electron from B and one from F); each F has three lone pairs; B has no lone pair and only 6 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 three B–F shared pairs; B1 three lone pairs on each F; B1 boron has 6 outer electrons (incomplete octet).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Beryllium chloride molecules, BeCl₂, exist in the gas phase. State the number of outer-shell electrons around beryllium.
parts.working: Two shared pairs = 4 electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why molecules such as BF₃ and BeCl₂ are described as 'electron-deficient', and predict how BF₃ reacts with a fluoride ion.
parts.answer: Their central atoms have fewer than eight outer electrons (empty orbitals), so they can accept a lone pair. BF₃ accepts a lone pair from F⁻ to form BF₄⁻ (a dative bond), giving B a full octet.
parts.working: M1 fewer than 8 electrons, can accept a lone pair; A1 BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻ (dative bond).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule CANNOT act as the electron-pair donor in a dative covalent bond?
A CH₄
B NH₃
C H₂O
D CO
parts.answer: A CH₄
parts.working: A donor needs a lone pair. CH₄ has none: all four carbon outer electrons are in C–H bonds. NH₃ (one lone pair on N), H₂O (two on O) and CO (a lone pair on C, which is how CO binds to iron in haemoglobin) can all donate. CO is the likely distractor because it already contains a dative bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen chloride to form ammonium chloride. Which statement about the ammonium ion formed is correct?
A All four N–H bonds are identical, and the H–N–H bond angle is 109.5°.
B The dative N–H bond is longer than the other three, and the ion is pyramidal.
C The nitrogen atom still has one lone pair, and the H–N–H bond angle is 107°.
D The hydrogen atom donates an electron pair to the nitrogen atom.
parts.answer: A All four N–H bonds are identical, and the H–N–H bond angle is 109.5°.
parts.working: N donates its lone pair to H⁺; once formed, the dative bond is identical to the other three N–H bonds, giving a regular tetrahedron (109.5°). C describes ammonia before reaction (main distractor). D reverses the donor and acceptor; H⁺ has no electrons to donate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a dative covalent (co-ordinate) bond.
parts.answer: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom.
parts.working: B1 shared pair of electrons, both provided by one atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how an ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, forms from an ammonia molecule and a hydrogen ion. Identify the donor and acceptor.
parts.answer: The lone pair on the nitrogen atom of NH₃ is donated into the empty 1s orbital of H⁺ to form a fourth N–H bond. N (NH₃) is the donor; H⁺ is the acceptor.
parts.working: M1 lone pair on N donated to H⁺; A1 donor N / acceptor H⁺ (H⁺ has an empty orbital).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe, in words, how the dative bond is usually shown in a displayed formula.
parts.answer: As an arrow pointing from the donor atom (N) to the acceptor atom (H).
parts.working: B1 arrow from N to H.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When hydrogen chloride dissolves in water, oxonium ions, H₃O⁺, form. Describe how the dative bond in H₃O⁺ forms.
parts.answer: One of the two lone pairs on the O atom of a water molecule is donated to an H⁺ ion, forming a third O–H bond.
parts.working: M1 lone pair on oxygen of H₂O; A1 donated to H⁺ (empty orbital).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of lone pairs on the oxygen atom in H₃O⁺ and give the shape of the ion.
parts.answer: 1 lone pair; pyramidal
parts.working: B1 one lone pair (two before − one used); B1 pyramidal (3 bp + 1 lp), about 107°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons (not just outer electrons) in one H₃O⁺ ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon monoxide is a dangerous product of incomplete combustion from badly ventilated gas heaters. The CO molecule has a triple bond, one of which is a dative bond from oxygen to carbon. Calculate the number of electrons in the outer shell of each atom in CO.
parts.working: B1 C: three shared pairs (6) + one lone pair (2) = 8; B1 O: three shared pairs (6) + one lone pair (2) = 8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which atom provides both electrons for the dative bond and why this is possible.
parts.answer: Oxygen. O has six outer electrons; after forming two normal shared pairs with C it still has two lone pairs, so it can donate one lone pair to carbon, which needs two more electrons to complete its octet.
parts.working: M1 oxygen donates; A1 O has a lone pair available and C has only 6 outer electrons after two normal bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Carbon monoxide is toxic because it bonds strongly to the Fe²⁺ ion in haemoglobin through the lone pair on its carbon atom. Name the type of bond formed between CO and Fe²⁺.
parts.answer: dative covalent (co-ordinate) bond
parts.working: B1 C donates a lone pair to Fe²⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ozone, O₃, in the upper atmosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation. One simple model of ozone has an O=O double bond and a dative bond from the central oxygen atom to the third oxygen atom. Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in O₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for this model of ozone. Give the number of lone pairs on each oxygen atom.
parts.answer: End O (double bond): two shared pairs with the central O, 2 lone pairs. Central O: 2 shared pairs to the first O, a dative pair (both its own electrons) to the third O, 1 lone pair. Third O: receives the dative pair, 3 lone pairs.
parts.working: B1 O=O double bond with two lone pairs on that terminal O; B1 dative O→O bond from the central O, which keeps one lone pair; B1 terminal O on the dative bond has three lone pairs. Check: 3 bonding pairs + 6 lone pairs = 9 pairs = 18 electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your diagram to predict whether ozone is linear or bent.
parts.answer: Bent — the central O has three regions of electron density including a lone pair.
parts.working: B1 bent (about 117°; accept 'just under 120°').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boron trifluoride reacts with a fluoride ion to form the tetrafluoroborate ion: BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻. Explain how the new bond forms, naming the type of bond.
parts.answer: A dative covalent bond: F⁻ donates one of its lone pairs into the empty orbital of the boron atom, which has only 6 outer electrons in BF₃.
parts.working: M1 lone pair from F⁻ donated; A1 to boron's vacant orbital (electron-deficient B) — dative bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the shape and F–B–F bond angle of BF₃ and of BF₄⁻.
parts.answer: BF₃ trigonal planar, 120°; BF₄⁻ tetrahedral, 109.5°
parts.working: B1 each species.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of outer-shell electrons around boron in BF₄⁻ and explain why all four B–F bonds in BF₄⁻ have the same length.
parts.answer: 8. Once formed, the dative bond is identical to the other bonds (a shared pair is a shared pair, whichever atom supplied it), so all four B–F bonds are equivalent.
parts.working: B1 8; B1 dative bond indistinguishable from the others once formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When aluminium chloride dissolves in water, the Al³⁺ ion becomes surrounded by six water molecules to form [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺. Describe the bonding between each water molecule and the Al³⁺ ion.
parts.answer: Dative covalent bonds: each water molecule donates a lone pair from its oxygen atom into an empty orbital of Al³⁺.
parts.working: M1 lone pair on O of water; A1 donated to Al³⁺ — dative bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of dative bonds in one [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ion, its shape and the O–Al–O bond angle.
parts.answer: 6 dative bonds; octahedral; 90°
parts.working: B1 six; B1 octahedral; B1 90°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons that the six water molecules donate to the aluminium ion.
parts.working: 6 bonds × 2 electrons = 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of lone pairs on a nitrogen atom in NH₃, on an oxygen atom in H₂O and on a fluorine atom in HF.
parts.answer: N in NH₃: 1; O in H₂O: 2; F in HF: 3
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student claims that HF should be the best electron-pair donor because the fluorine atom has the most lone pairs. Suggest why ammonia is in fact the best donor of the three.
parts.answer: Nitrogen is the least electronegative of N, O and F, so it holds its lone pair least tightly; the lone pair is more available to be donated. Fluorine holds its lone pairs very strongly.
parts.working: M1 N is less electronegative/has lower nuclear charge; A1 its lone pair is held less tightly and is more easily donated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of the ion formed when each of NH₃ and H₂O accepts a proton.
parts.answer: NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitric acid, HNO₃, has an H–O–N group, an N=O double bond and an N→O dative bond. Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in an HNO₃ molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for HNO₃. Show the dative bond and give the number of lone pairs on each oxygen atom.
parts.answer: O of the OH group: one pair shared with H, one with N, 2 lone pairs. O of N=O: two pairs shared with N, 2 lone pairs. O of the dative bond: receives a lone pair from N, 3 lone pairs. N: one single bond, one double bond and the dative pair, no lone pair (8 electrons).
parts.working: B1 H–O–N with two lone pairs on that O; B1 N=O with two lone pairs on O; B1 N→O dative bond from N's lone pair, that O has three lone pairs; B1 N has 8 outer electrons and no lone pair.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Check the total number of electrons in your diagram.
parts.answer: 5 bonding pairs (H–O, O–N, 2 in N=O, N→O) + 7 lone pairs = 12 pairs = 24 electrons
parts.working: B1 consistent count.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.400 g of aluminium bromide vapour occupies 34.3 cm³ at 550 K and 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the relative molecular mass of the vapour. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Mr of AlBr₃ is 266.7. Deduce the formula of the molecules in the vapour.
parts.answer: Al₂Br₆
parts.working: 533 ÷ 266.7 = 2.00, so dimers Al₂Br₆.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how two AlBr₃ units join together, and state the number of dative bonds in each molecule.
parts.answer: In AlBr₃, Al has only 6 outer electrons. A bromine atom of one AlBr₃ donates a lone pair to the Al atom of the other, and vice versa, forming two Br→Al dative bonds (bridging Br atoms). Each Al then has 8 outer electrons and is roughly tetrahedral.
parts.working: M1 Al electron-deficient (6 outer electrons); M1 lone pair on a Br atom donated to Al of other unit; A1 two dative bonds per dimer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonium chloride is used in dry cells and as a flux in soldering. Name the three types of bonding present in solid NH₄Cl and say where each is found.
parts.answer: Ionic bonding: between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Covalent bonds: three N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ (normal shared pairs). Dative covalent bond: the fourth N–H bond, where N supplied both electrons.
parts.working: B1 ionic between ions; B1 covalent N–H; B1 dative N→H (only one, but all four N–H bonds become identical).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons in one NH₄⁺ ion and in one Cl⁻ ion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When heated, solid NH₄Cl gives off NH₃ and HCl gases, which recombine as white smoke on the cooler part of the tube. Explain which bond is broken in the ammonium ion during this change.
parts.answer: One N–H bond breaks so that both its electrons stay with N (giving NH₃ with its lone pair back) and the H⁺ is transferred to Cl⁻ (giving HCl).
parts.working: B1 an N–H bond breaks heterolytically, the electron pair returning to N as a lone pair; proton passes to chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphine, PH₃, reacts with hydrogen iodide to form phosphonium iodide, PH₄I, which contains the PH₄⁺ ion. Explain how PH₄⁺ is formed and identify the dative bond.
parts.answer: PH₃ has a lone pair on P (P has 5 outer electrons, 3 used in bonding). This lone pair is donated to H⁺ from HI, forming a dative P→H bond.
parts.working: M1 lone pair on P donated; A1 to H⁺ — dative bond P→H.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape and bond angle of PH₄⁺.
parts.answer: tetrahedral; 109.5°
parts.working: B1 four bonding pairs, no lone pair → tetrahedral; B1 109.5°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Phosphine is a much weaker base than ammonia. Suggest one reason, in terms of the lone pair.
parts.answer: P is a larger atom, so its lone pair is more spread out (less concentrated/lower electron density) and is less effective at bonding to H⁺.
parts.working: B1 lone pair on larger P is more diffuse / in a larger orbital, less available for donation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in the PH₄⁺ ion.
parts.working: 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 (four bonding pairs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Marble workshops use saw blades tipped with small diamonds. Describe the structure of diamond.
parts.answer: A giant covalent lattice in which every carbon atom is bonded covalently to four other carbon atoms arranged tetrahedrally.
parts.working: B1 giant (covalent) lattice; B1 each C bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral (109.5°).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point.
parts.answer: Every atom is held in place by strong covalent bonds in three dimensions; a very large number of these bonds must be broken to scratch or melt it.
parts.working: M1 strong covalent bonds throughout in 3D; A1 many bonds must break — lots of energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: All four outer electrons of each carbon are used in localised covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons or ions to carry charge.
parts.working: B1 no delocalised/mobile electrons (all in bonds).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of graphite.
parts.answer: Flat layers of carbon atoms in hexagonal rings; each C is covalently bonded to three others; one electron per carbon is delocalised across the layer; layers are held together by weak intermolecular (van der Waals') forces.
parts.working: B1 layers of hexagons, each C bonded to 3; B1 delocalised electrons within layers; B1 weak forces between layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pencil 'lead' is mostly graphite mixed with clay. Explain why graphite leaves a mark on paper.
parts.answer: The weak forces between layers allow layers to slide off easily and stick to the paper.
parts.working: B1 layers slide/flake off because of weak forces between layers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why graphite can be used as a dry lubricant in locks.
parts.answer: The layers slide over each other easily, reducing friction, and graphite is solid so it does not run out of the lock.
parts.working: B1 layers slide easily (weak interlayer forces).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon is used to make solar cells. Silicon has the same structure as diamond. Describe this structure and give the bond angle around each silicon atom.
parts.answer: Giant covalent lattice with each Si atom bonded to four other Si atoms, tetrahedral; bond angle 109.5°.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent, each Si bonded to 4; B1 109.5°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Silicon melts at 1410 °C, but diamond does not melt until above 3500 °C. Suggest why silicon has the lower melting point.
parts.answer: Silicon atoms are larger than carbon atoms, so Si–Si bonds are longer and weaker than C–C bonds; less energy is needed to break them.
parts.working: M1 larger atoms/longer bonds; A1 weaker covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In diamond, each carbon atom forms four C–C bonds, but each bond is shared between two atoms. Show that there are 2 mol of C–C bonds per mole of carbon atoms.
parts.answer: 4 bonds per atom ÷ 2 atoms per bond = 2 bonds per atom

parts.label: b
parts.text: A diamond in a ring has a mass of 3.00 carats (1 carat = 0.200 g). Calculate the amount of carbon atoms in the diamond, in mol. (Ar C = 12.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of C–C bonds in the diamond. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 6.02 × 10²² bonds

parts.label: a
parts.text: The C–C bond length in diamond is 0.154 nm, but the C–C bond length within a layer of graphite is 0.142 nm. Explain why the bonds in a graphite layer are shorter.
parts.answer: In graphite each carbon forms three σ bonds and its fourth electron joins a delocalised π system over the layer, giving each C–C bond some double-bond character; the extra electron density between the atoms pulls them closer.
parts.working: M1 delocalised electrons add bonding between atoms within layers; A1 bonds are between single and double (partial double bond character), so shorter/stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The distance between neighbouring layers in graphite is 0.335 nm. Use this value to explain why graphite is soft and has a much lower density than diamond.
parts.answer: The layers are far apart compared with bond lengths (0.335 vs 0.142 nm), showing they are held only by weak forces and not covalent bonds, so they slide easily (soft). The large gaps between layers mean the atoms are less closely packed, so graphite has a lower density.
parts.working: M1 interlayer distance much larger than a covalent bond length; M1 only weak forces between layers → layers slide → soft; A1 atoms less closely packed → lower density.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick. Using your knowledge of graphite, explain why graphene conducts electricity.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom is bonded to three others and has one delocalised electron; the delocalised electrons can move across the sheet and carry charge.
parts.working: M1 one electron per C delocalised; A1 free to move through the layer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Graphene is extremely strong when it is stretched, but a lump of graphite is weak and flaky. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: Within the sheet every atom is held by strong covalent bonds (plus delocalised bonding), so the sheet is very strong; graphite breaks easily because the layers are held to each other only by weak forces and slide apart.
