parts.working: M1 strong covalent bonding within the layer; A1 graphite fails between layers (weak forces), not within a layer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the C–C–C bond angle in graphene and the hybridisation of each carbon atom.
parts.working: B1 120° (hexagonal, trigonal planar); B1 sp².

stem: Densities: graphite 2.26 g/cm³; diamond 3.51 g/cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume occupied by one mole of carbon atoms in graphite and in diamond. Give your answers in cm³ to 3 significant figures. (Ar C = 12.0)
parts.answer: graphite 5.31 cm³; diamond 3.42 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of structure, why diamond is denser than graphite.
parts.answer: In diamond every atom is bonded to four neighbours in a compact three-dimensional network. In graphite there is a large space between the layers, so the same number of atoms takes up more volume.
parts.working: M1 graphite layers far apart (0.335 nm gaps); A1 diamond's 3D tetrahedral network packs atoms more closely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Diamond can be made from graphite using very high pressure. Suggest why high pressure favours the formation of diamond.
parts.answer: Diamond occupies a smaller volume for the same mass, so high pressure favours the denser, smaller-volume form.
parts.working: B1 diamond has smaller molar volume; pressure favours smaller volume.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon carbide, SiC, is used as an abrasive in grinding wheels and does not melt below about 2700 °C. Suggest the structure of silicon carbide and describe how the atoms are arranged.
parts.answer: Giant covalent lattice similar to diamond: each Si atom bonded covalently to four C atoms and each C atom to four Si atoms, arranged tetrahedrally.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent; B1 each atom bonded to four of the other element; B1 tetrahedral arrangement (109.5°).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why silicon carbide is suitable as an abrasive.
parts.answer: It is extremely hard because strong covalent bonds extend in three dimensions; it can scratch and grind softer materials without wearing away quickly.
parts.working: M1 very hard; A1 due to strong covalent bonds throughout the 3D lattice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether silicon carbide conducts electricity well.
parts.answer: No (at most a poor semiconductor) — all outer electrons are in localised covalent bonds.
parts.working: B1 poor conductor, no delocalised electrons.

stem:
Data for five solids:
A: mp 2076 °C; does not conduct as solid or liquid; insoluble in water.
B: mp 772 °C; conducts only when molten or dissolved; soluble in water.
C: mp 114 °C; does not conduct; dissolves in hexane.
D: sublimes at about 3650 °C; conducts as a solid; insoluble in all solvents.
E: mp 1535 °C; conducts as solid and liquid; insoluble in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the TWO substances that have giant covalent structures.
parts.answer: A and D
parts.working: B1 each. A: very high mp, insoluble, non-conductor. D: very high mp, conducts as solid (graphite-like). (B is ionic: conducts when molten; C is simple molecular; E is metallic.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how substance D can conduct electricity as a solid even though it has a giant covalent structure.
parts.answer: It has delocalised electrons (as in graphite), which can move through the structure.
parts.working: B1 delocalised electrons in layers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the structure of substance B and explain the conductivity data.
parts.answer: Giant ionic. Ions cannot move in the solid, but are free to move when molten.
parts.working: B1 giant ionic; B1 ions mobile only when molten.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Standard enthalpy changes of atomisation: diamond +714.8 kJ/mol; graphite +716.7 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When diamond is atomised, each atom breaks 2 C–C bonds (each bond shared by two atoms). Calculate the average energy needed per C–C bond in diamond. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 357 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: In graphite each carbon atom forms three bonds within its layer, each shared by two atoms. Ignoring the weak forces between layers, calculate the average energy per C–C bond in graphite. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 478 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bonds in a graphite layer are stronger than the bonds in diamond.
parts.answer: In graphite the fourth electron of each carbon is delocalised over the layer, adding π bonding between neighbouring atoms, so each bond is partly a double bond; diamond has only C–C single (σ) bonds.
parts.working: M1 delocalised π electrons within layer; A1 bond order between 1 and 2 (stronger, shorter than a single bond).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the enthalpies of atomisation of diamond and graphite are almost the same even though the individual bonds differ in strength.
parts.answer: Diamond has more bonds per atom (2) but each is weaker; graphite has fewer bonds per atom (1.5) but each is stronger, so the total energy per mole of atoms is similar.
parts.working: B1 more but weaker bonds vs fewer but stronger bonds.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single crystal of graphite conducts electricity thousands of times better along the layers than at right angles to them. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are confined to each layer (in the π system formed from p orbitals within the layer), so they move freely along the layer. Between layers there is no delocalised bonding — the layers are 0.335 nm apart and held only by weak forces — so electrons cannot easily move from one layer to the next.
parts.working: M1 delocalised electrons in each layer; M1 free movement along layers; A1 large gap/no overlap between layers, so very little conduction perpendicular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Diamond is a very good conductor of heat but not of electricity. Suggest how heat can travel through diamond without delocalised electrons.
parts.answer: Vibrations of the atoms are passed very efficiently from one atom to the next through the rigid network of strong covalent bonds.
parts.working: M1 lattice vibrations; A1 transmitted through stiff, strong covalent bonds in all directions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexagonal boron nitride, BN, has a layered structure like graphite, with alternating B and N atoms in hexagonal rings. Calculate the total number of electrons in the outer shells of one B atom and one N atom, and compare with two C atoms.
parts.answer: B + N = 3 + 5 = 8; two C atoms = 8 (the same)
parts.working: B1 3 + 5 = 8 = 2 × 4 (BN is isoelectronic with C₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why hexagonal boron nitride is used as a lubricant at high temperatures.
parts.answer: Like graphite, its layers are held by weak forces and slide over each other; the strong covalent bonds within layers make it stable at high temperature.
parts.working: B1 layers slide easily (weak forces between layers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Unlike graphite, hexagonal boron nitride is an electrical insulator. Suggest an explanation in terms of electronegativity.
parts.answer: N is much more electronegative than B, so the electrons in the layer (including the π electrons from N's lone pair) are held mostly on the N atoms rather than being spread evenly; they are not free to move through the layer.
parts.working: M1 large electronegativity difference between B and N; A1 electrons localised on N atoms, not delocalised/mobile.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the B–N–B bond angle in a layer.
parts.working: B1 planar hexagons, 120°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a graphene sheet each carbon atom is shared by three hexagons. Show that there are, on average, 2 carbon atoms per hexagon.
parts.answer: 6 atoms per hexagon × 1/3 share each = 2

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of graphene has a mass of 0.0240 g. Calculate the number of hexagons in the sample. (Ar C = 12.0; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 6.02 × 10²⁰ hexagons

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each carbon in graphene forms three bonds, each shared by two atoms. Calculate the number of C–C σ bonds per hexagon.
parts.working: 2 atoms × 3 bonds ÷ 2 = 3 (or 6 bonds per hexagon, each shared by 2 hexagons).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the TWO conditions needed for hydrogen bonding between molecules of a substance.
parts.answer: A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom (N, O or F); a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule.
parts.working: B1 H attached to N, O or F (gives δ+ H); B1 lone pair on N/O/F of another molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these substances form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules? CH₃OH, CH₃OCH₃, NH₃, CH₄, HF, CH₃CHO
parts.answer: CH₃OH, NH₃ and HF
parts.working: 3 marks for all three and no extras; −1 for each error. CH₃OCH₃ and CH₃CHO have O lone pairs but no H on O; CH₄ has no N/O/F.

stem: Boiling points of the Group 15 hydrides: NH₃ −33 °C; PH₃ −88 °C; AsH₃ −62 °C; SbH₃ −17 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the boiling points increase from PH₃ to SbH₃.
parts.answer: The molecules have more electrons from PH₃ to SbH₃, so the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.
parts.working: M1 more electrons/larger molecules; A1 stronger id–id forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ammonia has a higher boiling point than phosphine even though it has fewer electrons.
parts.answer: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds: N is small and very electronegative, so the N–H hydrogen atoms are δ+ and are attracted to the lone pair on the N atom of a neighbouring molecule. P is much less electronegative, so PH₃ cannot hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than id–id forces, so more energy is needed to separate NH₃ molecules.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonding between NH₃ molecules; B1 δ+ H on N attracted to lone pair on N of another molecule (N very electronegative; P is not, so no hydrogen bonding in PH₃); B1 hydrogen bonds stronger than id–id forces → more energy needed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol is completely miscible with water, but hexane does not mix with water. Explain why ethanol dissolves in water.
parts.answer: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their O–H groups; these new hydrogen bonds replace those broken in the pure liquids.
parts.working: M1 hydrogen bonds between ethanol and water; A1 energy released compensates for bonds broken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hexane does not dissolve in water.
parts.answer: Hexane cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; the water molecules would have to break their strong hydrogen bonds to make room for hexane molecules, and only weak id–id forces would form instead.
parts.working: M1 hexane non-polar / no hydrogen bonding with water; A1 not enough energy released to break water's hydrogen bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glycerol, propane-1,2,3-triol (HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH), is used in cough syrups and soaps. State the number of O–H groups in a glycerol molecule and in a propan-1-ol molecule.
parts.answer: glycerol 3; propan-1-ol 1
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glycerol boils at 290 °C, propan-1-ol at 97 °C. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Each glycerol molecule has three O–H groups, so it forms many more hydrogen bonds with its neighbours; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: M1 more O–H groups → more hydrogen bonds per molecule; A1 stronger overall intermolecular attraction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why glycerol is a thick, viscous liquid at room temperature.
parts.answer: Extensive hydrogen bonding holds the molecules together, so they do not flow past one another easily.
parts.working: B1 many hydrogen bonds between molecules resist flow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of water molecules in ice.
parts.answer: Each water molecule is hydrogen bonded to four others arranged tetrahedrally, forming an open three-dimensional lattice with large spaces.
parts.working: B1 each molecule hydrogen bonded to four others (tetrahedral); B1 open structure with spaces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The density of ice is 0.917 g/cm³ and the density of liquid water at 0 °C is 1.000 g/cm³. Calculate the increase in volume when 1.00 kg of water freezes. Give your answer in cm³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 90.5 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Water pipes sometimes burst during cold winters in Murree. Use your answers to explain why.
parts.answer: When water freezes the open hydrogen-bonded lattice takes up about 9 % more volume, and the expanding ice pushes on the pipe walls until they crack.
parts.working: B1 expansion on freezing due to the open structure of ice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Urea, (NH₂)₂CO, is a very soluble fertiliser. State the number of hydrogen atoms in a urea molecule that can act as hydrogen-bond donors (δ+ H atoms bonded to N, O or F), and name the atom whose lone pairs are the best hydrogen-bond acceptor.
parts.answer: 4 hydrogen atoms (all on N); the oxygen atom of C=O
parts.working: B1 4 N–H hydrogens; B1 carbonyl oxygen (δ−, two lone pairs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why urea is very soluble in water.
parts.answer: Urea forms many hydrogen bonds with water molecules: its N–H hydrogens bond to the O of water, and water's H atoms bond to the O (and N) lone pairs of urea.
parts.working: M1 hydrogen bonds formed between urea and water; A1 both directions — urea donates (N–H) and accepts (C=O lone pairs).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe, in words, a hydrogen bond between the C=O group of urea and a water molecule. Include the partial charges and the bond angle at hydrogen.
parts.answer: A δ+ H atom of water is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− O of urea's C=O group; the O–H···O atoms lie in a straight line (about 180°).
parts.working: B1 δ+ H of water to lone pair on δ− O of urea; B1 linear, 180° at H.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butan-1-ol (bp 118 °C) and ethoxyethane, CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ (bp 35 °C), both have the formula C₄H₁₀O. Explain the difference in their boiling points.
parts.answer: Butan-1-ol molecules have an O–H group and form hydrogen bonds with each other. Ethoxyethane has no H attached to O, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other — only pd–pd and id–id forces. Hydrogen bonds are stronger, so butan-1-ol needs more energy to boil.
parts.working: B1 butan-1-ol hydrogen bonds (O–H); B1 ethoxyethane: no O–H, only pd–pd/id–id; B1 similar number of electrons, so the difference is due to hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethoxyethane dissolves in water to a small extent, even though it cannot form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules. Explain how it can form hydrogen bonds with water.
parts.answer: The O atom of ethoxyethane has lone pairs and is δ−, so it can accept a hydrogen bond from a δ+ H atom of a water molecule.
parts.working: M1 lone pairs on O of ether; A1 accepts a hydrogen bond from water's H.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a demonstration, a dry flask of ammonia gas is connected to a tube dipping into water. When a few drops of water enter the flask, water rushes up the tube as a fountain. Explain why ammonia is so soluble in water.
parts.answer: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with water molecules: N–H hydrogens bond to O lone pairs of water, and water's H atoms bond to the lone pair on N.
parts.working: M1 hydrogen bonding between NH₃ and H₂O; A1 described in at least one direction with correct atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water rushes into the flask.
parts.answer: Ammonia dissolves so quickly that the pressure in the flask falls; atmospheric pressure pushes water up the tube.
parts.working: B1 pressure drop in the flask as gas dissolves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why methane would not produce a fountain in the same experiment.
parts.answer: Methane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so it is almost insoluble.
parts.working: B1 no hydrogen bonding/non-polar → insoluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is used in nail-polish remover and mixes completely with water. Explain why propanone molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other.
parts.answer: None of its hydrogen atoms is bonded to N, O or F; all are bonded to carbon, so none is sufficiently δ+.
parts.working: B1 no H on an electronegative atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how propanone can form hydrogen bonds with water.
parts.answer: The O of the C=O group carries a δ− charge and has lone pairs; a δ+ H of water is attracted to one of these lone pairs.
parts.working: M1 δ− O with lone pairs in C=O; A1 accepts a hydrogen bond from H of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Propanone (bp 56 °C) evaporates from the skin much faster than water (bp 100 °C). Explain this in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.answer: Water molecules are held by extensive hydrogen bonding, whereas propanone molecules are held only by pd–pd and id–id forces, which are weaker, so propanone molecules escape from the liquid more easily.
parts.working: M1 water: hydrogen bonds; A1 propanone: weaker pd–pd/id–id forces only, so more volatile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butenedioic acid, HOOC–CH=CH–COOH, exists as two geometrical isomers. The cis isomer (maleic acid) melts at 135 °C; the trans isomer (fumaric acid) melts at about 287 °C. Draw no diagram, but explain why the cis isomer can form a hydrogen bond within one molecule but the trans isomer cannot.
parts.answer: In the cis isomer both COOH groups are on the same side of the C=C bond, close enough for the O–H of one group to hydrogen bond to the C=O oxygen of the other (intramolecular). In the trans isomer the groups are on opposite sides and too far apart.
parts.working: M1 COOH groups on same side in cis, close together; A1 intramolecular hydrogen bond possible; in trans the groups are too far apart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain the difference in melting points.
parts.answer: In the cis isomer, some O–H groups are used in intramolecular hydrogen bonds, so fewer hydrogen bonds form between molecules. The trans isomer forms all its hydrogen bonds between molecules, producing a strong network in the crystal; more energy is needed to melt it. (Trans molecules also pack more efficiently.)
parts.working: M1 intramolecular hydrogen bonding reduces intermolecular hydrogen bonding in cis; M1 trans: all hydrogen bonds intermolecular, extended network; A1 more energy needed to separate trans molecules → higher mp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The enthalpy change of vaporisation of water at 100 °C is +40.7 kJ/mol. Assume that evaporating one mole of water breaks two moles of hydrogen bonds and ignore all other forces. Estimate the strength of one mole of hydrogen bonds. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 20.4 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each water molecule forms, on average, two hydrogen bonds per molecule (even though it can take part in four).
parts.answer: Each molecule can take part in four hydrogen bonds (two via its H atoms, two via its lone pairs), but each hydrogen bond is shared between two molecules, so the number of bonds per molecule is 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
parts.working: M1 four possible (2 δ+ H + 2 lone pairs); A1 each bond counted for two molecules → 2 per molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A person in a hot summer in Jacobabad loses 250 g of water by evaporation of sweat. Calculate the energy removed from the body, assuming the same enthalpy of vaporisation. (Mr H₂O = 18.0) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 565 kJ

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the estimate in (a) is likely to be too high.
parts.answer: The enthalpy of vaporisation also includes overcoming id–id and pd–pd forces, so not all of the 40.7 kJ is used to break hydrogen bonds.
parts.working: B1 other intermolecular forces also overcome (also some hydrogen bonds already broken in liquid at 100 °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH (Mr 46), has more electrons than water (Mr 18), yet ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. Explain why water has the higher boiling point.
parts.answer: Each water molecule has two δ+ H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds (a 3D network). Each ethanol molecule has only one O–H hydrogen, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds on average. The extra hydrogen bonding in water outweighs ethanol's stronger id–id forces.
parts.working: M1 water: 2 H + 2 lone pairs → up to 4 hydrogen bonds per molecule; M1 ethanol: one δ+ H → fewer hydrogen bonds; A1 hydrogen bonding difference outweighs larger id–id forces in ethanol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, is an isomer of ethanol and boils at −24 °C. Explain why its boiling point is so much lower than ethanol's.
parts.answer: It has no H bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself; only weaker pd–pd and id–id forces act.
parts.working: B1 no O–H, so no intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Place H₂O, HF and NH₃ in order of increasing boiling point, and explain why NH₃ is lowest even though it has three hydrogen atoms per molecule.
parts.answer: NH₃ (−33 °C) < HF (20 °C) < H₂O (100 °C). N is less electronegative than O and F, so the N–H hydrogen is less δ+ and the hydrogen bonds are weaker; also N has only one lone pair, limiting the number of hydrogen bonds per molecule.
parts.working: B1 correct order; B1 N less electronegative → weaker hydrogen bonds / only one lone pair per N.

stem: Boiling points of the hydrogen halides: HF 20 °C; HCl −85 °C; HBr −67 °C; HI −35 °C. Electronegativities: H 2.2; O 3.4; F 4.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electronegativity difference in an H–F bond and in an O–H bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, a hydrogen bond between two HF molecules. Include the partial charges and the F–H···F bond angle.
parts.answer: The δ+ H atom of one HF molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− F atom of a neighbouring HF molecule; the F–H···F atoms lie in a straight line (about 180°).
parts.working: B1 δ+ H of one molecule attracted to a lone pair on δ− F of another; B1 F–H···F linear, 180°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why HF has the highest boiling point of the four.
parts.answer: F is the most electronegative element and is small with three lone pairs, so the very δ+ H of one HF molecule forms strong hydrogen bonds to a lone pair on F of another molecule (forming zig-zag chains). Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the forces between the other hydrogen halide molecules.
parts.working: M1 hydrogen bonding between HF molecules (H–F···H–F); A1 stronger than id–id/pd–pd forces in HCl, HBr, HI.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The H–F bond is more polar than the O–H bond, but water (100 °C) boils at a higher temperature than HF (20 °C). Suggest why.
parts.answer: Each HF molecule has only one δ+ H atom, so on average it forms one hydrogen bond per molecule (chains), even though F has three lone pairs. Each water molecule has two δ+ H atoms and two lone pairs, giving on average two hydrogen bonds per molecule and a 3D network.
parts.working: M1 HF: only one H per molecule → about one hydrogen bond per molecule; A1 water: two H and two lone pairs → about two per molecule, so more energy needed overall.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Butanal is warmed with Fehling's solution. What is seen?
A An orange precipitate forms.
B A silver mirror forms on the inside of the tube.
C The blue solution gives a red-brown precipitate.
D The orange solution turns green.
parts.answer: C The blue solution gives a red-brown precipitate.
parts.working: Fehling's solution contains a blue copper(II) complex; an aldehyde reduces Cu²⁺ to copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, a red-brown precipitate. A is the 2,4-DNPH result, B is Tollens' and D is acidified dichromate — all plausible tests for carbonyl or alcohol groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH AND a red-brown precipitate when warmed with Fehling's solution?
A butanone
B 2-methylpropanal
C butan-2-ol
D methyl propanoate
parts.answer: B 2-methylpropanal
parts.working: 2-Methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO, is an aliphatic aldehyde: its C=O group reacts with 2,4-DNPH and it is oxidised by Fehling's solution. Butanone is the main distractor: it is a ketone, so it gives the 2,4-DNPH precipitate but no reaction with Fehling's. Butan-2-ol has no C=O; the C=O of an ester does not give the 2,4-DNPH test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out the Tollens' test on a solution of glucose safely in a school laboratory. Include the observation for a positive result.
parts.answer: Add a few drops of the glucose solution to freshly prepared Tollens' reagent in a clean test tube; warm the tube in a beaker of hot water (no naked flame); a silver mirror (or grey/black precipitate) forms.
parts.working: B1 mix sample with Tollens' reagent in clean tube; B1 warm in a hot water bath; B1 silver mirror / grey-black precipitate of silver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The open-chain form of glucose contains an aldehyde group. Name the type of reaction the aldehyde group undergoes in the Tollens' test and state what happens to the silver ions.
parts.answer: The aldehyde is oxidised (to a carboxylate/carboxylic acid group); Ag⁺ ions are reduced to silver metal.
parts.working: B1 aldehyde oxidised; B1 Ag⁺ reduced to Ag (gains one electron).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student wants to show that a sample of honey contains a carbonyl compound but does not want to rely on Tollens' reagent. Name another reagent that could be used to show the presence of a C=O group and give the observation.
parts.answer: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH): orange (or yellow-orange) precipitate.
parts.working: B1 reagent and observation.

stem: A student uses Fehling's solution to estimate the amount of butanal in a sample. The aldehyde is warmed with excess Fehling's solution, and the red-brown precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and weighed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction, using RCHO for the aldehyde, given that the products are the carboxylate ion RCOO⁻, copper(I) oxide and water. The reaction takes place in alkaline solution (OH⁻ ions).
parts.answer: RCHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O
parts.working: M1 correct species; A1 balanced (charge −1 on both sides).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of copper(I) oxide that could form from 0.360 g of butanal. (Mr butanal 72.0; Mr Cu₂O 143.1) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student collects 0.601 g of dry Cu₂O. Calculate the percentage of the maximum mass obtained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest ONE practical reason why the mass obtained is less than the maximum.
parts.answer: Some precipitate passed through or stayed on the filter paper/apparatus; or some butanal evaporated (bp 75 °C) during warming; or the reaction was incomplete.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: There are seven carbonyl compounds with the formula C₅H₁₀O. State how many of them are aldehydes and how many are ketones.
parts.answer: 4 aldehydes; 3 ketones
parts.working: Aldehydes: pentanal, 2-methylbutanal, 3-methylbutanal, 2,2-dimethylpropanal. Ketones: pentan-2-one, pentan-3-one, 3-methylbutan-2-one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many of the seven give (i) an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and (ii) a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.
parts.working: B1 all carbonyl compounds react with 2,4-DNPH; B1 only the 4 aldehydes reduce Tollens'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compound X is one of the seven. X gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and has a chiral centre. Identify X by name and structural formula.
parts.answer: 2-methylbutanal, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CHO
parts.working: B1 name; B1 structure (C2 carries H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and CHO — four different groups).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Compound Y is the ketone with a branched carbon chain. Identify Y and state, with a reason, whether Y gives a pale yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine.
parts.answer: 3-methylbutan-2-one, CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂; yes — it contains the CH₃CO– group.
parts.working: B1 3-methylbutan-2-one (the other two ketones, pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one, are unbranched); B1 positive tri-iodomethane test because it is a methyl ketone (CH₃CO–).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction of propanal with HCN in the presence of KCN, which species attacks the carbonyl carbon atom in the first step?
A H⁺
B CN⁻
C HCN
D K⁺
parts.answer: B CN⁻
parts.working: The cyanide ion is the nucleophile: its lone pair on carbon attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, and the π bond electrons move onto oxygen. H⁺ (or HCN) only protonates the negatively charged intermediate in the second step, so C is the main distractor. K⁺ is a spectator ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Butanal reacts with HCN to give 2-hydroxypentanenitrile. The product does not rotate plane-polarised light. Why?
A The carbonyl group is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from either side equally and a racemic mixture forms.
B The product has no chiral centre.
C CN⁻ attacks only from one side because the ethyl group blocks the other side.
D The OH group can move between the two sides of the molecule.
parts.answer: A The carbonyl group is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from either side equally and a racemic mixture forms.
parts.working: The product CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CN does have a chiral centre (H, OH, CN and propyl on one carbon), so B is the main distractor. Because the C=O group and the atoms bonded to it are trigonal planar, attack from above and below is equally likely, giving a 50:50 (racemic) mixture of the two optical isomers, whose effects on polarised light cancel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some kernels of bitter almonds and apricots contain a compound that breaks down to benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, and HCN. In the laboratory, benzaldehyde reacts with HCN (with a trace of KCN) to form 2-hydroxy-2-phenylethanenitrile. Give the structural formula of this product.
parts.answer: C₆H₅CH(OH)CN
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction.
parts.answer: nucleophilic addition
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the relative molecular mass of the product. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, N 14.0, O 16.0)

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why this reaction is useful in organic synthesis.
parts.answer: It increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom (a new C–C bond is formed).
parts.working: B1 adds one carbon / forms C–C bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of propanone with HCN and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₃ + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN; 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student reacts 2.90 g of propanone (Mr 58.0) with excess HCN and obtains 3.40 g of product (Mr 85.1). Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: HCN is extremely toxic. Suggest why the reaction is carried out using KCN and a little dilute acid rather than pure HCN.
parts.answer: HCN gas is highly toxic and volatile; generating it in solution from KCN and acid avoids handling the gas (and provides CN⁻ ions, the nucleophile).
parts.working: B1 safer — avoids handling volatile toxic HCN / provides CN⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexanone, a cyclic ketone (C₆H₁₀O) used to make nylon, reacts with HCN. Describe, in words, the mechanism of this reaction. Say where each curly arrow starts and ends.
parts.answer: Step 1: the lone pair on the carbon of CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon (arrow from lone pair to C); at the same time the C=O π bond electrons move onto the O atom (arrow from the C=O bond to O), forming an anion with O⁻. Step 2: a lone pair on O⁻ attacks the H of HCN (arrow from O⁻ lone pair to H) and the H–CN bond electrons move onto CN (arrow from bond to C/N), regenerating CN⁻.
parts.working: B1 C=O polarised δ+ C, δ− O; B1 arrow from CN⁻ lone pair (on C) to carbonyl C; B1 arrow from C=O π bond to O, intermediate with O⁻; B1 O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN (or H⁺), regenerating CN⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product and state whether it has a chiral centre.
parts.answer: 1-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonitrile (1-hydroxycyclohexanecarbonitrile); no chiral centre
parts.working: B1 name (accept the structural description: OH and CN on the same ring carbon); B1 no chiral centre — the two paths round the ring from that carbon are identical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two different carbonyl compounds, J and K, each react with HCN to give a product with the molecular formula C₄H₇NO. Give the molecular formula of J and K, and identify the two possible carbonyl compounds.
parts.answer: C₃H₆O; propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, and propanone, CH₃COCH₃
parts.working: B1 C₄H₇NO − HCN = C₃H₆O; B1 propanal; B1 propanone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The product from J has a chiral centre but the product from K does not. Identify J and give the structural formula of its product.
parts.answer: J is propanal; product CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxybutanenitrile)
parts.working: B1 J propanal; B1 product — central carbon has H, OH, CN and C₂H₅.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why J reacts faster with HCN than K.
parts.answer: In a ketone the carbonyl carbon carries two alkyl groups, which push electron density towards it (reducing δ+) and also get in the way of the attacking nucleophile (steric hindrance); an aldehyde has only one alkyl group, so its carbonyl carbon is more δ+ and more accessible.
parts.working: M1 alkyl groups electron-donating reduce δ+ on C in ketone; A1 more steric hindrance in ketone.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound does NOT give a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
A ethanal
B butan-2-ol
C 1-phenylethanol, C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃
D pentan-3-ol
parts.answer: D pentan-3-ol
parts.working: A positive test needs a CH₃CO– group or a CH₃CH(OH)– group (which is oxidised to CH₃CO– by the iodine). Pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, has its OH carbon joined to two ethyl groups, so no CH₃ is next to the CH(OH). Ethanal has CH₃CO–; butan-2-ol and 1-phenylethanol have CH₃CH(OH)–. Students may wrongly reject 1-phenylethanol because of the benzene ring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the name, formula and colour of the precipitate formed in a positive tri-iodomethane test.
parts.answer: tri-iodomethane (iodoform), CHI₃, pale yellow
parts.working: B1 name and formula; B1 pale yellow (antiseptic smell).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the precipitate. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, I 126.9)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student tests butanal and butanone. Predict which compound gives a positive result and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, because it contains a CH₃CO– (methyl ketone) group; butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, has no CH₃ next to the C=O.
parts.working: B1 butanone; B1 contains CH₃C=O group, butanal does not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol gives a positive tri-iodomethane test even though it is an alcohol. Explain why, naming the carbonyl compound formed first.
parts.answer: Alkaline iodine is an oxidising agent: it first oxidises ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, to ethanal, CH₃CHO, which contains the CH₃CO– group and then reacts to give CHI₃.
parts.working: M1 iodine oxidises ethanol; A1 to ethanal (CH₃CHO), which has a CH₃C=O group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula of the organic ion left in solution when ethanal reacts in this test.
parts.answer: HCOO⁻ (methanoate ion)
parts.working: The CH₃ becomes CHI₃ and the rest of the molecule (H–C=O) becomes HCOO⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why methanol does not give a positive result.
parts.answer: Methanol (CH₃OH) is oxidised to methanal (HCHO), which has no CH₃ group next to C=O / methanol has no CH₃CH(OH)– group.
parts.working: B1 no CH₃CH(OH)– or CH₃CO– group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A methyl ketone, CH₃COR, reacts with alkaline iodine to give one mole of CHI₃ per mole of ketone. 0.430 g of an unknown methyl ketone, L, gives 1.97 g of CHI₃ (Mr 393.7) with a 100 % yield. Calculate the Mr of L. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: L contains only C, H and one O atom. Show that its molecular formula is C₅H₁₀O.
parts.working: B1 Mr of C₅H₁₀O = 86.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formulae and names of the TWO methyl ketones that fit this formula.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃ pentan-2-one; CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂ 3-methylbutan-2-one
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The precipitate is filtered off. The filtrate contains sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa. Deduce the structural formula and name of M.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₂CH₃, butanone
parts.working: M1 the R group of CH₃COR ends up in RCOO⁻; R = CH₃CH₂ (A1 butanone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: An alcohol N also gives CHI₃ and sodium propanoate in this test. Identify N and explain why it reacts.
parts.answer: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. It contains the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which alkaline iodine oxidises to CH₃CO–, forming butanone, which then reacts.
parts.working: B1 butan-2-ol; B1 oxidised to butanone (methyl ketone) first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of butanone with iodine and sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + CH₃CH₂COONa + 3NaI + 3H₂O
parts.working: M1 correct products; A1 balanced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why butan-1-ol, an isomer of N, gives no precipitate in this test.
parts.answer: Butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, has no CH₃CH(OH)– group; it would be oxidised to butanal, which has no CH₃CO– group.
parts.working: B1 no CH₃CH(OH)– group (its oxidation product butanal has no CH₃C=O).

author: HomiLabs
stem: A methyl ketone, M, is warmed with iodine and aqueous sodium hydroxide. A pale yellow precipitate forms.

In the tri-iodomethane reaction a methyl ketone reacts as follows:
CH₃COR + 3I₂ + 4OH⁻ → CHI₃ + RCOO⁻ + 3I⁻ + 3H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the equation to calculate the minimum volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ iodine solution needed to react completely with 0.00200 mol of butanone.
parts.answer: 60.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethanol is first oxidised by iodine: C₂H₅OH + I₂ + 2OH⁻ → CH₃CHO + 2I⁻ + 2H₂O. Ethanal then reacts in the same ratio as a methyl ketone. Write the overall equation for ethanol and calculate the minimum volume of the same iodine solution needed for 0.00200 mol of ethanol.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + 4I₂ + 6OH⁻ → CHI₃ + HCOO⁻ + 5I⁻ + 5H₂O; 80.0 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a student adds iodine solution until the brown colour remains, and then adds NaOH dropwise until the colour just disappears.
parts.answer: This ensures excess iodine is present for complete reaction while keeping the solution alkaline; the colour change shows the iodine has been converted to the reactive alkaline form without adding a large excess of NaOH.
parts.working: B1 ensures enough iodine and alkaline conditions (excess iodine indicated by brown colour).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name each compound and state whether it is an aldehyde or a ketone: (i) CH₃CH₂CHO  (ii) CH₃COCH₂CH₃  (iii) (CH₃)₂CHCHO  (iv) C₆H₅CHO
parts.answer: (i) propanal, aldehyde; (ii) butanone, ketone; (iii) 2-methylpropanal, aldehyde; (iv) benzaldehyde, aldehyde
parts.working: B1 each (name and class).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the structural difference between an aldehyde and a ketone.
parts.answer: In an aldehyde the C=O carbon is bonded to at least one H atom (C=O at the end of the chain); in a ketone the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents used to oxidise ethanol to ethanal in the laboratory, and the colour change seen.
parts.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇ with dilute H₂SO₄; orange to green.
parts.working: B1 reagents; B1 orange → green.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: The distillate is tested to confirm that it contains ethanal and to find out whether any ethanoic acid has also been formed. Give a test, with its positive result, for each compound.
parts.answer: Ethanal: warm with Tollens' reagent — silver mirror (or Fehling's solution — red-brown precipitate). Ethanoic acid: add sodium carbonate (or sodium hydrogencarbonate) — effervescence/bubbles of CO₂ (which turn limewater milky).
parts.working: B1 Tollens' → silver mirror, Fehling's → red-brown precipitate, or 2,4-DNPH → orange precipitate (ethanoic acid does not react with any of these); B1 Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ → effervescence of CO₂ (or a metal such as magnesium → H₂).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the reducing agent normally used in aqueous or alcoholic solution to reduce aldehydes and ketones.
parts.answer: sodium tetrahydridoborate, NaBH₄
parts.working: B1 (LiAlH₄ in dry ether also accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, using [H], for the reduction of propanal and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH; propan-1-ol
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 name.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the product formed when pentan-3-one is reduced in the same way, and classify it as a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol.
parts.answer: pentan-3-ol; secondary
parts.working: B1 name; B1 secondary (ketones reduce to secondary alcohols).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is the main ingredient of many nail-polish removers. It mixes with water in all proportions. Explain why.
parts.answer: The O atom of the polar C=O group has lone pairs and a δ− charge, so it can accept hydrogen bonds from δ+ H atoms of water molecules.
parts.working: M1 δ− O with lone pairs; A1 hydrogen bonds formed with water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Decanal, CH₃(CH₂)₈CHO, is responsible for part of the smell of orange peel. Suggest why decanal is almost insoluble in water.
parts.answer: Its long hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and cannot hydrogen bond with water; the single C=O group cannot form enough hydrogen bonds to make up for breaking water–water hydrogen bonds around the chain.
parts.working: M1 long non-polar chain; A1 cannot form hydrogen bonds with water / disrupts water's hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why propanone (bp 56 °C) has a lower boiling point than propan-2-ol (bp 82 °C).
parts.answer: Propan-2-ol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other (O–H group); propanone has no O–H, so only weaker pd–pd and id–id forces.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonding in alcohol, none between propanone molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: There are three carbonyl compounds with the molecular formula C₄H₈O. Give the structural formula and name of each.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO butanal; (CH₃)₂CHCHO 2-methylpropanal; CH₃COCH₂CH₃ butanone
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the name of the alcohol formed when each compound is reduced by NaBH₄, and state which of these alcohols is chiral.
parts.answer: butanal → butan-1-ol; 2-methylpropanal → 2-methylpropan-1-ol; butanone → butan-2-ol (chiral)
parts.working: B1 two primary alcohols named; B1 butan-2-ol; B1 butan-2-ol is chiral (C2 has H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which of the three carbonyl compounds could be made by oxidising a secondary alcohol?
parts.answer: butanone (from butan-2-ol)
parts.working: B1 ketones come from secondary alcohols.

stem: A student plans to make propanone by heating propan-2-ol with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI), then distilling the product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass of propanone that could be made from 6.00 g of propan-2-ol. (Mr: propan-2-ol 60.0; propanone 58.0)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student obtains 4.35 g of propanone. Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mixture was heated under reflux for 20 minutes before distillation. Explain why heating under reflux is suitable here but not when making an aldehyde.
parts.answer: Propanone is a ketone and is not oxidised further, so reflux (which keeps it in contact with the oxidising agent) does not lower the yield; an aldehyde would be oxidised to a carboxylic acid under reflux.
parts.working: M1 ketones resist further oxidation; A1 aldehydes would be oxidised to carboxylic acids — must be distilled off as formed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest TWO changes to the method that could increase the yield, and explain each.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g.: cool the receiving flask in ice so less of the volatile propanone (bp 56 °C) evaporates; heat under reflux for longer so that all the propan-2-ol is oxidised; use fewer transfers/seal the joints so less product is lost.
parts.working: B1 each for any two improvements with a valid reason (using excess oxidising agent does not score — the plan already uses excess).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Levulinic acid, CH₃COCH₂CH₂COOH, can be made from sugar-cane waste. Name the two functional groups present.
parts.answer: ketone (carbonyl) and carboxylic acid
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the organic product when levulinic acid reacts with NaBH₄.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂COOH
parts.working: M1 C=O reduced to CH(OH); A1 COOH unchanged (NaBH₄ does not reduce carboxylic acids).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the organic product when levulinic acid reacts with excess LiAlH₄ in dry ether, followed by careful addition of water.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (pentane-1,4-diol)
parts.working: M1 C=O → CH(OH); A1 COOH → CH₂OH (LiAlH₄ is a stronger reducing agent).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the C=O bond is polar.
parts.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the bonding electrons are pulled towards O, leaving C δ+ and O δ−.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the C=O group of an aldehyde is attacked by nucleophiles, but the C=C group of an alkene is attacked by electrophiles.
parts.answer: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ (electron-poor), so it attracts nucleophiles, which donate a lone pair to it. The C=C bond is non-polar but has a region of high electron density in its π bond, which attracts electrophiles (electron-pair acceptors).
parts.working: M1 C of C=O is δ+; M1 nucleophiles attracted to δ+ C/donate electron pair; A1 C=C electron-rich π bond attracts electrophiles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the shape around the carbonyl carbon and explain why this makes attack from either face of the molecule equally likely.
parts.answer: Trigonal planar (120°); the nucleophile can approach from above or below the plane of the C=O group with equal ease.
parts.working: B1 trigonal planar; B1 planar group accessible equally from both sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A few drops of each of butanal and butanone are warmed separately with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Give the observation with each.
parts.answer: butanal: orange solution turns green; butanone: stays orange
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, using [O], for the reaction that occurs and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO + [O] → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH; butanoic acid
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 name.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why butanone does not react.
parts.answer: Ketones have no H atom on the carbonyl carbon; oxidation would need a C–C bond to break, which mild oxidising agents cannot do.
parts.working: B1 no H on carbonyl carbon / would need to break C–C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name a reagent, other than acidified dichromate, that would distinguish the two compounds, and give the result with butanal.
parts.answer: Tollens' reagent — silver mirror (or Fehling's solution — red-brown precipitate)
parts.working: B1 reagent and positive observation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal can be made from 1-bromopropane in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediate formed.
parts.answer: Step 1: NaOH(aq), heat under reflux → propan-1-ol. Step 2: K₂Cr₂O₇ with dilute H₂SO₄, warm and distil the product off immediately → propanal.
parts.working: B1 NaOH(aq) heat/reflux; B1 propan-1-ol; B1 acidified dichromate; B1 distil off as formed (prevents oxidation to propanoic acid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Propanal is then converted into 2-hydroxybutanoic acid in two further steps. Give the reagent(s) for each step and the structural formula of the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 3: HCN with a trace of KCN (or KCN + dilute acid) → CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN. Step 4: heat under reflux with dilute HCl (acid hydrolysis) → CH₃CH₂CH(OH)COOH.
parts.working: B1 HCN/KCN; B1 intermediate 2-hydroxybutanenitrile CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN; B1 hydrolysis with dilute acid, heat under reflux.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall percentage yield if the four steps have yields of 85 %, 70 %, 80 % and 90 %. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A neutral compound P contains 66.7 % carbon, 11.1 % hydrogen and 22.2 % oxygen by mass. Calculate its empirical formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₈O

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Mr of P is 72. Deduce its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₈O
parts.working: Mr of C₄H₈O = 48 + 8 + 16 = 72, so the molecular formula is the empirical formula.

parts.label: c
parts.text: P gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but does not react with Fehling's solution. Identify P.
parts.answer: butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃
parts.working: Carbonyl compound (2,4-DNPH) that is not an aldehyde (Fehling's) → the only C₄H₈O ketone.

parts.label: d
parts.text: P is reduced by NaBH₄ to Q. Give the structural formula of Q and explain why the Q obtained does not rotate plane-polarised light, even though Q is chiral.
parts.answer: Q is CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (butan-2-ol). The H⁻ nucleophile attacks the planar C=O group equally from either side, so equal amounts of the two optical isomers form (racemic mixture) and their rotations cancel.
parts.working: B1 butan-2-ol; B1 planar carbonyl attacked from both sides equally → racemic mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: NaBH₄ acts as a source of hydride ions, H⁻. Name the type of mechanism by which the hydride ion reacts with the carbonyl group of propanone.
parts.answer: nucleophilic addition
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the two steps of this mechanism for propanone. Say where each curly arrow starts and ends.
parts.answer: Step 1: an arrow from the lone pair on H⁻ to the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the C=O π-bond electrons move onto O (arrow from the C=O bond to O), forming the anion (CH₃)₂CH–O⁻. Step 2: a lone pair on O⁻ attacks an H atom of a water (or acid) molecule, and the O–H bond electrons move onto the O of water (forming OH⁻), giving (CH₃)₂CHOH.
parts.working: B1 H⁻ attacks δ+ C; B1 π electrons move to O, alkoxide intermediate; B1 O⁻ protonated by water/H⁺ to give propan-2-ol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Propanone is reduced with NaBD₄, a source of deuteride ions, D⁻ (D = ²H), in aqueous solution (H₂O). Use the mechanism to give the structural formula of the product, showing where the D atom ends up.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₂CD–OH: the D is bonded to the former carbonyl carbon and the H on the oxygen comes from water.
parts.working: B1 D on the carbon atom (from D⁻ attack in step 1), OH hydrogen from H₂O (step 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cinnamaldehyde, C₆H₅CH=CHCHO, gives cinnamon (daalchini) its flavour. Calculate its Mr. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what is observed when cinnamaldehyde is added to (i) bromine water and (ii) 2,4-DNPH, and when it is (iii) warmed with Tollens' reagent.
parts.answer: (i) orange/brown bromine water decolourised; (ii) orange (orange-red) precipitate; (iii) silver mirror
parts.working: B1 each. (i) C=C addition; (ii) C=O present; (iii) aldehyde.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the organic product when cinnamaldehyde is reacted with (i) NaBH₄ and (ii) excess hydrogen with a nickel catalyst under conditions that do not affect the benzene ring.
parts.answer: (i) C₆H₅CH=CHCH₂OH; (ii) C₆H₅CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
parts.working: B1 NaBH₄ reduces only the C=O (nucleophilic H⁻ does not attack the C=C); B1 H₂/Ni reduces both the C=C and the C=O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a school food-science project in Faisalabad, a 0.80 g roasted chickpea is set alight on a mounted needle and held under a boiling tube containing 25.0 g of water. The water temperature rises by 18.4 °C. Use specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the energy released per gram of chickpea, in kJ/g. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The packet states a much larger value. Give two reasons why the experimental value is lower.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the surroundings/air and to the boiling tube; incomplete combustion (soot) / chickpea not fully burned.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: heat lost to air; heat absorbed by the glass tube and clamp; incomplete combustion / soot; not all of the chickpea burns; some energy lost before the tube is in place.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student mixes 50.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid with 50.0 cm³ of dilute sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup and uses q = mcΔT to find the energy released. Both solutions have a density of 1.00 g/cm³. Which value of m should be used?
A 50.0 g
B 100 g
C the mass of sodium chloride formed
D 100 g plus the mass of the polystyrene cup
parts.answer: B 100 g
parts.working: The energy heats the whole 100 cm³ of mixture (100 g), not just one solution. A (50.0 g) uses only one solution; the cup's heat capacity is taken as negligible for polystyrene, so D is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Experiment 1: 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl(aq) is mixed with 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ NaOH(aq); the temperature rises by 6.8 K.
Experiment 2: 50 cm³ of each of the same two solutions are mixed.
Experiment 3: 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ HCl(aq) is mixed with 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ NaOH(aq).
What are the temperature rises in experiments 2 and 3? (No heat losses.)
A Exp 2: 13.6 K; Exp 3: 13.6 K
B Exp 2: 6.8 K; Exp 3: 13.6 K
C Exp 2: 13.6 K; Exp 3: 6.8 K
D Exp 2: 6.8 K; Exp 3: 6.8 K
parts.answer: B Exp 2: 6.8 K; Exp 3: 13.6 K
parts.working: Exp 2: twice the moles of water formed but twice the mass to heat, so ΔT is unchanged (6.8 K). Exp 3: twice the moles in the same mass, so ΔT doubles (13.6 K). A forgets that the mass also doubles in Exp 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 50.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 5.4 K. Assume the mixture has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −56.4 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with 50.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol/dm³ aqueous ammonia in place of sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 4.9 K. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation in this case.
parts.answer: −51.2 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the value in (b) is less exothermic than the value in (a).
parts.answer: Ammonia is a weak base, only partly reacted/ionised; some energy is absorbed in ionising it (forming NH₄⁺ and OH⁻) as the reaction proceeds.
parts.working: B1 ammonia is a weak base / only partially ionised; B1 energy is needed to complete ionisation, so less energy is released overall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A copper calorimeter of mass 120 g contains 250 g of water. Burning 0.500 g of methanol, CH₃OH (Mr 32.0), under it raises the temperature of the calorimeter and water by 9.2 K. Specific heat capacities: water 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, copper 0.385 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol from these results, in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures. Include the energy absorbed by the copper.
parts.answer: −642 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard enthalpy change of combustion of methanol is −726 kJ/mol. Calculate the percentage of the energy released by the methanol that was transferred to the calorimeter and water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change to the apparatus that would make the result closer to −726 kJ/mol.
parts.answer: Use a draught shield / lid / insulate the calorimeter / put the flame closer to the calorimeter / use a flame calorimeter with a heat exchanger.
parts.working: Any one sensible change that reduces heat loss.

stem:
In a thermometric titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration is placed in a polystyrene cup. 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, also at 22.0 °C, is added 4.0 cm³ at a time and the highest temperature after each addition is recorded.
volume of HCl added / cm³: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32
temperature / °C: 22.0, 25.8, 28.6, 30.9, 32.7, 34.1, 33.2, 32.3, 31.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to state the volume of acid needed to neutralise the sodium hydroxide. Explain how the table shows this.
parts.answer: 20 cm³; the temperature is highest at 20 cm³ and falls after it (no more reaction; cold acid only dilutes/cools the mixture).
parts.working: B1 20 cm³; B1 maximum temperature at this volume, extra acid causes cooling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide, in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 1.60 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the maximum temperature to calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in kJ/mol. Assume the solution has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
parts.answer: −56.9 kJ/mol

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why plotting a graph of the results and finding where two best-fit lines cross would give a more reliable end-point than simply reading the highest value in the table.
parts.answer: The true maximum may fall between two additions (only 4 cm³ steps) / heat is lost during the experiment, so the highest reading may be below the true maximum; extrapolating the lines finds the true end-point.
parts.working: Any one valid point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bottle of camping spirit is a mixture of ethanol, C₂H₅OH (Mr 46.0), and water. 1.50 g of the spirit is burned completely under a can containing 200 g of water. The water temperature rises by 38.4 K. Only 80 % of the energy released reaches the water. ΔHc of ethanol = −1367 kJ/mol; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, released by the burning spirit.
parts.working: q to water = 200 × 4.18 × 38.4 = 32 102 J (M1); only 80 % transferred, so energy released = 32.10 ÷ 0.80 = 40.1 kJ (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of ethanol in the spirit. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption, other than the 80 % efficiency, made in your calculation.
parts.answer: Only the ethanol burns (water/other components release no energy) / combustion of ethanol is complete / the value of ΔHc applies under the experimental conditions.
parts.working: Any one.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 30.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid is added to 50.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide in an insulated flask. The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is −57.3 kJ/mol. Assume the mixture has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show which reactant is in excess and calculate the amount of water formed.
parts.answer: n(H⁺) = 0.0600 mol, n(OH⁻) = 0.100 mol, so NaOH is in excess; 0.0600 mol of water forms.
parts.working: M1 n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0300 mol so n(H⁺) = 0.0600; n(OH⁻) = 0.100; A1 0.0600 mol H₂O, NaOH in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both solutions start at 23.5 °C. Calculate the maximum temperature reached.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In a second run the acid starts at 22.0 °C and the alkali at 25.0 °C. Calculate the starting temperature that should be used, and the new maximum temperature.
parts.answer: Start = 23.9 °C; maximum = 34.2 °C

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ammonia is oxidised in the first stage of making nitric acid:
4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)
Standard enthalpy changes of formation / kJ/mol: NH₃(g) −46; NO(g) +90; H₂O(g) −242.
What is the enthalpy change of this reaction?
A −1276 kJ/mol
B −1092 kJ/mol
C −908 kJ/mol
D +908 kJ/mol
parts.answer: C −908 kJ/mol
parts.working: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = [4(+90) + 6(−242)] − [4(−46)] = −1092 + 184 = −908 kJ/mol. B ignores the reactants; A adds the reactant term with the wrong sign.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Standard enthalpy changes of combustion / kJ/mol: C₂H₄(g) −1411; H₂(g) −286; C₂H₆(g) −1560.
What is the standard enthalpy change of C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g)?
A −137 kJ/mol
B +137 kJ/mol
C −1697 kJ/mol
D −3257 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −137 kJ/mol
parts.working: Using combustion data, ΔH = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) = (−1411 − 286) − (−1560) = −137 kJ/mol. B uses products − reactants, which is the rule for formation data, not combustion data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆(s).
parts.answer: 6C(graphite) + 6H₂(g) + 3O₂(g) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s)
parts.working: Correct formulae, balancing and state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Standard enthalpy changes of combustion / kJ/mol: C(graphite) −394; H₂(g) −286; C₆H₁₂O₆(s) −2803. Use a Hess cycle to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of glucose.
parts.answer: −1277 kJ/mol
parts.working: Cycle: elements and glucose both burn to 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (M1); ΔHf = 6(−394) + 6(−286) − (−2803) (M1); = −1277 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this enthalpy change cannot be measured directly.
parts.answer: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen do not react together to form glucose (other products would form / no reaction under lab conditions).
parts.working: Any one valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Standard enthalpy changes of combustion / kJ/mol: C(graphite) −393.5; C(diamond) −395.4. Calculate the enthalpy change for C(graphite) → C(diamond).
parts.answer: +1.9 kJ/mol
parts.working: Both burn to CO₂(g) (M1); ΔH = −393.5 − (−395.4) = +1.9 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to state which form of carbon has more energy, and why graphite (not diamond) is used in equations for standard enthalpy changes of formation.
parts.answer: Diamond has 1.9 kJ/mol more energy; graphite is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions (its standard state).
parts.working: B1 diamond higher in energy; B1 graphite is the standard state of carbon.

stem:
Baking powder in a Karachi bakery releases CO₂ by the reaction 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Two reactions with excess dilute hydrochloric acid are measured:
NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)   ΔH₁ = +28.4 kJ/mol
Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)   ΔH₂ = −34.8 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a Hess cycle and calculate ΔH for the decomposition reaction.
parts.answer: +91.6 kJ/mol
parts.working: Both NaHCO₃ and Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ react with HCl to give 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) + 2CO₂(g) (M1); ΔH = 2ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ (M1); = 2(+28.4) − (−34.8) = +91.6 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, absorbed when 8.40 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate (Mr 84.0) decomposes in a cake.
parts.working: 0.100 mol NaHCO₃ = 0.0500 mol of reaction; 0.0500 × 91.6 = 4.58 kJ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ΔH for the decomposition cannot be found simply by heating sodium hydrogencarbonate in a calorimeter.
parts.answer: It needs continuous strong heating, so the energy absorbed by the reaction cannot be separated from the heat supplied/lost (and the reaction is slow/incomplete).
parts.working: Any one valid reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Railway tracks are welded with the thermite reaction: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s)   ΔH = −852 kJ/mol. The standard enthalpy change of formation of Fe₂O₃(s) is −824 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃(s).
parts.answer: −1676 kJ/mol
parts.working: ΔH = ΔHf(Al₂O₃) − ΔHf(Fe₂O₃) (M1); ΔHf(Al₂O₃) = −852 + (−824) = −1676 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in kJ, when 1.00 kg of aluminium reacts completely. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures. (Ar Al = 27.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the enthalpy change of formation of iron does not appear in your calculation.
parts.answer: Iron (like aluminium) is an element in its standard state, so its ΔHf is zero.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrazine, N₂H₄, is used as a rocket fuel. Reaction 1: N₂H₄(l) + 2H₂O₂(l) → N₂(g) + 4H₂O(g).
Standard enthalpy changes of formation / kJ/mol: N₂H₄(l) +50.6; H₂O₂(l) −187.8; H₂O(g) −241.8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for reaction 1, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −642.2 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per kilogram of reactant mixture for reaction 1. (Mr: N₂H₄ 32.0, H₂O₂ 34.0, O₂ 32.0)
parts.answer: 6422 kJ/kg
parts.working: Mass per mole of reaction = 32.0 + 68.0 = 100 g (M1); 642.2 kJ ÷ 0.100 kg = 6422 kJ/kg (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Reaction 2 uses liquid oxygen instead: N₂H₄(l) + O₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). Calculate the energy released per kilogram of reactants and state which oxidant gives more energy per kilogram. (Ignore the enthalpy change for liquefying oxygen.)
parts.answer: 8347 kJ/kg; oxygen gives more energy per kilogram

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ethanol is made by the hydration of ethene. Data / kJ/mol: ΔHc C₂H₄(g) −1411; ΔHc C₂H₅OH(l) −1367; enthalpy change of vaporisation of water +44; enthalpy change of vaporisation of ethanol +43.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l) → C₂H₅OH(l).
parts.answer: −44 kJ/mol
parts.working: Both sides burn to 2CO₂ + 3H₂O; water has no combustion (M1); ΔH = −1411 − (−1367) = −44 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In industry the reaction is carried out with all substances as gases: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g). Use the extra data to calculate ΔH for this reaction.
parts.answer: −45 kJ/mol
parts.working: Route: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l): −44 (M1); → C₂H₅OH(l): −44; → C₂H₅OH(g): +43 (M1); total = −44 − 44 + 43 = −45 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ΔHc of water does not appear in the cycle.
parts.answer: Water cannot burn further; it is already a combustion product (fully oxidised), so its ΔHc is zero.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of sodium carbonate?
A Na₂O(s) + CO₂(g) → Na₂CO₃(s)
B 2Na(s) + C(graphite) + 1½O₂(g) → Na₂CO₃(s)
C 2Na(g) + C(g) + 3O(g) → Na₂CO₃(s)
D 4Na(s) + 2C(graphite) + 3O₂(g) → 2Na₂CO₃(s)
parts.answer: B 2Na(s) + C(graphite) + 1½O₂(g) → Na₂CO₃(s)
parts.working: Formation: one mole of compound from its elements in their standard states. A starts from compounds; C uses gaseous atoms (not standard states); D forms two moles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is about −57 kJ/mol both for HCl(aq) with NaOH(aq) and for HNO₃(aq) with KOH(aq). Which statement explains this?
A Both acids and both alkalis are fully ionised, so the only reaction is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
B Sodium and potassium are in the same group of the Periodic Table.
C Both salts formed are soluble in water.
D Chloride ions and nitrate ions have the same charge.
parts.answer: A Both acids and both alkalis are fully ionised, so the only reaction is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
parts.working: Strong acids and strong bases are fully ionised; the metal ions and anions are spectator ions, so the same reaction (and the same energy change per mole of water) occurs. C is true but does not explain the equal values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term standard enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH°r.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when the amounts of reactants shown in the equation react to give products, under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa), all in their standard states.
parts.working: B1 amounts in the stated equation (molar quantities); B1 standard conditions / standard states.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)   ΔH°r = −572 kJ/mol. State the standard enthalpy change of formation of water and explain why it is different from ΔH°r.
parts.answer: −286 kJ/mol; ΔHf refers to one mole of water, but the equation forms two moles.
parts.working: B1 −286 kJ/mol; B1 explanation (per mole of product).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, that represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of methanol, CH₃OH(l).
parts.answer: CH₃OH(l) + 1½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
parts.working: One mole of methanol, liquid water, correct state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ammonia.
parts.answer: ½N₂(g) + 1½H₂(g) → NH₃(g)
parts.working: One mole of NH₃(g) from elements in standard states.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of solid calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂.
parts.answer: Ca(s) + N₂(g) + 3O₂(g) → Ca(NO₃)₂(s)
parts.working: Correct balancing and state symbols.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the equation in (b) needs fractions.
parts.answer: The definition requires exactly one mole of the product to form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.
parts.answer: No change takes place: forming the element from itself in the same state involves no energy change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these have a standard enthalpy change of formation of zero. Give a reason for each one you reject: O₂(g); O₃(g); Br₂(l); Br₂(g); C(diamond); Hg(l).
parts.answer: Zero: O₂(g), Br₂(l), Hg(l). Not zero: O₃(g) (not the standard form of oxygen); Br₂(g) (bromine is a liquid under standard conditions); C(diamond) (graphite is the standard state of carbon).
parts.working: B1 for the three zeros all correct; B1 each correct reason for O₃, Br₂(g), diamond.

stem: Standard enthalpy changes of combustion of alkanes / kJ/mol: methane −890; ethane −1560; propane −2219; butane −2877.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean change in ΔHc for each extra CH₂ group from methane to butane.
parts.answer: −662 kJ/mol per CH₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to predict ΔHc of pentane, C₅H₁₂(g).
parts.answer: about −3539 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of bonds, why each CH₂ group adds a roughly constant amount.
parts.answer: Each extra CH₂ adds one C–C and two C–H bonds to break and needs 1½O₂; it gives one more CO₂ and H₂O, so the same extra bonds are made each time.
parts.working: B1 same extra bonds broken (C–C, 2 C–H, 1½ O=O); B1 same extra bonds formed (2 C=O, 2 O–H).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid is neutralised by excess sodium hydroxide; 2.86 kJ of energy is released. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation.
parts.answer: −57.2 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the answer is calculated per mole of water and not per mole of sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change of neutralisation is defined for the formation of one mole of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, how the value would differ if ethanoic acid (in the right amount) were used instead.
parts.answer: Less exothermic (smaller magnitude); ethanoic acid is a weak acid and energy is needed to ionise it fully.
parts.working: B1 less exothermic; B1 weak acid / ionisation absorbs energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: "The standard enthalpy change of combustion of hydrogen is the same as the standard enthalpy change of formation of steam, H₂O(g)." ΔHc of H₂ = −286 kJ/mol and ΔHf of H₂O(g) = −242 kJ/mol. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Under standard conditions water is a liquid, so ΔHc of H₂ forms H₂O(l), not H₂O(g); ΔHc(H₂) equals ΔHf(H₂O(l)).
parts.working: B1 standard state of water is liquid; B1 ΔHc(H₂) = ΔHf of liquid water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the enthalpy change for H₂O(g) → H₂O(l).
parts.answer: −44 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ΔHc of carbon monoxide is not the same as ΔHf of carbon dioxide, even though both form one mole of CO₂(g).
parts.answer: ΔHf of CO₂ starts from the elements C(graphite) and O₂; ΔHc of CO starts from a compound, CO, so the energy of forming CO is not included.
parts.working: B1 formation must start from elements; B1 CO is a compound (difference = ΔHf of CO).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trekking group near Gilgit burns butane in a camping stove at 5 °C and 75 kPa. Steam escapes and some soot forms on the pan. Give four reasons why the value they measure is not the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane.
parts.answer: Temperature not 298 K; pressure not 100 kPa; water formed as gas, not liquid (standard state); incomplete combustion (soot/CO) so not complete combustion; also heat losses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: not 298 K; not 100 kPa; water is H₂O(g) not H₂O(l); incomplete combustion; heat loss to surroundings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the standard conditions used in thermochemistry.
parts.answer: 298 K (25 °C) and 100 kPa (1 bar); 1 mol/dm³ for solutions.
parts.working: B1 for 298 K and 100 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bond energies / kJ/mol: H–H 436; Cl–Cl 242; H–Cl 431. Calculate the enthalpy change for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
parts.answer: −184 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, making bonds releases energy; more energy is released forming the H–Cl bonds than is absorbed breaking H–H and Cl–Cl.
parts.working: B1 breaking endothermic/making exothermic; B1 energy released > energy absorbed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bond energies / kJ/mol: H–H 436; Br–Br 193; H–Br 366.
What is the enthalpy change for H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g)?
A −263 kJ/mol
B −103 kJ/mol
C +103 kJ/mol
D +263 kJ/mol
parts.answer: B −103 kJ/mol
parts.working: Broken: 436 + 193 = 629; made: 2 × 366 = 732; ΔH = 629 − 732 = −103 kJ/mol. D (+263) counts only one H–Br bond (629 − 366); C reverses the sign (made − broken).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term bond energy.
parts.answer: The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, with all species in the gaseous state.
parts.working: B1 energy to break one mole of bonds; B1 gaseous state.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The C–H bond energy is usually given as an average value of 410 kJ/mol. Explain why it is an average value.
parts.answer: The strength of a C–H bond depends on its environment (the other atoms in the molecule), so values from many different compounds are averaged.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The H–H bond energy (436 kJ/mol) is an exact value, not an average. Suggest why.
parts.answer: It only occurs in one molecule, H₂, so there is only one environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bond energies / kJ/mol: C=C 610; C–C 350; C–H 410; H–Cl 431; C–Cl 340. Propene reacts with hydrogen chloride: CH₃CH=CH₂(g) + HCl(g) → CH₃CHClCH₃(g). Calculate the enthalpy change of this reaction.
parts.answer: −59 kJ/mol
parts.working: Only changed bonds needed: broken C=C + H–Cl = 1041 (M1); made C–C + C–H + C–Cl = 1100 (M1); ΔH = −59 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why you do not need to count the other C–H bonds in propene.
parts.answer: They are present in both reactant and product, so the energy to break them equals the energy released when they re-form (they cancel).

stem: Bond energies / kJ/mol: C–H 410; C–C 350; C–O 360; O–H 460; O=O 496; C=O (in CO₂) 805.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₅OH(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(g).
parts.answer: −1272 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol is −1367 kJ/mol. Give two reasons for the difference.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values; under standard conditions ethanol and water are liquids (energy of vaporisation/condensation not included in the bond-energy calculation).
parts.working: B1 average bond energies; B1 standard states are liquids, not gases.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene reacts with bromine: C₂H₄(g) + Br₂(g) → C₂H₄Br₂(g)   ΔH = −107 kJ/mol. Bond energies / kJ/mol: C=C 610; C–C 350; Br–Br 193. Calculate the C–Br bond energy.
parts.answer: 280 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the reaction must be considered with all species as gases.
parts.answer: Bond energies are defined for gaseous species; any change of state would add extra energy terms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) + O₂(g).
Bond energies / kJ/mol: O–O 150; O–H 460; O=O 496.
What is the enthalpy change of this reaction?
A −196 kJ/mol
B +196 kJ/mol
C −346 kJ/mol
D +346 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −196 kJ/mol
parts.working: Broken: 2 × (2 O–H + O–O) = 2 × 1070 = 2140; made: 4 O–H + O=O = 2336; ΔH = 2140 − 2336 = −196 kJ/mol. C (−346) comes from breaking only one O–O bond (150 − 496), forgetting that two H₂O₂ molecules react.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrazine burns in oxygen: N₂H₄(g) + O₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). Bond energies / kJ/mol: N–N 160; N–H 390; O=O 496; N≡N 944; O–H 460. Calculate the enthalpy change of this reaction.
parts.answer: −568 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the bond energies to explain why forming N₂ makes a large contribution to the energy released.
parts.answer: The N≡N triple bond is very strong (944 kJ/mol), so a lot of energy is released when it forms.

stem: Data: standard enthalpy change of formation of CH₄(g) = −75 kJ/mol; C(graphite) → C(g)   ΔH = +717 kJ/mol; H–H bond energy = 436 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the mean C–H bond energy in methane.
parts.answer: 416 kJ/mol
parts.working: CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g): reverse formation +75, atomise carbon +717, break 2 H–H +872 (M1); total = +1664 kJ/mol (M1); ÷ 4 = 416 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this value differs from the average C–H bond energy of 410 kJ/mol used in data books.
parts.answer: The data-book value is an average over many compounds; in methane the C–H bond has its own particular value.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonia is being tested as a way to carry hydrogen fuel by ship. Bond energies / kJ/mol: N–H 390; N≡N 944; H–H 436; O=O 496; O–H 460.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use bond energies to calculate ΔH for 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g).
parts.answer: +88 kJ/mol
parts.working: Broken 6 N–H = 2340; made N≡N + 3 H–H = 2252 (M1); ΔH = +88 kJ/mol (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed, in MJ, to release 1.00 kg of hydrogen from ammonia. (Mr H₂ = 2.016)

parts.label: c
