parts.answer: E° values apply to aqueous ions under standard conditions; they do not apply to insoluble solids/complexes.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car's catalytic converter contains platinum and rhodium on a ceramic honeycomb. Write an equation for the removal of NO and CO.
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the metals are spread as a very thin layer on a honeycomb.
parts.answer: Gives a very large surface area for adsorption; less of the expensive metals is needed.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how lead compounds from leaded petrol would stop the converter working.
parts.answer: Lead is strongly adsorbed on the active sites and blocks them (catalyst poisoning).

parts.label: d
parts.text: A good catalyst adsorbs reactants neither too strongly nor too weakly. Explain why.
parts.answer: Too weak: reactants not held long enough / bonds not weakened; too strong: products are not released (desorbed), so sites stay blocked.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vegetable ghee (banaspati) is made by hydrogenating vegetable oils with a nickel catalyst. Write a general equation for the reaction of one C=C bond, and give the conditions.
parts.answer: –CH=CH– + H₂ → –CH₂–CH₂–; finely divided Ni, about 150 °C (heat), H₂ under pressure.
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nickel must be finely divided.
parts.answer: Large surface area / more active sites.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sulfur compounds in the oil must be removed first. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Sulfur poisons the nickel (strongly adsorbed, blocks active sites).

parts.label: d
parts.text: The nickel is a solid, while the oil is a liquid and hydrogen is a gas. Name this type of catalysis and explain the name.
parts.answer: Catalyst in a different phase from reactants: heterogeneous catalysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem: E° values: Cr₂O₇²⁻/Cr³⁺ +1.33 V; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V; MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ +1.52 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate E°cell for the reaction of acidified dichromate(VI) with Fe²⁺ ions, and state whether it is feasible.
parts.answer: +0.56 V; feasible

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E°cell for (i) dichromate(VI) with chloride ions and (ii) manganate(VII) with chloride ions. Predict whether each reaction is feasible.
parts.answer: (i) −0.03 V, not feasible; (ii) +0.16 V, feasible
parts.working: B1 each with prediction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why iron(II) can be titrated with dichromate in hydrochloric acid, but not with manganate(VII).
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ would also oxidise Cl⁻ from the acid to Cl₂, so extra titrant is used (titre too large); Cr₂O₇²⁻ does not oxidise Cl⁻ under standard conditions.
parts.working: B1 MnO₄⁻ oxidises Cl⁻ → high titre; B1 dichromate does not.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Concentrated HCl does react slowly with warm dichromate(VI). Suggest why, even though E°cell is negative.
parts.answer: Non-standard conditions: high [H⁺] and [Cl⁻] (and higher temperature) make the electrode potentials change, so the reaction becomes feasible.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem: Vanadium forms several oxides. Oxide A contains 56.0 % vanadium by mass. (Ar: V 50.9; O 16.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of oxide A and give the oxidation state of vanadium in it.
parts.answer: V₂O₅; +5

parts.label: b
parts.text: 1.82 g of A (Mr 181.8) is heated with a reducing agent and loses 0.160 g of oxygen, forming oxide B. Deduce the formula of B and the oxidation state of vanadium in B.
parts.answer: VO₂ (V₂O₄); +4
parts.working: n(A) = 0.0100 mol, so 0.0200 mol V and 0.0500 mol O; O lost = 0.0100 mol, so 0.0400 mol O left (M1); V : O = 1 : 2, VO₂, +4 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electronic structure, why vanadium can form compounds with several different oxidation states.
parts.answer: The 3d and 4s electrons are similar in energy, so different numbers of them (up to five) can be lost or used in bonding.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol/dm³ KMnO₄ is added to an alkaline solution containing sulfite ions, SO₃²⁻. Exactly 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol of SO₃²⁻ reacts (oxidised to SO₄²⁻).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of electrons gained by each MnO₄⁻ ion, and hence the oxidation state of manganese in the product.
parts.answer: 3 electrons; +4
parts.working: n(MnO₄⁻) = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ (M1); SO₃²⁻ → SO₄²⁻ gives 2e⁻ each, so 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol e⁻ (M1); 3 per Mn, +7 → +4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the manganese product, describe its appearance and write the ionic equation.
parts.answer: MnO₂, a brown/black solid; 2MnO₄⁻ + 3SO₃²⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + 3SO₄²⁻ + 2OH⁻
parts.working: B1 MnO₂ brown precipitate; B1 equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the product of reduction of MnO₄⁻ in acidic solution and the number of electrons gained per MnO₄⁻.
parts.answer: Mn²⁺; 5

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration, in the form [Ar]3dˣ4sʸ, of: Ti; Ti²⁺; V³⁺; Co²⁺; Ni; Zn²⁺.
parts.answer: Ti [Ar]3d²4s²; Ti²⁺ [Ar]3d²; V³⁺ [Ar]3d²; Co²⁺ [Ar]3d⁷; Ni [Ar]3d⁸4s²; Zn²⁺ [Ar]3d¹⁰
parts.working: 3 marks all six; 2 marks five; 1 mark four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the two species in (a) that have the same electronic configuration.
parts.answer: Ti²⁺ and V³⁺ (both [Ar]3d²)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configurations of chromium and copper atoms in the form [Ar]3dˣ4sʸ.
parts.answer: Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these configurations do not follow the expected pattern.
parts.answer: A half-filled (3d⁵) or completely filled (3d¹⁰) d subshell gives extra stability (lower energy), since the 3d and 4s energies are very close.
parts.working: B1 half-filled/full 3d more stable; B1 3d and 4s close in energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the configuration of Cu²⁺.
parts.answer: [Ar]3d⁹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of 3d electrons in each ion: Sc³⁺; Ti⁴⁺; V³⁺; Fe³⁺; Cu⁺; Cu²⁺; Zn²⁺.
parts.working: 2 marks all seven; 1 mark five or six.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to predict which of these ions form coloured complexes, and explain.
parts.answer: Coloured: V³⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺ – partly filled 3d subshell allows electrons to be promoted between split d orbitals (absorbing visible light); colourless: Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺ (no d electrons), Cu⁺, Zn²⁺ (full d subshell, no d–d transition possible).
parts.working: B1 correct coloured list; B1 partly filled d subshell; B1 d⁰/d¹⁰ cannot have d–d transitions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the five 3d orbitals.
parts.answer: 3dxy, 3dxz, 3dyz, 3dx²−y², 3dz²
parts.working: B1 all five.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sort the five orbitals into two groups: those with lobes along the x, y and z axes, and those with lobes between the axes.
parts.answer: Along axes: dx²−y², dz²; between axes: dxy, dxz, dyz
parts.working: B1 each group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In an octahedral complex the six ligands approach along the axes. State which group of orbitals is raised to higher energy, and why.
parts.answer: dx²−y² and dz²; their lobes point directly at the ligand lone pairs, so there is greater repulsion.
parts.working: B1 group; B1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configurations of Mn, Mn²⁺ and of manganese in the +7 state, as in MnO₄⁻.
parts.answer: Mn [Ar]3d⁵4s²; Mn²⁺ [Ar]3d⁵; Mn(+7) [Ar] (1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The maximum oxidation states of Sc, Ti, V, Cr and Mn are +3, +4, +5, +6 and +7. Explain this pattern in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: The maximum oxidation state equals the total number of 4s and 3d electrons, which increases by one from Sc to Mn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the energies of the five 3d orbitals of Cr³⁺ when six water ligands surround it octahedrally.
parts.answer: The five d orbitals split into two energy levels: three lower (dxy, dxz, dyz) and two higher (dx²−y², dz²).
parts.working: B1 split into two levels; B1 three lower / two higher.

parts.label: b
parts.text: [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs most strongly at about 575 nm. Calculate the energy gap ΔE in kJ/mol. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 208 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a solution of [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ appears violet.
parts.answer: It absorbs yellow–green light (around 575 nm); the remaining transmitted light (red and blue/violet) appears violet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a tetrahedral complex the d orbitals also split into two sets. State which set is higher in energy.
parts.answer: dxy, dxz, dyz (three orbitals) higher; dx²−y², dz² lower (opposite to octahedral).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The energy gap in a tetrahedral complex is smaller than in an octahedral complex of the same metal ion and ligand. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Only four ligands (not six), so less repulsion; no ligands point directly at any d orbital.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether a tetrahedral complex absorbs light of longer or shorter wavelength than the octahedral complex of the same ion with the same ligand.
parts.answer: Longer; ΔE is smaller and λ = hc/ΔE, so a smaller energy gap means a longer wavelength.
parts.working: B1 longer; B1 reasoning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each compound, give the oxidation state of the metal and the number of 3d electrons: K₂[NiCl₄]; [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃; K₃[Fe(CN)₆]; [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃; KMnO₄.
parts.answer: Ni +2, d⁸; Co +3, d⁶; Fe +3, d⁵; Cr +3, d³; Mn +7, d⁰
parts.working: B1 each compound (oxidation state and d count).

parts.label: b
parts.text: KMnO₄ is intensely purple. Use your answer to (a) to explain why its colour cannot be caused by d–d electron transitions.
parts.answer: Mn(+7) has no d electrons (d⁰), so no d–d transition is possible; the colour has another cause.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of Ti³⁺.
parts.answer: [Ar]3d¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs most strongly at about 500 nm. Calculate ΔE in kJ/mol. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 239 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the spectrum of this ion shows only one main absorption.
parts.answer: With one d electron there is only one possible transition: from the lower set to the upper set.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The ion is purple. Explain this colour using the wavelength absorbed.
parts.answer: It absorbs green–yellow light (around 500 nm); the transmitted red and blue/violet light combine to look purple.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the 3d electrons in the split d orbitals of [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and give the number of unpaired electrons.
parts.answer: Cr³⁺ is d³: one electron in each of the three lower orbitals (parallel spins); upper two empty; 3 unpaired.
parts.working: B1 arrangement; B1 three unpaired.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do the same for [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.answer: Ni²⁺ is d⁸: three lower orbitals full (6 electrons, paired); one electron in each of the two upper orbitals; 2 unpaired.
parts.working: B1 arrangement; B1 two unpaired.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why electrons in (a) occupy separate orbitals before pairing.
parts.answer: Electrons repel each other; occupying separate orbitals (of equal energy) with parallel spins minimises repulsion.

stem: When excess concentrated ammonia is added to pale blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate, a deep blue solution forms. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs most strongly at about 800 nm and [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ at about 600 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy gap ΔE, in kJ/mol, for each complex. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ 150 kJ/mol; [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ 200 kJ/mol
parts.working: E = hcL/λ for each (M1); both values (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in colour in terms of d-orbital splitting.
parts.answer: Ammonia ligands cause a larger split (greater ΔE) than water, so the complex absorbs light of higher energy (shorter wavelength, more orange/yellow), and the transmitted colour becomes a deeper/violet-blue.
parts.working: B1 NH₃ larger ΔE; B1 absorbs shorter λ, so colour changes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the ligand exchange and name the type of reaction.
parts.answer: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ ⇌ [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O; ligand substitution (exchange)
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 type.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a blue complex:
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the shape and coordination number of each cobalt complex.
parts.answer: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ octahedral, 6; [CoCl₄]²⁻ tetrahedral, 4
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use d-orbital splitting to explain why the two complexes have different colours.
parts.answer: Different ligands and geometry give different ΔE (tetrahedral splitting smaller); so different wavelengths of light are absorbed and different colours are transmitted.
parts.working: B1 different ΔE (tetrahedral smaller); B1 different λ absorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When the pink-violet equilibrium mixture is warmed it turns blue. Deduce the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction.
parts.answer: Positive (endothermic): raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, towards [CoCl₄]²⁻.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict the colour change when water is added to the blue solution, and explain.
parts.answer: Turns pink; adding water shifts the equilibrium to the left (dilution / more H₂O).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an octahedral complex of a metal ion, the d-orbital energy gap is 2.48 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per ion. Calculate the wavelength, in nm, of light absorbed. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)
parts.answer: 802 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A tetrahedral complex of the same ion with the same ligand has an energy gap about 4/9 of the octahedral value. Calculate the wavelength absorbed and state the region of the spectrum.
parts.answer: 1.80 × 10³ nm (about 1800 nm); infrared
parts.working: ΔE = 2.48 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4/9 = 1.10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (M1); λ = hc/ΔE = 1.80 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1.80 × 10³ nm, infrared – outside the visible region (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what this means for the colour caused by d–d transitions in the tetrahedral complex.
parts.answer: Its d–d absorption is not in the visible region, so (on this basis) it would absorb little visible light and appear nearly colourless/pale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gaseous ion M³⁺ of a Period 4 element has three unpaired electrons in its 3d subshell. Give the two possible numbers of 3d electrons.
parts.answer: 3 or 7 (d³ or d⁷)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the element for each possibility.
parts.answer: d³: chromium (Cr³⁺); d⁷: nickel (Ni³⁺)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: M also forms the yellow ion MO₄²⁻. Identify M and give the electronic configuration of M in MO₄²⁻.
parts.answer: Chromium (+6 in CrO₄²⁻); [Ar] (3d⁰)
parts.working: B1 Cr; B1 configuration.

stem: A student in Karachi wants to find the concentration of ethanoic acid in a bottle of white vinegar, which is expected to be about 0.85 mol/dm³. The only alkali available is 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of undiluted vinegar, and use your answer to explain why the vinegar must be diluted first.
parts.answer: 212.5 cm³; far more than one 50 cm³ burette can deliver, so the vinegar is diluted (e.g. 1 in 10) to give a titre of about 21 cm³.
parts.working: M1 0.85 × 25.0 ÷ 0.100 = 212.5 cm³; A1 too big for one burette filling / dilute ×10 to give ≈ 21 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should dilute the vinegar exactly ten times, naming the apparatus used.
parts.answer: Pipette 25.0 cm³ of vinegar into a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask, make up to the mark with distilled water and invert to mix.
parts.working: B1 25.0 cm³ pipette + 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask; B1 distilled water to the mark (bottom of meniscus) and invert/shake to mix.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a suitable indicator, give its colour change at the end point and explain why methyl orange is not suitable.
parts.answer: Phenolphthalein, colourless to (pale) pink. A weak acid–strong base titration has an end point pH of about 8–9, outside the range of methyl orange (about 3–4.5).
parts.working: B1 phenolphthalein colourless → pink; B1 reason about end-point pH / sharp pH change in alkaline region.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Oxygen is made by adding a small amount of manganese(IV) oxide to 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrogen peroxide.
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
Molar gas volume at room conditions = 24.0 dm³/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen, in cm³, that can be produced at room conditions.
parts.answer: 48.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two pieces of apparatus are available to collect the gas: a 100 cm³ gas syringe and a 25 cm³ measuring cylinder over water. Choose the better one and explain your choice.
parts.answer: The 100 cm³ gas syringe: its capacity is larger than 48 cm³, whereas the 25 cm³ cylinder would overflow.
parts.working: B1 gas syringe; B1 capacity argument using the answer to (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the reaction can be started without losing any oxygen before the bung is in place.
parts.answer: Place the MnO₂ in a small tube (or tied in a muslin bag) inside the sealed flask, then tip/shake it into the peroxide after the apparatus is connected.
parts.working: B1 any method that mixes reactants only after the system is sealed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to measure the temperature change when 5.35 g of ammonium chloride (Mr 53.5) dissolves in 50.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. ΔH(solution) of NH₄Cl is +14.8 kJ/mol. Assume 50.0 g of solution with specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected temperature change and state whether the temperature rises or falls.
parts.answer: Fall of 7.08 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the apparatus used to measure the 50.0 cm³ of water and the 5.35 g of solid.
parts.answer: A 50 cm³ measuring cylinder (or burette/pipette) and a balance reading to 0.01 g.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons for using a polystyrene cup rather than a glass beaker.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a good insulator so less heat is gained from the surroundings; it has a very low heat capacity so it absorbs little energy itself.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A laboratory has these measuring devices: 100 cm³ beaker; 50 cm³ measuring cylinder; 25.0 cm³ volumetric pipette; 50.00 cm³ burette; 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Choose the most suitable device for each task.
(i) Transferring exactly 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask for titration.
(ii) Adding about 20 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid, which is in excess, to a solid.
(iii) Adding 3.00, 6.00, 9.00, 12.00 and 15.00 cm³ of acid to five separate tubes.
(iv) Making up a standard solution.
parts.answer: (i) volumetric pipette; (ii) measuring cylinder; (iii) burette; (iv) volumetric flask.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a beaker should never be used to measure a volume in a quantitative experiment.
parts.answer: Beaker graduations are only approximate (large uncertainty, about ±5 %).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student in Lahore plans to find the solubility of calcium hydroxide in water at 25 °C. Excess solid Ca(OH)₂ is shaken with distilled water and left in a water bath at 25 °C. The mixture is filtered and 25.0 cm³ of the filtrate is titrated with 0.0500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid; the mean titre is 23.30 cm³.
Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O   (Mr Ca(OH)₂ = 74.1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why excess solid is used and why the mixture is left in the water bath for some time before filtering.
parts.answer: Excess solid ensures the solution is saturated; time at 25 °C lets the solution reach equilibrium (saturation) at the stated temperature.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the filter paper, funnel and collecting flask must be dry, and why any solid in the filtrate must be avoided.
parts.answer: Water would dilute the saturated solution, lowering the titre; solid Ca(OH)₂ in the filtrate would react with acid and make the titre too high.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of calcium hydroxide in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0233 mol/dm³; 1.73 g/dm³
parts.working: M1 n(HCl) = 1.165 × 10⁻³; M1 n(Ca(OH)₂) = 5.825 × 10⁻⁴ in 25.0 cm³; A1 0.0233 mol/dm³ and 1.73 g/dm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
To find x in washing soda, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, 3.58 g of crystals are dissolved and made up to 250.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions are titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl using methyl orange; the mean titre is 25.00 cm³.
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂   (Mr Na₂CO₃ = 106.0, H₂O = 18.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the crystals and hence x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the colour of methyl orange at the end point.
parts.answer: Orange (from yellow).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Washing soda crystals lose water when left in dry air. Explain how this would affect the calculated value of x if the crystals were left out before weighing.
parts.answer: More Na₂CO₃ per gram, so more moles and a larger titre; calculated Mr and so x would be too low.
parts.working: M1 more moles per gram / larger titre; A1 x too low.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen peroxide oxidises iodide ions in acid: H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O. A student plans an 'iodine clock' to find the order with respect to I⁻. Each mixture contains fixed volumes of H₂O₂, H₂SO₄, a small fixed amount of sodium thiosulfate and starch. The volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ KI is varied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Five experiments use 10.0, 8.0, 6.0, 4.0 and 2.0 cm³ of KI solution. State what must be added to each mixture and in what volumes, and explain why.
parts.answer: Distilled water: 0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0 cm³, so the total volume is the same in each and [I⁻] is proportional to the volume of KI.
parts.working: B1 water volumes; B1 total volume constant so concentration ∝ volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is timed and how a value proportional to the initial rate is obtained.
parts.answer: Time t from mixing until the blue-black colour appears; rate ∝ 1/t.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the amount of thiosulfate must be both small and the same in each experiment.
parts.answer: Small: only a small fraction of reactant is used, so the rate measured is the initial rate; same: the same amount of I₂ is formed before the colour appears, so 1/t is proportional to rate in every experiment.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the graph that would show the reaction is first order with respect to I⁻.
parts.answer: A straight line through the origin for 1/t against volume (or concentration) of KI.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid is found by injecting 0.120 g of it into a gas syringe held in an oven at 100 °C. After all the liquid has vaporised, the volume of vapour is 66.2 cm³. Pressure = 101 kPa; R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of vapour and the Mr of the liquid.
parts.working: M1 conversion to Pa, m³ and K; M1 n = pV/RT = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol; A1 Mr = 55.6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which of these liquids it is: ethanol (Mr 46.0), propanone (Mr 58.0), hexane (Mr 86.0).
parts.answer: Propanone
parts.working: B1 closest value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two practical points the student must take care with to obtain an accurate result.
parts.answer: Any two: read the syringe volume only when it is constant (all liquid vaporised); subtract any air already in the syringe; weigh the hypodermic syringe before and after injection to find the mass injected; oven temperature must be above the boiling point and constant.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student plans to find the percentage of iron in iron tablets, each containing about 65 mg of iron as iron(II). Five tablets are crushed, dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions are titrated with 0.0100 mol/dm³ KMnO₄.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O   (Ar Fe = 55.8)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected titre.
parts.answer: 11.6 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student wants a titre of about 23 cm³. Suggest one change to the plan that would achieve this.
parts.answer: Use 0.00500 mol/dm³ KMnO₄ (or use ten tablets in 250.0 cm³).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute sulfuric acid is used rather than dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ would oxidise Cl⁻ to chlorine, using up extra manganate(VII) and making the titre too high.
parts.working: B1 Cl⁻ oxidised; B1 titre too high.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why no indicator is needed and give the colour at the end point.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ is almost colourless, so the first permanent pale pink colour shows excess MnO₄⁻.
parts.working: B1 self-indicating; B1 pale pink permanent.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The enthalpy change for MgCO₃(s) → MgO(s) + CO₂(g) cannot be measured directly, so a student plans two experiments with excess 2.0 mol/dm³ HCl (50.0 cm³ each, in a polystyrene cup).
Experiment A: 1.00 g MgO; temperature rise 17.5 °C.
Experiment B: 2.00 g MgCO₃; temperature rise 5.5 °C.
Use 50.0 g of solution, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; Mr MgO = 40.3, MgCO₃ = 84.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the enthalpy change cannot be measured directly.
parts.answer: Decomposition needs continuous strong heating, so the heat taken in cannot be measured / the reaction does not go to completion quickly at room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction in experiment A and in experiment B, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: A: −147 kJ/mol; B: −48.5 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 q values 3657 J and 1150 J; M1 moles 0.02481 and 0.02372; A1 both with negative sign.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use Hess's law to calculate ΔH for the decomposition of MgCO₃.
parts.answer: +98.9 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = ΔH(B) − ΔH(A); A1 +98.9 kJ/mol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why experiment B has a larger percentage error from heat losses than experiment A.
parts.answer: Its temperature rise is much smaller, so the fixed thermometer uncertainty (and spray loss as CO₂ escapes) is a larger fraction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to find Kc for CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. 0.100 mol of ethanoic acid, 0.100 mol of ethanol and 1.00 cm³ of concentrated HCl (catalyst) are sealed in a flask and kept at 25 °C for one week. The mixture is then poured into ice-cold water and titrated with 1.00 mol/dm³ NaOH; titre 42.4 cm³. A separate titration of 1.00 cm³ of the concentrated HCl alone, diluted the same way, needs 12.0 cm³ of the NaOH (concentrated HCl is about 12 mol/dm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the flask is sealed and left for a week.
parts.answer: Sealed so no volatile reactants/products escape; a week because the reaction is slow and must reach equilibrium.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mixture is poured into ice-cold water before titrating.
parts.answer: Cooling and dilution slow the reaction so the equilibrium position does not shift appreciably during the titration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount of ethanoic acid at equilibrium, then Kc. Explain why Kc has no units here.
parts.answer: n(CH₃COOH) = 0.0304 mol; Kc = 5.24; no units because the moles (and volumes) cancel.
parts.working: M1 subtract HCl titre: 42.4 − 12.0 = 30.4 cm³; M1 0.0304 mol acid; M1 ester = water = 0.0696 mol, ethanol = 0.0304 mol; A1 Kc = 5.24, no units.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to find the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol with a spirit burner under a copper can containing 200 g of water. Results: mass of burner before 85.62 g, after 85.17 g; temperature rise of the water 14.5 °C. c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; Mr propan-1-ol = 60.0. Data-book value: −2021 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔHc of propan-1-ol from these results.
parts.answer: −1620 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the magnitude of the result is lower than the data-book value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons for the difference and, for each, one change to the plan to reduce it.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the surroundings → use a draught shield / lid / insulate the can; incomplete combustion (soot) → ensure good air supply, short flame; evaporation of alcohol from the wick → keep cap on burner when weighing and weigh promptly; heat absorbed by the can → include its heat capacity.
parts.working: 2 × (reason B1 + matching improvement B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution with hydrochloric acid from a burette. Before starting, the student rinses every piece of glassware with distilled water only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the titre of rinsing the burette with water only before filling it with acid.
parts.answer: Titre is too large: water left in the burette dilutes the acid, so more acid solution is needed.
parts.working: B1 larger; B1 acid diluted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the titre of rinsing the pipette with water only before taking the alkali.
parts.answer: Titre is too small: the alkali is diluted, so fewer moles of NaOH are in the 25.0 cm³ portion.
parts.working: B1 smaller; B1 fewer moles of alkali.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rinsing the conical flask with distilled water has no effect on the titre.
parts.answer: The number of moles of NaOH pipetted into the flask is unchanged by extra water.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student heats copper(II) carbonate in an open crucible for five minutes, lets it cool, weighs it once and calculates the mass of carbon dioxide lost.
CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heating for a fixed time and weighing only once is a source of error, and state its effect on the calculated mass of CO₂.
parts.answer: Decomposition may be incomplete, so the mass lost (CO₂) is too small.
parts.working: B1 incomplete decomposition; B1 mass of CO₂ too low.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the improvement.
parts.answer: Heat, cool (in a desiccator), weigh; repeat heating, cooling and weighing until two consecutive masses agree (constant mass).
parts.working: B1 repeat heat-cool-weigh; B1 until constant mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During heating some powder spits out of the crucible. State the effect on the calculated mass of CO₂ and suggest how to prevent it.
parts.answer: Mass of CO₂ too high; heat gently at first / use a lid placed slightly ajar.
parts.working: B1 too high; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student times the reaction between a 2 cm length of magnesium ribbon and 2.0 mol/dm³ HCl with a hand-held stopwatch. The ribbon disappears in 12 s. The student estimates that their reaction time when starting and stopping the watch adds an uncertainty of ±0.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a change to the experiment that would reduce this percentage uncertainty, and explain why it works.
parts.answer: Use more dilute acid (or a lower temperature) so the reaction takes longer; the same ±0.5 s is then a smaller fraction of the time.
parts.working: B1 change; B1 explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other reason why the measured time may not be reliable for such a fast reaction.
parts.answer: Any one: ribbon floats/sticks to the side; judging the exact moment the last piece disappears is hard; heat released raises temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To measure the enthalpy change of Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), a student records the temperature of the CuSO₄ solution, adds excess zinc powder, stirs, and records the temperature again after exactly 2 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why recording only one temperature after 2 minutes may give a temperature rise that is too small.
parts.answer: The maximum may have been reached earlier and the mixture is already cooling (or the reaction is not yet complete), so the reading is below the true maximum.
parts.working: B1 heat loss/cooling; B1 maximum missed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the method should be improved to obtain a more accurate temperature rise.
parts.answer: Record the temperature every 30 s for a few minutes before and after adding zinc; plot temperature against time; extrapolate the cooling line back to the time of mixing to find the maximum rise.
parts.working: B1 regular readings before and after; B1 plot graph; B1 extrapolate back to time of mixing.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each error as random or systematic.
(i) A student reads a burette sometimes from above and sometimes from below eye level.
(ii) A balance that was not zeroed reads 0.12 g too high every time.
(iii) A thermometer always reads 1.0 °C below the true value.
(iv) A student judges the end point colour slightly differently in each titration.
parts.answer: (i) random; (ii) systematic; (iii) systematic; (iv) random.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which type of error can be reduced by repeating readings and taking a mean.
parts.answer: Random error.

stem:
A student finds the Mr of the gas in a butane lighter. The lighter is weighed, gas is released under water into an inverted measuring cylinder full of water, and the lighter is dried and reweighed.
mass lost = 0.25 g; volume of gas = 102 cm³ at room conditions (molar volume 24.0 dm³). True Mr of butane = 58.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the gas from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student did not dry the lighter fully before the second weighing. State and explain the effect on the calculated Mr.
parts.answer: Mass lost appears smaller (water adds mass), so Mr would be too low.
parts.working: B1 mass loss too small; B1 Mr too low.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the volume reading is less precise in a 250 cm³ cylinder than in a 100 cm³ cylinder, and give one other improvement.
parts.answer: Larger cylinder has wider graduations (larger uncertainty). Other: equalise water levels inside and outside before reading / use a gas syringe / release gas slowly so none escapes.
parts.working: B1 graduations; B1 improvement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student heats hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, to find x. The expected value is 2.
mass of crucible = 15.20 g
mass of crucible + hydrated salt = 17.64 g
mass of crucible + residue = 17.32 g
(Mr BaCl₂ = 208.3; H₂O = 18.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate x from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the most likely reason for the low value and an improvement.
parts.answer: Not all water removed (not heated to constant mass); heat, cool and reweigh until the mass is constant.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 improvement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a balance reading to 0.01 g is a limitation here, and suggest a better balance.
parts.answer: Mass of water (0.32 g) has a percentage uncertainty of about 3 % (two readings ±0.005 g); use a balance reading to 0.001 g or a larger sample.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
To find the concentration of a sample of hydrochloric acid, a student adds excess calcium carbonate to 50.0 cm³ of the acid in an open flask on a balance and records the total mass loss: 0.95 g. The acid is actually 1.00 mol/dm³.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂   (Mr CO₂ = 44.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the acid from the student's result and the percentage error.
parts.answer: 0.864 mol/dm³; 14 % low
parts.working: M1 n(CO₂) = 0.0216 mol; M1 n(HCl) = 0.0432 mol; A1 0.864 mol/dm³ (14 % low).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the result is low.
parts.answer: Some CO₂ remains dissolved in the solution; the final mass was read before the reaction was complete.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons that make mass loss too small.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a different measurement that would give a more accurate concentration.
parts.answer: Titrate the acid directly with a standard alkali (e.g. NaOH or Na₂CO₃ solution).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three students each measure the time for a cross to disappear in a thiosulfate–acid reaction 'at 30 °C' and repeat it three times.
Student P: 45, 46, 45 s, but P's water bath was later found to be at 33 °C.
Student Q: 38, 55, 47 s at 30.0 °C.
Student R: 50, 51, 50 s at 30.0 °C.
The true value at 30 °C is 50 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each student, state whether the results are precise (repeatable) and whether they are accurate.
parts.answer: P: precise but not accurate (systematic error); Q: not precise, mean ≈ 47 s, not reliable; R: precise and accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark per student.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why repeating the experiment does not remove the error in P's results.
parts.answer: The bath temperature is wrong every time (systematic error), so every reading is shifted the same way; repeats only reduce random error.
parts.working: B1 systematic; B1 repeats reduce random errors only.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student mixes 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ NaOH in an insulated cup. The temperature rise is 6.4 °C. The student says: 'My value is less exothermic than the standard enthalpy of neutralisation (−57.1 kJ/mol) only because of heat losses.' Use 100 g of solution and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation from these results.
parts.answer: −53.5 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 q = 2675 J; A1 ÷ 0.0500 mol, negative sign.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the student's statement.
parts.answer: Partly wrong: ethanoic acid is a weak acid, so energy is absorbed to ionise it fully as it is neutralised; this makes ΔH less exothermic than −57.1 even with no heat loss. Heat losses may also contribute.
parts.working: B1 weak acid / partly ionised; B1 ionisation endothermic; B1 conclusion that heat loss is not the only reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find how much of the difference is due to heat losses.
parts.answer: Repeat the experiment in the same apparatus with HCl (strong acid) and compare with −57.1 kJ/mol, or use a cooling curve correction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: To find Ea for a reaction, a student measures the time t for a fixed amount of product to form at only two temperatures: 84 s at 25 °C and 22 s at 45 °C. Rate ∝ 1/t. During the 45 °C run the student notices the mixture cooled to 41 °C by the end. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Ea from the student's two results, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: 52.8 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain whether the cooling during the 45 °C run makes the calculated Ea too high or too low.
parts.answer: Too low: the reaction ran at a lower average temperature, so it was slower and t too long; the rate ratio used with T₂ = 318 K is too small.
parts.working: B1 too low; B1 reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the plan.
parts.answer: Use at least five temperatures and plot ln(1/t) against 1/T, Ea from the gradient; use a thermostatically controlled water bath / pre-heat both solutions; record the temperature at the start and end and use the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Standard copper(II) sulfate solutions (0 to 0.100 mol/dm³) give a straight calibration line of absorbance against concentration through the origin with gradient 9.80 dm³/mol; the 0.100 mol/dm³ standard gave absorbance 0.98. An unknown solution gives absorbance 1.45, and the student extrapolates the line to obtain its concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration the student obtains by extrapolation.
parts.answer: 0.148 mol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this value is unreliable.
parts.answer: It is outside the range of the standards; there is no evidence the line stays straight (absorbance may not be proportional to concentration at high absorbance).
parts.working: B1 outside range; B1 linearity not shown.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student instead dilutes 25.0 cm³ of the unknown to 50.0 cm³ with a pipette and volumetric flask; the diluted solution has absorbance 0.72. Calculate the concentration of the original unknown.
parts.answer: 0.147 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one other source of error in colorimetry and how to avoid it.
parts.answer: Fingerprints/scratches/bubbles on the cuvette → handle by frosted sides, wipe clean, tap out bubbles; or wrong filter → use the complementary (red/orange) filter for blue Cu²⁺.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's thermometer reads 1.5 °C too high at all temperatures, and the balance reads 0.020 g too high at all masses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an enthalpy experiment the student records an initial temperature of 21.5 °C and a maximum of 33.0 °C. Explain whether the thermometer error affects the calculated ΔH.
parts.answer: No: both readings are 1.5 °C too high, so the difference ΔT (11.5 °C) is unchanged.
parts.working: B1 no; B1 difference cancels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The balance readings for weighing by difference are 25.384 g (bottle + solid) and 24.132 g (bottle after tipping). Calculate the mass of solid transferred and explain whether the balance error matters.
parts.answer: 1.252 g; no effect, the offset cancels when subtracting.
parts.working: B1 1.252 g; B1 cancels.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one measurement in which the thermometer error would give a wrong result, and explain.
parts.answer: A melting point or boiling point, which is a single reading, would be 1.5 °C too high and could lead to a wrong identification/purity judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Potassium hydrogen phthalate, KHC₈H₄O₄ (Mr 204.2), is used as a primary standard for alkalis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass needed to make 250.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two properties that make this compound a good primary standard.
parts.answer: Any two: available very pure; does not absorb water from the air (not hygroscopic); stable / does not react with air (CO₂, O₂); high Mr so weighing error is a small percentage; soluble in water.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A stock solution of 0.500 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate is used to make 50.0 cm³ of each of four standards for colorimetry: 0.100, 0.200, 0.300 and 0.400 mol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of stock solution and of distilled water needed for each standard.
parts.working: M1 V = c × 50.0 ÷ 0.500; A1 all four with water volumes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the apparatus that should be used to measure these volumes accurately.
parts.answer: Burettes (one for stock, one for water), or graduated pipettes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solutions must be mixed thoroughly before measuring absorbance.
parts.answer: So the concentration is uniform throughout and the reading represents the whole solution.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Silver nitrate (Mr 169.9) solution is used in chloride titrations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of silver nitrate needed to make 100.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol/dm³ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the solution is stored in a brown bottle.
parts.answer: Silver compounds are decomposed by light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why distilled (deionised) water must be used rather than tap water.
parts.answer: Tap water contains chloride ions, which would precipitate AgCl and lower the Ag⁺ concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student describes how they made a standard solution of sodium carbonate:
1. Weighed 2.65 g of the solid on a piece of filter paper.
2. Tipped the solid straight into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask.
3. Added tap water until the level was just above the line.
4. Removed the extra water with a dropping pipette until the meniscus was on the line.
5. Labelled the flask.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four mistakes in this method and give the correct procedure for each.
parts.answer: Weighing on paper loses solid/not weighed by difference → weigh in a weighing bottle and reweigh it after tipping; solid tipped straight into flask → dissolve in a beaker first, transfer with washings; tap water → distilled water; overfilled and water removed (solution removed too) → add water dropwise near the mark; not mixed → stopper and invert several times.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four mistakes with corrections.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is 18.0 mol/dm³. A technician must make 500.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of concentrated acid needed.
parts.answer: 13.9 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the order of mixing, and explain it.
parts.answer: Add the acid slowly to about 300 cm³ of water (never water to acid), stirring, then make up to 500.0 cm³ once cool; dilution is very exothermic and adding water to acid can boil and spit.
parts.working: B1 acid to water; B1 exothermic explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solution should be cooled to room temperature before making up to the mark.
parts.answer: Volumetric flasks are calibrated at 20 °C; warm solution has a larger volume, so the final concentration would be wrong.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O (Mr 392.1), is used to make a standard Fe²⁺ solution for titration with manganate(VII).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass needed for 250.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The solid is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid rather than water. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The acid stops Fe²⁺ being oxidised by air / hydrolysing to give a precipitate, and supplies the H⁺ needed in the titration.
parts.working: B1 prevents oxidation/hydrolysis; B1 provides acid for titration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solution should be used on the day it is made.
parts.answer: Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidised to Fe³⁺ by dissolved oxygen, lowering its concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A household bleach is too concentrated to titrate directly. 10.0 cm³ of the bleach is pipetted into a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask and made up with distilled water. 25.0 cm³ of the diluted bleach is found to contain 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol of chlorate(I), ClO⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ClO⁻ in the diluted bleach.
parts.answer: 0.0412 mol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ClO⁻ in the original bleach.
parts.answer: 1.03 mol/dm³
parts.working: M1 dilution factor 25; A1 1.03 mol/dm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the dilution factor and explain why a pipette must be rinsed with bleach, not water, before use.
parts.answer: Factor 25; water left in the pipette would dilute the bleach, so fewer moles would be transferred.
parts.working: B1 25; B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaCl(aq) is mixed with 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ CaCl₂(aq). Assume volumes are additive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of chloride ions in the mixture.
parts.answer: 0.180 mol/dm³
parts.working: M1 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol from NaCl; M1 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol from CaCl₂; A1 ÷ 0.0500 dm³ = 0.180 mol/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of calcium ions in the mixture.
parts.answer: 0.0600 mol/dm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student weighs 1.325 g of a solid by difference on a balance reading to ±0.001 g per reading, then makes it up to 250.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask with uncertainty ±0.3 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass.
parts.working: B1 two readings: ±0.002 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume and the total percentage uncertainty in the concentration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the percentage uncertainty in the mass could be halved without changing the balance.
parts.answer: Weigh twice the mass and make up to 500.0 cm³ (or a larger mass in a larger flask).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Concentrated hydrochloric acid has a density of 1.18 g/cm³ and contains 36.0 % HCl by mass (Mr HCl = 36.5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the concentrated acid in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 11.6 mol/dm³
parts.working: M1 1 dm³ has mass 1180 g, of which 424.8 g is HCl; A1 11.6 mol/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the concentrated acid needed to make 1.00 dm³ of approximately 0.100 mol/dm³ acid.
parts.answer: 8.59 cm³
parts.working: B1 ecf.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the diluted acid cannot be used as a primary standard and must be standardised.
parts.answer: Concentrated HCl loses HCl gas (volatile) and the stated percentage is approximate, so its exact concentration is unknown; it must be titrated against a primary standard such as anhydrous Na₂CO₃.
parts.working: B1 volatile/inexact; B1 titrate against primary standard.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is standardised against potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP, Mr 204.2), a monoprotic acid. 0.510 g of KHP is weighed by difference into a conical flask, dissolved in water and titrated; 24.65 cm³ of NaOH is required.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium hydroxide cannot be weighed out to make a standard solution.
parts.answer: It absorbs water from the air (deliquescent) and reacts with CO₂ in air, so the mass weighed is not all NaOH.
parts.working: B1 water; B1 CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
parts.answer: 0.101 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the KHP is weighed directly into the conical flask rather than made up into a solution here, and why the volume of water used to dissolve it does not need to be measured accurately.
parts.answer: Weighing by difference straight into the flask gives the exact moles titrated; the moles of acid do not depend on the volume of water.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A buffer of pH 5.00 is to be made by mixing 0.200 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid with 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium ethanoate to give 100.0 cm³ in total. Ka of ethanoic acid = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio [CH₃COO⁻] ÷ [CH₃COOH] needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of each solution to mix.
parts.answer: ethanoic acid 36.5 cm³; sodium ethanoate 63.5 cm³
parts.working: M1 equal concentrations so volume ratio = 1.74; A1 both volumes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the apparatus used to measure these volumes and suggest how the pH should be checked.
parts.answer: Two burettes; use a pH meter calibrated with standard buffers.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student needs a 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³ solution of a dye from a 0.100 mol/dm³ stock. Apparatus: 10.00 cm³ pipette (±0.02 cm³) and 100.0 cm³ volumetric flasks (±0.10 cm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of stock that a single dilution to 100.0 cm³ would need, and explain why this is not practical.
parts.answer: 0.0100 cm³; far too small to measure accurately with normal apparatus.
parts.working: B1 0.0100 cm³; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a serial dilution to make the solution.
parts.answer: Four successive 1 in 10 dilutions: pipette 10.00 cm³ into a 100.0 cm³ flask, make up and mix; repeat with the new solution three more times (0.0100 → 1.00 × 10⁻³ → 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ → 1.00 × 10⁻⁵).
parts.working: B1 four ×10 steps; B1 correct technique.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the maximum percentage uncertainty in the final concentration.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
Molten lauric acid is left to cool and its temperature is recorded every minute.
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
temperature / °C: 60.0, 52.5, 46.0, 43.9, 43.9, 43.9, 43.8, 40.1, 35.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which variable goes on the x-axis and describe the shape of the line that should be drawn.
parts.answer: Time on the x-axis; a smooth falling curve, then a horizontal line (about 3–6 min), then a falling curve again.
parts.working: B1 time on x; B1 curve–plateau–curve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to give the freezing point of lauric acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the points must not be joined 'dot to dot' with straight ruled lines.
parts.answer: The temperature changes smoothly between readings; a best-fit smooth curve averages out random errors.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem: A student must plot the volume of gas collected (up to 87 cm³) against time (up to 300 s). The graph grid has 8 large squares across and 12 large squares up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for each axis and check that the points use more than half the grid in each direction.
parts.answer: x: 50 s per large square (300 s uses 6 of 8 squares); y: 10 cm³ per large square (87 cm³ uses about 9 of 12).
parts.working: B1 each sensible scale that uses > half the grid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a scale of 3 cm³ per large square would be a poor choice even though it fits.
parts.answer: Awkward to plot and read values (not 1, 2, 5 or 10 multiples), so errors are likely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what each axis label must include.
parts.answer: The quantity and its unit, e.g. 'volume of gas / cm³'.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
A teacher marks a student's graph of the mass of product against the mass of reactant. The teacher notes:
• points are plotted as large dots about 3 mm across
• consecutive points are joined with straight lines
• the y-axis is labelled 'mass' only
• the x-axis scale goes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12
• the line is forced through (0, 0) although the student's data show a clear intercept on the y-axis

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is wrong with each feature and how it should be corrected.
parts.answer: Large dots → use small neat crosses or dots with circles so the centre is exact; dot-to-dot → one best-fit straight line or smooth curve; label lacks unit → 'mass of product / g'; awkward scale → use 1, 2, 5 or 10 per square; forcing through origin → draw the best-fit line through the data, only through the origin if (0,0) is a genuine data point/expected.
parts.working: 1 mark per feature.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
The solubility of potassium nitrate in water was measured at several temperatures.
temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
solubility / g per 100 g water: 31.6, 45.8, 63.9, 85.5, 110.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether a straight line or a smooth curve should be drawn through these points, with a reason.
parts.answer: Smooth curve: the increase in solubility gets larger for each 10 °C rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the solubility at 45 °C by assuming a straight line between the 40 °C and 50 °C points.
parts.answer: 74.7 g per 100 g water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the value read from the best-fit curve at 45 °C would be slightly higher or lower than your estimate.
parts.answer: Lower: the curve bends upwards (concave up), so it lies below the straight line joining the two points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
Different masses of magnesium react with excess acid and the hydrogen is collected at room conditions (molar volume 24.0 dm³).
mass of Mg / g: 0.020, 0.040, 0.060, 0.080, 0.100
volume of H₂ / cm³: 19.5, 39.8, 59.0, 80.2, 98.9
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the best-fit line should pass through the origin.
parts.answer: No magnesium gives no hydrogen (volume ∝ mass).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The best-fit straight line through the origin passes through (0.100 g, 99.0 cm³). Calculate its gradient, with units.
parts.answer: 990 cm³/g

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the gradient to calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium.
parts.working: M1 1 g gives 990 cm³, so 1 mol (24 000 cm³) of H₂ comes from 24 000 ÷ 990 g of Mg; A1 24.2.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
A fixed amount of air in a sealed gas syringe is heated in a water bath at constant pressure.
temperature / °C: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
volume / cm³: 50.0, 53.4, 56.8, 60.2, 63.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the straight line.
parts.answer: 0.170 cm³ per °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the line to find the temperature, in °C, at which the volume would be zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is an extrapolation and comment on its reliability.
parts.answer: The value lies far outside the range of the data; it assumes the line stays straight (ideal gas behaviour) – the gas would liquefy before this, but the answer agrees closely with absolute zero (−273 °C).
parts.working: B1 outside range; B1 comment.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
In a thermometric experiment, the temperature of an acid is recorded every 0.5 min. At 3.5 min an alkali is added. Readings:
0.0–3.0 min: 21.0 °C (constant)
4.0 min: 31.2; 4.5 min: 30.9; 5.0 min: 30.6; 5.5 min: 30.3; 6.0 min: 30.0 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the two best-fit lines that should be drawn.
parts.answer: A horizontal line through the readings before mixing; a straight (cooling) line through the readings after 4.0 min, extended back to 3.5 min.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Extrapolate the cooling line to 3.5 min to find the maximum temperature and the corrected temperature rise.
parts.working: M1 cooling rate 0.6 °C/min; A1 31.5 °C and 10.5 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the extrapolated value is used instead of the highest reading.
parts.answer: Heat is lost while the reaction is still going on; extrapolating estimates the temperature if mixing and reaction were instantaneous with no loss.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem: A calibration graph of absorbance against concentration of iron(III) thiocyanate is drawn. The best-fit straight line passes through (0, 0.02) and (5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³, 1.02).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line, with units.
parts.answer: 2000 dm³/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample has absorbance 0.66. Use the line to find its concentration.
parts.answer: 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the line does not pass through the origin, and how this could be avoided.
parts.answer: The colorimeter was not zeroed with a blank (or the cuvette absorbs a little); zero the instrument with a cuvette of the solvent/blank before measuring.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 fix.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
Boiling points of straight-chain alkanes:
number of carbon atoms: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
boiling point / °C: −162, −89, −42, −1, 36, 69, 98

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether a straight line or a smooth curve best fits the data, using the differences between successive boiling points.
parts.answer: Smooth curve: the rises are 73, 47, 41, 37, 33, 29 °C – they get smaller, so the gradient decreases.
parts.working: M1 differences; A1 curve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the trend to estimate the boiling point of octane.
parts.answer: About 124 °C (next difference about 26 °C); accept 122–128 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.answer: More electrons/larger surface area → stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces → more energy to separate molecules; each extra CH₂ adds a smaller fraction to the total.
parts.working: B1 id-id forces increase; B1 smaller fractional increase.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
The initial rate of a reaction is measured at different concentrations of reactant A.
[A] / mol dm⁻³: 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80
initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴, 8.1 × 10⁻⁴, 3.2 × 10⁻³, 1.28 × 10⁻²
A graph of lg(rate) against lg[A] is plotted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate lg[A] and lg(rate) for the first and last experiments.
parts.working: B1 lg[A] pair; B1 lg(rate) pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line and state the order with respect to A.
parts.answer: gradient = 2.00; second order
parts.working: M1 gradient; A1 order 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the log–log graph is more useful than a graph of rate against [A] here.
parts.answer: It gives a straight line whose gradient is the order directly (rate = k[A]ⁿ → lg rate = n lg[A] + lg k), and the intercept gives lg k.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
Rate constants for a reaction at four temperatures:
T / K: 293, 303, 313, 323
k / s⁻¹: 0.0121, 0.0238, 0.0448, 0.0813
R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ln k = −Ea/(RT) + ln A

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what should be plotted on each axis to give a straight line.
parts.answer: ln k on the y-axis against 1/T on the x-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1/T and ln k for the first and last temperatures.
parts.working: B1 1/T values; B1 ln k values.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assuming the best-fit line passes through these two points, calculate Ea in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: 49.9 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 gradient = −Ea/R ≈ −6.0 × 10³ K; A1 Ea = 49.9 kJ/mol (accept 49–51).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the x-axis does not need to start at zero.
parts.answer: 1/T values lie in a narrow range (3.1–3.4 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹); starting at zero would squash the points into a small part of the grid.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
The concentration of a reactant B is measured over time in a first-order reaction.
t / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120
[B] / mol dm⁻³: 0.0800, 0.0567, 0.0401, 0.0284, 0.0201

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what should be plotted against t to give a straight line, and why.
parts.answer: ln[B]: for a first-order reaction ln[B] = ln[B]₀ − kt, so the graph is a straight line of gradient −k.
parts.working: B1 ln[B]; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first and last points, calculate k.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the half-life and check it against the data.
parts.answer: 60.2 s; [B] halves from 0.0800 to 0.0401 in 60 s, consistent.
parts.working: B1 t½ = 0.693/k; B1 check.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
stem:
A fixed amount of gas is compressed at 298 K.
pressure / kPa: 100, 125, 150, 200, 250
volume / cm³: 60.0, 48.0, 40.0, 30.0, 24.0
R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest what to plot to obtain a straight line through the origin, and calculate the value for p = 125 kPa.
parts.answer: V against 1/p; 1/p = 0.00800 kPa⁻¹ at 125 kPa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gradient of this line is 6000 kPa cm³. Calculate the amount of gas, in mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why plotting V against p would make it hard to check the relationship.
parts.answer: It gives a curve (hyperbola); it is hard to judge by eye whether a curve fits a particular law, whereas a straight line is easy to test.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student uses a thermometer marked every 1 °C, which can be read to the nearest 0.5 °C. The results table is headed 'Temp' and contains the readings: 25, 25.5, 26.0, 27, 26.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rewrite the readings as they should be recorded.
parts.working: B1 all to 1 decimal place (nearest 0.5 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a correct column heading.
parts.answer: temperature / °C (or T / °C)
parts.working: B1 quantity and unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why all readings from the same instrument should be recorded to the same number of decimal places.
parts.answer: They have the same precision; writing '25' suggests a lower precision than '25.5'.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the number of significant figures in each value.
(i) 0.0250 mol/dm³
(ii) 25.00 cm³
(iii) 1.20 × 10³ J
(iv) 0.00305 g
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: 2.46 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Mr 106.0) is dissolved in water and made up to 250.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the solution and give it to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0928 mol/dm³
parts.working: M1 n = 0.02321 mol; A1 0.0928 mol/dm³ to 3 s.f.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your choice of significant figures.
parts.answer: The least precise data (mass, 2.46 g) has 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The time t for a precipitate to obscure a cross is measured for five concentrations of thiosulfate.
t / s: 125, 84, 63, 50, 42
The student calculates a 'rate' for each, equal to 1000/t.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1000/t for each time to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 values; A1 all to 3 s.f. (8.00 and 20.0 with trailing zeros).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a suitable column heading for these values.
parts.answer: 1000/t (rate in 10⁻³ s⁻¹)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three portions of 0.150 mol/dm³ HCl are measured: 12.40 cm³, 18.60 cm³ and 24.80 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of HCl in each portion.
parts.working: M1 convert cm³ to dm³; A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: These are written in a table column headed 'amount of HCl / 10⁻³ mol'. State the numbers that appear in the column.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Potassium chlorate(V) is heated to constant mass in a boiling tube.
mass of tube = 21.36 g
mass of tube + KClO₃ = 23.81 g
mass of tube + residue = 22.85 g
(Mr KClO₃ = 122.6; O₂ = 32.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of KClO₃ used and the mass of oxygen given off.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of each and the ratio mol O₂ : mol KClO₃.
parts.answer: KClO₃ 0.0200 mol; O₂ 0.0300 mol; ratio 1.50
parts.working: M1 moles; A1 ratio 1.50.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the result agrees with the equation 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, and state how many significant figures the ratio deserves.
parts.answer: 3 : 2 = 1.50 – agrees; 2 s.f. at most, since 0.96 g has only 2 significant figures.
parts.working: B1 agreement; B1 2 s.f. with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student heats a small sample of a hydrated salt:
mass of crucible = 12.43 g
mass of crucible + hydrated salt = 12.98 g
mass of crucible + anhydrous salt = 12.91 g
The balance reads to ±0.005 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost and state how many significant figures it has.
parts.answer: 0.07 g; 1 significant figure

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of water (two readings).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a value of x calculated from these results cannot be quoted to 3 significant figures, and suggest how to improve the experiment.
parts.answer: The mass of water is known only to 1 s.f. (about ±14 %), so x is no better than 1 s.f.; use a much larger sample (several grams) so the mass loss is larger.
parts.working: B1 reasoning; B1 larger mass.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A sample of impure iron(II) sulfate crystals, FeSO₄·7H₂O (Mr 278.0), of mass 0.700 g is dissolved in acid and made up to 250.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions need a mean titre of 23.45 cm³ of 0.00200 mol/dm³ KMnO₄.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of FeSO₄·7H₂O in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage purity, to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.working: B1 value; B1 3 s.f. justified by 0.700 g and 0.00200 mol/dm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a rate experiment, each mixture contains V cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ Na₂S₂O₃, (50 − V) cm³ of water and 10.0 cm³ of HCl (total 60.0 cm³). V = 10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0 and 50.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of thiosulfate in each mixture, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these concentrations, rather than V, would be used if the results were compared with another group who used a total volume of 100 cm³.
parts.answer: Rate depends on concentration; the same V gives a different concentration in a different total volume.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a thermometric titration, 1.00 mol/dm³ HCl is added from a burette to 25.0 cm³ of NaOH and the highest temperature after each addition is recorded.
volume of HCl / cm³: 0, 5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 30.0, 35.0, 40.0
temperature / °C: 22.0, 24.4, 26.8, 29.2, 31.6, 31.0, 30.4, 29.8
The rising points lie on one straight line and the falling points on another.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of each line (T in terms of V).
parts.answer: rising: T = 22.0 + 0.48V; falling: T = 34.6 − 0.12V
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume at which the lines cross and the maximum temperature.
parts.working: M1 solve simultaneously; A1 both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
parts.answer: 0.840 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after the end point.
parts.answer: No more reaction (no more heat released); cooler acid is added and heat is lost to the surroundings.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.0485 g of magnesium reacts with excess acid to give 48.6 cm³ of hydrogen at room conditions (molar volume 24.0 dm³). Student X rounds n(H₂) to 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol before the next step; student Y keeps all figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Ar of Mg obtained by each student, to 4 significant figures for comparison.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why X's method is wrong even though X's answer is closer to the accepted value 24.3.
parts.answer: Rounding an intermediate value to 2 s.f. introduces an extra error (here about 1 %) unrelated to the data; the agreement is accidental. Intermediate values should be kept unrounded and only the final answer given to 3 s.f.
parts.working: B1 rounding error; B1 keep figures until end.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on Y's answer.
parts.answer: It is about 1.4 % low, so the gas volume was too large for the mass used: e.g. the gas was warmer than room temperature when read (reaction is exothermic), it contained water vapour, or the volume of acid added pushed extra air into the collector.
parts.working: B1 % low with a reason that makes the volume too large.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An oxide of copper is reduced to copper in a stream of hydrogen.
mass of tube = 31.24 g
mass of tube + oxide = 33.67 g
mass of tube + copper = 33.18 g
The balance reads to ±0.005 g. (Ar Cu = 63.5, O = 16.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts of copper and oxygen and deduce the formula of the oxide.
parts.answer: Cu 0.0306 mol; O 0.0306 mol; ratio 1 : 1, CuO
parts.working: M1 masses 1.94 g and 0.49 g; M1 moles; A1 CuO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of oxygen and explain whether the data could be consistent with Cu₂O.
parts.answer: 2.0 %; no – Cu₂O would need a 2 : 1 ratio, far outside a 2 % uncertainty.
parts.working: B1 2.0 %; B1 reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one safety precaution for this experiment.
parts.answer: Burn excess hydrogen at the outlet only after air has been flushed out (test for purity first) / keep H₂ flowing while the copper cools so it is not reoxidised.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
To find the purity of an ammonium sulfate fertiliser from a farm in Sindh, 1.50 g of fertiliser is boiled with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ NaOH until no more ammonia is given off. The remaining NaOH needs 54.70 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ HCl.
(NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O   (Mr (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 132.1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of NaOH that reacted with the fertiliser.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage purity, giving your answer to a suitable number of significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the answer cannot reasonably be given to more than 3 s.f. even though the titre has 4 s.f.
parts.answer: The mass (1.50 g) and the NaOH volume (50.0 cm³) have only 3 s.f.; also the answer depends on a difference, which increases the uncertainty.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student records burette readings as: initial 0.0, final 23.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is wrong with this recording and rewrite the readings correctly, assuming the meniscus was exactly on the lines.
parts.answer: Burette readings must be recorded to 2 decimal places (nearest 0.05 cm³): initial 0.00, final 23.40.
parts.working: B1 2 d.p./nearest 0.05; B1 0.00 and 23.40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the eye and the meniscus should be positioned when reading a burette.
parts.answer: Eye level with the bottom of the meniscus (to avoid parallax).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the titre.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Titres (cm³) for an acid–alkali titration:
rough: 24.85
run 1: 24.55
run 2: 24.60
run 3: 24.50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rough titre is not used in the mean.
parts.answer: It was done quickly (acid added fast) to find the approximate end point, so it overshoots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that runs 1–3 are concordant and calculate the mean titre.
parts.answer: All within 0.10 cm³ of each other; mean = 24.55 cm³
parts.working: B1 concordance; B1 24.55.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Give the reason for each step in a titration.
(i) Placing the conical flask on a white tile.
(ii) Swirling the flask continuously.
(iii) Adding the titrant drop by drop near the end point.
(iv) Washing the inside of the flask with a little distilled water near the end point.
parts.answer: (i) to see the colour change clearly; (ii) to mix the reactants so the indicator responds to the whole solution; (iii) so the end point is not overshot (one drop changes colour); (iv) to rinse titrant from the walls into the solution so it all reacts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Three accurate titres are 18.35, 18.75 and 18.45 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the titres that should be used to calculate the mean and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 18.35 and 18.45: they agree within 0.10 cm³; 18.75 does not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean titre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the student should do next to improve confidence in the mean.
parts.answer: Carry out another titration to obtain a third concordant titre.

author: HomiLabs

stem: State and explain the effect of each mistake on the titre measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An air bubble in the burette jet is expelled during the titration.
parts.answer: Titre too large: the volume of the bubble is read as liquid delivered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The funnel used to fill the burette is left in the top and drips into the burette during the titration.
parts.answer: Titre too small: extra liquid drips into the burette during the run, so the final reading is higher than it would be and the apparent volume delivered is smaller.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student reads both burette readings from above eye level.
parts.answer: Little or no effect on the titre: both readings are wrong in the same way, so the difference is roughly unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The pipette is not rinsed with the solution it is used for and contains drops of water.
parts.answer: Titre too small: the pipetted solution is diluted, so it contains fewer moles.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.0500 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid.
rough: initial 0.00, final 22.60
run 1: initial 0.10, final 22.20
run 2: initial 22.20, final 44.35
run 3: initial 0.00, final 22.05
2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the titres and the mean titre.
parts.answer: 22.10, 22.15, 22.05 cm³ (rough titre 22.60 not used); mean of runs 1–3 = 22.10 cm³
parts.working: B1 titres; B1 mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: 0.0884 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why run 2 started at 22.20 cm³ and why this is acceptable here.
parts.answer: The burette was not refilled; acceptable because there was enough acid left (more than one titre) in the 50 cm³ burette.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An iodine solution is titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium thiosulfate. 25.0 cm³ of the iodine solution needs a mean titre of 21.60 cm³.
I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe when starch is added and the colour change at the end point.
parts.answer: Add starch when the solution is pale yellow (near the end point); end point is blue-black to colourless.
parts.working: B1 when; B1 colour change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why starch is not added at the start.
parts.answer: With a lot of iodine the starch–iodine complex forms strongly and releases iodine slowly, making the end point hard to judge (late).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of iodine.
parts.answer: 0.0432 mol/dm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: Burette readings each have an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. A student obtains a mean titre of 12.30 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a titre of 12.30 cm³.
parts.working: B1 two readings, ±0.10 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty if the titre were 24.60 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two changes that would double the titre without changing the burette.
parts.answer: Use a titrant half as concentrated; use a 50.0 cm³ pipette (double the volume of solution titrated) / make the solution in the flask twice as concentrated.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
1.26 g of hydrated ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O (Mr 126.0), is made up to 250.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions, acidified and warmed to about 60 °C, are titrated with 0.0200 mol/dm³ KMnO₄.
2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂C₂O₄ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected titre.
parts.working: M1 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol acid per 25.0 cm³; M1 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol MnO₄⁻; A1 20.00 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pink colour disappears slowly with the first few drops but quickly later. Explain.
parts.answer: Mn²⁺ produced catalyses the reaction (autocatalysis); at first there is little Mn²⁺.
