parts.text: Explain why hydrogen must be passed through the apparatus for some time before heating starts.
parts.answer: To flush out the air; a mixture of hydrogen and air can explode when heated.
parts.working: B1 flush air; B1 explosive mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student can show that the air has been removed.
parts.answer: Collect a sample of the gas at the outlet in a test-tube and light it: it should burn quietly, not pop/squeak.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the hydrogen flow is continued while the copper cools.
parts.answer: To stop hot copper being re-oxidised by air entering the tube.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A technician prepares solutions from concentrated ammonia (about 15 mol/dm³) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (about 12 mol/dm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main hazards of these two reagents.
parts.answer: Concentrated ammonia gives off toxic/irritant ammonia gas (and is corrosive); concentrated HCl gives off corrosive HCl fumes (and is corrosive).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two precautions for diluting them.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard; wear goggles and gloves; keep the bottles apart/stoppered (NH₃ and HCl fumes form a white smoke of NH₄Cl).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Excess dilute HCl is added to calcium carbonate in a flask connected to a 100 cm³ gas syringe. Molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³/mol; Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced from 0.50 g of CaCO₃.
parts.answer: 120 cm³
parts.working: M1 n = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol; A1 120 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the safety and practical problem this causes, and calculate the maximum safe mass of CaCO₃.
parts.answer: The gas exceeds the syringe capacity: the plunger could be forced out or the bung blown off; maximum ≈ 0.417 g (use about 0.35 g).
parts.working: B1 problem; B1 0.417 g.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to react sodium with ethanol to make sodium ethoxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation and state the hazard from the gas produced.
parts.answer: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂; hydrogen is flammable/explosive with air.
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 hazard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how sodium should be stored and handled.
parts.answer: Stored under oil (paraffin); cut with a scalpel on a tile, handled with tongs, small pieces only, never touched with fingers.
parts.working: B1 storage; B1 handling.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why unused pieces of sodium are destroyed by adding them to ethanol rather than water.
parts.answer: Sodium reacts violently with water (H₂ may ignite); the reaction with ethanol is slower and controlled.
parts.working: B1 violent with water; B1 ethanol slower.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chlorine is made in a fume cupboard by adding concentrated HCl to 0.316 g of potassium manganate(VII) (Mr 158.0).
2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O
Molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of chlorine produced.
parts.answer: 120 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how excess chlorine leaving the apparatus can be made safe.
parts.answer: Pass it through (bubble into) aqueous sodium hydroxide, which absorbs it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the amounts of reagents used should be kept as small as possible.
parts.answer: Chlorine is toxic; less reagent means less chlorine can escape if something goes wrong.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student dissolves 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide pellets (Mr 40.0) in 50.0 g of water. ΔH(solution) of NaOH = −44.5 kJ/mol. Assume the solution has mass 54.0 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain two hazards of making concentrated NaOH solution, and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: The solution becomes hot (can boil/spit if large amounts are dissolved quickly) – add pellets slowly to cold water with stirring/cooling; the solution is corrosive – goggles and gloves.
parts.working: 1 mark each hazard + precaution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the solution should be cooled before being made up in a volumetric flask.
parts.answer: Warm solution occupies a larger volume (flask calibrated at 20 °C), so the concentration would be wrong; hot glass could crack.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student's plan contains this safety section: 'Wear safety glasses. Be careful with chemicals. Do everything in a fume cupboard. Wash hands at the end.' The experiment is the titration of aqueous ammonia (0.5 mol/dm³) with dilute hydrochloric acid (0.5 mol/dm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this safety section.
parts.answer: It is vague and not linked to specific hazards ('be careful' is not a precaution); a fume cupboard is unnecessary for dilute solutions; it does not mention the real hazards: dilute ammonia and HCl are irritant to eyes/skin; it omits pipette safety (use a pipette filler, never mouth pipette).
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid criticism (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite it as two specific precautions.
parts.answer: Use a pipette filler to fill the pipette with aqueous ammonia (irritant); wear goggles because both solutions are irritant to eyes, and rinse spills from the skin with water.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Propanone reacts with iodine in acid solution. Starch is added, and the time for the blue-black colour to appear is recorded. The total volume is kept at 50.0 cm³ with water, so the iodine and acid concentrations are the same in every experiment.
volume of propanone / cm³: 5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0
time to blue-black / s: 240, 120, 80, 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of 1000/t for each experiment, to 3 significant figures. Give units of 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
parts.working: B2 all four correct to 3 s.f. (B1 for two or three correct). 1000/240 = 4.17, 1000/60 = 16.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the volume of propanone and the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: The rate increases in direct proportion to the volume of propanone; doubling the volume roughly doubles the rate.
parts.working: B1 rate increases as volume increases; B1 directly proportional / doubling volume doubles rate (rate ∝ volume).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of reaction can be taken as 1/t.
parts.answer: The same amount of iodine is removed in every experiment, so the faster the reaction, the shorter the time t.
parts.working: B1 same amount of iodine reacts each time (fixed quantity); B1 rate ∝ 1/t, so a larger rate gives a shorter time.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrogen peroxide is poured into a conical flask with a spatula of manganese(IV) oxide. The flask, with a loose cotton-wool plug, sits on a top-pan balance as oxygen is released.
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180
mass of flask and contents / g: 100.00, 99.82, 99.66, 99.54, 99.46, 99.36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen lost at 60 s and at 180 s.
parts.working: B1 0.34 g at 60 s; B1 0.64 g at 180 s (100.00 minus the reading).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of oxygen lost by 60 s, and hence the amount of H₂O₂ that has decomposed by then.
parts.working: M1 0.34/32.0 = 0.010625 mol O₂; A1 2 × 0.010625 = 0.0213 mol H₂O₂ (2 mol H₂O₂ give 1 mol O₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of loss of mass over the first 60 s, in g/s, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the cotton wool plug is loose.
parts.answer: It lets oxygen escape so the pressure does not build up, but stops liquid spray being lost.
parts.working: B1 allows gas to escape; stops spray/liquid being lost (which would add to the mass loss).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sodium thiosulfate solution of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³ is diluted with water to a total of 50.0 cm³ in each experiment. Then 5.0 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is added and the time for a cross marked under the flask to disappear is recorded. Ignore the small dilution by the acid.
volume of Na₂S₂O₃ solution / cm³: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10
volume of water / cm³: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
time for cross to disappear / s: 18.0, 22.5, 30.0, 45.0, 90.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of Na₂S₂O₃ in the experiment using 30.0 cm³ of the stock solution.
parts.answer: 0.0600 mol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1/t for the experiment using 20.0 cm³ of stock solution, in s⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that 1/t is directly proportional to the concentration of thiosulfate, and state the order of reaction with respect to thiosulfate.
parts.answer: 1/t ÷ concentration is constant (0.0556 ÷ 0.100 = 0.0222 ÷ 0.0400 = 0.556 s⁻¹ per mol/dm³), so rate ∝ [S₂O₃²⁻]; first order.
parts.working: M1 1/t divided by concentration gives the same value for at least two experiments (e.g. 0.556); A1 first order with respect to thiosulfate (rate proportional to concentration).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the total volume and the volume of acid are kept the same in each experiment.
parts.answer: So that only the thiosulfate concentration changes (a fair test).
parts.working: B1 fair test: only the variable being investigated changes.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two experiments use 2.00 g of calcium carbonate and an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask on a balance. In experiment A the calcium carbonate is in lumps; in experiment B it is powdered. The loss in mass (CO₂ escaping) is recorded.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90
mass of CO₂ lost, lumps / g: 0.00, 0.18, 0.30, 0.38
mass of CO₂ lost, powder / g: 0.00, 0.42, 0.66, 0.80
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂   (Mr of CO₂ = 44.0; CaCO₃ = 100.1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the mass of CO₂ lost in the first 30 s for the powder compared with the lumps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in rate in terms of surface area and collisions between particles.
parts.answer: Powder has a much larger surface area, so more calcium carbonate is exposed to acid particles; collisions are more frequent and more successful, giving a faster rate.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area (powder); B1 more frequent collisions per unit time / more successful collisions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CO₂ lost from the lumps by 90 s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate that has reacted in the powder experiment by 90 s.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution is added to an excess of ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid) at 25 °C. Four potassium manganate(VII) solutions of different concentrations, with the same volume of each, are used. The time for the purple colour to disappear is recorded.
concentration of KMnO₄ / mol/dm³: 0.0050, 0.0100, 0.0200, 0.0400
time for purple colour to disappear / s: 160, 80, 40, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/t for the experiment with 0.0200 mol/dm³ KMnO₄, in s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment, and the variable that is kept constant.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of KMnO₄; dependent: time for the purple colour to disappear (or 1/t); constant: volume of KMnO₄ and the amount of ethanedioic acid (excess), temperature.
parts.working: B1 independent variable is concentration of KMnO₄; B1 dependent variable is time; (ignore temperature to avoid double-count) also B1 any named constant condition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ethanedioic acid is in excess.
parts.answer: So that the potassium manganate(VII) is the limiting reagent and all of it is used up at the same point / the colour change depends only on the KMnO₄ concentration.
parts.working: B1 ensures the KMnO₄ is completely reacted (limiting), so the time depends only on its concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sodium thiosulfate solution and dilute hydrochloric acid of the same concentrations are mixed at four temperatures. The time for a cross to disappear is measured each time.
temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50
time / s: 62, 33, 18, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/t at 20 °C and at 50 °C, in s⁻¹, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the factor by which the rate increases between 20 °C and 30 °C.
parts.answer: 1.88 (about 1.9 times)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, using collision theory, why the rate increases with temperature.
parts.answer: The particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so more collisions occur per second and a greater proportion of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy.
parts.working: B1 more frequent collisions (particles move faster); B1 more collisions have energy ≥ activation energy.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A colorimeter is used to measure absorbance of iodine solutions of known concentration. The calibration points are:
concentration / mol/dm³: 0.0000, 0.0200, 0.0400, 0.0600, 0.0800
absorbance: 0.000, 0.146, 0.292, 0.440, 0.585
A solution made from the same reaction mixture gives an absorbance of 0.372.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the calibration line through the origin, using the least-squares method (Σxy ÷ Σx²), to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.32 (absorbance per mol/dm³)
parts.working: M1 Σxy ÷ Σx² (or a line through the origin fitted to the data); A1 gradient = 7.317 ≈ 7.32.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the unknown solution, in mol/dm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0508 mol/dm³
parts.working: M1 concentration = absorbance ÷ gradient = 0.372 ÷ 7.317; A1 0.0508 ≈ 0.0508 mol/dm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a blank (for example distilled water) is used to set the colorimeter to zero before the readings are taken.
parts.answer: So that the absorbance measured is due only to the coloured iodine, not the solvent or the glass cuvette.
parts.working: B1 removes absorbance from solvent/cuvette so the reading reflects only the coloured species.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The concentration of reactant A is followed during a reaction by sampling at intervals.
time / s: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80
[A] / mol/dm³: 0.200, 0.176, 0.158, 0.144, 0.134, 0.118, 0.108

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction between 0 and 20 s, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 (0.200 − 0.158)/20 = 2.10 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (rate of disappearance of A).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate between 40 s and 80 s, and state how it compares with the rate at the start.
parts.answer: 6.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, about three times slower than the initial rate
parts.working: M1 (0.134 − 0.108)/40 = 6.50e-04; A1 slower than at the start (roughly one-third of the initial rate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.
parts.answer: The concentration of A falls, so there are fewer particles per unit volume and collisions are less frequent.
parts.working: B1 concentration of reactant decreases; B1 fewer (less frequent) effective collisions.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide (1.0 mol/dm³) decomposes to give oxygen. The volume of oxygen collected in a gas syringe is measured at intervals, once with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst and once without.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120
volume of O₂, with catalyst / cm³: 0, 20, 35, 45, 50
volume of O₂, without catalyst / cm³: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production over the first 30 s, with and without the catalyst, in cm³/s.
parts.answer: With catalyst: 0.67 cm³/s; without catalyst: 0.13 cm³/s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate between 30 s and 60 s with the catalyst, in cm³/s, and explain why it is lower than in the first 30 s.
parts.answer: (35 − 20)/30 = 0.50 cm³/s; the H₂O₂ concentration falls, so there are fewer collisions and the rate decreases.
parts.working: B1 0.50 cm³/s; B1 concentration of H₂O₂ falls so the rate decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have sufficient energy.
parts.working: B1 lower activation energy (alternative route); more particles have energy ≥ Ea.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Strips of magnesium ribbon of the same length are added to hydrochloric acid of different concentrations at 25 °C. The time for each strip to disappear completely is recorded.
concentration of HCl / mol/dm³: 1.00, 0.50, 0.25, 0.125
time for strip to disappear / s: 20.0, 42.0, 88.0, 185.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/t for each experiment, in s⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B2 all four correct to 3 s.f. (B1 for two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio: rate at 1.00 mol/dm³ HCl ÷ rate at 0.50 mol/dm³ HCl, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.1 (the rate at 1.00 mol/dm³ is about 2.1 times the rate at 0.50 mol/dm³)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to HCl, giving a reason from your answer.
parts.answer: First order: rate is roughly proportional to concentration (the rate roughly halves each time the concentration halves).
parts.working: B1 first order (rate ∝ [HCl], as 1/t approximately doubles when the concentration doubles).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Propanone reacts with iodine in acid: CH₃COCH₃ + I₂ → CH₃COCH₂I + H⁺ + I⁻. A fixed, small amount of iodine is used in each experiment; the reaction is timed until the iodine is all used up (the colour change from starch). Therefore rate = [I₂]₀ ÷ t.
Experiment | [propanone] / mol/dm³ | [H⁺] / mol/dm³ | [I₂]₀ / mol/dm³ | time / s
1 | 0.40 | 0.20 | 0.0010 | 120
2 | 0.80 | 0.20 | 0.0010 | 60
3 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.0010 | 60
4 | 0.40 | 0.20 | 0.0020 | 240

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction for experiment 1, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 8.33 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to propanone, H⁺ and I₂, using all four experiments. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Propanone: first order (doubling [propanone] halves the time, so doubles the rate, exp 1 → 2). H⁺: first order (doubling [H⁺] halves the time, exp 1 → 3). I₂: zero order (doubling [I₂] doubles the time, so the rate is unchanged, exp 1 → 4).
parts.working: B1 propanone first order (rate doubles, exp 1 → 2); B1 H⁺ first order (exp 1 → 3); B1 I₂ zero order (rate same in exps 1 and 4).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant k, with units, for rate = k[propanone][H⁺].
parts.answer: 1.04 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
parts.working: M1 rate = [I₂]₀/t = 8.33 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and [propanone][H⁺] = 0.080; A1 k = 1.04e-04 = 1.04 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A clock reaction is timed at five temperatures. The time t (for a fixed amount of product) is taken as proportional to 1/k, where k is the rate constant.
temperature / K: 293, 303, 313, 323, 333
time t / s: 100.0, 50.8, 26.9, 14.9, 8.5
Use ln(1/t) against 1/T. For the Arrhenius equation, ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT), with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/T and ln(1/t) at 293 K and at 333 K. Give 1/T to 4 significant figures and ln(1/t) to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line between these two points.
parts.answer: -6013 K (approximately -6012.9 K, negative)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your gradient to calculate the activation energy, Ea, in kJ/mol, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 50 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R; A1 Ea ≈ 50 kJ/mol (accept 48–52).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid. Rate is taken as 1/t, where t is the time for a cross to disappear.
Experiment | [S₂O₃²⁻] / mol/dm³ | [H⁺] / mol/dm³ | time / s
1 | 0.20 | 0.50 | 25
2 | 0.10 | 0.50 | 50
3 | 0.10 | 0.25 | 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to S₂O₃²⁻ and with respect to H⁺, giving your reasons from the data.
parts.answer: S₂O₃²⁻: first order (halving [S₂O₃²⁻] doubles t, so the rate halves, exp 1 → 2). H⁺: zero order (halving [H⁺] has no effect on t, exp 2 → 3).
parts.working: B1 first order with respect to thiosulfate; B1 reason (t doubles when concentration halves); B1 zero order with respect to H⁺ (same t when [H⁺] changes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant k, with units, for rate = k[S₂O₃²⁻]. Use the rate = 1/t.
parts.answer: 0.200 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the time for a cross to disappear when [S₂O₃²⁻] = 0.40 mol/dm³ and [H⁺] = 2.00 mol/dm³.
parts.working: M1 1/t = k[S₂O₃²⁻] (H⁺ has no effect) = 0.200 × 0.40 = 0.0800 s⁻¹; A1 t = 12.5 s.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student measures the rate of a gas-loss reaction as (mass of gas lost) ÷ (time). The mass lost is 0.240 g ± 0.005 g (balance reading). The time is 48.0 s ± 0.5 s (stopwatch and judgement of the end point).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass lost and in the time.
parts.answer: mass: 2.1 %; time: 1.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum percentage uncertainty in the rate of reaction, and the rate with its uncertainty range.
parts.answer: 3.1 % (rate = 5.00 × 10⁻³ g/s, with a range of about 4.84 to 5.16 × 10⁻³ g/s)
parts.working: M1 add the percentage uncertainties: 2.08 % + 1.04 %; A1 3.1 %, so the rate is 5.00 × 10⁻³ ± 0.16 × 10⁻³ g/s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the time.
parts.answer: Repeat the experiment several times and take a mean, or use a colour sensor / light sensor to judge the end point instead of the eye.
parts.working: B1 repeat and average, or use a sensor for the end point (to reduce judgement error).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
0.130 g of zinc is added to an excess of dilute sulfuric acid in a flask fitted with a gas syringe. 48.0 cm³ of hydrogen is collected at room conditions (molar volume 24.0 dm³/mol).
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of hydrogen collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to calculate the relative atomic mass of zinc.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the acid must be in excess.
parts.answer: So that all the zinc reacts; the amount of zinc, and so the amount of gas, is then fixed by the mass of zinc.
parts.working: B1 all zinc reacts / zinc is the limiting reagent so the gas volume depends only on its mass.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A gas syringe contains carbon dioxide at 25 °C. At this temperature 1 mol of gas occupies 24.8 dm³ (room conditions). The syringe reads 62.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide (Mr = 44.0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one precaution to take when reading the syringe so that the volume is accurate.
parts.answer: Read the scale at eye level with the bottom of the plunger (the flat end) and wait until the reading is steady.
parts.working: B1 eye level / plunger read at the correct point, gas at room temperature before reading.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student needs to collect four gases in the laboratory: hydrogen, carbon dioxide, ammonia and chlorine. Relevant properties: H₂ is insoluble in water and less dense than air; CO₂ is slightly soluble in water and denser than air; NH₃ is very soluble in water and less dense than air; Cl₂ is poisonous, denser than air and reacts with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each gas, state a suitable collection method from: over water, upward delivery, downward delivery, or a gas syringe in a fume cupboard. Give the reason for each choice.
parts.answer: H₂: over water (insoluble). CO₂: downward delivery (denser than air; slightly soluble, so not over water). NH₃: upward delivery (less dense than air; very soluble, so not over water). Cl₂: downward delivery in a fume cupboard (denser than air; toxic; reacts with water).
parts.working: B1 each gas with a suitable method; B1 each gas with a valid reason (1 mark each, max 4).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A gas syringe is connected to a flask through a delivery tube. Before a reaction is started the student wants to check that the apparatus has no leaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a simple leak test for this apparatus.
parts.answer: Seal the outlet (close the tap or pinch the delivery tube) so that only the syringe is open; pull the plunger out to a mark and release it. It should stay in place (or move only very slowly) if there is no leak; if it springs back, there is a leak.
parts.working: B1 seal/close the outlet so only the syringe is open; B1 move the plunger and release it; if it returns or does not hold the position, there is a leak.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a leak would affect the calculated relative atomic mass of a metal.
parts.answer: Less gas is collected, so the moles of gas are too low; the calculated Ar of the metal is too high.
parts.working: B1 less gas measured, so the calculated Ar is too high (since Ar = mass ÷ moles of gas).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Magnesium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe at 25 °C (molar volume 24.8 dm³/mol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of hydrogen needed to fill a syringe to 240 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium that must react to produce 240 cm³ of hydrogen (Ar Mg = 24.3).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student tests the purity of a sample of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (Mr = 106.0). 0.500 g of the impure solid is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. 96.0 cm³ of carbon dioxide is collected at room conditions (molar volume 24.0 dm³/mol). Assume that all the gas comes from sodium carbonate.
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of pure sodium carbonate in the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage purity of the sample.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one impurity that would make the purity appear too high, and explain why.
parts.answer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃), because it also reacts with acid to give CO₂, so more gas is collected than from the same mass of Na₂CO₃.
parts.working: B1 impurity that also gives CO₂ (e.g. NaHCO₃); B1 extra CO₂ produced so the calculated Na₂CO₃ is too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A white solid is a pure metal carbonate, MCO₃. 0.316 g of the solid is added to excess dilute acid. 90.0 cm³ of CO₂ is collected at room conditions (24.0 dm³/mol). The metal carbonate must be one of: magnesium carbonate (Mr 84.3), calcium carbonate (Mr 100.1) or zinc carbonate (Mr 125.4).
MCO₃ + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CO₂ collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the molar mass of the carbonate.
parts.answer: 84.3 g/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the carbonate, and state the formula of the chloride formed.
parts.answer: Magnesium carbonate, MgCO₃; the chloride is MgCl₂.
parts.working: B1 MgCO₃ (Mr 84.3, closest to the calculated value); MgCl₂ formed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zinc granules react with excess dilute sulfuric acid. The volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe is recorded every 20 seconds.
time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
volume of H₂ / cm³: 0, 22.0, 40.0, 52.0, 60.0, 66.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production over the first 20 s, in cm³/s.
parts.answer: 1.10 cm³/s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate between 60 s and 100 s, in cm³/s.
parts.answer: 0.35 cm³/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.
parts.answer: The concentration of sulfuric acid falls as it is used up, so collisions between H⁺ ions and zinc become less frequent.
parts.working: B1 acid concentration decreases (fewer H⁺ ions); B1 fewer frequent collisions between H⁺ and zinc surface (zinc surface may be covered).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Potassium hydrogencarbonate decomposes on heating:
2KHCO₃ → K₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂
The carbon dioxide is collected in a gas syringe at room conditions (24.0 dm³/mol). Mr of KHCO₃ = 100.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CO₂ collected when 400 cm³ of gas is collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of KHCO₃ that decomposed, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A sample of 3.80 g of KHCO₃ was heated. Calculate the percentage of the KHCO₃ that decomposed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Aluminium reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide, producing hydrogen:
2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂
0.135 g of aluminium (Ar 27.0) is used. The hydrogen is collected at 25 °C (molar volume 24.8 dm³/mol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of aluminium used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen expected, in cm³, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 186 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student measures 172 cm³. Calculate the percentage yield of hydrogen.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student reacts a metal M with excess acid and collects hydrogen. From the mass of metal used, the expected volume of hydrogen is calculated as 60.0 cm³ at 25 °C (molar volume 24.8 dm³/mol). Only 54.0 cm³ is collected: the student notices a small leak in the gas syringe connection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the volume of hydrogen collected.
parts.answer: 10.0 % (too low)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of hydrogen actually collected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the relative atomic mass calculated for M would be too high or too low, and why.
parts.answer: Too high: the amount of hydrogen measured is too small, so the moles of metal (equal to moles of H₂ for a 1:1 reaction) are underestimated and Ar = mass ÷ moles is too high.
parts.working: B1 fewer moles of gas recorded so the calculated moles of metal are too low; B1 Ar = mass ÷ moles is therefore too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dry 250 cm³ round-bottomed flask is evacuated, weighed, then filled with a gas at 20 °C (293 K) and 101.3 kPa. The increase in mass is 0.456 g. Use pV = nRT with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of gas in the flask.
parts.working: M1 n = pV/RT with p = 101 300 Pa, V = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and T = 293 K; A1 n = 0.01040 mol (≈ 1.04 × 10⁻² mol).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the molar mass of the gas, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 43.9 g/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a gas with a molar mass close to your answer, and explain why the result may be slightly different from the true value.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide (44.0) or propane (44.1). Possible reasons: the flask was not fully evacuated (air left in it), or a small leak or the gas was not at exactly 293 K.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ or propane (or another gas with Mr ≈ 44); B1 any valid source of error (incomplete evacuation / temperature not exactly 293 K / leak).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A metal M reacts with dilute acid and the hydrogen is collected over water at 20 °C. The water vapour pressure at 20 °C is 2.3 kPa and the atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa. The volume of gas collected in the inverted measuring cylinder is 50.0 cm³ (measured at the same level of water inside and outside). Assume that the molar volume at 101.3 kPa and 20 °C is 24.0 dm³/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the water vapour pressure must be subtracted from the atmospheric pressure before the volume is corrected.
parts.answer: The gas in the cylinder is a mixture with water vapour, which exerts a pressure; the pressure of the dry hydrogen is therefore lower than atmospheric pressure, so the moles of H₂ are not given by the volume read at 101.3 kPa.
parts.working: B1 the cylinder contains water vapour, which contributes to the total pressure; B1 the dry gas pressure is atmospheric minus 2.3 kPa, so the volume must be corrected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of dry hydrogen at 101.3 kPa, in cm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 48.9 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: A 0.0500 g sample of M gave the corrected volume of hydrogen. Calculate the relative atomic mass of M (assume a 1:1 ratio of M to H₂).

author: HomiLabs

stem: 100.0 cm³ of a mixture of hydrogen and carbon dioxide is collected at room conditions (24.0 dm³/mol). The mixture is passed into excess concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, which absorbs all the carbon dioxide by the reaction 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O. The remaining gas (hydrogen) is measured as 62.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume percentage of carbon dioxide in the original mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide absorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide needed to absorb all this carbon dioxide (Mr NaOH = 40.0).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the sodium hydroxide must be in excess.
parts.answer: So that all the carbon dioxide is absorbed; any CO₂ not absorbed would give a volume of gas that is too large.
parts.working: B1 ensures all CO₂ is absorbed so the volume of hydrogen is accurate (the remaining gas is only hydrogen).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution is placed in a polystyrene cup at 21.0 °C. 0.70 g of zinc powder is added and the mixture is stirred. The highest temperature reached is 31.5 °C.
Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
Assume the solution has density 1.00 g/cm³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Ar: Zn = 65.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CuSO₄ and of zinc, and identify the limiting reagent.
parts.answer: CuSO₄: 0.0100 mol; zinc: 0.0107 mol; CuSO₄ is limiting
parts.working: M1 n(CuSO₄) = 0.0500 × 0.200 = 0.0100 mol and n(Zn) = 0.70/65.4 = 0.0107 mol; A1 CuSO₄ is limiting (zinc in excess).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in J, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH, in kJ/mol, with its sign, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: -219 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = −q ÷ n = −2.1945 kJ ÷ 0.0100 mol; A1 ΔH = -219 kJ/mol (exothermic).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
2.00 g of solid ammonium nitrate (Mr 80.0) is added to 50.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature falls from 22.0 °C to 16.4 °C. Assume density 1.00 g/cm³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
NH₄NO₃(s) → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of NH₄NO₃ dissolved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed by the water, in J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution, ΔH, in kJ/mol, with its sign.
parts.answer: +46.8 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = +q ÷ n (heat absorbed) = 1.1704 kJ ÷ 0.0250 mol; A1 +46.8 kJ/mol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the process is exothermic or endothermic, and explain your answer in terms of energy.
parts.answer: Endothermic: energy is taken in from the water, so the temperature falls.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; energy is absorbed from the surroundings (the water cools).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
4.00 g of solid sodium hydroxide (Mr 40.0) is added to 100.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 20.0 °C to 27.6 °C. Assume density 1.00 g/cm³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
NaOH(s) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of NaOH dissolved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for dissolving NaOH, in kJ/mol, with its sign to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: -31.8 kJ/mol

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one reason why the value is less accurate than a neutralisation value.
parts.answer: Some heat is lost to the surroundings and the cup absorbs some heat, so the temperature rise is underestimated.
parts.working: B1 heat loss to surroundings / heat absorbed by the cup is ignored.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid at 20.0 °C is added to 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide at 20.0 °C in a polystyrene cup. The highest temperature reached is 32.5 °C. Assume density 1.00 g/cm³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of water formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise and the energy released, in J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in kJ/mol, with its sign.
parts.answer: -52.3 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A spirit burner contains ethanol (Mr 46.0). The standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol is −1367 kJ/mol.
C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of ethanol in 0.46 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released by burning 0.46 g of ethanol, in kJ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assuming all this energy heats water, calculate the mass of water that would be warmed by 20.0 °C. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A spirit burner of ethanol (Mr 46.0; ΔcH = −1367 kJ/mol) is used to heat 100.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 45.0 °C. The mass of the burner falls by 0.60 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed by the water, in kJ, with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released by the ethanol burned, in kJ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of the burner.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the efficiency is less than 100 %.
parts.answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings and the air, and the cup/container absorbs some of the heat.
parts.working: B1 heat lost to surroundings or absorbed by the container; incomplete combustion is also acceptable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student determines the energy content of a crisp by burning a 1.25 g sample under 150.0 g of water in a metal can. The temperature of the water rises by 18.4 °C. Assume c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ignore the heat absorbed by the can.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed by the water, in kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy content of the crisp, in kJ/g, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The label on the packet states 20 kJ/g. Suggest two reasons why the student's value is lower.
parts.answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings (air and the can); some of the crisp does not burn completely (soot/unburnt food); the can absorbs heat.
parts.working: B1 any reason for heat loss to surroundings / absorbed by the can; B1 incomplete combustion of the sample.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
50.0 cm³ of dilute acid at 21.0 °C is added to an excess of magnesium in a polystyrene cup and the mixture is stirred. Because the temperature falls after the reaction is complete, the temperature is recorded every minute after the reaction is over:
time / min: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
temperature / °C: 34.6, 34.2, 33.8, 33.4, 33.0
Assume the solution has a mass of 50.0 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use a graph or extrapolation back to the time of mixing (time 0) to find the maximum temperature.
parts.working: M1 the cooling rate is 0.40 °C per minute, so extrapolate back 3 min from 34.6 °C; A1 35.8 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise, and the energy released, in J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why extrapolation is necessary.
parts.answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings after mixing, so the highest reading taken is below the true maximum; extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing estimates the temperature with no heat loss.
parts.working: B1 heat is lost during the time of the measurements, so the true maximum is found by extrapolation back to the mixing time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two experiments neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ HCl with 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ NaOH (both at 20.0 °C), in polystyrene cups. Experiment A uses a lid; experiment B has no lid. Temperature rises: A = 12.5 °C; B = 11.6 °C. Assume c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and density 1.00 g/cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation for experiment A and for experiment B, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: A: -52.3 kJ/mol; B: -48.5 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the value for B is smaller than the value for A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lid gives a more accurate value.
parts.answer: The lid reduces heat lost to the surroundings (by evaporation and convection), so more of the heat released stays in the solution.
parts.working: B1 less heat lost to surroundings, so the temperature rise is not underestimated.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ethanol (Mr 46.0; ΔcH = −1367 kJ/mol) is burned in a spirit burner to heat 200 g of water from 20.0 °C to 50.0 °C. The burner is only 25 % efficient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat the water, in kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy that must be released by the ethanol, in kJ, to allow for the 25 % efficiency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethanol that must be burned, in g, to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an experiment, 50.0 cm³ of solution (mass 50.0 g ± 0.5 g) is used. The initial temperature is 20.0 °C and the highest temperature is 32.5 °C. Each thermometer reading is accurate to ±0.1 °C. The enthalpy change is calculated as ΔH = −mcΔT ÷ n, with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and n = 0.0500 mol (exact).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise ΔT (ΔT = 12.5 °C).
parts.working: B1 uncertainty in ΔT = ±0.2 °C (both readings) ; 0.2/12.5 × 100 = 1.6 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of solution, and the total percentage uncertainty in ΔH (add the percentage uncertainties).
parts.answer: mass: 1.0 %; total: 2.6 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence give the enthalpy change with its uncertainty, in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 ΔH = −52.25 kJ/mol (from ΔT = 12.5 and mass 50.0 g); A1 uncertainty = 1.36 kJ/mol, so −52.3 ± 1.4 kJ/mol.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two neutralisation experiments are compared. Each uses 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ acid and 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ NaOH (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, density 1.00 g/cm³). With ethanoic acid the temperature rise is 6.5 °C.
Accepted value for strong acid neutralisation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −57.3 kJ/mol
CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation for ethanoic acid, in kJ/mol, from the experiment.
parts.answer: -54.3 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a cycle (CH₃COOH → H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻, then H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O) to calculate the enthalpy change of ionisation of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq).
parts.answer: +3.0 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH(ionisation) = ΔH(experiment) − ΔH(H⁺ + OH⁻) = -54.3 − (−57.3); A1 +3.0 kJ/mol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the sign of your answer to (b).
parts.answer: The ionisation is endothermic: energy is absorbed to break the O–H bond and separate the ions, so less heat is released in the neutralisation.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; energy needed to ionise the weak acid.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
3.20 g of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (Mr 159.6) is added to 50.0 cm³ of water at 20.0 °C in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises to 26.3 °C.
CuSO₄(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CuSO₄ used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution, ΔH, in kJ/mol, with its sign.
parts.answer: -65.7 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the process is exothermic or endothermic, and suggest why the value for the hydrated salt (CuSO₄·5H₂O) would be different.
parts.answer: Exothermic (temperature rises). The hydrated salt has a different enthalpy of solution, because its Cu²⁺ ions are already surrounded by water of crystallisation in the solid; the lattice and hydration energy terms differ from those of the anhydrous salt, so the energy balance changes (the hydrated salt dissolves with a much smaller, endothermic enthalpy change).
parts.working: B1 exothermic (temperature rises); B1 the hydrate has a different enthalpy because its water of crystallisation changes the lattice and hydration energy balance.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ HCl and 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ NaOH are mixed in a polystyrene cup, rise 12.5 °C (from 20.0 °C to 32.5 °C). The cup itself has a heat capacity of 25 J/K. Assume c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the solution (mass 50.0 g) and 0.0500 mol of water is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heat absorbed by the solution and by the cup, and the total energy released, in J.
parts.answer: solution: 2612 J; cup: 312 J; total 2925 J

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation including the cup, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: -58.5 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the value including the cup is more accurate than a value calculated using only the solution.
parts.answer: The cup absorbs some of the heat released, so ignoring it underestimates the energy released and the magnitude of ΔH.
parts.working: B1 heat absorbed by the cup is part of the energy released; ignoring it gives a value that is too small in magnitude.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound A is a colourless organic liquid with the formula C₃H₆O. Results:
Test 1: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) reagent → orange precipitate.
Test 2: warm with Tollens' reagent → no silver mirror.
Test 3: warm with Fehling's solution → no red precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the functional group shown by test 1, and which type of compound (aldehyde or ketone) A must be, using tests 2 and 3.
parts.answer: Carbonyl group, C=O; A is a ketone (no reaction with Tollens' or Fehling's, so not an aldehyde).
parts.working: B1 carbonyl group (C=O) shown by 2,4-DNPH; B1 ketone, since aldehydes give a silver mirror / red precipitate and ketones do not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name compound A.
parts.answer: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃
parts.working: B1 propanone (the only ketone with formula C₃H₆O).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Tollens' reagent does not react with a ketone.
parts.answer: Ketones cannot be oxidised further under these conditions because the carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen atom attached to it.
parts.working: B1 ketones are not oxidised (no H on the C=O carbon); aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three colourless compounds are shaken with aqueous bromine (orange) in a test tube, in the dark:
Compound X: hexane — no change.
Compound Y: cyclohexene — the orange colour is lost immediately.
Compound Z: phenol — a white precipitate forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group in compound Y that causes the change in colour.
parts.answer: Carbon–carbon double bond (C=C), an alkene.
parts.working: B1 C=C (alkene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the observation for compound X and explain it.
parts.answer: No change, because hexane is a saturated alkane with no C=C bonds and does not react with bromine water.
parts.working: B1 no change; no C=C / saturated alkane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the name of the white precipitate formed with compound Z, and explain why bromine substitutes three positions.
parts.answer: 2,4,6-tribromophenol. The OH group activates the ring, so bromine substitutes at the positions 2, 4 and 6 (ortho and para to OH).
parts.working: B1 2,4,6-tribromophenol; B1 OH is electron-donating / activates the ring at 2, 4 and 6 positions.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound P, C₃H₈O, is tested with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution:
Compound Q (propan-1-ol) is warmed: the orange solution turns green.
Compound R (2-methylpropan-2-ol) is warmed: the solution stays orange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change expected for compound Q, and name the type of alcohol that gives this result.
parts.answer: Orange → green; Q is a primary alcohol (it is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 orange to green; B1 primary alcohol (also accept secondary alcohol, but Q is primary).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why compound R does not change colour.
parts.answer: R is a tertiary alcohol; the carbon bonded to the OH group has no hydrogen atom, so it cannot be oxidised.
parts.working: B1 tertiary alcohol; no H on the carbon with OH, so no oxidation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organic product formed by oxidising compound Q under these conditions, if the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms.
parts.answer: Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO.
parts.working: B1 propanal (aldehyde); on heating under reflux the product would be propanoic acid.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound H is a white solid that dissolves in water. When aqueous sodium carbonate is added to H, there is effervescence (fizzing). The gas produced turns limewater milky.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group in H.
parts.answer: Carboxylic acid, –COOH
parts.working: B1 carboxylic acid (–COOH).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the gas and give the equation for its formation.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; 2CH₃CH₂COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃CH₂COONa + H₂O + CO₂ (for propanoic acid as an example)
parts.working: B1 CO₂; B1 correct balanced equation or word equation: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen when the gas is passed into limewater.
parts.answer: The limewater turns milky (cloudy) white.
parts.working: B1 limewater turns milky (calcium carbonate formed).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound J is a solid. Tests:
Test 1: aqueous iron(III) chloride → violet colour.
Test 2: sodium metal added → hydrogen bubbles.
Test 3: aqueous sodium carbonate → no effervescence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group in J.
parts.answer: Phenol (–OH bonded directly to a benzene ring)
parts.working: B1 phenol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there is no effervescence with sodium carbonate.
parts.answer: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid, so it does not react with carbonate ions to release CO₂.
parts.working: B1 phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid (H₂CO₃); B1 so no CO₂ is produced, unlike carboxylic acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the observation when bromine water is added to J.
parts.answer: A white precipitate of a tribromophenol forms (decolourises the orange bromine).
parts.working: B1 white precipitate; bromine decolourised.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four compounds are tested with alkaline aqueous iodine (warmed) and the results are recorded.
Compound | Result
ethanol | yellow precipitate
propan-1-ol | no precipitate
propan-2-ol | yellow precipitate
propanone | yellow precipitate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural feature common to the three compounds that give a positive result.
parts.answer: A CH₃CO– group or a CH₃CH(OH)– group (a methyl group next to C=O or next to a CH–OH carbon).
parts.working: B1 CH₃ group attached to a C=O carbon (methyl ketone) or to a CH(OH) carbon; B1 both groups named or ethanol/propan-2-ol explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the result of this test for butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Positive (yellow precipitate), because it contains a CH₃CO– group.
parts.working: B1 positive: CH₃CO– group present.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the yellow precipitate.
parts.answer: Triiodomethane (iodoform), CHI₃
parts.working: B1 triiodomethane, CHI₃.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four compounds are tested: propanal, propanone, butanone and propanoic acid. The results are:
Test 1: Tollens' reagent, warm → silver mirror.
Test 2: sodium carbonate solution → effervescence.
Test 3: Fehling's solution, warm → red precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which compound(s) give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.
parts.answer: Propanal only.
parts.working: B1 propanal (the only aldehyde).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which compound gives effervescence with sodium carbonate, and name the gas.
parts.answer: Propanoic acid; carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 propanoic acid; B1 CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why propanal reduces Tollens' reagent, but propanone does not.
parts.answer: Propanal has a C=O group at the end of the chain with an H atom, so it is oxidised to propanoic acid and the silver ions are reduced to silver; propanone has no H atom on the carbonyl carbon, so it is not oxidised.
parts.working: B1 propanal has a –CHO group that is oxidised to a carboxylic acid; B1 propanone (ketone) cannot be oxidised, so no silver is formed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three halogenoalkanes are each warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide for several minutes. The mixture is then acidified with dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate is added:
1-chlorobutane: white precipitate, formed slowly.
1-bromobutane: cream precipitate, formed faster.
1-iodobutane: yellow precipitate, formed fastest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three precipitates, and write the ionic equation for the formation of the cream precipitate.
parts.answer: AgCl (white); AgBr (cream); AgI (yellow). Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s).
parts.working: B1 AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow (1 mark for all three correct, 2 for two); B1 Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mixture must be acidified with dilute nitric acid before adding silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To remove the excess OH⁻ ions, which would react with silver ions to form a brown precipitate of silver(I) oxide, hiding the halide precipitate.
parts.working: B1 removes OH⁻ (excess alkali); B1 otherwise silver oxide (brown) forms and confuses the result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the order of precipitation is I > Br > Cl.
parts.answer: The C–X bond strength decreases from C–Cl to C–I (C–I is weakest), so the iodoalkane hydrolyses fastest.
parts.working: B1 C–I bond is weakest (bond enthalpy C–Cl > C–Br > C–I), so it is broken fastest.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound X, C₅H₁₀O, is tested.
Test 1: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine → orange precipitate.
Test 2: Tollens' reagent, warm → no silver mirror.
Test 3: alkaline aqueous iodine, warm → yellow precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the functional group in X, and state whether X is an aldehyde or a ketone, using tests 2 and 3.
parts.answer: Carbonyl group, C=O; X is a ketone (Tollens' negative, so not an aldehyde); the yellow precipitate shows a CH₃CO– group.
parts.working: B1 carbonyl group (C=O) from test 1; B1 ketone, because aldehydes give a silver mirror in test 2 and X does not; the yellow precipitate (iodoform) shows a CH₃CO– group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name X and give its structural formula. Name the other ketone with formula C₅H₁₀O and state its result in test 3.
parts.answer: X is pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃. The other ketone, pentan-3-one (CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃), gives no yellow precipitate in test 3 because it has no CH₃CO– group.
parts.working: B1 pentan-2-one with the correct structure; B1 pentan-3-one gives a negative iodoform test (no CH₃CO– group).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why X cannot be pentanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO.
parts.answer: Pentanal would give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, but X does not.
parts.working: B1 pentanal is an aldehyde and gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound K, C₃H₆O₂, is tested:
Test 1: aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate → vigorous effervescence.
Test 2: 2,4-DNPH → no precipitate.
Test 3: alkaline aqueous iodine, warm → no precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group shown by test 1.
parts.answer: Carboxylic acid, –COOH
parts.working: B1 carboxylic acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name compound K and give its structural formula.
parts.answer: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
parts.working: B1 propanoic acid (structure given).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction in test 1.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃CH₂COONa + H₂O + CO₂
parts.working: B1 reactants; B1 products correct (salt, water, carbon dioxide).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound M, C₃H₆O, is tested:
Test 1: 2,4-DNPH → orange precipitate.
Test 2: Tollens' reagent, warm → silver mirror forms on the inside of the test tube.
Test 3: alkaline aqueous iodine, warm → no precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the functional group in M and name M.
parts.answer: Aldehyde, –CHO (C=O at the end of the chain, detected by DNPH and Tollens); M is propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO.
parts.working: B1 aldehyde (–CHO); B1 propanal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reduction of silver ions in Tollens' reagent.
parts.answer: Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s)
parts.working: B1 Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why test 3 is negative.
parts.answer: M has no CH₃CO– group and no CH₃CH(OH)– group; the only methyl group is attached to CH₂, so no triiodomethane (iodoform) is produced.
parts.working: B1 no CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group; B1 so the iodoform reaction cannot occur.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound N, C₇H₈O, is a phenol. Tests:
Test 1: aqueous iron(III) chloride → violet colour.
Test 2: aqueous bromine added → a white precipitate containing two bromine atoms per molecule of N.
The product of test 2 is 2,6-dibromo-4-methylphenol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bromine adds to positions 2 and 6 of the ring only.
parts.answer: The –OH group activates the ring and directs substitution to positions 2, 4 and 6; the position 4 is already occupied by the methyl group, so only positions 2 and 6 are substituted.
parts.working: B1 –OH directs to 2, 4, 6; B1 4-position occupied by CH₃ so only 2 and 6 are substituted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the name of compound N.
parts.answer: 4-methylphenol (p-cresol)
parts.working: B1 4-methylphenol with the CH₃ para to OH.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structural feature of N that is responsible for the violet colour in test 1.
parts.answer: The phenol –OH group bonded directly to the benzene ring forms a complex with iron(III).
parts.working: B1 OH bonded to benzene ring (phenol) forms a coloured complex with Fe³⁺.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Compound P, C₃H₆O, is tested:
Test 1: aqueous bromine → decolourised immediately.
Test 2: sodium metal → hydrogen gas is produced.
Test 3: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm → orange turns green.
Test 4: 2,4-DNPH → no precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two functional groups in P, using tests 1 and 2.
parts.answer: C=C (alkene, from test 1) and –OH (alcohol, from test 2).
parts.working: B1 C=C (alkene); B1 –OH (alcohol).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why test 4 is negative.
parts.answer: P has no C=O (carbonyl) group, so it does not react with 2,4-DNPH.
parts.working: B1 no C=O group in P.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the structural formula and name of P, and name the product expected in test 3 if the alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde.
parts.answer: P = prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH; oxidation product (aldehyde) is propenal, CH₂=CHCHO.
parts.working: B1 CH₂=CHCH₂OH with a C=C double bond and a primary –OH; B1 prop-2-en-1-ol; B1 propenal, CH₂=CHCHO (aldehyde).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two isomeric bromoalkanes, both C₄H₉Br, are each warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide, then acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with aqueous silver nitrate:
compound Q (1-bromobutane): cream precipitate forms slowly.
compound R (2-bromo-2-methylpropane): cream precipitate forms rapidly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the reagent mixture is acidified before silver nitrate is added.
parts.answer: To remove excess OH⁻, which would precipitate silver(I) oxide (brown) and hide the bromide precipitate.
parts.working: B1 remove OH⁻ ions; B1 otherwise brown Ag₂O forms and the cream AgBr precipitate cannot be seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why compound R reacts faster than compound Q.
parts.answer: R is a tertiary halogenoalkane and hydrolyses by an SN1 mechanism through a relatively stable tertiary carbocation, whereas Q, a primary halogenoalkane, hydrolyses by SN2 with a less stable transition state; the carbocation route is faster.
parts.working: B1 R is tertiary; B1 SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation (more stable than primary); B1 Q primary, SN2, slower.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organic product formed by hydrolysis of compound R.
parts.answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH
parts.working: B1 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what are the units of Kc?
A mol⁻¹ dm³
B mol⁻² dm⁶
C mol dm⁻³
D no units
parts.answer: B mol⁻² dm⁶
parts.working: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³), so units = (mol dm⁻³)^(2−4) = mol⁻² dm⁶. A and C do not follow from the powers. D is wrong because the powers do not cancel (4 gas molecules become 2).

stem: Carbon monoxide and steam are sealed in a 2.00 dm³ vessel at 900 K: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). At equilibrium the vessel contains 0.40 mol CO, 0.20 mol H₂O, 0.60 mol CO₂ and 0.60 mol H₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for Kc for this reaction.
parts.answer: Kc = [CO₂][H₂] / ([CO][H₂O])
parts.working: B1 correct expression with products on top

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of Kc at 900 K and state its units.
parts.answer: Kc = 4.50 (no units)
parts.working:
M1 concentrations: [CO] = 0.20, [H₂O] = 0.10, [CO₂] = 0.30, [H₂] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³
A1 Kc = 0.30 × 0.30 / (0.20 × 0.10) = 4.50; no units because the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sulfur dioxide and oxygen are sealed in a container at 700 K: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). At equilibrium [SO₂] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³, [O₂] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [SO₃] = 0.80 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kc for this equilibrium, giving its units.
parts.answer: Kc = 20.0 mol⁻¹ dm³
parts.working:
M1 Kc = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]²[O₂]) = 0.80² / (0.40² × 0.20)
A1 = 20.0; units (mol dm⁻³)^(2−3) = mol⁻¹ dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. State and explain how Kc changes if the temperature is raised.
parts.answer: Kc decreases, because a higher temperature favours the endothermic backward reaction and lowers the amount of SO₃ relative to SO₂ and O₂
parts.working: B1 decreases with a reason linked to the equilibrium shifting left

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nitrosyl chloride decomposes reversibly: 2NOCl(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) + Cl₂(g). A sealed container at 400 K is filled with 2.00 mol NOCl. At equilibrium it contains 1.00 mol NOCl, 1.00 mol NO and 0.50 mol Cl₂. The total pressure is 200 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the partial pressure of NOCl at equilibrium, in kPa.
parts.answer: 80 kPa
parts.working:
M1 mole fraction of NOCl = 1.00 / 2.50 = 0.400
A1 p(NOCl) = 0.400 × 200 = 80 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression for Kp for this equilibrium.
parts.answer: Kp = p(NO)² × p(Cl₂) / p(NOCl)²
parts.working: B1 correct expression

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Kp, giving its units.
parts.answer: Kp = 40 kPa

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gas X dissociates reversibly: X(g) ⇌ 2Y(g). A 1.00 dm³ sealed vessel initially contains 1.00 mol of X and no Y. At the temperature of the experiment Kc = 0.250 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let z mol dm⁻³ of X react by the time equilibrium is reached. Write the equilibrium concentrations of X and Y in terms of z.
parts.answer: [X] = (1.00 − z) mol dm⁻³; [Y] = 2z mol dm⁻³
parts.working:
B1 [X] = 1.00 − z
B1 [Y] = 2z, because 2 mol Y form for each mol X that reacts

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that z satisfies 4z² + 0.250z − 0.250 = 0.
parts.working:
M1 substitute into Kc = [Y]²/[X]
A1 rearrange to 4z² + 0.250z − 0.250 = 0

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve for z and calculate [Y] at equilibrium, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: z = 0.221 mol dm⁻³; [Y] = 2z = 0.441 mol dm⁻³
parts.working:
M1 use the quadratic formula with a = 4, b = 0.250, c = −0.250
M1 z = (−0.250 + √4.0625)/8 = 0.2207
A1 [Y] = 2z = 0.441 mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compounds A₂ and B₂ react reversibly: A₂(g) + B₂(g) ⇌ 2AB(g). A 1.00 dm³ sealed flask initially contains 1.00 mol A₂ and 1.00 mol B₂ and no AB. At equilibrium Kc = 9.00 at this temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for Kc.
parts.answer: Kc = [AB]² / ([A₂][B₂])
parts.working: B1 correct expression

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the amount of AB at equilibrium is 1.20 mol.
parts.answer: Let x mol of A₂ react: [AB] = 2x and [A₂] = [B₂] = (1 − x). Then (2x)²/(1 − x)² = 9.00, so 2x/(1 − x) = 3, x = 0.600 and n(AB) = 1.20 mol.
parts.working:
M1 define x and write equilibrium amounts (AB = 2x, A₂ = B₂ = 1 − x)
M1 (2x)²/(1 − x)² = 9.00 and take the square root
A1 x = 0.600, so n(AB) = 1.20 mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonia dissociates reversibly: 2NH₃(g) ⇌ N₂(g) + 3H₂(g). 0.500 mol of NH₃ is placed in a 2.00 dm³ sealed vessel at 700 K. At equilibrium the vessel contains 0.120 mol of H₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts, in mol, of N₂ and NH₃ at equilibrium.
parts.answer: n(N₂) = 0.0400 mol; n(NH₃) = 0.420 mol
parts.working:
M1 H₂ formed = 0.120 mol, so N₂ formed = 0.120 / 3 = 0.0400 mol
M1 NH₃ reacted = 2 × 0.0400 = 0.0800 mol, so NH₃ left = 0.500 − 0.0800 = 0.420 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression for Kc and calculate its value with units.
parts.answer: Kc = [N₂][H₂]³ / [NH₃]² = 9.80 × 10⁻⁵ mol² dm⁻⁶
parts.working:
M1 concentrations: [N₂] = 0.0200, [H₂] = 0.0600, [NH₃] = 0.210 mol dm⁻³
M1 Kc = 0.0200 × 0.0600³ / 0.210²
A1 = 9.80 × 10⁻⁵; units (mol dm⁻³)^(1+3−2) = mol² dm⁻⁶

author: HomiLabs

stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating in a sealed vessel: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g). At 1000 K, 0.250 mol of CO₂ is present in a sealed 5.00 dm³ vessel that also contains solid CaCO₃ and solid CaO. Treat CO₂ as an ideal gas, with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the solids do not appear in the expression for Kp.
parts.answer: Pure solids have a fixed concentration, so their terms are constant and are not included; only gases appear in Kp
parts.working: B1 solids have constant (fixed) concentration, so they are not included

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pressure of CO₂, in kPa, using pV = nRT.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the expression for Kp and state its value at 1000 K, with units.
parts.answer: Kp = p(CO₂) = 415.5 kPa
parts.working: B1 only one gas is present, so Kp equals the pressure found in part (b)

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the equilibrium A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g), Kc = 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ at 500 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kc at 500 K for the equilibrium 2B(g) + 2C(g) ⇌ 2A(g), giving units.
parts.answer: Kc = 625 mol⁻² dm⁶
parts.working:
M1 the reverse reaction gives 1/Kc, and doubling the equation squares it: Kc′ = 1/(0.0400)²
A1 = 625; units (mol⁻¹ dm³)² = mol⁻² dm⁶

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the value of Kc for the original equilibrium changes if its forward reaction is endothermic and the temperature rises. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Kc increases, because an endothermic forward reaction is favoured at higher temperature so the equilibrium shifts right
parts.working: B1 increases, with a reason based on the equilibrium shifting towards the products

author: HomiLabs

stem: Substance A dimerises reversibly: 2A(g) ⇌ B(g). At 350 K the equilibrium concentrations are [A] = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.300 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kc, giving its units.
parts.answer: Kc = 750 mol⁻¹ dm³
parts.working:
M1 Kc = [B]/[A]² = 0.300 / 0.0200²
A1 = 750; units (mol dm⁻³)^(1−2) = mol⁻¹ dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature is raised and Kc falls to 300 mol⁻¹ dm³. Deduce the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction and give a reason.
parts.answer: ΔH is negative (the forward reaction is exothermic). A higher temperature lowers Kc, so the equilibrium shifts left towards the endothermic backward reaction.
parts.working:
B1 ΔH negative (exothermic)
B1 reason: higher temperature shifts the equilibrium to the endothermic (backward) side, lowering Kc

author: HomiLabs

stem: The ionic product of water, Kw, is 2.40 × 10⁻¹³ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 350 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why pure water is still neutral at 350 K.

parts.text: Explain why hydrochloric acid is described as a strong acid.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: 1.12 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K) is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The two solutions react completely.

stem: A 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak acid HA is 2.4 % dissociated at 298 K.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Solutions of equal concentration are compared at 298 K: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pH of the ethanoic acid is higher than the pH of the hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³. Ethanoic acid is weak and only partly dissociated, so its [H⁺] is much lower (about 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³), giving a higher pH.
parts.working:
B1 HCl fully dissociated so [H⁺] is equal to the acid concentration
B1 ethanoic acid is weak, its equilibrium lies to the left and only a small fraction ionises
B1 lower [H⁺] in ethanoic acid, so higher pH

parts.working: B1 (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol³ dm⁻⁹

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt is described as an equilibrium.
parts.answer: Ions leave the surface of the solid and ions in solution return to it at equal rates. Because the rates are equal, the concentrations of the ions stay constant while undissolved solid is present.
parts.working:
B1 dissolving and crystallisation (solid ⇌ ions) occur at equal rates
B1 so the concentrations of the dissolved ions remain constant

stem: Calcium sulfate, CaSO₄ (Mr = 136.1), has Ksp = 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of CaSO₄ in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b

A1 = 0.681 g dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

stem: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, has Ksp = 5.60 × 10⁻¹² mol³ dm⁻⁹ at 298 K. Solid Mg(OH)₂ is shaken with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution until equilibrium is reached.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate [Mg²⁺] in the solution at equilibrium, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: [Mg²⁺] = 5.60 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³
parts.working:
M1 Ksp = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² with [OH⁻] ≈ 0.100 mol dm⁻³ from the NaOH
A1 [Mg²⁺] = 5.60 × 10⁻¹² / (0.100)² = 5.60 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of Mg(OH)₂ in pure water at 298 K, in mol dm⁻³, and explain why the [Mg²⁺] in (a) is much smaller than this value.
parts.answer: Solubility = 1.12 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ in pure water. The OH⁻ ions from the NaOH are a common ion; they shift Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) to the left, so much less Mg(OH)₂ dissolves.
parts.working:
M1 solubility s gives [Mg²⁺] = s and [OH⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³
A1 s = (5.60 × 10⁻¹² / 4)^(1/3) = 1.12 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³
B1 common ion (OH⁻) shifts the equilibrium to the left

author: HomiLabs

stem: Equal volumes of two solutions are mixed at 298 K: 50.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ Pb(NO₃)₂ and 50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaCl. Ksp for PbCl₂ is 1.60 × 10⁻⁵ mol³ dm⁻⁹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentrations of Pb²⁺ and Cl⁻ immediately after mixing.
parts.answer: [Pb²⁺] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³; [Cl⁻] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: B1 both solutions are diluted by 2: 0.0200/2 = 0.0100 and 0.100/2 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ionic product Q = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]² for this mixture.
parts.answer: Q = 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol³ dm⁻⁹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether a precipitate of PbCl₂ forms, with a reason.
parts.answer: Yes. Q (2.50 × 10⁻⁵) is greater than Ksp (1.60 × 10⁻⁵), so the solution is supersaturated and PbCl₂ precipitates.
parts.working: B1 Q > Ksp, so precipitation occurs

author: HomiLabs

stem: Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, is a sparingly soluble base. Its solubility product at 298 K is Ksp = 5.50 × 10⁻⁶ mol³ dm⁻⁹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for Ksp of Ca(OH)₂.
parts.answer: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]²
parts.working: B1 correct expression

parts.label: b

parts.answer: s = 1.11 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
parts.working:
M1 if s = solubility, Ksp = s × (2s)² = 4s³, so s = (Ksp / 4)^(1/3)
A1 s = (1.375 × 10⁻⁶)^(1/3) = 1.11 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c

A1 [F⁻] = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³

stem: Lead(II) fluoride, PbF₂, has Ksp = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ mol³ dm⁻⁹ at 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate [Pb²⁺] in a saturated solution of PbF₂ in 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium fluoride solution.
parts.answer: [Pb²⁺] = 1.32 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
parts.working:
M1 Ksp = [Pb²⁺][F⁻]² with [F⁻] ≈ 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ from the NaF
A1 [Pb²⁺] = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ / (0.0500)² = 1.32 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the solubility of PbF₂ in pure water, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: s = 2.02 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

parts.answer: The fluoride ions from NaF are a common ion. They shift PbF₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq) to the left, so [Pb²⁺] falls by a factor of about 150.
parts.working: B1 common ion effect: high [F⁻] shifts the equilibrium to the left, so [Pb²⁺] is about 150 times lower than in pure water

author: HomiLabs

stem: Silver chromate, Ag₂CrO₄, has Ksp = 1.10 × 10⁻¹² mol³ dm⁻⁹ at 298 K. Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq).

M1 [Ag⁺] = 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
A1 solubility of Ag₂CrO₄ = [Ag⁺]/2 = 5.24 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³

stem: For each mixture below, state whether it is a buffer solution and give a reason. Each mixture is made by combining the two solutions at 298 K.

parts.answer: Yes. 0.00250 mol CH₃COOH is left over (0.00500 mol acid minus 0.00250 mol NaOH), and 0.00250 mol CH₃COONa is formed, so a weak acid and its salt are present.

stem: A buffer is made from ammonia solution and ammonium chloride solution.

B1 added OH⁻ is removed by the NH₄⁺ (acid) component
B1 the change in [NH₃]/[NH₄⁺] is small, so pH hardly changes

stem: A buffer is made from 0.250 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.100 mol of sodium ethanoate in 1.00 dm³ of solution (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³). Then 0.0300 mol of HCl gas is dissolved in the buffer. Assume the volume stays at 1.00 dm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A chemist wants a buffer with pH 9.00 at 298 K. Start with 0.500 dm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ aqueous ammonia. Kb for NH₃ is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Solid NH₄Cl (Mr = 53.5) is added, and the volume stays at 0.500 dm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A buffer is made by mixing 60.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid with 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Ka for ethanoic acid is 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K.

A1 CH₃COOH = 9.00 × 10⁻³ − 3.00 × 10⁻³ = 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol; CH₃COO⁻ = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)   ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹
Which change increases the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
A adding a catalyst
B increasing the pressure at constant temperature
C increasing the temperature
D adding argon at constant volume
parts.answer: B increasing the pressure at constant temperature
parts.working: Four gas molecules become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right. A: a catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so yield is unchanged. C: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a higher temperature shifts it left. D: at constant volume argon does not change the partial pressures of N₂, H₂ or NH₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)   ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹
Which change increases the amount of CO₂ present at equilibrium?
A increasing the total pressure
B raising the temperature
C adding more solid CaCO₃
D adding more solid CaO
parts.answer: B raising the temperature
parts.working: The forward reaction is endothermic, so a higher temperature shifts it to the right and more CO₂ forms. A: higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (the left), so CO₂ falls. C and D: adding solids does not change the position of equilibrium because solids have constant concentration.

stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)   ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the effect of lowering the temperature on the equilibrium yield of SO₃.
parts.answer: The yield of SO₃ increases, because the forward reaction is exothermic and lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right to release heat.
parts.working:
B1 yield increases
B1 forward reaction exothermic, so lower temperature favours it

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium yield of SO₃.
parts.answer: The yield of SO₃ increases, because the right-hand side has fewer gas molecules (2 against 3), so the equilibrium shifts to the right to reduce the pressure.
parts.working:
B1 yield increases
B1 fewer gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts right

author: HomiLabs

stem: A solution containing Fe³⁺(aq) and SCN⁻(aq) is blood red because of the complex ion [Fe(SCN)]²⁺: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺(aq). Sodium fluoride solution is then added. F⁻ ions form a very stable complex with Fe³⁺ ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change seen after the sodium fluoride is added.
parts.answer: The red colour fades (becomes much paler).
parts.working: B1 red colour fades as [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ decreases

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour change in terms of the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: F⁻ removes Fe³⁺ ions from solution by forming a stable complex, so the equilibrium shifts to the left to replace the Fe³⁺ ions. Less [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ is present.
parts.working:
B1 F⁻ lowers [Fe³⁺], so the equilibrium shifts left
B1 less [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ forms, so the red colour fades

author: HomiLabs

stem: Argon, an unreactive gas, is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) in a container that can expand so that the total pressure stays constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of adding argon on the equilibrium yield of NH₃.
parts.answer: The volume increases at constant pressure, so the partial pressures of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ all fall. The equilibrium shifts towards the side with more gas molecules (the left), so the yield of NH₃ decreases.
parts.working:
B1 volume increases at constant pressure, so partial pressures fall
B1 the side with more gas molecules (left, 4 against 2) is favoured
B1 yield of NH₃ decreases

author: HomiLabs

stem: For an exothermic reaction, Kc = 4.0 at 500 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how Kc changes when the temperature is raised to 600 K, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Kc decreases. A higher temperature favours the endothermic backward reaction, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and the ratio of products to reactants falls.
parts.working:
B1 Kc decreases
B1 higher temperature shifts equilibrium to the left (backward, endothermic side)

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2A(g) ⇌ B(g)   ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹. A mixture is at equilibrium in a sealed container.

parts.label: a
