parts.text: Predict the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium yield of B. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The yield of B increases. The left side has 2 mol of gas and the right side has 1 mol, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right to reduce the total number of gas molecules.
parts.working:
B1 yield of B increases
B1 fewer gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts right

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of increasing the temperature on (i) the rate of the reaction and (ii) the equilibrium yield of B. Explain each answer.
parts.answer:
(i) The rate increases because more molecules have energy at least equal to the activation energy, so collisions are more successful.
(ii) The yield of B decreases because the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts to the left.
parts.working:
B1 (i) rate increases: more molecules exceed the activation energy
B1 (ii) yield of B decreases
B1 (ii) reason: forward reaction exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is carried out at about 450 °C. Given values for this question: at 450 °C the equilibrium yield of SO₃ is about 96 % at 1 atm and about 99 % at 5 atm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plant operates at about 2 atm rather than 5 atm, even though the yield at 5 atm is higher.
parts.answer: Raising the pressure increases the yield, but compressing the gases costs a lot of energy and needs stronger, more expensive equipment. Going from 2 atm to 5 atm gives only a small extra gain in yield, so the higher cost is not worthwhile.
parts.working:
B1 higher pressure raises yield (fewer gas molecules on the right)
B1 high cost: compression energy and stronger, more expensive equipment
B1 the extra yield above about 2 atm is small, so it is not economic

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dichromate and chromate ions are in equilibrium in aqueous solution: Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq). Dichromate ions are orange and chromate ions are yellow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the colour change when sodium hydroxide solution is added to the orange solution, and explain it.
parts.answer: The solution turns yellow. OH⁻ ions react with H⁺ ions, removing H⁺ from the equilibrium, so the equilibrium shifts to the right and more yellow CrO₄²⁻ forms.
parts.working:
B1 colour changes to yellow
B1 OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the equilibrium
B1 equilibrium shifts right, so more CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) forms

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Haber process, the ammonia formed is continuously removed from the reaction mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of continuously removing NH₃ on the equilibrium yield of NH₃.
parts.answer: Removing NH₃ lowers its concentration, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace it. More NH₃ forms, so the yield increases.
parts.working:
B1 removing product shifts the equilibrium to the right
B1 yield of NH₃ increases

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the equilibrium X(g) ⇌ Y(g), Kc = [Y]/[X]. Kc = 0.250 at 400 K and Kc = 0.0800 at 500 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction.
parts.answer: ΔH is negative (the forward reaction is exothermic), because Kc falls as the temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 negative ΔH, since Kc decreases with increasing temperature

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a) using Le Chatelier's principle.
parts.answer: When the temperature rises, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction, which is to the left (towards X). So [Y]/[X] falls and Kc decreases.
parts.working:
B1 higher temperature shifts equilibrium towards the endothermic (backward) side
B1 this lowers [Y]/[X], so Kc decreases; the forward reaction must be exothermic

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound R is shaken with hexane and water until equilibrium is reached.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an expression for the partition coefficient Kpc of R between hexane and water.
parts.answer: Kpc = [R in hexane] / [R in water]
parts.working: B1 concentration in hexane divided by concentration in water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the units of Kpc.
parts.answer: No units (it is a ratio of concentrations in the same units)
parts.working: B1 the units cancel

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound R is shared between ethoxyethane and water at 298 K. At equilibrium its concentration is 0.120 mol dm⁻³ in ethoxyethane and 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kpc for R between ethoxyethane and water.
parts.working:
M1 Kpc = [R in ethoxyethane]/[R in water] = 0.120/0.0400
A1 = 3.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which solvent R is more soluble in, and justify your answer from the value of Kpc.
parts.answer: Ethoxyethane, because Kpc is greater than 1, so the concentration in ethoxyethane is higher.
parts.working: B1 ethoxyethane; Kpc > 1 means more R dissolves in the ethoxyethane

author: HomiLabs

stem: A chemist wants to extract an organic compound from an aqueous solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two properties that a suitable solvent for this solvent extraction should have.
parts.answer: It must be immiscible with water (so two layers form), and the compound must be much more soluble in it than in water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: immiscible with water; the compound is much more soluble in it; it does not react with the compound; it can be easily separated (for example, low boiling point)

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2.00 g of a solute is dissolved in 50.0 cm³ of water. The solution is shaken with 50.0 cm³ of ethoxyethane. Kpc (ethoxyethane : water) = 6.0 at 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the relationship between the mass of solute in the ethoxyethane (m_e) and the mass in the water (m_w) at equilibrium, using equal volumes.
parts.answer: m_e / m_w = 6.0, because the volumes are equal so the mass ratio equals the concentration ratio
parts.working: B1 with equal volumes, m_e/m_w = Kpc = 6.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of solute extracted into the ethoxyethane.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A compound has Kpc (organic solvent : water) = 8.0 at 298 K. A total of 3.00 g of the compound is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water, and the solution is shaken with 25 cm³ of the organic solvent. At equilibrium the total mass of the compound is 3.00 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the mass in the organic solvent is twice the mass left in the water.
parts.answer: mass_organic / 25 ÷ (mass_water / 100) = 8.0, so mass_organic = 2 × mass_water

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the compound in the organic solvent.
parts.working: B1 m_o + m_w = 3.00 and m_o = 2 m_w, so m_w = 1.00 g and m_o = 2.00 g

author: HomiLabs

stem: A compound is shaken until equilibrium is reached between two solvents. In solvent X, 0.80 g of the compound is found in 20.0 cm³. In solvent Y, 0.25 g is found in 25.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kpc (solvent X : solvent Y).

author: HomiLabs

stem: 100 cm³ of water contains 2.00 g of compound Q. Kpc (ethoxyethane : water) = 5.0 at 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum volume of ethoxyethane needed for a single extraction that removes 95 % of Q from the water.
parts.answer: 380 cm³
parts.working:
M1 fraction remaining in water = V_w / (V_w + Kpc × V_o)
M1 0.05 = 100 / (100 + 5.0 × V_o)
A1 100 + 5.0 V_o = 2000, so V_o = 380 cm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, is dissolved in ethoxyethane. The ethoxyethane solution is shaken with aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃(aq).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why most of the benzoic acid moves into the aqueous layer.
parts.answer: Benzoic acid reacts with HCO₃⁻: C₆H₅COOH + HCO₃⁻ → C₆H₅COO⁻ + H₂O + CO₂. The ionic benzoate salt is very soluble in water and hardly soluble in ethoxyethane, so the equilibrium moves strongly into the aqueous layer.
parts.working:
B1 benzoic acid reacts with HCO₃⁻ to form an ionic salt
B1 the ionic benzoate is very soluble in water but not in ethoxyethane
B1 so the partition equilibrium moves into the aqueous layer

author: HomiLabs

stem: Iodine is far more soluble in hexane than in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why iodine is much more soluble in hexane than in water.
parts.answer: Iodine and hexane are both non-polar, so they are attracted to each other by van der Waals (London dispersion) forces that are similar in strength to those in each pure substance. Water molecules are polar and held together by hydrogen bonds, which iodine cannot replace, so iodine dissolves poorly in water.
parts.working:
B1 both iodine and hexane are non-polar
B1 they form induced dipole (van der Waals) forces with each other
B1 water has hydrogen bonding that iodine cannot replace, so solubility is low

author: HomiLabs

stem: 200 cm³ of aqueous solution contains 0.250 mol dm⁻³ of compound Q. It is shaken with 100 cm³ of dichloromethane, with Kpc (dichloromethane : water) = 6.5 at 298 K, and the layers are allowed to separate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the fraction of Q remaining in the water after one extraction is 0.235.
parts.working:
M1 fraction remaining = V_w / (V_w + Kpc × V_o)
A1 = 200/850 = 0.235

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of Q remaining in the water.
parts.working: B1 initial amount = 0.250 × 0.200 = 0.0500 mol; remaining = 0.0500 × 0.235 = 0.0118 mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student compares two ways of extracting a solute from 100 cm³ of water. Both use a total of 100 cm³ of the same organic solvent, which has Kpc (organic : water) = 5.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why two extractions of 50 cm³ each remove more solute than one extraction of 100 cm³.
parts.answer: Each extraction re-establishes the partition equilibrium with fresh solvent, so a fixed fraction of the solute still in the water is removed each time. Splitting the solvent into smaller portions therefore leaves less solute behind in total.
parts.working:
B1 each portion re-establishes the partition equilibrium with fresh solvent
B1 a fixed fraction of the remaining solute is removed each time
B1 so several small portions remove more solute than one large portion of the same total volume

author: HomiLabs

stem: A separating funnel is used to extract a compound from water with an organic solvent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two liquid layers form when the mixture is left to stand.
parts.answer: The two solvents are immiscible (they do not mix), so they separate into two layers.
parts.working: B1 immiscible solvents form separate layers

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the partition coefficient stays constant at a fixed temperature.
parts.answer: Kpc is an equilibrium constant, so its value depends only on temperature (and not on the amounts of solvents used).
parts.working: B1 Kpc is an equilibrium constant that depends only on temperature

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ + OH⁻, which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base?
A HCO₃⁻
B H₂O
C H₂CO₃
D OH⁻
parts.answer: A HCO₃⁻
parts.working: HCO₃⁻ accepts a proton from water to form H₂CO₃, so it is the base. Water donates a proton, so it is the acid. H₂CO₃ is a product, and OH⁻ is formed when water donates H⁺; neither accepts a proton in this reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base.
parts.answer: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor. A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor.
parts.working:
B1 acid: proton donor
B1 base: proton acceptor

stem: Identify the Brønsted–Lowry acid and the Brønsted–Lowry base in each reaction.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: HNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)
parts.answer: Acid: HNO₃; base: H₂O
parts.working: B1 HNO₃ donates H⁺; H₂O accepts H⁺

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
parts.answer: Acid: H₂O; base: CH₃COO⁻
parts.working: B1 H₂O donates H⁺ to form OH⁻; CH₃COO⁻ accepts H⁺ to form CH₃COOH

author: HomiLabs

stem: Give the formula of the species requested in each part.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The conjugate base of HSO₄⁻.
parts.answer: SO₄²⁻
parts.working: B1 removing one H⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: The conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻.
parts.answer: HPO₄²⁻
parts.working: B1 removing one H⁺

parts.label: c
parts.text: The conjugate acid of CO₃²⁻.
parts.answer: HCO₃⁻
parts.working: B1 adding one H⁺

author: HomiLabs

stem: Water can act both as an acid and as a base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an amphoteric substance. Write two equations to show HCO₃⁻ acting as (i) an acid and (ii) a base.
parts.answer:
An amphoteric substance can act as both a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a base.
(i) HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺ (HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺)
(ii) HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃ (HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺)
parts.working:
B1 can act as both acid (proton donor) and base (proton acceptor)
B1 equation (i) with HCO₃⁻ giving H⁺
B1 equation (ii) with HCO₃⁻ accepting H⁺

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid that partly dissociates in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for ethanoic acid reacting with water, and identify both conjugate acid–base pairs.
parts.answer: CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺. Pairs: CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O.
parts.working:
B1 correct equation with ⇌
B1 both pairs: CH₃COOH (acid)/CH₃COO⁻ (base) and H₃O⁺ (acid)/H₂O (base)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Consider the reactions of HCl (a strong acid) and CH₃COOH (a weak acid) with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid in terms of proton transfer to water and the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: A strong acid transfers its proton to water almost completely, so the equilibrium lies far to the right and the conjugate base is very weak. A weak acid transfers only a small fraction of its protons, so the equilibrium lies to the left.
parts.working:
B1 strong acid: complete proton transfer, equilibrium far right
B1 weak acid: partial transfer, equilibrium lies to the left
B1 conjugate base of a strong acid is very weak (or the reverse for weak acid)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonia gas reacts with hydrogen chloride gas to form ammonium chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for this reaction and identify both conjugate acid–base pairs.
parts.answer: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻). Pairs: NH₄⁺/NH₃ and HCl/Cl⁻.
parts.working:
B1 correct equation
B1 pairs: NH₄⁺ (acid)/NH₃ (base) and HCl (acid)/Cl⁻ (base)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Water is a Brønsted–Lowry base in some reactions and a Brønsted–Lowry acid in others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for water acting as a base towards HCl, and name the conjugate acid formed.
parts.answer: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻; the conjugate acid is H₃O⁺ (hydroxonium ion)
parts.working: B1 water accepts H⁺ to form H₃O⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for water acting as an acid towards NH₃, and explain why water is an acid in this reaction.
parts.answer: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Water donates a proton to NH₃, so it is the proton donor (acid) here.
parts.working:
B1 correct equation
B1 water donates H⁺ to NH₃, which accepts it

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, reacts with a concentrated strong acid: CH₃CH₂OH + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the Brønsted–Lowry base in this reaction.
parts.answer: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), because it accepts a proton
parts.working: B1 ethanol accepts H⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the conjugate base of CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂OH
parts.working: B1 removing H⁺ from CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ gives ethanol

author: HomiLabs

stem: H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → HPO₄²⁻(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the Brønsted–Lowry acid and the Brønsted–Lowry base in this reaction.
parts.answer: Acid: H₂PO₄⁻ (it loses H⁺ to form HPO₄²⁻). Base: CO₃²⁻ (it gains H⁺ to form HCO₃⁻).
parts.working:
B1 acid H₂PO₄⁻ (donates H⁺)
B1 base CO₃²⁻ (accepts H⁺)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the two conjugate acid–base pairs in this reaction.
parts.answer: H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ and HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻
parts.working: B1 HPO₄²⁻ is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻; HCO₃⁻ is the conjugate acid of CO₃²⁻

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrazine, N₂H₄, is a base. It accepts a proton to form the ion N₂H₅⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of the conjugate base of N₂H₅⁺.
parts.answer: N₂H₄
parts.working: B1 removing H⁺ from N₂H₅⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the conjugate acid of N₂H₄.
parts.answer: N₂H₅⁺
parts.working: B1 adding H⁺ to N₂H₄

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sodium carbonate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid in two stages: Stage 1: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻. Stage 2: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃ (which then decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In stage 1, identify the base and state its conjugate acid.
parts.answer: Base: CO₃²⁻; conjugate acid: HCO₃⁻
parts.working: B1 CO₃²⁻ accepts H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ is its conjugate acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: In stage 2, state whether HCO₃⁻ is acting as an acid or a base, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Base, because it accepts a proton (H⁺) to form H₂CO₃
parts.working: B1 HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ to form H₂CO₃, so it is a base

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why stage 1 happens before stage 2.
parts.answer: CO₃²⁻ is a stronger base than HCO₃⁻, so it accepts the first proton more readily.
parts.working: B1 CO₃²⁻ is the stronger base and reacts first

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change does NOT alter the position of an equilibrium?
A adding a catalyst to the reaction mixture
B adding more N₂ to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
C raising the temperature of an exothermic reaction
D increasing the pressure on N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)
parts.answer: A adding a catalyst to the reaction mixture
parts.working: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so the position of equilibrium is unchanged; it only reduces the time to reach equilibrium. B shifts the equilibrium to the right, C shifts it left, and D shifts it left (fewer gas molecules are on the left).

stem: A sealed flask contains ice and water at 0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this equilibrium is described as dynamic.
parts.answer: Water molecules continually freeze onto the ice and ice continually melts. The two processes occur at equal rates, so the amounts of ice and water stay constant.
parts.working:
B1 melting and freezing both continue
B1 at equal rates, so there is no net change

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conditions that must be met for a dynamic equilibrium to be established.
parts.answer: The reaction must be reversible, and the system must be closed (no substance can escape).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: reversible reaction; closed system; constant temperature (and pressure if gases are present)

stem: At equilibrium in a closed system, the rate of the forward reaction is 2.4 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the rate of the backward reaction at this moment, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2.4 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, because at equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal
parts.working: B1 equal rates at dynamic equilibrium

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student claims: 'Once equilibrium is reached, the reactions have stopped.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: The claim is incorrect. The forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant but are not stationary.
parts.working:
B1 claim is wrong: reactions do not stop
B1 forward and backward rates are equal, so there is no net change

author: HomiLabs

stem: A reversible reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) starts with pure A in a closed container.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rates of the forward and backward reactions change from the start until equilibrium is reached.
parts.answer: At the start the forward rate is highest because only A is present, and the backward rate is zero. As B forms, the forward rate falls and the backward rate rises. The two rates become equal at equilibrium and then remain constant.
parts.working:
B1 at the start: forward rate maximum, backward rate zero
B1 forward rate falls and backward rate rises as B forms
B1 rates become equal at equilibrium and stay constant

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a closed container the reaction A ⇌ B starts with 1.00 mol of A and no B. At equilibrium the container holds 0.70 mol of A and 0.30 mol of B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the original A that has been converted to B.
parts.working:
M1 amount of A converted = 0.30 mol (1 mol A gives 1 mol B)
A1 percentage = 0.30 / 1.00 × 100 = 30 %

author: HomiLabs

stem: A saturated solution of NaCl is in contact with excess solid NaCl in a sealed vessel at constant temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mass of undissolved solid stays constant.
parts.answer: NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) is a dynamic equilibrium. Ions leave the solid surface and ions in solution crystallise back onto the solid at equal rates. Because the rates are equal, the concentration of the solution and the mass of the solid stay constant.
parts.working:
B1 equilibrium between solid and dissolved ions is reversible
B1 rate of dissolving equals rate of crystallisation
B1 so the concentration and the mass of solid remain constant

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student says that the position of an equilibrium depends on how fast the reactions go.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is incorrect. The position of equilibrium depends on the conditions (temperature, pressure, concentrations) and the equilibrium constant; the rate only determines how quickly equilibrium is reached.
parts.working:
B1 position depends on conditions/Kc, not on rate
B1 rate only changes the time to reach equilibrium

author: HomiLabs

stem: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture that is not yet at equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the idea of activation energy, why the catalyst does not change the composition of the equilibrium mixture but does make equilibrium reached sooner.
parts.answer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy for both the forward and backward reactions. It increases both rate constants, but their ratio kf/kb (which equals Kc) is unchanged, so the equilibrium composition is the same. Equilibrium is simply reached sooner.
parts.working:
B1 lowers the activation energy of both forward and backward reactions
B1 kf/kb (= Kc) is unchanged, so the equilibrium composition is unchanged
B1 equilibrium is reached more quickly

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two identical sealed flasks are kept at the same temperature for the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g). Flask 1 starts with 2.00 mol of A and no B. Flask 2 starts with 1.00 mol of A and 1.00 mol of B. Both flasks reach equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the final equilibrium compositions and explain your answer.
parts.answer: The final compositions are the same. The equilibrium position depends only on the equilibrium constant at that temperature, not on the starting mixture, and the equilibrium can be approached from either side.
parts.working:
B1 same final composition in both flasks
B1 position depends only on K (and T), not on starting amounts
B1 equilibrium can be reached from either direction

author: HomiLabs

stem: The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH > 0). The temperature of an equilibrium mixture is raised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the forward rate increases more than the backward rate.
parts.answer: For an endothermic forward reaction, the activation energy of the forward reaction is greater than that of the backward reaction. A rise in temperature increases the rate constants exponentially, and a larger activation energy gives a bigger fractional increase, so the forward rate increases more and the equilibrium shifts right.
parts.working:
B1 ΔH > 0 means Ea(forward) > Ea(backward)
B1 higher temperature increases both rate constants, with the larger fractional rise for the forward reaction
B1 so the equilibrium shifts to the right

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the reversible reaction A ⇌ B, both steps are first order. The forward rate constant is kf = 0.20 s⁻¹ and the backward rate constant is kb = 0.050 s⁻¹. The total concentration of A and B is 1.00 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that at equilibrium [B]/[A] = kf/kb.
parts.answer: Rate forward = kf[A] and rate backward = kb[B]. At equilibrium these are equal, so kf[A] = kb[B] and [B]/[A] = kf/kb = 0.20/0.050 = 4.0.
parts.working:
M1 rate forward = rate backward: kf[A] = kb[B]
A1 [B]/[A] = kf/kb = 4.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of A and B.
parts.answer: [A] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³; [B] = 0.80 mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the catalyst and the typical operating conditions used.
parts.answer: Iron catalyst; temperature about 450 °C and pressure about 200 atm (in the range 150–300 atm)
parts.working:
B1 iron (Fe) catalyst
B1 temperature about 400–450 °C and pressure about 200 atm

author: HomiLabs

stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)   ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the sign of ΔH tells you about the forward reaction, and the effect of raising the temperature on the equilibrium yield.
parts.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic (heat is released). Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, so the yield of NH₃ falls.
parts.working:
B1 negative ΔH means the forward reaction is exothermic
B1 higher temperature shifts equilibrium left, lowering the yield

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Haber process, the temperature is a compromise between yield and rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used rather than a lower temperature.
parts.answer: A lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, but the rate of reaction would be too slow to produce ammonia economically. At about 450 °C the rate is acceptable, even though the yield is lower than the maximum possible.
parts.working:
B1 lower temperature gives a slow rate, which is uneconomic
B1 at about 450 °C the rate is acceptable with a reasonable yield

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonia is produced by the Haber process. The mass of 1.00 tonne = 1.00 × 10⁶ g of NH₃ (Mr = 17.0) is to be produced from N₂ (Mr = 28.0) at 100 % yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of NH₃ in 1.00 tonne.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of N₂ needed, in tonnes.
parts.answer: 0.824 tonnes
parts.working:
M1 amount of N₂ = 5.88 × 10⁴ / 2 = 2.94 × 10⁴ mol (1 N₂ : 2 NH₃)
A1 mass = 2.94 × 10⁴ × 28.0 = 8.24 × 10⁵ g = 0.824 tonnes

author: HomiLabs

stem: An iron catalyst is used in the Haber process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the catalyst and state its effect on the equilibrium yield.
parts.answer: The catalyst speeds up both the forward and backward reactions, so equilibrium is reached quickly and production is economic. It does not change the equilibrium yield, because it changes both rates equally.
parts.working:
B1 increases the rate so equilibrium is reached sooner
B1 no change in yield because forward and backward rates are increased equally

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Haber process the reaction mixture leaving the reactor contains unreacted N₂ and H₂ as well as NH₃. The NH₃ is separated by cooling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled, and why cooling is used to remove the NH₃.
parts.answer: Recycling returns unreacted gases to the reactor so that more of the feedstock is converted, which raises the overall yield and lowers the cost. Cooling liquefies NH₃, so it can be separated from the gases. Removing NH₃ shifts the equilibrium to the right to replace it.
parts.working:
B1 recycling returns unreacted gases, improving overall yield and cost
B1 cooling liquefies NH₃ so it can be separated
B1 removing NH₃ shifts the equilibrium right

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Contact process, sulfur trioxide is converted into sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why SO₃ is absorbed into concentrated sulfuric acid rather than directly into water.
parts.answer: Reacting SO₃ directly with water is highly exothermic and forms a fine mist (acid droplets) that is hard to collect. Absorbing SO₃ into concentrated (about 98 %) sulfuric acid avoids this mist, and the product is then diluted with water to give the required acid.
parts.working:
B1 direct reaction with water is very exothermic
B1 forms a fine acid mist that is hard to collect
B1 absorption into concentrated H₂SO₄ avoids the mist

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Haber and Contact processes both use temperatures near 450 °C, but they use different pressures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the pressures used in the two processes and suggest one reason for the difference.
parts.answer: The Haber process uses a high pressure (about 200 atm), while the Contact process uses about 1–2 atm. The Haber process has fewer gas molecules on the right (2 against 4), so a high pressure is needed for an acceptable yield. The Contact process already gives a high yield at low pressure.
parts.working:
B1 Haber about 200 atm; Contact about 1–2 atm
B1 Haber needs high pressure to shift equilibrium right; Contact already has a high yield at low pressure

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the Haber process the pressure is not increased much above 200 atm, even though a higher pressure increases the yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pressure is not increased further.
parts.answer: Compressing gases to higher pressures needs a lot of energy and stronger, more expensive equipment, which adds safety risks. The extra yield gained above 200 atm is small, so the cost is not justified.
parts.working:
B1 higher pressure costs more energy and stronger equipment
B1 the extra yield is small, so it is not economic

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sulfur is converted into sulfuric acid by the Contact process. Assume an overall yield of 97 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass, in tonnes, of H₂SO₄ (Mr = 98.1) produced from 1.00 tonne of sulfur (Ar = 32.1).
parts.answer: 2.96 tonnes
parts.working:
M1 1 mol S gives 1 mol H₂SO₄ (S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄)
M1 theoretical mass = 1.00 × 98.1/32.1 = 3.056 tonnes
A1 at 97 % yield: 3.056 × 0.97 = 2.96 tonnes

author: HomiLabs

stem: 500 mol of N₂ and 1500 mol of H₂ are mixed in the Haber process. The yield is 25 % of the theoretical maximum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of NH₃ (Mr = 17.0) produced, in kg.
parts.working:
M1 N₂ and H₂ are in the exact ratio 1 : 3, so theoretical NH₃ = 2 × 500 = 1000 mol
M1 actual amount = 25 % of 1000 = 250 mol
A1 mass = 250 × 17.0 = 4250 g = 4.25 kg

author: HomiLabs

stem: Excess oxygen is used in the Contact process: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain why excess oxygen increases the yield of SO₃.
parts.answer: Adding O₂ (a reactant) shifts the equilibrium to the right, so more SO₃ forms. It also helps the SO₂ to be converted more fully.
parts.working:
B1 extra reactant shifts equilibrium right
B1 more SO₂ converted to SO₃

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Haber process must balance rate and yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in temperature affects the rate and the yield, and why the industrial conditions are a compromise.
parts.answer: A higher temperature increases the rate because more molecules have enough energy to react. However, the forward reaction is exothermic, so a higher temperature lowers the equilibrium yield. A lower temperature gives a higher yield but a slower rate. The catalysed process at about 450 °C is a compromise giving an acceptable rate and a reasonable yield.
parts.working:
B1 higher T increases the rate
B1 higher T lowers the equilibrium yield (exothermic forward reaction)
B1 compromise: about 450 °C with a catalyst gives an acceptable rate and yield

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Contact process converts sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide in a reversible reaction at about 450 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for this reversible step, including state symbols and the formula of the catalyst used.
parts.answer: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst (V₂O₅)
parts.working:
B1 correct balanced equation with state symbols
B1 catalyst V₂O₅ (vanadium(V) oxide)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which monomer forms an addition polymer with the repeat unit –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–?
A CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ (2-methylpropene)
B CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (but-2-ene)
C CH₂=CHCH₃ (propene)
D CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂ (2-methylbut-2-ene)
parts.answer: A CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ (2-methylpropene)
parts.working: In addition polymerisation the C=C bond opens and the carbon atoms of the monomer become the backbone. The repeat unit –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂– has two backbone carbons (one CH₂ and one C(CH₃)₂), four carbons in total, so the monomer is CH₂=C(CH₃)₂. B gives –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–; C gives –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–; D gives a five-carbon repeat unit.

stem: Ethenyl ethanoate has the structure CH₂=CH–OCOCH₃. It polymerises by addition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw the repeat unit of the polymer in the form –CH₂–CH(X)–, and identify the group X.
parts.answer: Repeat unit: –CH₂–CH(OCOCH₃)–; X is the ethanoyloxy group, –OCOCH₃ (an ester group attached through oxygen)
parts.working:
B1 backbone –CH₂–CH– with the C=C opened
B1 X = OCOCH₃ attached to the second carbon

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A polymer is made by addition polymerisation of methyl propenoate, CH₂=CH–COOCH₃. Which is the repeat unit?
A –CH₂–CH(COOCH₃)–
B –CH₂–C(COOCH₃)–CH₂–
C –CH(COOCH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–
D –CH₂–CH(OCOCH₃)–
parts.answer: A –CH₂–CH(COOCH₃)–
parts.working: The C=C of the monomer opens to give a two-carbon backbone unit, with the ester group COOCH₃ as the side group on one carbon. B has an extra backbone carbon, C has three backbone carbons, and D is the repeat unit of ethenyl ethanoate, not of methyl propenoate.

stem: Poly(ethenyl ethanoate) has the repeat unit –CH₂–CH(OCOCH₃)–, with Mr = 86.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of the polymer has an average of 480 repeat units per chain. Calculate the average Mr of the chain, to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A copolymer is made by addition of chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, and ethenylbenzene (styrene), C₆H₅CH=CH₂, in a 1 : 1 ratio. The two monomers alternate along the chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw the section of chain that contains one repeat unit from each monomer, in the form –[…]–, in the correct order.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)– (this two-unit sequence repeats along the chain)
parts.working:
B1 each monomer C=C opens to give a –CH₂–CH(X)– unit
B1 X = Cl from chloroethene and X = C₆H₅ from ethenylbenzene
B1 the units alternate in the order –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–

author: HomiLabs

stem: Poly(propene) has the repeat unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, with Mr = 42.1. A 1.00 kg sample of poly(propene) is burned completely in excess oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of repeat units in 1.00 kg.
parts.answer: 23.8 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced, in kg. (Mr of CO₂ = 44.0)
parts.working: B1 each C₃H₆ unit gives 3 CO₂: 3 × 23.75 × 44.0 = 3135 g

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of H₂O produced, in kg. (Mr of H₂O = 18.0)
parts.working: B1 each C₃H₆ unit gives 3 H₂O: 3 × 23.75 × 18.0 = 1283 g

author: HomiLabs

stem: A section of an addition copolymer is: –CH₂–CF₂–CH₂–CHF–CH₂–CF₂–CH₂–CHF–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two monomers that form this copolymer, giving their structures.
parts.answer: CH₂=CF₂ (1,1-difluoroethene) and CH₂=CHF (fluoroethene)
parts.working:
B1 the –CH₂–CF₂– unit comes from CH₂=CF₂
B1 the –CH₂–CHF– unit comes from CH₂=CHF
B1 the two monomers alternate in a 1 : 1 ratio along the chain

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of linkage formed between monomers in (i) a polyester and (ii) a polyamide.
parts.answer: (i) Ester linkage, –CO–O– (–COO–); (ii) amide linkage, –CO–NH–
parts.working:
B1 ester linkage –COO– in a polyester
B1 amide linkage –CONH– in a polyamide

stem: A polyester is made from ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH, and butanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₂COOH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated each time one ester link forms.
parts.answer: Water, H₂O
parts.working: B1 an –OH from the acid and an –H from the alcohol combine to form H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of the polyester.
parts.answer: –O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₂–CO–
parts.working:
M1 –O–CH₂CH₂–O– from the diol
A1 –CO–(CH₂)₂–CO– from the diacid, giving two ester links per repeat unit

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nylon-6 is made from 6-aminohexanoic acid, H₂N(CH₂)₅COOH (Mr = 131.2). Each monomer loses one molecule of water as it joins the chain. The repeat unit of nylon-6 is –NH(CH₂)₅CO–, with Mr = 113.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of water molecules released per repeat unit formed.
parts.answer: One water molecule per repeat unit
parts.working: B1 one condensation step per monomer added

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water released when 1.00 kg of nylon-6 forms. Give your answer in g.
parts.working:
M1 amount of repeat units = 1000 / 113.2 = 8.83 mol, so 8.83 mol of H₂O is released
A1 mass = 8.83 × 18.0 = 159 g

author: HomiLabs

stem: A polyester chain is made from ethane-1,2-diol and butanedioic acid. Each repeat unit, –O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₂–CO–, has Mr = 144.1. The chain has 50 repeat units (ignore the end groups).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the chain, and give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A polyamide is made from 1,6-diaminohexane, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂, and benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride, ClCO–C₆H₄–COCl. The acid chloride reacts with the amine groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of this polyamide.
parts.answer: –NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–C₆H₄–CO–
parts.working:
M1 –NH–(CH₂)₆–NH– from the diamine
A1 –CO–C₆H₄–CO– from the benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl unit, with the two amide links

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated at each amide link.
parts.answer: Hydrogen chloride, HCl
parts.working: B1 Cl from the acid chloride and H from the amine combine to form HCl

author: HomiLabs

stem: 1.00 mol of 1,6-diaminohexane reacts completely with 1.00 mol of benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride to form a polyamide, releasing HCl at each amide link. Mr of HCl = 36.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of HCl released, in g.
parts.working:
M1 each molecule of diamine has two NH₂ groups and each acid chloride has two COCl groups, so 2 mol HCl is released
A1 mass = 2 × 36.5 = 73.0 g

author: HomiLabs

stem: A monomer used to make a condensation polymer must have two functional groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a monomer used in condensation polymerisation must have two functional groups.
parts.answer: Each monomer must react at both ends so that it can link to two other monomers and the chain can grow in two directions. A monomer with only one functional group would stop the chain from growing.
parts.working:
B1 two reactive groups allow linking at both ends, so the chain grows in both directions
B1 a single functional group would act as a chain end and stop growth

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms thermoplastic polymer and thermosetting polymer.
parts.answer: Thermoplastic: softens and can be remoulded on heating, because the chains are held by intermolecular forces that can be overcome. Thermosetting: has a cross-linked network of covalent bonds, so it does not soften on heating and it decomposes instead.
parts.working:
B1 thermoplastic: softens and can be remoulded on heating
B1 thermosetting: cross-linked network that does not soften on heating

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why high-density poly(ethene), HDPE, is denser than low-density poly(ethene), LDPE.
parts.answer: HDPE has fewer side branches, so its chains pack more closely together and form more crystalline regions. The closer packing gives a higher density.
parts.working:
B1 fewer branches allow the chains to pack more closely
B1 closer packing and higher crystallinity give a higher density

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a thermosetting polymer that make it rigid.
parts.answer: Covalent cross-links join the chains into a network; this network means the chains cannot slide past one another.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: covalent cross-links between chains; network structure; chains cannot slide past each other

stem: Polyesters and polyamides can be broken down in some environments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term biodegradable.
parts.answer: Able to be broken down by living organisms (such as microorganisms) into simpler natural substances.
parts.working: B1 broken down by living organisms into natural substances

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why polyesters can be broken down by hydrolysis.
parts.answer: Ester groups are hydrolysed by water (often catalysed by enzymes), breaking the polymer chain into smaller molecules.
parts.working: B1 ester links are hydrolysed by water, splitting the chain

author: HomiLabs

stem: Plastic waste is collected and sorted for mechanical recycling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of mechanical recycling.
parts.answer: Advantage: uses less energy and fewer new raw materials than making new polymer. Disadvantage: plastics must be sorted and cleaned, and repeated heating breaks chains, so the quality of the recycled plastic falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: any advantage (less energy or raw material use; less waste) and any disadvantage (sorting and cleaning needed; degradation of chains on reprocessing)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Unplasticised poly(chloroethene), PVC, is rigid. Plasticised PVC is soft and flexible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why adding a plasticiser makes PVC more flexible.
parts.answer: Small plasticiser molecules fit between the polymer chains and push them apart. This weakens the dipole–dipole forces between the polar C–Cl groups, so the chains slide past each other more easily.
parts.working:
B1 plasticiser molecules fit between the polymer chains
B1 they weaken dipole–dipole forces between the C–Cl groups
B1 chains can slide more easily, so the material is more flexible

author: HomiLabs

stem: Poly(propene) floats on water, and its density is about 0.90 g cm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why poly(propene) has a density less than that of water.
parts.answer: The chains are non-polar and held only by weak van der Waals forces, so they pack loosely. Water molecules are held closer together by hydrogen bonds, so water is denser.
parts.working:
B1 weak van der Waals forces only, so chains pack loosely
B1 water has stronger hydrogen bonding, so it is denser (1.00 g cm⁻³)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(alkene)s are very resistant to degradation in landfill sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why poly(alkene)s degrade so slowly, and describe how they break up into smaller pieces over time.
parts.answer: The C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar, and the polymer has no hydrolysable groups, so microorganisms cannot readily digest it. Ultraviolet light breaks C–C bonds in the chains through free-radical reactions, making the polymer brittle so that it breaks into small fragments (microplastics).
parts.working:
B1 strong non-polar bonds and no hydrolysable groups, so not biodegradable
B1 UV light initiates free-radical bond breaking (photodegradation)
B1 the polymer becomes brittle and forms smaller fragments (microplastics)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Burning PVC produces a gas that turns damp universal indicator paper red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas and explain why burning PVC is hazardous.
parts.answer: Hydrogen chloride, HCl. It is a toxic, corrosive gas, and it forms hydrochloric acid when it dissolves in water, damaging the lungs and equipment.
parts.working:
B1 hydrogen chloride (HCl)
B1 toxic and corrosive; forms hydrochloric acid with moisture

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pyrolysis of poly(ethene) means heating it in the absence of air. The products are a mixture of alkanes and alkenes of different chain lengths.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the products are a mixture of compounds and not a single compound.
parts.answer: The long chains break at random C–C bonds, so fragments of many different lengths form. The breaking occurs by a free-radical mechanism, which gives a range of alkanes and alkenes. Each fragment is a different size, so the product is a mixture.
parts.working:
B1 random C–C bond breaking along the chain gives fragments of many lengths
B1 free-radical mechanism gives a range of products
B1 alkanes (saturated) and alkenes (unsaturated) of different sizes form, so a mixture results

author: HomiLabs

stem: Poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE, has an average Mr of 1.20 × 10⁶. The repeat unit –CF₂–CF₂– has Mr = 100.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average number of repeat units in one molecule of PTFE.
parts.working:
M1 n = Mr(polymer) / Mr(repeat unit) = 1.20 × 10⁶ / 100.0
A1 n = 1.20 × 10⁴

author: HomiLabs

stem: Natural rubber is made of long unbranched chains and is soft. Vulcanised rubber is made by heating natural rubber with sulfur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why vulcanised rubber is harder, stronger and more elastic than natural rubber.
parts.answer: Sulfur forms cross-links between the chains. These cross-links stop the chains sliding past each other, so the rubber is harder and returns to its original shape after stretching.
parts.working:
B1 sulfur cross-links restrict the movement of chains
B1 the material is stronger and returns to shape (more elastic)

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nylon-6,6 is spun into fibres for carpets in busy shops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two properties of nylon-6,6 that make it suitable for hard-wearing carpet fibres, and explain each.
parts.answer: Strength: hydrogen bonds between the amide groups of neighbouring chains give high tensile strength. Durability: it is tough and resistant to wear, so nets last a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a property with an explanation, for example strength (hydrogen bonding) and durability or flexibility

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two samples of poly(ethene) have average Mr values of 2.0 × 10³ and 2.0 × 10⁵.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the sample with the higher average Mr is likely to have a higher melting point.
parts.answer: Longer chains have more contact points, so there are more van der Waals (London dispersion) forces between chains in total. More energy is needed to overcome these forces and separate the chains, so the melting point is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: longer chains give more points of contact and more van der Waals forces in total; more energy is needed to separate the chains; poly(ethene) has only van der Waals forces between chains

author: HomiLabs

stem: Poly(ethylene terephthalate), PET, has the repeat unit C₁₀H₈O₄ (Mr = 192.2). Polyesters can be hydrolysed, but PET is slow to degrade in practice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of repeat units in 50.0 g of PET.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced by complete combustion of 50.0 g of PET, to 3 significant figures. (Mr of CO₂ = 44.0)
parts.working:
M1 each repeat unit gives 10 CO₂, so 10 × 0.260 = 2.60 mol CO₂
A1 mass = 2.60 × 44.0 = 114 g

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student claims: 'All polymers that contain C=O groups are biodegradable.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this claim, giving examples.
parts.answer: The claim is incorrect. Ester and amide groups (C=O) can be hydrolysed, but many such polymers are slow to degrade in practice; PET and nylon-6,6 are examples. Poly(alkene)s contain no C=O groups and are not biodegradable. Biodegradation depends on the polymer structure, the conditions and the presence of microorganisms.
parts.working:
B1 claim is incorrect: C=O groups alone do not guarantee biodegradation
B1 ester/amide groups can be hydrolysed, but PET and nylon-6,6 degrade very slowly in practice
B1 degradation depends on structure, conditions and microorganisms; poly(alkene)s have no C=O and are not biodegradable

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl, in water was studied at 25 °C. Initial rates were measured for three mixtures:
Experiment 1: [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [OH⁻] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to (CH₃)₃CCl and with respect to OH⁻. Explain how the data show each order.
parts.answer: First order with respect to (CH₃)₃CCl; zero order with respect to OH⁻.
parts.working: 1 mark: doubling [(CH₃)₃CCl] doubles the rate (experiments 1 and 2), so first order. 1 mark: tripling [OH⁻] has no effect on the rate (experiments 1 and 3), so zero order. 1 mark: orders are found from the ratio of rates when only one concentration changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl]
parts.working: Only a reactant with a non-zero order appears in the rate equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, and give its units.
parts.working: k = rate ÷ [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.10 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. 1 mark rearrangement, 1 mark value, 1 mark units (s⁻¹, as the reaction is first order overall).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction has the rate equation rate = k[A]²[B]. The rate constant at the temperature used is k = 0.035 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.50 mol dm⁻³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.58 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = 0.035 × (0.30)² × 0.50 = 0.035 × 0.090 × 0.50 = 1.575 × 10⁻³ = 1.58 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. 1 mark squaring [A]; 1 mark the product; 1 mark 3 s.f. with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall order of this reaction.
parts.answer: 3 (second order in A and first order in B)
parts.working: Overall order is the sum of the individual orders: 2 + 1 = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction is zero order with respect to Y and first order with respect to X. Give the units of the rate constant, k.
parts.answer: s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = k[X], so k = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³) = s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate constant of a reaction has units dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Deduce the overall order of the reaction.
parts.answer: 2 (second order overall)
parts.working: For second order, rate = k[A]² so k = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the units of k depend on the overall order of the reaction, although the units of the rate do not.
parts.answer: The rate is always in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, but rate = k × (concentration terms), so k = rate ÷ (concentration)ⁿ and its units change with the overall order n.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate always has units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. 1 mark: k = rate ÷ concentration^(overall order), so the units of k depend on n.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A reaction is first order with respect to A and second order with respect to B. Deduce the units of k.
parts.answer: dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = k[A][B]², overall order 3. k = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹. 1 mark for the expression for k, 1 mark for the units.

stem:
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen: 2NO(g) + 2H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
Initial rates were measured at 1000 K:
Experiment 1: [NO] = 0.0050 mol dm⁻³, [H₂] = 0.0020 mol dm⁻³, rate = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [NO] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³, [H₂] = 0.0020 mol dm⁻³, rate = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [NO] = 0.0050 mol dm⁻³, [H₂] = 0.0040 mol dm⁻³, rate = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to NO, with respect to H₂ and the overall order.
parts.answer: Order 2 with respect to NO; order 1 with respect to H₂; overall order 3.
parts.working: 1 mark: [NO] doubled, rate × 4 so order 2. 1 mark: [H₂] doubled, rate × 2 so order 1. 1 mark: overall = 2 + 1 = 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, k, with its units.
parts.answer: rate = k[NO]²[H₂]; k = 2.4 × 10³ dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: k = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.0050² × 0.0020) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (2.5 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³) = 2400 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. 1 mark rate equation; 1 mark rearrangement; 1 mark value and units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the order with respect to H₂ is not the same as its coefficient in the equation.
parts.answer: The order is determined experimentally from the data and reflects the rate-determining step, which involves only one H₂ molecule; the equation’s coefficient does not necessarily give the order.
parts.working: 1 mark: orders come from experiments, not from the balanced equation. 1 mark: the rate-determining step (and so the rate equation) may involve fewer molecules than the equation shows.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Propanone reacts with bromine in acidic solution:
CH₃COCH₃(aq) + Br₂(aq) → CH₃COCH₂Br(aq) + HBr(aq)
Experiment 1: [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [Br₂] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [Br₂] = 0.0020 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
The rate equation is rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate does not change when [Br₂] is doubled.
parts.answer: The reaction is zero order with respect to bromine, so [Br₂] does not appear in the rate equation and does not affect the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: bromine is zero order (the rate equation contains no [Br₂] term). 1 mark: so changing [Br₂] has no effect on the rate, because the rate-determining step does not involve bromine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, with its units.
parts.answer: k = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
parts.working: k = rate ÷ ([CH₃COCH₃][H⁺]) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ (0.80 × 0.10) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. 1 mark for the value, 1 mark for the units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the initial rate when [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [Br₂] = 0.0050 mol dm⁻³ at the same temperature.
parts.answer: 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.40 × 0.25 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The bromine concentration makes no difference.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction 2X + Y → Z was studied at constant temperature:
Experiment 1: [X] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, [Y] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [X] = 0.60 mol dm⁻³, [Y] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, rate = 3.6 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [X] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, [Y] = 0.90 mol dm⁻³, rate = 1.2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the rate equation for the reaction, showing how the orders were found.
parts.answer: rate = k[X]²[Y]
parts.working: 1 mark: [X] × 3 gives rate × 9, so order 2 in X. 1 mark: [Y] × 3 gives rate × 3, so order 1 in Y. 1 mark: rate equation written with these orders.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, with its units, using experiment 1.
parts.answer: k = 3.3 × 10⁻² dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [X] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [Y] = 0.60 mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction P + Q → R was studied at 298 K. Initial rates were measured:
Experiment 1: [P] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [Q] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [P] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, [Q] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [P] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [Q] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, rate = 4.5 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 4: [P] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³, [Q] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = ? mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order with respect to P, the order with respect to Q and the overall order.
parts.answer: First order in P; second order in Q; overall order 3.
parts.working: 1 mark: [P] × 2 gives rate × 2, so first order in P; [Q] × 3 gives rate × 9, so second order in Q. 1 mark: overall order 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation and calculate k with units.
parts.answer: rate = k[P][Q]²; k = 0.50 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: k = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10²) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.50 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. 1 mark for the value, 1 mark for the units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the rate in experiment 4, then state the rate to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 8.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the orders cannot be deduced from the equation P + Q → R alone.
parts.answer: The orders must be found from experimental data, because the rate depends on the rate-determining step, which need not match the stoichiometry of the overall equation.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate equations come from experiments. 1 mark: the rate-determining step may involve different species or numbers of molecules from the overall equation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A gas-phase reaction A → products is studied at constant temperature. Initial rates were measured:
Experiment 1: [A] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [A] = 0.040 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to A, showing how the data give it.
parts.answer: Second order: quadrupling [A] gives a rate increase of 16 = 4², so the order is 2.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate ratio = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 16. 1 mark: 4² = 16, so the order is 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, k, with its units, using experiment 1.
parts.answer: rate = k[A]²; k = 0.20 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
parts.working: k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ (0.010)² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.20. Units: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.090 mol dm⁻³. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.6 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction A + B + C → products is studied. The rate is found to fit rate = k[A][B]/[C].
Experiment 1: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.20, [C] = 0.50 (all mol dm⁻³), rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.20, [C] = 1.00 (all mol dm⁻³), rate = ? mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the order with respect to C and explain what a negative order tells you about the effect of C.
parts.answer: Order −1 with respect to C. Increasing [C] decreases the rate, so C slows the reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: order −1 (the power of [C] is −1 in the rate equation). 1 mark: increasing [C] lowers the rate, so C acts as an inhibitor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, with its units, from experiment 1.
parts.working: k = rate × [C] ÷ ([A][B]) = 4.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.50 ÷ (0.10 × 0.20) = 0.10. Units: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)(mol dm⁻³) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = s⁻¹. 1 mark rearrangement, 1 mark value, 1 mark units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate in experiment 2.
parts.answer: 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.20 ÷ 1.00 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (doubling [C] halves the rate from 4.0 × 10⁻³).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a rate equation with a negative order is unlikely from a single-step reaction, and suggest a type of mechanism that could give it.
parts.answer: A single elementary step cannot have a negative order. A fast reversible step X ⇌ Y + C, where Y is a reactant of the slow step, gives [Y] = K[X] ÷ [C], so the rate falls as [C] rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: the order of an elementary step equals its molecularity, which is never negative. 1 mark: a fast equilibrium that produces C makes [Y] proportional to 1/[C].

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A first-order reaction has a rate constant k = 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Calculate the half-life in minutes, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 33.0 min

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the half-life of a first-order reaction changes if the initial concentration is doubled.
parts.answer: It does not change.
parts.working: A constant half-life is the defining feature of first-order kinetics; t½ = ln 2 ÷ k depends only on k.

stem: The decomposition of azomethane, (CH₃)₂N₂, is first order. The half-life at a certain temperature is 20 minutes. The initial concentration of azomethane is 0.400 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of azomethane remaining after 60 minutes.
parts.answer: 0.125 (one-eighth)
parts.working: 60 min = 3 half-lives. Fraction remaining = (1/2)³ = 0.125.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of azomethane after 60 minutes.
parts.answer: 0.0500 mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term half-life of a reaction.
parts.answer: The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half of its initial value.
parts.working: Must refer to the reactant concentration (or amount) halving over a given time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the expression for the half-life of a first-order reaction in terms of the rate constant, k.
parts.answer: t½ = ln 2 ÷ k  (or t½ = 0.693 ÷ k)
parts.working: Standard result for first-order reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the half-life of a second-order reaction would change as the reaction proceeds.
parts.answer: For a second-order reaction the rate depends on [A]², so as [A] falls the rate falls faster and each successive halving takes longer; the half-life is not constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate depends on concentration squared / the rate falls as [A] falls. 1 mark: each halving therefore takes longer, so the half-life lengthens.

stem:
The first-order decomposition of azomethane at 600 K was followed. Concentrations of azomethane were measured at intervals:
Time / s: 0, 500, 1000, 1500
[(CH₃)₂N₂] / mol dm⁻³: 0.200, 0.121, 0.0736, 0.0446

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln[(CH₃)₂N₂] for each measured concentration at t = 500 s, 1000 s and 1500 s. Give each value to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: ln 0.121 = −2.112; ln 0.0736 = −2.609; ln 0.0446 = −3.110. 1 mark for two correct values, 1 mark for all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plot ln[(CH₃)₂N₂] against time would give a straight line for a first-order reaction. Use the gradient of this line to determine the rate constant, k, and state its units.
parts.answer: gradient ≈ −1.00 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, so k = 1.00 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: Gradient from (500, −2.112) and (1500, −3.110) = (−3.110 + 2.112) ÷ 1000 = −9.98 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. 1 mark for gradient, 1 mark for k = −gradient, 1 mark units s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the half-life of the reaction using your value of k.
parts.answer: about 693 s (accept 690–700 s)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 45 s. Calculate the time taken for 90% of the reactant to be used up. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Remaining fraction = 0.10 = (1/2)ⁿ, so n = log 10 ÷ log 2 = 3.32 half-lives. Time = 3.32 × 45 = 149 s. 1 mark for 0.10 = (½)ⁿ, 1 mark for n = 3.32, 1 mark for the time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for 99% of the reactant to be used up, and compare it with your answer to (a).
parts.answer: About 299 s, roughly twice the 149 s needed for 90%.
parts.working: 0.01 = (½)ⁿ gives n = 6.64 half-lives; 6.64 × 45 = 299 s. 1 mark for n = 6.64 (or equivalent log method), 1 mark for the time and the comparison (about double).

stem:
A student studied the reaction X → products at 310 K using two different starting concentrations. The half-lives measured were:
Experiment 1: [X]₀ = 0.50 mol dm⁻³, t½ = 24 min
Experiment 2: [X]₀ = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, t½ = 120 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Second order with respect to X (it is not first order).
parts.working: 1 mark: [X]₀ is 5 times smaller, and the half-life is 5 times longer. 1 mark: for a first-order reaction the half-life would be constant. 1 mark: for second order, t½ ∝ 1/[X]₀, which matches the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: rate = k[X]²
parts.working: Order equals power of concentration in rate equation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The hydrolysis of an ester in a very large excess of water is effectively first order in the ester. In experiment A the pseudo-first-order rate constant at 298 K is k = 2.6 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by pseudo-first-order kinetics in this situation.
parts.answer: The concentration of water is so large that it is effectively constant during the reaction, so the rate depends only on the ester concentration, which gives first-order kinetics.
parts.working: 1 mark: [H₂O] is almost unchanged (very large excess). 1 mark: the rate depends on [ester] only, so the reaction behaves as first order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the half-life of the ester in hours, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of ester remaining after 24 hours.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 7.70 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. Calculate the half-life in hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the reactant remaining after 10.0 hours.
parts.working: Number of half-lives = 10.0 ÷ 2.50 = 4; fraction = (½)⁴ = 0.0625.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the half-life of a first-order reaction is more useful than the initial rate when comparing reactions at different starting concentrations.
parts.answer: Half-life is independent of starting concentration for a first-order reaction, so it allows the rate constant to be compared directly without knowing the starting concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: half-life does not depend on initial concentration for first order. 1 mark: makes comparison of k or reaction speed simpler.

stem:
The reaction A → 2B is first order in A. It is studied in a sealed vessel at 500 K, starting with pure A at 20.0 kPa. The total pressure is measured at intervals.
Total pressure at 300 s = 25.2 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why P(A) = 40.0 − P(total) at any time, and use this to find the partial pressure of A at 300 s.
parts.answer: At time t, if x kPa of A has reacted, P(A) = 20.0 − x and P(B) = 2x, so P(total) = 20.0 + x and P(A) = 40.0 − P(total). At 300 s, P(A) = 40.0 − 25.2 = 14.8 kPa.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct expressions for partial pressures in terms of x and P(total). 1 mark: P(A) = 14.8 kPa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, for the first-order reaction, with units.
parts.working: k = ln(P₀ ÷ P) ÷ t = ln(20.0 ÷ 14.8) ÷ 300 = 0.3011 ÷ 300 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. 1 mark for ln form, 1 mark for the value, 1 mark for units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total pressure at 600 s, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 29.0 kPa

author: HomiLabs

stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 30 s. At time zero the concentration of reactant is 0.80 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of reactant after 90 s.
parts.answer: 0.10 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: 90 s = 3 half-lives; concentration = 0.80 × (½)³ = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the concentration to fall to 0.050 mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: 0.80 → 0.050 is a factor of 16 = 2⁴, so 4 half-lives = 4 × 30 = 120 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch in words how the graph of concentration against time differs from a graph for a second-order reaction with the same starting concentration.
parts.answer: The first-order graph is an exponential curve: each equal time interval removes the same fraction of reactant. For a second-order reaction successive half-lives get longer, so the curve levels off more gradually at low concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: first-order curve has constant half-life (falls by same fraction each interval). 1 mark: second-order half-life lengthens as reaction proceeds, so the curve flattens more slowly at low concentration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction, and is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
parts.working: Must mention increasing the rate and being unchanged (regenerated) overall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one homogeneous catalysed reaction and one heterogeneous catalysed reaction. For each, give the state of the catalyst relative to the reactants.
parts.answer: Homogeneous: H⁺(aq) catalysing hydrolysis of an ester in aqueous solution (catalyst and reactants both aqueous). Heterogeneous: manganese(IV) oxide, a solid, catalysing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct homogeneous example and phase. 1 mark: correct heterogeneous example and phase. 1 mark: explanation that homogeneous means the same phase, heterogeneous means a different phase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in three stages, how a nickel catalyst increases the rate of the reaction C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
parts.answer: 1. Adsorption: ethene and hydrogen molecules are attracted to and bond to the nickel surface at active sites. 2. The H–H and C=C bonds are weakened (H atoms bonded to Ni). 3. Desorption: ethane (product) is released, freeing the active sites.
parts.working: 1 mark each: adsorption onto the surface/active sites; bonds weakened (in H₂ and C=C) so the reaction needs less energy; desorption of the product, freeing the surface for further reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of the following catalysed systems as homogeneous or heterogeneous:
(i) platinum gauze catalysing the oxidation of ammonia by oxygen
(ii) Fe²⁺(aq) ions catalysing the decomposition of aqueous hydrogen peroxide
(iii) solid zeolite catalysing the cracking of gaseous hydrocarbons
(iv) H⁺(aq) catalysing the hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate in water
parts.answer: (i) heterogeneous; (ii) homogeneous; (iii) heterogeneous; (iv) homogeneous.
parts.working: Homogeneous: catalyst in same phase as reactants (aqueous with aqueous). Heterogeneous: catalyst in different phase, usually a solid with gas or liquid reactants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A powdered catalyst gives a faster reaction than the same mass of catalyst in a single lump. Explain why.
parts.answer: A powder has a much larger surface area, giving more active sites for adsorption, so more reactant molecules are held in position and collide with each other per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area (more active sites). 1 mark: more reactant molecules adsorbed/brought together, so the rate increases.

stem: A homogeneous catalyst is used at 0.0040 mol. Each mole of catalyst converts 0.50 mol of reactant to product per second (turnover frequency 0.50 mol s⁻¹ per mol of catalyst). The product is ethane, C₂H₆ (Mr = 30.0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of ethane produced in 60 s.
parts.answer: 0.12 mol
parts.working: Amount of product = 0.0040 mol × 0.50 mol s⁻¹ per mol × 60 s = 0.12 mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethane produced in 60 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the catalyst is consumed in the reaction and explain your answer.
parts.answer: No, it is not consumed; it is regenerated at the end of each cycle and is still 0.0040 mol.
parts.working: A catalyst is chemically unchanged overall; the stated amount of catalyst is still present.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nickel catalyst used in a hydrogenation process is 'poisoned' by a trace of a sulfur compound. Explain how poisoning reduces the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: The sulfur compound bonds strongly to the active sites of the nickel surface, so these sites are blocked. Fewer sites are available for reactant molecules to be adsorbed, so fewer reactions occur per second and the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: impurity adsorbs strongly/bonds to active sites. 1 mark: fewer active sites available for reactants. 1 mark: fewer adsorbed reactants so the rate falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one step a manufacturer could take to avoid poisoning.
parts.answer: Remove the sulfur compound from the feedstock before the reaction (purify the reactants).
parts.working: Any sensible purification step is acceptable.

stem:
Iron(III) ions catalyse the reaction between tin(II) ions and dichromate(VI) ions in acidic solution. The steps are:
Step 1: Fe³⁺ oxidises Sn²⁺ to Sn⁴⁺
Step 2: Dichromate oxidises Fe²⁺ back to Fe³⁺
Both steps occur in the same solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for step 1 and step 2 as balanced equations.
parts.answer: Step 1: 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺. Step 2: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O.
parts.working: 1 mark each for correctly balanced charges and atoms (step 1 needs 2Fe³⁺ and Sn²⁺; step 2 needs 6Fe²⁺ and 14H⁺).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Combine the equations to give the overall equation, cancelling species that appear on both sides. Show that Fe³⁺ is a catalyst.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3Sn²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3Sn⁴⁺ + 7H₂O. Fe³⁺ appears in step 1 and is regenerated in step 2, so it is unchanged overall and is a catalyst.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct overall equation with multiplied step 1 (×3). 1 mark: Fe³⁺ is used then regenerated, so unchanged overall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether Fe³⁺ is a homogeneous or heterogeneous catalyst and give a reason.
parts.answer: Homogeneous: Fe³⁺ is aqueous, in the same phase as the reacting ions.
parts.working: Reactants and catalyst are all in aqueous solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a catalyst does not change the enthalpy change of a reaction.
parts.answer: A catalyst does not change the energy of the reactants or products; it provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so ΔH (the difference between reactant and product energies) stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: the energies of reactants and products are unchanged. 1 mark: the catalyst lowers activation energy only, so ΔH is unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lower activation energy increases the rate of the reaction, referring to the Boltzmann distribution.
parts.answer: A larger proportion of molecules have energy equal to or greater than the lower activation energy, so more successful collisions occur per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea. 1 mark: more successful collisions per unit time.

stem: The reaction between manganate(VII) ions and ethanedioate ions in acid is slow at the start. Mn²⁺ ions are formed as a product during the reaction, and the reaction speeds up as Mn²⁺ builds up. The rate later falls as the reactants are used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term autocatalysis.
parts.answer: A reaction in which one of the products acts as a catalyst for the same reaction.
parts.working: Product catalyses the reaction that produces it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate is slow at the start of the reaction.
parts.answer: At the start there is little or no Mn²⁺, so the catalysed pathway is not available; the uncatalysed reaction has a high activation energy and proceeds slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark: no/little Mn²⁺ present initially (no autocatalyst). 1 mark: uncatalysed route with high Ea is slow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate eventually falls.
parts.answer: The reactants are used up, so their concentrations fall and the rate decreases.
parts.working: Concentrations of reactants fall as the reaction proceeds.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph of rate against time for this reaction.
parts.answer: Rate starts low, rises to a maximum (a peak) as Mn²⁺ builds up, then falls towards zero as reactants are used up.
parts.working: Rate rises as Mn²⁺ builds up, peaks, then falls as reactants are used.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Iron is used as a finely divided solid catalyst in the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). The reaction is run at about 450 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of heterogeneous catalysis on the iron surface, giving the three stages in detail and referring to active sites.
parts.answer: 1. Adsorption: N₂ and H₂ molecules bond to active sites on the iron surface. 2. The N≡N and H–H bonds are weakened and broken on the surface, forming nitrogen and hydrogen atoms. 3. NH₃ forms on the surface and desorbs, freeing the active sites.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: adsorption onto active sites; N≡N and H–H bonds weakened or broken on the surface; NH₃ formed on the surface; NH₃ desorbs and frees the sites for further reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Haber process is run at about 450 °C rather than at a lower temperature, even though the forward reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: A lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia, but the rate would be too slow to be economic. The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a useful rate is reached at this compromise temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (higher yield) but gives a slower rate. 1 mark: the catalyst allows a reasonable rate at a moderate temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction have the same pre-exponential factor, A. The activation energy is 75.0 kJ mol⁻¹ without the catalyst and 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹ with the catalyst. The temperature is 298 K. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an expression for the ratio k(catalysed) ÷ k(uncatalysed) in terms of the activation energies, and state why the pre-exponential factors cancel.
parts.answer: k(cat) ÷ k(uncat) = exp[(Ea(uncat) − Ea(cat)) ÷ RT]; the pre-exponential factors cancel because they are the same for both.
parts.working: 1 mark: ratio of exponentials with difference in Ea over RT. 1 mark: pre-exponential factor A is the same, so it cancels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(catalysed) ÷ k(uncatalysed) at 298 K, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide solution is decomposed by iodide ions: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)
The reaction is thought to occur by this two-step mechanism:
Step 1: H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻ (slow)
Step 2: H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻ (fast)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the intermediate and the catalyst in this mechanism.
parts.answer: Intermediate: IO⁻ (formed in step 1 and used up in step 2). Catalyst: I⁻ (used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2).
parts.working: 1 mark: IO⁻ is formed then consumed, so it is an intermediate. 1 mark: I⁻ is used then regenerated, so it is the catalyst.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that adding the two steps gives the overall equation, cancelling species that appear on both sides.
