parts.answer: Adding: 2H₂O₂ + I⁻ + IO⁻ → 2H₂O + IO⁻ + O₂ + I⁻. Cancelling I⁻ and IO⁻ gives 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: the intermediate IO⁻ appears on both sides and cancels. 1 mark: the remaining equation is the overall equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which step is rate-determining and write the rate equation predicted by the mechanism.
parts.answer: Step 1 is rate-determining; rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻].
parts.working: 1 mark: step 1 is the slow step. 1 mark: the rate equation contains only the species in step 1; IO⁻ does not appear.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ozone is destroyed in the upper atmosphere by a chlorine radical, Cl•, which acts as a catalyst. The mechanism is:
Step 1: O₃ + Cl• → ClO• + O₂ (slow)
Step 2: ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂ (fast)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the two steps.
parts.answer: O₃ + O → 2O₂
parts.working: Add the two steps and cancel Cl• and ClO•.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the catalyst and the intermediate in this mechanism.
parts.answer: Catalyst: Cl• (it is used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2). Intermediate: ClO• (formed in step 1 and used up in step 2).
parts.working: 1 mark each: catalyst regenerated; intermediate formed then consumed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate equation for a reaction between A and B is rate = k[A][B]. Three possible single-step or slow-step reactions are being considered:
Step X: A + B → C
Step Y: A → C + D
Step Z: 2A + B → C + D

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the molecularity of each step, and identify which step(s) are consistent with the rate equation.
parts.answer: Step X is bimolecular (A + B) and matches rate = k[A][B]. Step Y is unimolecular, giving rate = k[A] (does not match). Step Z is trimolecular and would give rate ∝ [A]²[B] (does not match).
parts.working: 1 mark each for molecularity; 1 mark for correct conclusion that only step X gives the rate equation. Alternative: state that the rate equation only includes species in the slow step.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term rate-determining step.
parts.answer: The slowest step in a reaction mechanism; it controls the overall rate of the reaction.
parts.working: Must refer to slowest step and overall rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the species in the rate-determining step appear in the rate equation, but species in faster steps do not.
parts.answer: The overall rate cannot exceed the rate of the slowest step, so only species that take part in the slow step (and any pre-equilibrium needed to form them) determine the rate; fast steps happen so quickly that they do not limit the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: the slow step limits the overall rate. 1 mark: species in faster steps are not in the rate equation because they do not limit the rate.

stem:
The reaction 2NO(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2NOCl(g) is thought to occur by this mechanism:
Step 1: NO + Cl₂ ⇌ NOCl₂ (fast equilibrium, equilibrium constant K)
Step 2: NOCl₂ + NO → 2NOCl (slow)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate equation cannot be deduced from the overall equation alone.
parts.answer: The orders must be determined from experiment or from the mechanism; the coefficients in the overall equation do not give the orders of the rate-determining step.
parts.working: The rate equation is determined from the slow step and the pre-equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation for step 2 in terms of [NOCl₂] and [NO].
parts.answer: rate = k₂[NOCl₂][NO]
parts.working: The slow step is bimolecular with these reactants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the equilibrium constant K for step 1 to show that [NOCl₂] = K[NO][Cl₂]. Hence deduce the rate equation for the overall reaction and its order with respect to NO and Cl₂.
parts.answer: K = [NOCl₂] ÷ ([NO][Cl₂]), so [NOCl₂] = K[NO][Cl₂]; rate = k₂K[NO]²[Cl₂]; order 2 with respect to NO and 1 with respect to Cl₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: rearrangement of K for [NOCl₂]. 1 mark: substitution gives rate = k₂K[NO]²[Cl₂] and the orders.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain whether this mechanism is consistent with the overall equation and state the overall order.
parts.answer: Yes: adding steps 1 and 2 gives NO + Cl₂ + NOCl₂ + NO → NOCl₂ + 2NOCl, cancelling NOCl₂ gives 2NO + Cl₂ → 2NOCl. Overall order is 3.
parts.working: 1 mark: intermediate NOCl₂ cancels when steps are added to give the overall equation. 1 mark: overall order 2 + 1 = 3.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ozone decomposes in the upper atmosphere: 2O₃(g) → 3O₂(g). The experimental rate equation is rate = k[O₃]² ÷ [O₂].
A proposed mechanism is:
Step 1: O₃ ⇌ O₂ + O (fast equilibrium, constant K = [O₂][O] ÷ [O₃])
Step 2: O + O₃ → 2O₂ (slow)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the two steps add up to the overall equation.
parts.answer: Adding: O₃ + O + O₃ → O₂ + O + 2O₂. Cancelling O gives 2O₃ → 3O₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: the intermediate O appears on both sides and cancels. 1 mark: the remaining equation is 2O₃ → 3O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation for the slow step 2. Use K to replace [O], and deduce the rate equation of the mechanism.
parts.answer: rate = k₂[O][O₃]; [O] = K[O₃] ÷ [O₂], so rate = k₂K[O₃]² ÷ [O₂].
parts.working: 1 mark: rate = k₂[O][O₃]. 1 mark: rearranging K gives [O] = K[O₃]/[O₂], and substitution gives rate = k₂K[O₃]²/[O₂].

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to O₂, and state whether the mechanism is consistent with the experimental rate equation.
parts.answer: Order −1 with respect to O₂ (the rate falls as [O₂] rises). Yes, the mechanism gives [O₃]² ÷ [O₂], the same as the experimental rate equation.
parts.working: 1 mark: order −1 from the [O₂] term in the denominator. 1 mark: the predicted rate equation matches the experimental one.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) has the experimental rate equation rate = k[NO]²[O₂].
A two-step mechanism is proposed:
Step 1: NO + NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast equilibrium, constant K = [N₂O₂] ÷ [NO]²)
Step 2: N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂ (slow)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the rate equation for the slow step, and identify the intermediate.
parts.answer: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂]; the intermediate is N₂O₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate expression from the slow step's reactants. 1 mark: N₂O₂ is formed in step 1 and used in step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the equilibrium constant K to replace [N₂O₂] and hence deduce the rate equation of the mechanism.
parts.answer: [N₂O₂] = K[NO]², so rate = k₂K[NO]²[O₂].
parts.working: 1 mark: rearrangement of K. 1 mark: rate = k₂K[NO]²[O₂].

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the mechanism is consistent with the experimental rate equation.
parts.answer: Yes: the predicted rate equation has the same orders (2 in NO, 1 in O₂) as the experimental rate equation.
parts.working: Compare the orders from the mechanism with the experimental orders.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A reaction A + B → P is thought to proceed through an intermediate I:
Step 1: A ⇌ I (fast; equilibrium established)
Step 2: I + B → P (slow)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the rate equation for the slow step 2 and use the equilibrium in step 1 to write the rate equation in terms of [A] and [B].
parts.answer: rate = k₂[I][B]; with K = [I] ÷ [A], [I] = K[A], so rate = k₂K[A][B].
parts.working: 1 mark: rate = k₂[I][B]. 1 mark: K = [I]/[A] rearranged. 1 mark: rate = k₂K[A][B].

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the rate if [A] is doubled and [B] is kept constant.
parts.answer: The rate doubles, since rate ∝ [A].
parts.working: From rate = k₂K[A][B], rate is directly proportional to [A].

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Consider the mechanism for reaction A + B → P, with an intermediate I. The step equilibrium in step 1 is set up quickly.
Step 1: A ⇌ I (fast, equilibrium constant K = [I] ÷ [A] = 0.40, no units)
Step 2: I + B → P (slow, rate constant k₂ = 3.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹)
The initial concentrations are [A] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of I at equilibrium in step 1.
parts.answer: 0.10 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of the reaction, using the rate of the slow step.
parts.answer: 0.060 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: rate = k₂[I][B] = 3.0 × 0.10 × 0.20 = 0.060 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. 1 mark for using [I] from part (a), 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate depends on the concentration of I, which is not a reactant.
parts.answer: I is formed from A in the fast equilibrium, and its concentration is set by [A] through K; therefore the rate depends on [A] indirectly, even though I is not a starting reactant.
parts.working: 1 mark: I is in the rate equation because it is a reactant in the slow step. 1 mark: [I] is controlled by the equilibrium with A, so it depends on [A].

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction 2X + Y → Z is studied at constant temperature. The initial rates are:
Experiment 1: [X] = 0.10, [Y] = 0.10 (mol dm⁻³), rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [X] = 0.20, [Y] = 0.10 (mol dm⁻³), rate = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [X] = 0.10, [Y] = 0.30 (mol dm⁻³), rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Two mechanisms are proposed:
Mechanism P: Step 1: X + X → X₂ (slow); Step 2: X₂ + Y → Z (fast)
Mechanism Q: Step 1: X + Y → W (slow); Step 2: W + X → Z (fast)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the experimental rate equation from the data.
parts.answer: rate = k[X]²[Y]^0 = k[X]² (zero order in Y)
parts.working: Doubling [X] gives rate × 4 (order 2); tripling [Y] has no effect (order 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation predicted by mechanism P and by mechanism Q, using the rate-determining (slow) step in each.
parts.answer: Mechanism P: rate = k[X]² (slow step is 2X). Mechanism Q: rate = k[X][Y].
parts.working: 1 mark each: rate from the slow step's reactants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which mechanism is consistent with the data and explain why.
parts.answer: Mechanism P is consistent: its rate equation matches the experimental order of 2 in X and zero in Y. Mechanism Q would give first order in Y, which the data do not show.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct mechanism. 1 mark: reasoning using the zero order in Y.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A two-step reaction goes through an intermediate. Activation energies for each step are: step 1 (slow) Ea = 84 kJ mol⁻¹, step 2 (fast) Ea = 22 kJ mol⁻¹. The overall reaction is exothermic with ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which step is rate-determining and justify your answer using the activation energies.
parts.answer: Step 1 is rate-determining because it has the larger activation energy (84 kJ mol⁻¹), giving the highest energy barrier and the slowest step.
parts.working: 1 mark: step 1. 1 mark: higher activation energy means a slower step / highest barrier.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the energy profile for the reaction, referring to the intermediate and the positions of the reactants and products.
parts.answer: Reactants start at a higher energy than products (exothermic). The first peak (transition state for step 1) is highest; between the two peaks is the intermediate at a local energy minimum; step 2 peak is lower; products are 40 kJ mol⁻¹ below reactants.
parts.working: 1 mark: products below reactants by 40 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic). 1 mark: intermediate in a valley between two peaks, with the first peak (step 1) highest.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A mechanism has three steps:
Step 1: A + B → C (slow)
Step 2: C + A → D (fast)
Step 3: D → E + B (fast)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the rate equation for the reaction from the mechanism.
parts.answer: rate = k[A][B]
parts.working: Only the reactants in the rate-determining step (step 1) appear; steps 2 and 3 are faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why A has an order of 1 in the rate equation, even though A is a reactant in both step 1 and step 2.
parts.answer: Only step 1 is slow and it contains one A. The A in step 2 is used in a fast step after the rate-determining step, so it does not affect the overall rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: only the slow step determines the rate. 1 mark: A in step 2 is in a fast step, so it does not contribute to the rate equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify B in the mechanism: is it a reactant, product or catalyst overall?
parts.answer: B is a catalyst: it is used in step 1 and regenerated in step 3.
parts.working: Overall equation: 2A → E (B is used in step 1 and regenerated in step 3, so it cancels).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Boltzmann distribution is drawn for a gas at two temperatures, T₁ and T₂, where T₂ > T₁. Describe two differences between the curve at T₂ and the curve at T₁.
parts.answer: The peak of the curve at T₂ is lower and further to the right (more molecules have higher energies); the curve is broader/flatter, so the proportion of molecules with energy at or above the activation energy is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: peak moves to higher energy; peak is lower; curve is broader; greater proportion of molecules above Ea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of the curve that stays the same at both temperatures, and explain why.
parts.answer: The total area under the curve is the same, because the total number of molecules does not change.
parts.working: Area under curve represents total number of molecules, which is constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the Boltzmann distribution and collision theory, why the rate of a reaction increases when temperature is raised.
parts.answer: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so a larger proportion of molecules have energy at or above the activation energy (Boltzmann). More collisions have energy ≥ Ea, so more successful collisions occur per second; the average collision frequency also increases slightly.
parts.working: 1 mark: molecules have more kinetic energy/average energy rises. 1 mark: larger proportion of molecules have E ≥ Ea. 1 mark: more successful collisions per unit time. 1 mark: collisions occur more frequently (small effect).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change increases the fraction of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, without changing the activation energy?
A Adding more reactant at the same concentration ratio
B Increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction mixture at constant temperature
C Increasing the temperature of the mixture
D Adding a catalyst
parts.answer: C Increasing the temperature of the mixture
parts.working: Raising temperature shifts the Boltzmann distribution so a larger fraction of molecules have E ≥ Ea. A changes nothing about the fraction; B changes collision frequency, not the fraction; D changes the activation energy itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The activation energy of a reaction is 50 kJ mol⁻¹. Show that the factor by which the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K is about 1.9. Use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and the expression ratio = exp[(Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)].
parts.answer: ratio = exp[(50 000 ÷ 8.314)(1/300 − 1/310)] = exp(6013 × 1.075 × 10⁻⁴) = exp(0.6467) = 1.91; so the fraction increases by a factor of about 1.9.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct expression with Ea in J mol⁻¹. 1 mark: difference of reciprocals 1/300 − 1/310 = 1.075 × 10⁻⁴. 1 mark: exp(6013 × 1.075 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.91.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'Heating the reaction mixture makes the molecules move twice as fast, so the rate doubles.' Explain why this reasoning is incomplete and the explanation is misleading.
parts.answer: The average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, so molecular speed rises only slightly (speed is proportional to √T; for 300 K to 310 K about 1.7 %). The main reason the rate roughly doubles for a 10 K rise is the large increase in the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea, not the speed of the molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark: speed is proportional to √T, so a 10 K rise changes speed by only about 2 %. 1 mark: the main effect is the increase in the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea. 1 mark: a 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate for typical Ea values, not because molecules move twice as fast.

stem: For a reaction at 300 K, the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases by a factor of 3.50 when the temperature is raised to 320 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation that links the ratio of the two fractions to Ea, R, T₁ and T₂.
parts.answer: ln(ratio) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)
parts.working: Standard form of the Boltzmann-based (Arrhenius-type) relation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy, Ea, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Ea = R × ln(3.50) ÷ (1/300 − 1/320) = 8.314 × 1.2528 ÷ 2.083 × 10⁻⁴ = 49 990 J mol⁻¹ ≈ 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹. 1 mark for ln(3.50), 1 mark for reciprocal difference, 1 mark for the value and units.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two reactions occur in the same vessel at the same temperature. Reaction P has an activation energy of 40 kJ mol⁻¹ and reaction Q has an activation energy of 90 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factor by which the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases for reaction P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the factor for reaction Q.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of reaction Q is more sensitive to the temperature rise than the rate of reaction P.
parts.answer: Reaction Q has the higher activation energy, so the Boltzmann fraction it depends on changes more rapidly with temperature; a larger fraction of molecules gain enough energy to react.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher Ea means the fraction increases more when T rises. 1 mark: explanation using the exponential Boltzmann relationship.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The table shows the percentage of molecules in a gas that have energy in each range, at two temperatures.
Energy range / kJ mol⁻¹ | 300 K (%) | 320 K (%)
0–20 | 40 | 30
20–40 | 35 | 33
40–60 | 18 | 22
60–80 | 6 | 11
80 and above | 1 | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the percentage in the 0–20 kJ mol⁻¹ range is lower at 320 K.
parts.answer: More molecules have gained energy and moved into the higher energy ranges, so fewer molecules remain in the lowest range.
parts.working: Total must remain 100%; the proportion moved up as temperature rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of molecules with energy of 60 kJ mol⁻¹ or more at each temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the percentage at 320 K to that at 300 K for molecules with energy of at least 60 kJ mol⁻¹, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a rise of 20 K in temperature may cause a greater rate increase than a rise of 20 K would for a reaction with a lower activation energy.
parts.answer: A larger activation energy means the proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea increases more steeply with temperature; so a reaction with high Ea gains proportionally more from the same temperature rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: proportion of molecules above Ea rises faster for higher Ea. 1 mark: the rate increase depends on the Boltzmann fraction, which is more sensitive when Ea is larger.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch in words how the Boltzmann distribution of a gas at 350 K differs from the distribution at 300 K, describing the peak and the area under the curve.
parts.answer: At 350 K the peak is lower and moves to a higher energy; the curve is broader and flatter, with a longer tail to high energies. The total area under the curve is the same at both temperatures.
parts.working: 1 mark: peak lower. 1 mark: peak at higher energy/curve broader. 1 mark: area equal (same number of molecules).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why changing the pressure of a gaseous reaction at constant temperature does not change the shape of the Boltzmann distribution.
parts.answer: The distribution depends on temperature only, since it describes the spread of molecular kinetic energies; increasing pressure increases the concentration (and collision frequency) but does not change the energies of the molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark: distribution depends only on temperature. 1 mark: pressure affects concentration/collision frequency, not molecular energy distribution.

stem: A reaction has an activation energy of 65 kJ mol⁻¹. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea at 308 K to the fraction at 298 K, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: ratio = exp[(65 000 ÷ 8.314)(1/298 − 1/308)] = exp(0.8523) = 2.34. 1 mark for correct expression, 1 mark for reciprocal difference (1.09 × 10⁻⁴), 1 mark for value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on whether this ratio would be a good estimate of the rate ratio for a reaction with the same activation energy.
parts.answer: It is a reasonable estimate of the effect of temperature on the rate, but rate also depends on collision frequency, which increases slightly with T, and on orientation; so the real ratio may differ.
parts.working: Credit any sensible comment that the rate ratio also depends on collision frequency and orientation factors.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the effects of raising the temperature and raising the pressure of a gaseous reaction on the number of molecules with energy greater than the activation energy.
parts.answer: Raising temperature increases the number of molecules with E ≥ Ea (a larger fraction, shifting the Boltzmann curve); raising pressure at constant temperature increases the number of molecules per unit volume but does not change their energy distribution or the fraction above Ea.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature increases fraction above Ea. 1 mark: pressure does not change the fraction. 1 mark: pressure increases the total number of molecules per unit volume / collision frequency, so total successful collisions rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why most molecules in a gas sample have energies close to the average energy, and only a few have very high or very low energies.
parts.answer: Molecules collide and exchange energy randomly, so energies spread out around an average; extreme energies are rare because they need many collisions to be produced by chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: random collisions transfer energy between molecules. 1 mark: most molecules cluster around the average, with few at extremes.

stem: A reaction has an activation energy of 50.0 kJ mol⁻¹. At 298 K the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is f. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature, T₂, at which the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea would be exactly twice f. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: ln 2 = (Ea/R)(1/298 − 1/T₂); 1/T₂ = 1/298 − (R ln 2)/Ea = 3.356 × 10⁻³ − 1.152 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.2405 × 10⁻³; T₂ = 308.6 K. 1 mark for correct equation, 1 mark for rearrangement, 1 mark for reciprocal value, 1 mark for T₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on whether a 10.6 K rise in temperature is typical for a doubling of the rate of many reactions near room temperature.
parts.answer: Yes: a rise of about 10 K roughly doubles the rate for many reactions, as the Boltzmann fraction and the rate both depend strongly on temperature.
parts.working: Accept any sensible comment on the rule of thumb that rate doubles per 10 K.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student investigates the reaction of sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid, using a 'disappearing cross' method. The time for a cross to disappear is recorded for four concentrations of sodium thiosulfate, with the total volume kept the same by adding water:
[Na₂S₂O₃] / mol dm⁻³: 0.050, 0.100, 0.150, 0.200
Time, t / s: 80, 40, 27, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/t for each concentration to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: 1/80 = 0.01250; 1/40 = 0.02500; 1/27 = 0.03704; 1/20 = 0.05000 s⁻¹. 1 mark for at least three correct; 1 mark for all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between 1/t and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate, and explain why 1/t is used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: 1/t is directly proportional to the concentration (doubling concentration doubles 1/t). The rate is proportional to 1/t because the reaction is complete when the cross disappears, so the time is inversely proportional to the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: directly proportional. 1 mark: time is inversely proportional to rate, so 1/t is proportional to rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes slowly to oxygen. A gas syringe records the volume of oxygen collected at room temperature (molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹):
Time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90
Volume of O₂ / cm³: 0, 22, 38, 48

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of oxygen collected in the first 30 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction, in mol s⁻¹, over the first 30 s.
parts.answer: 3.06 × 10⁻⁵ mol s⁻¹
parts.working: 9.17 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 30 = 3.06 × 10⁻⁵ mol s⁻¹. 1 mark for dividing by time, 1 mark for the value with units.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the reaction mixture should be kept at a constant temperature during a rate experiment.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the rate strongly (more molecules have E ≥ Ea), so a changing temperature would change the rate during the experiment and make the results unreliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature changes the rate. 1 mark: constant temperature needed so only the independent variable changes the rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term rate of reaction.
parts.answer: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
parts.working: Must include change in concentration and per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the units of rate of reaction when concentration is measured in mol dm⁻³ and time in seconds.
parts.answer: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: Concentration per time.

stem:
A flask on a balance contains an excess of marble chips and dilute acid; the carbon dioxide escapes, so the total mass falls. Readings:
Time / s: 0, 60, 120, 180
Total mass / g: 120.00, 119.10, 118.40, 117.90

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of CO₂ lost in each of the three 60 s intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of mass loss, in g s⁻¹, for each interval, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in these rates.
parts.answer: The rate falls because the acid concentration decreases as it reacts with the marble chips, so collisions become less frequent.
parts.working: Any sensible explanation based on reactant concentration falling.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A graph of concentration of reactant A against time was plotted. A tangent was drawn to the curve at t = 40 s. The tangent passes through the points (20.0 s, 0.70 mol dm⁻³) and (60.0 s, 0.55 mol dm⁻³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the tangent, with units.
parts.answer: −3.75 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the rate of reaction at t = 40 s.
parts.answer: 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
parts.working: Rate = −gradient of the concentration–time curve, so the rate is the positive value of the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gradient of a tangent at t = 0 gives the initial rate.
parts.answer: At t = 0 the reaction has just started and the concentrations have not changed much, so the tangent at t = 0 gives the rate when the concentrations are the starting ones.
parts.working: The tangent at t = 0 corresponds to initial concentrations.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide is added to acidified potassium iodide. The reaction produces iodine, I₂, which is measured by titration. At intervals a 10.0 cm³ sample is quickly removed, cooled and titrated with 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium thiosulfate solution. The titre is 18.2 cm³ at one time.
Iodine and thiosulfate react: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the sample is cooled and quickly removed before titration.
parts.answer: To stop (quench) the reaction, so the iodine concentration does not change during the titration.
parts.working: Quenching stops the reaction at the time of sampling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of thiosulfate ions in the titre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount of iodine in the 10.0 cm³ sample, then its concentration in mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: I₂ = ½ × thiosulfate = 4.55 × 10⁻⁴ mol; concentration = 4.55 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.0100 dm³ = 0.0455 mol dm⁻³.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why measuring the time for a visible change, such as a cross disappearing, is a less reliable measure of rate than a continuous method.
parts.answer: The end point depends on the observer judging when the change is visible, which introduces error; a continuous method such as a colorimeter or gas syringe records changes continuously and avoids this subjective judgement.
parts.working: 1 mark: subjective judgement of end point. 1 mark: visible change may happen late or early depending on the observer or lighting. 1 mark: continuous method (colorimeter, gas syringe) gives many readings and is objective.

stem:
The volume of gas produced in a first-order decomposition at constant temperature was measured. The reaction goes to completion, giving V∞ = 50.0 cm³.
Time / s: 0, 100, 200
Volume of gas, V / cm³: 0, 16.48, 27.53

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln(V∞ − V) at t = 100 s and t = 200 s, to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for V∞ − V values (33.52 and 22.47); 1 mark for both logarithms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the rate constant, k, from the gradient of a graph of ln(V∞ − V) against time, and state its units.
parts.working: Gradient = (3.112 − 3.512) ÷ 100 = −4.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; k = 4.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Units s⁻¹ because the reaction is first order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of V∞ − V for a first-order reaction at any time, and explain why the expression works for determining order.
parts.answer: V∞ − V is proportional to the concentration of reactant remaining, so ln(V∞ − V) against time is linear with gradient −k for a first-order reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: V∞ − V is proportional to remaining reactant concentration. 1 mark: first order gives a straight line.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student repeats a timed experiment three times and gets 25.0 s, 24.5 s and 26.0 s. Each time is measured to the nearest 0.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time and the percentage uncertainty in a single time measurement, based on ±0.5 s.
parts.answer: Mean = 25.2 s; percentage uncertainty = 0.5 ÷ 25.2 × 100 ≈ 2.0%

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate is proportional to 1/t. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the rate using the mean time.
parts.answer: About 2.0% (the same as the percentage uncertainty in t, since rate ∝ 1/t).
parts.working: Percentage uncertainty in 1/t equals the percentage uncertainty in t, so 2.0%.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The concentration of a reactant, A, was measured at intervals. It fell from 0.80 mol dm⁻³ to 0.40 mol dm⁻³ in 60 s and to 0.20 mol dm⁻³ in 120 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the data show about the order of reaction with respect to A.
parts.answer: The half-life is 60 s at both stages, which is constant, so the reaction is first order with respect to A.
parts.working: 1 mark: half-life is constant. 1 mark: constant half-life indicates first order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, in s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction when [A] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 4.6 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: Four repeat timings for the same experiment were recorded as 38 s, 41 s, 37 s and 56 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain how you decide it should be excluded from the mean.
parts.answer: 56 s is anomalous: it is far from the other three values (38, 41, 37), which agree within 4 s. Excluding it is reasonable only if the anomaly has a known cause, such as a delayed start, and the reason is recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark: 56 s identified as anomalous. 1 mark: decision based on consistency with other repeats and a recorded cause, not just convenience.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean time after excluding the anomaly, and then the rate, taken as 1/t, in s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for mean 38.7 s; 1 mark for 1/t = 0.0258 s⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the order of reaction with respect to a reactant X, using initial rates. Include the variables, the apparatus or measurement you would use, the concentrations you would test and how you would process the results.
parts.answer: Plan points: independent variable = [X] (at least four concentrations, others kept constant including temperature and total volume); dependent variable = initial rate measured by a continuous method (e.g. gas syringe or colorimeter) or 1/t for a clock reaction; controlled variables (temperature, concentrations of other reactants, volume, same catalyst mass and surface area); repeats and mean; plot rate against [X] or log rate against log [X]; the gradient of log–log plot gives the order; a straight line through the origin means first order, a parabola/proportional-square means second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: independent variable with a range; dependent variable and method; controlled variables; repeats/average; initial rate found from tangent or 1/t; graph processing (log–log or rate vs concentration) to deduce order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the Contact process, sulfur dioxide is oxidised using a vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, catalyst. Write two equations to show how V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.
parts.answer: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄; V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅ (or 2V₂O₄ + O₂ → 2V₂O₅).
parts.working: 1 mark: first step reduces V₂O₅ to V₂O₄ while SO₂ is oxidised. 1 mark: second step regenerates V₂O₅ with oxygen (balanced).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst is described as 'regenerated' rather than 'used up'.
parts.answer: V₂O₅ is formed again in the second step, so the same amount of catalyst is present at the end.
parts.working: Catalyst is chemically unchanged overall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why industrial processes often use a catalyst to achieve a suitable rate, rather than simply raising the temperature.
parts.answer: Raising the temperature increases the rate but may reduce the equilibrium yield of an exothermic reaction, raise energy costs and lead to side reactions or equipment damage. A catalyst lowers the activation energy so a reasonable rate is achieved at a lower temperature without these problems.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher temperature may lower yield (exothermic) or cause side reactions. 1 mark: higher temperatures cost more energy/damage equipment. 1 mark: catalyst allows a useful rate at a lower temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change increases the rate of a reaction catalysed by a solid catalyst by increasing the number of active sites exposed?
A Using one large lump of the same mass of catalyst
B Grinding the same mass of catalyst into a fine powder
C Cooling the reaction mixture
D Adding more of a product to the mixture
parts.answer: B Grinding the same mass of catalyst into a fine powder
parts.working: B: a finer powder has a much larger surface area, so more active sites are exposed. A: one large lump has fewer exposed sites. C: cooling lowers the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea. D: a product does not add active sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student adds a few drops of copper(II) sulfate solution to a reaction mixture and the rate increases. Describe one test the student should carry out to show the copper(II) ions are not used up.
parts.answer: Measure the rate in repeat experiments using a second, fresh portion of copper(II) ions (or recover the copper and check its mass or concentration at the end); if it is unchanged after the reaction, the ions were not used up.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid test (recover and weigh, or measure concentration at end). 1 mark: reasoning that unchanged amount/rate confirms catalyst.

stem:
Ammonia is oxidised over a platinum–rhodium gauze catalyst at about 850 °C:
4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen monoxide produced from 34.0 g of ammonia (Mr of NH₃ = 17.0; Mr of NO = 30.0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to react with this 34.0 g of ammonia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gauze is made of very fine wires or mesh, and state the role of the catalyst.
parts.answer: Fine wire gauze has a large surface area so many active sites are available for adsorbing the reactants; the catalyst lowers the activation energy so the reaction proceeds fast enough at this temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: large surface area / many active sites. 1 mark: catalyst lowers activation energy.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Esters are hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide (saponification): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + C₂H₅OH. Explain why OH⁻ is not described as a catalyst in this reaction.
parts.answer: The hydroxide ion is used up: it reacts with the ester to form the ethanoate ion and ethanol, and is not regenerated, so it is a reactant rather than a catalyst.
parts.working: 1 mark: OH⁻ appears in the equation as a reactant. 1 mark: it is consumed and not regenerated. 1 mark: a catalyst must be unchanged/regenerated at the end.

stem: A solid catalyst has a mass of 0.50 g. Its molar mass is 195.1 g mol⁻¹. Each mole of active catalyst converts 1.5 × 10⁴ mol of reactant to product over its lifetime (turnover number).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of catalyst used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total amount of product that could be formed by this catalyst over its lifetime.
parts.answer: 38.4 mol
parts.working: 2.56 × 10⁻³ × 1.5 × 10⁴ = 38.4 mol. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An uncatalysed reaction has a single step with activation energy 120 kJ mol⁻¹. With a catalyst the reaction takes place by a two-step route. Step 1 has activation energy 60 kJ mol⁻¹ and step 2 has activation energy 45 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change of the reaction is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the rate-determining step of the catalysed route and give its activation energy.
parts.answer: Step 1 is rate-determining, with activation energy 60 kJ mol⁻¹ (the larger of the two).
parts.working: The slower step is the one with the larger activation energy (the highest energy barrier).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the reduction in activation energy for the rate-determining step.
parts.answer: 60 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the enthalpy change of the reaction is the same with and without the catalyst.
parts.answer: The catalyst changes only the pathway; the reactants and products have the same energies, so the overall enthalpy change, ΔH, is unchanged.
parts.working: 1 mark: energies of reactants and products unchanged. 1 mark: catalyst changes route/activation energy only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the Boltzmann distribution, how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without changing the temperature.
parts.answer: The Boltzmann distribution (the spread of molecular energies) is unchanged at the same temperature. The catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a larger proportion of molecules have energy equal to or greater than the new, lower activation energy. This increases the number of successful collisions per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: distribution unchanged at constant T. 1 mark: Ea is lowered. 1 mark: more molecules have E ≥ Ea. 1 mark: more successful collisions per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A catalytic converter contains a metal catalyst on a ceramic support. Describe the sequence of events on the catalyst surface that converts CO and NO into CO₂ and N₂.
parts.answer: CO and NO molecules are adsorbed onto active sites on the metal surface; their bonds weaken, which lowers the activation energy; the atoms react to form CO₂ and N₂ on the surface; the products are desorbed, freeing the sites for further reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each: adsorption onto active sites; bond weakening; reaction to form products on the surface; desorption of CO₂ and N₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of the reaction on the surface levels off when the concentrations of the gases are very high.
parts.answer: All the active sites on the surface are occupied, so adding more gas cannot increase the number of adsorbed molecules; the rate is then limited by the number of active sites.
parts.working: 1 mark: surface active sites become saturated. 1 mark: rate depends on sites available, not gas concentration.

stem: A reaction is catalysed by a solid catalyst. Two forms of the same mass of catalyst are compared: one large lump with radius 1.0 cm, and many small spherical grains each with radius 0.010 cm. The total volume is the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of grains that could be made from the lump, if the grains are spheres of radius 0.010 cm and the same total volume.
parts.answer: 1.0 × 10⁶ grains

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the total surface area of the grains to the surface area of the lump, and comment on the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: Ratio = 100 (the surface area increases 100-fold, since the ratio is R ÷ r); the rate increases, because there are many more active sites exposed to reactants.
parts.working: Total area ratio = N × r² ÷ R² = R/r = 100.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student investigates a solid catalyst. She measures the rate of a reaction with 1.0 g of the catalyst, then with 2.0 g. The rate doubles. She concludes that the catalyst has been used up in proportion to its mass and the reaction is limited by the catalyst amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion, identifying the flaw in her reasoning and suggesting one improvement to the experiment.
parts.answer: Doubling the mass of catalyst increases the number of active sites, so a higher rate is expected; this shows the rate depends on catalyst amount but does not show the catalyst was 'used up'. The conclusion that the catalyst is used up is not supported: she did not measure the catalyst afterwards. Improvement: weigh and test the catalyst after the reaction to check its mass is unchanged, and use the same surface area and conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate depends on active sites (catalyst amount) so the result is expected. 1 mark: no evidence the catalyst is used up. 1 mark: needs recovery and weighing/testing of catalyst. 1 mark: control variables (surface area, temperature) to keep fair.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of a reaction catalysed on a solid surface varies as the pressure of a gaseous reactant is increased from low pressure to very high pressure at constant temperature.
parts.answer: At low pressure the rate increases roughly in proportion to the pressure because more active sites are available for adsorption. At high pressure the active sites become saturated, so the rate levels off and does not increase further.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate rises with pressure at low pressure. 1 mark: rate levels off as sites are saturated. 1 mark: rate limited by surface sites at high pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term rate constant, k.
parts.answer: The proportionality constant in the rate equation, which links the rate to the concentrations of reactants raised to their orders.
parts.working: Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; k is a constant for a given reaction at a given temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that change the value of k and one factor that does not.
parts.answer: Temperature and the presence of a catalyst change k; the concentration of reactants does not change k.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two factors (temperature, catalyst) and 1 mark for concentration not changing k (accept pressure of gases too).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why k does not change when the concentration of a reactant is changed.
parts.answer: k is a constant for a given reaction at a fixed temperature, and concentration changes affect the rate through the concentration terms, not k.
parts.working: Concentration appears in the rate equation separately from k.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what each symbol represents in the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), and give the units of A.
parts.answer: A is the pre-exponential factor (frequency factor); e is the exponential constant; Ea is the activation energy (J mol⁻¹); R is the gas constant (8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); T is the absolute temperature (K). A has the same units as k.
parts.working: 1 mark for A and its units (same as k). 1 mark for Ea, R and T with units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the following temperatures to kelvin and calculate 1/T for each, to 4 significant figures: 25 °C and 45 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for conversions (298 K and 318 K). 1 mark for both reciprocal values to 4 s.f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Arrhenius equation can be written as ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). State what should be plotted to obtain a straight line, and the value of the gradient.
parts.answer: Plot ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis). The gradient is −Ea/R, and the intercept is ln A.
parts.working: 1 mark: ln k against 1/T. 1 mark: gradient −Ea/R. 1 mark: intercept ln A.

stem: The rate constant for a reaction is 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and 6.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 320 K. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy, Ea, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 71.5 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: ln(k₂/k₁) = ln 6.0 = 1.792. Ea = R × ln(k₂/k₁) ÷ (1/T₁ − 1/T₂) = 8.314 × 1.792 ÷ (3.333 × 10⁻³ − 3.125 × 10⁻³) = 8.314 × 1.792 ÷ 2.083 × 10⁻⁴ = 71 500 J mol⁻¹. 1 mark for the ln ratio, 1 mark for the reciprocal difference, 1 mark for rearranging, 1 mark for the value.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A reaction has an activation energy of 60.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The rate constant at 298 K is 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant at 308 K, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate constant rises by a factor of about 2 for a 10 K rise in this reaction.
parts.answer: The Boltzmann fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea increases by a factor of about 2 over this range, so k (and the rate) approximately doubles.
parts.working: Exponential dependence on 1/T.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate constant k was measured at four temperatures:
T / K: 290, 300, 310, 320
k / s⁻¹: 1.15 × 10⁻³, 2.00 × 10⁻³, 3.36 × 10⁻³, 5.45 × 10⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln k and 1/T for T = 290 K and T = 320 K, using the data (ln k to 2 decimal places, 1/T to 4 significant figures in K⁻¹ ×10⁻³).
parts.working: 1 mark for two ln k values; 1 mark for two 1/T values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the two points from (a) to calculate the gradient of ln k against 1/T, and hence the activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
parts.working: 1 mark: gradient ≈ −4800 K. 1 mark: Ea ≈ 40 kJ mol⁻¹ (accept 39–41).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the pre-exponential factor, A, represents in the Arrhenius equation.
parts.answer: The frequency of collisions with the correct orientation (a measure of how often collisions with correct geometry occur).
parts.working: A relates to collision frequency and orientation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two factors that would change A for a reaction without changing Ea.
parts.answer: The steric factor (the proportion of collisions with the correct orientation) and the collision frequency, for example through the size or shape of the reacting molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible factors: steric factor (orientation requirement); collision frequency (size or shape of the molecules affects how often they collide with the right orientation).

stem: A plot of ln k against 1/T for a reaction gives a straight line with gradient −4800 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy, Ea, in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: 39.9 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Ea = −gradient × R = 4800 × 8.314 = 39 907 J mol⁻¹ = 39.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the gradient is negative.
parts.answer: As temperature rises, 1/T falls and ln k rises; so ln k increases as 1/T decreases, meaning ln k falls as 1/T increases, giving a negative gradient.
parts.working: Gradient = −Ea/R is negative because Ea is positive.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A reaction has an activation energy of 75.0 kJ mol⁻¹. At 300 K its rate constant is 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which the rate constant becomes 5.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Give your answer to the nearest kelvin.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two reactions, X and Y, have the same pre-exponential factor. The activation energy of X is 55 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of Y is 85 kJ mol⁻¹. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which reaction has the larger rate constant at 310 K, and explain why.
parts.answer: Reaction X, because it has the lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of molecules has enough energy to react.
parts.working: Lower Ea gives a larger exponential term e^(−Ea/RT).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(X) ÷ k(Y) at 310 K, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for expression, 1 mark for exponent, 1 mark for value. exp[30 000 ÷ (8.314 × 310)] = exp(11.640) = 1.14 × 10⁵.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plots ln k against T (in kelvin, not 1/T) and reads Ea from the gradient. Explain why this method is wrong.
parts.answer: The Arrhenius relationship is linear in 1/T, not T; plotting ln k against T gives a curve, so the gradient does not equal −Ea/R.
parts.working: 1 mark: the relationship is linear in 1/T. 1 mark: a plot against T is curved, so a gradient gives no meaningful Ea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the correct plot and how Ea is found from it.
parts.answer: Plot ln k against 1/T (T in kelvin); the gradient is −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R.
parts.working: 1 mark: ln k vs 1/T. 1 mark: Ea = −gradient × R.

stem: A student wants to determine the activation energy of the reaction between a dye and bleach, using a colorimeter to measure the rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method, including how the rate constant is found at each temperature and how Ea is then determined.
parts.answer: Choose five temperatures (e.g. 20–50 °C) using a water bath; at each temperature measure the time or absorbance change to find the initial rate, and use the known order to calculate k; plot ln k against 1/T with T in kelvin; the gradient is −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature control and range (water bath, several temperatures). 1 mark: k from rate and concentrations/order at each temperature. 1 mark: plot ln k against 1/T, Ea = −gradient × R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two control variables and one source of error in the investigation.
parts.answer: Control variables: initial concentrations of the reactants, volume, and the same colorimeter/cuvette or wavelength. Error: the temperature of the reaction mixture may change slightly during the measurement, or the sample may not reach the bath temperature before mixing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible controls; 1 mark for a valid source of error with cause.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: A higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so the particles collide more frequently per second; more collisions per second means more successful collisions and a faster rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: more particles per unit volume give more frequent collisions. 1 mark: more successful collisions per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to a total volume of 100.0 cm³. Calculate the new concentration of the acid.
parts.answer: 0.050 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: moles of HCl unchanged: 0.20 × 0.0250 = 0.0050 mol; new concentration = 0.0050 ÷ 0.100 = 0.050 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the rate of reaction of this dilution, assuming the rate is proportional to [H⁺].
parts.answer: The rate falls by a factor of 4, because the concentration falls by a factor of 4 (0.20 to 0.050), so there are fewer collisions per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why increasing the surface area of a solid reactant increases the rate of reaction?
A It increases the activation energy of the reaction.
B It increases the energy of the particles that collide.
C It increases the number of collisions per second between particles at the surface.
D It makes the enthalpy change of the reaction more negative.
parts.answer: C It increases the number of collisions per second between particles at the surface.
parts.working: A and D are false (Ea and ΔH are unaffected by surface area); B is false because surface area does not change the energy of the particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term collision frequency and state two factors that increase it in a reaction mixture.
parts.answer: Collision frequency is the number of collisions per unit volume per second. Two factors: increasing concentration, increasing temperature (or pressure of gases, or surface area).
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark each for two factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two identical lumps of zinc are placed in dilute acid. One is stirred and one is not. The stirred mixture reacts faster. Explain why stirring increases the rate.
parts.answer: Stirring moves the acid past the surface of the zinc so fresh acid reaches the surface; a layer of depleted solution (or hydrogen/products) is removed, so more acid particles collide with the zinc surface per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: fresh reactant brought to the surface. 1 mark: depleted layer removed. 1 mark: more collisions per second with the zinc surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A marble chip of 1 cm side (a cube) is crushed into small cubes of side 1 mm, keeping the total volume the same. Calculate the total surface area of the 1 mm cubes, in cm², and the factor by which the surface area increases. (Each cube has six faces; 1 cm = 10 mm.)
parts.answer: 1 cm cube: 6 cm²; 1000 cubes of side 1 mm: each has 6 mm² = 0.06 cm²; total = 1000 × 0.06 = 60 cm²; factor = 60 ÷ 6 = 10.
parts.working: 1 mark: surface area of large cube 6 cm². 1 mark: number of 1 mm cubes = 1000. 1 mark: total area 60 cm². 1 mark: factor 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of iodide ions in the mixture.
parts.answer: 0.32 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the rate is proportional to [I⁻], calculate the factor by which the rate falls compared with the original 0.60 mol dm⁻³ solution.
parts.working: The rate falls by the ratio of the concentrations: 0.60 ÷ 0.32 = 1.875, about 1.9.

author: HomiLabs
stem: 30.0 cm³ of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ potassium iodide solution is mixed with 70.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ potassium iodide solution. The total volume of the mixture is 100.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why most collisions between reactant particles do not lead to a reaction, referring to the two conditions for a successful collision.
parts.answer: For a successful collision, the particles must have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and they must collide with the correct orientation (the reactive parts must meet). Most collisions fail because the energy is too low (most molecules have less than Ea) or the orientation is wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark: energy at least Ea. 1 mark: correct orientation. 1 mark: most molecules have E < Ea so most collisions have too little energy. 1 mark: many collisions have the wrong orientation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A spherical granule of calcium carbonate of radius 2.0 mm is broken into 8 identical smaller spheres of the same total volume. Calculate the ratio of the total surface area of the 8 spheres to that of the original sphere.
parts.answer: Each small sphere has radius 1.0 mm (volume 1/8 of the original, so radius is half). Total area = 8 × 4π(1.0)² = 32π mm²; original = 4π(2.0)² = 16π mm²; ratio = 2.0.
parts.working: 1 mark: radius of small spheres 1.0 mm. 1 mark: 8 spheres each 4π(1.0)². 1 mark: original 4π(2.0)². 1 mark: ratio 2 (equivalently R/r).

stem: In a reaction, the collision frequency Z is 4.0 × 10²⁷ collisions per dm³ per second. The fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea and correct orientation is f = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of successful collisions per dm³ per second, using rate of successful collisions = Z × f.
parts.answer: 1.0 × 10²² per dm³ per s
parts.working: 4.0 × 10²⁷ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.0 × 10²² successful collisions per dm³ per s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The concentration of one reactant is doubled, with f unchanged. Calculate the new number of successful collisions per dm³ per second.
parts.answer: 2.0 × 10²² per dm³ per s
parts.working: Doubling the concentration doubles Z (more particles per unit volume), so Z = 8.0 × 10²⁷ and successful collisions = 8.0 × 10²⁷ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 × 10²².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why raising the temperature increases f, but doubling the concentration does not change f.
parts.answer: A higher temperature increases the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ Ea (f rises). Doubling concentration changes only the number of particles per unit volume, so Z increases but the fraction f with enough energy and correct orientation is unchanged.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature increases the Boltzmann fraction above Ea. 1 mark: concentration affects Z only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'Increasing the surface area of a solid always increases the rate of reaction.' Evaluate this statement, giving one situation in which increasing surface area would have little or no effect.
parts.answer: Partly true: more surface area means more collisions with the solid, so the rate rises when the reaction is controlled by collisions at the surface. But if the solid is in large excess, or if the rate is limited by another step (for example the concentration of a dissolved reactant, or the rate of diffusion/removal of products), a larger surface area has little effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct link with more collisions at surface. 1 mark: qualification that it depends on the rate-determining step. 1 mark: example with little effect (e.g. solid in excess, or diffusion/solution concentration limits). 1 mark: balanced conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why collision theory helps to explain why the rate of a single-step reaction is proportional to the product of the concentrations of its reactants.
parts.answer: In a single bimolecular step, the number of collisions per second between A and B is proportional to [A] × [B], since each collision requires one A and one B particle; if the fraction with enough energy and orientation is constant, the rate is proportional to [A][B].
parts.working: 1 mark: collisions between A and B depend on the number of each per unit volume. 1 mark: product of concentrations. 1 mark: fraction successful constant at fixed T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why collision theory cannot reliably predict the orders of more complex reactions.
parts.answer: Complex reactions involve several steps, and the slowest step may not contain the species seen in the overall equation; the orders must come from experiment.
parts.working: Accept rate-determining step point.

stem: A reaction of hydrochloric acid with marble chips is first order in H⁺ and proportional to the surface area of the chips. With 1.0 mol dm⁻³ acid and marble chips of surface area A, the initial rate is 0.20 cm³ s⁻¹ of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the initial rate with 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid and marble with ten times the surface area, all other conditions the same.
parts.answer: 4.0 cm³ s⁻¹
parts.working: Rate ∝ [H⁺] × surface area: rate = 0.20 × 2.0 × 10 = 4.0 cm³ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the prediction in (a) may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: The surface area of the chips may not be proportional to the rate if the reaction is partly limited by diffusion of acid to the surface, or if the powder is not evenly spread; also, the tenfold area may not be exactly tenfold in practice.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate may not be proportional to area (diffusion or packing). 1 mark: a valid practical reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the reaction profile (energy profile) of an exothermic reaction, labelling the reactants, products, activation energy and enthalpy change.
parts.answer: Reactants start at a higher energy than products. The activation energy is the height of the energy barrier (peak) above the reactants; ΔH is the difference between the energy of products and reactants, shown as negative (products lower).
parts.working: 1 mark: products lower than reactants (exothermic, ΔH negative). 1 mark: Ea is the energy from reactants to the peak/transition state.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The activation energy of a reaction is 84 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy needed by a single molecule, in J, to 3 significant figures. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)
parts.working: 84 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.395 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is 1.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to 3 s.f. 1 mark for dividing by L, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction is exothermic overall, but a mixture of the reactants needs heating or a spark to start. Explain why.
parts.answer: The reactant molecules must first overcome the activation energy, which is the energy needed to break bonds and start the reaction; the overall exothermicity does not supply this energy at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark: activation energy must be supplied first. 1 mark: the energy released later does not provide this initial energy.

stem: A reaction X ⇌ Y has an energy profile with the following values relative to X (taken as 0 kJ mol⁻¹): the energy of the peak (transition state) is +85 kJ mol⁻¹, and the energy of Y is −40 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the forward reaction, X → Y.
parts.answer: 85 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Ea forward = energy of peak − energy of reactants = 85 − 0 = 85 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, for X → Y, and state whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹; exothermic
parts.working: ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants = −40 − 0 = −40 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction, Y → X.
parts.answer: 125 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Ea(reverse) = energy of peak − energy of Y = 85 − (−40) = 125 kJ mol⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a reaction with a high activation energy is usually slow at room temperature, even if it is strongly exothermic.
parts.answer: A high activation energy means only a very small fraction of molecules at room temperature have enough energy to react, so successful collisions are rare and the rate is low.
parts.working: 1 mark: few molecules have E ≥ Ea. 1 mark: few successful collisions, so slow rate (regardless of ΔH).

stem: A reaction is studied at two temperatures using a clock method (rate taken as 1/t). At 298 K the clock time is 120 s; at 318 K it is 45 s. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming rate ∝ 1/t and the same concentrations, calculate the ratio of the rate constants k(318 K) ÷ k(298 K).
parts.working: k ∝ rate ∝ 1/t, so ratio = 120 ÷ 45 = 2.67.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 38.6 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: ln(2.67) = (Ea/R)(1/298 − 1/318); Ea = 8.314 × 0.981 ÷ (2.110 × 10⁻⁴) = 38 600 J mol⁻¹. 1 mark for ln ratio, 1 mark for reciprocal difference, 1 mark for value.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen at room temperature does not react noticeably, even though the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is strongly exothermic. Explain why, and state what happens when a spark is added.
parts.answer: The activation energy is high, so very few molecules at room temperature have enough energy to react. The spark supplies the activation energy to a few molecules, which then release enough energy to start a chain of reactions that sustains the reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: high Ea, few molecules above Ea at room T. 1 mark: spark supplies activation energy. 1 mark: exothermic release of energy sustains the reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy in kJ mol⁻¹ equivalent to 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per molecule. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)
parts.answer: 289 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is larger or smaller than a typical activation energy for a reaction and give one implication.
parts.answer: It is larger than most activation energies (which are typically 20–150 kJ mol⁻¹), so such a reaction would be very slow unless a catalyst were present or the temperature were very high.
parts.working: Comparison with typical Ea range.

stem: Three reactions, P, Q and R, have activation energies of 40 kJ mol⁻¹, 65 kJ mol⁻¹ and 110 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. They have the same pre-exponential factor. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which reaction is fastest at 298 K, and which is slowest.
parts.answer: P is fastest; R is slowest.
parts.working: Lower Ea gives a larger rate constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(P) ÷ k(R) at 298 K, to 2 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The rate constants of two reactions A and B are compared at 298 K. Both have the same pre-exponential factor. Reaction A has Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹, reaction B has Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(B) ÷ k(A) at 298 K, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(B) ÷ k(A) at 500 K, assuming both reactions keep the same pre-exponential factor. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: ratio = exp[(100 000 − 50 000) ÷ (8.314 × 500)] = exp(12.03) = 1.7 × 10⁵. 1 mark for the expression using the difference in Ea, 1 mark for the value.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why one measurement of rate at a single temperature cannot give the activation energy of a reaction, and describe the minimum set of measurements needed.
parts.answer: Ea appears in an exponential relationship with temperature; a single rate gives only one value of k, which cannot separate Ea from A. At least two (preferably 4–5) temperatures are needed, with the rate constant (k) found at each, so the ratio or gradient of ln k against 1/T gives Ea.
parts.working: 1 mark: one rate gives one k, which cannot separate A and Ea. 1 mark: need at least two temperatures. 1 mark: k at each temperature. 1 mark: ratio or gradient of ln k against 1/T gives Ea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea at 298 K when Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, using f = e^(−Ea/RT). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why, even though this fraction is very small, reactions with this activation energy still take place at room temperature, given a very large number of collisions per second.
parts.answer: The number of collisions per second in a gas or solution is enormous, so even a tiny fraction of successful collisions gives a measurable number of reactions per second; the rate is set by fraction × collision frequency.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate = collision frequency × fraction. 1 mark: collision frequency is very large. 1 mark: small fraction still gives many reactions.

stem: A two-step reaction X → Y goes through an intermediate I. Step 1: X → I, with ΔH = +20 kJ mol⁻¹ and activation energy 70 kJ mol⁻¹ (from X). Step 2: I → Y, with activation energy 30 kJ mol⁻¹ (from I). Energies are relative to X at 0 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of the intermediate I and the energy of the peak for step 2, both relative to X.
parts.answer: I is at +20 kJ mol⁻¹; the peak for step 2 is at 20 + 30 = +50 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark: intermediate at +20 kJ. 1 mark: step 2 peak at 50 kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the rate-determining step and the overall activation energy of the reaction as measured from X.
parts.answer: Step 1 is rate-determining; the overall activation energy is 70 kJ mol⁻¹ (the highest peak, which is step 1).
parts.working: 1 mark: step 1 is the highest barrier. 1 mark: 70 kJ mol⁻¹ from X.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic, given that the final product Y lies at −30 kJ mol⁻¹ relative to X.
parts.answer: Exothermic, because Y is lower in energy than X (ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.working: Compare final energy with X.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A reaction with activation energy 90.0 kJ mol⁻¹ is timed by a clock method, with rate taken as 1/t. At 298 K the clock time is 50.0 s. R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Assume the same concentrations at both temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio k(330 K) ÷ k(298 K).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the clock time at 330 K, to 2 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term dynamic equilibrium in terms of the rates of the forward and reverse reactions.
parts.answer: A state in a closed system where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant; both reactions continue.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate forward = rate reverse. 1 mark: both reactions still occur (dynamic), so concentrations constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium. Explain, in terms of rates, why the equilibrium position does not change.
parts.answer: The catalyst increases the rate of the forward and the reverse reactions by the same factor, because it lowers the activation energy for both directions equally. The forward and reverse rates remain equal, so the equilibrium composition is unchanged; only the time to reach equilibrium changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: catalyst increases both rates. 1 mark: by the same amount, so forward = reverse still. 1 mark: equilibrium position unchanged but reached faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentrations of reactants and products do not change at equilibrium, even though both reactions continue.
parts.answer: The forward reaction removes reactants at the same rate as the reverse reaction forms them (and vice versa for products), so there is no net change in concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: forward and reverse rates equal. 1 mark: no net change in amounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, the temperature is raised. Both the forward and the reverse rates increase. Explain why the reverse rate increases by more than the forward rate.
parts.answer: Raising the temperature increases the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ Ea for both reactions. For an exothermic reaction the activation energy of the reverse reaction is larger than that of the forward reaction (Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH|), so the reverse rate increases by a larger factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: both rates increase because more molecules exceed Ea. 1 mark: Ea of reverse reaction is larger for exothermic reaction. 1 mark: larger Ea gives a larger increase in rate for the same temperature rise, so reverse increases more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction vessel contains only the products of a reversible reaction at time zero. State which of the forward or reverse rates is zero at the start, and explain why.
parts.answer: The forward rate is zero at the start, because there are no reactants present; the reverse rate starts at a positive value because the products are present and react.
parts.working: 1 mark: forward rate zero. 1 mark: no reactant to react.

stem: The equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is established in a sealed syringe at constant temperature. The pressure is then increased by pushing the plunger in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which rate increases by the larger factor when the pressure is increased, the forward rate or the reverse rate, and explain your answer in terms of collisions.
parts.answer: The reverse rate increases by the larger factor. The reverse reaction depends on collisions between two NO₂ molecules (rate ∝ [NO₂]²), while the forward reaction depends on a single N₂O₄ molecule breaking up (rate ∝ [N₂O₄]). When pressure rises, concentrations rise; the reverse rate increases with the square of the concentration factor, so it increases more.
parts.working: 1 mark: reverse rate increases more. 1 mark: forward rate is proportional to [N₂O₄] (one molecule). 1 mark: reverse rate ∝ [NO₂]² (two molecules must collide). 1 mark: concentrations increase, so the faster-increasing rate is the reverse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of this change on the equilibrium position.
parts.answer: The equilibrium moves to the side with fewer gas molecules (N₂O₄), since the reverse rate becomes greater than the forward rate until equilibrium is re-established.
parts.working: Fewer gas molecules favoured by increased pressure.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the equilibrium PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at a fixed temperature, Kc = [PCl₃][Cl₂] ÷ [PCl₅] = 0.0250 mol dm⁻³. At equilibrium [PCl₅] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [PCl₃] = [Cl₂].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate [PCl₃] at equilibrium, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.071 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: [PCl₃] = [Cl₂] = x, so x² = Kc × [PCl₅] = 0.0250 × 0.20 = 5.0 × 10⁻³. x = √(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 0.0707, which is 0.071 mol dm⁻³ to 2 s.f. 1 mark for the rearrangement, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: PCl₅ dissociation is endothermic. State and explain the effect of raising the temperature on the value of Kc.
parts.answer: Kc increases. The forward reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature increases the forward rate more than the reverse rate, so the equilibrium moves to the right and the value of [PCl₃][Cl₂] ÷ [PCl₅] increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: Kc increases. 1 mark: an endothermic forward reaction is favoured by a higher temperature, so the equilibrium moves to the right.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the reaction A + B ⇌ C, the rate constants are kf = 4.0 × 10⁻³ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ and kr = 0.20 s⁻¹. A mixture has [A] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [C] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the forward rate and the reverse rate for this mixture.
parts.answer: forward = 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; reverse = 2.0 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the mixture is at equilibrium and, if not, in which direction the net reaction proceeds.
parts.answer: Not at equilibrium: the reverse rate is larger, so the net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction (C → A + B) until the forward and reverse rates are equal.
parts.working: 1 mark: not equilibrium (rates unequal). 1 mark: net reverse direction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of collisions, why the reverse reaction rate increases as the concentration of product increases in a reversible reaction at constant temperature.
parts.answer: More product molecules per unit volume give more collisions between products per second; a larger fraction of these collisions can react, so the reverse rate increases until it equals the forward rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: more product molecules per volume. 1 mark: more collisions per second between them. 1 mark: more successful collisions so reverse rate rises until balance.

stem: A reversible reaction has forward activation energy 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and reverse activation energy 110 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, of the forward reaction and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) = 80 − 110 = −30 kJ mol⁻¹; exothermic.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct difference of Ea values. 1 mark: negative, exothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a rise in temperature affects the position of this equilibrium, using the rates of forward and reverse reactions.
parts.answer: Raising temperature increases both rates, but the reverse reaction has the larger activation energy so its rate increases by the larger factor. The reverse rate now exceeds the forward rate, so the equilibrium moves to the left (towards reactants).
parts.working: 1 mark: both rates rise. 1 mark: reverse Ea larger, so reverse rate increases more. 1 mark: equilibrium shifts left.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at 700 K, the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I₂] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [HI] = 0.80 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kc for this equilibrium.
parts.answer: Kc = 32

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the units of Kc and explain your answer.
parts.answer: No units: there are 2 mol of gas on each side, so the units cancel.
parts.working: 1 mark: the number of moles of gas on each side is equal, so the units of Kc cancel (both expressions have units (mol dm⁻³)⁰).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure at constant temperature on the position of this equilibrium.
parts.answer: No change in position. Both sides contain 2 mol of gas, so the forward and reverse rates increase by the same factor and remain equal.
parts.working: 1 mark: no shift, since there is no change in the number of gas molecules. 1 mark: the forward and reverse rates both increase by the same factor.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to show that, at equilibrium, the forward and reverse rates are equal but the concentrations are constant. Include the reaction you would choose, how you would start it, how you would measure concentrations over time, and how you would show that no net change occurs.
parts.answer: Choose a reversible reaction with a visible or measurable change (for example one with a coloured species or a measurable pressure change); start from reactants and from products separately; take readings of concentration (or absorbance/pressure) at intervals until constant; show the same final composition from both starting points; the constant composition with continuing reactions shows dynamic equilibrium.
