parts.working: 1 mark: suitable reversible reaction with measurable property. 1 mark: measurements over time. 1 mark: start from both sides to show same equilibrium. 1 mark: explanation that constant composition is consistent with equal forward and reverse rates.

stem: For the equilibrium A(g) ⇌ B(g) at constant temperature, the equilibrium concentrations are [A] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.75 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kc for this equilibrium.
parts.answer: Kc = 3.0 (no units)
parts.working: Kc = [B] ÷ [A] = 0.75 ÷ 0.25 = 3.0. The units cancel because the expression is concentration over concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: More B is added at constant temperature and a new equilibrium is established. Explain, in terms of the forward and reverse rates, why the equilibrium moves towards A, but Kc is unchanged.
parts.answer: Adding B increases the reverse rate at once, so the reverse rate is greater than the forward rate and the net reaction proceeds towards A until the two rates are equal again. Kc depends only on temperature, so it stays at 3.0.
parts.working: 1 mark: the reverse rate rises first, so the net reaction moves towards A. 1 mark: Kc depends only on temperature, so it is unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: At equilibrium, extra reactant is added to a reaction mixture. Describe how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions change with time until a new equilibrium is established.
parts.answer: The forward rate increases immediately, because the reactant concentration has increased. The reverse rate then increases gradually as more product forms. The forward rate falls back as reactants are used, and the two rates become equal again at a new equilibrium, which has a higher concentration of products than before the addition.
parts.working: 1 mark: forward rate jumps up at once. 1 mark: reverse rate increases as product builds up. 1 mark: forward falls as reactant is used. 1 mark: rates become equal at a new equilibrium.

parts.answer: B 0.150 mol/dm³

parts.text: Explain why starch indicator is added only when the solution is pale yellow, near the end point.
parts.answer: Starch forms an intense blue-black complex with iodine. If it is added while iodine is still concentrated, the iodine is bound slowly and the end point is blurred; adding it near the end point gives a sharp colour change.
parts.working: 1 mark: starch complex with iodine is strong and binds iodine slowly if added early. 1 mark: adding near the end point gives a sharp blue-to-colourless change.

parts.text: State the empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.
parts.answer: CH₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: CH₂O (C : H : O = 6 : 12 : 6, divided by 6).

stem: A hydrocarbon burns completely. 0.260 g of it forms 0.880 g of carbon dioxide and 0.180 g of water. [Ar C 12.0, H 1.0; Mr CO₂ 44.0, H₂O 18.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the empirical formula is CH.
parts.answer: Mass C = 0.240 g and mass H = 0.020 g; moles C : H = 0.0200 : 0.0200 = 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass is 78.0. Deduce the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₆H₆

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phosphorus forms an oxide that contains 43.7 % phosphorus by mass. Deduce its empirical formula. [Ar P 31.0, O 16.0]
parts.answer: P₂O₅

stem: Magnesium burns in nitrogen to form magnesium nitride. 2.43 g of magnesium gives 3.35 g of magnesium nitride. [Ar: Mg 24.3, N 14.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen that combined with the magnesium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the empirical formula of magnesium nitride.
parts.answer: Mg₃N₂

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose has the empirical formula CH₂O and a relative molecular mass of 180. Calculate the number of empirical units in one molecule and state the molecular formula. [Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0]
parts.answer: 6 units; C₆H₁₂O₆
parts.working: M1 Mr(CH₂O) = 30.0; n = 180 ÷ 30.0 = 6. A1 molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound has the empirical formula C₂H₅ and a relative molecular mass of 58.0. Deduce its molecular formula. [Ar C 12.0, H 1.0]
parts.answer: C₄H₁₀

parts.label: a
parts.text: 5.00 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until its mass is constant. 3.20 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ remains. Calculate x. [Mr: CuSO₄ 159.6, H₂O 18.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrated sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄·xH₂O, is 55.9 % water by mass. Calculate x. [Mr: Na₂SO₄ 142.0, H₂O 18.0]

stem: A student heats a hydrated salt, MgCl₂·xH₂O, in a tube. Mass of tube = 22.40 g; mass of tube + hydrated salt = 26.47 g. After heating to constant mass, mass of tube + anhydrous salt = 24.31 g. [Mr: MgCl₂ 95.3, H₂O 18.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of anhydrous salt.
parts.working: M1 mass of anhydrous salt = 24.31 − 22.40 = 1.91 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost.
parts.working: M1 mass of water = 4.07 − 1.91 = 2.16 g (the hydrated salt was 26.47 − 22.40 = 4.07 g).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate x.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 2.86 g sample of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. 20.0 cm³ of acid is needed (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂). Calculate x. [Mr: Na₂CO₃ 106.0, H₂O 18.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, is 51.1 % water by mass. Calculate x. [Ar: Mg 24.3, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that a hydrated salt has been fully dehydrated when its mass stops changing on heating. Explain why the salt is heated again and weighed until the mass is constant.
parts.answer: Heating for a set time may not remove all the water; repeating the heating and weighing until two masses agree shows that all the water of crystallisation has been driven off.
parts.working: 1 mark: a single heating may leave some water. 1 mark: repeated heating and weighing until the mass is constant shows complete dehydration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of sodium carbonate with 10 molecules of water of crystallisation.
parts.answer: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: the water is written after a dot, with the number of water molecules before H₂O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the formula of magnesium sulfate with 7 molecules of water of crystallisation.
parts.answer: MgSO₄·7H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: the water is written after a dot, with the number of water molecules before H₂O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is used to make a 0.100 mol/dm³ solution. Calculate the mass of the crystals needed to make 500 cm³ of this solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr CuSO₄·5H₂O = 249.7]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in CuSO₄·5H₂O. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr CuSO₄·5H₂O = 249.7; H₂O = 18.0 × 5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Barium chloride dihydrate, BaCl₂·2H₂O, has Mr = 244.3. A student dissolves 3.00 g of the crystals in water. Calculate the mass of barium ions in the sample. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. [Ar Ba = 137.3]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·6H₂O, is pink. On heating it loses water and becomes blue. Write the equation for the dehydration.
parts.answer: CoCl₂·6H₂O → CoCl₂ + 6H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation with 6H₂O released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the colour change seen when water is added back to the blue solid, and state what this shows about the reaction.
parts.answer: Blue to pink; the reaction is reversible, so the colour change can be used as a test for water.
parts.working: 1 mark: colour changes from blue to pink. 1 mark: the hydration is reversible, so the test detects water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·xH₂O, has mass 2.87 g. On heating, 1.26 g of water is lost. Calculate x. [Mr: ZnSO₄ 161.4, H₂O 18.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, how many moles of chlorine are needed to react completely with 0.60 mol of aluminium?
A 0.40 mol
B 0.60 mol
C 0.90 mol
D 1.20 mol
parts.answer: C 0.90 mol
parts.working: Mole ratio Al : Cl₂ = 2 : 3, so n(Cl₂) = 0.60 × 3/2 = 0.90 mol. A uses the inverse ratio; B assumes a 1 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Balance each equation: (i) NH₃ + O₂ → NO + H₂O (ii) C₄H₁₀ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (iii) K + H₂O → KOH + H₂
parts.answer: (i) 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (ii) 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O (iii) 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂
parts.working: 1 mark each. Balance the atoms that appear in one formula each first (N, then C, then H, and O last).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lithium burns in nitrogen: 6Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N. Calculate the mass of lithium nitride formed from 2.10 g of lithium. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. [Ar: Li 6.9, N 14.0]

stem: Ammonia is made in the laboratory from ammonium chloride: Ca(OH)₂ + 2NH₄Cl → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O. [Mr: Ca(OH)₂ 74.1, NH₄Cl 53.5; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium hydroxide needed to react with 5.35 g of ammonium chloride. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: 2.40 dm³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene reacts with bromine: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Calculate the mass of 1,2-dibromoethane formed from 2.80 g of ethene, assuming bromine is in excess and the reaction is complete. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, Br 79.9; Mr C₂H₄ 28.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper(II) oxide is reduced by hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Calculate the mass of copper formed from 4.00 g of copper(II) oxide. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Ar: Cu 63.5, O 16.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. 10.6 g of sodium carbonate is added to 100 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at room temperature and pressure, and state whether the acid or the carbonate is in excess. [Mr Na₂CO₃ = 106.0; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 2.40 dm³ of CO₂; neither is in excess (exact stoichiometry)
parts.working: M1 n(Na₂CO₃) = 10.6 ÷ 106.0 = 0.100 mol; n(HCl) = 2.00 × 0.100 = 0.200 mol. M1 HCl needed = 2 × 0.100 = 0.200 mol, exactly the amount available. A1 n(CO₂) = 0.100 mol, V = 2.40 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. 25.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol/dm³ hydrogen peroxide is decomposed completely. Calculate the volume of oxygen produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm³.
parts.answer: 240 cm³

stem: Silver nitrate solution reacts with sodium chloride solution: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ silver nitrate is added to excess sodium chloride solution. [Ar: Ag 107.9, Cl 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of silver chloride precipitated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass is found from the silver nitrate and not from the sodium chloride.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride is in excess, so the silver nitrate is the limiting reagent and determines the amount of precipitate.
parts.working: 1 mark: NaCl is in excess. 1 mark: AgNO₃ limits the amount of AgCl formed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: 1 mark: correct products, balancing and state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for sodium with water.
parts.answer: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: 1 mark: correct products, balancing and state symbols.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for zinc with dilute sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: 1 mark: correct products, balancing and state symbols.

stem: 0.240 g of metal M, with relative atomic mass 24.0, reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. 240 cm³ of hydrogen is produced at room temperature and pressure. [Molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of hydrogen produced, in mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the equation for the reaction and the formula of the chloride of M formed.
parts.answer: M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂; the chloride is MCl₂
parts.working: M1 M : H₂ = 1 : 1 (0.0100 mol of M gives 0.0100 mol of H₂), so M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂. M1 M is +2, so its chloride is MCl₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify M, using its relative atomic mass.
parts.answer: M is magnesium (Mg).
parts.working: M1 n(M) = 0.240 ÷ 24.0 = 0.0100 mol, so Ar = 24.0. A1 the element with Ar closest to 24.0 is magnesium (24.3).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Methane burns completely: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What amount of oxygen is needed to burn 0.0500 mol of methane?
A 0.0250 mol
B 0.0500 mol
C 0.100 mol
D 0.200 mol
parts.answer: C 0.100 mol
parts.working: Mole ratio CH₄ : O₂ = 1 : 2, so n(O₂) = 2 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol. B uses 1 : 1; D multiplies by 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term percentage yield, and give the equation used to calculate it.
parts.answer: Percentage yield = (actual mass or amount of product obtained ÷ theoretical mass or amount of product) × 100 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: actual yield compared with the theoretical (maximum possible) yield. 1 mark: the correct ratio multiplied by 100 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the atom economy for the production of hydrogen. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Ar: Zn 65.4, Cl 35.5, H 1.0]
parts.working: M1 total Mr of reactants = 65.4 + 2 × 36.5 = 138.4. M1 Mr of desired product H₂ = 2.0. A1 atom economy = 2.0 ÷ 138.4 × 100 = 1.4 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 10.0 g of calcium carbonate gives 4.80 g of calcium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1; CaO = 56.1]

parts.label: a
parts.text: A two-step synthesis has a yield of 80 % in step 1 and 75 % in step 2. Calculate the overall percentage yield.
parts.working: M1 overall yield = 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60. A1 overall yield = 60 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose ferments to ethanol: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for the production of ethanol. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr: C₆H₁₂O₆ 180.0; C₂H₅OH 46.0]
parts.working: M1 mass of desired products = 2 × 46.0 = 92.0. A1 atom economy = 92.0 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron is extracted from 40.0 g of iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃, in a process with an 85 % yield. Calculate the mass of iron obtained. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Ar: Fe 55.8, O 16.0; Mr Fe₂O₃ = 159.6]
parts.working: M1 theoretical moles of Fe = 2 × 40.0 ÷ 159.6 = 0.501 mol. M1 theoretical mass = 0.501 × 55.8 = 27.97 g. A1 actual mass = 0.85 × 27.97 = 23.8 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium chlorate(V) decomposes on heating: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. 2.45 g of KClO₃ is heated and 0.816 g of oxygen is collected. Calculate the percentage yield of oxygen. [Mr KClO₃ = 122.5; O₂ = 32.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the percentage yield of a reaction is usually less than 100 % in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Any two of: some product is lost during transfer or filtration; the reaction is reversible or does not go to completion; side reactions form other products; impure reactants.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: loss during transfer/filtration/purification; reversible or incomplete reaction; side reactions; impure reactants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium oxide is made by heating calcium carbonate: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for making calcium oxide. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1; CaO = 56.1]
parts.working: M1 mass of desired product = 56.1 out of 100.1 total reactant mass. A1 atom economy = 56.1 ÷ 100.1 × 100 = 56.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene is converted to ethanol by reaction with steam: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. 5.60 g of ethene is converted to ethanol (Mr 46.0) with a percentage yield of 65 %. Calculate the mass of ethanol obtained. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 n(C₂H₄) = 5.60 ÷ 28.0 = 0.200 mol. M1 theoretical mass of ethanol = 0.200 × 46.0 = 9.20 g. A1 actual mass = 0.65 × 9.20 = 5.98 g.

stem: A three-step synthesis has yields of 90 %, 80 % and 70 % in the three steps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overall percentage yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the theoretical mass of the final product is 20.0 g, calculate the actual mass obtained.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol can be dehydrated to ethene: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Calculate the atom economy for the production of ethene. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [Mr: C₂H₅OH 46.0; C₂H₄ 28.0]
parts.working: M1 mass of desired product = 28.0 out of total reactant mass 46.0. A1 atom economy = 28.0 ÷ 46.0 × 100 = 60.9 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the atom economy of a reaction is important, even when the percentage yield is 100 %.
parts.answer: A reaction with a high yield can still waste many atoms as by-products. Atom economy measures how much of the reactant mass ends up as the desired product, so low atom economy means more waste to dispose of and more raw material used.
parts.working: 1 mark: by-products are wasted atoms even with high yield. 1 mark: atom economy measures the proportion of reactant mass in the desired product, showing waste and resource use.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the correct formula of ammonium carbonate?
A NH₄CO₃
B (NH₄)₂CO₃
C NH₄(CO₃)₂
D (NH₄)₃CO₃
parts.answer: B (NH₄)₂CO₃
parts.working: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻; two NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻. A has the wrong charge balance; C and D have the wrong numbers of ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the correct formula of lead(II) phosphate?
A Pb₂(PO₄)
B Pb₃(PO₄)₂
C Pb(PO₄)₂
D Pb₂PO₄
parts.answer: B Pb₃(PO₄)₂
parts.working: Pb²⁺ and PO₄³⁻: the least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so 3 Pb²⁺ and 2 PO₄³⁻ give Pb₃(PO₄)₂. C would need Pb⁴⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of each compound: (i) potassium manganate(VII) (ii) calcium nitrate (iii) aluminium oxide (iv) sodium hydrogencarbonate.
parts.answer: (i) KMnO₄ (ii) Ca(NO₃)₂ (iii) Al₂O₃ (iv) NaHCO₃
parts.working: 1 mark each. Use the ion charges: K⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, O²⁻, Na⁺, HCO₃⁻, NO₃⁻ and MnO₄⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name each compound: (a) Cr₂O₃ (b) Fe(OH)₃ (c) Mn(NO₃)₂ (d) CuSO₄·5H₂O.
parts.answer: (a) chromium(III) oxide (b) iron(III) hydroxide (c) manganese(II) nitrate (d) copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate
parts.working: 1 mark each. Work out the metal's oxidation state from the anion, then write it in Roman numerals (e.g. Cr₂O₃: 2 Cr = +6, so Cr is +3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the formula of (a) tin(IV) oxide (b) tin(II) chloride. Tin(IV) is Sn⁴⁺ and tin(II) is Sn²⁺.
parts.answer: (a) SnO₂ (b) SnCl₂
parts.working: 1 mark each: SnO₂ (2 O²⁻ balance Sn⁴⁺); SnCl₂ (2 Cl⁻ balance Sn²⁺).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of each compound: (a) magnesium hydrogensulfate (b) lithium dichromate(VI) (c) iron(III) carbonate.
parts.answer: (a) Mg(HSO₄)₂ (b) Li₂Cr₂O₇ (c) Fe₂(CO₃)₃
parts.working: 1 mark each. Hydrogensulfate is HSO₄⁻, dichromate is Cr₂O₇²⁻, carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Fe³⁺ needs 3 carbonates for every 2 iron ions: Fe₂(CO₃)₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrated iron(III) sulfate, Fe₂(SO₄)₃·xH₂O, has mass 5.00 g. On analysis it contains 0.993 g of iron. Calculate x. [Ar: Fe 55.8, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the oxidation state of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇ and of manganese in K₂MnO₄. Use the fact that the oxidation states of potassium (+1) and oxygen (−2) are fixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium iron(II) sulfate hexahydrate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O. [Ar: N 14.0, H 1.0, Fe 55.8, S 32.1, O 16.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of each ion: (a) sulfite (b) hydrogencarbonate (c) phosphate (d) ammonium.
parts.answer: (a) SO₃²⁻ (b) HCO₃⁻ (c) PO₄³⁻ (d) NH₄⁺
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of each salt formed: (a) sulfuric acid with calcium hydroxide (b) nitric acid with lead(II) oxide. Write the balanced equation for each, showing water as a product.
parts.answer: (a) H₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaSO₄ + 2H₂O, salt CaSO₄ (b) 2HNO₃ + PbO → Pb(NO₃)₂ + H₂O, salt Pb(NO₃)₂
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct salt formula. 1 mark for each balanced equation with water as a product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of (a) copper(I) oxide (b) copper(II) oxide.
parts.answer: (a) Cu₂O (b) CuO
parts.working: 1 mark each: Cu⁺ needs 2 ions per O²⁻; Cu²⁺ needs 1 O²⁻.

stem: Aluminium and chlorine form an ionic compound. [Ar: Al 27.0, Cl 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of aluminium chloride.
parts.answer: AlCl₃
parts.working: 1 mark: Al³⁺ and Cl⁻ give AlCl₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its relative formula mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chloride ions in 26.7 g of aluminium chloride.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which Period 3 element has the highest electronegativity?
A sodium
B silicon
C phosphorus
D chlorine
parts.answer: D chlorine
parts.working: Electronegativity increases across Period 3 as nuclear charge rises with similar shielding. Argon is excluded because it has no value. B and C are in the middle of the period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
parts.answer: Aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than the 3s sub-shell of magnesium, so it is removed more easily. The 3p electron is also slightly further from the nucleus, and the 3s electrons shield it. Magnesium's 3s² pair is a full, stable sub-shell.
parts.working: 1 mark: Al's outer electron is in 3p, which is higher in energy than 3s. 1 mark: 3p electron is further from the nucleus / more shielded. 1 mark: Mg's 3s² is a stable full sub-shell that is harder to disturb.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The atomic radius of sodium is 186 pm and that of chlorine is 99 pm. Calculate the percentage decrease in atomic radius from sodium to chlorine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 decrease = 186 − 99 = 87 pm. A1 percentage = 87 ÷ 186 × 100 = 46.8 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ionic radius of P³⁻ is larger than that of Cl⁻, even though P³⁻ and Cl⁻ have the same number of electrons (18).
parts.answer: P³⁻ has 15 protons and Cl⁻ has 17 protons. The nuclear charge is lower for P³⁻, so it attracts the 18 electrons less strongly and its electron cloud is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: both ions have 18 electrons (isoelectronic). 1 mark: Cl⁻ has more protons (17 against 15). 1 mark: greater nuclear attraction pulls the electron cloud in, so Cl⁻ is smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first six successive ionisation energies of an element X in Period 3 are: 1012, 1907, 2914, 4964, 6274, 21 267 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate the ratio IE₆ ÷ IE₅ to 2 decimal places. (b) Deduce the group of X and identify X.
parts.answer: (a) 3.39 (b) Group 15 (five outer electrons, big jump after the 5th); X is phosphorus
parts.working: (a) M1 21 267 ÷ 6274 = 3.39. (b) M1 the large jump occurs after 5 electrons, so X has 5 outer electrons. A1 Group 15. A1 X is phosphorus (P).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why electronegativity increases across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
parts.answer: Nuclear charge increases across the period. The outer electrons are in the same shell and shielding is similar, so the nucleus attracts the bonding electron pair more strongly.
parts.working: 1 mark: nuclear charge (protons) increases. 1 mark: outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding. 1 mark: greater attraction for bonding electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a sodium atom is larger than a magnesium atom.
parts.answer: Magnesium has one more proton, so its nucleus has a greater charge. The outer electrons of both atoms are in the 3rd shell with similar shielding, so the extra nuclear charge pulls the outer shell closer.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg has a larger nuclear charge. 1 mark: outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding, so they are pulled closer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the second ionisation energy of an element is always higher than its first ionisation energy.
parts.answer: After the first electron is removed the ion is positive, so the remaining electrons are held more strongly by the same nucleus; the attraction increases, so the next electron is harder to remove.
parts.working: 1 mark: the ion formed has a positive charge. 1 mark: the same nucleus holds fewer electrons more strongly, so the next removal needs more energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average increase in first ionisation energy per element, in kJ/mol, from sodium to argon. The first ionisation energies are: Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 786, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 146.4 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 total increase from Na to Ar = 1521 − 496 = 1025 kJ/mol over 7 steps. A1 average = 1025 ÷ 7 = 146.4 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio IE₃ ÷ IE₂ for magnesium (IE₂ = 1451, IE₃ = 7733) and for silicon (IE₂ = 1577, IE₃ = 3232), both in kJ/mol. Give each ratio to 2 decimal places. Explain why the magnesium ratio is so much larger.
parts.answer: Mg: 5.33; Si: 2.05. Mg²⁺ has a stable neon-like configuration, so removing a third electron must break into the full inner shell, giving a large jump; Si still has electrons in its outer shell, so its ratio is smaller.
parts.working: M1 7733 ÷ 1451 = 5.33. M1 3232 ÷ 1577 = 2.05. A1 explanation: Mg²⁺ is a stable, full-shell ion, so removing a third electron breaks into the inner shell. A1 Si still has electrons in its outer shell at this stage, so the ratio is smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance has the lowest melting point?
A magnesium oxide
B aluminium
C chlorine
D silicon(IV) oxide
parts.answer: C chlorine
parts.working: Chlorine is simple molecular with weak London forces between Cl₂ molecules, so little energy is needed to melt it. MgO is giant ionic, aluminium is metallic and SiO₂ is giant covalent, so all three need much more energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of silicon and of phosphorus, and state how this affects their melting points.
parts.answer: Silicon is a giant covalent lattice of atoms, each bonded to four others, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it (high m.p.). Phosphorus (P₄) is simple molecular with tetrahedral P₄ molecules held by weak London forces, so it melts at a low temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: silicon is giant covalent. 1 mark: each Si bonded to 4 others in a lattice. 1 mark: phosphorus is simple molecular (P₄). 1 mark: weak forces between molecules make P's m.p. low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur exists as S₈ molecules and phosphorus as P₄ molecules. Explain why sulfur has a higher melting point than phosphorus (115 °C against 44 °C).
parts.answer: S₈ molecules are larger, with more electrons, so they have stronger London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces between molecules. More energy is needed to overcome these forces.
parts.working: 1 mark: both are simple molecular with London forces between molecules. 1 mark: S₈ has more electrons / a larger molecule. 1 mark: stronger London forces need more energy to overcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of ions in 1.00 g of sodium chloride, NaCl. [Mr NaCl = 58.5; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 2.06 × 10²² ions
parts.working: M1 n(NaCl) = 1.00 ÷ 58.5 = 0.0171 mol. M1 each formula unit gives 2 ions, so n(ions) = 0.0342 mol. A1 number = 0.0342 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.06 × 10²² ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why magnesium chloride melts at 714 °C but silicon(IV) chloride, SiCl₄, melts at −70 °C.
parts.answer: MgCl₂ is an ionic giant lattice, with strong electrostatic attraction between Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in all directions, which needs a lot of energy to break. SiCl₄ is simple molecular with only weak London forces between molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark: MgCl₂ is giant ionic with strong electrostatic forces. 1 mark: SiCl₄ is simple molecular. 1 mark: weak London forces are overcome at low temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why silicon conducts electricity poorly but aluminium conducts well.
parts.answer: Aluminium has delocalised electrons that can move through the metal lattice to carry charge. Silicon has no free-moving electrons in its covalent structure; it is a semiconductor, conducting only weakly.
parts.working: 1 mark: Al has delocalised (mobile) electrons. 1 mark: Si's electrons are fixed in covalent bonds, so it conducts poorly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂, has a very high melting point, but carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it. CO₂ is simple molecular, so only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules must be overcome, which needs little energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: SiO₂ giant covalent with strong bonds throughout. 1 mark: CO₂ simple molecular. 1 mark: weak forces between CO₂ molecules are easily overcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the structure and bonding of each: (a) sodium chloride (b) magnesium chloride (c) silicon(IV) chloride (d) chlorine.
parts.answer: (a) giant ionic lattice (b) giant ionic lattice (c) simple molecular, covalent (d) simple molecular, covalent
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: Argon has the lowest melting point in Period 3 (−189 °C), and the melting point of silicon is 1414 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between these two melting points in °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why argon (−189 °C) melts at a lower temperature than chlorine (−101 °C).
parts.answer: Cl₂ has a larger Mr (71 against 40) and more electrons (34 against 18), so its London forces are stronger; argon atoms are held by weaker London forces, so less energy is needed to melt it.
parts.working: 1 mark: Cl₂ has more electrons / larger Mr than Ar. 1 mark: stronger London forces between Cl₂ molecules. 1 mark: weaker forces between Ar atoms mean a lower m.p.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in terms of structure and bonding, the trend in melting point across Period 3, from sodium to argon.
parts.answer: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals with metallic bonding that strengthens from Na to Al, so the melting point rises. Silicon is giant covalent with the highest melting point. Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon are simple molecular with weak London forces, so their melting points are much lower; S₈ is highest of these and argon is lowest.
parts.working: 1 mark: metallic bonding strengthens from Na to Al. 1 mark: silicon is giant covalent with the highest m.p. 1 mark: P, S, Cl₂ and Ar are simple molecular. 1 mark: weak London forces give low m.p., with larger molecules higher.

subtopic: Period 3 elements: reactions with oxygen & chlorine

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Phosphorus burns in an excess of oxygen. Which product is formed?
A P₄O₆
B P₄O₁₀
C PO
D PH₃
parts.answer: B P₄O₁₀
parts.working: Phosphorus burns in excess oxygen to give phosphorus(V) oxide, P₄O₁₀; P₄O₆ is formed when oxygen is limited.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Period 3 elements: reactions with oxygen & chlorine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when sulfur is burned in air.
parts.answer: Sulfur burns with a blue flame and forms a colourless, choking gas (sulfur dioxide).
parts.working: 1 mark: blue flame. 1 mark: colourless gas formed (sulfur dioxide, with a choking smell).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 2.30 g sample of sodium is burned in an excess of oxygen to form sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂. Write the equation for the reaction and calculate the mass of sodium peroxide formed. [Ar Na 23.0; Mr Na₂O₂ 78.0]
parts.answer: 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂; 3.90 g
parts.working: M1 equation: 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂. M1 n(Na) = 2.30 ÷ 23.0 = 0.100 mol. M1 n(Na₂O₂) = 0.050 mol (2 : 1). A1 mass = 0.050 × 78.0 = 3.90 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium reacts with chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. Calculate the mass of chlorine needed to react completely with 0.500 g of aluminium. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. [Ar Al 27.0; Cl 35.5]

subtopic: Period 3 elements: reactions with oxygen & chlorine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon burns in chlorine: Si + 2Cl₂ → SiCl₄. Calculate the volume of chlorine, in dm³ at room temperature and pressure, needed to react completely with 2.80 g of silicon. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [Ar Si 28.1; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 4.78 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of phosphorus with an excess of chlorine to form phosphorus(V) chloride. Use P₄ as the form of phosphorus.
parts.answer: P₄ + 10Cl₂ → 4PCl₅
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct formulae; 1 mark for balancing (4 P, 10 Cl).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Period 3 elements: reactions with oxygen & chlorine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium foil does not burn easily in air, but aluminium powder burns vigorously. Explain both observations.
parts.answer: Aluminium forms a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide on its surface that protects the metal from further reaction. Powder has a much larger surface area for oxygen to react with, so it burns vigorously.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxide layer on the foil protects the metal. 1 mark: powder has a much larger surface area. 1 mark: more area gives a faster reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the oxidation state of phosphorus in P₄O₁₀ and of sulfur in SO₂.

parts.text: Phosphorus burns in a limited supply of oxygen to form phosphorus(III) oxide, P₄O₆ (Mr = 220.0). Calculate the mass of P₄O₆ formed when 3.10 g of phosphorus (P₄, Mr = 124.0) burns. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Calculate the volume of chlorine, in cm³ at room temperature and pressure, that reacts with 25.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. [Molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 120 cm³

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Period 3 elements: reactions with oxygen & chlorine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur burns in excess oxygen: S + O₂ → SO₂. Calculate the volume of sulfur dioxide, in cm³ at room temperature and pressure, formed from 0.800 g of sulfur. Give your answer to the nearest cm³. [Ar S 32.1; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 598 cm³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium oxide melts at a much higher temperature than sodium oxide. Explain this in terms of the ions present.
parts.answer: In MgO both ions are more highly charged (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ against Na⁺ and O²⁻ in Na₂O) and the Mg²⁺ ion is smaller, so the electrostatic attraction in the giant ionic lattice is stronger and more energy is needed to melt it.
parts.working: 1 mark: giant ionic lattice in both. 1 mark: higher ionic charges (2+ and 2−) in MgO. 1 mark: smaller ions put the charges closer, so attraction is stronger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mean bond enthalpies: C–F 484 kJ mol⁻¹, C–Cl 346 kJ mol⁻¹, C–Br 290 kJ mol⁻¹, C–I 228 kJ mol⁻¹. Describe how the C–X bond enthalpy changes from C–F to C–I, and state how this change affects the rate of hydrolysis of CH₃F, CH₃Cl, CH₃Br and CH₃I by aqueous NaOH.
parts.answer: Bond enthalpy decreases from C–F to C–I. The weaker the C–X bond, the more easily it is broken, so the rate of hydrolysis increases in the order CH₃F (slowest) < CH₃Cl < CH₃Br < CH₃I (fastest).
parts.working: B1 bond enthalpy decreases C–F → C–Cl → C–Br → C–I (C–F strongest, C–I weakest); B1 weaker C–X bond is broken more easily, so rate increases C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why CH₃F does not undergo hydrolysis by aqueous NaOH under normal laboratory conditions.
parts.answer: The C–F bond is very strong, so it is very hard to break.
parts.working: B1 strong C–F bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl, is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide. Rate experiments at 25 °C gave these results: [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ gives a rate of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Doubling [(CH₃)₃CCl] doubles the rate. Doubling [OH⁻] has no effect on the rate. Deduce the order with respect to each reactant and write the rate equation.
parts.answer: First order with respect to (CH₃)₃CCl; zero order with respect to OH⁻; rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl]
parts.working: B1 first order in (CH₃)₃CCl and zero order in OH⁻; B1 rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant k, with its units, using the first experiment.
parts.working: M1 k = rate / [(CH₃)₃CCl] = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.10; A1 2.4 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (units s⁻¹ because the rate equation has only one concentration term).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which mechanism these results support, and identify the slow step.
parts.answer: SN1; the slow step is the heterolysis of the C–Cl bond to form (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Cl⁻.
parts.working: B1 SN1; B1 slow step is C–Cl breaking (carbocation formed), not involving OH⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bromoethane reacts faster than chloroethane when each is heated with aqueous NaOH.
parts.answer: The C–Br bond is weaker (lower bond enthalpy) than the C–Cl bond, so it breaks more easily; Br⁻ is a better leaving group than Cl⁻ because it is a weaker base.
parts.working: B1 C–Br weaker / lower bond enthalpy than C–Cl; B1 C–Br is broken more easily, lower activation energy; B1 Br⁻ is a better leaving group (weaker base).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the hydrolysis of primary (1-bromopropane), secondary (2-bromopropane) and tertiary (2-bromo-2-methylpropane) halogenoalkanes by the SN1 mechanism. State the order of SN1 rate, from fastest to slowest.
parts.answer: tertiary > secondary > primary
parts.working: B1 tertiary fastest, primary slowest for SN1; B1 explanation via carbocation stability (more alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge by electron donation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The SN2 mechanism shows the opposite trend for these three compounds. Explain why, in terms of the attacking nucleophile.
parts.answer: In SN2 the OH⁻ must approach the carbon from the side opposite the halogen; alkyl groups crowd this site, so primary halogenoalkanes react fastest and tertiary ones react least (steric hindrance).
parts.working: B1 OH⁻ approaches from the opposite side to C–X (backside attack); B1 more alkyl groups cause steric hindrance, so primary is fastest.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the SN1 hydrolysis of (CH₃)₃CBr, what happens in the rate-determining step?
A hydroxide ion attacks the carbon atom and bonds to it at the same time as the C–Br bond breaks
B the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to give (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻
C a proton is removed from a methyl group to give an alkene
D water donates a lone pair to form a C–O bond with a Br⁻ ion already present
parts.answer: B the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to give (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻
parts.working: SN1 has two steps; the first, slow step is heterolytic fission of the C–Br bond to a carbocation. Option A describes SN2 (single step), C describes elimination, D is not a step.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Optically active 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH. Explain why the product obtained by an SN1 pathway is optically inactive.
parts.answer: The planar carbocation intermediate can be attacked by OH⁻ from either face, giving equal amounts of the two mirror-image alcohols, a racemic mixture.
parts.working: B1 planar carbocation (sp² carbon); B1 attack from both faces equally gives 50:50 mixture of enantiomers (racemic, optically inactive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Neopentyl bromide, 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br, is a primary halogenoalkane but reacts extremely slowly by both SN1 and SN2 mechanisms. Explain why it reacts so slowly by SN2 and why it also reacts slowly by SN1.
parts.answer: SN2: the bulky (CH₃)₃C– group next to CH₂Br blocks the backside approach of OH⁻ (severe steric hindrance). SN1: a primary carbocation would be very unstable, so the first step is very difficult.
parts.working: B1 bulky tert-butyl group adjacent to C–Br; B1 blocks backside attack by nucleophile (steric hindrance) so SN2 slow; B1 SN1 needs primary carbocation which is very unstable; B1 so the slow ionisation step is also very slow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction profile for the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is described as follows. The energy rises to a first peak, then falls to a shallow valley (intermediate), then rises to a second, lower peak, then falls to the products. Identify which step has the higher activation energy and explain why this step controls the rate.
parts.answer: The first step (C–Br bond breaking to form the carbocation) has the higher activation energy, so it is the rate-determining step.
parts.working: B1 first step has the higher energy peak (larger Ea); B1 slowest step determines overall rate; B1 the intermediate is a carbocation, formed in the first step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the intermediate in part (a) is not formed in SN2.
parts.answer: SN2 is a single concerted step; no intermediate forms as the nucleophile attacks as the leaving group departs.
parts.working: B1 concerted one-step mechanism, no intermediate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an experiment on the reaction RX + Y⁻ → product, three rate experiments were carried out at 25 °C.
Experiment 1: [RX] 0.10, [Y⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³; rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [RX] 0.20, [Y⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³; rate 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [RX] 0.10, [Y⁻] 0.30 mol dm⁻³; rate 6.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Deduce the orders and calculate the rate constant k with units.
parts.answer: Order 1 with respect to RX and order 1 with respect to Y⁻; k = 0.20 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 doubling [RX] doubles rate → order 1; B1 tripling [Y⁻] triples rate → order 1; B1 k = rate/([RX][Y⁻]) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.20 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-chlorobutane is heated with ethanolic sodium hydroxide. Name the major alkene formed and state the rule that predicts it.
parts.answer: But-2-ene; the more substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product (Zaitsev's rule).
parts.working: B1 but-2-ene; B1 more substituted alkene forms as major product (Zaitsev).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1-chloropentane is heated with (i) aqueous NaOH (ii) NaOH dissolved in ethanol. Give the organic product in each case.
parts.answer: (i) pentan-1-ol; (ii) pent-1-ene
parts.working: B1 (i) substitution gives pentan-1-ol; B1 (ii) elimination gives pent-1-ene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction in part (a)(ii), including the other products.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ + Cl⁻ + H₂O
parts.working: B1 correct organic reactant and product (pent-1-ene); B1 Cl⁻ and H₂O as products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the elimination of HBr from 2-bromo-3-methylbutane using ethanolic NaOH. Name the major organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CHBrCH(CH₃)CH₃ + OH⁻ → CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₃ + Br⁻ + H₂O; major product 2-methylbut-2-ene
parts.working: B1 structure CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₃; B1 Br⁻, H₂O and organic product as products; B1 named 2-methylbut-2-ene (more substituted alkene, major).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (C₅H₁₁Br) is heated with ethanolic KOH. The alkene is formed in 62 % yield. Given that 6.04 g of the bromoalkane is used, calculate the mass of alkene obtained. [Mr: C₅H₁₁Br 150.9; C₅H₁₀ 70.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which product forms when 2-bromopropane is heated with ethanolic KOH?
A propan-1-ol
B propan-2-ol
C propene
D propanone
parts.answer: C propene
parts.working: Heating with ethanolic KOH causes elimination of HBr to give an alkene; propene is CH₃CH=CH₂. Propan-2-ol would come from substitution with aqueous KOH and propanone from oxidation, not from this reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bromoalkane C₆H₁₃Br gives only one alkene, 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, when heated with ethanolic KOH. Give the name and structure of the bromoalkane.
parts.answer: 1-bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane, BrCH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₃
parts.working: B1 1-bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane; B1 the only β-hydrogens are on the CH₂ next to CH₂Br, so only one alkene forms (BrCH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₃ → CH₂=CHC(CH₃)₃ + HBr).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethanol is used as the solvent, rather than water, when a halogenoalkane is heated with NaOH to make an alkene.
parts.answer: Ethanol is less polar than water, so OH⁻ is less solvated and acts more as a base (removing H⁺) than as a nucleophile; heating under these conditions favours elimination.
parts.working: B1 OH⁻ acts as a base (removes H⁺) rather than nucleophile; B1 ethanol is a less polar solvent / OH⁻ less solvated; B1 heating favours elimination; HBr formed is neutralised by the excess base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Heating (CH₃)₃CBr with ethanolic KOH gives 2-methylpropene as the main product. Propose why substitution (SN2) is negligible for this tertiary halide.
parts.answer: Tertiary halide: the three alkyl groups block backside attack by OH⁻, so SN2 is very slow; the C–Br bond is also easily broken, and OH⁻ acts as a base to remove a proton from a methyl group (elimination).
parts.working: B1 steric hindrance blocks SN2 backside attack; B1 OH⁻ acts as a base; B1 proton removed from adjacent CH₃ giving C=C (elimination) favoured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name all the alkenes, including stereoisomers, formed by elimination of HBr from 2-bromopentane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₂CH₃, using ethanolic KOH. State which one is the major product.
parts.answer: pent-1-ene (minor); (E)-pent-2-ene (major); (Z)-pent-2-ene (minor)
parts.working: B1 pent-1-ene; B1 (E)-pent-2-ene and (Z)-pent-2-ene; B1 (E) is major (more stable, Zaitsev, trans arrangement less steric strain).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 10.0 g of 2-chlorobutane is heated with ethanolic NaOH and 4.20 g of but-2-ene is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield of but-2-ene. [Mr: C₄H₉Cl 92.5; C₄H₈ 56.0]
parts.working: M1 moles of 2-chlorobutane = 10.0/92.5 = 0.1081 mol; M1 theoretical mass = 0.1081 × 56.0 = 6.05 g; A1 4.20/6.05 × 100 = 69.4 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is stronger than the C–Cl bond in chloroethane.
parts.answer: A lone pair on Cl overlaps with the π-electron system of the ring, so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is shorter and stronger.
parts.working: B1 lone pair on Cl delocalised into the benzene ring (p-orbital overlap); B1 partial double bond character, shorter and stronger C–Cl bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions for the substitution of benzene by chlorine to form chlorobenzene.
parts.answer: Cl₂ with a halogen carrier catalyst such as AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) at room temperature in the dark (no UV light).
parts.working: B1 Cl₂ with AlCl₃ / FeCl₃ catalyst; B1 room temperature, in the dark (not UV, which would give side-chain reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, does not hydrolyse readily with aqueous NaOH, unlike chloroethane. Explain why.
parts.answer: The C–Cl carbon is sp² hybridised and the C–Cl bond has partial double bond character from delocalisation of a chlorine lone pair; the bond is strong, and the π electron density of the C=C repels the incoming OH⁻.
parts.working: B1 C–Cl in chloroethene has partial double bond character / lone pair delocalisation; B1 stronger C–Cl bond, harder to break; B1 electron-rich C=C repels nucleophile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of aluminium chloride. Show how AlCl₃ generates the electrophile, giving an equation.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻
parts.working: B1 AlCl₃ polarises / accepts a pair of electrons from Cl₂; B1 equation Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ (Cl⁺ is the electrophile).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why chlorobenzene is much less reactive than 1-chloropropane towards nucleophilic substitution by NaOH(aq).
parts.answer: The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is stronger (partial double bond character); the phenyl cation that would form in SN1 is unstable (not stabilised by alkyl groups), and ring electron density repels the nucleophile.
parts.working: B1 stronger C–Cl bond due to delocalisation of lone pair into ring; B1 SN1 carbocation (phenyl cation) too unstable / SN2 repelled by π electrons of ring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ring C–Cl bond is not affected when 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene is heated with NaOH(aq) under normal conditions, but the side-chain C–Cl of (chloromethyl)benzene is hydrolysed easily.
parts.answer: In (chloromethyl)benzene the Cl is on an sp³ carbon, a normal halogenoalkane, so it is hydrolysed by SN1/SN2; in the ring the Cl is attached to sp² carbon with delocalisation, so it is unreactive.
parts.working: B1 side chain C–Cl is on sp³ carbon (halogenoalkane-type); B1 ring C–Cl is on sp² carbon with lone pair delocalisation; B1 ring C–Cl strong and unreactive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene and benzene both contain π electrons and both react with chlorine. Ethene reacts with Cl₂ at room temperature without a catalyst by addition, whereas benzene needs AlCl₃ and gives a substitution product. Name the product from ethene and explain the difference in terms of the π electrons of the two molecules.
parts.answer: Ethene gives 1,2-dichloroethane by addition. The C=C π bond is localised and reacts directly with Cl₂. In benzene the π electrons are delocalised over the ring, which makes the ring very stable, so it does not react with Cl₂ alone; AlCl₃ produces the stronger electrophile Cl⁺, and substitution keeps the delocalised ring intact, whereas addition would destroy it.
parts.working: B1 product from ethene is 1,2-dichloroethane (addition); B1 ethene's localised C=C π bond is reactive, benzene's delocalised π system is more stable; B1 AlCl₃ is needed to form the electrophile Cl⁺ for benzene; B1 substitution keeps the aromatic ring (delocalisation) whereas addition would break it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 g of benzene (Mr 78.0) is monochlorinated with chlorine using AlCl₃ as catalyst, so that only chlorobenzene forms. 26.5 g of chlorobenzene (Mr 112.5) is isolated. Calculate the percentage yield.
parts.working: M1 moles of benzene = 25.0/78.0 = 0.3205 mol; M1 theoretical mass of chlorobenzene = 0.3205 × 112.5 = 36.06 g; A1 26.5/36.06 × 100 = 73.5 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of electrophilic substitution in the chlorination of benzene, from the attack of Cl⁺ to the regeneration of the aromatic ring. Mention the intermediate formed and the role of AlCl₄⁻.
parts.answer: Ring π electrons attack Cl⁺ forming a carbocation intermediate with the positive charge spread over the ring (delocalised, not an aromatic ring); AlCl₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the ring carbon, restoring the aromatic ring; HCl and AlCl₃ are regenerated.
parts.working: B1 π electrons of benzene attack Cl⁺ (electrophile); B1 carbocation intermediate with delocalised positive charge (arenium ion); B1 AlCl₄⁻ removes H⁺; B1 aromatic ring regenerated; B1 HCl and AlCl₃ released (catalyst regenerated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane with the attempted SN1 hydrolysis of chlorobenzene. State the cation each would need to form and explain why only the first undergoes SN1 readily.
parts.answer: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane forms (CH₃)₃C⁺, a tertiary carbocation stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups; chlorobenzene would need to form a phenyl cation, C₆H₅⁺, in which the vacant orbital is sp² in the ring plane and is not stabilised, so it is very unstable.
parts.working: B1 (CH₃)₃C⁺ tertiary carbocation; B1 alkyl groups stabilise the cation by electron donation; B1 phenyl cation C₆H₅⁺ needed for chlorobenzene; B1 phenyl cation very unstable (vacant sp² orbital in the plane, no stabilisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions needed to convert 1-iodobutane into (i) pentanenitrile (ii) butan-1-ol.
parts.answer: (i) KCN dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux; (ii) NaOH(aq) (dilute aqueous alkali), heated under reflux.
parts.working: B1 KCN in ethanol, reflux; B1 aqueous NaOH, heat under reflux.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1-bromobutane is heated in a sealed tube with an excess of ammonia dissolved in ethanol. Name the main organic product and explain why ammonia is used in excess.
parts.answer: Butylamine (butan-1-amine); excess ammonia makes it more likely that a bromoalkane molecule meets NH₃ rather than the amine product, reducing further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.
parts.working: B1 butan-1-amine (butylamine); B1 excess NH₃ makes the first substitution more likely; B1 reduces further reaction to form secondary/tertiary amines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give reagents and conditions for each step of a two-step synthesis of pentanoic acid from 1-bromobutane, naming the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux, giving pentanenitrile (CH₃(CH₂)₃CN). Step 2: dilute HCl(aq) (or dilute acid), heat under reflux, giving pentanoic acid (and NH₄Cl).
parts.working: B1 step 1 KCN, ethanol, reflux; B1 intermediate pentanenitrile; B1 step 2 dilute HCl(aq) with reflux gives pentanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent and conditions convert 1-iodopropane into propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂?
A KCN in ethanol, heated under reflux
B NaOH dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux
C excess NH₃ in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
D dilute HCl(aq), heated under reflux
parts.answer: C excess NH₃ in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
parts.working: Ammonia is a nucleophile; with excess NH₃ in a sealed tube, 1-iodopropane undergoes substitution to give propylamine. KCN would give a nitrile with one more carbon (butanenitrile), NaOH in ethanol causes elimination to propene, and dilute HCl does not replace the iodine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2.00 g of bromoethane is heated under reflux with excess dilute aqueous NaOH. Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that could be formed. [Mr: C₂H₅Br 108.9; C₂H₅OH 46.0]
parts.working: M1 moles of bromoethane = 2.00/108.9 = 0.01837 mol, so maximum ethanol = 0.01837 mol; A1 0.01837 × 46.0 = 0.845 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN is carried out in ethanol rather than water.
parts.answer: Halogenoalkanes are not soluble in water but dissolve in ethanol; ethanol dissolves both the organic halide and the ionic KCN, so the two can react together.
parts.working: B1 halogenoalkane is insoluble (or poorly soluble) in water; B1 ethanol is a common solvent for both the organic halide and the ionic KCN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound X, C₃H₇Br, reacts with KCN in ethanol to give Y, C₄H₇N. Y is a straight-chain nitrile. Compound X also reacts with NaOH(aq) to give Z, C₃H₈O. Identify X, Y and Z and write an equation for the reaction of Y to form a carboxylic acid.
parts.answer: X = 1-bromopropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Br; Y = butanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂CN; Z = propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH; hydrolysis: CH₃CH₂CH₂CN + 2H₂O + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + NH₄⁺
parts.working: B1 X = 1-bromopropane (straight chain); B1 Y = butanenitrile (CN adds one carbon); B1 Z = propan-1-ol; B1 hydrolysis equation to butanoic acid; B1 the balanced ammonium / H⁺ ion equation (or NH₄Cl).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a three-step route from ethanol to propanoic acid, giving the reagents and conditions for each step and naming the two intermediates. State how many carbon atoms the route adds to the chain and where they come from.
parts.answer: Step 1: PBr₃ (or NaBr with conc H₃PO₄, heated) gives bromoethane. Step 2: KCN dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux, gives propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN. Step 3: dilute HCl(aq) (or other dilute acid), heated under reflux, gives propanoic acid. One carbon is added, from the CN⁻ ion (the carbon of the nitrile group).
parts.working: B1 step 1 PBr₃ or NaBr/conc H₃PO₄ gives bromoethane; B1 step 2 KCN in ethanol under reflux, intermediate propanenitrile; B1 step 3 dilute acid under reflux gives propanoic acid; B1 one carbon added, from the CN group of CN⁻ (2 C to 3 C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemist made pentanenitrile from 5.00 g of 1-bromobutane using KCN in ethanol and isolated 2.27 g of pentanenitrile. Calculate the percentage yield. [Mr: C₄H₉Br 136.9; C₅H₉N 83.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions needed to convert 2-bromopropane into propan-2-amine.
parts.answer: Excess ammonia dissolved in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube (under pressure).
parts.working: B1 excess NH₃ (ammonia) in ethanol; B1 heat in a sealed tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the formation of propylamine from 1-bromopropane and excess ammonia, and name the salt formed as the by-product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br
parts.working: B1 propylamine as organic product; B1 NH₄Br (ammonium bromide) as by-product, with second NH₃ acting as base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the reaction CN⁻ + CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃ → CH₃CH(CN)CH₂CH₃ + Br⁻, identify the nucleophile and the leaving group.
parts.answer: Nucleophile: CN⁻ (lone pair on carbon); leaving group: Br⁻
parts.working: B1 CN⁻ is the nucleophile (donates a lone pair); B1 Br⁻ is the leaving group (departs with the pair from the C–Br bond).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the equation for the slow first step of the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂C(Br)CH₂CH₃, and explain why the rate of this step does not depend on the concentration of water or hydroxide ions.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₂C(Br)CH₂CH₃ → (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃ + Br⁻. Only the halogenoalkane is involved in this slow step, so water or OH⁻ does not appear in its rate.
parts.working: B1 equation with a carbocation (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃ and Br⁻ formed; B1 C–Br bond breaks heterolytically in the slow step; B1 the nucleophile (water or OH⁻) is involved only in the fast second step, so it is not in the rate equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of 1-iodopropane with ammonia. Use words to describe where each curly arrow starts and ends, and state whether the transition state is a single species.
parts.answer: NH₃ lone pair attacks the δ⁺ carbon from the side opposite the iodine; the arrow starts at the N lone pair and ends at the C; the C–I bond arrow starts at the C–I bond and ends on I (I⁻ leaves). Transition state is a single species with partial N–C and partial C–I bonds.
parts.working: B1 N lone pair attacks C (arrow from lone pair on N to C); B1 curly arrow from C–I bond to I; B1 backside attack (opposite side to I); B1 single transition state with partial bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 3-bromo-3-methylpentane by water. Include both steps and the curly arrows described in words.
parts.answer: Step 1: C–Br bond breaks heterolytically; the arrow starts at the C–Br bond and ends on Br (Br⁻ leaves), giving a planar tertiary carbocation. Step 2: a lone pair on the oxygen of H₂O attacks the cation; the arrow starts at the O lone pair and ends on C. Then a proton is lost from H₂O⁺ to give the alcohol.
parts.working: B1 step 1 C–Br breaks, arrow to Br, carbocation formed; B1 step 2 H₂O lone pair attacks C⁺, arrow to C; B1 proton lost (arrow from O–H to base); B1 slow first step / carbocation intermediate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, what is the intermediate?
A (CH₃)₃C–OH (the final alcohol product)
B (CH₃)₃C⁺
C (CH₃)₃C⁻
D CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺
parts.answer: B (CH₃)₃C⁺
parts.working: SN1 forms a planar tertiary carbocation as its intermediate: the slow first step gives (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻. (CH₃)₃C–OH is the final product, a carbanion (CH₃)₃C⁻ would be very unfavourable, and CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ is a primary cation that is not formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the SN2 reaction of bromomethane with hydroxide ions, and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻; methanol
parts.working: B1 CH₃OH and Br⁻ as products (OH⁻ attacks C, Br⁻ leaves); B1 named methanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why hydroxide ions attack 2-bromopropane by an SN2 mechanism more readily than water does.
parts.answer: OH⁻ carries a negative charge and has a higher electron density, so it is a stronger nucleophile than neutral H₂O, which has a lone pair but no charge.
parts.working: B1 OH⁻ is negatively charged / higher electron density; B1 stronger nucleophile than water, so faster SN2 reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the C–Br carbon in bromoethane is electrophilic (attracted to nucleophiles).
parts.answer: Br is more electronegative than C, so the C–Br bond is polar; the carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺) and is attracted to nucleophiles.
parts.working: B1 Br more electronegative than C, bond polarised; B1 carbon has δ⁺ charge, attracted to lone pairs / nucleophiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethylamine reacts with bromoethane to give diethylamine, (C₂H₅)₂NH. Describe the mechanism of this second substitution, identifying the nucleophile and the reason ethylamine is more nucleophilic than ammonia.
parts.answer: The lone pair on the N of ethylamine attacks the δ⁺ C of bromoethane by SN2 (curly arrow from N lone pair to C; C–Br bond breaks, Br⁻ leaves), then the (C₂H₅)₂NH₂⁺ ion loses H⁺ to give diethylamine. Ethylamine is more nucleophilic because the electron-donating ethyl group increases the electron density on N (positive inductive effect).
parts.working: B1 N lone pair of ethylamine is nucleophile; B1 SN2 with curly arrow from N to C and from C–Br to Br; B1 product protonated then H⁺ lost to give diethylamine; B1 ethyl group donates electrons to N, making it more nucleophilic than NH₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Optically active (R)-2-chloropentane is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH by an SN2 mechanism. Name the organic product, give its configuration, and explain the inversion of configuration in terms of the transition state.
parts.answer: (S)-pentan-2-ol. OH⁻ attacks from the side opposite the Cl; in the transition state the carbon has partial C–O and C–Cl bonds and the other three groups are flattened, like an umbrella turning inside out, so the spatial arrangement is inverted (Walden inversion). The priorities are unchanged, so the descriptor changes from R to S.
parts.working: B1 product (S)-pentan-2-ol (same priority order, so R becomes S); B1 OH⁻ attacks from the side opposite Cl (backside attack); B1 transition state with partial C–O and C–Cl bonds and the other three groups flattened; B1 inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) as the groups flip like an umbrella.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the transition state formed in the SN2 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with hydroxide ions, and explain why this reaction is negligibly slow compared with that of 1-bromopropane.
parts.answer: The transition state is five-coordinate: the carbon has a partial bond to O from OH⁻ and a partial bond to Br, the arrangement is trigonal bipyramidal and the overall charge is −1. The three bulky CH₃ groups block the backside approach of OH⁻, so this crowded transition state is too high in energy and SN2 is negligible; the reaction goes by SN1 instead.
parts.working: B1 five-coordinate carbon with partial C–O and partial C–Br bonds; B1 trigonal bipyramidal arrangement with overall charge −1; B1 three bulky CH₃ groups block the backside approach of OH⁻ (steric hindrance); B1 crowded transition state has high activation energy, so SN2 is negligible (SN1 instead).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when 1-chloropentane is (i) heated under reflux with aqueous NaOH (ii) heated under reflux with KCN dissolved in ethanol (iii) heated with excess NH₃ dissolved in ethanol in a sealed tube.
parts.answer: (i) pentan-1-ol; (ii) hexanenitrile; (iii) pentan-1-amine (pentylamine)
parts.working: B1 pentan-1-ol; B1 hexanenitrile; B1 pentan-1-amine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the organic product when 3-bromopentane is warmed with dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.answer: pentan-3-ol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the class of alcohol produced in part (a).
parts.answer: secondary
parts.working: B1 (carbon bearing OH is bonded to two carbon atoms).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is warmed with water, and name its class (primary, secondary or tertiary).
parts.answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol; tertiary
parts.working: B1 2-methylpropan-2-ol; B1 tertiary (C bearing OH bonded to three other carbon atoms).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2.42 g of 1-chloropropane (Mr 78.5) is heated under reflux with excess aqueous NaOH and 1.64 g of propan-1-ol (Mr 60.0) is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
parts.working: M1 moles of 1-chloropropane = 2.42/78.5 = 0.03083 mol; M1 theoretical mass of propan-1-ol = 0.03083 × 60.0 = 1.85 g; A1 1.64/1.85 × 100 = 88.7 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the organic product when 2-chloropropane is heated under reflux with aqueous NaOH?
A propan-1-ol
B propan-2-ol
C propene
D propanone
parts.answer: B propan-2-ol
parts.working: Aqueous NaOH causes nucleophilic substitution: OH⁻ replaces Cl on the same carbon, giving propan-2-ol. Propan-1-ol would need the Cl on carbon 1; propene is from ethanolic (elimination) conditions; propanone needs oxidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, with 1-bromopropane that forms the ammonium salt (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₂NH₂⁺Br⁻ as the product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + CH₃CH₂CH₂Br → (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₂NH₂⁺Br⁻
parts.working: B1 nitrogen lone pair of propylamine attacks the C–Br carbon and Br⁻ leaves; B1 correct formula of the salt (dipropylammonium bromide), which gives dipropylamine when treated with base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of 2-bromopropane with ethanolic KCN and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CHBrCH₃ + KCN → CH₃CH(CN)CH₃ + KBr; product 2-methylpropanenitrile.
parts.working: B1 correct equation with KBr; B1 2-methylpropanenitrile (CN on the central carbon).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 3.00 g of bromoethane is heated with excess ethanolic KCN and the product, propanenitrile, is isolated in 68 % yield. Calculate the mass of propanenitrile formed. [Mr: C₂H₅Br 108.9; C₃H₅N 55.0]
parts.working: M1 moles of bromoethane = 3.00/108.9 = 0.02755 mol; M1 theoretical mass = 0.02755 × 55.0 = 1.515 g; A1 1.515 × 0.68 = 1.03 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Excess ethanolic ammonia reacts with 1-bromobutane in a sealed tube. Explain why the product is a mixture of amines and a quaternary ammonium salt, and state how the use of excess ammonia affects the proportions.
parts.answer: Each amine produced is itself a nucleophile, so it reacts with more bromobutane: butylamine → dibutylamine → tributylamine → quaternary ammonium bromide. Excess ammonia makes it more likely that a bromoalkane meets NH₃, so butylamine forms mainly.
parts.working: B1 primary amine is a nucleophile and reacts further; B1 secondary and tertiary amines form; B1 quaternary ammonium salt formed by further alkylation; B1 excess NH₃ favours primary amine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound A, C₅H₁₁Br, is hydrolysed by warm aqueous NaOH to give compound B, C₅H₁₂O. B does not change the colour of hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Identify A and B, and calculate the Mr of B. [Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0]
parts.answer: A: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂C(Br)CH₂CH₃; B: 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃, Mr = 88.0
parts.working: B1 B is tertiary alcohol (not oxidised); B1 A is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; B1 B is 2-methylbutan-2-ol; B1 Mr = 5(12.0) + 12(1.0) + 16.0 = 88.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1-iodobutane, 1.50 g, is heated with excess ethanolic KCN. Calculate the theoretical mass of pentanenitrile that could be formed. [Mr: C₄H₉I 183.9; C₅H₉N 83.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when 2-bromobutane is heated with ethanolic KCN.
parts.answer: 2-methylbutanenitrile
parts.working: B1 CN attaches to C2 giving 2-methylbutanenitrile (CH₃CH(CN)CH₂CH₃).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of butan-1-ol with concentrated hydrobromic acid, HBr, heated, giving 1-bromobutane.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br + H₂O
parts.working: B1 1-bromobutane; B1 water as the other product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the product when propene reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, and name the type of reaction.
parts.answer: 2-bromopropane; electrophilic addition
parts.working: B1 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov addition); B1 electrophilic addition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine reacts with methane in the presence of ultraviolet light. Write an equation for the initiation step.
parts.answer: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
parts.working: B1 homolytic fission of Cl–Cl bond gives two chlorine radicals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent needed to convert ethanol into bromoethane, and the other product formed with PBr₃.
parts.answer: PBr₃; phosphonic acid H₃PO₃ (or phosphorus compound) is the other product.
parts.working: B1 phosphorus(III) bromide PBr₃ (or PBr₅ alternative); B1 H₃PO₃ formed as by-product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol is converted into bromoethane. Name the reagent and conditions needed and state why concentrated sulfuric acid is not used with sodium bromide.
parts.answer: NaBr with concentrated H₃PO₄, heated under reflux. H₂SO₄ oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂, so the bromoethane is contaminated with bromine.
parts.working: B1 NaBr with conc H₃PO₄ (heat under reflux); B1 H₃PO₄ is non-oxidising, whereas H₂SO₄ oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂; B1 Br₂ contaminates the product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-methylpropene reacts with hydrogen bromide. Name the major organic product and explain why it is the major product.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, Br to the carbon with fewer H, giving the more stable tertiary carbocation intermediate.
parts.working: B1 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; B1 Markovnikov rule; B1 tertiary carbocation intermediate more stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propane is chlorinated by Cl₂ in UV light. Give the names of the two monochloro products and explain why a mixture forms.
parts.answer: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane; the radical chain can remove any hydrogen; secondary and primary H atoms are both attacked, and multiple substitution also occurs.
parts.working: B1 1-chloropropane; B1 2-chloropropane; B1 free-radical substitution attacks different C–H bonds (and further substitution occurs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 12.5 g of butan-1-ol (Mr 74.0) is refluxed with excess conc HBr and 14.0 g of 1-bromobutane (Mr 136.9) is isolated. Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the crude bromoalkane made from butan-1-ol with NaBr and H₂SO₄ is shaken with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, and name one impurity that this removes.
parts.answer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate neutralises remaining acid (HBr / H₂SO₄) in the crude product, releasing CO₂ gas (so the funnel must be vented); the acid impurity is removed.
parts.working: B1 neutralises acid; B1 CO₂ gas produced (vent the funnel); B1 impurity acid (HBr / H₂SO₄) removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why conc H₃PO₄ rather than conc H₂SO₄ is used to make iodoalkanes from alcohols and sodium iodide, and why the product, if formed with H₂SO₄, is coloured.
parts.answer: H₂SO₄ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ (brown/purple), so the product is contaminated; H₃PO₄ is not strong enough to oxidise I⁻.
parts.working: B1 H₂SO₄ oxidises I⁻ to I₂; B1 I₂ dissolved gives brown/purple colour; B1 H₃PO₄ does not oxidise iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chloromethane, CH₃Cl, formed when 2.00 mol of chlorine reacts with excess methane in UV light, assuming only CH₃Cl and HCl are formed and the yield is 80 %. [Mr: CH₃Cl 50.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why PCl₅ must be kept dry when used to prepare chloroalkanes from alcohols, and why misty fumes are seen.
parts.answer: PCl₅ reacts with water (hydrolysis) and gives HCl gas, which forms misty fumes with moist air; water would also reduce the yield of the chloroalkane.
parts.working: B1 PCl₅ hydrolysed by water; B1 HCl gas produced; B1 HCl fumes form misty droplets with water vapour in air and water lowers yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the reagents SOCl₂ and PCl₅ for converting butan-2-ol into 2-chlorobutane. Explain why SOCl₂ is often preferred.
parts.answer: SOCl₂ gives the chloroalkane plus gaseous SO₂ and HCl, which escape from the mixture, so the product is easier to purify; PCl₅ is a solid and gives POCl₃ liquid by-product, which must be separated by distillation.
parts.working: B1 both give 2-chlorobutane from butan-2-ol; B1 SOCl₂ gives gaseous by-products (SO₂ and HCl); B1 PCl₅ gives a liquid by-product (POCl₃) that must be separated; B1 SOCl₂ therefore gives a purer product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each halogenoalkane as primary, secondary or tertiary: (i) 1-iodobutane (ii) 3-iodopentane (iii) 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.
parts.answer: (i) primary; (ii) secondary; (iii) tertiary
parts.working: B1 (i) C–I carbon bonded to one other carbon: primary; B1 (ii) bonded to two carbons: secondary; B1 (iii) bonded to three carbons: tertiary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two structural isomers of C₃H₇Cl and classify each.
parts.answer: 1-chloropropane (primary) and 2-chloropropane (secondary)
parts.working: B1 both correct names; B1 classified correctly (1-chloropropane primary, 2-chloropropane secondary).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four structural isomers of C₄H₉I.
parts.answer: 1-iodobutane, 2-iodobutane, 1-iodo-2-methylpropane, 2-iodo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: B1 1-iodobutane and 2-iodobutane; B1 1-iodo-2-methylpropane and 2-iodo-2-methylpropane (all four correct).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw the condensed structural formula of (i) a primary bromoalkane, C₃H₇Br (ii) a secondary bromoalkane, C₃H₇Br (iii) a tertiary bromoalkane, C₄H₉Br. Name each compound.
parts.answer: (i) CH₃CH₂CH₂Br, 1-bromopropane; (ii) CH₃CHBrCH₃, 2-bromopropane; (iii) (CH₃)₃CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: B1 (i) Br on an end carbon bonded to one other carbon: 1-bromopropane; B1 (ii) Br on a carbon bonded to two carbons: 2-bromopropane; B1 (iii) Br on a carbon bonded to three carbons: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound D, C₅H₁₁Cl, has Mr 106.5 and is tertiary. Identify D. [Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, Cl 35.5]
parts.answer: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂C(Cl)CH₂CH₃
parts.working: M1 Mr = 5(12.0) + 11(1.0) + 35.5 = 106.5 confirms formula; A1 only tertiary isomer is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (C bearing Cl bonded to three carbons).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bromoalkane has formula C₅H₁₁Br. Name the number of primary, secondary and tertiary bromoalkane isomers, giving the total.
parts.answer: Primary: 4; secondary: 3; tertiary: 1; total: 8
parts.working: B1 primary 4 (1-bromopentane, 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-bromo-3-methylbutane, 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane); B1 secondary 3; B1 tertiary 1 (2-bromo-2-methylbutane), total 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why 1-chlorobutane has a higher boiling point than 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.
parts.answer: Both are polar, but the branched 2-chloro-2-methylpropane has a smaller surface area, so weaker van der Waals forces (id-id) between molecules; 1-chlorobutane has stronger intermolecular forces.
parts.working: B1 1-chlorobutane has larger surface area / stronger van der Waals forces; B1 branching reduces surface contact in the tertiary isomer, so lower boiling point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrolysis of 2-chlorobutane, 1-chlorobutane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane by NaOH(aq) each gives an alcohol. Name each alcohol and classify it. State which alcohol is not oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: butan-2-ol (secondary); butan-1-ol (primary); 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary); 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised
parts.working: B1 three alcohols named correctly; B1 classification primary/secondary/tertiary; B1 tertiary alcohol not oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a tertiary halogenoalkane gives an alkene more readily than a primary one when heated with ethanolic NaOH.
parts.answer: Tertiary halogenoalkanes ionise to a stable tertiary carbocation, and the tertiary structure gives more β-hydrogens; OH⁻ can act as a base removing a proton, so elimination competes well and forms alkenes.
parts.working: B1 tertiary carbocation stable / easily formed; B1 more β-hydrogens available; B1 OH⁻ acts as base and elimination favoured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of structural isomers of C₃H₆Cl₂ and name each.
parts.answer: 4: 1,1-dichloropropane; 1,2-dichloropropane; 1,3-dichloropropane; 2,2-dichloropropane
parts.working: B1 1,1- and 1,2-dichloropropane; B1 1,3- and 2,2-dichloropropane; B1 total count 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'primary halogenoalkane' and explain why no primary halogenoalkane can be chiral at the carbon bearing the halogen.
parts.answer: A primary halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon bonded to one other carbon (and two hydrogens). That carbon has two identical H atoms, so it cannot have four different groups, and cannot be a chiral centre.
parts.working: B1 halogen on carbon bonded to one other C; B1 carbon has two H atoms; B1 two identical groups, so not chiral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound E is a dihalogenoalkane, C₃H₆Br₂, in which both bromines are on the same carbon atom. Name E and explain how its classification differs from that of 1,2-dibromopropane.
parts.answer: E is 1,1-dibromopropane (both Br on C1); it is a primary dihalide because the Br-bearing carbon is bonded to only one other carbon; 1,2-dibromopropane has one Br on a secondary carbon.
parts.working: B1 1,1-dibromopropane; B1 C1 bonded to one other carbon (primary); B1 1,2-dibromopropane has a secondary C–Br.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A halogenoalkane F has the formula C₄H₉Cl and is secondary. Identify F, and explain why it is more reactive than a primary chloroalkane in SN1 but less reactive than a tertiary one.
parts.answer: F is 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH₃. A secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation (two alkyl groups donate electrons), so SN1 is faster than for primary; it is less stable than tertiary (only two electron-donating groups).
parts.working: B1 2-chlorobutane; B1 secondary cation stabilised by two alkyl groups, more stable than primary; B1 less stable than tertiary cation with three alkyl groups; B1 correct SN1 reasoning.

parts.label: a
