parts.text: Identify the isomer of C₄H₉Br, with a chiral centre, that is secondary and is hydrolysed to a secondary alcohol (butan-2-ol). Explain why the two enantiomers of the alcohol cannot be separated by simple distillation.
parts.answer: 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃; enantiomers have identical physical properties (boiling points, density), so simple distillation cannot separate them.
parts.working: B1 2-bromobutane (C2 chiral, four different groups); B1 enantiomers have identical boiling points and physical properties; B1 separation needs chiral method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of 1-bromopropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Br. For each peak give the approximate δ value, the relative number of hydrogen atoms and the splitting pattern.
parts.answer: δ ≈ 1.0, 3H, triplet (CH₃); δ ≈ 1.9, 2H, sextet (middle CH₂); δ ≈ 3.4, 2H, triplet (CH₂Br)
parts.working: B1 three peaks; B1 CH₃ at δ ~1.0, 3H, triplet (2 neighbouring H); B1 middle CH₂ at δ ~1.9, sextet (5 neighbours); B1 CH₂Br at δ ~3.4, 2H, triplet (2 neighbours).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound X, C₄H₁₀O, gives a ¹H NMR spectrum with two peaks: δ 1.2 (6H, triplet) and δ 3.4 (4H, quartet). Identify X and explain why only two peaks are seen although the molecule has ten hydrogen atoms.
parts.answer: X is diethyl ether, CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃. Both ethyl groups are identical, so the six CH₃ hydrogens are equivalent, as are the four CH₂ hydrogens. Each CH₃ is split by the two neighbouring CH₂ hydrogens (triplet); each CH₂ by the three CH₃ hydrogens (quartet).
parts.working: B1 identifies diethyl ether; B1 two equivalent ethyl groups give two environments; B1 triplet/quartet from n+1 rule (2 neighbours and 3 neighbours); B1 number of H in each peak consistent (6:4 = 3:2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound with formula C₂H₄Cl₂ gives a ¹H NMR spectrum with two peaks: δ 2.1 (doublet, 3H) and δ 5.9 (quartet, 1H). Identify the compound and explain each splitting pattern.
parts.answer: 1,1-dichloroethane, CH₃CHCl₂. The CH₃ (3H) is a doublet because it is next to one CH hydrogen; the CHCl₂ (1H) is a quartet because it is next to three CH₃ hydrogens. Its δ is high because the two Cl atoms are electron-withdrawing.
parts.working: B1 1,1-dichloroethane identified; B1 CH₃ doublet (1 neighbour); B1 CH quartet (3 neighbours); B1 high δ for CHCl₂ due to two electronegative Cl atoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound Y, C₄H₁₀O, gives these ¹H NMR peaks: δ 1.2 (singlet, 9H) and δ 2.1 (singlet, 1H). The peak at δ 2.1 disappears when D₂O is shaken with the sample. Identify Y and explain (i) why both peaks are singlets (ii) why the δ 2.1 peak disappears.
parts.answer: Y is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH. (i) The nine CH₃ hydrogens are equivalent and attached to a carbon with no hydrogens, so there are no neighbouring H atoms to split them; the OH hydrogen is also not split. (ii) The OH hydrogen exchanges with deuterium (OH → OD) in D₂O, so this peak disappears.
parts.working: B1 2-methylpropan-2-ol; B1 nine equivalent CH₃ H atoms, no adjacent H, singlet; B1 OH singlet with no adjacent H; B1 OH exchanges with D₂O to give OD, which is not seen in ¹H NMR; B1 integration 9:1 consistent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, gives two molecular ion peaks. State their m/e values, their relative heights, and explain the ratio.
parts.answer: m/e 108 and 110, roughly equal heights (1:1)
parts.working: B1 m/e 108 (C₂H₅⁷⁹Br⁺) and 110 (C₂H₅⁸¹Br⁺); B1 relative heights about 1:1; B1 because ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br occur in almost equal abundance (about 50 % each).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound would show molecular ion peaks at M and M+2 in a ratio of about 3 : 1?
A CH₂Br₂
B CH₃Cl
C CH₃Br
D CH₃I
parts.answer: B CH₃Cl
parts.working: Chlorine has isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in about 3 : 1 ratio, so a single chlorine gives M and M+2 in 3 : 1. Bromine (1 : 1) gives the pattern for CH₃Br and CH₂Br₂ (which gives 1 : 2 : 1 at three peaks); iodine is monoisotopic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The molecular ion peak of a hydrocarbon is at m/e 78 with relative height 100, and its M+1 peak has relative height 6.6. Assume the M+1 peak is due only to ¹³C (about 1.1 % of the M+ height per carbon atom). Deduce the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.
parts.answer: 6 carbon atoms
parts.working: M1 6.6 / 1.1 = 6.0; A1 6 carbon atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon in part (a).
parts.answer: C₆H₆
parts.working: M1 6 C = 72, so the remaining 78 − 72 = 6 hydrogens: C₆H₆.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the mass spectrum of propanone, CH₃COCH₃, which ion is responsible for the peak at m/e 43?
A CH₃CO⁺
B CH₃⁺
C C₃H₇O⁺
D CO⁺
parts.answer: A CH₃CO⁺
parts.working: Propanone has Mr 58. Cleavage of a C–C bond next to the C=O gives the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺ (m/e 43) and a neutral CH₃ radical. CH₃⁺ would be m/e 15; C₃H₇O⁺ is m/e 59; CO⁺ is m/e 28.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tertiary alcohols often show a very weak molecular ion peak. Explain why, and name the ion usually responsible for the strong peak at M – 15 in the mass spectrum of 2-methylpropan-2-ol (Mr 74).
parts.answer: The tertiary structure breaks very readily to give a stable ion; the molecular ion is therefore weak. The strong peak at m/e 59 is (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, formed by loss of a CH₃ radical.
parts.working: B1 molecular ion is unstable and fragments readily; B1 fragmentation gives a stable ion / tertiary structure; B1 m/e 59, (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, formed by loss of CH₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromochloromethane, CH₂BrCl, gives a cluster of molecular ion peaks. Give the m/e values of the three different molecular ion peaks and their relative heights. [Ar: C 12, H 1, Cl 35 or 37, Br 79 or 81]
parts.answer: m/e 128, 130 and 132, with relative heights 3 : 4 : 1
parts.working: M1 128 = ⁷⁹Br³⁵Cl; 130 = ⁸¹Br³⁵Cl + ⁷⁹Br³⁷Cl; 132 = ⁸¹Br³⁷Cl; M1 relative intensities 1 × 3 : (1 × 3 + 1 × 1) : 1 × 1; A1 3 : 4 : 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound with Mr 60 gives a mass spectrum with its base peak at m/e 45 and a smaller peak at m/e 31. It reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen, and it is oxidised by hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to a ketone. Identify the compound by considering the ions responsible for each peak.
parts.answer: Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH. The base peak at m/e 45 is CH₃CHOH⁺ formed by loss of a CH₃ radical; m/e 31 is CH₂OH⁺ (less favoured here). Propan-1-ol would give a base peak at m/e 31 (CH₂OH⁺), not 45.
parts.working: B1 Mr 60 is C₃H₈O; B1 m/e 45 = CH₃CHOH⁺ from loss of CH₃ (characteristic of 2-alcohol); B1 m/e 31 = CH₂OH⁺; B1 propan-2-ol, not propan-1-ol, since propan-1-ol base peak is m/e 31.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boron has two isotopes, ¹⁰B (19.9 %) and ¹¹B (80.1 %). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the wavenumber range, in cm⁻¹, of the N–H stretch in a primary amine, and state how many absorptions a primary amine usually shows in this region.
parts.answer: 3300–3500 cm⁻¹; two absorptions (symmetric and asymmetric N–H stretches)
parts.working: B1 3300–3500 cm⁻¹; B1 two (medium) peaks for –NH₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butanenitrile shows a sharp absorption at about 2250 cm⁻¹. State the bond responsible and give the usual wavenumber range for it.
parts.answer: C≡N (nitrile); 2200–2260 cm⁻¹
parts.working: B1 C≡N triple bond; B1 range 2200–2260 cm⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the O–H absorption of a carboxylic acid is much broader than that of an alcohol.
parts.answer: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, so O–H bonds have a wide range of strengths and environments, giving a very broad band from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonding (dimers) in carboxylic acids; B1 wide range of O–H environments gives a broad band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal and propanone both contain C=O. State one absorption present in the IR spectrum of propanal but absent from propanone, and give its wavenumber range.
parts.answer: Aldehyde C–H stretch: weak absorption at about 2700–2900 cm⁻¹
parts.working: B1 C–H (aldehyde) stretch; B1 2700–2900 cm⁻¹ (weak).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the IR spectrum would show that ethanoic acid has been converted into ethyl ethanoate by reaction with ethanol.
parts.answer: The broad O–H band at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ of the acid disappears; the C=O band moves from about 1700–1725 cm⁻¹ (acid) to about 1735–1750 cm⁻¹ (ester); a C–O band at about 1000–1300 cm⁻¹ is present in the ester.
parts.working: B1 broad O–H (2500–3300 cm⁻¹) of the acid disappears; B1 C=O shifts from about 1700–1725 (acid) to about 1735–1750 (ester); B1 C–O absorption (1000–1300 cm⁻¹) present in the ester.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which absorption is present in the IR spectrum of ethanoic acid but absent from ethyl ethanoate?
A C=O at about 1700–1750 cm⁻¹
B C–H at about 2850–3000 cm⁻¹
C broad O–H at about 2500–3300 cm⁻¹
D C–O at about 1000–1300 cm⁻¹
parts.answer: C broad O–H at about 2500–3300 cm⁻¹
parts.working: Ethyl ethanoate is an ester with no O–H group, so it lacks the very broad O–H absorption. Both compounds have C=O, C–H and C–O bonds, so A, B and D are present in both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexanol is dehydrated to cyclohexene. Describe two changes in the IR spectrum that show the reaction has occurred.
parts.answer: Loss of the broad O–H absorption at about 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; appearance of a C=C absorption at about 1620–1680 cm⁻¹ (and =C–H stretch just above 3000 cm⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 broad O–H band (3200–3600) disappears; B1 C=C absorption (1620–1680) appears; B1 =C–H stretch above 3000 cm⁻¹ (accept).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound S, C₄H₈O, shows a strong absorption at about 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption above 2500 cm⁻¹. Name two compounds that fit this data, and suggest a second technique that could tell them apart.
parts.answer: Butanone (CH₃COCH₂CH₃) and butanal (CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO) both have C=O; a second technique such as ¹H NMR (aldehyde H at δ ~9–10, a singlet/triplet) or ¹³C NMR (aldehyde C at δ ~200 vs ketone C at δ ~210) would distinguish them.
parts.working: B1 butanone; B1 butanal; B1 IR cannot easily distinguish aldehyde and ketone C=O; B1 suggest ¹H NMR (δ 9–10 aldehyde H) or ¹³C NMR / mass spectrometry as the second technique.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the C=O absorption of an amide (about 1640–1690 cm⁻¹) occurs at a lower wavenumber than that of an ester (about 1735–1750 cm⁻¹).
parts.answer: In an amide the lone pair on N is delocalised into the C=O (resonance), giving the C=O more single-bond character, so the bond is weaker and absorbs at lower wavenumber. In an ester the O lone pair is less strongly delocalised.
parts.working: B1 lone pair on N delocalises into C=O (resonance); B1 gives C=O partial single-bond character; B1 weaker bond, lower frequency / wavenumber.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound T, C₂H₅NO, shows two N–H absorptions at about 3180 and 3350 cm⁻¹ and a strong C=O absorption at about 1650 cm⁻¹. Identify the functional group and suggest T. Explain why two N–H absorptions are seen.
parts.answer: T is ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂ (a primary amide). Two N–H stretches arise from the two N–H bonds of –NH₂ (symmetric and asymmetric), the usual pattern for a primary amide.
parts.working: B1 primary amide; B1 ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂) identified; B1 two N–H bonds on the –NH₂ give two stretches (symmetric and asymmetric); B1 strong C=O at ~1650 is amide (lower wavenumber than ester).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a TLC experiment the solvent front travels 7.0 cm from the baseline and a spot of an amino acid travels 4.2 cm. Calculate the Rf value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the solvent level in a TLC tank must be kept below the baseline of the plate, and why the tank is covered during development.
parts.answer: If the solvent is above the baseline, the spots dissolve into the solvent pool and are lost. A covered tank is saturated with solvent vapour, so the solvent front rises evenly and Rf values are reproducible.
parts.working: B1 spots would dissolve into the solvent and be lost if the solvent is above the baseline; B1 covered tank is saturated with solvent vapour, so the front runs evenly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two amino acids are spotted on a TLC plate. After the run, the solvent front is 9.0 cm from the baseline; amino acid X travels 3.6 cm and amino acid Y travels 5.4 cm. Calculate the Rf value of each and state which is more soluble in the mobile phase.
parts.answer: X: Rf = 0.40; Y: Rf = 0.60; Y is more soluble in the mobile phase (moves further)
parts.working: M1 Rf(X) = 3.6/9.0 = 0.40; M1 Rf(Y) = 5.4/9.0 = 0.60; A1 Y travels further, so is more soluble in (and less retained by) the mobile phase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An unknown alcohol is analysed by gas chromatography under the same conditions as a sample of pure butan-1-ol, which has a retention time of 4.2 min. The unknown has a retention time of 4.2 min. Suggest what can and cannot be concluded.
parts.answer: The unknown is probably butan-1-ol, but this is not certain: other compounds could have the same retention time. Confirmation needs co-injection (spiking) or a second technique such as mass spectrometry.
parts.working: B1 probably butan-1-ol (same retention time under identical conditions); B1 cannot be certain because other compounds may coincide; B1 confirm by co-injection or GC–MS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A GC analysis of a fragrance mixture gives these peak areas (arbitrary units), with equal response for each compound: linalool 3.0, geraniol 5.0, limonene 2.0 and citronellol 2.0. Calculate the percentage of each compound in the mixture.
parts.answer: linalool 25.0 %; geraniol 41.7 %; limonene 16.7 %; citronellol 16.7 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, in gas chromatography, a compound with a higher boiling point usually has a longer retention time.
parts.answer: A compound with a higher boiling point has stronger intermolecular forces with the stationary phase and spends more time dissolved in it, so it is retained longer and elutes later.
parts.working: B1 higher boiling point = stronger intermolecular forces / less volatile; B1 more time in the stationary phase so longer retention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A TLC plate has a reference spot of a known food dye, a spot of the sample, and a spot of both mixed (co-spotted) at the same place. After development, the sample spot and the reference spot run to the same Rf value. Explain what can and cannot be concluded.
parts.answer: The sample probably contains the reference dye, because it moves the same distance; but another dye could have the same Rf in that solvent, so confirmation with a second solvent is needed. The co-spot shows a single spot if they are the same substance.
parts.working: B1 same Rf suggests same substance; B1 different substances can share an Rf in one solvent; B1 co-spot gives a single spot only if the substances are identical, so a second solvent or co-spot check is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student reports Rf = 0.45 for a dye from a TLC run in a solvent of unknown composition. Explain why the value can only be compared with another Rf if the solvent, the plate and the temperature are the same, and explain why Rf can never be greater than 1.0.
parts.answer: Rf depends on the balance between solubility in the mobile phase and adsorption on the stationary phase; changing the solvent, plate or temperature changes this balance, so only results obtained under identical conditions can be compared. Rf is the distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent front, and a spot cannot travel further than the front, so Rf ≤ 1.0.
parts.working: B1 Rf depends on the balance between solubility in the mobile phase and adsorption to the stationary phase; B1 changing solvent, plate or temperature changes this balance; B1 results are comparable only under identical conditions; B1 a spot cannot move further than the solvent front, so Rf ≤ 1.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) combines the two techniques, and what the mass spectrometer provides for each peak that the GC alone does not.
parts.answer: The GC separates components by retention time; each component passes into the mass spectrometer as it elutes. The MS gives a mass spectrum for each peak, showing the molecular ion and fragment ions, which identifies the compound (and confirms its purity).
parts.working: B1 GC separates the mixture; B1 each separated component enters the MS as it elutes; B1 MS gives a mass spectrum (M+ and fragments) for each peak; B1 identifies compound from Mr / fragmentation, beyond retention time alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A GC analysis of a mixture uses a response correction. Compound A gives a peak area of 60 units and compound B gives a peak area of 40 units. The relative response factor of B is 1.25 (corrected amount = area ÷ response factor, with A taken as 1.00). Calculate the percentage of A in the mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 4 peaks
parts.working: B1 4 peaks; B1 four different carbon environments (C=O, CH₂, CH₃ next to C=O, CH₃ of ethyl group).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, and give the approximate δ range for the carbon bonded to Cl.
parts.answer: 4 peaks; δ about 50–70 ppm for C–Cl
parts.working: B1 4 peaks (four different carbons); B1 C–Cl at δ ~50–70.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate ¹³C chemical shift ranges (δ, ppm) for: (i) a ketone C=O (ii) an ester or carboxylic acid C=O (iii) an aromatic ring carbon.
parts.answer: (i) about 200–220; (ii) about 160–180; (iii) about 110–150
parts.working: B1 ketone C=O 200–220; B1 ester/acid C=O 160–180; B1 aromatic C 110–150.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of (i) 1,2-dichlorobenzene (ii) 1,4-dichlorobenzene. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: (i) 3 peaks; (ii) 2 peaks
parts.working: B1 (i) 3 peaks: a mirror plane through the midpoint of the C1–C2 bond gives equivalent pairs C1/C2, C3/C6 and C4/C5; B1 (ii) 2 peaks: C1/C4 are equivalent and the four CH carbons C2, C3, C5 and C6 are all equivalent by symmetry; B1 both answers from symmetry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene gives a single peak in its ¹³C NMR spectrum at about δ 128. Explain why.
parts.answer: All six carbon atoms are in identical environments because of the symmetry of the ring and the delocalised π system, so they give one peak.
parts.working: B1 all six carbon atoms are equivalent; B1 symmetry of the ring (delocalised, identical environments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃, and name the carbon environments that give them.
parts.answer: 4 peaks
parts.working: B1 4 peaks; B1 two equivalent CH₃ on C2, quaternary C2, CH₂, and the CH₃ of the ethyl group (four environments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pent-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃, and the number of peaks in the ¹³C spectrum of pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: pent-1-ene: 5 peaks; pentan-3-one: 3 peaks
parts.working: B1 pent-1-ene has five non-equivalent carbons (5 peaks); B1 pentan-3-one has three environments (C=O; two equivalent CH₂; two equivalent CH₃), giving 3 peaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, and name the carbon environments.
parts.answer: 6 peaks
parts.working: B1 6 peaks; B1 CH₃, CH₂, ipso C, ortho pair, meta pair and para carbon (six environments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound V, C₄H₁₀O, gives three ¹³C NMR peaks at δ 19 (2 C), δ 30 (1 C) and δ 68 (1 C). Identify V and assign each peak.
parts.answer: V is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH. δ 19: the two equivalent CH₃ carbons; δ 30: the CH carbon; δ 68: the CH₂OH carbon (bonded to O, deshielded).
parts.working: B1 2-methylpropan-1-ol; B1 δ 19 two equivalent CH₃; B1 δ 30 CH; B1 δ 68 CH₂ bonded to O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of cyclohexanone, and give the approximate δ of its carbonyl carbon. Explain why the two carbons next to C=O give one peak.
parts.answer: 4 peaks; C=O at about δ 210
parts.working: B1 4 peaks; B1 C=O δ ~205–215 (ketone); B1 the two α-carbons are equivalent by the ring's symmetry (mirror plane through C=O and C4), so they give one peak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the relative heights of peaks in a ¹³C NMR spectrum are not used to count the carbon atoms in the way that they are in ¹H NMR.
parts.answer: In routine ¹³C NMR spectra the signals are proton-decoupled and the intensity of a signal depends on the number of attached H atoms and relaxation times, not reliably on the number of carbons; so peak heights are not a reliable measure of the number of C atoms.
parts.working: B1 spectra are proton-decoupled, so each carbon gives a single peak regardless of H count; B1 peak intensity is not proportional to carbon number (relaxation, nuclear Overhauser effects); B1 so the number of peaks, not height, gives the environments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student spots too much of a sample onto a TLC plate and the spot runs as a long smear rather than a compact spot. Suggest the cause and how the result can be improved.
parts.answer: The plate is overloaded, so the sample dissolves into the solvent in a wide band. Use a more dilute solution and apply a smaller spot, drying between applications.
parts.working: B1 too much sample / overloading causes streaking; B1 dilute the sample or apply a smaller spot (and let it dry between spots).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectra of (i) propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO (ii) 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄.
parts.answer: (i) 3 peaks; (ii) 2 peaks
parts.working: B1 propanal: three environments (CHO, CH₂, CH₃); B1 2,2-dimethylpropane: the four CH₃ are equivalent and the central C is a different environment, giving 2 peaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two conditions a molecule must meet to show cis/trans (E/Z) isomerism.
parts.answer: (1) Restricted rotation about a C=C double bond (or within a ring); (2) each carbon atom of the restricted bond carries two different groups.
parts.working: 1 mark for each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, does not show cis/trans isomerism.
parts.answer: One carbon of the C=C bond carries two identical CH₃ groups, so no two different arrangements of groups are possible.
parts.working: 1 mark: two identical groups on one carbon of the C=C bond; 1 mark: so only one arrangement exists (no cis/trans isomers).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound has a pair of geometric (cis/trans) isomers?
A (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃
B CH₂=CCl₂
C CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂
D CHBr=CHBr
parts.answer: D CHBr=CHBr
parts.working: D: each carbon of the C=C bond carries one H and one Br, so cis and trans forms exist. A has two identical CH₃ groups on one carbon; B has two Cl atoms on one carbon; C has two H atoms on C1.

stem: Three compounds have molecular formula C₄H₈: but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the compound that shows cis/trans isomerism.
parts.answer: But-2-ene
parts.working: But-1-ene has two H atoms on C1; 2-methylpropene has two CH₃ groups on C2; only but-2-ene has two different groups on each carbon of the C=C bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the arrangement of the two CH₃ groups in the trans isomer of this compound.
parts.answer: The two CH₃ groups are on opposite sides of the C=C bond (one above and one below the plane of the double bond).
parts.working: 1 mark: CH₃ groups on opposite sides; 1 mark: described relative to the plane of the C=C bond (or equivalent).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why 1-chloropropene, CH₃CH=CHCl, shows cis/trans isomerism.
parts.answer: Restricted rotation about the C=C bond; C1 carries H and Cl, and C2 carries H and CH₃, so each carbon has two different groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: restricted rotation about C=C; 1 mark: each carbon of the C=C bond has two different groups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the isomer in which the Cl and the CH₃ group are on the same side of the C=C bond.
parts.answer: cis-1-chloropropene (Z-1-chloroprop-1-ene)
parts.working: Same side = cis = Z, because Cl has higher priority than H on C1 and CH₃ has higher priority than H on C2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a ring can show cis/trans isomerism, using 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (ring of three carbon atoms, one CH₃ on each of two adjacent ring carbons) as the example.
parts.answer: The ring bonds cannot rotate freely, so the two CH₃ groups can lie on the same face of the ring (cis) or on opposite faces (trans).
parts.working: 1 mark: restricted rotation in the ring; 1 mark: CH₃ groups on the same or opposite faces of the ring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane.
parts.answer: C₅H₁₀
parts.working: Ring: 3 C and 4 H (one CH₂ and two CH); two CH₃ groups: 2 C and 6 H; total C₅H₁₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cis isomer of but-2-ene has a slightly higher boiling point than the trans isomer. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why.
parts.answer: The cis isomer has a permanent dipole because its bond dipoles do not cancel, so it has permanent dipole–dipole forces in addition to London forces; the trans isomer has bond dipoles that cancel, so only London forces.
parts.working: 1 mark: cis isomer has a net (permanent) dipole whereas trans does not; 1 mark: extra permanent dipole–dipole forces in cis need more energy to overcome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the difference in boiling points is small.
parts.answer: Both are small molecules with the same molecular formula, and London (dispersion) forces are the main intermolecular forces in both.
parts.working: 1 mark: London forces dominate in both isomers, and permanent dipoles are small.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexa-2,4-diene, CH₃CH=CH–CH=CHCH₃, has two C=C bonds. Explain why each C=C bond can show cis/trans isomerism.
parts.answer: Each C=C bond has restricted rotation, and each carbon of each C=C bond carries one H and one alkyl group (CH₃ or CH=), so each carbon has two different groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: restricted rotation at both C=C bonds; 1 mark: each carbon of each C=C has H and an alkyl group, which are different.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hexa-2,4-diene has three stereoisomers, not four. Explain why.
parts.answer: The stereoisomers are (2E,4E), (2Z,4Z) and (2E,4Z). The (2E,4Z) form is the same molecule as (2Z,4E), because the molecule is symmetrical and numbering from the other end swaps the descriptors.
parts.working: 1 mark: three distinct forms named; 1 mark: (2E,4Z) and (2Z,4E) are the same molecule because the chain is symmetrical.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many stereoisomers, counting cis/trans isomers, does pent-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, have?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
parts.answer: B 2
parts.working: Pent-2-ene has one C=C bond with two different groups on each carbon, giving E and Z forms; it has no chiral centre, so there are 2 stereoisomers. C and D would count a non-existent extra form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the systematic name of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: 2-methylpentane
parts.working: Longest chain has 5 carbons; methyl branch on C2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the systematic name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂Br.
parts.answer: 1-bromo-2-methylbutane
parts.working: Longest chain has 4 carbons, Br on C1 and CH₃ on C2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the systematic name of CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: pentan-3-one
parts.working: Five-carbon chain with the C=O on C3, which is the middle carbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound has the same molecular formula as pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃?
A pentanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO
B pentane, C₅H₁₂
C pentan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃
D 2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃
parts.answer: A pentanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO
parts.working: Pentan-2-one is C₅H₁₀O. Pentanal is also C₅H₁₀O. B and D are C₅H₁₂ and C is C₅H₁₂O, so they have different formulae.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three compounds have molecular formula C₃H₈O and one of them is an ether. Name the two alcohols with this formula.
parts.answer: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol
parts.working: 1 mark each: OH on C1 gives propan-1-ol; OH on C2 gives propan-2-ol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the ether with molecular formula C₃H₈O.
parts.answer: methoxyethane, CH₃–O–CH₂CH₃
parts.working: Ethers have a C–O–C linkage; this is the only ether with formula C₃H₈O.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many structural isomers with molecular formula C₃H₆O₂ are either carboxylic acids or esters?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
parts.answer: C 3
parts.working: Carboxylic acid: propanoic acid (1). Esters: methyl ethanoate and ethyl methanoate (2). Total 3. Option B misses one of the esters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the molecular formula of 3-methylpentane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₄
parts.working: Six carbons; saturated, so H = 2(6) + 2 = 14.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the name of one structural isomer of 3-methylpentane whose longest carbon chain has four carbon atoms.
parts.answer: 2,2-dimethylbutane (or 2,3-dimethylbutane)
parts.working: 1 mark: C₆H₁₄ isomer with a longest chain of four carbons; 1 mark: correct systematic name with two methyl branches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound X and compound Y both have molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. X reacts with sodium carbonate solution to give carbon dioxide. Name X.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
parts.working: Carboxylic acids release CO₂ with carbonates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Y is an ester made from methanol and methanoic acid. Name Y and state the type of isomerism shown by X and Y.
parts.answer: Y is methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃; X and Y are functional group isomers.
parts.working: 1 mark: methyl methanoate; 1 mark: functional group isomerism (different functional groups, same formula).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the systematic name of (CH₃)₂CHCH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH.
parts.answer: 3,4-dimethylpentan-1-ol
parts.working: 1 mark: longest chain containing the OH carbon has 5 carbons (pentan-1-ol); 1 mark: methyl groups on C3 and C4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify this alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Primary: the carbon bearing the OH group (CH₂OH) is bonded to only one other carbon.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct classification with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound M is 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO, which has molecular formula C₄H₈O. Name the ketone that is also C₄H₈O.
parts.answer: butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃
parts.working: The C=O sits within the chain (C2 of a four-carbon chain) in a ketone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why butanone and 2-methylpropanal are functional group isomers.
parts.answer: They have the same molecular formula (C₄H₈O) but different functional groups: butanone is a ketone (C=O inside the chain) and 2-methylpropanal is an aldehyde (–CHO at the end of the chain).
parts.working: 1 mark: same molecular formula; 1 mark: different functional groups (ketone and aldehyde).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two conditions a molecule must meet to show optical isomerism.
parts.answer: (1) It has a chiral centre (a carbon with four different groups attached); (2) the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable.
parts.working: 1 mark for each condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound is optically active?
A 2-chloropropane, (CH₃)₂CHCl
B 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃
C 1,1-dichloroethane, CH₃CHCl₂
D 1,2-dichloroethane, ClCH₂CH₂Cl
parts.answer: B 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃
parts.working: In B, C2 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups. A has two CH₃ groups on the carbon bearing Cl; C has two Cl atoms on one carbon; D has no carbon with four different groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-bromo-3-methylbutanoic acid is (CH₃)₂CH–CHBr–COOH. Identify its chiral centre.
parts.answer: C2 (the CHBr carbon)
parts.working: C2 carries H, Br, COOH and CH(CH₃)₂. C3 carries two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not chiral.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this acid can exist as two optical isomers.
parts.answer: It has one chiral centre, so the molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed.
parts.working: 1 mark: one chiral centre gives a non-superimposable mirror image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)COOH, is optically active. Identify the chiral centre and state how many optical isomers it has.
parts.answer: C2 is the chiral centre (H, OH, COOH and CH₂CH₃ are all different); there are two optical isomers (a pair of enantiomers).
parts.working: 1 mark: C2 identified with four different groups; 1 mark: two enantiomers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why CH₂Cl₂ is not optically active.
parts.answer: The carbon has two identical H atoms and two identical Cl atoms, so it is not chiral and the molecule has a plane of symmetry.
parts.working: 1 mark: two identical groups on the carbon so no chiral centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solution of a single enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light by +25°. A 50:50 mixture of the two enantiomers (a racemic mixture) shows no optical activity. Explain why.
parts.answer: The two enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions (+25° and −25°), which cancel out in the mixture.
parts.working: 1 mark: equal and opposite rotations; 1 mark: they cancel, giving zero net rotation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2,4-dichloropentane is CH₃CHClCH₂CHClCH₃. Identify the chiral centres.
parts.answer: C2 and C4
parts.working: Each of C2 and C4 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and a different CH₂-containing group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that there are three stereoisomers, and state which one is optically inactive even though it has two chiral centres.
parts.answer: The (2R,4R) and (2S,4S) forms are a pair of enantiomers, both optically active. The (2R,4S) form is a meso compound with a plane of symmetry, so it is optically inactive; RS and SR are the same molecule, giving three stereoisomers.
parts.working: 1 mark: RR, SS and RS forms, with RS and SR the same compound (three in total); 1 mark: the meso (R,S) form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, reacts with HCN, with a trace of KCN as a catalyst, to give a single product. Name the product.
parts.answer: 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN
parts.working: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving a hydroxynitrile with the carbon bearing OH, CN, H and C₂H₅.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the product is formed as a racemic mixture.
parts.answer: The planar C=O group is attacked by CN⁻ from either face with equal probability, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers (a 50:50 mixture) with no net optical activity.
parts.working: 1 mark: planar carbonyl attacked from either side; 1 mark: equal amounts of both enantiomers (50:50).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Enzymes in the body make only one optical isomer of lactic acid. Explain why.
parts.answer: Enzymes have a three-dimensional chiral active site that fits only one enantiomer, so only that enantiomer is made.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes are chiral / active site is 3D and chiral; 1 mark: only one enantiomer fits the active site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-aminobutanoic acid is CH₃CH₂CH(NH₂)COOH. Identify its chiral centre.
parts.answer: C2 (the carbon bearing NH₂, COOH, H and C₂H₅)
parts.working: This carbon has four different groups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of optical isomers 2-aminobutanoic acid has.
parts.answer: 2 (a pair of enantiomers)
parts.working: One chiral centre gives two enantiomers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms electrophile and nucleophile.
parts.answer: Electrophile: a species that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond. Nucleophile: a species that donates a pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃.
parts.answer: Addition
parts.working: Two molecules join to give one product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr.
parts.answer: Substitution (nucleophilic substitution; hydrolysis)
parts.working: Br is replaced by OH.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Classify CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (with concentrated phosphoric acid).
parts.answer: Elimination (dehydration)
parts.working: Water is removed to form a C=C bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation is the initiation step in the free-radical chlorination of methane?
A Cl₂ → 2Cl•
B Cl• + CH₄ → CH₃• + HCl
C CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
D 2CH₃• → C₂H₆
parts.answer: A Cl₂ → 2Cl•
parts.working: Initiation creates radicals by homolytic fission of Cl–Cl (in UV light). B and C are propagation steps, and D is a termination step.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromine reacts with ethene by electrophilic addition. Explain why Br₂ acts as an electrophile in this reaction.
parts.answer: The electron-rich C=C bond attracts one Br atom of the Br–Br molecule, polarising it so that one Br is δ+; the π electrons of the C=C bond form a new bond to this Br, and Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.
parts.working: 1 mark: C=C is electron-rich (π electrons); 1 mark: Br–Br is polarised, so one Br is δ+; 1 mark: the π electrons form a C–Br bond, then Br⁻ adds to the carbocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two different termination steps for the free-radical chlorination of methane that form ethane and chloromethane.
parts.answer: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ and CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl (either two different termination steps)
parts.working: 1 mark each; a termination step joins two radicals and removes them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, to give 2-bromopropane as the major product. Describe in words the first step of the mechanism, showing the movement of an electron pair, and name the intermediate formed.
parts.answer: The π electron pair of C=C attacks the δ+ H of HBr and a C–H bond forms at C1 (the CH₂ carbon) while the H–Br bond breaks, so the positive charge sits on C2. The intermediate is a secondary carbocation, CH₃CH⁺CH₃ (propan-2-yl cation).
parts.working: 1 mark: π electron pair of C=C attacks H of HBr, with H–Br bond breaking; 1 mark: C–H bond forms at C1 and the positive charge sits on C2; 1 mark: named secondary carbocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromoethane reacts faster than chloroethane when warmed with aqueous NaOH. Explain why.
parts.answer: The C–Br bond is weaker (lower bond enthalpy) than the C–Cl bond, so it is broken more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: C–Br bond weaker / lower bond enthalpy than C–Cl; 1 mark: so less energy is needed to break it and the substitution is faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethane reacts with chlorine in sunlight to give a mixture of chloroethanes. Explain why a mixture of products forms.
parts.answer: Chloroethane still has H atoms that can be replaced by radicals, so further substitution gives dichloroethanes; the radical chain reaction has no selectivity between H atoms.
parts.working: 1 mark: the product can undergo further substitution; 1 mark: radical substitution is not selective, giving a mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromoethane reacts with aqueous cyanide ions. Write the equation for the reaction and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻; the product is propanenitrile.
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation with ions; 1 mark: product named propanenitrile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a free radical, and state the number of unpaired electrons in a chlorine free radical, Cl•.
parts.answer: A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons; Cl• has one unpaired electron.
parts.working: 1 mark: species with one or more unpaired electrons; 1 mark: one unpaired electron in Cl•.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of bond fission in the initiation step of free-radical chlorination, and explain why.
parts.answer: Homolytic fission: each Cl atom takes one electron from the Cl–Cl bond, forming two radicals.
parts.working: 1 mark: homolytic fission; 1 mark: each atom receives one electron forming radicals.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the functional group in each compound.
(i) CH₃CH₂CHO
(ii) CH₃COCH₃
(iii) CH₃CH₂NH₂
parts.answer: (i) aldehyde (–CHO); (ii) ketone (C=O); (iii) primary amine (–NH₂)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound contains both a hydroxyl group and a carbonyl group?
A ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
B propanone, CH₃COCH₃
C 2-hydroxypropanal, CH₃CH(OH)CHO
D 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl
parts.answer: C 2-hydroxypropanal, CH₃CH(OH)CHO
parts.working: C has an –OH and a –CHO group. A has an OH only, B has a C=O only, and D has a halogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Serine has the structure HOCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH. Name the three functional groups present.
parts.answer: hydroxyl (alcohol, –OH); amino (–NH₂); carboxylic acid (–COOH)
parts.working: 1 mark for each group named correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each compound by its functional group.
(i) CH₂=C(CH₃)₂
(ii) CH₃CH₂Cl
(iii) CH₃COOCH₂CH₃
parts.answer: (i) alkene; (ii) halogenoalkane; (iii) ester
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound T is CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃. State the two functional groups present.
parts.answer: a C=C double bond (alkene) and an ester group (–COO–)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: CH₃OCH₃ and CH₃CH₂OH both have molecular formula C₂H₆O. State the name of the functional group in CH₃OCH₃.
parts.answer: ether (C–O–C)
parts.working: Two alkyl groups linked by an oxygen atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why CH₃OCH₃ and CH₃CH₂OH are functional group isomers.
parts.answer: They have the same molecular formula but different functional groups: the ether has C–O–C, the alcohol has –OH.
parts.working: 1 mark: same molecular formula; 1 mark: different functional groups (ether vs alcohol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, contains an amide group. Name the functional group and give the products formed when ethanamide is hydrolysed by refluxing with dilute acid.
parts.answer: Amide (–CONH–); ethanoic acid and ammonium ions (NH₄⁺).
parts.working: 1 mark: amide; 1 mark: ethanoic acid and ammonium ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the functional group in CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and the class of compound it belongs to.
parts.answer: The C–Cl (halogen) group; it is a halogenoalkane (chloroalkane).
parts.working: 1 mark: C–Cl group; 1 mark: halogenoalkane.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary, and give its systematic name.
(i) (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH
(ii) (CH₃)₂CHC(CH₃)₂OH
(iii) CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
parts.answer: (i) primary, 2-methylpropan-1-ol; (ii) tertiary, 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol; (iii) secondary, pentan-3-ol
parts.working: 1 mark each compound for the correct class and name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound with molecular formula C₅H₈O₂ contains an ester group and a C=C double bond. Give one possible structural formula and its name.
parts.answer: CH₂=CHCOOCH₂CH₃, ethyl prop-2-enoate (any other valid example, such as methyl but-3-enoate, CH₂=CHCH₂COOCH₃, is acceptable).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct ester with C=C and C₅H₈O₂; 1 mark: correct name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a functional group, using the –OH group in alcohols as an example.
parts.answer: A group of atoms in a molecule that determines its characteristic chemical reactions; the –OH group in alcohols determines reactions such as oxidation and reaction with sodium.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition; 1 mark: –OH example with a characteristic reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexanoic acid is CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH. Give its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₂
parts.working: Six carbons; 12 H; two O atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the empirical formula of hexanoic acid.
parts.answer: C₃H₆O
parts.working: Divide C₆H₁₂O₂ by 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the compound CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O
parts.working: Six carbons; C=O counts one oxygen; saturated with one C=O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the compound CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₂CH₃.
parts.answer: hexan-3-one
parts.working: Six-carbon chain with C=O on C3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexane is a ring of six carbon atoms, each with two H atoms. Give its molecular and empirical formulae.
parts.answer: Molecular C₆H₁₂; empirical CH₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-methylbutan-2-ol is (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃. Give its molecular formula and its empirical formula.
parts.answer: Molecular: C₅H₁₂O; empirical: C₅H₁₂O (already the simplest ratio).
parts.working: 1 mark each; the ratio 5:12:1 has no common factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and relative molecular mass 180.0 (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0). Find n, where molecular formula = (CH₂O)n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆
parts.working: (CH₂O)₆.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. Calculate its empirical formula (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0).
parts.answer: CH₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanedioic acid is HOOC–COOH. Give its molecular formula and empirical formula.
parts.answer: Molecular C₂H₂O₄; empirical CHO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.300 g of an organic compound containing only C, H and O burns to give 0.440 g of CO₂ and 0.180 g of H₂O. Calculate the masses of C, H and O in the sample (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass is 60.0. Give the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₄O₂
parts.working: Moles: C 0.010, H 0.020, O 0.010, so empirical CH₂O (Mr 30); n = 60/30 = 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound has empirical formula C₂H₅ and relative molecular mass 58.0. Give its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₁₀
parts.working: C₂H₅ has Mr 29.0; 58.0 ÷ 29.0 = 2, so C₄H₁₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound has empirical formula C₂H₄O and relative molecular mass 88.0. Give its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₈O₂
parts.working: C₂H₄O has Mr 44.0; 88.0 ÷ 44.0 = 2, so C₄H₈O₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the empirical formula of benzene, C₆H₆.
parts.answer: CH
parts.working: Divide 6 C and 6 H by 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A skeletal formula shows a zig-zag chain of four carbon atoms, with a C=C double bond between the two carbons at one end and an –OH group on the carbon at the other end. Give the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₈O
parts.working: Four carbons with one C=C and one OH: C₄H₈O (one degree of unsaturation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the compound.
parts.answer: but-3-en-1-ol, HOCH₂CH₂CH=CH₂
parts.working: Number from the OH end so the OH carbon is C1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A compound contains 52.2% C, 13.0% H and 34.8% O by mass, and its relative molecular mass is 46.0 (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0). Find its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₆O
parts.working: Moles: C 4.35, H 13.0, O 2.175; divide by 2.175 gives 2 : 6 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₂H₆O (Mr 46.0), which is also the molecular formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the general formula of alkanes and give the molecular formula of the alkane with five carbon atoms.
parts.answer: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; C₅H₁₂ (pentane)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the general formula of alkenes and of cycloalkanes.
parts.answer: CₙH₂ₙ for both.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the general formula of saturated monohydric alcohols.
parts.answer: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
parts.working: One –OH group replaces one H of the alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bromobutane has the formula C₄H₉Br. Show that it fits the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X, and state the value of n.
parts.answer: 2n + 1 = 9 gives n = 4, so C₄H₉Br fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X with n = 4.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct substitution 2n + 1 = 9; 1 mark: n = 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why successive members of a homologous series differ by a CH₂ unit, and give the difference in relative molecular mass between pentane and hexane (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0).
parts.answer: Each member adds one CH₂ unit (one carbon and two hydrogens) to the chain; the Mr difference is 14.0.
parts.working: 1 mark: one CH₂ added; 1 mark: Mr difference 14.0 (12.0 + 2 × 1.0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carboxylic acids have general formula CₙH₂ₙO₂. Calculate the relative molecular mass of hexanoic acid (n = 6; Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the boiling point increases steadily down a homologous series such as the alkanes.
parts.answer: Larger molecules have more electrons, so London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark: more electrons / larger molecules, stronger London forces; 1 mark: more energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alkane has relative molecular mass 86.0 (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0). Find its molecular formula, showing your working.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₄
parts.working: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: 14n + 2 = 86, so n = 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the member of the alkene homologous series with four carbon atoms, and give its molecular formula.
parts.answer: but-1-ene (or but-2-ene); C₄H₈
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ketones have general formula CₙH₂ₙO (n ≥ 3). Show that propanone (C₃H₆O) has relative molecular mass 58.0 (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0).
parts.working: 1 mark for the Mr sum; 1 mark for stating 58.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alkynes have general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. An alkyne has relative molecular mass 54.0. Find n and name a structural isomer of the alkyne.
parts.answer: n = 4 (C₄H₆); but-1-yne, CH≡CCH₂CH₃ (or but-2-yne).
parts.working: 1 mark: 14n − 2 = 54, n = 4; 1 mark: C₄H₆ is CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ with n = 4; 1 mark: correct name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the general formula of alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂).
parts.answer: The C=C double bond (one π bond) means two fewer H atoms are needed per molecule; equivalently, one ring or double bond reduces H by two.
parts.working: 1 mark: C=C double bond (or a ring) reduces H by two; 1 mark: this gives CₙH₂ₙ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene (C₃H₆) and but-1-ene (C₄H₈) are both alkenes. State whether they belong to the same homologous series, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes. Both fit the general formula CₙH₂ₙ (n = 3 and n = 4), and they differ by one CH₂ unit.
parts.working: 1 mark: yes, both fit CₙH₂ₙ; 1 mark: they differ by one CH₂ unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propan-1-ol (Mr 60.0) belongs to a homologous series. Name this series, and give the molecular formula of the member of the series with Mr 74.0. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
parts.answer: Alcohols (alkanols); C₄H₁₀O
parts.working: 1 mark: alcohols (alkanols); 1 mark: C₄H₁₀O, since C₄H₁₀O has Mr 74.0 (4 × 12.0 + 10 × 1.0 + 16.0) and the alcohol series is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound is LESS acidic than phenol?
A ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
B carbonic acid, H₂CO₃
C ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
D hydrochloric acid, HCl
parts.answer: C ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
parts.working: Ethanol does not form a delocalised anion and is a much weaker acid than phenol. Ethanoic acid, carbonic acid and HCl are all stronger acids than phenol.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Phenol is treated with excess bromine water at room temperature. What is the main organic product?
A 2-bromophenol
B 4-bromophenol
C 2,4,6-tribromophenol
D 1,3,5-tribromobenzene
parts.answer: C 2,4,6-tribromophenol
parts.working: The –OH group activates positions 2, 4 and 6 of the ring, so all three are brominated without a catalyst, giving a white precipitate. D has no –OH group and would not form from phenol in this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.
parts.answer: The phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the ion is stabilised. In ethanol, the ethoxide ion's charge is localised on O and the electron-donating alkyl group destabilises it.
parts.working: 1 mark: delocalisation of the negative charge into the ring stabilises phenoxide; 1 mark: ethoxide charge is localised and destabilised by alkyl donation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal.
parts.answer: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂
parts.working: Phenol behaves as an acid, releasing H₂ and forming sodium phenoxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one observation seen when sodium is added to phenol.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is given off (effervescence/fizzing) and the sodium gradually disappears.
parts.working: Any one observation of gas production or sodium reacting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenol has Ka = 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Calculate Kb for the phenoxide ion, C₆H₅O⁻, giving your answer in mol dm⁻³ to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Kb = 7.7 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pH of a 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ solution of sodium phenoxide. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Name the organic product.
parts.answer: butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃
parts.working: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change of the reagent.
parts.answer: Orange to green
parts.working: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
2-methylpropan-1-ol is heated under reflux with an excess of acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which organic product forms?
A 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO
B 2-methylpropanone, (CH₃)₂CO
C 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH
D No reaction; the solution stays orange.
parts.answer: C 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH
parts.working: A primary alcohol heated under reflux with excess oxidant is oxidised fully to the carboxylic acid. A is only obtained if the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms; B needs a secondary alcohol; D is wrong because primary alcohols are oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanal, using [O].
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O
parts.working: One [O] removes two H atoms: one from the OH and one from the adjacent CH₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how Tollens' reagent can show that a distillate contains propanal rather than unreacted propan-1-ol.
parts.answer: Warm the sample with Tollens' reagent: propanal reduces the silver ions and a silver mirror (or grey precipitate) forms; propan-1-ol gives no reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: warm with Tollens' reagent; 1 mark: propanal gives a silver mirror and propan-1-ol gives no change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2.30 g of ethanol (Mr 46.0) is oxidised to ethanoic acid (Mr 60.0) with a percentage yield of 75.0%. Calculate the mass of ethanoic acid formed, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Moles of ethanol = 2.30 / 46.0 = 0.0500 mol; theoretical mass = 0.0500 × 60.0 = 3.00 g; actual = 3.00 × 0.750 = 2.25 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alcohol M, C₄H₁₀O, has an unbranched carbon chain. It is oxidised by warm acidified dichromate(VI) to an aldehyde (no ketone is possible). Name M and explain why M is not chiral.
parts.answer: M is butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (a primary alcohol with an unbranched chain). It is not chiral because no carbon has four different groups: C1 carries two H atoms and the other carbons each carry two H atoms or two identical groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: butan-1-ol; 1 mark: primary alcohol forms an aldehyde; 1 mark: C1 has two H atoms so no chiral centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which alcohol gives a ketone when heated under reflux with acidified dichromate(VI)?
A 2-methylpropan-2-ol
B pentan-3-ol
C propan-1-ol
D ethanol
parts.answer: B pentan-3-ol
parts.working: Pentan-3-ol is secondary and gives pentan-3-one. Propan-1-ol and ethanol are primary and give aldehydes or acids; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary and is not oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanoic acid in acidic solution.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H₂O → CH₃CH₂COOH + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
parts.working: 1 mark: H₂O added and organic species balanced; 1 mark: 4H⁺ and 4e⁻ on the right (charge and atoms balanced).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two reagents that, together, convert propan-2-ol into 2-bromopropane, and state the condition needed.
parts.answer: Potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid, heated (these generate HBr in situ); or HBr directly.
parts.working: 1 mark: KBr with concentrated H₂SO₄ (or HBr); 1 mark: heat/reflux.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main organic product when propan-1-ol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid.
parts.answer: propene
parts.working: Dehydration removes H₂O and forms a C=C bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: correct organic reactant and product; 1 mark: H₂O shown as the second product.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which alcohol gives exactly two different alkenes on dehydration, ignoring stereoisomers?
A ethanol
B propan-1-ol
C butan-2-ol
D 2-methylpropan-2-ol
parts.answer: C butan-2-ol
parts.working: Butan-2-ol gives but-1-ene and but-2-ene. Ethanol gives ethene only, propan-1-ol gives propene only, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol gives 2-methylpropene only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass, in g, of 1-chloropropane (C₃H₇Cl, Mr 78.5) that could be formed from 5.50 g of propan-1-ol (Mr 60.0).
parts.working: Moles of propan-1-ol = 5.50 / 60.0 = 0.09167 mol; theoretical mass = 0.09167 × 78.5 = 7.20 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 5.50 g of 1-chloropropane is actually obtained. Calculate the percentage yield to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why thionyl chloride, SOCl₂, is often preferred to PCl₅ for converting an alcohol into a chloroalkane.
parts.answer: Both by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, so the chloroalkane is left behind and is easier to purify; PCl₅ gives a liquid by-product (POCl₃) that must be separated.
parts.working: 1 mark: SO₂ and HCl escape as gases; 1 mark: the product is easier to purify (no liquid by-product to separate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of the SN2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ions.
parts.answer: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon atom from the side opposite the C–Br bond (backside attack) in a single step; a transition state forms in which the C–O and C–Br bonds are partly formed and partly broken; the C–Br bond breaks and Br⁻ leaves, giving butan-1-ol.
parts.working: 1 mark: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon from the opposite side to C–Br; 1 mark: one-step (concerted) process with a transition state; 1 mark: Br⁻ leaves and butan-1-ol forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 3.00 g of propan-2-ol (Mr 60.0) is dehydrated to propene. Calculate the volume of propene formed at room temperature and pressure (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³) if the percentage yield is 60.0%. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.72 dm³
parts.working: Moles = 3.00 / 60.0 = 0.0500 mol; theoretical volume = 0.0500 × 24.0 = 1.20 dm³; actual = 1.20 × 0.600 = 0.72 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is shaken with concentrated hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl
parts.working: A tertiary alcohol reacts with HCl at room temperature by substitution of –OH by –Cl.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this reaction is fast for a tertiary alcohol.
parts.answer: Loss of water gives a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilised by the three electron-donating alkyl groups; the carbocation forms easily so the reaction is fast.
parts.working: 1 mark: tertiary carbocation formed on loss of water; 1 mark: stabilised by three alkyl groups (inductive electron donation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanol with sodium.
parts.answer: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂
parts.working: 1 mark: correct reactants and products; 1 mark: balanced with 2 mol Na and 1 mol H₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Propan-1-ol is warmed with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. What is the main organic product?
A propyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃
B propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
C ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃
D sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa
parts.answer: A propyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃
parts.working: Esterification joins the alcohol's alkyl group to the acid's carboxyl group, giving propyl ethanoate. C would need ethanol and propanoic acid; B and D are not formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction between methanol and propanoic acid, using structural formulae or condensed formulae.
parts.answer: CH₃OH + CH₃CH₂COOH ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ + H₂O
parts.working: Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the ester formed.
parts.answer: methyl propanoate
parts.working: Alkyl group from methanol (methyl) and acyl group from propanoic acid (propanoate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of the concentrated sulfuric acid in this reaction.
parts.answer: It acts as a catalyst and absorbs the water formed, shifting the equilibrium towards the ester.
parts.working: 1 mark for catalyst; 1 mark for removing water (either point credited separately as part of the answer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2.30 g of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol, Mr 92.0) reacts with excess sodium. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Moles of glycerol = 2.30 / 92.0 = 0.0250 mol; each molecule has three OH groups, giving 1.5 mol H₂ per mol glycerol: 0.0375 mol H₂ × 24.0 = 0.900 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the observations when phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl₅, is added to ethanol.
parts.answer: The reaction is vigorous and steamy white fumes of hydrogen chloride are seen.
parts.working: 1 mark: vigorous reaction; 1 mark: white/steamy fumes of HCl.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethanol is a weaker acid than water.
parts.answer: The ethyl group is electron-donating (inductive effect), which pushes electron density onto the oxygen of the ethoxide ion and destabilises it, so ethanol releases H⁺ less readily than water.
parts.working: 1 mark: alkyl group donates electrons to O; 1 mark: ethoxide is destabilised, so less dissociation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol (Mr 46) has a much higher boiling point than ethane (Mr 30), although the two molecules have similar sizes. Explain why.
parts.answer: Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds between its –OH groups, which are stronger than the London forces holding ethane molecules together.
parts.working: 1 mark: hydrogen bonding in ethanol; 1 mark: stronger than London forces in ethane, so more energy needed to boil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propan-2-ol is warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine. A yellow precipitate forms. State the formula of the yellow precipitate.
parts.answer: CHI₃ (triiodomethane)
parts.working: Iodoform test: a CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group gives CHI₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the sodium salt formed as the other organic product.
parts.answer: sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa
parts.working: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + 4I₂ + 6NaOH → CHI₃ + CH₃COONa + 5NaI + 5H₂O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sodium reacts more slowly with propan-2-ol than with ethanol.
parts.answer: Propan-2-ol has two alkyl groups on the carbon bearing OH, which donate electrons to the O–H bond and make the alcohol less acidic; the bulkier alkoxide is also hindered from reacting.
parts.working: 1 mark: more alkyl groups make the O–H less acidic (electron donation); 1 mark: steric hindrance around the bulkier alkoxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol (0.100 mol) and ethanoic acid (0.100 mol) are heated under reflux with a catalyst. The yield of ethyl ethanoate is 65.0%. Calculate the mass of ethyl ethanoate (Mr 88.0) formed, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Theoretical moles of ester = 0.100 mol; theoretical mass = 0.100 × 88.0 = 8.80 g; actual = 8.80 × 0.650 = 5.72 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) that distinguishes primary and secondary alcohols from tertiary alcohols.
parts.answer: Warm each with acidified dichromate(VI): primary and secondary alcohols turn the reagent from orange to green; tertiary alcohols do not react and the solution stays orange.
parts.working: 1 mark: orange to green for primary and secondary alcohols; 1 mark: tertiary alcohol gives no colour change (stays orange).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions for making ethanol by fermentation of glucose.
parts.answer: Yeast enzymes in aqueous glucose solution, under anaerobic conditions, at about 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark: yeast/enzymes in aqueous glucose; 1 mark: anaerobic and about 25–37 °C (about 30 °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the industrial hydration of ethene to ethanol.
parts.answer: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH
parts.working: Addition of water across the C=C bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the preparation of ethanol from bromoethane and aqueous sodium hydroxide, and state the type of reaction.
parts.answer: C₂H₅Br + NaOH → C₂H₅OH + NaBr (or with OH⁻ ions); nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct equation; 1 mark: nucleophilic substitution / hydrolysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fermentation alone cannot give ethanol of concentration above about 15%, and state how a more concentrated product is obtained.
parts.answer: Ethanol is toxic to yeast and kills it at about 15%, so fermentation stops; concentrated ethanol is obtained by fractional distillation.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanol kills the yeast at about 15%; 1 mark: fractional distillation of the mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage atom economy for the hydration of ethene, C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0).
parts.working: Mass of desired product = 46.0; total mass of reactants = 28.0 + 18.0 = 46.0; 46.0 / 46.0 × 100 = 100%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, Mr 180.0) is fermented: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the mass of ethanol (Mr 46.0) formed from 90.0 g of glucose at a yield of 80.0%.
parts.working: Moles of glucose = 90.0 / 180.0 = 0.500 mol; theoretical ethanol = 1.00 mol = 46.0 g; actual = 46.0 × 0.800 = 36.8 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why hydration of ethene is carried out at high pressure, but not at the highest possible temperature.
parts.answer: Fewer gas molecules are formed (2 mol of gas react to give 1 mol), so high pressure increases the yield. The reaction is exothermic, so high temperature lowers the equilibrium yield, though it speeds up the reaction; a compromise is used.
parts.working: 1 mark: high pressure favours fewer gas moles so gives higher yield; 1 mark: high temperature lowers yield (exothermic) so a compromise is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage atom economy for the preparation of ethanol from bromoethane: C₂H₅Br + NaOH → C₂H₅OH + NaBr (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Br 79.9). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Mass of ethanol = 46.0; total mass of products and reactants = 108.9 + 40.0 = 148.9; 46.0 / 148.9 × 100 = 30.9%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butanal is reduced to butan-1-ol. Name a suitable reducing agent and write an equation using [H].
parts.answer: Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), NaBH₄ (or hydrogen with a nickel catalyst); CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable reducing agent; 1 mark: equation balanced with 2[H].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanone is reduced by hydrogen over a nickel catalyst. Write an equation for the reaction and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₃ + H₂ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propan-2-ol); this is a reduction (addition of hydrogen).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct equation and product; 1 mark: reaction described as reduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene is hydrated with steam and an acid catalyst. Name the main alcohol formed and explain which carbon atom bears the –OH group.
parts.answer: propan-2-ol; H adds to C1 (the CH₂ carbon) and –OH to C2, because the more stable secondary carbocation forms as the intermediate.
parts.working: 1 mark: propan-2-ol; 1 mark: the –OH goes to C2 via the more stable secondary carbocation (Markovnikov).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the microorganism used to ferment sugar solutions such as molasses to make ethanol, and state one advantage of hydration of ethene over fermentation.
parts.answer: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae); hydration is a continuous, faster process that does not depend on crops or yeast cultures.
parts.working: 1 mark: yeast; 1 mark: a valid advantage such as continuous, faster or not dependent on biological material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethanol cannot be concentrated above about 95% by simple distillation of an ethanol–water mixture.
parts.answer: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope (a constant-boiling mixture) at about 95% ethanol, so simple distillation cannot separate them further.
parts.working: 1 mark: azeotrope formed; 1 mark: constant-boiling mixture so simple distillation cannot give a purer product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of ethene, at room temperature and pressure (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³), needed to make 9.20 g of ethanol at a yield of 75.0% by hydration. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 6.40 dm³
parts.working: Moles of ethanol = 9.20 / 46.0 = 0.200 mol; ethene needed = 0.200 / 0.750 = 0.267 mol; volume = 0.267 × 24.0 = 6.40 dm³.

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lattice energy of lithium fluoride, LiF (−1036 kJ mol⁻¹), is more exothermic than that of potassium fluoride, KF (−821 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: Li⁺ is much smaller than K⁺, so the ions in LiF are closer together and the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is stronger.
parts.working: 1 mark: Li⁺ is smaller (higher charge density) than K⁺; 1 mark: shorter separation of oppositely charged ions gives stronger electrostatic attraction.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf⦵ KCl(s) = −437; ΔHat⦵ K(s) = +89; 1st ionisation energy of K = +419; ΔHat⦵ Cl (½Cl₂ → Cl) = +122; 1st electron affinity of Cl = −349.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the lattice energy of potassium chloride, KCl. Give your answer in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: −718 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: ΔHf = ΔHat(K) + IE(K) + ΔHat(Cl) + EA(Cl) + LE, so LE = −437 − (89 + 419 + 122 − 349) = −718 kJ mol⁻¹. 1 mark: Born–Haber route; 1 mark: substitution; 1 mark: answer with sign.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf⦵ BaCl₂(s) = −858; ΔHat⦵ Ba(s) = +180; 1st IE of Ba = +503; 2nd IE of Ba = +965; ΔHat⦵ Cl (per mole of Cl atoms) = +122; 1st electron affinity of Cl = −349.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of barium chloride, BaCl₂. Remember that two chlorine atoms are involved.
parts.answer: −2052 kJ mol⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf⦵ Li₂O(s) = −598; ΔHat⦵ Li(s) = +159; 1st IE of Li = +520; ΔHat⦵ O (½O₂ → O) = +249; 1st electron affinity of O = −141; 2nd electron affinity of O = +798.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of lithium oxide, Li₂O, in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: −2862 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 2ΔHat(Li) = 318; 2 × IE(Li) = 1040; ΔHat(O) = 249; EA1(O) = −141; EA2(O) = +798; sum = 2264. LE = −598 − 2264 = −2862 kJ mol⁻¹. 1 mark each for the two Li terms, the O terms and the final answer.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHat⦵ Mg(s) = +148; 1st IE of Mg = +738; 2nd IE of Mg = +1451; ΔHat⦵ Cl (per mole of Cl atoms) = +122; 1st EA of Cl = −349; lattice energy of MgCl₂ = −2526.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the predicted standard enthalpy change of formation of MgCl₂(s) from these data, in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: −643 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experimental value is −641 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest one reason why the predicted value differs slightly from it.
parts.answer: The lattice energy is calculated from a purely ionic model (the bonding has some covalent character), and the data are rounded.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason (model assumptions, covalent character, or rounding of data).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the standard enthalpy change of solution.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in sufficient water to form an infinitely dilute solution, under standard conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: one mole of solute; 1 mark: in sufficient water to give an infinitely dilute solution (standard conditions).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation linking the enthalpy change of solution of an ionic compound MX(s) to its lattice energy and the hydration enthalpies of M⁺(g) and X⁻(g). State the sign convention used for the lattice energy.
parts.answer: ΔHsol = −LE + ΔHhyd(M⁺) + ΔHhyd(X⁻), where LE is the (negative) lattice energy, so −LE is the positive energy needed to separate the lattice.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct cycle with −LE (lattice broken) and both hydration enthalpies; 1 mark: LE stated as a negative value so −LE is positive.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Hypothetical data (kJ mol⁻¹, not data-book values): lattice energy of NaBr = −747; ΔHhyd⦵ Na⁺(g) = −419; ΔHhyd⦵ Br⁻(g) = −337.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of solution of NaBr, and state whether its dissolving is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −9 kJ mol⁻¹; exothermic (only slightly).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHsol⦵ KBr = +19.9; lattice energy of KBr = −671; ΔHhyd⦵ K⁺(g) = −322.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of hydration of Br⁻(g), in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: −329 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: ΔHhyd(Br⁻) = ΔHsol + LE − ΔHhyd(K⁺) = 19.9 + (−671) − (−322) = −329.1, which rounds to −329 kJ mol⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the hydration enthalpy of Mg²⁺ (−1920 kJ mol⁻¹) is much more exothermic than that of Ba²⁺ (−1360 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is smaller, so it has a higher charge density; water molecules are attracted more strongly to it (stronger ion–dipole attraction).
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg²⁺ smaller / higher charge density; 1 mark: stronger attraction to water molecules (ion–dipole).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: A student dissolves 2.50 g of potassium nitrate, KNO₃ (Mr 101.1), in 50.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the water falls by 2.2 °C. Assume the density of water is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heat energy absorbed by the water, in J, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: q = m c ΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 2.2 = 459.8 J (the water has mass 50.0 g since its density is 1.00 g cm⁻³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of KNO₃ in kJ mol⁻¹, including its sign, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: +18.6 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Moles of KNO₃ = 2.50 / 101.1 = 0.02473 mol; ΔH = +459.8 J ÷ 0.02473 mol = +18 600 J mol⁻¹ = +18.6 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature fell, so the process is endothermic (positive).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the method: identify two sources of error and suggest one improvement for each.
parts.answer: Heat loss to the surroundings (through the cup and the air): use a lid and a better insulated container and record the temperature until it is steady, extrapolating back to the time of mixing. Incomplete dissolving: stir continuously or use powdered KNO₃. Also: thermometer resolution (use a digital thermometer reading to 0.1 °C) and measuring volume (use a measuring cylinder or burette rather than an estimate).
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid source of error with a sound improvement (up to 4 marks).

author: HomiLabs
stem: A student determines the enthalpy change of solution of KNO₃ by dissolving 2.50 g of KNO₃ in 50.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup; the temperature falls by 2.2 °C. The student's value (+18.6 kJ mol⁻¹) is noticeably different from the data-book value.

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Hypothetical data for NH₄Cl (kJ mol⁻¹): lattice energy = −698; ΔHhyd⦵ NH₄⁺(g) = −284; ΔHhyd⦵ Cl⁻(g) = −364.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of solution of NH₄Cl using these hypothetical data, and state whether dissolving it is endothermic or exothermic.
parts.answer: +50 kJ mol⁻¹; endothermic.
parts.working: ΔHsol = −(−698) + (−284) + (−364) = 698 − 648 = +50 kJ mol⁻¹, a positive value, so endothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this dissolving process could be used in an instant cold pack.
parts.answer: The process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the solution (and the pack) becomes colder.
parts.working: 1 mark: endothermic process takes in heat from surroundings.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the first ionisation energy of an element.
parts.answer: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: per mole of gaseous atoms; 1 mark: removal of one electron to form a gaseous 1+ ion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic.
parts.answer: The O⁻ ion is already negative, so the incoming electron is repelled by it; energy must be supplied to overcome this repulsion.
parts.working: 1 mark: repulsion between the incoming electron and the negative O⁻ ion; 1 mark: energy must be supplied to overcome it.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
