parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium (578 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of magnesium (738 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: The outer electron of Al is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy and more shielded than the 3s electrons of Mg, so it is removed more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: Al's outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p orbital; 1 mark: it is more shielded, so less energy is needed.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert 0.500 mol of gaseous aluminium atoms into Al³⁺(g) ions. Use IE1 = 578, IE2 = 1817 and IE3 = 2745 kJ mol⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of oxygen (1314 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: Oxygen has a paired electron pair in a 2p orbital; the repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove. Nitrogen has three unpaired electrons in its half-filled 2p subshell, which is more stable.
parts.working: 1 mark: paired electrons in O 2p cause repulsion; 1 mark: N's half-filled subshell is more stable, so more energy is needed.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 17 from fluorine (1681 kJ mol⁻¹) to iodine (1008 kJ mol⁻¹), and explain it.
parts.answer: The first ionisation energy decreases down the group, because the atomic radius and the shielding increase, so the outer electron is less strongly attracted to the nucleus.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease; 1 mark: atomic radius and shielding increase, so the outer electron is less strongly attracted.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in eV per atom, needed to remove one electron from a gaseous sodium atom if the first ionisation energy is 496 kJ mol⁻¹. Use 1 eV per atom = 96.5 kJ mol⁻¹, and give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.1 eV

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations, with state symbols, for the first ionisation of calcium and for the first electron affinity of chlorine.
parts.answer: Ca(g) → Ca⁺(g) + e⁻ and Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)
parts.working: 1 mark each; state symbols are needed.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the second ionisation of magnesium.
parts.answer: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻
parts.working: The second electron is removed from the gaseous 1+ ion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert 5.00 g of solid calcium into gaseous Ca²⁺ ions. Use ΔHat⦵ Ca(s) = +178, 1st IE = +590 and 2nd IE = +1145 kJ mol⁻¹, and Ar of Ca = 40.1. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 239 kJ
parts.working: Energy per mole = 178 + 590 + 1145 = 1913 kJ mol⁻¹; moles = 5.00 / 40.1 = 0.1247 mol; energy = 0.1247 × 1913 = 238.5 kJ, which is 239 kJ to 3 s.f.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first electron affinity of a noble gas is endothermic (positive).
parts.answer: The added electron would have to occupy a new, higher-energy shell or subshell, so no stable configuration is gained; there is also repulsion from the electrons already present, so energy must be supplied.
parts.working: 1 mark: electron enters a higher-energy shell/subshell with no stability gain; 1 mark: repulsion from the existing full shell means energy is needed.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first electron affinity of chlorine (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more exothermic than that of fluorine (−328 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: Fluorine's added electron enters a small 2p subshell where electron–electron repulsion is large, whereas chlorine's larger 3p subshell has less repulsion, so chlorine releases more energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: F's small 2p subshell has large electron–electron repulsion; 1 mark: Cl's larger 3p subshell has less repulsion, so more energy is released.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy of beryllium (900 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of boron (801 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy than the 2s orbital holding Be's outer electrons, so it is removed more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: B's outer electron is in a higher-energy 2p orbital; 1 mark: it is less strongly held than Be's 2s electron pair.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ to 3 significant figures, needed to remove one electron from 0.250 mol of gaseous potassium atoms, given that the first ionisation energy of K is +419 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: 105 kJ

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The successive ionisation energies of an element X (kJ mol⁻¹) are: 1st 578, 2nd 1817, 3rd 2745, 4th 11 577. Deduce the group of X and explain the large jump between the 3rd and 4th values.
parts.answer: Group 13 (X is aluminium). After three electrons are removed, the ion has a stable noble gas-like configuration, and the 4th electron is removed from an inner shell that is much closer to the nucleus and much less shielded, so far more energy is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: three outer electrons, so Group 13; 1 mark: after 3 removals a stable configuration is reached; 1 mark: the 4th electron comes from an inner shell with less shielding.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first ionisation energy of sodium is 496 kJ mol⁻¹ and the second is about 4560 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain the very large increase.
parts.answer: After one electron is removed, Na⁺ has a stable, full [Ne] configuration; the second electron is removed from this full shell, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so much more energy is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: Na⁺ has a stable noble gas configuration; 1 mark: the next electron is removed from an inner shell with less shielding.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first ionisation energies of lithium and sodium are 520 and 496 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. Explain why sodium's value is lower.
parts.answer: Sodium's outer electron is in the 3s subshell, which is further from the nucleus and more shielded by the extra inner shell, so less energy is needed to remove it than from lithium's 2s electron.
parts.working: 1 mark: outer electron further from the nucleus (extra shell); 1 mark: more shielding, so less energy is needed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene is warmed with fuming sulfuric acid (concentrated H₂SO₄ containing dissolved SO₃). Name the organic product and state the type of reaction.
parts.answer: Benzenesulfonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H; electrophilic substitution (an H atom of the ring is replaced by –SO₃H).
parts.working: 1 mark benzenesulfonic acid (C6H5SO3H); 1 mark electrophilic substitution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the electrophile in this reaction and explain why it is attracted to the benzene ring.
parts.answer: SO₃ (sulfur trioxide). The S atom is electron-deficient and accepts a pair of electrons from the delocalised π electrons of the ring.
parts.working: 1 mark SO3 as electrophile; 1 mark electron-deficient S attracted to the high electron density of the π system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene reacts with 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: (2-methylpropan-2-yl)benzene, C₆H₅C(CH₃)₃ (tert-butylbenzene).
parts.working: A tert-butyl group replaces one H on the ring (Friedel–Crafts alkylation); HCl is also formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of aluminium chloride in this reaction.
parts.answer: It is a catalyst (Lewis acid): it accepts a lone pair from Cl, polarising and breaking the C–Cl bond to form a carbocation electrophile.
parts.working: 1 mark accepts an electron pair from Cl (Lewis acid) or polarises C–Cl; 1 mark forms the carbocation electrophile.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of the electrophile formed from 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₃C⁺
parts.working: A tertiary carbocation; it is attacked by the π electrons of the benzene ring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the formation of the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, from concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻
parts.working: 1 mark NO2+ formed with H3O+ and HSO4- as products; 1 mark correct balancing (2 H2SO4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the first step of the mechanism of nitration of benzene with NO₂⁺, including the curly arrow(s) and the intermediate formed.
parts.answer: A π-electron pair from the ring forms a bond to the N of NO₂⁺ (curly arrow from the ring C=C to N⁺). An arenium (σ-complex) intermediate forms, with positive charge spread over the ring and one sp³ carbon bearing both H and NO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark curly arrow from the π bond to N⁺; 1 mark intermediate with delocalised positive charge; 1 mark sp³ carbon bearing H and NO₂ (ring temporarily loses its delocalised aromatic system).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of HSO₄⁻ in the final step of the mechanism.
parts.answer: It removes an H⁺ from the intermediate, restoring the delocalised ring and regenerating H₂SO₄ (catalyst).
parts.working: 1 mark: removes H⁺ and restores the aromatic ring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the mononitration of benzene using concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: equation balanced with H2O as a product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrobenzene formed from 5.00 g of benzene at a yield of 78.0 %. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₆H₆ = 78.0; C₆H₅NO₂ = 123.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrobenzene is nitrated much more slowly than benzene. Using the electron-withdrawing effect of the NO₂ group, explain why.
parts.answer: NO₂ withdraws electron density from the ring (by induction and resonance), so the ring is less electron-rich and less attractive to the electrophile NO₂⁺. The reaction is slower and needs more forcing conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark NO2 is electron-withdrawing; 1 mark ring electron density is reduced / less attractive to NO2+; 1 mark reaction slower and needs harsher conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Dinitration of nitrobenzene gives mainly the meta-dinitro product. Explain why attack at the ortho and para positions is less favourable.
parts.answer: When the electrophile attacks at the ortho or para position, one resonance form of the intermediate puts the positive charge on the carbon bearing NO₂, next to a strongly electron-withdrawing group. This is destabilising. Attack at the meta position never places the positive charge on that carbon, so the meta intermediate is more stable.
parts.working: 1 mark ortho/para intermediate has + charge on the C bearing NO2 (destabilised); 1 mark meta intermediate avoids this; 1 mark meta product therefore favoured (lower energy pathway).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene (7.80 g) is mixed with bromine (20.0 g) and a little FeBr₃. Show by calculation which reagent is limiting. (Mr: C₆H₆ = 78.0; Br₂ = 159.8)
parts.answer: Benzene is limiting. n(C₆H₆) = 0.100 mol and n(Br₂) = 0.125 mol; the reaction is 1:1, so only 0.100 mol Br₂ is needed and bromine is in excess.
parts.working: M1 moles of both reagents calculated; M1 1:1 ratio, so the smaller amount (benzene, 0.100 mol) is limiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass of bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br (Mr = 156.9), that can be formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In practice 12.6 g of bromobenzene is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene does not decolourise bromine water in the dark, yet it reacts with liquid bromine only in the presence of FeBr₃ (or iron filings). Cyclohexene reacts with bromine without any catalyst. Explain why a catalyst is needed for benzene.
parts.answer: The delocalised π system of benzene is stable (aromatic), so a strong electrophile is needed to attack it. FeBr₃ polarises Br–Br to give a strongly electrophilic species. Cyclohexene has a localised, electron-rich C=C π bond that polarises Br₂ directly, so no catalyst is needed. Addition would destroy the stable ring, so benzene undergoes substitution instead.
parts.working: 1 mark delocalised ring stable/less reactive; 1 mark FeBr3 polarises Br2 to give a stronger electrophile; 1 mark cyclohexene's localised C=C is reactive enough without a catalyst; 1 mark substitution keeps the aromatic ring whereas addition would destroy it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound is the major product when 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, reacts with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst?
A 2-methylpropan-1-ol
B 2-methylpropan-2-ol
C butan-2-ol
D 2-methylpropane-1,2-diol
parts.answer: B 2-methylpropan-2-ol
parts.working: Acid-catalysed hydration is electrophilic addition. H⁺ adds to the CH₂ carbon, giving a tertiary carbocation, which is the more stable carbocation; water then attacks it. A would need the less stable primary carbocation; C has the wrong carbon skeleton; D has two OH groups and is not formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to ethene, which species acts as the electrophile?
A Br⁻
B the δ⁻ bromine atom of HBr
C the δ⁺ hydrogen atom of HBr (H⁺)
D Br⁺
parts.answer: C the δ⁺ hydrogen atom of HBr (H⁺)
parts.working: HBr is polar (Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻). The electron-poor H is attracted to the π electrons of C=C and forms a bond to one carbon. Br⁻ is then the nucleophile that attacks the carbocation. The δ⁻ bromine is not electrophilic, Br⁻ is not the electrophile, and Br⁺ is not formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene reacts with bromine dissolved in an inert solvent such as tetrachloromethane. Write the equation for the reaction and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₃CHBrCH₂Br; product is 1,2-dibromopropane.
parts.working: 1 mark correct equation with one Br₂ added across the C=C; 1 mark name 1,2-dibromopropane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is observed when the bromine solution is added to propene.
parts.answer: The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears (the solution becomes colourless).
parts.working: 1 mark: decolourisation of bromine; this is the test for C=C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene reacts with bromine. Write the equation for the reaction and give the Mr of the product, 1,2-dibromoethane. (Mr: C₂H₄ = 28.0; C₂H₄Br₂ = 187.8)
parts.answer: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂; Mr = 187.8
parts.working: 1 mark equation; 1 mark Mr of C2H4Br2 = 187.8 (using Br = 79.9).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 1,2-dibromoethane formed from 1.40 g of ethene at a yield of 85.0 %. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alkene, CnH2n, reacts with bromine in a 1:1 mole ratio. A 0.392 g sample of the alkene reacts exactly with 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ bromine solution. Calculate the amount, in mol, of bromine that reacted.
parts.working: n(Br₂) = 0.0200 dm³ × 0.200 mol dm⁻³ = 0.00400 mol (2 marks for correct working and answer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the alkene.
parts.working: Mr = 0.392 g / 0.00400 mol = 98.0 (1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the molecular formula of the alkene.
parts.answer: C₇H₁₄
parts.working: CnH2n: 14n = 98, so n = 7; C7H14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alkanes do not react with bromine in the dark, but alkenes decolourise bromine quickly at room temperature. Explain this difference in terms of the π electrons of C=C.
parts.answer: The C=C bond has a region of high electron density (the π electrons) above and below the bond plane. This attracts the δ⁺ bromine atom of the polarised Br–Br bond, so an addition reaction occurs. Alkanes have only σ bonds with no accessible region of high electron density, so they do not react with Br₂ under these conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark π electrons form a region of high electron density; 1 mark this attracts/polarises Br₂ (electrophile); 1 mark alkanes contain only C–C and C–H σ bonds with no such electron-rich site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 3-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CH–CH(CH₃)₂, reacts with HBr. Name the carbocation formed when H⁺ adds to C1, and state whether it is primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: CH₃–CH⁺–CH(CH₃)₂ (positive charge on C2 of the chain): a secondary carbocation.
parts.working: 1 mark correct carbocation structure; 1 mark secondary (carbon bonded to two other carbons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: This carbocation rearranges by a hydride shift to form a more stable carbocation. Describe the shift and draw (write) the structure of the new carbocation.
parts.answer: A hydrogen with its bonding pair moves (as H⁻) from the adjacent CH(CH₃)₂ carbon to the positive carbon, giving CH₃CH₂–C⁺(CH₃)₂, a tertiary carbocation.
parts.working: 1 mark hydride (H⁻) shift from adjacent carbon; 1 mark tertiary carbocation CH3CH2C+(CH3)2 is more stable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the major product of the addition of HBr to 3-methylbut-1-ene.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane
parts.working: Br⁻ attacks the tertiary carbocation, CH₃CH₂C(Br)(CH₃)₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene reacts with bromine dissolved in water. The major organic product is 1-bromopropan-2-ol. Name the type of this product and identify which carbon bears the OH group.
parts.answer: A bromohydrin (a halogenated alcohol); the OH is on C2 (the central carbon) and Br is on C1.
parts.working: 1 mark bromohydrin / bromo-alcohol; 1 mark OH on C2 and Br on C1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water attacks the carbon at C2 rather than C1, using the cyclic bromonium ion intermediate.
parts.answer: Br₂ is polarised by the π electrons and adds to form a cyclic bromonium ion across C1 and C2. The bromonium ion opens so that the positive charge is better stabilised on the more substituted carbon (C2). Water, a nucleophile, attacks the carbon with more δ⁺ character, which is C2, so the OH ends up on C2.
parts.working: 1 mark cyclic bromonium ion formed; 1 mark positive charge better stabilised on the more substituted carbon (C2); 1 mark water attacks C2 (more δ⁺), giving OH on C2 and Br on C1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: But-1-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide to give two possible products. Name both, and state which is the major product.
parts.answer: 2-bromobutane is the major product; 1-bromobutane is the minor product.
parts.working: 1 mark 2-bromobutane (major) from the secondary carbocation; 1 mark 1-bromobutane (minor) from the primary carbocation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the stability of carbocations, why 2-bromobutane is the major product.
parts.answer: Protonation gives a secondary carbocation (CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃) which is more stable than the primary carbocation (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂⁺) formed by protonation at C2. Alkyl groups donate electron density to the positive carbon, stabilising it; the major pathway proceeds via the more stable carbocation.
parts.working: 1 mark secondary carbocation more stable than primary; 1 mark alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect) and stabilise the + charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation represents a termination step in the free-radical chlorination of methane?
A CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl
B Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
C Cl₂ → 2Cl•
D CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
parts.answer: B Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
parts.working: Termination joins two radicals to form a stable molecule and removes radicals. A and D are propagation steps (each uses a radical and makes a new one); C is the initiation step (homolytic fission of Cl₂ by UV light).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term free radical and describe what is meant by homolytic fission.
parts.answer: A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons. Homolytic fission is the breaking of a covalent bond so that each atom takes one electron from the shared pair.
parts.working: 1 mark free radical has an unpaired electron; 1 mark homolytic fission: each atom keeps one electron of the bond pair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one condition needed for methane to react with chlorine at room temperature, and name the mechanism of the reaction.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet light (or sunlight) is needed; the mechanism is free-radical substitution.
parts.working: 1 mark UV light (sunlight); 1 mark free-radical substitution (accept chain reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the reaction of methane with chlorine to form chloromethane.
parts.answer: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl
parts.working: 1 mark balanced equation (UV light may be stated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chloromethane formed from 4.00 g of methane at a yield of 64.0 %. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: CH₄ = 16.0; CH₃Cl = 50.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butane is chlorinated in UV light. Name the two monochloro products formed in the chain propagation step.
parts.answer: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct name (both needed; 1 mark for the pair if one correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 2-chlorobutane is formed in greater amount than 1-chlorobutane, even though there are six primary H atoms (on C1 and C4) and only four secondary H atoms (on C2 and C3).
parts.answer: Chlorine radicals attack the C–H bonds that lead to the more stable radical. Removal of an H from C2 gives a secondary radical, which is more stable than the primary radical formed from C1, so more 2-chlorobutane forms.
parts.working: 1 mark secondary radical (from loss of H at C2) is more stable than the primary radical from C1; 1 mark the stability of the intermediate outweighs the statistical advantage of 6 primary H atoms, so more 2-chlorobutane forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethane reacts with excess chlorine in UV light to form hexachloroethane, C₂Cl₆, and hydrogen chloride only. Write the equation for this overall reaction.
parts.answer: C₂H₆ + 6Cl₂ → C₂Cl₆ + 6HCl
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of hydrogen chloride formed from 3.00 g of ethane. (Mr: C₂H₆ = 30.0; HCl = 36.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2,2-dimethylpropane, C(CH₃)₄, is chlorinated in UV light. Give the name of the only monochloro product that forms.
parts.answer: 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct name (its structure is (CH3)3C–CH2Cl).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why only one monochloro structural isomer is formed.
parts.answer: All twelve hydrogen atoms are on primary carbon atoms and are equivalent, so substitution of any one of them gives the same compound.
parts.working: 1 mark all hydrogens are equivalent; 1 mark all are on primary (CH₃) carbons, so one product only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorination of methane with excess chlorine gives a mixture of CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. Explain why this happens.
parts.answer: The product CH₃Cl still has C–H bonds, which a chlorine radical can attack, so further substitution occurs; each product is attacked in turn.
parts.working: 1 mark CH3Cl still contains C–H bonds; 1 mark further propagation steps substitute more H atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using an excess of methane increases the proportion of chloromethane in the product.
parts.answer: With excess methane, a chlorine radical is more likely to collide with a CH₄ molecule than with a CH₃Cl molecule, so the first substitution is favoured over further substitution.
parts.working: 1 mark chlorine radicals more likely to meet CH4 than CH3Cl; 1 mark so monosubstitution is favoured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the chlorination of ethane, ethyl radicals (C₂H₅•) are formed. Write equations for two termination steps: one that forms butane and one that forms chloroethane.
parts.answer: C₂H₅• + C₂H₅• → C₄H₁₀ (butane); C₂H₅• + Cl• → C₂H₅Cl (chloroethane).
parts.working: 1 mark each correct termination equation (each joins two radicals and removes them); 1 mark both steps are termination steps (not propagation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the initiation step of the chlorination of methane, and state the energy source needed.
parts.answer: Cl₂ → 2Cl•; energy from ultraviolet light (UV).
parts.working: 1 mark Cl2 → 2Cl• (homolytic fission, both radicals shown); 1 mark UV light supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of 2.00 mol of methane and 1.00 mol of chlorine is exposed to UV light. Assume the reaction gives only CH₃Cl and HCl. Identify the limiting reagent.
parts.answer: Chlorine is limiting; 1.00 mol Cl₂ can react with only 1.00 mol CH₄.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine limiting (1:1 ratio, 1.00 mol Cl2 vs 2.00 mol CH4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of CH₃Cl formed and of unreacted CH₄.
parts.answer: CH₃Cl = 1.00 mol; unreacted CH₄ = 1.00 mol.
parts.working: 1 mark CH3Cl = 1.00 mol (1:1 with Cl2); 1 mark CH4 left = 2.00 − 1.00 = 1.00 mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ethene is shaken with cold, dilute, neutral potassium manganate(VII) solution. Which organic product is formed?
A ethanol
B ethanal
C ethane-1,2-diol
D ethanoic acid
parts.answer: C ethane-1,2-diol
parts.working: Under cold dilute conditions the C=C bond is oxidised to a diol, with the manganate reduced to brown MnO₂. Ethanol and ethanal need reduction/loss of oxygen; ethanoic acid needs the C–C bond to break, which happens only under hot, concentrated conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclopentene is shaken with cold, dilute, neutral potassium manganate(VII) solution. State two observations.
parts.answer: The purple colour of the solution disappears (it decolourises); a brown solid (MnO₂) forms.
parts.working: 1 mark purple colour disappears; 1 mark brown precipitate of MnO2 forms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organic product of this reaction.
parts.answer: cis-Cyclopentane-1,2-diol, C₅H₈(OH)₂ (the ring C=C is converted to two adjacent OH groups).
parts.working: 1 mark: cyclopentane-1,2-diol (accept cis or unspecified stereochemistry).

parts.label: a
parts.text: But-1-ene is heated with hot, concentrated, acidified potassium manganate(VII). Name the organic product and the gas evolved.
parts.answer: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, and carbon dioxide gas.
parts.working: 1 mark propanoic acid; 1 mark CO2 (from the =CH₂ terminal carbon).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alkene X, C₄H₈, gives only ethanoic acid when heated with hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanoic acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the structure and name of X.
parts.answer: CH₃CH=CHCH₃, but-2-ene (either the cis or the trans isomer).
parts.working: 1 mark for the structure with the C=C between C2 and C3; 1 mark named but-2-ene (cis or trans accepted).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alkene M, C₇H₁₄, gives butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, and propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, when heated with hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄. Explain which carbon atom of the C=C bond gives the C=O of butanone and which gives the COOH of propanoic acid.
parts.answer: The C=C carbon bearing a CH₃ and a CH₂CH₃ group gives the ketone (C=O) of butanone because it has no H to leave as COOH. The C=C carbon bearing one H and a CH₂CH₃ group gives an aldehyde that is oxidised further to propanoic acid.
parts.working: 1 mark quaternary alkene carbon (two alkyl groups) forms the ketone; 1 mark CH carbon forms an aldehyde, oxidised to the COOH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula and name of M.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CHCH₂CH₃; 3-methylhex-3-ene.
parts.working: 1 mark structure and name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the change in oxidation state of manganese when MnO₄⁻ is reduced in acidic conditions.
parts.answer: From +7 to +2 (Mn²⁺).
parts.working: 1 mark: +7 to +2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In cold, dilute, neutral conditions the manganese product is a brown solid. Name it.
parts.answer: Manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: MnO2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the product is a brown solid under cold, neutral conditions but a colourless solution under hot, acidified conditions.
parts.answer: Under neutral conditions MnO₄⁻ is reduced only to MnO₂ (Mn +4, insoluble); in acid, it is reduced to Mn²⁺ (Mn +2), which is colourless and dissolves.
parts.working: 1 mark: different reduction product (MnO2 insoluble vs Mn2+ soluble in acid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexene is heated with hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: Hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH.
parts.working: 1 mark: hexanedioic acid; 1 mark correct (CH2)4 chain with COOH at both ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the C=C bond in the ring is cleaved to give a single chain with a COOH at each end.
parts.answer: The C=C bond breaks: each alkene carbon, which bears one ring CH₂ group and one H, becomes a C=O that is oxidised to COOH. The C–C ring bond between the two carbons is replaced by two separate chain ends, so a single open chain forms.
parts.working: 1 mark C=C cleaved; 1 mark each former alkene carbon becomes a COOH group (ring opened to a chain).

stem: Three colourless liquids, hexane, cyclohexene and benzene, were tested. Test 1: 2 cm³ of each was shaken with a few drops of cold dilute acidified KMnO₄. Results: hexane, purple colour unchanged; cyclohexene, purple colour disappeared quickly; benzene, purple colour unchanged. Test 2: 2 cm³ of each was shaken with bromine water. Results: hexane, orange colour unchanged; cyclohexene, orange colour disappeared; benzene, orange colour unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the liquid that gives a positive result in both tests.
parts.answer: Cyclohexene
parts.working: 1 mark: cyclohexene (has a C=C bond; decolourises both reagents).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why benzene gives negative results in both tests, even though it has six π electrons.
parts.answer: The six π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, which makes benzene aromatic and stable. There is no localised C=C bond with high electron density for the electrophilic/oxidising reagent to attack, and substitution rather than addition would be needed, so no rapid reaction occurs.
parts.working: 1 mark π electrons delocalised, giving a stable aromatic ring; 1 mark no localised C=C to react rapidly with Br2 or MnO4⁻ under these conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution for Test 2 and one reason why only 2 cm³ of each liquid should be used.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard (bromine is toxic and volatile), or wear goggles; small volumes limit the amount of hazardous reagent or volatile liquid used.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible precaution (fume cupboard / goggles / gloves) for bromine; 1 mark for the reason for 2 cm³ (small volume limits the amount of hazardous or volatile liquid).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethene decolourises cold, dilute KMnO₄ but ethane does not.
parts.answer: Ethene has a π bond, a region of high electron density that is attacked by the oxidising reagent. Ethane has only σ C–C and C–H bonds, with no such site, so there is no reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark π bond in ethene is electron-rich and reactive; 1 mark ethane has only σ bonds with no site for oxidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene is shaken with cold, dilute, neutral KMnO₄. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: Propane-1,2-diol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂OH
parts.working: 1 mark: propane-1,2-diol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of propane-1,2-diol formed from 0.420 g of propene, assuming a 100 % yield. (Mr: C₃H₆ = 42.0; C₃H₈O₂ = 76.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pent-2-ene is heated with hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄. Name the two organic products.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.
parts.working: 1 mark each product correctly named (C=C cleaved: CH3CH= gives ethanoic acid; =CHCH2CH3 gives propanoic acid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the oxidation of ethene to ethane-1,2-diol using [O] to represent the oxidising agent from KMnO₄ under cold, dilute conditions.
parts.answer: C₂H₄ + [O] + H₂O → HOCH₂CH₂OH
parts.working: 1 mark C2H4 + H2O + [O] as reactants; 1 mark HOCH2CH2OH as product (balanced).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C. Write the equation and name the product.
parts.answer: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆; ethane.
parts.working: 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark ethane named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: But-1-ene is shaken with bromine dissolved in tetrachloromethane. Write the equation for the reaction and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃; 1,2-dibromobutane.
parts.working: 1 mark equation with one Br2 added across the C=C; 1 mark 1,2-dibromobutane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethene (2.50 dm³ at room temperature and pressure) is hydrogenated completely at a yield of 80.0 %. Calculate the mass of ethane formed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Molar volume at rtp = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹; Mr of C₂H₆ = 30.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: But-1-ene is hydrated by steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Name the major organic product.
parts.answer: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
parts.working: 1 mark: butan-2-ol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why butan-2-ol rather than butan-1-ol is the major product.
parts.answer: The H⁺ adds to C1, giving a secondary carbocation on C2, which is more stable than the primary carbocation that would form on C1 by addition to C2. Water attacks the secondary carbocation, so OH goes on C2.
parts.working: 1 mark secondary carbocation more stable than primary; 1 mark OH therefore ends up on C2 (butan-2-ol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrocarbon X, C₅H₈ (Mr = 68.0), is acyclic (has no rings) and contains no triple bonds. 0.340 g of X reacts exactly with 0.0100 mol of hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. Calculate the amount, in mol, of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mole ratio of X to H₂ and deduce the number of C=C bonds in X.
parts.answer: X : H₂ = 1 : 2, so each X molecule adds two H₂ molecules, giving two C=C bonds per molecule.
parts.working: 1 mark mole ratio 1:2 (0.0100 / 0.00500); 1 mark each C=C adds one H2; 1 mark two C=C bonds (a C≡C would also need 2 H2, but none is present).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogenation of an alkene is an addition reaction. Explain why the carbon atoms of the C=C bond are reduced during this reaction, using oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: In ethene each C is bonded to two H atoms and to the other C, so its oxidation number is −2. In ethane each C has three H atoms and one C, giving −3. The oxidation number of each carbon decreases from −2 to −3, so the carbon is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark oxidation number of C in ethene = −2; 1 mark in ethane = −3; 1 mark decrease in oxidation number means reduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexene reacts with hydrogen bromide to form a single organic product. Write the equation and name the product.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₀ + HBr → C₆H₁₁Br; bromocyclohexane.
parts.working: 1 mark equation; 1 mark bromocyclohexane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of reaction and the species that acts as the electrophile.
parts.answer: Electrophilic addition; the electrophile is the δ⁺ hydrogen (H⁺) of HBr.
parts.working: 1 mark electrophilic addition (accept the H⁺ as electrophile).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene is hydrated by steam using a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure. Write the equation and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃; propan-2-ol.
parts.working: 1 mark equation; 1 mark propan-2-ol (secondary alcohol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hex-1-ene, C₆H₁₂ (Mr = 84.0), is added to bromine. Calculate the mass of 1,2-dibromohexane (Mr = 243.8) formed from 0.700 g of hex-1-ene at a yield of 90.0 %. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the addition of hydrogen to an alkene needs a nickel catalyst and heating, whereas bromine adds to an alkene at room temperature without a catalyst.
parts.answer: H₂ is a non-polar molecule with a strong H–H bond, so it is not polarised by the C=C π electrons and needs a catalyst surface to break the H–H bond. Bromine is polarised and can be attacked by the π electrons directly, so it adds without a catalyst.
parts.working: 1 mark H2 is non-polar and the H–H bond is strong; 1 mark a catalyst is needed to break H–H (adsorbs H2); 1 mark Br2 is polarisable and reacts directly with the π electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An unsaturated fatty acid has three C=C bonds in each molecule. Calculate the amount, in mol, of hydrogen needed to saturate 0.250 mol of the fatty acid.
parts.working: 3 × 0.250 mol = 0.750 mol (1 mark for the ratio, 1 mark for the answer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of this hydrogen at room temperature and pressure (molar volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: 18.0 dm³
parts.working: 0.750 mol × 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 18.0 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the addition of hydrogen chloride to ethene and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl; chloroethane.
parts.working: 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark chloroethane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylbenzene is heated under reflux with acidified potassium manganate(VII). Name the organic product and state the colour change seen in the solution.
parts.answer: Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH. The purple colour of the manganate(VII) disappears (solution becomes colourless or pale).
parts.working: 1 mark benzoic acid; 1 mark purple colour disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylbenzene is oxidised by hot acidified KMnO₄ to benzoic acid, but tert-butylbenzene, C₆H₅C(CH₃)₃, is not oxidised under the same conditions. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Side-chain oxidation needs at least one hydrogen atom on the carbon attached to the ring (a benzylic hydrogen). Methylbenzene has three H atoms on that carbon, so it is oxidised to COOH. tert-Butylbenzene has no hydrogen on the carbon attached to the ring, so no oxidation occurs.
parts.working: 1 mark benzylic C–H needed; 1 mark methylbenzene CH3 has H atoms so oxidised to COOH; 1 mark tert-butylbenzene's attached carbon has no H, so no reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light. Name the organic product and the type of reaction.
parts.answer: (Chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl (benzyl chloride); free-radical substitution in the side chain.
parts.working: 1 mark (chloromethyl)benzene; 1 mark free-radical substitution (UV light; the CH3 side chain reacts, not the ring).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that benzene decolourises acidified KMnO₄ in the same way as cyclohexene. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: Benzene has a delocalised, stable aromatic π system with no localised C=C bond that is easily attacked. It does not react with the oxidising reagent under these conditions, so the purple colour is not decolourised.
parts.working: 1 mark delocalised, stable ring (no localised C=C); 1 mark so no reaction / no decolourisation at room temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the oxidation of methylbenzene to benzoic acid, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent.
parts.answer: C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] → C₆H₅COOH + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced with 3[O] and H2O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of benzoic acid formed from 2.00 g of methylbenzene at a yield of 75.0 %. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₆H₅CH₃ = 92.0; C₆H₅COOH = 122.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product formed when 1,2-dimethylbenzene (o-xylene) is heated with hot, acidified KMnO₄.
parts.answer: Benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid).
parts.working: 1 mark: benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both methyl groups are oxidised and why the benzene ring is not broken.
parts.answer: Each CH₃ group has hydrogen atoms on the carbon attached to the ring, so each is oxidised to COOH. The aromatic ring is stable and is not attacked under these conditions, so it remains intact.
parts.working: 1 mark each CH3 has benzylic H so both are oxidised; 1 mark the aromatic ring is stable and remains intact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Styrene (phenylethene) is shaken with bromine in tetrachloromethane. Name the organic product.
parts.answer: (1,2-dibromoethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CHBrCH₂Br.
parts.working: 1 mark: product named (addition across the side-chain C=C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the benzene ring does not react with bromine under these conditions.
parts.answer: The ring's delocalised π system is stable (aromatic). Adding Br₂ to the ring would destroy this stability, so no addition occurs. Only the localised C=C bond in the side chain reacts.
parts.working: 1 mark ring stability (aromatic delocalisation) would be lost on addition; 1 mark only the side-chain C=C is localised and reacts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorobenzene does not react with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide under conditions that hydrolyse chloroethane. Explain why.
parts.answer: In chlorobenzene one lone pair on Cl overlaps with the π system of the ring, so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is shorter and stronger. The carbon is sp² and the ring repels the incoming nucleophile, so hydrolysis does not occur easily.
parts.working: 1 mark lone pair on Cl delocalised into the ring; 1 mark C–Cl bond is stronger / has partial double-bond character; 1 mark the sp² carbon and electron-rich ring repel OH⁻ (no easy substitution).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzene reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light, not in the presence of AlCl₃, to form C₆H₆Cl₆. Write the equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 Cl2 on the reactant side; 1 mark C6H6Cl6 product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of reaction and explain why it is an addition reaction rather than a substitution.
parts.answer: Free-radical addition; each Cl₂ adds across a double bond of the ring, forming a saturated ring, so no H atom is replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark: addition (no H atoms replaced; ring becomes saturated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, is oxidised completely to benzoic acid. Calculate the mass of benzoic acid formed from 3.00 g of ethylbenzene, assuming a 100 % yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ = 106.0; C₆H₅COOH = 122.0)
parts.working: M1 n(ethylbenzene) = 3.00/106.0 = 0.0283 mol; M1 1:1 ratio, so n(benzoic acid) = 0.0283 mol; A1 mass = 0.0283 × 122.0 = 3.45 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the other product formed from the side-chain carbon that is lost.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide, CO₂ (the CH₂CH₃ side chain loses its extra carbon as CO₂ and water is formed).
parts.working: 1 mark: CO2 (accept carbon dioxide and water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in UV light by substitution in the side chain, whereas chlorination of the ring needs a catalyst such as AlCl₃ in the dark.
parts.answer: UV light causes homolytic fission of Cl₂ to give chlorine radicals, which attack the weak benzylic C–H bond of the side chain by a free-radical mechanism. For ring substitution, the ring's π electrons attack an electrophilic Cl⁺ species; AlCl₃ polarises Cl–Cl to make this electrophile. The ring's π system needs a catalyst because it is stable.
parts.working: 1 mark UV gives Cl• radicals that attack the side chain (free-radical); 1 mark ring substitution is electrophilic and needs AlCl3 to polarise Cl2; 1 mark the ring is stable so needs a stronger electrophile (catalyst).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the dimethylbenzene that gives benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) on oxidation with hot, acidified KMnO₄.
parts.answer: 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene).
parts.working: 1 mark: 1,4-dimethylbenzene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the 1,2- and 1,3-dimethylbenzenes give different dicarboxylic acids from the 1,4 isomer.
parts.answer: Oxidation converts each CH₃ group to COOH without changing its position on the ring. The positions of the two CH₃ groups are kept, so the 1,2 isomer gives the 1,2-dicarboxylic acid, the 1,3 isomer gives 1,3, and the 1,4 isomer gives the 1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Each isomer therefore gives a different product.
parts.working: 1 mark CH3 groups keep their ring positions (become COOH); 1 mark each isomer gives a different dicarboxylic acid, so the product identifies the starting isomer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, is shaken with cold, dilute, neutral KMnO₄ solution. State the observation.
parts.answer: The purple colour remains (no reaction occurs; the solution stays purple).
parts.working: 1 mark: purple colour unchanged; the side chain is not oxidised under cold, dilute, neutral conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the side chain is not oxidised under these conditions, but is oxidised to a COOH group by hot, acidified KMnO₄.
parts.answer: Side-chain oxidation needs heat and acidified (strong) KMnO₄; cold, dilute, neutral KMnO₄ is too weak an oxidising agent to attack the C–H bonds next to the ring.
parts.working: 1 mark: needs hot, acidified (strong oxidising) conditions; 1 mark cold, dilute, neutral KMnO₄ is not strong enough (insufficient energy/oxidising power).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alkanes such as hexane are almost insoluble in water. Explain why, in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.answer: Alkanes are non-polar and can only form weak van der Waals (London) forces. They cannot form hydrogen bonds or other attractions with water molecules, so the energy released on mixing is not enough to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark alkanes are non-polar and only have van der Waals forces; 1 mark no attractions with water to offset the hydrogen bonds broken in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of pentane, C₅H₁₂, and name the two products.
parts.answer: C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O; carbon dioxide and water.
parts.working: 1 mark balanced equation (8 O2, 5 CO2, 6 H2O); 1 mark both products named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propane burns with a limited supply of oxygen to form carbon monoxide and water only. Write the balanced equation.
parts.answer: C₃H₈ + 3.5O₂ → 3CO + 4H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: CO and H2O products; 1 mark balanced (3.5 O2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one hazard of carbon monoxide produced in this way.
parts.answer: It is poisonous: it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, reducing oxygen transport in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: toxic; binds to haemoglobin (accept 'colourless, odourless, toxic gas').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of propane.
parts.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 10.0 g of propane burns completely. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₃H₈ = 44.0; CO₂ = 44.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the complete combustion of methane.
parts.answer: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of methane in 2.00 g. (Mr: CH₄ = 16.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, at room temperature and pressure (molar volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹), needed for complete combustion of 2.00 g of methane.
parts.answer: 6.00 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexane is cracked to produce one molecule of butene and one molecule of ethane. Write the equation and name the alkene product.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₄ → C₄H₈ + C₂H₆; the alkene is but-1-ene (or but-2-ene).
parts.working: 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark alkene named (but-1-ene or but-2-ene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conditions used for cracking.
parts.answer: High temperature (around 500–700 °C) and a catalyst such as zeolite (or aluminium oxide).
parts.working: 1 mark high temperature; 1 mark catalyst (zeolite / aluminium oxide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cracking is important in the petroleum industry.
parts.answer: Large alkanes in the fractions are less useful and are in less demand than shorter alkanes. Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes for petrol and gas, and into alkenes that are needed to make plastics and other chemicals.
parts.working: 1 mark more demand for short-chain fuels/petrol than long-chain fractions; 1 mark cracking breaks C–C bonds to make shorter alkanes; 1 mark alkenes are produced for chemical (e.g. polymer) manufacture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the boiling points of alkanes increase as the chain length increases.
parts.answer: Longer chains have more electrons, so the van der Waals (London) forces between molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark more electrons / larger molecular size; 1 mark stronger van der Waals forces; 1 mark more energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrocarbon X burns completely in oxygen. 0.100 mol of X produces 0.300 mol of CO₂ and 0.400 mol of H₂O. Deduce the number of carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms in one molecule of X.
parts.working: 1 mark 3 carbon atoms; 1 mark 8 hydrogen atoms (each H2O gives 2 H).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the molecular formula of X and state the homologous series it belongs to, assuming X is an alkane.
parts.answer: C₃H₈; propane, a member of the alkane homologous series.
parts.working: 1 mark: C3H8 (alkane, general formula CnH2n+2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen monoxide is formed inside petrol engines. Write the equation for its formation from nitrogen and oxygen, and explain why it forms only at high temperatures.
parts.answer: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO. The N≡N triple bond is very strong and requires a large activation energy to break. High temperatures in the engine supply enough energy for the N₂ and O₂ molecules to react; at lower temperatures the reaction is too slow.
parts.working: 1 mark N2 + O2 → 2NO (balanced); 1 mark N≡N bond very strong, large activation energy; 1 mark high engine temperature provides the energy so the reaction occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Octane burns with a smoky, luminous flame when the air supply is limited. Explain why soot forms, and write an equation for the formation of carbon monoxide from octane.
parts.answer: With insufficient oxygen, complete combustion does not occur and carbon is released as soot (carbon particles). Carbon monoxide forms: C₈H₁₈ + 8.5O₂ → 8CO + 9H₂O.
parts.working: 1 mark incomplete combustion because of limited oxygen; 1 mark carbon released as soot; 1 mark balanced equation for CO (8CO + 9H2O).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the general equation for the complete combustion of an alkane, CnH2n+2.
parts.answer: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + [(3n + 1)/2] O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark products nCO2 and (n+1)H2O; 1 mark oxygen term (3n+1)/2 correctly balanced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈.
parts.answer: C₈H₁₈ + 12.5O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation (12.5 O2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of oxygen needed to burn 0.500 mol of octane completely.
parts.answer: 6.25 mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of this oxygen at room temperature and pressure (molar volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: 150 dm³
parts.working: M1 6.25 mol × 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 150 dm³; A1 correct to 3 s.f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The C–C bond length in benzene is 0.139 nm. Compare this with typical C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm) bond lengths, and explain the value.
parts.answer: 0.139 nm lies between the single (0.154 nm) and double (0.134 nm) bond lengths. This is because the six π electrons are delocalised over all six C–C bonds, so each bond has a bond order of about 1.5.
parts.working: 1 mark value lies between C–C and C=C; 1 mark delocalisation gives each bond an intermediate bond order (about 1.5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of σ bonds and the number of delocalised π electrons in one molecule of benzene.
parts.answer: 12 σ bonds (6 C–C and 6 C–H); 6 π electrons delocalised over the ring.
parts.working: 1 mark 12 σ bonds (6 C–C, 6 C–H); 1 mark 6 delocalised π electrons (one from each carbon).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all bond angles in benzene are 120° and why the molecule is planar.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom is sp² hybridised with three σ bonds arranged in a trigonal planar arrangement, giving bond angles of 120°. The unhybridised p orbital on each carbon is perpendicular to the plane, so the ring is flat and the p orbitals overlap sideways to form the delocalised π system.
parts.working: 1 mark each C is sp² with three σ bonds (trigonal planar); 1 mark bond angles 120°; 1 mark unhybridised p orbitals perpendicular to the plane, overlapping sideways to make the ring planar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Biphenyl, C₁₂H₁₀, is two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond. Deduce the number of σ bonds and the number of π bonds in its Kekulé structure.
parts.answer: 23 σ bonds (13 C–C and 10 C–H); 6 π bonds.
parts.working: 1 mark 13 C–C σ bonds (12 within the two rings + 1 linking bond); 1 mark 10 C–H σ bonds; 1 mark 6 π (C=C) bonds (3 per ring).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyclohexene decolourises bromine water readily, but benzene does not. Explain this difference in terms of the π electrons.
parts.answer: The π electrons of cyclohexene are localised in one C=C bond, so they are readily available to attack the electrophile Br⁺/polarised Br₂. In benzene the π electrons are delocalised over six carbons, which gives extra stability (delocalisation energy); attack would destroy this, so benzene undergoes substitution only with a catalyst and not addition.
parts.working: 1 mark localised π bond in cyclohexene is accessible; 1 mark delocalised π in benzene gives extra stability; 1 mark addition would destroy the ring's stability so benzene does not add bromine readily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1,4-dichlorobenzene has no net dipole moment, but 1,2-dichlorobenzene has one. Explain this using the positions of the Cl atoms and the bond dipoles.
parts.answer: Each C–Cl bond is polar. In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions (they are at 180° to each other), so they cancel out. In 1,2-dichlorobenzene the bond dipoles are at 60° to each other and do not cancel, so the molecule has a net dipole moment.
parts.working: 1 mark each C–Cl bond is polar; 1 mark 1,4 dipoles are opposite and cancel (180°); 1 mark in 1,2 the dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Kekulé suggested a structure for benzene with three alternating C=C and C–C bonds. Explain why benzene is better described by a delocalised model than by either of the two Kekulé structures.
parts.answer: The two Kekulé structures have alternating single and double bonds, which would predict two different C–C bond lengths. Experimentally all six C–C bonds are equal (0.139 nm). The real structure is a resonance hybrid, in which the π electrons are spread over the whole ring, so every bond has the same intermediate character.
parts.working: 1 mark Kekulé forms predict unequal bond lengths (alternating); 1 mark experiment shows all bonds equal at 0.139 nm; 1 mark real structure is a resonance hybrid with delocalised π electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the π electron cloud above and below the benzene ring attracts electrophiles.
parts.answer: The delocalised π electrons form a region of high electron density above and below the plane of the ring. Electrophiles (electron-pair acceptors) are attracted to this electron-rich region.
parts.working: 1 mark π electrons above and below the plane give high electron density; 1 mark electrophiles are attracted to this electron-rich region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (C₆H₁₀ + H₂ → C₆H₁₂) is −120 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene is hydrogenated to cyclohexane with ΔH = −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the delocalisation energy of benzene and explain what it shows.
parts.answer: Three C=C bonds would give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹; the actual value is −208 kJ mol⁻¹, so benzene is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable (delocalisation energy = 152 kJ mol⁻¹). This shows that the delocalised π system of benzene is more stable than a localised cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene would be.
parts.working: 1 mark 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹ for a localised model; 1 mark −360 − (−208) = −152, so the delocalisation energy is 152 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark delocalisation makes benzene less exothermic on hydrogenation, i.e. more stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the hybridisation of each carbon atom in benzene and the orbital that is not involved in hybridisation.
parts.answer: Each carbon is sp²; the unhybridised orbital is a p orbital, which is perpendicular to the ring plane.
parts.working: 1 mark sp²; 1 mark unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two features of a molecule that make it aromatic.
parts.answer: The molecule is cyclic and planar, with a continuous ring of p orbitals that contains delocalised π electrons (4n + 2 π electrons, e.g. 6 in benzene).
parts.working: 1 mark cyclic, planar, conjugated ring of p orbitals; 1 mark delocalised π electrons (4n + 2, e.g. 6 for benzene).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with localised double bonds would have alternating C=C and C–C bonds. Predict the two bond lengths this structure would have, and state which experimental result rules it out.
parts.answer: C=C about 0.134 nm and C–C about 0.154 nm alternating round the ring. Experiment shows all six C–C bonds in benzene are equal at 0.139 nm, so this structure is ruled out.
parts.working: 1 mark 0.134 nm and 0.154 nm alternating; 1 mark X-ray evidence shows all bonds equal (0.139 nm).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the formula for degrees of unsaturation, DoU = C − H/2 + 1, to show that benzene (C₆H₆) has four degrees of unsaturation. Explain what these four units represent.
parts.answer: DoU = 6 − 6/2 + 1 = 4. These are one ring and three double bonds (in the Kekulé picture), i.e. four units of unsaturation.
parts.working: 1 mark working gives 4; 1 mark one ring plus three C=C (or equivalent π bonds).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container?
A The gas molecules are attracted to the walls.
B The gas molecules collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
C The gas molecules are at rest and press on the walls.
D The gas molecules expand to fill the container.
parts.answer: B The gas molecules collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
parts.working: Gas molecules move randomly and constantly; their collisions with the container walls give a force per unit area, which is the pressure. Gas molecules are not attracted to walls (A), not at rest (C), and expansion (D) describes the result of motion, not the cause of pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hydrogen (Mr = 2.0) and oxygen (Mr = 32.0) are at the same temperature. Which statement is correct?
A Hydrogen molecules have a greater average kinetic energy than oxygen molecules.
B Oxygen molecules have a greater average kinetic energy than hydrogen molecules.
C Both gases have the same average kinetic energy, but hydrogen molecules move faster.
D Both gases have the same average kinetic energy, but oxygen molecules move faster.
parts.answer: C Both gases have the same average kinetic energy, but hydrogen molecules move faster.
parts.working: The average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends only on absolute temperature, so it is the same for both gases. For equal kinetic energies, ½mv² is the same, so the lighter hydrogen molecules must move faster. A and B are wrong because kinetic energy does not depend on the molar mass at the same temperature; D reverses the speed relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends on the absolute temperature.
parts.answer: It is directly proportional to the absolute (kelvin) temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: directly proportional to absolute temperature (not Celsius).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of one gas molecule at 300 K. Use the relationship KE = 3/2 kT with k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Give your answer in J to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid are placed at opposite ends of a 100.0 cm glass tube. A white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube. State which end of the tube the ring is nearer to.
parts.answer: The ring is nearer to the hydrochloric acid end (HCl end).
parts.working: NH₃ (Mr 17.0) is lighter and diffuses faster than HCl (Mr 36.5), so it travels further before meeting the HCl; the ring forms nearer the HCl end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use Graham's law to calculate the distance from the ammonia end to the white ring. (Mr: NH₃ = 17.0; HCl = 36.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using kinetic theory, how the rate of diffusion of a gas depends on its temperature and on its molar mass.
parts.answer: Rate of diffusion increases with temperature because the molecules have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently and more energetically. Rate decreases with molar mass because, at the same temperature, heavier molecules have the same average kinetic energy but lower speed (½mv² is constant).
parts.working: 1 mark higher temperature gives more kinetic energy and faster molecules; 1 mark at the same temperature heavier molecules move more slowly (same KE, larger m); 1 mark diffusion rate is inversely related to √M (Graham's law).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Graham's law of effusion/diffusion in words or as a formula.
parts.answer: At constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass: rate ∝ 1/√M.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate ∝ 1/√M at constant T and p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Under the same conditions, neon (Mr = 20.2) diffuses 1.22 times as fast as an unknown gas Y. Calculate the Mr of Y.
parts.working: M1 rate(Ne)/rate(Y) = √(MY/MNe), so MY = MNe × 1.22² = 20.2 × 1.4884; A1 MY = 30.1 (3 s.f.).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a formula for a possible identity of Y.
parts.answer: C₂H₆ (ethane, Mr 30.0).
parts.working: 1 mark: C2H6 (other Mr≈30 gases such as NO are also acceptable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a gas has no fixed volume and fills the whole of any container it is placed in.
parts.answer: Gas molecules move randomly and rapidly with large spaces between them. The forces between molecules are very weak, so they keep moving apart until they hit the container walls.
parts.working: 1 mark molecules move randomly with large spaces and weak forces; 1 mark so they spread to fill the whole container.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plunger of a gas syringe is pushed in slowly at constant temperature. Use kinetic theory to explain why the pressure of the gas increases.
parts.answer: The same number of molecules is in a smaller volume, so the molecules hit the walls and plunger more often per unit area. The total force per unit area (pressure) increases.
parts.working: 1 mark more collisions per unit area per second (smaller volume); 1 mark force per unit area (pressure) therefore increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen (Mr = 2.0) takes 20.0 s to diffuse through a porous plug under fixed conditions of temperature and pressure. Using Graham's law, calculate the time taken for the same volume of sulfur dioxide (Mr = 64.1) to diffuse through the same plug under the same conditions. Give your answer in s to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 time is proportional to √M (rate ∝ 1/√M); M1 t(SO₂)/t(H₂) = √(64.1/2.0) = 5.66; A1 t = 20.0 × 5.66 = 113 s (3 s.f.).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to show that two gases diffuse at different rates, using a glass tube, cotton wool and concentrated solutions.
parts.answer: Soak cotton wool in concentrated ammonia and in concentrated hydrochloric acid. Place one plug at each end of a horizontal glass tube at the same time, close the ends, and leave the tube undisturbed. Note the position of the white ring of NH₄Cl after a set time (or measure its distance from each end).
parts.working: 1 mark two plugs placed at opposite ends at the same time, tube sealed/undisturbed; 1 mark measure distance of ring from each end and compare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two precautions for this experiment.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard (both solutions give toxic/irritant fumes); wear eye protection and gloves; keep the tube horizontal and not disturbed (not heated); use the same mass or size of cotton wool.
parts.working: 1 mark any safety precaution (fume cupboard, goggles, gloves); 1 mark a fair-test/accuracy precaution (same cotton wool, tube kept still, same length of time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why gases are easy to compress, whereas liquids are almost incompressible.
parts.answer: Gas molecules are far apart with large spaces between them, so pressure can push them closer together. In liquids the molecules are already touching (close together), so there is little space to compress them further.
parts.working: 1 mark gas molecules are far apart / large spaces; 1 mark pressure can reduce the spaces; 1 mark liquid molecules are already close together, so little compression is possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen (Mr = 2.0) and carbon dioxide (Mr = 44.0) are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Calculate how many times faster hydrogen diffuses than carbon dioxide. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.7 times faster

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the compressibility factor, Z, of a real gas, and state its value for an ideal gas.
parts.answer: Z = pV/nRT, where p is the measured pressure, V the volume, n the amount in mol and T the temperature in K. For an ideal gas Z = 1.
parts.working: 1 mark Z = pV/nRT (with p, V, n, T defined or the equation given); 1 mark Z = 1 for an ideal gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At 300 K and 101 kPa, helium is closer to ideal behaviour than carbon dioxide. Explain why, in terms of the size of the molecules and the forces between them.
parts.answer: Helium atoms are very small and have only very weak London (van der Waals) forces, so their own volume and attractions are negligible. CO₂ molecules have more electrons, so stronger van der Waals forces and a larger molecular volume, so they deviate more from ideal behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark He is small with negligible volume and very weak forces; 1 mark CO2 has more electrons, stronger attractions and larger molecular volume, so deviates more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.500 mol of a gas is in a container of volume 10.0 dm³ at 300 K. Calculate the pressure the gas would have if it behaved ideally. Give your answer in Pa to 3 significant figures. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The measured pressure of the gas is 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the compressibility factor, Z, to 3 significant figures and state whether the gas is more or less compressible than an ideal gas.
parts.answer: Z = 0.963; Z < 1, so the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas (attractive forces dominate).
parts.working: M1 Z = pV/nRT = (1.20 × 10⁵ × 0.0100)/(0.500 × 8.31 × 300) = 0.963; A1 Z < 1 means more compressible / attractive forces dominate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a real gas deviates strongly from ideal behaviour when it is cooled to a temperature close to its boiling point.
parts.answer: Near the boiling point the molecules have low kinetic energy and move slowly, so intermolecular attractions become significant. The molecules are pulled together and the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas (Z < 1), so it approaches liquefaction.
parts.working: 1 mark low kinetic energy / slow molecules at low temperature; 1 mark intermolecular attractions become significant; 1 mark molecules attract, so Z < 1 and the gas behaves less ideally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas equation for two effects. State the two effects and, for each, say whether it increases or decreases the measured pressure compared with the ideal pressure.
parts.answer: (1) The molecules have a finite volume, so the free space available is less than the container volume; this increases the pressure. (2) Intermolecular attractions pull molecules back from the walls, so the impact force is reduced; this decreases the pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark finite molecular volume (reduces free volume); 1 mark this increases the pressure; 1 mark attractions reduce the pressure (molecules pulled inwards).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the molar volume of an ideal gas at 298 K and 100 kPa. Give your answer in dm³ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 24.8 dm³ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: A real gas has a measured molar volume of 24.6 dm³ mol⁻¹ under the same conditions. Calculate its compressibility factor, Z, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 Z = measured Vm / ideal Vm, using the unrounded ideal Vm = 24.76 dm³ mol⁻¹: Z = 24.6/24.76 = 0.993; A1 Z < 1, so the gas is slightly more compressible than an ideal gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the volume correction for molecular size becomes significant at high pressure.
parts.answer: At high pressure the gas is compressed, so the molecules are forced close together and the volume they occupy becomes a large fraction of the container's volume. The space actually free for movement is then noticeably less than the total volume, so the measured pressure is higher than the ideal value.
parts.working: 1 mark at high pressure molecules occupy a significant fraction of the volume; 1 mark the free volume is less than the container volume, so the pressure is greater than ideal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gas X: 1.00 mol at 300 K and 2.00 dm³ has a measured pressure of 1.13 MPa. Calculate the ideal pressure and the compressibility factor Z. Give Z to 3 significant figures. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: Ideal p = 1.25 MPa; Z = 0.907.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether attractive or repulsive forces dominate in gas X under these conditions. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Attractive forces dominate because Z < 1 (the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas).
parts.working: 1 mark attractive forces (Z < 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas has Z = 0.85 at 250 K. State whether attractive or repulsive intermolecular forces are dominant, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Attractive forces dominate. Z < 1 means the measured pressure is less than the ideal pressure, so the molecules are attracting each other and reducing the pressure at the walls.
parts.working: 1 mark attractive forces dominate; 1 mark Z < 1 means pressure is lower than ideal because molecules attract each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon dioxide (Mr 44.0) and methane (Mr 16.0) are compared at the same temperature and pressure, close to room temperature. State which gas deviates more from ideal behaviour and explain your answer, referring to the forces between molecules.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide deviates more. CO₂ has more electrons, so its van der Waals (London) forces are stronger than those of CH₄ and its molecules attract each other more strongly. These attractions are significant at room temperature, so CO₂ has a Z value further below 1. Methane has fewer electrons, weaker attractions, and behaves more ideally.
parts.working: 1 mark CO₂ has stronger van der Waals forces (more electrons, larger molecule); 1 mark these attractions make CO₂ deviate more (Z further from 1); 1 mark CH₄ has weaker forces so behaves more ideally.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The compressibility factor Z of gases P and Q is measured at two temperatures, both at 10 MPa:
Gas P: Z = 0.86 at 200 K; Z = 0.95 at 300 K.
Gas Q: Z = 0.97 at 200 K; Z = 0.99 at 300 K.
State which gas is closer to ideal behaviour at 200 K and which has stronger intermolecular forces.
parts.answer: Gas Q is closer to ideal at 200 K (Z closer to 1). Gas P has stronger intermolecular forces (its Z is further below 1 at both temperatures).
parts.working: 1 mark Q closer to ideal; 1 mark P has stronger intermolecular forces (larger deviation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both gases move closer to ideal behaviour as the temperature increases from 200 K to 300 K.
parts.answer: At higher temperature the molecules have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and their attractions are less able to hold them together; the attractive effects become smaller relative to kinetic energy, so Z moves towards 1.
parts.working: 1 mark more kinetic energy at higher temperature; 1 mark intermolecular attractions less significant, so Z moves towards 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of gas has Z = 1.02. Calculate the volume occupied by 0.100 mol of this gas at 400 K and 150 kPa. Give your answer in dm³ to 3 significant figures. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 2.26 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance has a giant ionic lattice?
A carbon dioxide, CO₂
B magnesium chloride, MgCl₂
C silicon, Si
D iodine, I₂
parts.answer: B magnesium chloride, MgCl₂
parts.working: MgCl₂ is an ionic compound: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction. CO₂ and I₂ are simple molecular substances; silicon is a giant covalent (giant atomic) structure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sheet of sodium metal can be hammered into a new shape without shattering. Which explanation is correct?
A The metal bonds are covalent and break when the metal is bent.
B Layers of positive ions can slide over each other, while the delocalised electrons still hold the structure together.
C The electrons leave the metal and the ions are free to move apart.
D The positive ions and electrons swap places when the metal is bent.
parts.answer: B Layers of positive ions can slide over each other, while the delocalised electrons still hold the structure together.
parts.working: Metallic bonding is non-directional: the cations are held by a sea of delocalised electrons, which keeps the structure intact when layers slide. A describes covalent bonding, which is not present in metals. C would make the metal lose electrons and not be a solid; D is not a physical process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of sodium chloride, and state the coordination number of each ion.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arranged alternately in a regular three-dimensional cubic pattern. Each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ ion by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
parts.working: 1 mark giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in three dimensions; 1 mark regular/cubic arrangement held by electrostatic attraction; 1 mark each ion has 6 neighbours of opposite charge (6:6).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ionic solids such as sodium chloride are brittle, whereas metals can be bent.
parts.answer: When an ionic crystal is struck, layers of ions shift. This brings ions of the same charge next to each other, which repel, so the crystal splits along the plane. In a metal the layers of cations can slide because the delocalised electrons move with them and still hold the layers together.
parts.working: 1 mark shifting layers bring like charges together; 1 mark like charges repel, so the crystal breaks; 1 mark in metals the delocalised electrons allow layers to slide without fracture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium. Explain this in terms of the metallic bonding in each metal.
parts.answer: Each Mg atom contributes two delocalised electrons, compared with one for Na. Mg²⁺ ions are also smaller and more highly charged than Na⁺. This gives a stronger electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons, so more energy is needed to melt magnesium.
parts.working: 1 mark Mg contributes 2 delocalised electrons (Na contributes 1); 1 mark Mg²⁺ is smaller and more highly charged; 1 mark stronger metallic bonding, so higher melting point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of carbon atoms in 6.00 g of diamond. (Ar of C = 12.0; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.01 × 10²³ atoms

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four solids, A, B, C and D, were tested.
A: melting point 734 °C; does not conduct as a solid; conducts when molten; dissolves in water.
B: melting point 1085 °C; conducts when solid and when molten; can be hammered into sheets.
C: melting point 115 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water.
D: melting point 3550 °C; does not conduct as a solid; very hard; insoluble in water.
Classify each solid by type of structure and bonding, and give one reason for each classification.
parts.answer: A: giant ionic (e.g. KBr); ions are fixed when solid but mobile when molten or dissolved. B: metallic (e.g. copper); delocalised electrons conduct in the solid and liquid, and layers can slide. C: simple molecular (e.g. sulfur, S₈); weak van der Waals forces give a low melting point and no mobile charge. D: giant covalent (e.g. diamond); a strong network of covalent bonds with no mobile electrons, giving a very high melting point and hardness.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct classification with a reason (ionic: conducts only when ions mobile; metallic: delocalised electrons; molecular: low mp, no ions or electrons; giant covalent: very high mp, hard, no mobile charge).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid ionic compounds such as sodium chloride dissolve in water, whereas silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂, is insoluble. Explain this difference.
