parts.answer: Water molecules are polar and surround the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, forming ion–dipole attractions that release enough energy to overcome the lattice energy. In SiO₂ the atoms are linked by a three-dimensional network of very strong covalent bonds, which water cannot break; there are no separate ions to be solvated.
parts.working: 1 mark polar water molecules solvate ions (ion–dipole attraction); 1 mark this releases energy to overcome the ionic lattice; 1 mark SiO₂ is a covalent network that water cannot break, with no ions to solvate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Caesium chloride has a coordination number of 8:8 (each ion surrounded by eight ions of the opposite charge), whereas sodium chloride is 6:6. Explain this difference in terms of the sizes of the ions.
parts.answer: The Cs⁺ ion is much larger than Na⁺, so the ratio of the cation radius to the anion radius is larger. A larger cation can have eight chloride ions touching it, whereas a smaller Na⁺ ion can only touch six Cl⁻ ions without the ions overlapping/repelling the neighbours.
parts.working: 1 mark Cs⁺ is larger (larger radius ratio); 1 mark a larger cation can fit eight anions around it; 1 mark smaller Na⁺ fits only six, giving 6:6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of Mg²⁺ ions in 2.40 g of magnesium oxide, MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24.3; O = 16.0; L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.59 × 10²² Mg²⁺ ions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why graphite has a very high melting point and why it is soft and slippery.
parts.answer: Graphite is a giant covalent lattice of carbon atoms in layers. Strong covalent bonds within each layer must be broken to melt it, giving a high melting point. The layers are held together only by weak van der Waals forces, which are easily overcome, so the layers slide over each other and the solid is soft and slippery.
parts.working: 1 mark strong covalent bonds within layers (high mp); 1 mark weak van der Waals forces between layers; 1 mark layers slide, so soft/slippery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium oxide, MgO, melts at about 2850 °C, whereas sodium chloride, NaCl, melts at 801 °C. Explain this difference in terms of the charges and sizes of the ions in each lattice.
parts.answer: MgO contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, whereas NaCl contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The electrostatic attraction between ions is proportional to the product of their charges divided by their separation. The charges in MgO are twice as large on each ion, so the attraction is about four times larger for the same separation. The ions in MgO are also smaller, so the separation is smaller, giving a much stronger lattice that needs far more energy to melt.
parts.working: 1 mark MgO has 2+ and 2− ions (larger charges); 1 mark electrostatic attraction depends on charge product and inversely on separation; 1 mark smaller ions in MgO give a stronger lattice and a higher melting point.

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution of sodium bromide, giving a cream precipitate. Concentrated aqueous ammonia is then added to the precipitate. What is observed?
A The precipitate turns black and no solid remains
B The precipitate dissolves to give a colourless solution
C The precipitate is unchanged and a yellow solid forms
D The precipitate dissolves to give a blue solution
parts.answer: B The precipitate dissolves to give a colourless solution
parts.working: Silver bromide dissolves in concentrated ammonia to form the colourless complex [Ag(NH3)2]+. Silver chloride would dissolve even in dilute ammonia; silver iodide (yellow) does not dissolve at all. Option D is wrong because no copper is present.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A white solid X gives steamy fumes when warmed with concentrated sulfuric acid. A solution of X, acidified with dilute nitric acid, gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution that dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. What is X?
A sodium bromide
B sodium chloride
C sodium iodide
D sodium sulfate
parts.answer: B sodium chloride
parts.working: Chloride gives steamy HCl with concentrated H2SO4 (no redox). AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia. Bromide gives a cream precipitate, iodide a yellow one, and sulfate gives no steamy fumes.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three white solid sodium halides, P, Q and R, were each placed in a dry test tube and warmed with concentrated sulfuric acid. Observations:
P: steamy colourless fumes only.
Q: steamy fumes, a red-brown vapour and a choking smell.
R: a purple vapour that condenses as a grey-black solid on the cooler part of the tube, a yellow solid forms, and a smell of rotten eggs is detected.
Identify the halide ion in P, Q and R.
parts.answer: P chloride (Cl⁻); Q bromide (Br⁻); R iodide (I⁻)
parts.working: 1 mark each. P: HCl only, no redox. Q: HBr reduces H2SO4 to SO2 and is oxidised to Br2. R: HI reduces H2SO4 to S and H2S, and is oxidised to I2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction in which Q forms the red-brown vapour.
parts.answer: 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct formulae; 1 mark for balancing (2 Br, 4 H and 4 O on each side).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why R gives a yellow solid and a rotten-egg smell, but P does not.
parts.answer: Iodide ions are the strongest reducing agent of the three, so they reduce H₂SO₄ beyond SO₂ to sulfur (yellow solid) and to H₂S (rotten-egg smell). Chloride ions are too weak a reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid at all.
parts.working: 1 mark: iodide is the best reducing agent (most easily oxidised). 1 mark: sulfur is formed by reduction of S(+6) to S(0) and H2S by reduction to S(−2); chloride cannot reduce H2SO4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly describes bromine at room temperature?
A solid, black
B liquid, red-brown
C gas, pale green
D liquid, colourless
parts.answer: B liquid, red-brown
parts.working: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Chlorine is a pale green gas and iodine a black solid. No halogen is a colourless liquid at room temperature.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bond enthalpies: Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹; Br–Br 193 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement best explains why the Br–Br bond is weaker?
A Bromine has a higher electronegativity, so the bond is more polar.
B The Br–Br bond is longer, so the overlap between the bonding orbitals is smaller.
C Bromine atoms have more protons, so their nuclei repel the bonding pair.
D Each bromine atom has more lone pairs, which repel and weaken the bond.
parts.answer: B The Br–Br bond is longer, so the overlap between the bonding orbitals is smaller.
parts.working: Bond length rises from about 199 pm in Cl2 to about 228 pm in Br2, so the shared pair is further from the nuclei and the overlap is weaker. Bromine is less electronegative than chlorine (A is wrong). Nuclear repulsion of the bonding pair is not the cause (C). Cl2 and Br2 both have three lone pairs on each atom (D).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table gives data for the first four halogens.
Halogen | Mr | Boiling point / °C
F₂ | 38.0 | −188
Cl₂ | 70.9 | −34
Br₂ | 159.8 | 59
I₂ | 253.8 | 184
State the trend in boiling point from F₂ to I₂.
parts.answer: Boiling point increases down the group, from −188 °C to 184 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for the trend, with the direction stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend in terms of the forces between molecules.
parts.answer: The molecules are non-polar, so the forces between them are instantaneous induced dipole–induced dipole (London/van der Waals) forces. Larger halogen molecules have more electrons and larger electron clouds, so these forces are stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: the forces are induced dipole–induced dipole (van der Waals) forces. 1 mark: larger molecules have more electrons, so the forces are stronger. 1 mark: stronger forces need more energy to overcome, so boiling points rise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of iodine in 25.0 g of I₂ (Mr = 253.8). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436; Cl–Cl 242; I–I 151; H–Cl 431; H–I 299.
Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, for 2HCl(g) → H₂(g) + Cl₂(g).
parts.answer: +184 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Bonds broken: 2 × 431 = 862. Bonds formed: 436 + 242 = 678. ΔH = 862 − 678 = +184 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g).
parts.answer: +11 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Bonds broken: 2 × 299 = 598. Bonds formed: 436 + 151 = 587. ΔH = 598 − 587 = +11 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why hydrogen iodide decomposes on heating much more readily than hydrogen chloride.
parts.answer: The H–I bond is weaker (299 against 431 kJ mol⁻¹), and the enthalpy change for HI decomposition is much smaller (+11 against +184 kJ mol⁻¹), so far less energy is needed to break the bonds and the reaction is almost energy-neutral.
parts.working: 1 mark: H–I bond is weaker than H–Cl. 1 mark: the enthalpy change is much smaller, so less energy is needed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
First ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl 1251; Br 1140; I 1008.
State the trend in first ionisation energy from Cl to I and explain it.
parts.answer: The first ionisation energy decreases down the group. The outer electron is further from the nucleus, and is more shielded by the inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct trend. 1 mark: larger atoms, more shielding and a weaker attraction for the outer electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in first ionisation energy from Cl to I. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): F–F 158; Cl–Cl 242; H–H 436; H–F 565.
Calculate the enthalpy change for H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g).
parts.answer: −536 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Bonds broken: 436 + 158 = 594. Bonds formed: 2 × 565 = 1130. ΔH = 594 − 1130 = −536 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The F–F bond enthalpy (158) is lower than the Cl–Cl bond enthalpy (242), even though the F–F bond is shorter. Explain why.
parts.answer: Fluorine atoms are very small, so the lone pairs on the two atoms are close together and repel each other strongly. This repulsion weakens the shared pair of electrons, so less energy is needed to break the F–F bond.
parts.working: 1 mark: fluorine atoms are small, so the atoms and their lone pairs are close. 1 mark: lone-pair repulsion between the two F atoms. 1 mark: this weakens the bond, giving a low bond enthalpy.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Standard electrode potentials, E°: Cl₂/Cl⁻ = +1.36 V; Br₂/Br⁻ = +1.07 V; I₂/I⁻ = +0.54 V.
Calculate E°cell for Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E°cell for Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why bromine displaces iodide ions, but iodine does not displace bromide ions.
parts.answer: E°cell is positive for Br₂ + 2I⁻, so this reaction is feasible. The reverse reaction, 2Br⁻ + I₂, would have E°cell = −0.53 V, so it is not feasible.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive E°cell means the reaction is feasible. 1 mark: the reverse reaction has a negative E°cell.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict whether chlorine oxidises iodide ions, and give the E°cell for this reaction.
parts.answer: Yes. E°cell = 1.36 − 0.54 = +0.82 V, which is positive, so the reaction is feasible.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct E°cell value. 1 mark: positive, so the reaction occurs.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pauling electronegativities: H 2.2; F 4.0; Cl 3.0; Br 2.8; I 2.5.
Calculate the electronegativity difference for each H–X bond: H–F, H–Cl, H–Br and H–I.
parts.working: 1 mark: differences calculated. 1 mark: all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen fluoride has the most polar H–X bond, yet it is a weak acid, while hydrogen iodide is a strong acid. Explain this.
parts.answer: Acid strength depends on how easily the H–X bond breaks to release H⁺. The H–I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy (299 kJ mol⁻¹), so it breaks most easily. The H–F bond is the strongest, so HF releases few H⁺ ions despite its high polarity.
parts.working: 1 mark: acid strength depends on the ease of breaking the H–X bond. 1 mark: H–I is the weakest bond. 1 mark: H–F is the strongest bond, so polarity is not the main factor.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide:
3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O
How many moles of electrons are transferred per mole of Cl₂ that reacts?
A 0.33
B 0.67
C 1.67
D 5.00
parts.working: Five Cl atoms are reduced from 0 to −1, gaining 5 electrons, and one Cl atom is oxidised from 0 to +5, losing 5 electrons, per 3 mol Cl₂. So 5 ÷ 3 = 1.67 mol electrons per mol Cl₂. Option A is 1 ÷ 3; B is 2 ÷ 3; D forgets to divide by 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: correct products Cl⁻ and ClO⁻. 1 mark: balanced for atoms and charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using oxidation numbers, why this is a disproportionation reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine (oxidation number 0 in Cl₂) is oxidised to +1 in ClO⁻ and reduced to −1 in Cl⁻. The same element is both oxidised and reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxidation numbers 0, +1 and −1 correctly identified. 1 mark: the same element is both oxidised and reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of the solution formed.
parts.answer: Household bleach or disinfectant (sodium chlorate(I) solution).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct use.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 2.00 dm³ sample of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaOH reacts completely with chlorine: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
Calculate the amount, in mol, of NaOH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine, Cl₂ (Mr 70.9), needed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of NaClO (Mr 74.5) formed.
parts.working: Amount NaClO = 0.400 mol; mass = 0.400 × 74.5 = 29.8 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine dissolves in water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. Explain why chlorine water first turns litmus paper red and then turns it white.
parts.answer: HCl is a strong acid, so it turns litmus red. HClO is an oxidising agent that bleaches the coloured indicator, so the paper is then decolourised to white.
parts.working: 1 mark: HCl is an acid giving red colour. 1 mark: HClO bleaches (oxidises) the dye.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sodium carbonate solution is added to chlorine water and effervescence occurs. Name the gas and write the ionic equation for the reaction of the acid present.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide. 2H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → H₂O + CO₂
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon dioxide. 1 mark: correct ionic equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, disproportionates when warmed: 3ClO⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻.
Explain, using oxidation numbers, why this is a disproportionation reaction.
parts.answer: The Cl in ClO⁻ is +1. It is reduced to −1 in Cl⁻ and oxidised to +5 in ClO₃⁻. The same element is both reduced and oxidised.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct oxidation numbers for all three species. 1 mark: the same element is both reduced and oxidised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaClO solution is warmed until all the ClO⁻ has reacted by this equation. Calculate the mass of ClO₃⁻ formed, as NaClO₃ (Mr 106.5). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction only occurs at a useful rate when the solution is warmed.
parts.answer: Warming increases the kinetic energy of the ions, so more collisions have enough energy to exceed the activation energy. At room temperature the change is very slow.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher temperature gives more particles with energy above the activation energy. 1 mark: at room temperature the reaction is slow.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
100 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is shaken at room temperature with 0.0800 mol of chlorine: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
Show which reactant is in excess.
parts.answer: NaOH needed = 2 × 0.0800 = 0.160 mol. NaOH available = 0.100 × 2.00 = 0.200 mol. The NaOH is in excess, so chlorine is the limiting reactant.
parts.working: 1 mark: NaOH needed is 0.160 mol. 1 mark: NaOH available is 0.200 mol, so NaOH is in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of NaOH left unreacted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of NaClO (Mr 74.5) formed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NaClO = 0.0800 mol; mass = 0.0800 × 74.5 = 5.96 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypochlorous acid, HClO, is a weak acid with Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³. Write the expression for Ka of HClO.
parts.answer: Ka = [H⁺][ClO⁻] ÷ [HClO]
parts.working: Standard acid dissociation expression.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HClO. Assume [H⁺] = [ClO⁻] and [HClO] ≈ 0.10 mol dm⁻³. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why HClO is a more effective disinfectant at lower pH.
parts.answer: At lower pH the concentration of H⁺ is higher, so the equilibrium HClO ⇌ H⁺ + ClO⁻ moves to the left and more chlorine is present as HClO. HClO is the species that kills micro-organisms; ClO⁻ is much less effective.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the left, giving more HClO. 1 mark: HClO is the active killing species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why chlorine water bleaches coloured dyes.
parts.answer: Chlorine reacts with water to form HClO. HClO is an oxidising agent that destroys the coloured molecules of the dye, so the colour is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: HClO is formed from chlorine and water. 1 mark: HClO oxidises the dye and destroys its colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give an equation for the decomposition of HClO in sunlight, which also produces oxygen.
parts.answer: 2HClO → 2HCl + O₂
parts.working: Balanced: 2 H, 2 Cl and 2 O on each side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hot concentrated NaOH gives chlorate(V), ClO₃⁻, whereas cold dilute NaOH gives chlorate(I), ClO⁻. Explain the effect of temperature on the products.
parts.answer: Warming gives the ClO⁻ ions enough energy to overcome the activation energy for their disproportionation, which gives ClO₃⁻ and Cl⁻. In the cold, the ClO⁻ does not react further, so it remains the main product.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher temperature gives more particles above the activation energy. 1 mark: ClO⁻ disproportionates to ClO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ when warm. 1 mark: cold conditions keep the reaction slow, so ClO⁻ is the major product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of chlorine, measured at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹), needed to make 500 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaClO solution by reaction with cold dilute NaOH.
parts.answer: 1.20 dm³
parts.working: Amount NaClO = 0.500 × 0.100 = 0.0500 mol. One mol Cl₂ gives one mol NaClO, so 0.0500 mol Cl₂ × 24.0 = 1.20 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium chloride. What is observed?
A The solution turns orange-brown
B No visible change; the solution remains yellow-green
C A white precipitate forms
D The solution turns purple
parts.answer: B No visible change; the solution remains yellow-green
parts.working: Chlorine cannot oxidise chloride ions, so no reaction occurs and the chlorine water keeps its colour. Orange-brown would show bromine formed from bromide, and purple would show iodine formed from iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution containing starch. Describe the colour seen.
parts.answer: A blue-black colour.
parts.working: Iodine formed reacts with starch to give a blue-black colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
parts.working: 1 mark for correct formulae and balancing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the blue-black colour shows.
parts.answer: Iodine (I₂) has been formed, so chlorine has displaced iodide ions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electron transfer and oxidising power, why chlorine displaces bromide ions from solution but bromine does not displace chloride ions.
parts.answer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine; it gains electrons more readily. Cl₂ takes electrons from Br⁻, forming Br₂ and Cl⁻. Bromine is a weaker oxidising agent, so it cannot take electrons from Cl⁻ (chloride is harder to oxidise than bromide).
parts.working: 1 mark: Cl₂ is the stronger oxidising agent. 1 mark: Cl₂ oxidises Br⁻ by transferring electrons. 1 mark: Br₂ is too weak an oxidising agent to oxidise Cl⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each halogen solution was added to a potassium halide solution in a test tube, cyclohexane was added and the mixture was shaken. Results:
Tube 1: chlorine water + potassium chloride: no new colour in the cyclohexane layer.
Tube 2: chlorine water + potassium bromide: cyclohexane layer turns orange-brown.
Tube 3: chlorine water + potassium iodide: cyclohexane layer turns purple.
Tube 4: bromine water + potassium chloride: no new colour.
Tube 5: bromine water + potassium iodide: cyclohexane layer turns purple.
Tube 6: iodine solution + potassium bromide: no new colour.
Identify the tubes in which a reaction occurred, and the halogen formed in each.
parts.answer: Tubes 2, 3 and 5. Tube 2 forms bromine; tubes 3 and 5 form iodine.
parts.working: 1 mark: the three correct tubes. 1 mark: the halogen formed in each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an ionic equation for the reaction in tube 5.
parts.answer: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂
parts.working: 1 mark: correct formulae. 1 mark: balanced with correct charges.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Place chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of oxidising power, and justify your order from the results.
parts.answer: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide, bromine displaces iodide but not chloride, and iodine displaces neither.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct order. 1 mark: justified from the displacement results, with the more oxidising halogen displacing the less oxidising halide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why there is no change in tube 6.
parts.answer: Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine, so it cannot oxidise bromide ions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
0.0400 mol of potassium iodide reacts completely with excess bromine water: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.
Calculate the amount, in mol, of iodine formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iodine formed (Mr = 253.8). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 0.0200 × 253.8 = 5.076 g, which is 5.08 g to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 3.00 g mixture of potassium chloride and potassium iodide is dissolved in water and excess chlorine water is added. Only the iodide ions react: 2KI + Cl₂ → 2KCl + I₂. The solution is evaporated and the iodine is removed by heating. The solid left has a mass of 2.41 g. (Mr: KCl 74.6; KI 166.0.)
Calculate the mass of potassium iodide in the original mixture. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Let x g be the mass of KI. Each mole of KI gives one mole of KCl, so the final solid mass = (3.00 − x) + x × 74.6 ÷ 166.0. Then 2.41 = 3.00 − 0.5506x, so x = 0.59 ÷ 0.5506 = 1.07 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mass of potassium chloride in the original mixture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iodine solution is added to aqueous sodium fluoride. Predict whether a reaction occurs and explain your answer.
parts.answer: No reaction. Iodine is a much weaker oxidising agent than fluorine, so it cannot remove electrons from fluoride ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: no reaction. 1 mark: I₂ is too weak an oxidising agent to oxidise F⁻ (fluorine is the most oxidising halogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine gas, 2.40 dm³ at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹), is bubbled through excess potassium bromide solution. Calculate the amount, in mol, of chlorine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of bromine formed (Br₂, Mr = 159.8). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, so 0.100 mol Br₂ is formed. Mass = 0.100 × 159.8 = 15.98 g, which is 16.0 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to show that a solution contains bromide ions.
parts.answer: Add chlorine water and shake the mixture with cyclohexane. An orange-brown colour in the cyclohexane layer shows that bromine has been formed, so bromide ions were present.
parts.working: 1 mark: add chlorine water (oxidising agent). 1 mark: shake with an organic solvent such as cyclohexane. 1 mark: orange-brown layer shows Br₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ potassium iodide solution is treated with chlorine water of concentration 0.0300 mol dm⁻³ until the iodide is just used up. Calculate the mass of iodine formed (Mr = 253.8).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of chlorine water needed to react completely with the iodide ions, in cm³.
parts.answer: 33.3 cm³
parts.working: 2I⁻ + Cl₂ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, so amount Cl₂ = 0.00100 mol. Volume = 0.00100 ÷ 0.0300 = 0.0333 dm³ = 33.3 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For the reaction Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, state the change in oxidation number of bromine.
parts.answer: −1 to 0 (an increase of 1, so bromine is oxidised).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent: Cl₂. Reducing agent: Br⁻.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: Predict whether a reaction occurs when bromine water is added to aqueous sodium chloride. Write an equation if a reaction occurs.
parts.answer: No reaction. Bromine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine and cannot oxidise Cl⁻.
parts.working: 1 mark: no reaction, with a reason based on oxidising power.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: Predict whether a reaction occurs when iodine solution is added to aqueous sodium bromide. Write an equation if a reaction occurs.
parts.answer: No reaction. Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine and cannot oxidise Br⁻.
parts.working: 1 mark: no reaction, with a reason based on oxidising power.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.text: Predict whether a reaction occurs when chlorine water is added to aqueous sodium iodide. Write an equation if a reaction occurs.
parts.answer: Reaction occurs: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent).
parts.working: 1 mark: reaction occurs. 1 mark: correct balanced ionic equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine is added to drinking water to kill bacteria. Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with water.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO
parts.working: 1 mark: HCl and HClO as products. 1 mark: balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the dissociation of HClO in water, and name the ion formed.
parts.answer: HClO ⇌ H⁺ + ClO⁻; the ion formed is the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct equation with the ⇌ sign. 1 mark: hypochlorite ion (chlorate(I) ion), ClO⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why only a low concentration of chlorine is used in drinking water.
parts.answer: Chlorine is toxic, and a high concentration gives an unpleasant taste and smell and harms health.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one micro-organism that chlorine kills easily and one micro-organism that is resistant to chlorine.
parts.answer: E. coli (a bacterium) is killed easily. Cryptosporidium (a parasite with a tough protective shell, the oocyst) is resistant to chlorine.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A water plant treats 3.60 × 10⁶ dm³ of water each day with a chlorine dose of 2.0 mg dm⁻³. Calculate the mass of chlorine used each day, in kg.
parts.answer: 7.2 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Excess chlorine can be removed with sodium thiosulfate: S₂O₃²⁻ + 4Cl₂ + 5H₂O → 2SO₄²⁻ + 8Cl⁻ + 10H⁺.
Give the average oxidation number of S in S₂O₃²⁻ and the oxidation number of S in SO₄²⁻.
parts.answer: +2 (average) in S₂O₃²⁻; +6 in SO₄²⁻
parts.working: S₂O₃²⁻: 2x + 3(−2) = −2, so x = +2 (average). SO₄²⁻: x + 4(−2) = −2, so x = +6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium thiosulfate, Na₂S₂O₃ (Mr 158.1), needed to remove 0.500 g of chlorine (Mr 70.9). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hypochlorous acid, HClO, has pKa = 7.5. The fraction of total chlorine present as HClO can be estimated by fraction = 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(pH − pKa)).
Calculate this fraction at pH 6.5 and at pH 8.5. Give each to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which pH gives the better disinfection and why.
parts.answer: pH 6.5 gives better disinfection, because about 91 % of the chlorine is present as HClO, the active killing species, compared with about 9 % at pH 8.5.
parts.working: 1 mark: pH 6.5 is better. 1 mark: a much higher fraction of HClO is present at pH 6.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chloroform, CHCl₃ (Mr 119.4), can form when chlorine reacts with organic matter in water. A water sample contains 25.0 µg of chloroform per dm³. Calculate the amount, in mol, of chloroform in 5.00 dm³ of this water. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water containing excess chlorine is treated with sodium thiosulfate before it is discharged into a river. Explain why this treatment is needed.
parts.answer: Chlorine and HClO are toxic to fish, plants and other aquatic organisms. Thiosulfate reduces the chlorine to harmless chloride ions before discharge.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine is toxic to aquatic life. 1 mark: thiosulfate converts chlorine to chloride ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water companies test for a small residual of chlorine at the tap.
parts.answer: A residual chlorine level shows that disinfectant is still present to kill any bacteria that may have entered the pipes after treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine is still present (not used up). 1 mark: it kills bacteria that enter the distribution pipes after treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water treatment companies must balance the benefits and risks of adding chlorine.
parts.answer: Benefit: chlorine kills pathogenic bacteria and viruses, preventing diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Risk: chlorine reacts with dissolved natural organic matter to form chlorinated by-products such as chloroform, some of which may be harmful in the long term. Companies therefore remove organic matter first and control the dose to keep chlorine low but effective.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine kills pathogens. 1 mark: chlorine forms harmful by-products with organic matter. 1 mark: the dose must be controlled to keep by-products low. 1 mark: organic matter is removed before chlorination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of chlorine measured at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) needed to treat 500 dm³ of water at a dose of 2.0 mg dm⁻³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 339 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine can be made by electrolysis of concentrated brine: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH. Calculate the mass of NaCl (Mr 58.5) needed to make 1.00 kg of chlorine. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims: 'Adding more chlorine always makes water safer.' Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: Partly wrong. More chlorine gives more HClO and better disinfection, but excess chlorine is toxic, gives an unpleasant taste and smell, and increases harmful chlorinated by-products. A controlled low dose gives the best balance.
parts.working: 1 mark: a higher dose kills more micro-organisms. 1 mark: excess chlorine is harmful and forms by-products. 1 mark: a controlled dose is the correct conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At pH 6.5, 0.909 of the chlorine-containing species present is HClO (the rest is ClO⁻). A water sample contains 1.50 mg dm⁻³ of chlorine, Cl₂, which is converted to HClO and HCl by reaction with water. Calculate the mass of HClO, in mg dm⁻³, present at pH 6.5. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: HClO 52.5; Cl₂ 70.9.)
parts.answer: 1.01 mg dm⁻³
parts.working: Each mol Cl₂ gives one mol HClO, so the mass of Cl₂ converted is 1.50 mg dm⁻³. Mass of HClO = 0.909 × 1.50 × 52.5 ÷ 70.9 = 1.01 mg dm⁻³. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At pH 8.5 only about 9.09 % of the chlorine is HClO. Explain what this means for the chlorine dose needed.
parts.answer: A higher total chlorine dose is needed at pH 8.5 to give the same amount of HClO and so the same disinfection.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of: (a) Br in BrF₅; (b) Br in BrO₃⁻; (c) I in IO₃⁻; (d) I in I₂O₅.
parts.working: (a) Five F at −1 gives Br +5. (b) 3 O at −2 and charge −1 gives Br +5. (c) Same as (b) gives I +5. (d) Two I atoms share +10, so each is +5. 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of: (a) chlorate(VII) ion; (b) chlorate(III) ion; (c) chlorate(I) ion.
parts.answer: (a) ClO₄⁻; (b) ClO₂⁻; (c) ClO⁻
parts.working: Chlorine oxidation numbers +7, +3 and +1 respectively, with oxygen −2 and an overall ionic charge of −1 in each case. 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium chlorite, NaClO₂ (Mr 90.5), is used to make chlorine dioxide. Calculate the percentage by mass of chlorine in NaClO₂. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Mass of Cl = 35.5 in Mr 90.5; percentage = 35.5 ÷ 90.5 × 100 = 39.2 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iodine monochloride, ICl, is an interhalogen compound. State the oxidation numbers of I and Cl in ICl.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine has the negative oxidation number in ICl, using electronegativity values (Cl 3.0; I 2.5).
parts.answer: Chlorine is the more electronegative element, so it takes the negative oxidation number.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why fluorine never shows a positive oxidation number in its compounds.
parts.answer: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so it always attracts the shared electrons and takes the oxidation number −1.
parts.working: 1 mark: fluorine is most electronegative. 1 mark: it always gains electron density, so its oxidation number is −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine dioxide is made by: 2NaClO₂ + Cl₂ → 2ClO₂ + 2NaCl. Explain, with oxidation numbers, which substance is the oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent: Cl₂ (Cl 0 → −1 in NaCl). Reducing agent: NaClO₂ (Cl +3 → +4 in ClO₂).
parts.working: 1 mark: Cl in NaClO₂ goes from +3 to +4, so it is oxidised. 1 mark: Cl₂ goes from 0 to −1, so it is reduced. 1 mark: the oxidising agent is Cl₂ and the reducing agent is NaClO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ClO₂ (Mr 67.5) formed from 10.0 g of NaClO₂ (Mr 90.5), assuming complete reaction. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NaClO₂ = 10.0 ÷ 90.5 = 0.110 mol. This gives 0.110 mol ClO₂ (1:1). Mass = 0.110 × 67.5 = 7.46 g.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: Sodium chlorate(V), NaClO₃, decomposes on heating: 2NaClO₃ → 2NaCl + 3O₂. State the oxidation number changes of Cl and O.
parts.answer: Cl: +5 → −1 (reduced); O: −2 → 0 (oxidised).
parts.working: 1 mark for Cl (+5 to −1, reduced). 1 mark for O (−2 to 0, oxidised).

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen formed from 10.0 g of NaClO₃ (Mr 106.5). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NaClO₃ = 10.0 ÷ 106.5 = 0.0939 mol. O₂ = 1.5 × 0.0939 = 0.1408 mol. Mass = 0.1408 × 32.0 = 4.51 g. 1 mark for the amount of O₂, 1 mark for the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Household bleach contains NaClO. Mixing bleach with acid (HCl) gives: NaClO + 2HCl → NaCl + H₂O + Cl₂. Identify the element that is reduced and state the change in its oxidation number.
parts.answer: Chlorine in NaClO is reduced, from +1 to 0.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine is reduced. 1 mark: change +1 to 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mixing bleach with acid releases a toxic gas.
parts.answer: Acid converts the hypochlorite to chlorine gas, which is toxic and escapes, so bleach and acid should never be mixed.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorine gas is formed from the chlorine in NaClO (+1) and HCl (−1), and it is toxic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxidation number of Cl in HClO₄, ClO₂ and Cl₂O.
parts.answer: HClO₄: +7; ClO₂: +4; Cl₂O: +1
parts.working: HClO₄: H +1, 4 O −8, so Cl = +7. ClO₂: 2 O −4, so Cl = +4. Cl₂O: O −2, so each Cl = +1. 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine dioxide preparation: 5NaClO₂ + 4HCl → 4ClO₂ + 5NaCl + 2H₂O. Identify the element that is both oxidised and reduced, and give its oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: Chlorine in chlorite, NaClO₂: +3 is oxidised to +4 in ClO₂ and reduced to −1 in NaCl.
parts.working: 1 mark for the oxidation (+3 to +4). 1 mark for the reduction (+3 to −1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ClO₂ (Mr 67.5) formed from 5.00 g of NaClO₂ (Mr 90.5), assuming complete reaction. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NaClO₂ = 5.00 ÷ 90.5 = 0.05525 mol. ClO₂ = 0.05525 × 4/5 = 0.04420 mol. Mass = 0.04420 × 67.5 = 2.98 g. 1 mark for the amount of ClO₂, 1 mark for the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine dioxide is made by 2NaClO₂ + Cl₂ → 2ClO₂ + 2NaCl. A student uses 10.0 g of NaClO₂ (Mr 90.5) and obtains an actual yield of 6.00 g of ClO₂ (Mr 67.5). Calculate the percentage yield, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Theoretical mass: 10.0 ÷ 90.5 × 67.5 = 7.46 g (1:1 ratio of NaClO₂ to ClO₂). Percentage yield = 6.00 ÷ 7.46 × 100 = 80.4 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bleaching powder contains calcium chlorate(I), Ca(ClO)₂ (Mr 143.1). Excess hydrochloric acid releases chlorine: Ca(ClO)₂ + 4HCl → CaCl₂ + 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the mass of Cl₂ (Mr 70.9) released from 10.0 g of Ca(ClO)₂. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount Ca(ClO)₂ = 10.0 ÷ 143.1 = 0.0699 mol. Amount Cl₂ = 2 × 0.0699 = 0.1398 mol. Mass = 0.1398 × 70.9 = 9.91 g. 1 mark for the amount of Cl₂, 1 mark for the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the highest oxidation number that chlorine, bromine and iodine each show in their oxoanions, and explain why fluorine cannot show a similar oxoanion.
parts.answer: Chlorine +7 (ClO₄⁻), bromine +7 (BrO₄⁻) and iodine +7 (IO₄⁻). Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so it cannot have a positive oxidation number and cannot form oxoanions with oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the three highest oxidation numbers (Cl, Br, I). 1 mark for the fluorine explanation: it is the most electronegative element, so it cannot have a positive oxidation number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium chlorate(V), KClO₃ (Mr 122.5), decomposes on heating: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Calculate the mass of KClO₃ needed to produce 1.00 dm³ of oxygen at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount O₂ = 1.00 ÷ 24.0 = 0.04167 mol. Amount KClO₃ = 0.04167 × 2/3 = 0.02778 mol. Mass = 0.02778 × 122.5 = 3.40 g. 1 mark for the amount of KClO₃, 1 mark for the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxidation number of Mn in MnO₄⁻ and the average oxidation number of S in S₄O₆²⁻.
parts.answer: Mn: +7; S (average): +2.5
parts.working: MnO₄⁻: Mn + 4(−2) = −1, so Mn = +7. S₄O₆²⁻: 4S + 6(−2) = −2, so 4S = +10 and the average is +2.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation shows a reaction in which nitrogen is reduced?
A 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O
B 2NO → N₂ + O₂
C 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂
D N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
parts.answer: B 2NO → N₂ + O₂
parts.working: In NO, nitrogen is +2; in N₂ it is 0, so nitrogen gains electrons and is reduced. In A, N goes from −3 to +2 (oxidised); in C, N goes from +2 to +4 (oxidised); in D, N goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Selective catalytic reduction of nitrogen oxides uses ammonia: 6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O. How many moles of N₂ are formed per mole of NO₂ that reacts?
A 0.86
B 1.17
C 1.33
D 1.75
parts.working: 7 mol N₂ are formed from 6 mol NO₂, so 7 ÷ 6 = 1.17 mol N₂ per mol NO₂. Option A is the inverted ratio (6 ÷ 7); C is 8 ÷ 6, which uses the NH₃ ratio; D is 7 ÷ 4 with no basis in the equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why ammonia acts as a Lewis base?
A It donates a proton to water.
B It has a lone pair of electrons that it can donate to form a dative covalent bond.
C It has an empty orbital that accepts an electron pair.
D It carries a positive charge.
parts.answer: B It has a lone pair of electrons that it can donate to form a dative covalent bond.
parts.working: A Lewis base donates an electron pair. Ammonia uses its lone pair on nitrogen, for example to form [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ or NH₄⁺. Donating a proton describes a Brønsted–Lowry base, not a Lewis base; ammonia has no empty orbital; and NH₃ is neutral.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous ammonia? Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K, and Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.
A 9.1
B 10.9
C 11.1
D 12.9
parts.working: [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pOH = 2.87; pH = 14.00 − 2.87 = 11.1. Options A and D do not come from this method; B is a value below the correct pH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated aqueous ammonia and concentrated hydrochloric acid are brought close together. A white smoke forms. Name the white solid and write the equation for its formation.
parts.answer: Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl. NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl
parts.working: 1 mark: correct name of the solid. 1 mark: balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the Brønsted–Lowry acid and the Brønsted–Lowry base in this reaction.
parts.answer: Acid: HCl (proton donor). Base: NH₃ (proton acceptor).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonia is made by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the heat released when 1.00 kg of NH₃ (Mr 17.0) is formed. Give your answer in kJ to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NH₃ = 1000 ÷ 17.0 = 58.8 mol. Each mol NH₃ releases 92 ÷ 2 = 46 kJ. Heat released = 58.8 × 46 = 2.71 × 10³ kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect on the equilibrium position of removing ammonia as it forms, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: The equilibrium moves to the right, giving a higher yield of ammonia.
parts.working: 1 mark: equilibrium moves right. 1 mark: removing a product lowers its concentration, so the position moves to restore it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ aqueous ammonia is diluted with water to 250 cm³. Calculate the new concentration of ammonia, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.0200 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pH of the diluted solution. Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Assume [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zinc sulfide is roasted in air: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Give two sources of sulfur dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur (such as coal or oil); roasting of sulfide ores; volcanoes (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the change in oxidation number of sulfur in this reaction and whether sulfur is oxidised or reduced.
parts.answer: −2 to +4; sulfur is oxidised.
parts.working: 1 mark for the change; 1 mark for oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6), and why sulfur dioxide makes rain more acidic. Give equations where relevant.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide dissolves in rain to form weak carbonic acid, giving pH about 5.6. SO₂ dissolves to form H₂SO₃, which is oxidised to H₂SO₄, a strong acid, so the pH falls to below 5.6.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ forms a weak acid giving pH 5.6. 1 mark: SO₂ forms sulfuric acid, a strong acid, which lowers the pH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 2.00 kg sample of ZnS (Mr 97.5) is roasted completely by 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Calculate the mass of SO₂ (Mr 64.1) formed. Give your answer in kg to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The SO₂ from part (a) is oxidised completely to H₂SO₄ by hydrogen peroxide, SO₂ + H₂O₂ → H₂SO₄. Calculate the mass of H₂SO₄ (Mr 98.1) formed, in kg.
parts.working: Amount H₂SO₄ = amount SO₂ = 20.5 mol. Mass = 20.5 × 98.1 = 2012 g = 2.01 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Flue gas desulfurisation uses limestone: 2CaCO₃ + 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄ + 2CO₂. Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ (Mr 100.1) needed to remove 1.00 kg of SO₂ (Mr 64.1). Give your answer in kg to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount SO₂ = 1000 ÷ 64.1 = 15.6 mol. CaCO₃ needed = 15.6 mol (1:1). Mass = 15.6 × 100.1 = 1562 g = 1.56 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of the calcium sulfate produced.
parts.answer: Making plasterboard (gypsum) or cement.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain the effect of increasing the temperature on (i) the equilibrium yield and (ii) the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: (i) A higher temperature moves the equilibrium to the left (the endothermic direction), so the yield of SO₃ falls. (ii) The rate increases because the molecules have more energy and collide more frequently with enough energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: yield falls on heating (exothermic forward reaction). 1 mark: equilibrium shifts left. 1 mark: rate increases with temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plant operates at only 1–2 atm, although increasing pressure would favour SO₃. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The yield is already high at 1–2 atm, so the extra yield from higher pressure does not justify the cost of stronger equipment and higher energy use.
parts.working: 1 mark: yield is already high enough; higher pressure costs more than it gains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A marble statue is attacked by acid rain: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ (Mr 100.1) that reacts completely with 0.400 mol of H₂SO₄.
parts.working: 1 mol H₂SO₄ reacts with 1 mol CaCO₃, so 0.400 mol CaCO₃ are used. Mass = 0.400 × 100.1 = 40.0 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas given off in this reaction.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two effects of acid rain on the environment, and one way to reduce the sulfur dioxide released from power stations.
parts.answer: Effects: acidification of lakes that harms fish and other aquatic life; damage to limestone and marble buildings and statues; damage to forests and soils (any two). Reduction: fit flue gas desulfurisation, or burn low-sulfur fuel.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two correct effects; 1 mark for a valid reduction method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur dioxide is tested by passing it into acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution. State the colour change seen.
parts.answer: Orange to green.
parts.working: 1 mark: Cr(VI) (orange) is reduced to Cr(III) (green).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the change in oxidation number of sulfur, and explain why SO₂ is the reducing agent in this test.
parts.answer: +4 to +6. Sulfur is oxidised, so SO₂ is the reducing agent that reduces the dichromate.
parts.working: 1 mark: +4 to +6. 1 mark: sulfur is oxidised, so SO₂ is the reducing agent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rain contains 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ of H₂SO₄. Assume the first dissociation is complete and ignore the second. Calculate the pH of the rain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare this with normal rain (pH about 5.6) and state what this shows about acid rain.
parts.answer: This rain is more acidic (lower pH) than normal rain, so it shows acid rain.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower pH than normal rain. 1 mark: confirms the rain is acid rain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water: SO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₃. Explain why the solution is acidic.
parts.answer: H₂SO₃ partially dissociates to release H⁺ ions, which make the solution acidic.
parts.working: 1 mark: H₂SO₃ is an acid that releases H⁺. 1 mark: partial dissociation (weak acid) gives a solution that is acidic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a solution of H₂SO₃ has a higher pH than an H₂SO₄ solution of the same concentration.
parts.answer: H₂SO₃ is a weak acid, so it dissociates only partially and gives fewer H⁺ ions. H₂SO₄ is a strong acid and dissociates fully in its first step, giving more H⁺ ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: H₂SO₃ is weak (partial dissociation). 1 mark: H₂SO₄ is strong (complete first dissociation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cargo ship burns 800 kg of heavy fuel oil per hour, containing 2.7 % sulfur by mass. Assume all the sulfur is converted into SO₂. Calculate the mass of SO₂ (Mr 64.1) formed per hour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way the sulfur content of ship fuel can be reduced.
parts.answer: Use low-sulfur fuel, or fit exhaust scrubbers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of nitrogen gas that depend on its lack of reactivity.
parts.answer: Filling food packaging to prevent oxidation and spoilage; filling light bulbs or providing an inert atmosphere for welding (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in a nitrogen molecule, N₂, in terms of shared electron pairs.
parts.answer: There is a triple covalent bond between the two N atoms: one σ bond and two π bonds, making three shared pairs. Each N atom also has one lone pair.
parts.working: 1 mark: triple bond with three shared pairs (one σ and two π). 1 mark: one lone pair on each nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): N≡N 944; O=O 496; N=O 631. Calculate the enthalpy change for N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g).
parts.answer: +178 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Bonds broken: 944 + 496 = 1440. Bonds formed: 2 × 631 = 1262. ΔH = 1440 − 1262 = +178 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this reaction does not occur in the atmosphere at room temperature, but does occur in a car engine.
parts.answer: The reaction is endothermic and has a high activation energy because of the strong N≡N bond. Only at the high temperature of a car engine do enough molecules have enough energy to react.
parts.working: 1 mark: high activation energy from the N≡N bond. 1 mark: high temperature gives enough molecules above the activation energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen and oxygen react together only at high temperatures, such as in lightning, although the reaction is endothermic. Use the idea of activation energy in your answer.
parts.answer: The N≡N bond is very strong, so the activation energy for the reaction is high. At high temperatures, many more molecules have energy greater than the activation energy, so the rate of reaction increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong N≡N bond gives a high activation energy. 1 mark: high temperature increases the proportion of molecules with energy above the activation energy. 1 mark: the rate increases so the reaction becomes significant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): N≡N 944; H–H 436; N–H 391. Calculate the enthalpy change for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ using these values.
parts.answer: −94 kJ mol⁻¹ (for 2 mol NH₃)
parts.working: Bonds broken: 944 + 3 × 436 = 2252. Bonds formed: 6 × 391 = 2346. ΔH = 2252 − 2346 = −94 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the enthalpy change per mole of NH₃ formed, and state the sign of the change.
parts.answer: −47 kJ mol⁻¹ per mole of NH₃; the reaction is exothermic.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Despite the reaction being exothermic, nitrogen and hydrogen do not react at room temperature. Explain.
parts.answer: The N≡N bond is very strong, so the activation energy is high. At room temperature very few molecules have enough energy to react, so the rate is extremely slow without a catalyst.
parts.working: 1 mark: high activation energy. 1 mark: few molecules have enough energy at room temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Liquid air is fractionally distilled to obtain nitrogen. Nitrogen boils at −196 °C and oxygen boils at −183 °C. Explain which gas is collected first when the liquid is warmed.
parts.answer: Nitrogen is collected first, because it has the lower boiling point and so it evaporates first.
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrogen has the lower boiling point. 1 mark: it vaporises first and is collected first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonium nitrite decomposes on heating: NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the volume of N₂, at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹), formed from 100 g of NH₄NO₂ (Mr 64.0).
parts.answer: 37.5 dm³
parts.working: Amount NH₄NO₂ = 100 ÷ 64.0 = 1.5625 mol. Amount N₂ = 1.5625 mol. Volume = 1.5625 × 24.0 = 37.5 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 5.00 dm³ cylinder contains nitrogen at a pressure of 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 298 K. Use pV = nRT (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) to calculate the mass of N₂ (Mr 28.0) in the cylinder. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen molecules are non-polar, although the N≡N bond is a covalent bond between two atoms. Explain why N₂ has no permanent dipole.
parts.answer: Both nitrogen atoms are the same element with the same electronegativity, so the bonding electron pairs are shared equally. The molecule is symmetrical, so no bond dipole is present.
parts.working: 1 mark: the two atoms have equal electronegativity, so the shared pairs are shared equally. 1 mark: the symmetrical linear molecule has no net dipole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the N≡N bond (bond enthalpy 944 kJ mol⁻¹) is much stronger than a single N–N bond (bond enthalpy 163 kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: The triple bond has three shared pairs of electrons (one σ and two π bonds), compared with one shared pair in the N–N bond. The greater electron density between the nuclei holds the atoms more strongly, so the bond is stronger and shorter.
parts.working: 1 mark: three shared pairs (one σ and two π) against one. 1 mark: more electron density between the nuclei, so a stronger, shorter bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen is converted to ammonia by the Haber process. Calculate the mass of N₂ (Mr 28.0) needed to make 1.00 tonne (1.00 × 10⁶ g) of NH₃ (Mr 17.0) with 100 % yield. Give your answer in tonnes to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Amount NH₃ = 1.00 × 10⁶ ÷ 17.0 = 58 824 mol. Amount N₂ = half of this = 29 412 mol. Mass = 29 412 × 28.0 = 8.24 × 10⁵ g = 0.824 t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The yield of the process is only 40 %. Calculate the mass of N₂ needed to make 1.00 tonne of NH₃ at this yield, in tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Air contains 78.0 % nitrogen by volume. Calculate the volume of nitrogen, in dm³, in 2.50 × 10⁴ dm³ of air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen compounds, not nitrogen gas, must be supplied to crops, using the bond strength of N≡N in your answer.
parts.answer: The N≡N triple bond is very strong, so plants cannot use N₂ directly. Nitrogen must be converted into compounds such as nitrates or ammonium ions. Bacteria in the roots of legumes and lightning fix atmospheric nitrogen into these compounds.
parts.working: 1 mark: N≡N is strong and unreactive. 1 mark: plants need nitrogen in compound form (nitrate or ammonium). 1 mark: fixation by bacteria or lightning (any valid method).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the appearance and solubility of nitrogen gas at room temperature, and state one reason it is chemically unreactive.
parts.answer: Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless gas that is only slightly soluble in water. It is unreactive because the N≡N triple bond is very strong (bond enthalpy 944 kJ mol⁻¹), so a large amount of energy is needed to break it.
parts.working: 1 mark: colourless, odourless gas. 1 mark: only slightly soluble in water. 1 mark: strong triple bond with high bond enthalpy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonia is oxidised to nitrogen monoxide over a hot platinum catalyst (first step of the Ostwald process). Write the balanced equation.
parts.answer: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark: correct products. 1 mark: correct balancing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the Ostwald process, nitrogen dioxide is absorbed in water: 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO. Explain why the NO formed is recycled.
parts.answer: NO is oxidised by oxygen back to NO₂ (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂), which can be absorbed again, so the nitrogen is recycled and less is wasted.
parts.working: 1 mark: NO reacts with O₂ to form NO₂ again. 1 mark: the NO₂ is re-used in the absorption step.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of nitrogen in NH₃, NO, NO₂ and HNO₃.
parts.answer: NH₃: −3; NO: +2; NO₂: +4; HNO₃: +5
parts.working: 1 mark for two correct values; 1 mark for all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the reaction 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO, identify the nitrogen that is both oxidised and reduced, and explain.
parts.answer: Nitrogen in NO₂ (+4) is both oxidised to +5 (in HNO₃) and reduced to +2 (in NO). This is a disproportionation reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: N(+4) is oxidised to +5 and reduced to +2. 1 mark: the same element changes in both directions, so it is disproportionation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper reacts with dilute nitric acid: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O. Calculate the volume of NO, measured at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹), formed when 3.00 g of copper (Mr 63.5) reacts completely. Give your answer in cm³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 756 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated nitric acid reacts with copper: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O. State the colour of the gas formed.
parts.answer: Brown.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the gas and the products differ from those formed with dilute nitric acid.
parts.answer: Dilute acid gives NO rather than NO₂ (nitrogen is reduced to +2 rather than +4), and copper(II) nitrate and water are formed in both cases.
parts.working: 1 mark: dilute acid forms NO (nitrogen reduced to +2, not +4). 1 mark: nitrogen is reduced less far with concentrated acid NO₂ (+4), so the products differ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the change in oxidation number of nitrogen, why the nitrogen in HNO₃ is reduced to NO₂ in the reaction with concentrated nitric acid.
parts.answer: Nitrogen falls from +5 in HNO₃ to +4 in NO₂. A decrease in oxidation number is reduction (the nitrogen gains electrons).
parts.working: 1 mark: N changes from +5 to +4. 1 mark: a decrease in oxidation number means reduction (gain of electrons).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated nitric acid is 70 % HNO₃ by mass, with a density of 1.42 g cm⁻³. Calculate its concentration in mol dm⁻³ (Mr of HNO₃ = 63.0). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 15.8 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Mass of HNO₃ in 1 dm³ = 1420 g × 0.70 = 994 g. Amount = 994 ÷ 63.0 = 15.8 mol. Concentration = 15.8 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of nitric acid is neutralised by 18.5 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ calcium hydroxide solution: 2HNO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the nitric acid, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.148 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Amount Ca(OH)₂ = 0.0185 × 0.100 = 0.00185 mol. Amount HNO₃ = 2 × 0.00185 = 0.00370 mol. Concentration = 0.00370 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.148 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂ (Mr 164.1), formed in the neutralisation. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium nitrate decomposes on heating: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Calculate the amount, in mol, of NO₂ formed from 16.41 g of Ca(NO₃)₂ (Mr 164.1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of gas formed, at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: 6.00 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium nitrate decomposes on heating to give potassium nitrite and oxygen. Write the equation and state the test for oxygen.
parts.answer: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
parts.working: 1 mark: balanced equation. 1 mark: relights a glowing splint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium nitrate decomposes to MgO, NO₂ and O₂, whereas potassium nitrate decomposes only to the nitrite and O₂. Explain this difference in terms of the cations.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is small and has a high charge density, so it distorts the nitrate ion strongly and weakens the N–O bonds, favouring full decomposition to a stable oxide. K⁺ has a much lower charge density and does not distort the nitrate ion, so only the nitrite forms.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mg²⁺ has high charge density. 1 mark: this distorts and weakens the nitrate ion. 1 mark: K⁺ has a low charge density, so only the nitrite is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the brown ring test for nitrate ions.
parts.answer: Add aqueous iron(II) sulfate to the test solution, then carefully add concentrated sulfuric acid down the side of the tube. A brown ring forms at the junction of the two layers, showing nitrate ions are present.
parts.working: 1 mark: iron(II) sulfate added. 1 mark: concentrated sulfuric acid added slowly down the side. 1 mark: brown ring at the junction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fertiliser must supply 14.0 kg of nitrogen. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr 80.0), needed. Give your answer in kg.
parts.working: Amount N needed = 14 000 ÷ 14.0 = 1000 mol. Each NH₄NO₃ contains 2 N atoms, so amount NH₄NO₃ = 500 mol. Mass = 500 × 80.0 = 40 000 g = 40.0 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Ostwald process converts 1.00 tonne of NH₃ (Mr 17.0) into HNO₃ (Mr 63.0) with a yield of 90 %. Calculate the mass of HNO₃ formed, in tonnes, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Theoretical HNO₃ = 1.00 × 63.0 ÷ 17.0 = 3.71 t (one N atom per molecule in each case). Actual = 3.71 × 0.90 = 3.34 t.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute nitric acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Write the ionic equation for the reaction and name the gas formed.
parts.answer: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂O + CO₂. The gas is carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct ionic equation and gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hexaaquacopper(II) ions react with ammonia: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O. Which statement about this ligand exchange is correct?
A The coordination number of copper falls from 6 to 4.
B The coordination number stays at 6, and four water ligands are replaced by ammonia.
C Water is a stronger ligand than ammonia, so the equilibrium lies to the left.
D The product is colourless because all the d electrons are paired.
parts.answer: B The coordination number stays at 6, and four water ligands are replaced by ammonia.
parts.working: Four H₂O ligands are replaced by four NH₃ ligands, and copper still has six ligands. Ammonia is the stronger ligand, so the equilibrium lies to the right (C is wrong). The product is deep blue, not colourless, because d–d transitions occur (D is wrong).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The stability constants (lg Kstab) are: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ = 7.2; [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ = 21.1. By what factor is Kstab of [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ larger than Kstab of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
A 13.9
B 7.9 × 10¹³
C 1.4 × 10⁷
D 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁴
parts.working: Factor = 10^(21.1 − 7.2) = 10^13.9 = 7.9 × 10¹³. Option A is the difference in lg values, not the ratio. Option C is not a ratio of these values. Option D is the reciprocal (10^−13.9 = 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁴) and would mean the cyanide complex is less stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aqueous cobalt(II) chloride contains the pink ion [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added until the solution turns blue, due to the equilibrium: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. State the change in coordination number and in shape of cobalt.
parts.answer: Coordination number falls from 6 to 4; shape changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.
parts.working: 1 mark for coordination number. 1 mark for shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why diluting the blue solution with water turns it pink again.
parts.answer: Adding water increases the concentration of H₂O, so the equilibrium moves to the left (Le Chatelier's principle). The pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ion forms again.
parts.working: 1 mark: water is a product, so adding water shifts the equilibrium left. 1 mark: pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ reforms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for the forward reaction.
parts.answer: ΔS is positive. The forward reaction increases the number of particles from 5 to 7, which increases disorder.
parts.working: 1 mark: ΔS positive. 1 mark: 5 particles change to 7 particles (more disorder).

parts.label: a
parts.text: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ ⇌ [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻ + 2NH₃. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant, K, of this ligand exchange.
parts.answer: K = [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻ × [NH₃]² ÷ ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ × [S₂O₃²⁻]²)
parts.working: Products over reactants, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: lg Kstab values: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ = 7.2; [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻ = 13.5. Calculate K for the exchange. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the value of K tells you about the position of the equilibrium, and why.
parts.answer: K is much greater than 1, so the equilibrium lies to the right: the thiosulfate complex is much more stable than the ammonia complex.
parts.working: 1 mark: K ≫ 1, so products are favoured. 1 mark: the thiosulfate complex has a much larger stability constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide is added dropwise to aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and then excess sodium hydroxide is added. Describe what is seen, and write an ionic equation for the first reaction.
parts.answer: A pale blue precipitate forms, and it does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
parts.working: 1 mark: pale blue precipitate. 1 mark: precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH (unlike the ammonia reaction, which forms a soluble complex). 1 mark: correct ionic equation.

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the shape of the tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion, [CoCl₄]²⁻?
A octahedral
B square planar
C tetrahedral
D linear
parts.answer: C tetrahedral
parts.working: Four ligands around cobalt give a coordination number of 4, and a tetrahedral shape. Octahedral needs six ligands; square planar and linear shapes are not adopted by [CoCl₄]²⁻.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a hexadentate ligand?
A ethanedioate, C₂O₄²⁻
B ethane-1,2-diamine, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂
C EDTA⁴⁻ (ethylenediaminetetraacetate)
D cyanide, CN⁻
parts.answer: C EDTA⁴⁻ (ethylenediaminetetraacetate)
parts.working: EDTA⁴⁻ has six donor atoms (two N and four O), so it can bond at six sites. Ethanedioate and ethane-1,2-diamine are bidentate, and cyanide is monodentate.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the shape and coordination number of each complex: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.
parts.answer: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: square planar, CN 4. [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺: tetrahedral, CN 4. [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: octahedral, CN 6.
parts.working: 1 mark for each complex with both shape and coordination number correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar rather than tetrahedral.
parts.answer: Ni²⁺ is d⁸. The strong-field CN⁻ ligands cause a large splitting, so the d electrons pair up in the lower orbitals, leaving the d(x²−y²) orbital empty. This favours a square planar arrangement.
parts.working: 1 mark: d⁸ with strong-field ligands gives electron pairing. 1 mark: an empty d orbital favours square planar geometry.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nickel(II) chloride hexahydrate, [Ni(H₂O)₆]Cl₂ (Mr 237.7; Ar Ni = 58.7), is used as a source of Ni²⁺. Calculate the mass of nickel in 1.00 g of the compound. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in [Ni(H₂O)₆]Cl₂. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex [Cr(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ contains three ethanedioate (C₂O₄²⁻) ligands. Calculate the oxidation number of chromium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordination number of chromium in this complex.
parts.working: Each ethanedioate is bidentate, so 3 ligands give 6 donor atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the systematic name of the complex ion.
parts.answer: tris(ethanedioato)chromate(III) ion (or trioxalatochromate(III))
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct name.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'bidentate' and why complexes with bidentate ligands are described as more stable.
parts.answer: A bidentate ligand bonds to the metal through two donor atoms, forming a chelate ring. Chelate rings increase the stability of the complex, because breaking the ring is less favourable.
parts.working: 1 mark: two donor atoms bond to the metal. 1 mark: chelate ring gives greater stability.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ is formed. Identify the two ligands in the complex ion.
parts.answer: NH₃ and Cl⁻ (the Cl⁻ inside the square brackets; the outer Cl⁻ ions are counter-ions).
parts.working: 1 mark for NH₃. 1 mark for Cl⁻ bonded to cobalt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the oxidation number of cobalt and its coordination number.
parts.answer: Oxidation number +3; coordination number 6.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Excess aqueous silver nitrate is added to 1 mol of the complex. State the amount, in mol, of AgCl formed.
parts.answer: 2 mol
parts.working: Only the two Cl⁻ outside the complex ion are free to precipitate, giving 2 mol AgCl.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many geometric (cis–trans or fac–mer) isomers does the octahedral complex [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃] have?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
parts.answer: B 2
parts.working: There are two geometric isomers: facial (the three NH₃ on one face) and meridional (the three NH₃ in one plane). No other arrangement is possible for the MA₃B₃ type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The octahedral complex [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]⁺ has cis and trans isomers. Describe the position of the two chloride ligands in each isomer.
parts.answer: Cis: the two Cl⁻ ligands are at 90° to each other (adjacent). Trans: the two Cl⁻ ligands are at 180° to each other (opposite).
parts.working: 1 mark for cis. 1 mark for trans.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which isomer has a permanent dipole moment, and explain why the other does not.
parts.answer: The cis isomer has a permanent dipole moment, because its bond dipoles do not cancel. In the trans isomer the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, so it has no dipole moment.
parts.working: 1 mark: cis has a dipole. 1 mark: trans bond dipoles cancel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether either isomer is optically active, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Neither is optically active: each has a plane of symmetry, so each is superimposable on its mirror image.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex [Co(en)₂(NH₃)₂]³⁺ contains two bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine (en) ligands and two NH₃ ligands in an octahedral arrangement. State the number of geometric isomers.
parts.answer: 2 geometric isomers (cis and trans).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of stereoisomers, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 3 stereoisomers. The cis isomer is chiral and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (two optical isomers); the trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is achiral, giving one form.
parts.working: 1 mark: cis gives a pair of optical isomers. 1 mark: trans is achiral; total 2 + 1 = 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the trans isomer is not optically active.
parts.answer: It has a plane of symmetry, so it is superimposable on its mirror image.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrated chromium(III) chloride exists as two isomers with formula CrCl₃·6H₂O (Mr 266.5): violet [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ and green [CrCl(H₂O)₅]Cl₂·H₂O. Name the type of isomerism shown.
parts.answer: Hydrate (solvate) isomerism.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Separate 5.00 g samples of each isomer are dissolved in water and treated with excess aqueous silver nitrate. Calculate the amount, in mol, of AgCl formed from each sample. Give each to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Violet: 0.0563 mol; green: 0.0375 mol
parts.working: Amount of each = 5.00 ÷ 266.5 = 0.01876 mol. Violet has 3 Cl⁻ outside the complex: 3 × 0.01876 = 0.0563 mol. Green has 2 Cl⁻ outside the complex: 2 × 0.01876 = 0.0375 mol. 1 mark each for the two values; 1 mark for the method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) Define geometric isomerism. Then state whether each of these arrangements can show cis–trans isomerism: (i) octahedral MA₄B₂; (ii) tetrahedral MA₂B₂; (iii) square planar MA₂B₂.
parts.answer: Geometric isomers have the same molecular formula and bonding but a different spatial arrangement of ligands. (i) Yes, octahedral MA₄B₂ shows cis–trans isomerism. (ii) No, tetrahedral MA₂B₂ does not. (iii) Yes, square planar MA₂B₂ shows cis–trans isomerism.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (same formula and bonding, different spatial arrangement). 1 mark: (i) and (iii) can show cis–trans isomerism. 1 mark: (ii) cannot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many geometric (cis–trans) isomers does the octahedral complex [Co(NH₃)₂Cl₄]⁻ have?
parts.answer: 2 (cis and trans)
parts.working: With two NH₃ ligands, the isomers are the one with the two NH₃ adjacent (cis) and the one with them opposite (trans).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether either geometric isomer of [Co(NH₃)₂Cl₄]⁻ is optically active, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Neither isomer is optically active. Each isomer has a plane of symmetry, so it is superimposable on its mirror image.
parts.working: 1 mark: no optical isomers. 1 mark: justified by the plane of symmetry in each isomer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ contains three bidentate ethanedioate ligands. Explain why this complex shows optical isomerism.
parts.answer: The complex has an octahedral arrangement of three identical bidentate ligands, which gives a non-superimposable mirror image pair (Λ and Δ forms). The two forms are optical isomers.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-superimposable mirror images. 1 mark: three bidentate ligands in an octahedral arrangement give chirality.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of optical isomers, and whether geometric isomers are possible.
parts.answer: 2 optical isomers (a pair of enantiomers). No geometric isomers, since all six donor positions are equivalent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complex [Pt(en)Cl₂] is square planar, where en is the bidentate ligand ethane-1,2-diamine. Explain why [Pt(en)Cl₂] has no geometric isomers, whereas [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has two.
parts.answer: In [Pt(en)Cl₂], the en ligand occupies two adjacent positions. The two Cl⁻ ligands must then occupy the other two adjacent positions, so only one arrangement is possible. In [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], the NH₃ and Cl⁻ are monodentate, so they can be arranged cis or trans.
parts.working: 1 mark: en occupies adjacent positions. 1 mark: the Cl⁻ must therefore also be adjacent, so only one isomer. 1 mark: [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has monodentate ligands that can be cis or trans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ shows geometric isomerism or optical isomerism, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Neither. All six ligands are identical NH₃, so there is only one possible arrangement, and the complex has symmetry that makes it achiral.
parts.working: 1 mark: no geometric isomers, because all ligands are identical. 1 mark: no optical isomers, because the complex is achiral.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ion has a d¹⁰ configuration and is colourless in aqueous solution?
A Cu²⁺
B Zn²⁺
C Fe³⁺
D Co²⁺
parts.answer: B Zn²⁺
parts.working: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so all d orbitals are full and no d–d transition is possible; it is colourless. Cu²⁺ (d⁹), Fe³⁺ (d⁵) and Co²⁺ (d⁷) all have partly filled d orbitals and are coloured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A complex ion absorbs light of wavelength 580 nm. Calculate the energy of one photon of this light, in J. Use E = hc/λ with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy per mole of photons, in kJ mol⁻¹, and state the colour of the light absorbed and the colour observed.
parts.answer: 206 kJ mol⁻¹. Yellow light is absorbed, so the solution appears violet-blue (its complementary colour).
parts.working: 1 mark: energy per mole 3.43 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.02 × 10²³ = 206 kJ mol⁻¹. 1 mark: yellow absorbed and violet-blue observed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of unpaired electrons in each ion: Cu²⁺, Ni²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Sc³⁺.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ (d⁹): 1; Ni²⁺ (d⁸): 2; Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰): 0; Sc³⁺ (d⁰): 0
parts.working: 1 mark for each ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two octahedral complexes contain the same metal ion. Complex X has water ligands and absorbs at 500 nm. Complex Y has ammonia ligands and absorbs at 430 nm. Calculate the energy gap, ΔE, per ion for X and for Y, in J. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, giving each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: X: 3.98e-19 J per ion, Y: 4.63e-19 J per ion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which complex has the larger d-orbital splitting, and how this relates to the colours observed.
parts.answer: Complex Y has the larger splitting, because NH₃ is a stronger ligand than H₂O. Its absorption is at a shorter wavelength (higher energy), so the colour transmitted differs from complex X.
parts.working: 1 mark: NH₃ is a stronger field ligand, so Δ is larger for Y. 1 mark: larger Δ means higher energy, shorter wavelength absorbed, so the colour changes.

parts.label: a
