parts.text: [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is green, but [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ is blue-violet. Explain why replacing water with ammonia changes the colour.
parts.answer: NH₃ is a stronger ligand than H₂O, so the d-orbital splitting Δ is larger. The d–d transition then needs a different energy, so light at a different wavelength is absorbed and the colour of the transmitted light changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: NH₃ gives a larger Δ. 1 mark: a different wavelength is absorbed, so the colour changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the wavelength of the absorption changes.
parts.answer: The absorption moves to a shorter wavelength (higher energy).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Students prepared copper(II) sulfate solutions of different concentrations and measured their absorbance at 600 nm, using water as the blank in the colorimeter. Results (absorbance): 0.10 mol dm⁻³ → 0.12; 0.20 mol dm⁻³ → 0.24; 0.30 mol dm⁻³ → 0.36; 0.40 mol dm⁻³ → 0.48. Describe the relationship between concentration and absorbance.
parts.answer: Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration (a straight line through the origin), consistent with the Beer–Lambert law.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the calibration line, in absorbance per mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 1.2 (absorbance per mol dm⁻³)
parts.working: Gradient = 0.48 ÷ 0.40 = 1.2 (absorbance units per mol dm⁻³).

parts.label: c
parts.text: An unknown solution has an absorbance of 0.42. Calculate its concentration, in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.35 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Concentration = 0.42 ÷ 1.2 = 0.35 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why water is used as the blank, and suggest one source of error in this experiment.
parts.answer: Water is used to set the zero absorbance, so that the absorbance measured is only due to the copper(II) ions and not to the cuvette or the solvent. A source of error: a fingerprint or bubble on the cuvette, or using a cuvette that is not wiped clean.
parts.working: 1 mark: the blank corrects for absorbance by the cuvette and solvent. 1 mark: a valid source of error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A complex absorbs energy of 200 kJ mol⁻¹, which corresponds to the energy of one mole of photons of a single wavelength. Calculate the wavelength, in nm, to the nearest nm, and state the colour of the light absorbed and the colour observed.
parts.answer: 599 nm. Orange light is absorbed, so the solution appears blue.
parts.working: E per photon = 200 000 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. λ = hc ÷ E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.99 × 10⁻⁷ m = 599 nm. 1 mark each for the wavelength, the absorbed colour and the observed colour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the full electron configuration, in the form [Ar] 3d…, of each ion: Fe²⁺, Co³⁺, Cu⁺ and Ti³⁺.
parts.answer: Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶; Co³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶; Cu⁺: [Ar] 3d¹⁰; Ti³⁺: [Ar] 3d¹
parts.working: 1 mark for each ion. The 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons on ionisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons), but [CoF₆]³⁻ is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons. Explain this difference, referring to the ligand field strength, the size of the splitting Δ and the pairing energy.
parts.answer: NH₃ is a strong-field ligand, so Δ is larger than the pairing energy. The d⁶ electrons pair in the lower t₂g orbitals (low spin), giving no unpaired electrons. F⁻ is a weak-field ligand, so Δ is smaller than the pairing energy. Electrons occupy the higher eg orbitals before pairing (high spin, t₂g⁴e_g²), giving four unpaired electrons.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong field gives Δ greater than pairing energy, so electrons pair (low spin). 1 mark: weak field gives Δ smaller than pairing energy, so electrons occupy eg first (high spin). 1 mark: correct counts of unpaired electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complex A absorbs light at 580 nm and complex B absorbs at 450 nm. Calculate the ratio of the energy per photon for B to that for A. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: E ∝ 1/λ, so the ratio = 580 ÷ 450 = 1.29.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which complex has the larger d-orbital splitting, Δ, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Complex B has the larger splitting, because it absorbs the higher-energy (shorter wavelength) photons.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Standard electrode potentials: Mg²⁺(aq)/Mg(s) E° = −2.37 V; Ag⁺(aq)/Ag(s) E° = +0.80 V. Calculate E°cell for a cell made from these two half-cells. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for E°cell = E°(positive) − E°(negative) using the correct sign; 1 mark for 3.17 V

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the spontaneous cell reaction.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)
parts.working: Mg is oxidised (more negative E°), so it is the negative electrode; Ag⁺ is reduced. Balance for 2 electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
parts.answer: From the magnesium electrode to the silver electrode
parts.working: Electrons leave the negative electrode (Mg) and travel through the wire to the positive electrode (Ag).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Standard electrode potentials: Ni²⁺(aq)/Ni(s) E° = −0.25 V; Sn²⁺(aq)/Sn(s) E° = −0.14 V. A cell is built from these two half-cells under standard conditions. Calculate E°cell.
parts.working: 1 mark for using E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative); 1 mark for 0.11 V

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the positive electrode and state which metal is oxidised.
parts.answer: Sn is the positive electrode; Ni is oxidised
parts.working: Positive electrode is the half-cell with the more positive E°, Sn²⁺/Sn; Ni (more negative E°) is the negative electrode and loses electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A standard chlorine electrode, Cl₂(g)/Cl⁻(aq), has E° = +1.36 V. It is connected to a standard Pb²⁺(aq)/Pb(s) electrode, E° = −0.13 V. Calculate E°cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the chlorine electrode is the positive electrode in this cell, and write the half-equation for the reaction at it.
parts.answer: Cl₂ has the more positive E°, so it is reduced and is the positive electrode. Half-equation: Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻(aq)
parts.working: 1 mark: more positive E° means reduction occurs; 1 mark: positive electrode; 1 mark: correct half-equation with 2e⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one practical difficulty in setting up the chlorine electrode in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Chlorine is a toxic gas, so it must be handled in a fume cupboard or the apparatus must be sealed.
parts.working: Accept any sensible difficulty: toxicity, need for a platinum electrode, gas supply, dissolving chlorine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Standard electrode potentials: Fe³⁺(aq)/Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V; I₂(aq)/I⁻(aq) E° = +0.54 V. Use these values to decide whether Fe³⁺(aq) can oxidise I⁻(aq) under standard conditions. Justify your answer with a calculated E°cell.
parts.answer: Yes. Fe³⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent (more positive E°). E°cell = +0.77 − (+0.54) = +0.23 V, which is positive, so the reaction is feasible.
parts.working: 1 mark: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ is more positive so Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻; 1 mark: E°cell = +0.23 V; 1 mark: positive E°cell so feasible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + I₂(aq)
parts.working: Fe³⁺ gains one electron each; I⁻ loses one electron each to form I₂; balance with 2 mol of each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student adds 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ KI to 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Fe(NO₃)₃. Calculate the amount, in mol, of iodine formed, assuming the reaction goes to completion.
parts.working: n(Fe³⁺) = 0.0250 × 0.100 = 0.00250 mol; I⁻ also 0.00250 mol; from 2I⁻ → I₂, I₂ = 0.00125 mol. Mark: 1 for limiting-reagent reasoning, 1 for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the oxidation number of manganese in the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻?
A +5
B +6
C +7
D +8
parts.working: Oxygen is −2, so 4 × (−2) = −8; the ion has overall charge −1, so Mn = +7. The distractor +8 comes from ignoring the ion's charge; +5 and +6 come from sign or arithmetic slips with the −8 total.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction 2Cu²⁺(aq) + 4I⁻(aq) → 2CuI(s) + I₂(aq), which species is reduced?
A Cu²⁺
B I⁻
C I₂
D CuI
parts.answer: A Cu²⁺
parts.working: Cu goes from +2 in Cu²⁺ to +1 in CuI, a gain of electrons, so Cu²⁺ is reduced. I⁻ is oxidised (−1 to 0) to I₂; B is the oxidised species, the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of nitrogen in each of: NH₃, NO₂⁻, NO₃⁻.
parts.answer: NH₃: −3; NO₂⁻: +3; NO₃⁻: +5
parts.working: 1 mark each. NO₂⁻: N + 2(−2) = −1 gives N = +3. NO₃⁻: N + 3(−2) = −1 gives N = +5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nitrogen in NO₂⁻ could be oxidised or reduced depending on the reagent used.
parts.answer: Its oxidation number, +3, lies between the extremes of −3 in NH₃ and +5 in NO₃⁻, so it can go up or down.
parts.working: Accept any statement that +3 can increase to +5 or decrease to −3 or lower.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). State the oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O₂, in H₂O and in O₂.
parts.answer: H₂O₂: −1; H₂O: −2; O₂: 0
parts.working: 1 mark each. In H₂O₂, 2 O atoms share −2, so each is −1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the species that is oxidised and the species that is reduced. Explain why this is called disproportionation.
parts.answer: Oxidised: O in H₂O₂ going to O₂ (−1 to 0). Reduced: O in H₂O₂ going to H₂O (−1 to −2). Disproportionation because the same element is both oxidised and reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the two changes, and 1 mark for a reason based on one element changing in both directions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium chlorate(V), KClO₃, decomposes on heating: 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g). State the change in oxidation number of chlorine and of oxygen.
parts.answer: Chlorine goes from +5 to −1 (reduced, change −6). Oxygen goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised, change +2 per atom).
parts.working: 1 mark for chlorine; 1 mark for oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons transferred when 0.150 mol of KClO₃ decomposes completely.
parts.working: Each Cl gains 6 electrons, so 0.150 × 6 = 0.900 mol. 1 mark for the 6 electrons per Cl; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In acidic solution, manganate(VII) ions oxidise iron(II) ions: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) + 5Fe³⁺(aq). State the change in oxidation number of manganese per ion.
parts.answer: +7 to +2, a decrease of 5 (each Mn gains 5 electrons)
parts.working: Mn is reduced; the change is 5 per Mn atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ MnO₄⁻(aq) is needed to react completely with an iron(II) solution. Calculate the amount, in mol, of Fe²⁺ ions that reacted.
parts.working: n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.0250 × 0.0200 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol; mole ratio MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5, so n(Fe²⁺) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The peroxodisulfate ion, S₂O₈²⁻, contains two sulfur atoms, each bonded to four oxygen atoms in total; six of the eight oxygen atoms are bonded to sulfur only, and two oxygen atoms form an O–O peroxo link. Explain why the average oxidation number of sulfur is +6, and why the oxygen atoms in the O–O link are −1 rather than −2.
parts.answer: Sum over the ion: 2S + 6(−2) + 2(−1) = −2, so 2S = +12 and S = +6 for each sulfur. Each O in the O–O link is bonded to another O atom, so the shared electrons do not create an electronegativity difference and that O is −1 rather than −2.
parts.working: Let S be the oxidation number of each S: 2S + 6(−2) + 2(−1) = −2, so 2S = +12 and S = +6. The O–O link is bonded to another O of the same element, so the shared electrons do not count towards an electronegativity difference, and each peroxo O is −1. 1 mark for the sum; 1 mark for S = +6; 1 mark for the O–O explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why peroxodisulfate is a stronger oxidising agent than sulfate, with reference to the O–O bond.
parts.answer: The O–O bond is weak and easily broken, so it can accept electrons to form SO₄²⁻ readily.
parts.working: 1 mark for weak O–O bond; 1 mark for reduction to sulfate giving a favourable product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hot concentrated sodium hydroxide reacts with chlorine: 3Cl₂(g) + 6OH⁻(aq) → 5Cl⁻(aq) + ClO₃⁻(aq) + 3H₂O(l). Show that this is a disproportionation reaction by giving the oxidation numbers of chlorine in Cl₂, Cl⁻ and ClO₃⁻.
parts.answer: Cl₂: 0; Cl⁻: −1; ClO₃⁻: +5. Chlorine is both oxidised (0 to +5) and reduced (0 to −1) in the same reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the three oxidation numbers; the conclusion is part of the reasoning mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student reacts 14.2 g of chlorine with excess hot NaOH. Calculate the amount, in mol, of ClO₃⁻ formed. (Ar Cl = 35.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Manganate(VI) ions, MnO₄²⁻, disproportionate in acid: 3MnO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) → 2MnO₄⁻(aq) + MnO₂(s) + 2H₂O(l). State the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄²⁻, MnO₄⁻ and MnO₂.
parts.answer: MnO₄²⁻: +6; MnO₄⁻: +7; MnO₂: +4
parts.working: 1 mark each. Mn + 4(−2) = −2 gives +6; Mn + 4(−2) = −1 gives +7; Mn + 2(−2) = 0 gives +4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which change is oxidation and which is reduction, and explain why this is a disproportionation.
parts.answer: Oxidation: +6 to +7 (to MnO₄⁻); reduction: +6 to +4 (to MnO₂). It is disproportionation because one species is both oxidised and reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct statement with both changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxidation number of carbon in: (i) CH₃OH (ii) HCOOH.
parts.working: CH₃OH: 4 H (+1 each) and 1 O (−2), so C = −2. HCOOH: 2 H (+1), 2 O (−2), so C = +2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Methanol is oxidised to methanoic acid by acidified dichromate(VI). State the change in oxidation number of carbon.
parts.answer: −2 to +2, an increase of 4
parts.working: Carbon loses 4 electrons in the change from methanol to methanoic acid, which is oxidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A current of 0.800 A is passed for 45.0 minutes through aqueous copper(II) sulfate using inert electrodes. Calculate the charge passed, in coulombs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Cu = 63.5)
parts.working: 1 mark for n(e⁻) = Q/F; 1 mark for n(Cu) = n(e⁻)/2 from Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; 1 mark for the mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Write half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer: Cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
parts.working: 1 mark each for correct species and balanced electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no hydrogen is produced in this electrolysis, and state the physical state of the sodium formed at the cathode.
parts.answer: There is no water, so H⁺ ions are not present to be discharged. Sodium is liquid because the cell operates above its melting point of 98 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for no water or H⁺; 1 mark for liquid sodium above its melting point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes using a current of 2.00 A for 25.0 minutes. Calculate the total charge passed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of hydrogen and oxygen produced at room conditions, in cm³ to 3 significant figures. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; molar gas volume = 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: Hydrogen: 373 cm³; oxygen: 187 cm³
parts.working: Hydrogen: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, so n(H₂) = n(e⁻)/2. Oxygen: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so n(O₂) = n(e⁻)/4. 1 mark each for the mole relation, 1 mark for the volumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium is produced by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite. Write the half-equation at the cathode.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
parts.working: Aluminium ions gain three electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cell operates at a steady current of 5000 A for 1.00 hour. Calculate the mass of aluminium produced. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Al = 27.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zinc is deposited from aqueous zinc sulfate. Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn
parts.working: Zn²⁺ gains two electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time, in minutes to 3 significant figures, needed to deposit 1.00 g of zinc using a current of 3.00 A. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Zn = 65.4)
parts.answer: 16.4 min
parts.working: n(Zn) = 1.00/65.4; n(e⁻) = 2n; Q = n(e⁻) × F; t = Q/I, then divide by 60.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student passes different charges through silver nitrate solution and weighs the silver deposited at the cathode. Charge (C) and mass of silver (g): 500 C, 0.560 g; 1000 C, 1.120 g; 1500 C, 1.680 g; 2000 C, 2.240 g; 2500 C, 2.800 g. Use the gradient of a mass-against-charge graph to calculate the value of the Faraday constant F in C mol⁻¹, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar Ag = 107.9)
parts.working: 1 mark for gradient; 1 mark for mass per mol relation M/(nF) with n = 1; 1 mark for the value 9.63 × 10⁴.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The data book value is 96 500 C mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage error in the student's value, to 1 significant figure.
parts.working: Error = (96 500 − 96 300)/96 500 × 100 ≈ 0.2%. 1 mark for method; 1 mark for value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nickel is electroplated onto a metal spoon using an aqueous solution of nickel(II) sulfate, with the spoon as the cathode. Write the half-equation for the reaction at the spoon.
parts.answer: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni
parts.working: Ni²⁺ ions gain two electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A current of 3.50 A flows for 1 hour 20 minutes. Calculate the mass of nickel deposited. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Ni = 58.7)

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the chlor-alkali industry, concentrated brine is electrolysed in a diaphragm cell with a current of 1.50 × 10³ A for 24.0 hours. Write the half-equation for the production of chlorine.
parts.answer: 2Cl⁻(aq) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻
parts.working: Chloride ions lose electrons at the anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine produced in this time. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Cl = 35.5)
parts.working: Q = 1.50 × 10³ × 86 400 = 1.30 × 10⁸ C; n(Cl₂) = Q/(2F) = 671.5 mol; mass = 671.5 × 71.0 = 4.77 × 10⁴ g = 47.7 kg. 1 mark for Q; 1 mark for n(Cl₂); 1 mark for the value to 3 s.f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is refined by electrolysis. An impure copper anode and a pure copper cathode are placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. A current of 2.00 A flows for 1.00 hour. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Cu = 63.5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass lost by the anode can be greater than the mass gained by the cathode.
parts.answer: Less reactive metals in the impure anode (such as silver or gold) do not dissolve and fall to the bottom as sludge, so they are lost from the anode without depositing on the cathode.
parts.working: 1 mark for less reactive impurities falling as anode sludge; 1 mark for those impurities not being deposited at the cathode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolysed with a constant current of 40.0 A for 2.00 hours. Calculate the mass of magnesium produced. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Mg = 24.3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode during this electrolysis.
parts.answer: 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻
parts.working: Chloride ions are oxidised at the anode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Chlorine, not oxygen, is produced at the anode. Standard electrode potentials are: Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V; O₂/H₂O +1.23 V (at pH 7 this is +0.82 V). Explain why chlorine is produced.
parts.answer: Water is oxidised to O₂ at a lower potential, but O₂ is formed only at a high overpotential at a graphite/platinum anode. Chloride is present at a high concentration, which, by the Nernst equation, favours its oxidation. Chlorine therefore forms in preference to oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark for mentioning overpotential/kinetic hindrance of O₂ evolution; 1 mark for high [Cl⁻] favouring Cl₂; 1 mark for concluding that Cl₂ is formed preferentially.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the product at the cathode changes if dilute sodium chloride is used instead, and explain briefly.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is produced at the cathode in both cases, but with dilute solution oxygen can be produced at the anode.
parts.working: Water is reduced to H₂ at the cathode whatever the concentration; at the anode, lower [Cl⁻] makes O₂ more likely.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Alkaline manganate(VII) ions oxidise sulfite ions: MnO₄⁻ + SO₃²⁻ + OH⁻ → MnO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + H₂O (not yet balanced). What is the coefficient of OH⁻ in the balanced equation with the smallest whole numbers?
A 1
B 2
C 4
D 8
parts.answer: B 2
parts.working: Balanced: 2MnO₄⁻ + 3SO₃²⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + 3SO₄²⁻ + 2OH⁻. Check: O 18 = 18, charge −8 = −8. A and C/D come from half-equation slips.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the reaction of hydrogen peroxide with iodide ions in acid, which species is the oxidising agent?
2I⁻ + H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O
A I⁻
B H₂O₂
C H⁺
D H₂O
parts.answer: B H₂O₂
parts.working: H₂O₂ is reduced (O from −1 to −2 in H₂O), so it is the oxidising agent. I⁻ is oxidised; H⁺ and H₂O are not redox-active.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) ions, Cr₂O₇²⁻, to chromium(III) ions in acid.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
parts.working: Balance Cr first, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of iron(II) to iron(III).
parts.answer: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻
parts.working: One electron lost per Fe²⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Combine the two half-equations to give the balanced ionic equation for the reaction between acidified Cr₂O₇²⁻ and Fe²⁺.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O
parts.working: Multiply the Fe half-equation by 6 so that electrons cancel; 1 mark for balance of electrons, 1 mark for correct species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In acid, hydrogen peroxide oxidises iron(II) ions: H₂O₂ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Fe³⁺ + H₂O (not balanced). Balance the equation.
parts.answer: H₂O₂ + 2Fe²⁺ + 2H⁺ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for the electrons (one e⁻ per Fe²⁺, so 2 Fe²⁺ per H₂O₂); 1 mark for H and O balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of H₂O₂ that reacts with 0.0100 mol of Fe²⁺ ions.
parts.working: Mole ratio H₂O₂ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 2, so 0.0100/2 = 0.00500 mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zinc metal reduces nitrate ions to ammonium ions in acid: Zn + NO₃⁻ + H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + NH₄⁺ + H₂O. Write the balanced ionic equation.
parts.answer: 4Zn + NO₃⁻ + 10H⁺ → 4Zn²⁺ + NH₄⁺ + 3H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for electrons: each Zn loses 2e⁻, NO₃⁻ gains 8e⁻; 1 mark for H and O balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of zinc needed to reduce 0.0500 mol of nitrate ions completely. (Ar Zn = 65.4)
parts.working: n(Zn) = 4 × 0.0500 = 0.200 mol (from the balanced equation); mass = 0.200 × 65.4 = 13.1 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Acidified manganate(VII) is titrated against ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄. The products are Mn²⁺ and CO₂. Write the balanced ionic equation.
parts.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O (using C₂O₄²⁻; or with H₂C₂O₄ and H⁺ adjusted equivalently)
parts.working: 1 mark for 10 electrons transferred (Mn 7 → 2, C +3 → +4 for each of the 5 ethanedioate ions); 1 mark for correct H and O balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ MnO₄⁻(aq) reacts completely with ethanedioate ions. Calculate the mass of ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄ (Mr = 90.0), that is oxidised, in g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Manganate(VII) ions react with hydrogen peroxide in acid: MnO₄⁻ + H₂O₂ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + O₂ + H₂O. Balance the equation using the ion-electron method and show the number of electrons in each half-equation.
parts.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O
parts.working: Mn half: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O; H₂O₂ half: H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. 1 mark each for the half-equations, 1 mark for the combined equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of O₂, in dm³ at room conditions, produced when 0.0100 mol of MnO₄⁻ reacts completely. (Molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³)
parts.working: 5 mol O₂ per 2 mol MnO₄⁻: n(O₂) = 0.0100 × 5/2 = 0.0250 mol; volume = 0.0250 × 24.0 = 0.600 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper(I) oxide is converted into copper and copper(II) ions in acid: Cu₂O(s) + H⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l). Balance the equation.
parts.answer: Cu₂O(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l)
parts.working: Balance electrons and charges: left +2 equals right +2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the change in oxidation number of copper in each of the two changes that occur, and state the name for this type of reaction.
parts.answer: Cu⁺ → Cu: +1 to 0 (reduction, gain of 1 e⁻). Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺: +1 to +2 (oxidation, loss of 1 e⁻). This is disproportionation.
parts.working: 1 mark for the two changes; 1 mark for disproportionation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide react: 2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 3S(s) + 2H₂O(l). State the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂S, in SO₂ and in S, and identify the species that is oxidised and the species that is reduced.
parts.answer: H₂S: −2; SO₂: +4; S: 0. H₂S is oxidised (S from −2 to 0); SO₂ is reduced (S from +4 to 0).
parts.working: 1 mark for the three oxidation numbers; 1 mark for identifying H₂S as oxidised and SO₂ as reduced. Electrons balance: each S of H₂S loses 2 e⁻ (2 × 2 = 4 e⁻), and the S of SO₂ gains 4 e⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of sulfur formed when 0.300 mol of SO₂ reacts completely with excess H₂S.
parts.working: Mole ratio SO₂ : S = 1 : 3, so n(S) = 0.300 × 3 = 0.900 mol. 1 mark for the ratio; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tin(II) ions reduce acidified manganate(VII) ions: MnO₄⁻ + Sn²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺ + H₂O. Balance the equation.
parts.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5Sn²⁺ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5Sn⁴⁺ + 8H₂O
parts.working: Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ loses 2e⁻; MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ gains 5e⁻; so 5 Sn and 2 Mn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of tin(II) ions, Sn²⁺, that can be oxidised by 0.0200 mol of MnO₄⁻ in this reaction. (Ar Sn = 118.7)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrode potential of a Ni²⁺(aq)/Ni(s) half-cell at 298 K in which [Ni²⁺(aq)] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Use E = E° + (0.059/z) log[Ni²⁺] with E° = −0.25 V. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for substituting z = 2 and log(0.0010) = −3; 1 mark for −0.34 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fe³⁺(aq)/Fe²⁺(aq) E° = +0.77 V. Calculate E for this half-cell in which [Fe³⁺] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ and [Fe²⁺] = 0.00500 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Use E = E° + 0.059 log([Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺]). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for ratio [Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺] = 10 with log 10 = 1; 1 mark for +0.83 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Cu²⁺(aq)/Cu(s) half-cell has [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³. It is connected to a Zn²⁺(aq)/Zn(s) half-cell with [Zn²⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³. Use E° values of +0.34 V (Cu) and −0.76 V (Zn). Calculate E for each half-cell.
parts.working: 1 mark for the Cu half-cell using z = 2 and log(0.01) = −2; 1 mark for the Zn half-cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. of the cell, to 2 decimal places, and state which electrode is positive.
parts.answer: 1.07 V; the copper electrode is positive
parts.working: 1 mark for E_cell = E(positive) − E(negative); 1 mark for 1.07 V and the positive electrode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the Nernst equation for the half-equation Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), in the form E = E° + ... (use log₁₀).
parts.answer: E = E° + (0.059/2) log₁₀[Cu²⁺]
parts.working: Solids and pure metals have activity 1 and are omitted; z = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Cu²⁺/Cu electrode potential is required to be +0.30 V at 298 K. Calculate the concentration of Cu²⁺(aq) needed, in mol dm⁻³, to 3 significant figures. (E° = +0.34 V)
parts.answer: 0.0441 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: 0.30 = 0.34 + 0.0295 log[Cu²⁺]; log[Cu²⁺] = −1.3559; [Cu²⁺] = 10^−1.3559 = 4.41 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³. 1 mark for rearranging; 1 mark for log value; 1 mark for 0.0441 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Ag⁺(aq)/Ag(s) half-cell has E° = +0.80 V. Calculate the electrode potential when [Ag⁺] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electrode potential becomes less positive as the silver ion concentration falls.
parts.answer: A lower [Ag⁺] makes it less favourable for Ag⁺ to gain electrons (equilibrium shifts towards Ag⁺), so the reduction is less easily driven and E becomes less positive.
parts.working: 1 mark for less favourable reduction at lower [Ag⁺]; 1 mark for equilibrium position or E being less positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The half-equation for chlorine is Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻(aq), E° = +1.36 V. Show that the Nernst equation for this half-cell can be written as E = E° − 0.059 log[Cl⁻] when the chlorine pressure is 1 atm.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reaction quotient Q = [Cl⁻]²/p(Cl₂) with p(Cl₂) = 1 atm, giving the (0.059/2) log[Cl⁻]² term; 1 mark for simplifying (0.059/2) × 2 = 0.059 to give E = E° − 0.059 log[Cl⁻].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E for this half-cell when [Cl⁻] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell has E° = −0.76 V. Calculate E when [Zn²⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for substitution with log(10⁻²) = −2, giving −0.76 + 0.0295 × (−2); 1 mark for −0.819 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether this zinc electrode is more or less likely to act as the negative electrode than under standard conditions.
parts.answer: It is more likely to be the negative electrode, because the more negative E is, the more readily zinc is oxidised. The dilution makes the potential more negative than −0.76 V.
parts.working: 1 mark for more negative E; 1 mark for linking to oxidation/negative electrode.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell (E° = +0.34 V) is connected to a Pb²⁺/Pb half-cell (E° = −0.13 V). The Cu²⁺ concentration is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ and the Pb²⁺ concentration is 1.00 mol dm⁻³. Calculate the e.m.f. of the cell at 298 K, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for E(Cu) with log(0.001) = −3 giving 0.25 V; 1 mark for E(Pb) = −0.13 V; 1 mark for E_cell = 0.38 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the e.m.f. changes if the Cu²⁺ solution is diluted tenfold, and explain.
parts.answer: The e.m.f. falls, because [Cu²⁺] decreases, making the Cu²⁺/Cu potential less positive and reducing the cell e.m.f. (The Pb²⁺/Pb potential is unchanged.)
parts.working: 1 mark for a lower e.m.f.; 1 mark for the reason based on the Nernst equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for the e.m.f. of a cell in which the positive electrode is Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ and the negative electrode is Zn²⁺/Zn, in terms of E° values and concentrations.
parts.answer: E_cell = E(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) − E(Zn²⁺/Zn), each with its Nernst term: E = E° + 0.059 log([Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺]) and E = E° + 0.0295 log[Zn²⁺]
parts.working: 1 mark for E_cell = E(positive) − E(negative); 1 mark for both Nernst forms with correct z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect on the e.m.f. when [Fe²⁺] is increased, and explain.
parts.answer: The e.m.f. decreases, because increasing [Fe²⁺] lowers the ratio [Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺], making the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ potential less positive.
parts.working: Reduction potential depends on [oxidised]/[reduced].

parts.label: a
parts.text: The e.m.f. of a cell made from Ag⁺/Ag and Zn²⁺/Zn half-cells is 1.56 V when [Ag⁺] = [Zn²⁺] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³ (standard conditions). E° Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V; E° Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V. Keeping [Zn²⁺] at 1.00 mol dm⁻³, calculate the [Ag⁺] needed to give an e.m.f. of 1.52 V at 298 K, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: [Ag⁺] ≈ 0.21 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Use E_cell = E(Ag) − E(Zn) with E(Zn) = −0.76 V: E(Ag) = 0.76 V; then log[Ag⁺] = (0.76 − 0.80)/0.059 = −0.678; [Ag⁺] ≈ 0.21 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol is oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI) to ethanoic acid. Write the balanced half-equation for the oxidation of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, to ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, using H₂O and H⁺ as needed.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
parts.working: 1 mark for the species and the water; 1 mark for 4H⁺ and 4e⁻ with balanced oxygen and charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the reduction half-equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, combine it with the ethanol oxidation half-equation to write the balanced ionic equation for the reaction of ethanol with acidified dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: 3C₂H₅OH + 2Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 3CH₃COOH + 4Cr³⁺ + 11H₂O
parts.working: Multiply the oxidation half-equation by 3 (12 e⁻) and the reduction by 2 (12 e⁻), then add and cancel. 1 mark for the electron balance; 1 mark for the balanced equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Pb²⁺(aq)/Pb(s) half-cell has E° = −0.13 V. Calculate E at 298 K when [Pb²⁺] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³, to 2 decimal places. Use E = E° + (0.059/2) log[Pb²⁺].

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Sn⁴⁺(aq)/Sn²⁺(aq) half-cell has E° = +0.15 V. Write the half-equation and the Nernst equation with z = 2. Then calculate E at 298 K when [Sn⁴⁺] = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ and [Sn²⁺] = 0.200 mol dm⁻³, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for the half-equation and z = 2; 1 mark for the ratio [Sn⁴⁺]/[Sn²⁺] = 0.1; 1 mark for E = +0.12 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For the reaction Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), E°cell = +2.71 V. Calculate ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures, using ΔG° = −nFE°cell. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: -523 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the negative sign of ΔG° shows about the reaction under standard conditions.
parts.answer: The reaction is feasible (spontaneous) under standard conditions.
parts.working: A negative ΔG° means the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ni(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). Ni²⁺/Ni has E° = −0.25 V and Ag⁺/Ag has E° = +0.80 V. Calculate E°cell and ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: E°cell = +1.05 V; ΔG° = -203 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for E°cell = 1.05 V; 1 mark for n = 2; 1 mark for ΔG° = −203 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Sn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). The standard electrode potentials are Sn²⁺/Sn −0.14 V and Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V. Calculate E°cell and ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: E°cell = +0.94 V; ΔG° = −181 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.14) = 0.94 V; 1 mark for n = 2; 1 mark for ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 0.94 = −181 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction has ΔG° = −38.9 kJ mol⁻¹ and one electron is transferred per mole of reaction. Calculate E°cell, to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether E°cell is positive or negative for a feasible reaction, and give the reason.
parts.answer: Positive, because ΔG° is negative and ΔG° = −nFE°cell.
parts.working: Negative ΔG° requires positive E°cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The reaction H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) has ΔG° = −237.1 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH° = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Calculate the standard e.m.f. of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell producing liquid water, to 2 decimal places. (2 electrons per H₂)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum percentage of the enthalpy change that can be converted into electrical work, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrolysis of water needs a minimum voltage equal to the magnitude of E°cell for the reaction 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Using ΔG° = +474.2 kJ mol⁻¹ for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g), calculate the minimum voltage, to 2 decimal places. (4 electrons per O₂ formed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cell is operated at 2.00 V. Calculate the electrical energy supplied per mole of H₂ produced, in kJ, assuming all the energy is used for electrolysis (2 e⁻ per H₂). Calculate the efficiency based on ΔG° = +237.1 kJ mol⁻¹ for H₂O → H₂ + ½O₂.
parts.answer: Energy supplied = 2 × 96 500 × 2.00 = 386 kJ per mole of H₂; efficiency = 237.1/386 = 61.4%
parts.working: 1 mark for energy = nFE with n = 2; 1 mark for 386 kJ; 1 mark for efficiency 61.4%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium reacts with silver ions: Al(s) + 3Ag⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + 3Ag(s). E° for Al³⁺/Al is −1.66 V and for Ag⁺/Ag is +0.80 V. Calculate ΔG° per mole of Al reacting, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: -712 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: E°cell = 2.46 V; n = 3 per mole of Al; ΔG° = −3 × 96 500 × 2.46 = −712 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), with E°cell = +3.17 V, gives ΔG° per mole of Mg. Calculate it and state which metal gives more energy per mole of metal.
parts.answer: -612 kJ mol⁻¹; aluminium gives more energy per mole
parts.working: 1 mark for −612 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for aluminium giving more energy per mole (−712 kJ vs −612 kJ).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) has E°cell = +1.10 V. Explain why ΔG° negative does not tell you how fast the reaction occurs.
parts.answer: ΔG° gives feasibility (thermodynamics) only. The rate depends on kinetics (activation energy, surface area, concentration), so a feasible reaction may be very slow.
parts.working: 1 mark for feasibility versus rate; 1 mark for a factor affecting rate such as activation energy or surface area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for this reaction in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −212 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data in a table: E° for Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V and for Cl₂/Cl⁻ = +1.36 V. A student electrolyses aqueous copper(II) chloride. Calculate the minimum voltage needed to make copper and chlorine from CuCl₂(aq), and the ΔG° for this process in kJ mol⁻¹ (n = 2).
parts.answer: Minimum voltage = 1.02 V; ΔG° = +197 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for E°cell = 0.34 − 1.36 = −1.02 V; 1 mark for minimum voltage 1.02 V; 1 mark for ΔG° = +197 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the copper chloride electrolysis needs an energy input while a Zn/Cu cell (E°cell = +1.10 V) releases energy.
parts.answer: The electrolysis has a negative E°cell and positive ΔG°, so it is not spontaneous and needs electrical energy input. The Zn/Cu cell has a positive E°cell and negative ΔG°, so it releases energy.
parts.working: 1 mark for sign of E°cell/ΔG° for each process; 1 mark for the energy direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lead–acid cell. Overall reaction: Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 2H₂SO₄(aq) → 2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l). Standard electrode potentials: PbO₂/PbSO₄ +1.69 V; PbSO₄/Pb −0.36 V. Calculate E°cell and ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures (n = 2, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: E°cell = +2.05 V; ΔG° = −396 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for E°cell = 1.69 − (−0.36) = 2.05 V; 1 mark for n = 2; 1 mark for ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 2.05 = −396 kJ mol⁻¹ (−395.65 kJ).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is feasible under standard conditions, and give the reason in terms of the sign of ΔG°.
parts.answer: Feasible, because ΔG° is negative (E°cell is positive).
parts.working: A negative ΔG° means the reaction is feasible; ΔG° = −nFE°cell, so a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cell reaction has E°cell = +0.95 V and n = 1. Calculate ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures. Then calculate the E°cell that would correspond to ΔG° = −183.5 kJ mol⁻¹ with the same n = 1.
parts.answer: ΔG° = −91.7 kJ mol⁻¹; E°cell = 1.90 V
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔG° = −1 × 96 500 × 0.95 = −91.7 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for E°cell = −ΔG°/(nF) = 183 500/96 500 = 1.90 V; 1 mark for stating that E is proportional to ΔG° when n is fixed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption this method makes about the cell conditions.
parts.answer: Standard conditions (298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions, 1 atm gases) are assumed.
parts.working: ΔG° and E°cell refer to standard conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cell reaction has ΔG° = −377 kJ mol⁻¹ and E°cell = +1.95 V. Calculate the number of electrons, n, transferred in the equation as written, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
parts.working: 1 mark for rearranging ΔG° = −nFE° to n = −ΔG°/(FE°); 1 mark for n = 2.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with propan-1-ol, and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃COCl + CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ + HCl; the product is propyl ethanoate
parts.working: 1 mark for correct equation with HCl; 1 mark for naming the ester (propyl ethanoate).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason this reaction is preferred to heating ethanoic acid with propan-1-ol.
parts.answer: It is faster and goes to completion, because the reaction is not reversible.
parts.working: Acyl chloride esterification is not an equilibrium, unlike the acid-catalysed esterification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzoyl chloride, C₆H₅COCl, reacts with water: C₆H₅COCl + H₂O → C₆H₅COOH + HCl. Calculate the maximum mass of benzoic acid, in g to 3 significant figures, formed from 3.50 g of benzoyl chloride. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0, Cl 35.5; Mr benzoic acid = 122.0)
parts.working: 1 mark for Mr(C₇H₅ClO) = 140.5 and n = 0.0249 mol; 1 mark for 1:1 ratio; 1 mark for 3.04 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why benzoyl chloride must be kept dry and stored away from moist air.
parts.answer: It hydrolyses with water vapour in air, giving HCl fumes and benzoic acid.
parts.working: Acyl chlorides are moisture sensitive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoyl chloride reacts with excess methylamine, CH₃NH₂. Write the equation for the reaction and name the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂COCl + 2CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CH₂CONHCH₃ + CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻; the product is N-methylpropanamide
parts.working: 1 mark for organic product and amide; 1 mark for the second equivalent of amine forming the salt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why two moles of methylamine are needed for each mole of acyl chloride.
parts.answer: One mole acts as the nucleophile; the second neutralises the HCl formed, which would otherwise protonate the amine and stop the reaction.
parts.working: Accept any statement that one amine is used to neutralise HCl.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A liquid acyl chloride, X, contains by mass: C 38.9%, H 5.4%, Cl 38.3%, O 17.3%. Calculate its empirical formula. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, Cl 35.5, O 16.0)
parts.answer: C₃H₅ClO
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing by Ar: C 3.24, H 5.4, Cl 1.08, O 1.08; 1 mark for dividing by 1.08 to get the simplest ratio; 1 mark for C₃H₅ClO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Its Mr is 92.5. Name X and give its structural formula.
parts.answer: Propanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl
parts.working: The empirical and molecular formulae are the same; propanoyl chloride is the acyl chloride with this formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.845 g of propanoyl chloride, C₂H₅COCl (Mr = 92.5), is added to excess water. The solution is titrated with 0.250 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Explain why 2 mol of NaOH are needed for each mole of propanoyl chloride.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis gives propanoic acid and HCl, which together provide two acidic protons per mole of acyl chloride.
parts.working: 1 mark for propanoic acid and HCl formed; 1 mark for two H⁺ per mole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of NaOH, in cm³ to 3 significant figures, needed to neutralise all the acid formed.
parts.answer: 73.1 cm³
parts.working: n(acyl chloride) = 0.845/92.5 = 9.14 × 10⁻³ mol; n(NaOH) = 2 × that = 1.83 × 10⁻² mol; volume = 1.83 × 10⁻²/0.250 = 73.1 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenol is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide and ethanoyl chloride is added. Write an equation for the reaction and name the ester formed.
parts.answer: C₆H₅O⁻Na⁺ + CH₃COCl → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + NaCl; the ester is phenyl ethanoate
parts.working: 1 mark for the ester and salt products; 1 mark for the name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reaction with phenol is carried out in aqueous NaOH rather than with phenol alone.
parts.answer: NaOH converts phenol into the more nucleophilic phenoxide ion, which attacks the acyl chloride faster; the NaOH also neutralises the HCl formed.
parts.working: 1 mark for phenoxide being more nucleophilic; 1 mark for neutralising HCl or driving the reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoyl chloride (3.93 g) is mixed with ethanol (2.50 g). Calculate the amounts in mol of each reactant, and identify the limiting reagent. (Mr: CH₃COCl 78.5, C₂H₅OH 46.0)
parts.answer: Ethanoyl chloride: 0.0501 mol; ethanol: 0.0543 mol; limiting reagent is ethanoyl chloride
parts.working: 1 mark for both amounts; 1 mark for identifying the limiting reagent with the 1:1 ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass, in g, of ethyl ethanoate that can form. (Mr ethyl ethanoate = 88.0)
parts.working: Maximum from the limiting reagent: 0.0501 × 88.0 = 4.41 g. Using 0.0500 mol gives 4.40 g; either is accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The actual yield of ethyl ethanoate is 3.30 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pKa values are: ethanoic acid 4.76; chloroethanoic acid 2.86; propanoic acid 4.87; phenol 9.95. Place these four compounds in order of increasing acidity (weakest first).
parts.answer: Phenol < propanoic acid < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct order; 1 mark for explaining higher acidity means lower pKa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chloroethanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: The electron-withdrawing Cl atom pulls electron density from the O–H bond, stabilising the anion and making H⁺ easier to release.
parts.working: 1 mark for electron-withdrawing inductive effect; 1 mark for stabilising the carboxylate ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chloroethanoic acid has Ka = 1.38 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (pKa 2.86). Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ chloroethanoic acid at 298 K. Assume that [H⁺] = √(Ka × c). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for [H⁺] = √(1.38 × 10⁻³ × 0.100) = 1.17 × 10⁻²; 1 mark for taking −log₁₀; 1 mark for pH = 1.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason the pH calculated in (a) is an approximation.
parts.answer: Some of the acid is not fully dissociated, so the [H⁺] used is an approximation and the true value is slightly lower.
parts.working: The approximation assumes the dissociation is small.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoic acid has pKa = 4.87. Calculate Ka for propanoic acid at 298 K, in mol dm⁻³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.35e-05 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁸⁷ = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the pKa of ethanol is much higher than that of ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: Ethanol has no delocalised carboxylate anion; its conjugate base (alkoxide) is not stabilised by resonance, so the O–H is much less acidic.
parts.working: 1 mark for the anion stability; 1 mark for the comparison with the carboxylate resonance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanol with sodium metal, and calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, produced at room conditions when 0.460 g of ethanol reacts completely. (Mr C₂H₅OH = 46.0; molar gas volume = 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂; 120 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark for equation; 1 mark for n(ethanol) = 0.0100 mol; 1 mark for 0.00500 mol H₂ × 24 000 = 120 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2,4,6-Trichlorophenol is a stronger acid than phenol. Explain this in terms of the stability of the phenoxide ion formed on losing H⁺.
parts.answer: The electron-withdrawing Cl atoms withdraw electron density from the ring, spreading the negative charge of the phenoxide ion and stabilising it. This makes H⁺ loss easier, so the acid is stronger than phenol.
parts.working: 1 mark for electron-withdrawing Cl; 1 mark for stabilising the phenoxide anion; 1 mark for linking to easier H⁺ loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the pKa of 2,4,6-trichlorophenol compares with that of phenol.
parts.answer: The pKa is lower than that of phenol (9.95).
parts.working: Stronger acid means lower pKa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A monoprotic weak acid HX of concentration 0.200 mol dm⁻³ has pH = 2.45 at 298 K. Calculate [H⁺], then calculate Ka, giving Ka to 2 significant figures. Use Ka = [H⁺]²/([HX] at equilibrium), where [HX] = 0.200 − [H⁺].
parts.answer: [H⁺] = 3.55e-03 mol dm⁻³; Ka = 6.4e-05 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: 1 mark for [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁴⁵ = 3.55 × 10⁻³; 1 mark for [HX] at equilibrium = 0.196; 1 mark for Ka = 6.4 × 10⁻⁵.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is necessary to use [HX] equilibrium rather than 0.200 in this calculation.
parts.answer: Dissociation is significant; using 0.200 would give a Ka slightly too small, so the equilibrium concentration is more accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark for the dissociated acid being taken away from the starting concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzoic acid has pKa = 4.20 and phenol has pKa = 9.95 at 298 K. Calculate the ratio Ka(benzoic acid) : Ka(phenol). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why benzoic acid, not phenol, liberates CO₂ from aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate.
parts.answer: Benzoic acid is strong enough to donate H⁺ to HCO₃⁻, which forms carbonic acid that decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Phenol is too weak an acid (pKa 9.95) to do this.
parts.working: 1 mark for benzoic acid being stronger than carbonic acid; 1 mark for phenol being weaker than carbonic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas ethanoic acid and ethanol need a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst and heating. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: The C–Cl bond in the acyl chloride is much more polar than the C–OH in the acid, so the carbonyl carbon is far more electrophilic and attacked readily. The reaction is also not reversible, so no catalyst or heating is needed to drive it.
parts.working: 1 mark for more electrophilic carbonyl carbon; 1 mark for the reaction being non-reversible/faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenol has pKa = 9.95 at 298 K. Calculate Ka for phenol in mol dm⁻³, giving your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.12 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of reactants gives methyl butanoate on esterification?
A butanoic acid and methanol
B methanoic acid and butan-1-ol
C ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol
D propanoic acid and ethanol
parts.answer: A butanoic acid and methanol
parts.working: Methyl butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃, is made from butanoic acid (acid part) and methanol (alcohol part). B gives butyl methanoate; C and D give different esters.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ethyl benzoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which products are formed?
A benzoic acid and ethanol
B sodium benzoate and ethanol
C sodium ethanoate and phenol
D benzoic acid and sodium ethoxide
parts.answer: B sodium benzoate and ethanol
parts.working: Base hydrolysis (saponification) gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol. A forms the free acid, which is not produced directly in alkali.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the formation of methyl methanoate from methanoic acid and methanol, and name the catalyst used in the reaction.
parts.answer: HCOOH + CH₃OH ⇌ HCOOCH₃ + H₂O; catalyst is concentrated sulfuric acid
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation including water; 1 mark for concentrated H₂SO₄ as the catalyst.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid (5.00 g, Mr = 60.0) is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid. 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate (Mr = 88.0) is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
parts.working: 1 mark for the theoretical mass: 5.00/60.0 × 88.0 = 7.33 g; 1 mark for the ratio; 1 mark for 72.0%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃ (Mr = 74.0), is hydrolysed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH needed to hydrolyse 2.20 g of the ester completely. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 149 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark for n(ester) = 2.20/74.0 = 0.0297 mol; 1 mark for 1:1 ratio; 1 mark for 149 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ester X has molecular formula C₅H₁₀O₂. On hydrolysis with dilute acid, X gives ethanol and a carboxylic acid Y. Deduce the structural formula and name of Y, and write the name of X.
parts.answer: Y is propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH; X is ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃
parts.working: 1 mark for ethanol identifying the alcohol part; 1 mark for propanoic acid; 1 mark for the name ethyl propanoate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ester has the percentage composition by mass: C 58.8%, H 9.8%, O 31.4%. Calculate its empirical formula. (Ar: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
parts.answer: C₅H₁₀O₂
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing by Ar to get C 4.90, H 9.8, O 1.96; 1 mark for the ratio 5 : 10 : 2 giving C₅H₁₀O₂ (Mr 102).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Mr of the ester is 102. Give the molecular formula and suggest the name of one ester with this formula.
parts.answer: C₅H₁₀O₂; for example ethyl propanoate
parts.working: The empirical formula equals the molecular formula here (Mr 102 = empirical mass 102).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism for the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, RCOOR′, using NaOH. Name the type of mechanism and describe each step.
parts.answer: Nucleophilic addition–elimination. OH⁻ attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond breaks and a tetrahedral intermediate forms; the C–OR′ bond breaks, expelling the alkoxide R′O⁻; the alkoxide removes a proton from RCOOH to form RCOO⁻ and R′OH.
parts.working: 1 mark for nucleophilic addition–elimination; 1 mark for OH⁻ attacking the carbonyl carbon; 1 mark for tetrahedral intermediate and elimination of the alkoxide; 1 mark for the final proton transfer giving carboxylate and alcohol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the ester formed from butanoic acid and propan-2-ol.
parts.answer: propan-2-yl butanoate
parts.working: 1 mark for the alcohol part named as propan-2-yl; 1 mark for the acid part butanoate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent reduces butanone to butan-2-ol but does not reduce butanoic acid?
A sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), NaBH₄
B lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄
C acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
D water with a platinum catalyst
parts.answer: A NaBH₄
parts.working: NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids. LiAlH₄ reduces both; dichromate is an oxidant and water/Pt does not reduce butanone.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Propan-2-one is reduced by NaBH₄, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the organic product?
A propan-1-ol
B propan-2-ol
C propanal
D propanoic acid
parts.answer: B propan-2-ol
parts.working: The ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol, propan-2-ol. A is a primary alcohol (wrong carbonyl position), C is an aldehyde, D is an oxidation product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reduction of pentanoic acid, CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH, to pentan-1-ol using [H] to represent the reducing agent.
parts.answer: CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH + 4[H] → CH₃(CH₂)₃CH₂OH + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for four [H] atoms; 1 mark for water as a by-product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 3.00 g of pentanoic acid (Mr = 102.0) is reduced to give 2.24 g of pentan-1-ol (Mr = 88.0). Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for theoretical mass 3.00/102.0 × 88.0 = 2.59 g; 1 mark for the ratio; 1 mark for 86.5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the products when each compound is reduced with NaBH₄: (i) 2-methylpropanal (ii) cyclohexanone.
parts.answer: (i) 2-methylpropan-1-ol (2-methylpropanol); (ii) cyclohexanol
parts.working: 1 mark each for the alcohol; aldehyde gives primary, ketone gives secondary alcohol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, is reduced by NaBH₄ in aqueous solution, followed by acidification. Name the organic product, and explain why an ester such as ethyl ethanoate present in the same solution is not reduced.
parts.answer: Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. NaBH₄ is a mild source of hydride ions that reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters, because the ester carbonyl carbon is less electrophilic (its C=O is conjugated with the lone pair on the alkoxy oxygen).
parts.working: 1 mark for propan-1-ol (primary alcohol); 1 mark for NaBH₄ being too mild for esters; 1 mark for the ester carbonyl carbon being less electrophilic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the hydride ion, why LiAlH₄ reduces a carboxylic acid but NaBH₄ does not.
parts.answer: LiAlH₄ is a stronger source of H⁻ (more reactive, as the Al–H bonds are weaker/more polar), which can attack the less electrophilic carboxyl carbon. NaBH₄ delivers H⁻ less readily and is not reactive enough for the acid.
parts.working: 1 mark for LiAlH₄ being the more powerful hydride donor; 1 mark for NaBH₄ being too mild for the carboxyl group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethyl benzoate is reduced by LiAlH₄ in dry ether, followed by water. Give the names and structural formulae of both organic products.
parts.answer: Phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol), C₆H₅CH₂OH, and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
parts.working: 1 mark for phenylmethanol; 1 mark for ethanol; 1 mark for the structural formulae of both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butanal and butanone are each reduced with NaBH₄. Name each product and state whether the product of butanone reduction has a chiral centre.
parts.answer: Butanal gives butan-1-ol (no chiral centre); butanone gives butan-2-ol, which has a chiral centre at C2.
parts.working: 1 mark for both alcohols; 1 mark for stating chirality in butan-2-ol with reason (four different groups on C2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the reduction of a carboxylic acid is usually done with LiAlH₄ in dry ether rather than with H₂ and a nickel catalyst at room temperature.
parts.answer: Carboxylic acids are not reduced by H₂/Ni under mild conditions; LiAlH₄ is a strong hydride donor that reduces the carboxyl group effectively at room temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for H₂/Ni not reducing carboxylic acids easily; 1 mark for LiAlH₄ being a strong enough hydride donor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas is evolved when ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate?
A hydrogen
B oxygen
C carbon dioxide
D ethyne
parts.answer: C carbon dioxide
parts.working: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from hydrogencarbonate, giving CO₂ with effervescence. Hydrogen is produced with reactive metals, not with hydrogencarbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of butanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution, and name the salt formed.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + NaOH → CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa + H₂O; sodium butanoate
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation; 1 mark for the salt name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.240 g of magnesium ribbon (Ar Mg = 24.3) reacts completely with excess ethanoic acid. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room conditions, in cm³ to 3 significant figures. (Molar gas volume = 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 237 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark for n(Mg) = 0.240/24.3 = 9.88 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 mark for 1:1 H₂ ratio (Mg + 2CH₃COOH → …); 1 mark for 237 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution of hydrochloric acid has pH 1.0, while a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution of ethanoic acid has a pH of about 2.9. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: HCl is fully dissociated, giving [H⁺] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³; ethanoic acid is a weak acid that only partially dissociates, so [H⁺] is much less than 0.100 mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: 1 mark for complete dissociation of HCl; 1 mark for partial dissociation of ethanoic acid giving a lower [H⁺].

parts.label: a
parts.text: 25.0 cm³ of propanoic acid solution is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. 20.0 cm³ of NaOH is needed for complete neutralisation. Calculate the concentration of the acid, in mol dm⁻³, assuming it is monoprotic.
parts.answer: 0.0800 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: 1 mark for n(NaOH) = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 mark for 1:1 ratio; 1 mark for 2.00 × 10⁻³/0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoic acid reacts with magnesium carbonate: 2CH₃CH₂COOH + MgCO₃ → (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Mg + CO₂ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in g to 3 significant figures, produced when 2.00 g of MgCO₃ reacts completely with excess acid. (Mr MgCO₃ = 84.3; Mr CO₂ = 44.0)
parts.working: 1 mark for n(MgCO₃) = 2.00/84.3 = 2.37 × 10⁻² mol; 1 mark for 1:1 ratio of MgCO₃ to CO₂; 1 mark for 1.04 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous ammonia to form a salt. Write an equation for the reaction and name the salt formed.
parts.answer: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COONH₄; ammonium ethanoate
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation (neutralisation); 1 mark for ammonium ethanoate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoic acid (0.100 mol) reacts with sodium carbonate: 2CH₃CH₂COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃CH₂COONa + CO₂ + H₂O. Calculate the volume of CO₂, in dm³ at room conditions, produced when 0.100 mol of propanoic acid reacts completely with excess sodium carbonate. (Molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 1.20 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why phenol does not liberate CO₂ when it reacts with sodium carbonate under the same conditions.
parts.answer: Phenol (pKa 9.95) is too weak an acid to react with carbonate; it cannot donate H⁺ to form carbonic acid.
parts.working: Carboxylic acids are stronger than carbonic acid; phenol is weaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.440 g of an organic acid, Mr = 88.0, is dissolved and titrated with 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the volume of NaOH, in cm³, needed for complete neutralisation if the acid is monoprotic.
parts.answer: 25 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark for n(acid) = 0.440/88.0 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 mark for 25.0 cm³ (1:1 ratio).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student finds that 50.0 cm³ of the same NaOH is needed for the same mass of acid. Deduce whether the acid is monoprotic or diprotic.
parts.answer: Diprotic. Twice the volume of NaOH means each mole of acid releases two H⁺ ions (two carboxyl groups), so the acid is diprotic.
parts.working: 1 mark for doubling the volume; 1 mark for two acidic protons per molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄ (Mr = 90.0), is a diprotic acid. Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH needed to neutralise 0.450 g of ethanedioic acid completely.
parts.answer: 100 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark for n(H₂C₂O₄) = 0.450/90.0 = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 mark for NaOH = 2 × 5.00 × 10⁻³ = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol; 1 mark for 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid (b.p. 118 °C) and propan-1-ol (b.p. 97 °C) both have Mr = 60.0. Explain why ethanoic acid has the higher boiling point.
parts.answer: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, with two H-bonds per pair of molecules, which are stronger in total than the H-bonds between alcohol molecules. More energy is needed to separate the dimers.
parts.working: 1 mark for hydrogen bonding; 1 mark for dimer formation; 1 mark for more energy needed to overcome the dimer's intermolecular forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzoic acid is added to aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate. Describe what is seen and write an ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Effervescence (fizzing) as a colourless gas is produced and the solid dissolves. C₆H₅COOH + HCO₃⁻ → C₆H₅COO⁻ + CO₂ + H₂O.
parts.working: 1 mark for effervescence/fizzing and dissolving; 1 mark for correct ionic equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid by heating under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Explain why an excess of oxidising agent is used.
parts.answer: An excess of oxidising agent ensures the propanal intermediate is fully oxidised to propanoic acid, rather than stopping at the aldehyde.
parts.working: 1 mark for the aldehyde being oxidised further; 1 mark for complete oxidation to acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid. Write an equation for the formation of ethanoic acid from ethanenitrile, using H⁺ and H₂O, and name the ammonium-containing product.
parts.answer: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + H⁺ → CH₃COOH + NH₄⁺; the ammonium product is ammonium chloride in solution (or NH₄⁺)
parts.working: 1 mark for the carboxylic acid; 1 mark for NH₄⁺ (ammonium) product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2.30 g of ethanol (Mr = 46.0) is oxidised to ethanoic acid (Mr = 60.0), and 2.40 g of ethanoic acid is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
parts.working: 1 mark for theoretical mass 2.30/46.0 × 60.0 = 3.00 g; 1 mark for the ratio; 1 mark for 80.0%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal is oxidised to propanoic acid. Write an equation for this oxidation using [O] to represent the oxidising agent.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CHO + [O] → CH₃CH₂COOH
parts.working: One oxygen atom is added to the aldehyde to form the acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoic acid can be made from 1-chloropropane in two steps: (1) heating with NaCN in ethanol; (2) hydrolysis of the nitrile with dilute acid. Write the equation for step (1) and name the organic product of step (1).
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN + Cl⁻; the product is butanenitrile
parts.working: 1 mark for the nucleophilic substitution equation; 1 mark for butanenitrile (note: one carbon added to the chain).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the name of the final carboxylic acid after hydrolysis, and explain why this route adds one carbon atom to the chain.
parts.answer: Butanoic acid; the CN⁻ carbon becomes the carboxyl carbon, so the chain gains one carbon.
parts.working: 1 mark for the name; 1 mark for the CN carbon becoming part of COOH.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Butanoic acid can be made from 1-chloropropane in two steps: (1) heating with NaCN in ethanol; (2) hydrolysis of the nitrile with dilute acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butan-1-ol (1.85 g, Mr = 74.0) is oxidised completely to butanoic acid (Mr = 88.0). Calculate the maximum mass of butanoic acid that can be obtained, in g to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: n(butanol) = 1.85/74.0 = 0.0250 mol; maximum butanoic acid = 0.0250 × 88.0 = 2.20 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an aldehyde is distilled off during oxidation of a primary alcohol, but the carboxylic acid is obtained by heating under reflux.
parts.answer: Distilling the aldehyde as it forms removes it before it can be oxidised further, so the aldehyde is the product. Heating under reflux keeps the reaction mixture at the boiling point, returning vapour so that oxidation continues to the carboxylic acid.
parts.working: 1 mark for removing aldehyde as it forms; 1 mark for reflux returning vapour; 1 mark for complete oxidation to acid under reflux.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylbenzene is heated under reflux with acidified potassium manganate(VII). Name the organic product and state its use.
parts.answer: Benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH); used as a food preservative or in the manufacture of plasticisers.
parts.working: 1 mark for benzoic acid; 1 mark for a valid use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethyl propanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write the equation for the formation of the carboxylate salt, and state the step needed to obtain propanoic acid itself.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃CH₂COONa + C₂H₅OH; acidify the salt with dilute HCl (or H₂SO₄) and separate the acid.
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation; 1 mark for acidifying the sodium salt to release the free acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to prepare pure ethanoic acid from ethanol in the laboratory. Describe the method (reagent, conditions, and how the product is separated) and state one safety precaution.
parts.answer: Warm ethanol with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux; then distil off the ethanoic acid (b.p. 118 °C) from the mixture; precaution: use a fume cupboard and wear gloves and goggles because dichromate is toxic and the mixture is corrosive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for oxidant and reflux; 1 mark for distillation to separate; 1 mark for a valid safety point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid is a more efficient route than the hydrolysis of a nitrile for a school laboratory, giving one reason that favours each route.
parts.answer: Oxidation of alcohols uses readily available reagents at reflux in one step, without the toxic cyanide needed for nitrile preparation. Hydrolysis of a nitrile gives high purity but needs cyanide, which is hazardous; so oxidation is preferred in school labs.
parts.working: 1 mark for oxidation simplicity/availability; 1 mark for nitrile route needing cyanide; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of the ideal method for converting an alcohol into a carboxylic acid in industry, and explain one of them in terms of atom economy.
parts.answer: Features: high selectivity to the acid, with little over-oxidation or side products, and a cheap oxidant such as air or oxygen. Atom economy: O₂ gives water as its only by-product, so most of its atoms end up in the acid; a chromium(VI) oxidant gives Cr³⁺ waste and lowers atom economy.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid feature; 1 mark for a clear atom-economy explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid in a process with a 75.0% yield. Calculate the mass of ethanol, in g to 3 significant figures, needed to produce 5.00 g of ethanoic acid. (Mr ethanol = 46.0; Mr ethanoic acid = 60.0)
parts.working: 1 mark for theoretical ethanol = 5.00/60.0 × 46.0 = 3.83 g; 1 mark for dividing by 0.750; 1 mark for 5.11 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate ΔH° (kJ mol⁻¹) and ΔS° (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at 298 K.
parts.answer: ΔH° = -92.2 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = -199.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K, in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures, and state whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K.
parts.answer: ΔG° = -32.9 kJ mol⁻¹; feasible
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −92.2 − 298 × (−0.1991) = −32.9 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for feasible since ΔG° < 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the temperature, in K to the nearest whole number, above which the reaction is no longer feasible.
parts.working: ΔG° = 0 when T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 92 200/(−199.1) with signs: T = 463 K; above this temperature ΔG° becomes positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water gas reaction: C(s) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + H₂(g). Data at 298 K: ΔfH° values are H₂O(g) −241.8 kJ mol⁻¹, CO(g) −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹, and C(s) 0; S° values are C(s) 5.7, H₂O(g) 188.8, CO(g) 197.7, H₂(g) 130.7 (all J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Calculate ΔH° and ΔS°.
parts.answer: ΔH° = +131.3 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +133.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature, in K, at which the reaction becomes feasible.
parts.working: ΔG° = 0 at T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 131 300/133.9 = 981 K. Minimum temperature 981 K (ΔG° ≤ 0 above this).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reaction has ΔH = −85 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −120 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Write the equation linking ΔG, ΔH, ΔS and T, and calculate the temperature at which ΔG = 0.
parts.answer: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; T = ΔH/ΔS = 708 K
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation; 1 mark for converting units (−85 000 J mol⁻¹); 1 mark for T = 708 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is feasible at 600 K and at 800 K, giving reasons.
parts.answer: Feasible at 600 K (below 708 K, ΔG < 0); not feasible at 800 K (above 708 K, ΔG > 0).
parts.working: 1 mark for the sign at 600 K; 1 mark for the sign at 800 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron(III) oxide is reduced by hydrogen: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3H₂(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O(g). Data: ΔfH° Fe₂O₃ −824.2, H₂O(g) −241.8 (kJ mol⁻¹); S° Fe₂O₃ 87.4, Fe 27.3, H₂ 130.7, H₂O(g) 188.8 (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Calculate ΔH° and ΔS°.
parts.answer: ΔH° = +98.8 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +141.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and the minimum temperature, in °C, at which the reduction becomes feasible.
parts.answer: ΔG° = +56.6 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K (not feasible); T = 698 K = 425 °C
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔG° = +56.6 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 698 K; 1 mark for conversion to 425 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonia is oxidised: 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g). Data (298 K): ΔfH° NO(g) +90.3, H₂O(g) −241.8, NH₃(g) −46.1 (kJ mol⁻¹); S° NO(g) 210.8, H₂O(g) 188.8, NH₃(g) 192.3, O₂(g) 205.2 (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for the reaction.
parts.answer: ΔH° = -905.2 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +180.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and state whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature. Explain the sign of ΔS°.
parts.answer: ΔG° = -959.1 kJ mol⁻¹; feasible. ΔS° is positive because the number of gas molecules rises from 9 (4 NH₃ + 5 O₂) to 10 (4 NO + 6 H₂O), giving more disorder.
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔG° = −959.1 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for feasible; 1 mark for gas moles increase giving positive ΔS°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ΔG° of a reaction was measured at four temperatures: 300 K, 0.0 kJ mol⁻¹; 400 K, −20.1 kJ mol⁻¹; 500 K, −40.0 kJ mol⁻¹; 600 K, −59.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Plot ΔG° against T and use the line of best fit to find the gradient, in kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Gradient = -0.199 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for plotting the four points and drawing a best-fit line; 1 mark for gradient ≈ −0.199 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (accept −0.198 to −0.201).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the gradient to find ΔS° in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and the intercept to find ΔH° in kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: ΔS° = +199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔH° = +60 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: Gradient = −ΔS°, so ΔS° ≈ +199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (accept +198 to +201); the intercept at T = 0 gives ΔH° ≈ +60 kJ mol⁻¹ (about +59.8).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the temperature, in K, at which the reaction becomes feasible.
parts.working: Feasible when ΔG° < 0, i.e. T > ΔH°/ΔS° = 60 000/200 = 300 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium carbonate decomposes in a lime kiln: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). ΔH° = +178.3 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +160.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° at 1200 K, in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: -14.5 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔS° check and substitution: ΔG° = 178.3 − 1200 × 0.1607 = −14.5 kJ mol⁻¹; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the kiln must be hot even though the reaction is feasible above about 1110 K, and state the minimum temperature from the data.
parts.answer: The reaction is slow at low temperature; the kiln must run at about 1200 K so that the rate is useful. Minimum feasible T = 1110 K.
parts.working: 1 mark for kinetic reasoning; 1 mark for T = about 1110 K from ΔH°/ΔS° (178 300/160.7 = 1109.5 K).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A process has ΔH = +12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +45 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate the temperature, in K to the nearest whole number, above which the process becomes feasible.
parts.working: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 12 500/45 = 278 K; the process is feasible above 278 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of ΔG at 250 K and at 300 K, and give the temperature range of feasibility as a summary.
parts.answer: At 250 K, ΔG > 0 (not feasible); at 300 K, ΔG < 0 (feasible). Feasible for T > 278 K.
parts.working: 1 mark for the signs; 1 mark for the stated range.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether ΔS is positive or negative for each reaction, and give a reason for each.
(i) Br₂(l) → Br₂(g)
(ii) N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g)
(iii) 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
(iv) Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s)
parts.answer: (i) positive; (ii) positive; (iii) negative; (iv) negative
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) liquid to gas; (ii) 1 mole gas becomes 2 moles; (iii) 3 mol gas becomes liquid; (iv) aqueous ions form a solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use S° values: CO(g) 197.7, O₂(g) 205.2, CO₂(g) 213.8 (all J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Calculate ΔS° for 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g), and state its sign.
parts.answer: ΔS° = −173.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (negative)
parts.working: 1 mark for 2 × 213.8 − (2 × 197.7 + 205.2) = −173.0; 1 mark for negative sign with the reason (3 gas moles to 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The enthalpy of fusion of ice at 273 K is +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔS for melting 2.00 mol of ice at this temperature, in J K⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: ΔS_fus = ΔH/T = 6010/273 = 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; for 2.00 mol, ΔS = 44.0 J K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the entropy change of melting is positive.
parts.answer: Molecules in a liquid have more freedom of movement and more disorder than in an ordered solid lattice.
parts.working: Solid to liquid increases disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The standard enthalpy of combustion of methane is −890 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Calculate ΔS_surr for the surroundings, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to 4 significant figures, assuming the heat is transferred at 298 K.
parts.answer: +2987 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (about +2987)
parts.working: ΔS_surr = −ΔH_sys/T = +890 000/298 = 2987 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 1 mark for the sign convention; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ΔS_surr is large and positive for this exothermic combustion.
parts.answer: Heat released to the surroundings increases the random motion of their particles, so surroundings gain entropy; the large value arises because 890 kJ is divided by only 298 K.
parts.working: Exothermic: ΔS_surr is positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place 1 mol of each of these gases in order of increasing standard entropy, lowest first, and give the S° value of each: O₂(g), O₃(g), N₂(g). Data (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): O₂ 205.2; O₃ 238.9; N₂ 191.6.
parts.working: 1 mark for the order; 1 mark for the values quoted correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why O₃ has a higher standard entropy than O₂ at the same conditions.
parts.answer: O₃ is a larger molecule with more atoms, so more vibrational and rotational modes are available and more ways of arranging energy.
parts.working: Greater molar mass and atomicity lead to higher S°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexane boils at 342 K, where its enthalpy of vaporisation is +28.9 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔS_vap in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 84.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
parts.working: ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap/T = 28 900/342 = 84.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how this value compares with ethanol and water and suggest why water has a higher value than hexane, if it does.
parts.answer: Hexane (84.5) is typical of a non-polar liquid; ethanol and water (hydrogen bonded) have higher values, because hydrogen bonding in the liquid makes it more ordered, so vaporisation increases disorder by more.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparison; 1 mark for a reason based on hydrogen bonding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potassium chloride dissolves: KCl(s) → K⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): KCl(s) 82.6, K⁺(aq) 102.5, Cl⁻(aq) 56.5. Calculate ΔS° for the process.
parts.answer: +76.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the positive sign in terms of the ions in solution.
